High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report XXI

1 Executive Summary
The world-class research infrastructure at the US Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science (SC) provides
the research community with premier observational, experimental, computational, and network capabilities.
Each user facility is designed to provide unique capabilities to advance the core DOE mission in science and
technology for its SC program to stimulate rich scientific discoveries and enhance its innovation ecosystem.
Research communities gather and flourish around each user facility, bringing together new and enhanced
perspectives. The continual reinvention of the practice of science — as users and staff forge novel approaches
expressed in research workflows — unlocks new discoveries and propels scientific progress.

Within this research ecosystem, the high-performance computing (HPC) and networking user facilities stewarded
by the SC’s Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) program play a dynamic cross-cutting role,
enabling complex workflows demanding high-performance data, networking, and computing solutions. The
ASCR facilities enterprise seeks to understand and meet the needs and requirements across SC and DOE domain
science programs and priority efforts, highlighted by the formal requirements review methodology.

Between July and December 2024, the Energy Sciences Network (ESnet) and the Office of High Energy
Physics (HEP) of the DOE-SC organized an ESnet requirements review of HEP-supported program activities.
Preparation for these events included identification of key stakeholders: program and facility management,
research groups, and technology providers. Each stakeholder group was asked to prepare formal case study
documents about its relationship to the HEP program to build a complete understanding of the current, near-
term, and long-term status, expectations, and processes that will support the science going forward.

This review includes case studies from the following HEP user facilities, experiments, and joint collaborative efforts:

 • Cosmological Simulation Research
 • Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI)
 • Vera C. Rubin Observatory
 • Dark Energy Science Collaboration (DESC)
 • Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB)
 • Muon Experimentation at Fermilab: Muon g-2 and Mu2e
 • Belle-II Experiment
 • Neutrino experiments at Fermilab: Short-Baseline Neutrino (SBN) and Deep Underground
 Neutrino Experiment (DUNE)

 • Large Hadron Collider (LHC): A Toroidal LHC Apparatus (ATLAS) Experiment
 • LHC: Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) Experiment
 • LHC: LHC Operations
 • LHC: HL-LHC and Network Research
 • Super Cryogenic Dark Matter Search (SuperCDMS)
 • Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS) Experiment

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 1

Additionally, technical profiles are presented in this document reflecting the current state of support offered by
DOE SC-funded laboratories and user facilities in collaboration with HEP-supported activities. The laboratories
and user facilities profiled include:

 • National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC)
 • Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF)
 • Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF)
 • Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory (Fermilab)
 • Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL)
 • SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory (SLAC)
 • Argonne National Laboratory (ANL)
A summary of each case study and profile is presented prior to the case study document, along with a “Discussion
Summary” that highlights key areas of conversation from authors and attendees. These brief write-ups are not
meant to replace a full review of the case study, but provide a snapshot of the discussion and focus during the
in-person review.

Review participants spanned the following roles:

 • Subject-matter experts from the HEP program activities listed previously;
 • ESnet Site Coordinators Committee (ESCC) members from HEP activity host institutions,
 including the following DOE national laboratories and facilities: ALCF, ANL, BNL, Fermilab,
 High-Performance Data Facility (HPDF), Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL),
 NERSC, OLCF, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), and SLAC;

 • DOE-SC staff spanning ASCR and HEP; and
 • ESnet staff.
In recent years, the research communities around the DOE-SC user facilities have begun experimenting with
and demanding solutions directly integrated with HPC and data infrastructure. This rise of integrated-science
approaches is well documented, and there is a broad need for integrated computational, data, and networking
solutions. In response to these drivers, DOE has developed a vision for an Integrated Research Infrastructure
(IRI)1 to empower researchers to meld DOE’s world-class research tools, infrastructure, and user facilities
seamlessly and securely in novel ways to radically accelerate discovery and innovation.

The IRI vision is fundamentally about establishing new data-management and computational paradigms. Within
these, DOE SC user facilities and their research communities build bridges across traditional silos to improve
existing capabilities and create new possibilities. Implementation of IRI solutions will give researchers simple
and powerful tools with which to implement multifacility research data workflows. This work will also extend
analysis done on IRI patterns2 and discuss ways future HEP workflows can benefit from the approach.

1 "Integrated Research Infrastructure Architecture Blueprint Activity (Final Report 2023)", https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1984466/
2 "ESnet Requirements Review Program Through the IRI Lens: A Meta-Analysis of Workflow Patterns Across DOE Office of Science
Programs", https://www.osti.gov/biblio/2205078/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 2

1.1 Summary of Review Findings
The requirements review produced several important findings from the case studies and subsequent
virtual conversations.

1.1.1 Facility Management and Readiness
 • A common theme of the HEP case studies are challenges of data access throughout a
 collaboration. Some collaborations feature highly structured ecosystems that facilitate access
 to groups and individuals via a number of tools that manage identity and permissions. Other
 collaborations that have less structure may struggle with the available tools and are investigating
 other solutions (e.g., neutral site hosting through cloud providers, or adopting the policies of the
 strictest member of a collaboration). [Section 8]

 • Removing the need to worry about data locality allows researchers to invest more time on
 the science, versus spending energy in activities to stage data and allocate technology
 resources. It also prevents half-measures being used today to create mechanisms to perform
 analysis on partial data sets, or adopt streaming approaches that are not always
 successful on some of the larger computational resources not designed to support that mode
 of operation. [Section 6.1], [Section 8]

1.1.2 Scientific Data Management
 • The Rubin Observatory expects ~30 TB of continuous image and metadata to flow from Chile
 to the US each night. To support the Rubin Observatory, the US Data Facility (USDF) at SLAC
 will curate 5 PB/yr of data, with ancillary and other image data products that could add up to
 500 PB by the end of survey in 2035. A very demanding application is Data Release Processing
 and Alert Production, where 12.7 GB of pixel data need to be transferred in seven-second
 bursts from the observatory to the USDF. Two such bursts occur approximately every minute of
 nighttime observing. The bursts need to be sustained for approximately 355 days each
 year. [Section 6.4]

 • DUNE will produce ~45 PB of data per year at full operation. The first full DUNE detector is
 slated to begin full operation in mid-2029, and a second module will come online in 2030–2031.
 Transfer of the raw data produced from the DUNE detectors is likely to be the largest single
 network task for the experiment. In addition to beam and calibration data, the signal of
 neutrinos produced from a nearby supernova burst presents a significant challenge due to the
 large volume of data collected in a very short period (i.e., up to 600 TB in 100 seconds) and the
 time-critical nature of analyzing that data for optical astronomical observations. [Section 6.8]

1.1.3 Scientific Workflow
 • All LHC Tier-1 and Tier-2 computing infrastructure sites are expected to have perfSONAR
 nodes deployed to monitor network performance. perfSONAR allows network administrators to
 identify potential network issues that could impact data-transfer rates, both intersite and with
 CERN. It plays a vital role in the global transfer of data across the Worldwide LHC Computing
 Grid (WLCG). [Section 6.11]

 • Given the volume of data involved, making all Rubin releases available on fast storage for the
 duration of the project is not feasible. Rubin will keep the two most-recent releases available
 for rapid access, and archive older releases to tape. Users will not be able to perform database
 queries against these archived releases. However, they would be made available for bulk
 download. [Section 6.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 3

1.1.4 Computational and Storage Requirements
 • Cosmological simulation continues to be substantially limited by the availability of storage,
 particularly when considering how to distribute the simulation data to collaborators. This issue
 has several associated dimensions to consider: [Section 6.1]

 ° Sizes and numbers of simulations will increase.

 ° Locations producing simulations are expected to increase.

 ° Support spans different funding agencies.

 ° Usefulness over time, and to different communities, is increasing.

 • The impact of HL-LHC on storage and compute resources is significant. The corresponding
 increase in LHC luminosity not only generates significantly more data, but also significantly
 more complex events, which require more processing to resolve. [Section 6.12]

1.1.5 Remote Collaboration and Operational Requirements
 • Data movement of cosmological simulation data between facilities is not a critical problem, but
 broad access for the user community remains challenging. Simplifying access with updated
 portal software, or tools like Globus, has improved data mobility. The next step is to combine
 this with dynamic access to computing resources. [Section 6.1]

 • All the Rubin collaborations, as well as independent scientists, will access and analyze data
 through either the hybrid cloud-based US Data Access Centers (DACs; cloud-based Rubin
 Science Platform (RSP) and USDF back-end data services) or Independent Data Access Centers
 (IDACs) operated by in-kind contributor communities. The RSP is a set of web applications
 and services that will be used to access, visualize, interact with, and analyze data. Data will be
 exposed to users through the web portal (interactive use cases), the Jupyter Notebook interface
 (custom user use cases), and machine-accessible application program interfaces (APIs; remote
 tools/analyses use cases). [Section 6.3]

1.1.6 Multifacility Computational Workflows
 • The network speeds between major DOE HPC centers are not a limitation, and transferring
 PB-sized data sets is effectively routine. Data set sizes are expected to increase in the coming
 years, but will be within the capabilities of ESnet and the DOE HPC resources. [Section 6.1]

 • Having reliable mechanisms to transfer data into HPC facilities from the LHC Tier-1 and
 Tier-2 computing centers is of growing importance. HPCs are different from other resources
 used by the LHC primarily because they provide significant CPU resources but very limited
 disk resources, and because network access to or from HPC compute nodes is typically
 limited or not allowed. The broader LHC community has considered how to best utilize these
 resources within operational constraints. Unlike most HPC users, the LHC community cannot
 concentrate its efforts on using one or a handful of HPC facilities, but instead is motivated to
 use HPC facilities worldwide. Network access and data management are important aspects of
           this. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 4

1.1.7 Networking for Local and Wide-Area Data Mobility
 • Data volumes at the two large LHC experiments, ATLAS and CMS, can average 5 PB a day,
 with volumes exceeding this level during busy periods when the LHC is in full operation. The
 Tier-1 and Tier-2s within the US can see data flows of tens to hundreds of Gbps on a routine
 basis. Most are connected via 100 Gbps or 400 Gbps diverse connections to ESnet, or regional
 networking providers. All US Tier-2 sites are strongly encouraged to provide at least 100 Gbps
 connectivity, preferably with resilience. The intent is to have multiple 400 Gbps connectivity for
 each Tier-2 by the time HL-LHC starts. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10], [Section 8]

 • ESnet will investigate ways to integrate resources into LHCONE at non-LHC-affiliated sites.
 DOE HPC centers (e.g., NERSC) and AFs (e.g., SLAC) could benefit from being connected to
 better identify and prioritize traffic. [Section 6.9], [Section 8]

 • Networking has been fundamental to the success of LHC computing to date, enabling the
 exploitation of globally distributed resources for computationally limited science. This will
 remain the case to meet the budget-constrained computing challenges of HL-LHC. Strategies
 for HL-LHC computing are based on extensive use of powerful networks to reduce data
 replication by streaming over the network, and consolidating distributed resources into cohesive
 virtual federations such as data lakes. HL-LHC data and processing scales are large enough that
 optimizing for efficient bandwidth use will be essential. [Section 6.12]

1.1.8 Emerging Needs
 • Commercial cloud resources are an intriguing addition to HEP simulation workflow structures.
 While the cost of using these resources remains high, augmenting existing resources during
 periods of heavy use and justifying the increased expenditure may be possible. One could
 imagine a situation where the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML)
 frameworks becomes an instantaneous source of large-scale data; if challenges exist in
 allocating local computational and storage resources to meet the demand, these workflows may
 need to be integrated with commercial cloud infrastructure that can expand as needed to fit the
 needs. [Section 8]

 • DESI has used emerging Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites at the remote telescope site as a
 back-up connection for when the primary Internet is down. This was especially critical in 2022
 after a wildfire resulted in a multi-month outage of the fiber optic connection to the mountain.
 The LEO connection was sufficient for command and control of the telescope, but was not
 sufficient for transferring observational data, which required driving hard disks up and down
 the mountain. [Section 6.2]

 • SENSE (SDN for End-to-End Networked Science at the Exascale) uses Software-Defined
 Network (SDN) to dynamically manage network paths, prioritize traffic, and provide optimized
 routing. This setup is ideal for data-intensive tasks, as it can allocate resources in real time based
 on network conditions and experimental priorities. Rucio, developed by CERN in part for the
 LHC experiments, complements SENSE by managing large-scale data distribution across the
 network. [Section 6.11]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 5

1.1.9 IRI Responsiveness
 • Long-term storage of data remains a critical problem throughout HEP. The IRI program and
 HPDF facility should present a possible solution to this problem, providing a deterministic way
 for long-running efforts can be cataloged, stored, and found by the global community.
 If a single location cannot become the home for data sets, efforts must be made to unify a
 cataloging system to enable locality searches, despite the distributed nature of the data.
 [Section 6.1], [Section 8]

 • An area of friction for a number of HEP experiments involves the mechanisms used to manage
 identity and permissions for the large population of scientific users. A common problem is the
 management of credentials to access computation and storage across facilities, and how these
 may differ from accounts used to manage other aspects of the scientific workflow (e.g., home
 institutional accounts). [Section 8]

 • HEP experiments and facilities can benefit from IRI, especially if the DOE HPC centers and
 the newly awarded HPDF make resources available for use: [Section 6.4], [Section 6.9],
           [Section 6.10], [Section 6.12]

 ° IRI would provide the opportunity to implement near real-time workflows for
 critical payloads.

 ° Incorporating HPC resources typically come with some, potentially substantial, work to
 set up given facility specific configurations and constraints. A common interface (or access
 requirements) across DOE HPC sites and models for sustained access are potential
 IRI benefits.

 ° Workflows that are more compute intensive could possibly branch out across multiple sites
 in the future without having to invest heavily in software and hardware integration steps.

1.2 Summary of Review Actions
Lastly, ESnet plans to follow up with review participants on a number of high-level actions identified. These
items are listed as guidance for future collaboration, and do not reflect formal project timelines. ESnet will review
these with HEP participations on a yearly basis, until the next requirements review process begins.

1.2.1 Facility Management and Readiness
 • The HL-LHC predictions show a mismatch between the computing and storage resources
 the experiments can afford versus the resources needed to reach the HL-LHC science goals.
 In response to this gap, the experiments are exploring alternatives in how to utilize storage,
 computing, and network infrastructure. The network baseline currently being planned is
 composed of terabit-scale (1–2 Tbps) backbone networks with the largest resource sites
 connected at multiple 400G scale (800 Gbps+). Network use will be at least a factor of 10 larger
 than those in the LHC Run 3 program. [Section 6.12]

1.2.2 Scientific Data Management
 • The cosmological community is interested in advancing a data management model that
 would help reduce the number of times and locations that need to be involved to archive
 long-term data products, and is looking for assistance in scoping and realizing this design goal.
 Establishing permanent storage facilities would allow the community to establish a more regular
 pattern of collaboration: a smaller set of data portals that can be used to catalog and retrieve
 long-term campaigns of products along with a simplified way to support analysis activities,
 potentially leveraging interactive computing approaches, at a well-known number of sites.
           [Section 6.1], [Section 8], [Section 5.2]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 6

1.2.3 Scientific Workflow
 • DESI uses Globus for transfers of collaboration data, and users report positive experiences with
 Globus when they want to download an entire directory tree. But they have found the interface
 lacking for the more common use case of selecting a subset of data from a complex directory
 tree (e.g., all files matching a given regex regardless of where they appear in the directory
 structure). Discussions with Globus may be useful to help facilitate ways to address this use
 case. [Section 6.2]

1.2.4 Computational and Storage Requirements
 • The barrier to using DOE HPC resources within the LHC community remains, particularly in
 integrating the systems as resources into the software components, and normalizing the way the
 resources could be accounted for (expected versus ad hoc or opportunistic). More specifically,
 there is a desire to create agreements or other forms of arrangements, similar to an Service
 Level Agreement (SLA), with DOE HPC facilities such that resources can be considered
 pledged, like how Tier-1s and Tier-2s operate. This helps with planning for both the HEP
 community and the ASCR resources. Some of this may require discussion at the programmatic
 level. [Section 6.12], [Section 8]

 • The LHC community experiences sub-optimal performance when supporting a streaming-based
 workflow at large HPC facilities. Workarounds have been established to support this, either by
 allowing the worker nodes to stream directly or by leveraging caches and data lakes that are
 deployed close topologically. All these design choices come with trade-offs, which implies a set
 of R&D activities that will extend in the coming years. [Section 6.12], [Section 8]

1.2.5 Remote Collaboration and Operational Requirements
 • Several facilities are not connected to LHC Open Network Environment (LHCONE)
 currently, despite being heavily involved in LHC-affiliated computation and storage activities.
 These include major computational sites, AFs, and potentially commercial clouds. No formal
 agreement with any of these facilities exists now to be part of the LHC collaboration in a
 structured way, but investigating their ability to connect to LHCONE to support several
 important use cases is recommended. [Section 8]

1.2.6 Multifacility Computational Workflows
 • Using a single centralized HPC facility to support a given HEP experiment is beneficial, since
 there’s a single ecosystem to learn and it requires minimal overhead to share results with
 collaborators from other institutions. At the same time, it can also become a single point of
 failure and requires mitigations to be developed on how to proceed with operations during
 downtime. The limiting factors are not networking for data transfer, but rather the tools for
 making that data sharing automated and transparent for hundreds of users accessing PBs of data
 stored in millions of files. [Section 8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 7

1.2.7 Networking for Local and Wide-Area Data Mobility
 • The DOE HEP and DOE ASCR program offices are working out the specifics of the connectivity
 to SURF that ESnet will need to complete for the proper connection. The efforts are planned to
 converge by the end of fiscal year 2026. [Section 6.8], [Section 8]

 • LHCONE runs a hybrid approach to supporting Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) currently.
 The upcoming government mandate (e.g., M-21-07) will imply that Fermilab and BNL must
 move toward IPv6 capabilities, and subsequently the associated LHC Tier-2s will have to move
 toward dual stack support. One critical issue that cannot be solved by the US community will
 be the ability of CERN to deliver IPv6 capabilities from its service infrastructure. ESnet will
 continue to work with US collaborators on this to ease the transition to IPv6 operation. [Section 8]

 • Several international networking partners factored heavily into the requirements review
 discussions; connectivity to Europe, South America, and the Asia-Pacific region is accomplished
 through relationships with several R&E partners. ESnet maintains peering relations with most
 of these partners, and their connectivity carries significant amounts of HEP traffic daily. ESnet
 will continue to work with these partners to ensure networking access to international science
 locations. [Section 8]

1.2.8 Emerging Needs
 • Rucio’s adoption throughout the HEP community for distributed data management provides an
 opportunity for ESnet and other Research and Education (R&E) networks to explore data-
 movement intentions and required quality of service (QoS) or deadline requirements. ESnet
 will continue to work with the LHC community on co-design efforts such as this, along with
 SENSE, SciTags, and other potential opportunities. [Section 6.11], [Section 6.12], [Section 8]

 • Several HEP case studies outlined their interest in commercial cloud resources. ESnet is
 identifying additional ways to assist, and will continue to help with connectivity and peering
 when applicable. Networking can be a bottleneck in certain situations: mainly when traffic
 remained within a cloud versus being allowed to egress and use more predicable R&E routing
 and transit. ESnet can engage with experiments, sites, and cloud-providers to suggest potential
 solutions. [Section 8]

1.2.9 IRI Responsiveness
 • The discussions within the HEP community touched on several factors that should be
 considered by the IRI effort. A first step will be to establish a hierarchy of needs: an example
 being that accessing a set of resources or tools which span administrative boundaries is very
 different than the ability to use different tools and resources within the same location. A similar
 policy language and control structure could solve both, if ways to differentiate the needs and
 articulate the required control structures exist. [Section 8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 8

2 Requirements Review Overview
ESnet and ASCR use requirements reviews to discuss and analyze current and planned science use cases and
anticipated data output of a particular program, user facility, or project to inform ESnet’s strategic planning,
including network operations, capacity upgrades, and other service investments.

2.1 Purpose and Process
The requirements review process, when performed regularly and comprehensively, surveys major science
stakeholders’ plans and processes to investigate data-management requirements over the next 5–10 years.
Questions crafted to explore this space include the following:

 • How, and where, will new data be analyzed and used?
 • How will the process of doing science change over the next 5–10 years?
 • How will changes to the underlying hardware and software technologies influence
 scientific discovery?
Requirements reviews help ensure that key stakeholders have a common understanding of the issues and the
actions that ESnet may need to undertake to offer solutions. The ESnet Science Engagement team leads the
effort and relies on collaboration from other ESnet teams. ESnet meets with each individual program office
within the DOE SC every three years, with an intermediate virtual update scheduled between the full review.
ESnet collaborates with the relevant program managers to identify the appropriate principal investigators, and
their information technology partners, to participate in the review process. ESnet organizes, convenes, executes,
and shares the outcomes of the review with all stakeholders.

Requirements reviews are a critical part of a process to understand and analyze current and planned science use
cases across the DOE SC. This is done by eliciting and documenting the anticipated data outputs and workflows
of a particular program, user facility, or project to better inform strategic planning activities. These include, but
are not limited to, network operations, capacity upgrades, and other service investments for ESnet, as well as a
complete and holistic understanding of science drivers and requirements for the program offices.

We achieve these goals through reviewing the case study documents, discussions with authors, and general
analysis of the materials. The resulting output is a set of review findings and actions that will guide future
interactions between HEP, ASCR, and ESnet. These terms are defined as follows:

 • Findings: key facts or observations gleaned from the entire review process that highlight
 specific challenges, particularly those shared among multiple case studies.

 • Actions: potential strategic or tactical activities, investments, or opportunities that can be
 evaluated and potentially pursued to address the challenges laid out in the findings.

2.2 Structure
The requirements review process is hybrid, and relies on a combination of asynchronous and synchronous
activities to understand specific facility and experimental use cases. The review is a highly conversational process
through which all participants gain shared insight into the salient data-management challenges of the subject
program/facility/project. Requirements reviews help ensure that key stakeholders have a common understanding
of the issues and the potential actions that can be implemented in the coming years.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 9

2.2.1 Background
Through a case study methodology, the review provides ESnet with information about the following:

 • Existing and planned data-intensive science experiments and/or user facilities, including the
 geographical locations of experimental site(s), computing resource(s), data storage, and
 research collaborator(s).

 • For each experiment/facility project, a description of the “process of science,” including the
 goals of the project and how experiments are performed and/or how the facility is used. This
 description includes information on the systems and tools used to analyze, transfer, and store the
 data produced.

 • Current and anticipated data output on near- and long-term timescales.
 • Timeline(s) for building, operating, and decommissioning of experiments, to the degree these
 are known.

 • Existing and planned network resources, usage, and “pain points” or bottlenecks in transferring
 or productively using the data produced by the science.

2.2.2 Case Study Methodology
The case study template and methodology are designed to provide stakeholders with the following information:

 • Identification and analysis of any data-management gaps and/or network bottlenecks that are
 barriers to achieving the scientific goals.

 • A forecast of network capacity requirements by area of science, particularly in geographic
 regions where data production/consumption is anticipated to increase or decrease.

 • A survey of the data-management needs, challenges, and capability gaps that could inform
 strategic investments in solutions.
The case study format seeks a network-centric narrative describing the science, instruments, and facilities
currently used or anticipated for future programs; the network services needed; and how the network will be
used over three timescales: the near term (immediately and up to two years in the future); the medium term (two
to five years in the future); and the long term (greater than five years in the future).

The case studies address the following sections with review participants:

Science Background: a brief description of the scientific research performed or supported, the high-level
context, goals, stakeholders, and outcomes. The section includes a brief overview of the data life cycle and how
scientific components from the target use case are involved.

Collaborators: aims to capture the breadth of the science collaborations involved in an experiment or facility
focusing on geographic locations and how datasets are created, shared, computed, and stored.

IRI Readiness: Research communities that use DOE SC user facilities are experimenting with and demanding
solutions integrated with HPC and data infrastructure. The Integrated Research Infrastructure Architecture
Blueprint Activity (IRI-ABA) brought together domain experts from all DOE SC Programs to look for common
patterns within diverse workflows across a range of scientific disciplines. Participants discovered three
common patterns:

 • Time-sensitive pattern.
 • Data integration–intensive pattern.
 • Long-term campaign pattern.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 10

Instruments and Facilities: description of the instruments and facilities used, including any plans for major
upgrades, new facilities, or similar changes. When applicable, descriptions of the instrument or facility’s compute,
storage, and network capabilities are included. An overview of the composition of the datasets produced by the
instrument or facility (e.g., file size, number of files, number of directories, total dataset size) is also included.

Process of Science: documentation on the way in which the instruments and facilities are and will be used for
knowledge discovery, emphasizing the role of networking in enabling the science (where applicable). This should
include descriptions of the science workflows, methods for data analysis and data reduction, and the integration of
experimental data with simulation data or other use cases.

Remote Science Activities: use of any remote instruments or resources for the process of science and how this
work affects or may affect the network. This could include any connections to or between instruments, facilities,
people, or data at different sites.

Software Infrastructure: discussion of the tools that perform tasks, such as data-source management (local and
remote), data-sharing infrastructure, data-movement tools, processing pipelines, collaboration software, etc.

Network and Data Architecture: the network architecture and bandwidth for the facility and/or laboratory and/
or campus. The section includes detailed descriptions of the various network layers (local-area network [LAN],
metropolitan-area network [MAN], and wide-area network [WAN]) capabilities that connect the science
experiment/facility/data source to external resources and collaborators.

Emerging Technology Use: The use of new technologies in the scientific process is a constant evolution. Cloud
services, artificial intelligence (AI) / machine learning (ML) technologies, and the use of nonterrestrial networking
are growing in popularity to support research activities around the world. This section asks questions about the
role these technologies, and potentially others, are playing in the overall trajectory of the scientific use case.

Cloud Services: if applicable, cloud services that are in use or planned for use in data analysis, storage,
computing, or other purposes.

Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML): Outlining how the laboratory or facilities have invested
in AI/ML technologies. This could be the purchase and operation of on-site capabilities available for use or
partnerships with other entities (research and education [R&E], commercial, etc.) to use remote resources.

Remote or Field Research: Discussing aspects of a scientific workflow that depend on resources that may be
located in an isolated area, e.g., a sensor array or instrument deployed far from terrestrial networking that may
need access to cellular or satellite connectivity.

Data-Related Resource Constraints: any current or anticipated future constraints that affect productivity, such
as insufficient data-transfer performance, insufficient storage system space or performance, difficulty finding or
accessing data in community data repositories, or unmet computing needs.

Data Mobility Endpoints: If a facility or experiment has dedicated infrastructure to facilitate data sharing, ESnet
is interested in learning more about how it is constructed and maintained. ESnet maintains a set of well-tuned
test endpoints, and recommends regular testing to evaluate data-transfer capabilities.

Outstanding Issues: an open-ended section where any relevant challenges, barriers, or concerns not discussed
elsewhere in the case study can be addressed by ESnet.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 11

2.3 ESnet
ESnet is the high-performance network user facility for the US DOE SC and delivers highly reliable data
transport capabilities optimized for the requirements of data-intensive science. In essence, ESnet is the data
circulatory system that enables the DOE science mission by connecting all its laboratories and facilities in the US
and abroad. ESnet is funded and stewarded by the ASCR program and managed and operated by the Scientific
Networking Division at LBNL. ESnet is widely regarded as a global leader in the R&E networking community.

ESnet interconnects DOE national laboratories, user facilities, and major experiments so that scientists can use
remote instruments and computing resources as well as share data with collaborators, transfer large datasets, and
access distributed data repositories. ESnet is specifically built to provide a range of network services tailored to
meet the unique requirements of the DOE’s data-intensive science.

In short, ESnet’s mission is to enable and accelerate scientific discovery by delivering unparalleled network
infrastructure, capabilities, and tools. ESnet’s vision is summarized by these three points:

 1. Scientific progress will be completely unconstrained by the physical location of instruments, people,
 computational resources, or data.
 2. Collaborations at every scale, in every domain, will have the information and tools they
 need to achieve maximum benefit from scientific facilities, global networks, and emerging
 network capabilities.
 3. ESnet will foster the partnerships and pioneer the technologies necessary to ensure that these
 transformations occur.

2.4 About ASCR
The mission of the ASCR program is to discover, develop, and deploy computational and networking capabilities
to analyze, model, simulate, and predict complex phenomena important to the DOE. A particular challenge
of this program is fulfilling the science potential of emerging computing systems and other novel computing
architectures, which will require numerous significant modifications to today’s tools and techniques to deliver on
the promise of exascale science.

To accomplish its mission and address the challenges described previously, the ASCR program is organized into
three subprograms:

 • The Mathematical, Computational, and Computer Sciences Research subprogram develops
 mathematical descriptions, models, methods, and algorithms to describe and understand
 complex systems, often involving processes that span a wide range of time and/or length scales.

 • The HPC and Network Facilities subprogram delivers forefront computational and networking
 capabilities and contributes to developing next-generation capabilities through support of
 prototypes and test beds.

 • The Advanced Computing Technology Division supports research focused on the development
 of emerging computing technologies such as quantum information systems (QIS) and
 neuromorphic efforts as well as investments in microelectronics in partnership with the other
 Office of Science program offices, the Exascale Computing Project (ECP), Research and
 Evaluation Prototypes (REP), and ASCR-specific investments in cybersecurity.

2.5 About the Office of HEP
HEP explores what the world is made of and how it works at the smallest and largest scales, seeking new
discoveries from the tiniest particles to the outer reaches of space. This quest inspires young minds, trains an
expert workforce, and drives innovation that improves the nation’s health, wealth, and security.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 12

Our research is inspired by some of the biggest questions about our universe. What is it made of? What forces
govern it? How did it become the way it is today? Finding these answers requires the combined efforts of some of
the largest scientific collaborations in the world, using some of the most sensitive detectors in the world, at some
of the largest scientific machines in the world.

HEP supports US researchers who play leading roles in these international efforts and world-leading facilities
at our national laboratories that make this science possible. We also develop new accelerator, detector, and
computational tools to open new doors to discovery science, and through Accelerator Stewardship work to make
transformational accelerator technology widely available to science and industry.

HEP is organized into six subprograms:

 • Energy Frontier: Researchers at the Energy Frontier use the world’s largest and highest-energy
 particle accelerator to recreate the universe as it was a billionth of a second after the big bang.

 • Intensity Frontier: Researchers at the Intensity Frontier investigate some of the rarest particle
 interactions in nature and subtle effects that require large data sets to observe and measure.

 • Cosmic Frontier: Researchers at the Cosmic Frontier use naturally occurring cosmic particles
 and phenomena to reveal the nature of dark matter, cosmic acceleration, and more.

 • Theoretical, Computational, and Interdisciplinary Physics: Theoretical and computational
 physics provide the vision and the framework for extending our knowledge of particles and
 the universe.

 • Advanced Technology R&D: Cutting-edge research in the physics of particle accelerators,
 particle beams, and particle detection enables scientists to stay on the threshold of discovery.

 • Accelerator Stewardship: Supporting use-inspired basic research in accelerator science and
 technology to make particle accelerator technology widely available to science and industry.

3 Assessment of 2020 HEP Requirement Review
ESnet recorded a set of action items from the 2020 HEP Network Requirements Review, with the goal of
continuing support of collaborations funded by the HEP program beyond the publication of the report. ESnet
performed regular check-ins with HEP between the reviews (holding webinars with the community in 2022
and 2023) to ensure progress was made on these identified areas of mutual interest. These sections outline the
previous actions and discuss progress made since the publication of the report.

3.1 Prior Action Items
The actions identified during the 2020 HEP Network Requirements Review included:

 • ESnet will work with laboratories, user facilities, experiments, domestic networking peers,
 universities, partners, and international peers in the coming years to evaluate and upgrade
 network connections to support essential science missions.

 • ESnet will continue to provide leadership in the development, implementation, and operation
 of cyberinfrastructure components (e.g., the Science DMZ, Data Transfer Nodes (DTNs),
 perf SONAR, and the Modern Research Data Portal) used by the scientific user community.
 Emerging testbeds and technologies, including AutoGOLE, Adaptive ProgrammaBle Research
 Infrastructure for Computer Science and Science Applications (FABRIC), and Software-Defined
 Networking (SDN) for End-to-End Networked Science at the Exascale (SENSE), will see
 increased adoption as they are deployed more widely in the coming years.

 • ESnet will continue to evaluate and expand international connectivity options in support of
 international scientific requirements.

 • ESnet will continue to work closely with LHC R&D efforts to develop and deploy new
 capabilities and services that address scientific use cases. These efforts include methods to better
 measure and track network traffic, manage and provision networks, and improve in-network
 caching capabilities.

 • ESnet will remain active in the design, implementation, and operation of the Large Hadron
 Collider Open Network Environment (LHCONE) effort as it expands scope and usage to
 support the LHC and affiliated scientific experiments.

 • ESnet will collaborate with ASCR computing facilities to ensure connectivity matches scientific
 data requirements at all stages of operation (intake, dissemination, etc.).

3.2 Assessment
The 2020 HEP Network Requirements Review action items were assessed and reviewed with the HEP
community. This section does not offer a line-by-line response for each, but instead provides an update on several
major initiatives undertaken by the DOE SC programs, along with individual actions by ASCR, HEP, and ESnet.

3.2.1 ESnet Actions
Since the 2020 review, ESnet completed the design, procurement, and installation of ESnet6, the next-generation
networking platform that is currently running to deliver on DOE SC mission requirements. This was a multiyear
project that involved complete replacement of the underlying optical and routed network that ESnet operates
and resulted in upgraded capacities across the backbone and to connected laboratories and facilities.

Supporting HEP through transatlantic (TA) connectivity continues through the current time, with many upgrades
and changes implemented since the previous review cycle. ESnet continues to collaborate with international
partners (e.g., GÉANT) to establish networking spectrum on subsea cable resources. Efforts are underway to

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 14

share this resource across several diverse cable resources on a long-term basis (e.g., 10- to 15-year contracts). This
will result in approximately 10 Tbps of aggregate connectivity, across multiple connections, that will be available
to support the US and EU science missions, addressing the requirements of the LHC community projections for
Run 4 data production. By the 2027 time frame, 3.2 Tbps of capacity is expected to be available.

ESnet has also initiated the following efforts and programs that address some of the actions from the 2020 HEP
Network Requirements Review:

 • Upgrading the connectivity to support the LHC T1 sites in the US to support increased data
 volumes, and planning for more upgrades when technology and procurement of equipment
 become available:

 ° BNL now supports 1.6 Tbps.

 ° Fermilab now supports 2.4 Tbps.

 • Discussing connectivity upgrade options with regional networking partners that support LHC
 T2 facilities, and setting a schedule to upgrade connection capacities, peering locations, and
 downstream connections to campuses. All regional networks now support at least 100 Gbps
 connections, with many also upgrading to 400 Gbps, or slating to do so within the 2025 to 2026
 time frame. Downstream campuses are also connected using multiple connections of at least 100
 Gbps, or supporting 400 Gbps.

 • Fully adopting and supporting the LHCONE networking overlay, and the ability of other
 affiliated scientific efforts (e.g., DUNE, Belle II, etc.) to utilize this for network traffic that
 traverses similar computational sites and network paths.

 • Creating a program (i.e., the Fasterdata DTN framework) as a mechanism to support data
 mobility needs across the backbone and regional networking infrastructure, as well as
 touchpoints in campus environments.

 • Deploying the Stardust measurement and monitoring platform, which allows ESnet connectors
 to visualize and categorize their scientific network patterns.

 • Upgrading to all perfSONAR and DTN hardware to at least 100 Gbps-capable speeds.
 • Participating (continued) in LHC-affiliated R&D efforts including SENSE and Rucio
 integration, Scientific Network Tags (SciTags), deployment of networking caching, exploration of
 data lake performance, and others.

 • Making an organizational commitment to participate in “co-design” efforts. These joint
 projects between ESnet engineering staff, along with scientific experts at other facilities and
 projects, facilitate access to technical expertise and build strong relationships throughout the
 scientific community.

3.2.2 DOE SC Actions
A major focus for ASCR, along with other DOE SC programs like HEP, in the time between the 2020 and 2024
HEP Network Requirements Review was the convening of groups to discuss ways that the future generation
of technology provided on the network, and within computational facilities, will grow to meet the demands of
scientific experimentation.

The complexity of scientific pursuits is increasing rapidly with aspects that require dynamic integration of
experiment, observation, theory, modeling, simulation, visualization, ML, AI, and analysis. Research projects
across the DOE are increasingly data and compute intensive. Innovative research teams are accelerating the pace
of discovery by using high-performance computational and data tools in their research workflows and leveraging
multiple research infrastructures. DOE SC has embraced what can be possible with this integration and has

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 15

adopted a vision for IRI3: to empower researchers to meld DOE’s world-class research tools, infrastructure, and
user facilities seamlessly and securely in novel ways to radically accelerate discovery and innovation.

IRI defined three core patterns during its early work:

 • Time-sensitive pattern: requires real-time, or near real-time, response across more than one
 facility or resource for timely decision-making and experiment steering.

 • Data integration–intensive pattern: requires combining and analyzing data from multiple
 sources, e.g., sites, experiments, and/or computational runs, to deepen and expand context.

 • Long-term campaign pattern: requires sustained access to more than one facility or resource,
 often centered around rare or unique scientific instruments, over years or decades to accomplish
 a well-defined objective.
These activities address some of the actions from the 2020 HEP Network Requirements Review, namely in
trying to define a sensible set of requirements that DOE HPC facilities can deliver to assist the future needs of
experimental workflows and better scale service offerings for emerging efforts. These observations come from the
broader work to classify ESnet Requirements Reviews through the IRI lens.4

IRI acknowledges that data movement, be it in the form of bulk or streaming requirements, is a core goal and
must be supported fully by all experimental facilities that connect to ESnet. ESnet is committed to working with
HEP, and other DOE SC programs, to execute on the vision of IRI starting with the items identified in the 2024
HEP Network Requirements Review.
