4 Review Findings
The requirements review process helps to identify important facts and opportunities from the programs and user
facilities that are profiled. The following sections outline a set of findings from the HEP and ESnet requirements
review. These points summarize important information gathered during the review discussions surrounding case
studies and the HEP-managed user program in general. These findings are organized by topic area for simplicity
and by common themes:

 • Facility management and readiness.
 • Scientific data management.
 • Scientific workflow.
 • Computational and storage requirements.
 • Remote collaboration and operational requirements.
 • Multifacility computational workflows.
 • Networking for local and wide-area data mobility.
 • Emerging needs.
 • IRI responsiveness.

4.1 Facility Management and Readiness
 • Cosmological simulations provide theoretical predictions to understanding physical phenomena.
 These data products help to analyze and interpret results from cosmological surveys, and aid in
 survey design, optimization, and error estimates. [Section 6.1]

 • DESI is a DOE-led cosmology collaboration that will operate through at least 2026 and create
 the world’s largest 3D map of the universe. DESI utilizes the Mayall 4-meter telescope, located
 at Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). NERSC is used as the primary scientific analysis
 center for DESI. [Section 6.2]

 • The Rubin Observatory, an NSF-DOE funded partnership operated by NOIRLab and SLAC,
 will carry out the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), using the Simonyi Survey
 Telescope and the Rubin Observatory LSST Camera. It will take repeated images of the
 southern sky, and the resulting dataset will provide a static census of approximately 40 billion
 objects. The primary deliverables for Rubin Observatory include a real-time stream of “alerts”
 of transient events, prompt data products, annual data-release data products, and a science
 platform. [Section 6.3]

 • Rubin Observatory pre-operations ran early versions of all the data production elements
 between 2021 and 2023 in a commercial cloud environment (i.e., the “Interim Data Facility”
 [IDF]) using precursor data sets. Transition from the IDF to the permanent US Data Facility
 (USDF) was completed in FY24. Pre-operations will culminate with data production at full-
 scale testing in FY25. The full LSST will run for 10 years, and final data processing will take
 place after that for two years. Survey data taking ends in FY35. [Section 6.3]

 • The DESC international science collaboration will make high-accuracy measurements of
 fundamental cosmological parameters using data gathered from the LSST produced by the
 Rubin Observatory, and investigate the nature of dark energy and dark matter over 10 years.
 The DESC collaboration currently comprises some 1,270 members, originating from 23
 countries and more than 200 institutions. Of the members, about 50% are from the United
 States, 9% from the United Kingdom, and 7% from France. [Section 6.4]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 17

 • The CMB, or relic radiation, consists of photons created in the Big Bang that have been
 propagating through the universe continuously until detected in current times. CMB-S4, a
 joint project between the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the DOE, is the “Stage 4”
 ground-based CMB experiment, bringing the entire US community together to build a
 single experiment capable of detecting the faintest CMB signals. The CMB-S4 collaboration
 currently consists of 520 members at 142 institutions in 24 countries and 26 US states. The
 institutions include DOE, NASA, and Department of Commerce laboratories, as well as a host
 of universities. [Section 6.5]

 • In mid-2024, the NSF was not able to commit to funding for portions of the project that involved
 experimentation to be conducted at the South Pole.5 Thus, the information provided by CMB-S4
 in this report assumes the entirety of the observatory will be based in Chile. The experimentation
 will produce three coordinated surveys from Chile between 2028 to 2035: [Section 6.5]

 ° A wide and deep survey of ~70% of the sky using 2 x 6m telescopes that operate with a
 daily cadence.

 ° An ultra-deep survey of ~3% of the sky using 18 x 0.5m telescopes.

 ° An ultra-deep survey of the same ~3% of the sky using a different 5m telescope.

 • The Muon g-2 experiment at Fermilab collected data from 2018 until summer of 2023 and had
 two major releases of results: the first in 2021 based on Run 1 data and the second in 2023 based
 on Runs 2+3 data. The collaboration is analyzing the remaining data (Runs 4–6) and expects to
 make a final measurement during FY25. [Section 6.6]

 • The Mu2e collaboration features a total of 239 scientists from 39 institutions in six countries:
 China, Germany, Italy, Russia, the UK, and the US. Mu2e will start taking cosmic-ray
 commissioning data early in mid CY 2025 and will begin commissioning with beam operations
 late in calendar 2026. The first physics run will begin early in CY 2027 and will continue to the
 end of CY 2027. During 2028 and 2029 Fermilab accelerator operations will pause for upgrades
 to the accelerator complex in preparation for the Long-Baseline Neutrino Facility (LBNF).
 Mu2e will resume running in 2030 and continue until the 2033 summer shutdown. [Section 6.6]

 • The Belle II experiment collects data at the SuperKEKB asymmetric electron-positron collider
 at the Japanese High-Energy Accelerator Research Organization KEK in Tsukuba, Japan.
 Belle II’s goal is to accumulate about 50 times more data than Belle. Operations began in 2019,
 and about half as much data as Belle collected has been collected. The plan is to increase the
 amount of data collected per year to reach the goal by the 2030s. The Belle II collaboration
 comprises 1,183 members from 125 institutions and 28 countries around the world. There are
 118 US collaborators from 16 institutions, including BNL. [Section 6.7]

 • Belle II recently resumed data taking in March 2024 after a 19-month shutdown to replace
 the innermost vertex detector and a portion of the particle-identification detector as well
 as complete an upgrade of the data acquisition (DAQ). A SuperKEKB upgrade with a
 corresponding ~1.5 year shutdown, tentatively scheduled for 2029, will be required to reach
 design goals. [Section 6.7]

 • The Short-Baseline Neutrino (SBN) program consists of three detectors — the Short-Baseline
 Near Detector (SBND), MicroBooNE, and the short-baseline far detector Imaging Cosmic
 And Rare Underground Signals (ICARUS T600) — each detecting neutrinos from Fermilab’s
 Booster Neutrino Beamline (BNB). The design of the SBN detectors will prepare for the future
5 Scientific research using CMB data continues to be a priority for DOE and NSF, an initiative that provides crucial information on the
fundamental nature of matter and energy in the universe. However, DOE and NSF jointly decided in calendar year 2025 that they can no
longer support the P5-envisioned CMB-S4 project. Nevertheless, DOE and NSF will continue to partner with the CMB science community
to explore the potential science that can be achieved with limited upgrades to existing experiments to further this important U.S.-led research.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 18

 long-baseline neutrino experiment: DUNE. The SBN international collaborations include
 approximately 250 scientists from more than 50 institutions across the US, CERN, Italy, the UK,
 Switzerland, Spain, Turkey, and Brazil. [Section 6.8]

 • DUNE will study the fundamental nature of neutrinos through measurements of neutrino
 oscillations from both neutrino beam and other natural neutrino sources. In addition to studying
 neutrino oscillations, DUNE has a broader physics program that includes searches for proton
 decay, detection of neutrinos from supernova collapse, and other exotic phenomena. The
 DUNE Collaboration comprises approximately 1,500 scientists from more than 200 institutions
 in 39 countries around the world. These institutions include both national laboratories and
 universities. [Section 6.8]

 • The core facilities of DUNE are the near and far detectors, located on-site at Fermilab (Illinois)
 and in the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in South Dakota respectively, and
 will interact with the beam of the future LBNF at Fermilab. The network that connects SURF
 to the R&E network infrastructure will be critical to the success of DUNE’s operation.
           [Section 6.8]

 • DUNE has built two prototypes at CERN: ProtoDUNE Horizontal Drift (ProtoDUNE-HD)
 and ProtoDUNE Vertical Drift (ProtoDUNE-VD). ProtoDUNE-HD just completed a three-
 month beam run at CERN in the fall of 2024, and ProtoDUNE-VD is anticipated to start a
 roughly yearlong test period in summer 2025. [Section 6.8]

 • The work of SBN and the ProtoDUNE experiments at CERN will prepare for DUNE, which is
 scheduled to start in several years’ time. Both experiments will use grid-computing approaches
 provided by Open Science Grid (OSG), Worldwide LHC Computing Grid (WLCG), and HEP-
 community software for data movement, cataloging, simulation, and analysis. [Section 6.8]

 • The LHC at CERN is the most powerful particle accelerator in the world. The LHC collides
 protons more than a billion times every second, out of which the detector experiments select
 interesting collisions for recording at a rate of a thousand times every second. Over 2,000 hours
 of data collection every year when the LHC is running means a huge data sample for physicists
 to analyze. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]

 • ATLAS is the largest of four particle detectors that measure and record the particle collisions at
 the LHC, and consists of a global collaboration of physicists, engineers, technicians, students,
 and support staff from around the world. It is one of the largest collaborative efforts, with over
 5,500 members and almost 3,000 scientific authors. [Section 6.9]

 • The CMS experiment at the LHC is designed to probe new phenomena at the energy frontier.
 The CMS collaboration is made up of more than 3,000 members from more than 50 countries.
 Researchers at US institutions comprise about 30% of the collaboration. [Section 6.10]

 • CERN facilities are used to provide the ATLAS and CMS data reconstruction, to support
 detector commissioning work as well as physics analysis work. Then globally distributed Tier-1
 and Tier-2 facilities are responsible for data archiving, simulated data generation, analysis data
 storage, and physics analysis activities. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]

 • The LHC schedule has operating periods (called “runs”) interspersed with maintenance and
 upgrade periods (called “long shutdowns”). The first run of the LHC was 2009–2012 followed
 by long shutdown 1 (LS1) from 2012–2014. The second run (Run 2) was from 2014–2018,
 followed by LS2 from 2019–2021. Run 3 started in 2022 and will continue until 2026. The LHC
 will be upgraded to increase its luminosity during LS3, from 2026–2029. The new accelerator,
 HL-LHC, will start producing collisions in Run 4 in 2030. ATLAS and CMS are expected to
 produce 10 times more data in Run 4, compared with what will be produced in Run 3.
           [Section 6.11]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 19

 • The collaborators involved with LHC operations are the four main LHC experiments
 (ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb) as well as the technical teams running the accelerator
 and the globally distributed middleware (OSG, European Grid Infrastructure [EGI], Rucio,
 perf SONAR, File Transfer Service [FTS], etc.) and infrastructures (the various Tier-x sites)
 supporting the activities of the experiments. [Section 6.11]

 • SuperCDMS SNOLAB is a next-generation experiment aiming to detect sub-giga-electronvolt
 (GeV) dark matter particles funded and operated under the DOE SC HEP program in the
 Cosmic Frontier, and co-funded by NSF. Non-US funding is provided through the Canadian
 Foundation for Innovation (CFI). The SuperCDMS collaboration is spread between many
 institutions in the US, Canada, Germany, India, Spain, United Arab Emirates, and United
 Kingdom. The approximate count is about 130 collaborators in 28 institutions. [Section 6.13]

 • The SuperCDMS SNOLAB experiment is currently in the installation phase at SNOLAB
 (Canada), 2 km underground. Commissioning is expected to start in fall 2025, and science
 operations are expected to start at the beginning of 2026 and to last for at least three years,
 leaving open the possibility of upgrades (more detectors and/or new technology to leverage the
 cryogenic facility). [Section 6.13]

 • AMS is a precision particle physics detector installed on the International Space Station (ISS) in
 May 2011, conducting a unique, long-duration mission of fundamental physics research in space
 that is not replicable on earth. AMS is the largest instrument, and is scheduled to run until the
 ISS project ends, estimated to be after 2030. Since 2011, AMS has collected more than 200
 billion events. The AMS collaboration is composed of about 600 physicists and 44 institutes and
 organizations from 14 countries. [Section 6.14]

 • NERSC supplies supercomputing, data storage, networking, auxiliary equipment, and technical
 consulting to projects supported by the DOE SC. NERSC supports approximately 100 HEP
 projects, both simulation and data focused. NERSC-10 is expected in the 2027 time frame, and
 is anticipated to have 10 times the aggregate performance of Perlmutter. [Section 7.1]

 • The ALCF operates multiple supercomputing systems and enclaves that support all
 communities, including HEP. The ALCF-4 system is in the early planning stages, and expected
 in the three- to four-year time frame. [Section 7.2]

 • The OLCF operates Frontier, and other systems, to support DOE SC communities such as
 HEP. OLCF is preparing for the commissioning of the next HPC system, OLCF-6 and
 titled “Discovery.” The next system is expected in the 2027–2028 time frame. [Section 7.3]

 • Fermilab is the DOE’s particle physics and accelerator laboratory. It is a single-purpose
 laboratory, with a mission to support DOE-sponsored HEP experiments and activities.
 Fermilab is the US Tier-1 center for the LHC/CMS experiment, hosting roughly 40% of CMS
 experiment data. The laboratory is also the host institution for the DUNE experiment and
 supports the Tier-0 center for the experiment. Other active Fermilab-based experiments include
 SBN and SBD, NuMI Off-axis νe Appearance (NOvA), Mu2e, Muon g-2, ICARUS,
 and MicroBoone. [Section 7.4]

 • The Scientific Data and Computer Center (SDCC) at BNL began in 1997 when the Relativistic
 Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and ATLAS Computing Facility were established. SDCC provides
 dedicated data processing, storage, and analysis resources for a set of diverse, expansive
 experiments with general computing capabilities and support for users. [Section 7.5]

 • The primary scientific computation and storage facilities at SLAC are provisioned in the
 SLAC Shared Scientific Data Facility (S3DF). The S3DF is a compute, storage, and network
 architecture designed to support massive-scale analytics required by all SLAC experimental

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 20

 facilities and programs. The S3DF infrastructure is optimized for data analytics and is
 characterized by large, massive throughput, high-concurrency storage systems. [Section 7.6]

4.2 Scientific Data Management
 • Cosmology data sets are typically owned by the team that generated them, unless the work
 was specifically part of, or commissioned by, a collaborative activity. The transition toward
 open science, along with increased use for new domains, has led to more interest in placing
 simulation results in the public domain. Funding agencies often require datasets to be publicly
 available; the barrier to compliance is a lack of technical resources (e.g., computing, storage) to
 make this possible. [Section 6.1], [Section 8]

 • Cosmology simulations tend not to lose value over time. Older simulation catalogs continue
 to have high value and are being used in emerging work that utilizes AI and ML to
 construct generative models. Simulations can never truly be reproduced, even if the original
 codes and inputs are retained: differences in the underlying behavior of the systems that
 are used to generate are common, resulting in almost entirely new simulations. Older
 simulations will always have an intrinsic value, since they are unique and nonreproducible.
 However, the community understands that it is infeasible to keep every data set around
 forever, and mechanisms exist to archive sets that may not receive as much use as
 others. [Section 6.1], [Section 8]

 • Data storage needs for cosmological simulations post mid-2020s are likely to be in the 300
 petabyte (PB) range of spinning disk equivalent, requiring transfer rates of >300 Gbps on an
 intermittent basis when data mobility is required. [Section 6.1]

 • The network requirements for DESI must support transfer of an entire night’s observation (e.g.,
 100 GB or more). Tools including rsync are used help to keep a sliding window of 40 terabyte (TB)
 of previous observations up to date. In a worst-case scenario, transportable media could be
 used to take an evening’s worth of data manually down to the base station, or through a slower
 network path such as a low Earth orbit (LEO) Satellite (e.g., Starlink). [Section 6.2], [Section 8]

 • At NERSC, the DESI data volume is projected to grow at a rate of ~1 PB/year from 2020 to
 2025, reaching ~10 PB by the end of 2026. Approximately 1–2 PB originating from the Rubin
 Observatory with each yearly data release will be in this calculation, along with simulations
 produced at the DOE HPC facilities, which are expected to be several 100 TB, and data
 catalogs produced during the analysis process, which are estimated to be 20 TB. Extensions to
 the DESI effort have been proposed; if approved, these would continue the data growth at a
 similar rate through the mid-2030s. [Section 6.2]

 • Public DESI datasets will be curated by the Astro Data Lab at NOIRLab to be available
 beyond project completion. The intention is to also host the public DESI dataset via the
 Cosmology Data Repository at NERSC, though long-term funding commitment for that is not
 guaranteed. [Section 6.2]

 • The Rubin Observatory expects ~30 TB of continuous image and metadata to flow from
 Chile to the US each night. Real-time transfer over dedicated high-bandwidth segments is
 required to analyze each image at the USDF (hosted at SLAC) and broadcast alerts to the
 community. To support the Rubin Observatory, the USDF at SLAC will curate 5 PB/yr of data,
 with ancillary and other image data products that could add up to 500 PB by end of survey in
           2035. [Section 6.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 21

 • Once in full operations, major Rubin Observatory data releases for static cosmology analyses
 will be generated yearly. The bulk of data will originate with Rubin and be of the order of 1–2
 PB to be transferred every two to three years, and, assuming some data reduction strategies,
 could eventually be yearly. [Section 6.4]

 • DESC has tested Globus transfers of tens and hundreds of TB between NERSC and
 international sites, with transfer rates of 400 MB/s and 180 MB/s respectively. [Section 6.4]

 • DESC simulation activities will require data movement from other computing centers to
 NERSC. Data transfers will be on the order of 100 TB initially. When the Rubin
 Observatory Data Previews are present at SLAC, an additional 10–100 TB will be transferred
 to NERSC; this is expected in May 2025 and early 2026. The goal is to support PB-scale
 transfers between the facilities, and potentially to international collaborators to prepare for full
 production. [Section 6.4]

 • In operations, CMB-S4 will produce a data rate of approximately 2 Gbps. Data will be
 transferred in real time over fiber networks to the primary data center at the DOE’s NERSC,
 and copied to the secondary data center at the DOE’s ALCF. 20 TB of data are expected daily
 during operations (~7 PB of data annually). Along with the raw data files CMB-S4 will create,
 the primary data products will be the frequency maps: [Section 6.5]

           °    Daily (7 years x 365 days): 150 TB in 51,000 files.

 ° Monte Carlo (MC) (1,000 realizations x 7 years): 450 TB in 150,000 files.

 • CMB-S4 will deploy several telescope resources starting in 2030. These resources have the
 potential to produce 8 PB/year of data, sent to the US nightly in 20 TB sets. Local computation
 and storage resources can support storing a buffer of data for up to a month if necessary due to
 network degradation or downtime. [Section 6.5]

 • CMB-S4 will conduct a series of data challenges, starting in 2025 and running yearly
 through 2029, to help prepare for the operational challenge of data mobility from Chile to the
 US, and the analysis pipeline being constructed using DOE- and NSF-funded computing
 resources. [Section 6.5]

 • The Muon g-2 experiment will complete its studies with nearly 7 PB of raw experimental
 data, and an additional 1.5 PB of processed results. All data are planned to remain on tape
 at Fermilab, and at the current time no backup is planned or required. Once the processing
 is complete, the collaboration does not anticipate reprocessing will happen at this
 time. [Section 6.6], [Section 8]

 • The first aspect of operational Mu2e science will be to handle cosmic-ray events, which are
 expected to produce up to 500 TB of event data per year. Most of this effort will be computed
 through Fermilab, but there is a possibility that some computation could occur at other
 WLCG sites; a project goal is to consider up to half of computing needs occurring off-site.
 Regular operational data from Mu2e will top 7 PB of raw data a year. All data will be stored at
 Fermilab, with back-up copies stored at partner sites in Europe (locations are being
 determined). [Section 6.6], [Section 8]

 • Mu2e expects that many institutions will request copies of analysis-format datasets and that these
 will be stored locally at each institution. At this time, it is estimated that one copy of the analysis-
 format dataset for the full experiment will be, at most, on the scale of 50 TB. [Section 6.6]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 22

 • Belle II was an active participant in the LHC’s DC24 activities, and showed expected results for
 operations during this period; observation showed the experiment reached 250 TB/day, which
 is more than six times the maximum throughput expected at the end of the decade. A primary
 reason was testing of new software components shared with the LHC experiments. At the
 current time, Belle II does not anticipate participating in DC27. [Section 6.7], [Section 8]

 • Two copies of the raw data coming out of the Belle II DAQ at KEK are permanently stored: one
 copy at KEK and a second copy distributed between BNL (30%), Canada (15%), France (15%),
 Germany (20%), and Italy (20%). All raw data centers are connected to LHCONE. BNL houses
 approximately 3 PB of Belle II data, and anticipates having 5 PB of tape and 5 PB of disk storage
 available approaching 2028. [Section 6.7]

 • The SBN detectors (ICARUS and SBND) will produce approximately 5 PB of data per year that
 will be stored at Fermilab, and at backups sites. The SBN ICARUS detector has been taking
 data since 2021. The SBND detector is completing the commissioning phase and is expected to
 take physics-quality data in fall 2024. [Section 6.8]

 • ProtoDUNE efforts have produced approximately 5 PB of data per year at CERN during the
 initial run, and will exhibit a similar pattern for a second run between 2025 and 2026. [Section 6.8]

 • DUNE will produce 45 PB of data per year at full operation. This includes the near and far
 detectors, and 10 PB of processed data. The first full DUNE Far Detector, FD-VD, is slated to
 begin full operation at SURF in Lead, South Dakota, in mid-2029. A second module will come
 online in 2030–2031. These systems will require significant testing and calibration. They are
 projected to produce 10–15 PB of data per year per module to start and will be capped at 30 PB/
 year when in full operation. This includes tests of supernova burst sensitivity that will produce
 around 320 TB over a few hours. Steady rates of 100 TB/day are anticipated. [Section 6.8]

 • Transfer of the raw data produced from the DUNE detectors is likely to be the largest single
 network task for the experiment. It is anticipated that along with initial processing, annual
 reprocessing of all data accumulated to date will occur. In addition to beam and calibration data,
 the signal of neutrinos produced from a nearby supernova burst presents a significant challenge
 due to the large volume of data collected in a very short period (up to 600 TB in 100 seconds) and
 the time-critical nature of analyzing that data for optical astronomical observations. [Section 6.8]

 • DUNE participated in the DC24 activities with the LHC sites, and learned a lot about their
 approach to software and data management. DUNE anticipates participating in future DCs as
 well, due to the overlap with other WLCG computing resources. DUNE will also conduct its
 own DC activities on an annual basis. Being able to handle production traffic from the
 detector, as well as a supernova activity, will be an area of focus. This part of the DC will rely
 on the connection between SURF and Fermilab when the network is provisioned (expected in
 2026 or 2027). For the DC activities prior to this, BNL will currently serve as a stand-in for
 SURF. [Section 6.8], [Section 8]

 • LHC analyses are done by small and large groups that share data at a Tier-2 center, at a local
 Tier-3, or on other local computing facilities. An “average” event can be processed 50–100
 times by analysts. This means that LHC analysts are processing hundreds of PBs each year just
 to carry out the initial analysis steps, which process data created by the production
 system. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 23

 • Datasets in ATLAS are collections of files organized by category/workflow. These datasets are the
 fundamental units in ATLAS, fully integrated into the Rucio data management system, and used
 for workflow, transfers, and user analysis. Individual datasets vary greatly in size: [Section 6.9]

 ° Raw datasets are in the range of 1 TB to about 250 TB.

 ° Analysis Object Data (AOD) datasets are in the range of 1 GB to about 100 TB.

 ° DAOD datasets are in the range of 1 GB to about several TB.

 ° HITS datasets are in the order of several TB.

 • The Data Challenges (the last being DC24) were incredibly useful for the ATLAS experiment
 as well as the entire LHC community. Several issues were identified, including with the
 FTS tool, which limited productivity because there was no way to convey network capacity
 information to help influence performance. Simply stated, poor performance of some transfers
 limited the deployment of more to better-connected sites. Additional work to move from Virtual
 Organization Membership Service (VOMS), which is based on x.509 certificates, to HTTP-based
 tokens is also underway. FTS (and Rucio) are developed at CERN, and have limited resources to
 implement fixes. The timing of the next DC is still being discussed, and is tentatively scheduled
           for 2027. [Section 6.9], [Section 8]

 • The LHC provides data to CMS in roughly 10-hour data-taking periods with minimal downtime
 (typically a few hours) between periods. A roughly constant stream of data is therefore available
 during operation. Event rates of around 1 kHz of physics events are typical today and for Run 3,
 and 7.5 kHz is expected for HL-LHC. This translates into raw data volumes of: [Section 6.10]

 ° Run 2: 45 PB written during four years (2015–2018).

           °    Run 3: approximately 120 PB (2022–2024).

           °    Run 4: 270 PB/yr (estimated in 2022).

 • CMS has produced simulations with output that scales in size with the luminosity collected.
 CMS has about 70 PB (170 PB) of Run 3 (Run 2) MC simulation datasets stored on tape,
 representing around 75 billion (250 billion) MC events. [Section 6.10]

 • A paper was published after DC24 with several findings. The LHC collaborators’ DC24 activity
 revealed several weaknesses in the software stack, namely with the way that FTS performed
 globally when faced with bottlenecks at certain locations. The discussion in CMS about the
 use of alternative data formats, and the use of other R&D efforts such as Caching, may also
 influence how much bandwidth is needed between facilities, with the TA links being a main
 focus area. ESnet’s TA strategy has not changed substantially since the previous HEP review,
 and will continue to add capacity (mainly through using more flexible spectrum agreements, and
 sharing resources with GÉANT across multiple connections). [Section 6.11], [Section 8]

 • LHC Run 3 will be completed by the end of 2026, and the network traffic is expected to keep
 growing at the usual rate until then; the LHC community sees an annual increase of 20–30% of
 traffic in Large Hadron Collider Optical Private Network (LHCOPN) and LHCONE, the two
 networks dedicated to transfers between WLCG sites. The current networking capacities are
 typically 100 Gbps WAN links, with many sites already having resilience (multiple) 100 Gbps
 connections. This will need to evolve as the LHC community prepares for Run 4. The expected
 traffic during Run 4 beyond 2030, when the HL-LHC comes into operation, will significantly
 increase. ATLAS and CMS have estimated this increase in network traffic to be a factor of 10
 compared with Run3. [Section 6.11]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 24

 • In preparation for HL-LHC, the LHC experiments have defined a calendar of “data challenges”
 to progressively test the capabilities of the WLCG software and hardware infrastructure to meet
 the requirements. Here is the way they have estimated the network bandwidth: [Section 6.11]

 ° ATLAS & CMS T0 to T1 per experiment:

 • 350 PB raw data per year; average of 50 Gbps or 400 Gbps during LHC running time.
 • Another 100 Gbps estimated for prompt reconstruction data tiers (AOD, other
 derived output).

 • Estimated 1 Tbps for CMS and ATLAS summed.
 • ALICE & LHCb T0 Export
 ° 100 Gbps per experiment estimated from Run 3 rates.

 • The CMS experiment anticipates the following annual data volume for each data type during
 HL-LHC operation: [Section 6.12]

           °    Raw data: 250 PB.

           °    AOD data: 210 PB.

 ° MiniAOD data: 27 PB.

 ° NanoAOD data: 0.6 PB.

 • The ATLAS experiment anticipates the following annual data volume for each data type during
 HL-LHC operation: [Section 6.12]

           °    Raw data: 168 PB.

           °    AOD data: 200 PB.

 ° DAOD data: 76 PB.

 ° DAOD_PHYSLITE Data: 2.6 PB.

 • The estimated data volume of SuperCDMS SNOLAB is 350 TB/year, including calibration data
 and simulated data. [Section 6.13]

 • AMS produces ~40 TB of raw data per year, which are transmitted to CERN, and then
 reconstructed to 170 TB data per year available for analysis by collaboration members. The
 production is performed incrementally every six months. Reprocessing is performed only when
 changes to reconstruction software occur. Each version of full reproduction is called a “pass.”
 AMS has acquired over 500 TB of raw data, from which 2 PB of pass 8 data have been produced
 and copied to collaborators’ institutions for further analyses. [Section 6.14]

 • AMS data analysis requires massive MC simulation, performed by computing centers on a
 regular time basis. Currently, 23 PB of MC data have been produced since the start of the
           project in 2011. [Section 6.14]

 • AMS has more than 300K readout channels and 1,500 temperature sensors. More than 500
 microprocessors are onboard, which reduce the data rate from 7 Gbps to 10 Mb/s. Data taken
 on board of the ISS by AMS consist of raw events, and these are logically grouped in sequences
 called runs. Events inside one run are numbered in sequence. Every quarter of the orbit, a
 scientific run starts. The duration of each run corresponds to 23 minutes, and every run contains
 on average 700k events. The average size of a raw event is 2 KB; thus yearly raw data yield is 40
           TB. [Section 6.14]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 25

 • By the end of 2025, AMS will undergo a significant upgrade on the ISS; it will involve the
 addition of a new tracker layer at the top of the instrument. This advancement is essential
 for progressing dark matter searches and improving precision measurements. The new
 configuration of AMS will require a complete overhaul of simulations and data analysis tools,
 which will be developed over the next three to five years. The total volume of data is expected
 to increase to 50 PB over the next five years. [Section 6.14]

4.3 Scientific Workflow
 • Cosmological simulation data streams typically involve moving between 10–100 TB of bulk data,
 when an entire data set is needed. Smaller downloads that may target a subset of a data set for
 individual analysis may involve <1 TB chunks of data. Progress in remote visualization methods
 is allowing real-time visualization of many large data sets. [Section 6.1]

 • Over the next two to five years, an evolution in cosmological simulation workflow tools to
 manage local and remote simulation data analysis will occur. This effort to design more
 approachable ways to manage download sizes, and ease of location, will allow users more power
 over their analysis behaviors. [Section 6.1]

 • Every ~15 minutes, DESI obtains spectra of 5,000 astronomical objects, resulting in 1–2 GB
 of raw data per exposure. Data are then processed at NERSC in semi-real time (minutes to
 hours after capture), which results in a processed file size of ~10 GB per exposure. DESI
 projects that the total data volume will grow to O(10 PB) by the end of the survey. Every 1–2
 years, DESI reprocesses all the data taken to date using the latest data-processing code and
 calibrations. [Section 6.2]

 • Science analyses using DESI data are primarily performed at NERSC. The scale of
 analyses varies from single-core Jupyter Notebook use cases, to large parallel-batch jobs
 consuming many cores and machines. Many of the analyses make use of simulated datasets
 generated at NERSC, while others are generated at other DOE HPC facilities and
 transferred to NERSC. [Section 6.2]

 • Transfers of DESI's processed data from NERSC to the NOIRLab and University of
 Utah mirrors use Globus for the initial bulk transfer, then use rsync to pick up any later
 differences. [Section 6.2]

 • DESI experiences friction with the management of data mobility outside of NERSC. Data can
 be egressed via approaches like Globus, but this typically is an option only for users who are
 familiar with the tool and have the necessary credentials to manage it. An efficient method like
 commercial tools (e.g., Dropbox, iPhoto, etc.) may appeal to users less sophisticated with data
 mobility. Users often do not want to be bothered with the functional details of a data mobility
 tool and just want things to work efficiently and simply. That DESI would adopt some of the
 other tools the HEP community has championed (e.g., Rucio) is unlikely, as the cultural shift
 required to do so is not very strong. [Section 6.2], [Section 8]

 • Rubin alerts are required to be broadcast via at least five community-developed brokers in 60
 seconds from the time the camera shutter closes on the mountain top in Chile. Other “prompt
 data products” are made available to the community after an 80-hour embargo period. The
 embargo period is implemented to prevent prompt detection of artificial satellites in the LSST
 data stream. In 2021, Rubin completed selection of the community alert brokers. These include
 seven international teams: ANTARES (NOIRLab), ALeRCE (Chile), Lasair (UK), Pitt-Google
 (University of Pittsburgh), Fink (France), AMPEL (Germany), and Babamul (California Institute
 of Technology). Two downstream brokers that operate off one of the primary brokers were also
 endorsed by the Science Advisory Committee (SAC): SNAPS (Northern Arizona University) and
 POI (Vanderbilt University). [Section 6.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 26

 • All image data will be carried to the project’s Archive Center at the USDF, hosted within the
 S3DF. The total northbound data from Rubin to the Archive Center is approximately 30 TB/
 night. A very demanding application using these flows is Data Release Processing and Alert
 Production, where 12.7 GB (uncompressed) of pixel data need to be transferred from the Base
 Facility in La Serena Chile to the Archive Center in seven-second bursts. Two such bursts
 occur approximately every minute of nighttime observing. The bursts need to be sustained for
 approximately 355 days each year. The required reliability level for these flows is very high and
 is seen to require a path-diverse network with nearly lossless networking. [Section 6.3]

 • Over its 10 years of planned operations, Rubin Observatory will produce annual data releases.
 Each data release will include reprocessing of all data from the start of the survey up to the
 cutoff date for that release. [Section 6.3]

 • The DESC project is investigating the use of Rucio and FTS, as is the Rubin Observatory, to
 see if these would be a good fit for the data management aspects of the project. The use of any
 software comes with risks: the project strives to ensure that individual users can easily interact
 with the systems they create, and will gravitate toward things that are easy to install, use, and
 support long term. The latter observation holds true for managing access for scientific users:
 the lack of a cohesive multi-institutional way to manage credentials is also a challenge for this
 collaboration. [Section 6.4], [Section 8]

 • DESC is exploring ways to perform multimodal analysis using other streams of research data.
 Some possibilities include the European Space Agency’s Euclid mission6 and the Nancy Grace
 Roman Space Telescope.7 The effort is early, and questions remain about ways to get access to
 the data and how the data can be integrated through software and computational hardware.
 One question is that with the portal system for these three data products (and in general, all
 individual collaborations that produce a data set that others may want to use), no uniformity
 exists in how the data can be retrieved. This causes a challenge for the greater scientific
 community. [Section 6.4], [Section 8]

 • DESC is exploring the use of Independent Data Access Centers (IDACs) for the Rubin
 Observatory, which are being developed as in-kind contributions to the observatory by
 institutions around the world. Some of the IDAC resources will be made available to DESC and
 other LSST science collaborations for science analyses and could potentially provide specialized
 capabilities. [Section 6.4]

 • When CMB-S4 is operating, each day of data will be immediately reduced to a map of the
 observed sky, using US agency computing resources (DOE HPC, NSF High-Throughput
 Computing [HTC], and potentially FABRIC). These maps will be analyzed to identify transient
 sources, with alerts issued to the entire scientific community via the Community Alert Broker,
 and for data quality and telescope health checks. [Section 6.5]

 • Given the size and complexity of the CMB-S4 data set (~100 PB), collecting, transporting, and
 reducing the raw data from time streams of detector samples to well-characterized sky maps is
 the responsibility of the CMB-S4 project. Given the extraordinary range of science these maps
 support and their relatively small size (~100 TB), analyzing these maps is the responsibility of
 the CMB-S4 collaboration and the scientific community. [Section 6.5]

7 https://roman.gsfc.nasa.gov/
