 • Current and near-term work in data movement to support CMB-S4 will focus on building a
 test stand for both data and metadata into the baseline data movement tool (Rucio). These tests
 will primarily involve local operations within NERSC: running Rucio as a service on the Spin
 container-based service and ingesting simulated data into the Community File System (CFS).
 CMB-S4 will also practice moving data between local filesystems using Rucio. By the end of
 this time frame, transfers between NERSC and ALCF, or another large computing center, will
 be tested to validate performance expectations. [Section 6.5]

 • Mu2e will be adopting Rucio and other tools that are well-known to the HEP community to
 manage workflow and data mobility. The project is limited in exploration of alternative software
 and computational platforms due to funding and staff. Adopting new workflows is not something
 Mu2e has the time or resources to explore currently, but Mu2e has been able to make its
 simulation and analysis code work at NERSC and ALCF. During long shutdowns, or extended
 technical stops, it may be possible to explore other use cases. [Section 6.6], [Section 8]

 • Simulations for Mu2e will be run on Fermigrid resources, OSG resources, at NERSC, and at
 the ALCF. The simulated events and reconstructed simulated events will be stored at Fermilab.
 Mu2e expects that many institutions will request copies of the analysis-format datasets derived
 from the simulated events; these datasets are likely to be about a few times the volume of the
 corresponding experimental datasets. [Section 6.6]

 • All Mu2e data can be processed on Fermigrid, but for planning purposes it is assumed that
 about half will be processed on Fermigrid and half on opportunistic OSG. On average, Mu2e
 expects to process each event twice, leading to an estimate of 4 TB/year of outbound data and
 2.5 TB/year of inbound data. Discussions have taken place that may lead to some calibration
 work being done in the UK or at the Italian Institute for Nuclear Physics (INFN), using
 resources provided by their funding agencies. For this exercise, Mu2e assumes that about 0.5
 PB/year will be transferred to each location. [Section 6.6]

 • Belle II has a grid-computing model with a three-level hierarchical structure (“tiers”) of
 computing sites: raw data centers (Tier-1), regional data centers (Tier-2), and MC (simulated
 data) production centers (Tier-3). Many of the Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites in Belle II are part of
 the WLCG collaboration and shared with LHC experiments. This also includes the network
 connecting these sites, particularly the ones connected by LHCOne. The sites without
 LHCOne connection are small and can be used without LHCOne. [Section 6.7]

 • Belle II reprocessing campaigns based on improved calibration run typically once per year or
 biyearly. Reprocessing will be every other year beginning 2025. [Section 6.7]

 • Belle II chose to migrate from its bespoke data management solution to Rucio in January 2021.
 Since then, Rucio, with FTS as back-end transfer system, has managed all production and
 analysis data production on the grid. Rucio ensures the replication of raw data from KEK to
 the other data centers. Rucio also ensures the replication of the dataset output generated by
 the production system and makes a second copy of user or group data to other sites. Since the
 migration to Rucio in 2021, no network bottlenecks have been observed. [Section 6.7]

 • In addition to detector data, DUNE will produce large quantities of simulation that in some
 cases will rival the size of the detector data. These data will be produced at distributed
 compute facilities and be cataloged and stored in storage elements around the globe. DUNE is
 currently using more than 20 compute facilities and more than 10 storage facilities to achieve its
 computing tasks. This number is expected to grow between now and late 2028, when the first
 far detector module will become operational. [Section 6.8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 28

 • Three DUNE prototype detectors will be active over the next two years: ProtoDUNE-HD,
 ProtoDUNE-VD, and ND-LAr 2x2 demonstrator. The ProtoDUNE detectors are at CERN,
 while the demonstrator is at Fermilab. The raw data arrive from the ProtoDUNE detectors at a
 steady rate of approximately 1 TB/hr (~300 MB/s), and from the 2x2 detector at approximately
 42 GB/hr (~15 MB/s). The ProtoDUNE data are delivered to CERN on site, and a second
 copy of the ProtoDUNE data is also transferred to Fermilab. The raw data are made available
 for immediate processing, which is accessed via XRootD to run on the WLCG. For the 2x2
 demonstrator, the data are automatically stored at Fermilab, and then transferred in batches to a
 DUNE allocation at NERSC for processing. [Section 6.8]

 • DUNE data acquisition for the first far detector module will commence post 2029, and the
 output of the module will be roughly 30 PB/year going to archival storage. Offline processing
 and data flows will look very similar to prototype operations but with slightly different
 endpoints. (e.g., instead of data coming from CERN, data will be created at SURF). There
 is no significant change in the software or process of science between the activities of the
 prototypes and the actual DUNE detectors by design. It is anticipated that the current design
 of the DUNE computing model implemented with the prototypes will scale and be sufficient to
 achieve the science goals of DUNE. [Section 6.8]

 • For data management software, DUNE uses the Rucio replica management service, which has
 wide support in the high energy physics community. This is combined with the MetaCat data
 catalog which tracks the provenance of the data and can also interface with other databases,
 such as the run conditions database. Rucio can work with the FTS system, which in turn uses
 primarily https-based transfers to move the data sets to and from remote data sets. It can also
 use Globus as a transport mechanism, and DUNE expects to get data to and from the leadership
 facilities. There is a distributed global disk model in which current data sets are hosted at a set
 of 15 storage elements in the US and Europe. [Section 6.8]

 • The ATLAS grid infrastructure consists of the Tier-0 computing site at CERN, 9 Tier-1s, 70
 Tier-2s, and about 50 Tier-3 sites distributed worldwide. Any workflow can be executed at any
 location with memorandums of understanding (MOUs) established for the Tier-0, Tier-1, and
 Tier-2 sites specifically. Tape storage to store raw and AOD files is available at the Tier-0 and
 Tier-1 sites and a small subset of Tier-2 sites. ATLAS Tier-3 sites at most universities are usually
 smaller local central processing unit (CPU) clusters with several TBs of disk storage attached. At
 these sites individual end-user analysis happens without any production activity. [Section 6.9]

 • Data from the ATLAS detector are calibrated, reconstructed, and automatically distributed all
 around the world by the ATLAS Data Management system. The ATLAS Production System
 then filters through these events and selects the ones needed for a particular type of analysis.
 This brings the data set down to a manageable size for someone doing an analysis on a laptop.
 All members of the ATLAS Collaboration have equal access possibilities to all ATLAS data,
 independently of their geographical location, thanks to the WLCG. [Section 6.9]

 • The open-source software framework Rucio is used to organize, manage, and access the ATLAS
 data. The data are distributed across heterogeneous data centers at widely distributed locations
 worldwide. The Production and Distributed Analysis System (PanDA) ecosystem manages all
 workflows and workloads in ATLAS. PanDA uses the HTCondor system for job submission to
 most computing resources. [Section 6.9]

 • The data rates that CMS originally estimated for Run 3 (i.e., in 2020, just prior to the run
 beginning) were smaller than what was witnessed by a factor of two to three times beyond
 the 2018 values, and four to six times beyond the 2017 values. This increase in size has not

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 29

 translated directly into increased traffic on network connections; however, some of the R&E
 efforts to improve data mobility tools and workflow management have helped mitigate big
 spikes in traffic. [Section 6.10], [Section 8]

 • CMS globally has seven Tier-1s, including Fermilab in the US. The collection of Tier-1s is
 responsible for operating a distributed archive of all centrally produced data, including a
 second copy of the raw. The copy of the raw across the Tier-1s is considered the “active
 copy”; i.e., the raw copy at CERN is considered strictly a backup. In addition, the Tier-1s
 provide computing resources to the experiment that are primarily used for centrally organized
 processing. The US CMS Tier-1 Center at Fermilab is the largest of CMS Tier-1 facilities,
 currently providing 40% of the total CMS Tier-1 capacity. CMS has roughly 50 Tier-2s globally.
 The collection of the Tier-2s is responsible for all data analysis and some simulations. Tier-2s
 also provide disk space to host data for analysis, and a moderate amount of disk space for staging
 in data for processing. [Section 6.10]

 • CMS Tier-3 sites are typically university-hosted clusters smaller than Tier-2 sites and typically
 without dedicated support to ensure high resource availability. Those in the US are not funded
 through the US CMS operations program. Tier-3 sites can be part of the data management
 system of CMS and receive official datasets, or can access data through streaming. These sites
 can also provide disk space to hold user data as required by the local community. [Section 6.10]

 • CMS uses compute resources beyond the tiered computing centers. These include HPC centers
 in the US. During 2023, the CMS usage of shared HPC facilities funded by DOE and NSF
 amounted to about 10% of the overall computing budget globally. This increased substantially
 in the recent past, by around four times in relative fraction of CMS compute since 2020 (and
 a substantially greater increase in absolute terms), and substantially increased again in 2024.
 CMS expects that this model will change for the HL-LHC to include larger allocations on HPC
 facilities. [Section 6.10]

 • HPC centers funded by DOE and NSF as shared facilities across multiple science domains
 do not generally provide the full functionality required from an LHC Tier-2 or Tier-1 center
 (e.g., they normally do not provide any substantial amount of storage under the control of the
 experiment). Data access at HPC centers relies on either temporarily staging in input data on
 storage at the HPC site or streaming access, if the site setup allows access to the wider network.
 In general, HPC centers run only compute-dominated applications that have modest IO/
 CPU requirements (e.g., the central production workflows involved in central processing and
 simulations). Output is archived back to the Tier-1 sites, either directly from the application or
 through other mechanisms. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]

 • The centrally produced data from CMS comes in multiple formats ranging from the most
 versatile and complete (raw and AOD) to the easiest, smallest, and fastest to use (MiniAOD
 and NanoAOD). CMS has been moving toward the use of NanoAOD, a data format designed
 for interactive end-user analysis, and produced centrally. CMS adoption of this format has
 already grown in Run 3 to around 50% of analyses using the NanoAOD as their primary data
 tier. [Section 6.10]

 • CMS currently uses Rucio for bulk-data transfer activities, having fully switched from its
 previous system based on PhEDEx and Dynamo tools, to manage dataset storage and dataset
 transfers. Rucio has become a community solution for data management. Rucio uses the FTS to
 manage scheduling and file transfer. For bulk transfers via Rucio and executed by FTS, US CMS
 has moved to Third Party Copy (TPC) https implemented via XRootD servers and away from
 GridFTP. [Section 6.10]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 30

 • Failures in data streaming are a large source of job failures in CMS. This has also become an
 issue for analysis-facing activities, where a greater variety of tools are used to access CMS data.
 While CMS can instrument its centrally maintained software with retry mechanisms and other
 fallback logic, extending this to community-developed tools is more difficult. Reliable and high-
 capacity streaming of input data, either raw or pileup simulation, considerably reduces the disk
 requirements of CMS at HPC and other nondedicated computing facilities. [Section 6.10]

 • For LHC operations, the use of either pledged or opportunistic HPC resources located away
 from traditional tiered sites is currently very difficult because each HPC facility is “special” in
 terms of bespoke hardware, network access, storage policies, and job submission. This means
 each experiment using such facilities needs to dedicate significant resources to operating and
 maintaining the HPC for its use case. HEP experiments have developed in-house mechanisms,
 like HEPCloud and Harvester, to manage access to disparate resources. Therefore, the LHC
 community would greatly benefit from a unified security model across DOE (and NSF) HPC
 facilities and a unified resource brokering API via efforts such as IRI. [Section 6.11]

 • The LHC community maintains some common efforts to provide software used throughout the
 ecosystem: [Section 6.11]

 ° Rucio, a distributed data management system.

 ° FTS, responsible for reliably transferring data while not overloading end-systems.

 ° Monitoring:

 • SciTags, to label flows and/or IPv6 packets by experiment and activity.
 • WLCG Site Network Monitoring to track each site’s IN/OUT traffic.
 ° Networking orchestration:

 • SENSE/Rucio to integrate SDN with distributed data management.
 • NOTED, a tool to identify network congestion and move large flows to other
 paths dynamically.

 • All LHC Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites are expected to have perfSONAR nodes deployed to monitor
 network performance. These nodes are integrated into a mesh configuration, enabling regular
 tests such as latency and bandwidth checks between sites. perfSONAR allows network
 administrators to identify potential network issues that could impact data-transfer rates, both
 intersite and with CERN. It plays a vital role in the global transfer of data across the LHC
 Computing Grid (LCG). [Section 6.11]

 • The exact computing model for the HL-LHC has not been finalized, given that the LHC Run
 4 is not expected to start till 2030. It is assumed that the current computing models will be the
 baseline model, with some small improvements. No fixed hierarchy of computing sites will
 exist for most data processing and data access services. To improve usage efficiency, sites will
 be primarily categorized by size, service level, and capability. Hence the location of datasets
 and users is not deterministic. Tier-1s will need additional capacity to handle worldwide traffic,
 and Tier-2s will be scoped larger for national traffic needs. The network capacity should be
 provisioned to match the scale of the available resources at each site. [Section 6.12]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 31

 • ATLAS has chosen to evaluate two scenarios based on how aggressively it is anticipated that the
 HL-LHC storage and computing R&D program will deliver improvements: [Section 6.12]

 ° “Conservative” R&D is a program where work can be completed with the existing person-
 power. The R&D activities currently underway to support Run 3 will be put into place, and
 will encourage an almost universal adoption of the DAOD_PHYSLITE format.

 ° A full program of “aggressive” higher-risk R&D can be completed only with new person-
 power. ATLAS implements new developments that very significantly improve the speed
 and storage volumes of workflows that currently are heavy consumers of resources.

 • SuperCDMS SNOLAB data will be acquired underground at SNOLAB, transferred to the
 surface, and then transferred to SLAC where they will be processed. To ensure access to data to
 all members of the SuperCDMS collaboration (access to SLAC resources is restricted for some
 collaborators), processed data will also be copied on the Open Storage Network (OSN) and the
 Digital Research Alliance of Canada (DRAC). [Section 6.13]

 • SuperCDMS will not rely on SNOLAB for data analysis. Data analysis will happen primarily at
 SLAC, DRAC, the OSN, NSF ACCESS facilities, and at other smaller institutions. SNOLAB
 is minimally equipped with software, and each experiment has a dedicated subnetwork with
 limited bandwidth. Given the small amount of data to be moved from SNOLAB to SLAC,
 automated transfer tools based on rsync (single stream), with the option to move to bbcp
 (multiple streams, four by default), will be used. The limited outgoing bandwidth and the single
 destination make the use of such simple approaches ideal for this scenario. [Section 6.13]

 • Due to limitations in the available bandwidth that Tracking and Data Relay Satellite (TDRS)
 can deliver, and the number of use cases that exist on the ISS, AMS is able to access only
 about 14 Mbps of space-to-ground transmission. This limitation has not forced the adoption of
 high-speed data migration tools, as the data volumes will always remain small for this aspect of
 the workflow. NASA has been evaluating whether the use of other satellite technologies (e.g.,
 Starlink) could serve as an augmented communication mechanism, or a replacement for TDRS,
 but this would not be something AMS has control over. [Section 6.14], [Section 8]

 • The AMS project creates many simulations during its process of science; over 20 PB
 have been produced since the start of the project. With the pending upgrade to AMS
 hardware in the coming years, it is anticipated that all produced MC will have to be
 reprocessed. [Section 6.14], [Section 8]

 • Recorded data are packed to fixed length packets and transmitted via the TDRS satellites to
 ground at White Sands, New Mexico, and then relayed to NASA’s Marshall Space Flight
 Center (MSFC) in Alabama. At MSFC data are first transferred to the AMS relay computers
 using the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) and finally to the AMS Science Operation
 Center (SOC) at CERN, in Geneva, Switzerland, with bbftp software. Sustained transferring
 speed from MSFC to SOC up to 50 Mbit/sec is achieved. [Section 6.14]

 • AMS previously used Globus for cross-site data moving, but as CERN dropped Globus support,
 AMS now uses XRDCP to transfer data across sites. [Section 6.14]

4.4 Computational and Storage Requirements
 • As increased computational power becomes available, large-volume cosmological simulations
 with gas dynamics and subgrid modeling of astrophysical mechanisms have become possible,
 which were previously the domain of gravity-only simulations. Increased computational power
 will enable large-scale ensemble simulations that can be used directly for inference or to
 construct generative models using AI/ML techniques that can be then used for this purpose.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 32

 The level of resolution and volume required of cosmological simulations will continue to
 increase in the coming years, driving data volumes significantly upwards due to these
 factors. [Section 6.1]

 • Cosmological simulations can generate far more data than optical and microwave observations.
 This is expected to be the case when data become available from the Rubin Observatory, the
 largest of the imaging surveys. Estimation of statistical errors relies on hundreds to tens of
 thousands of simulated examples, and cosmologists often need to simulate results obtained
 from dozens to hundreds of varying simulation input conditions. While the on-sky pixel-level
 data can in some cases be larger, the simulated catalogs are already at the level of PBs for large
 simulation suites. [Section 6.1]

 • The size, sophistication, and realism of simulated sky catalogs has improved significantly, which
 puts further stress on storage and data-transfer capabilities. Typical simulation products can be
 a TB in size, approaching a PB for some of the wide-ranging simulations or those that contain
 more detail due to improvements in the modeling techniques. [Section 6.1]

 • Cosmological simulation continues to be substantially limited by the availability of storage,
 particularly when considering how to distribute the simulation data beyond the group that
 performed the simulation. Further, the need for storage beyond the initial computing project is
 critical; the lifetime of the need is often set by the life cycle of the analysis, which is happening
 in larger collaborations, and as the projects become more complex, over longer timelines.
 Some projects are more storage-limited than they are compute-limited. This issue has several
 associated dimensions to consider: [Section 6.1]

 ° Sizes and numbers of simulations will increase.

 ° Locations producing simulations are expected to increase.

 ° Funding spans different agencies.

 ° Usefulness over time, and to different communities, is increasing.

 • The DESI collaboration space at NERSC will eventually host 10 PB of experimental data. These
 data are processed nightly, and analyzed by users that access NERSC from remote locations.
 Backups are performed to High-Performance Storage System (HPSS) at NERSC, and mirrored
 to partner facilities (NOIRLab in Tucson, AZ, and the University of Utah). [Section 6.2]

 • Given the volume of data involved, making all Rubin releases available on fast storage for the
 duration of the project is not feasible. Instead, Rubin will keep the two most-recent releases
 available for rapid access, and archive older releases to tape. Users will not be able to perform
 database queries against these archived releases. However, they would be made available for
 bulk download. [Section 6.3]

 • Rubin requires a constant 1,188 CPU cores throughout the survey period to perform prompt
 processing. These cores will be used during the night for alert generation, and during the day
 for catch-up (where necessary) and solar system processing. Each core will have access to 5 GB
 of memory, and all these cores are located at the USDF. [Section 6.3]

 • In FY24 the Rubin Observatory IDF transitioned to the hybrid-cloud US Data Access Center
 (US DAC) model, with the user-facing Rubin Science Platform (RSP) remaining in Google
 Cloud and the back-end data holdings and data services hosted at the USDF at SLAC. The
 RSP is implemented in a virtualization framework that is portable across cloud providers or
 Kubernetes-based on-premises infrastructure. [Section 6.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 33

 • DESC analyses will be carried out primarily at NERSC, and SLAC is the primary data source
 for Rubin Observatory data. ESnet current connectivity between these sites is sufficient for
 DESC’s early needs, and planned upgrades in future years should ensure the data volumes are
 managed efficiently. During this period, DESC foresees testing and carrying out workflows
 across multiple sites as supplementary computing, trying to minimize data movement. In the
 next two to five years, NERSC will be migrating to NERSC-10, and DESC will be testing the
 incorporation of IDACs and other IRI platforms to these analyses. [Section 6.4]

 • The current computing needs of Mu2e are dominated by simulation campaigns to provide
 datasets of simulated events for the purpose of value engineering the design, validating the
 design, and providing input for the development of trigger, reconstruction, calibration, and
 analysis algorithms. At first the simulations were done on OSG, including Fermilab, but in
 recent years resources on Theta at ALCF and on Cori and Perlmutter at NERSC have been
 used. The output of each of these simulation campaigns is on the scale of 250 TB. [Section 6.6]

 • Mu2e has had preliminary discussions with groups in Italy and in the UK to provide computing
 resources for the calibration of subsystems. If these plans are realized, outbound datasets will be
 on the scale of 0.5 PB/year to each location, and inbound datasets will accumulate to tens of TB/
 year. If additional computing resources are available in collaborating institutions, Mu2e plans to
 use them for simulation campaigns; in this case there will be little outbound traffic and inbound
 traffic of up to a few hundred TB/year. [Section 6.6]

 • Belle II uses a grid model initially developed to support the computing needs of the LHC
 experiments. This model has a hierarchical structure with a Tier-0 site (e.g., KEK) that produces
 and hosts a primary copy of the raw data produced by the experiment Tier-1 sites that host a
 secondary copy of the raw data, and that are used for prompt processing and reprocessing. and
 Tier-2 sites mainly dedicated to MC production and user analysis. [Section 6.7]

 • In addition to use of Fermilab central computing, SBN will onboard computing at the national
 center of INFN (CNAF), CERN, and the UK to further facilitate general production and
 analysis work. SBN also plans to make use of HPC facilities like Polaris at ALCF and Perlmutter
 at NERSC to further enable general production processing. [Section 6.8]

 • For reconstruction processing of data, DUNE needs to have an amount of outbound network
 traffic from the disk elements equal to the output of the detectors so that processing can keep
 up with the production of raw data. Data need to be delivered to wherever that production is
 running: we expect this to be a combination of computing resources from around the world.
 DUNE expects data input/output rates to be tape/disk input/output (I/O) limited for the
 foreseeable future. [Section 6.8]

 • For SBN’s ICARUS reconstruction processing, computing jobs need to have data delivered at
 a consistent average rate of up to 2 TB/hr to satisfy demands during data production campaigns
 (~60 days in length). Data will be written back to Fermilab for storage at a rate of ~1 TB/
 hr. Data need to be delivered to wherever that production is running: SBN expects this to be
 largely Fermilab computing resources, but it will include some fraction of jobs to available OSG
 sites across the US and Europe, and to CNAF computing in Italy. For SBND, these numbers
 will peak at approximately 1 TB/hr for data reading and ~0.8 TB/hr for data write-back in this
 similar two-year period. [Section 6.8]

 • The WLCG collects resources worldwide and enables their usage by the LHC experiments
 as a distributed computing facility. The mission of the WLCG is to provide global computing
 resources to store, distribute, and analyze the ~50 to 70 PB of data expected every year of
 operations from the LHC at CERN. WLCG is coordinated by CERN. It is managed and
 operated by a worldwide collaboration between the experiments (ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, and
 LHCb) and the participating computer centers. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 34

 • ATLAS has a long history of successfully using HPC resources during Run 2 and Run 3 at the
 LHC. From 2016 to 2020, US-based HPC resources supported 10–25% of ATLAS simulation
 production. This share decreased after several HPC resources were commissioned in Europe.
 In the first half of 2024, 21% of the worldwide ATLAS CPU resources came from HPC
 resources with 70% of them from the European HPC Vega in Slovenia, 8% from Perlmutter
 at NERSC, and 5% from CSCS (the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre) in Switzerland.
 European HPC resources are mostly used through grid interfaces. US resources at NERSC
 and Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC) require special edge services to run ATLAS
 jobs. Only simulations were carried out, since they are not data intensive. In the future, ATLAS
 plans to adapt all workloads to run on HPC resources. This will put much higher demands on
 networking. [Section 6.9]

 • ATLAS computing is fully distributed. All processing and reprocessing of the data is managed
 by PanDA, and Rucio is used for data cataloging and data transfer. All computing activities are
 free to occur at any site, irrespective of their tier, and based on intelligent brokering of tasks
 and jobs. Distributed analysis jobs are also brokered by site capability; users are discouraged
 from choosing a specific site. Four distinct storage types are used by ATLAS computing
 environments: disk, tape, cloud, and cache storage. [Section 6.9]

 ° Disk storage is the main bulk of the storage: 1042M files with the volume of 412 PB are in
 disk storage. In the US, 198M files with the volume of 98.5 PB are in disk storage.

 ° Tape storage is used as a main data archival system: 370M files with the volume of 639 PB
 are stored in the tape archive system. In the US, 63M files with the volume of 107 PB are
 stored in the BNL Tier-1 HPSS system.

 ° S3 type storage is used for temporary output of event service jobs.

 ° XRootD XCache storage is used for unmanaged disk data cache for input of user
 analysis jobs.

 • Changes made to CMS analysis formats have also had a large impact on network traffic. The
 NanoAOD format, which was introduced late in Run 2, is becoming more widely used. The
 format is smaller, and thus occupies less network bandwidth and can run faster on CPUs. More
 than 50% of all physics analysis activities are now based on NanoAOD, with another 40% or
 more to be based on MiniAOD. The use of the larger AOD format is now minimal, despite it
 occupying a lot of disk space. At future HL-LHC scales, CMS expects to keep AOD on tape
 archives only. [Section 6.10], [Section 8]

 • The LHC computing and storage infrastructure is organized in a tiered computing model
 including four tiers, 0–3. Originally, when the connectivity among the sites was extremely
 limited, the tiers were hierarchical in that Tier-N+1 was connected only to an associated Tier-N
 above and associated Tier-N+2 below. Data were not allowed to flow from Tier-N+2 to Tier-N.
 This rigid concept has been eliminated over the last decade as network capacity and capability
 have progressed. [Section 6.10]

 • CMS acknowledges that the data volume that can be handled by the networks within and
 coming out of the CMS detector facility far exceeds what can be handled offline within current
 CPU, storage, and networking infrastructures. This bottleneck will remain for the foreseeable
 future, as network growth patterns move faster than storage and computation. [Section 6.10]

 • WLCG’s hardware choices for the next major cycles will have a huge influence on the
 performance of the overall computation and storage system, as witnessed during the LHC
 collaborators’ DC24 activity. Since funding requests must be made in advance, and hardware
 choice and prices fluctuate, uncertainty exists about what capabilities may exist. As a result

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 35

 of this, a series of mini-DC activities will occur on a regular basis to evaluate aspects of the
 ecosystem: computing, storage, software, and networking, culminating in the larger complete
 DC activities that focus on major goal milestones. [Section 6.11], [Section 8]

 • The impact of HL-LHC on ATLAS and CMS storage and compute resources is significant. The
 increase in luminosity not only generates significantly more data but also significantly more
 complex events, which require more processing to resolve. [Section 6.12]

 • The expanded use of High-Performance Computing (HPC) will also have an impact on the
 compute resources (storage and networking). These HPC centers are increasing in computing
 power, and several exaflop-scale machines will be operational during the start of the HL-LHC.
 These centers are more capable of processing larger and larger volumes of data; this means the
 workloads that will run on these machines will evolve. HPCs will be capable of producing a
 large volume of simulated data. [Section 6.12]

 • SuperCDMS SNOLAB’s raw data, in compressed Maximum Integrated Data Acquisition
 System (MIDAS) format, will be processed at SLAC, and the reconstructed output data, in
 ROOT format, can be directly used for data analyses. Collaborators will access and analyze
 processed data stored at SLAC using local computing resources. The data will also be
 transferred from SLAC to Fermilab, where they will be stored on tape for additional backup.
 Simulated data are generated at Texas A&M, transferred to SLAC, and then transferred to
 Fermilab for tape backup and to other sites as needed. [Section 6.13]

 • Currently, a new data analysis and computing center is being developed at the University of
 Hawaii at Mānoa to support AMS. This will be the first computing and analysis center on US
 soil dedicated exclusively to AMS data. About 20,000 CPU cores and 10 PB of data storage will
 be employed for AMS data production, analysis, MC simulations, and archiving. [Section 6.14]

4.5 Remote Collaboration and Operational Requirements
 • Removing the need to worry about data locality allows researchers focused on developing
 cosmological simulation to invest more time on the science, versus spending energy in activities
 to stage data and allocate technology resources. It also prevents half-measures being used today
 to create mechanisms to perform analysis on partial data sets, or adopt streaming approaches
 that are not always successful on some of the larger computational resources not designed to
 support that mode of operation. [Section 6.1], [Section 8]

 • Data movement of cosmological simulation data between facilities is not a critical problem, but
 broad access for the user community remains challenging. Simplifying access with updated
 portal software, or tools like Globus, has improved data mobility. The next step is to combine
 this with dynamic access to computing resources. [Section 6.1]

 • The ratio of the cosmological simulation user community to the size of the simulation groups
 will increase as the role of simulations advances; dataflow patterns will likely become more
 diverse, and pressure will increase on data-transfer facilities that serve the resulting simulation
 outputs. Although the main focus is the continental US, the geographical locations of the
 endpoints are worldwide. The diversity of endpoints and the number of geographical locations
 is expected to grow significantly. [Section 6.1]

 • DESI computing is done using interactive computing methods at NERSC, namely Jupyter
 Notebooks. DESI has considered moving to more widely available computing options not tied
 to a single facility, such as a cloud platform (like those that the Rubin Observatory has adopted);
 a core concern lies in the user community, however, who are slow to adopt new approaches to
 computing and are making do with legacy tools for a lot of the analysis process. Investment into
 a new system halfway through an experiment is not feasible. [Section 6.2], [Section 8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 36

 • The primary data access mode for DESI is for collaborators to login to NERSC directly, and
 perform work at the location of the data. Collaborators can download a subset of data for
 processing at local institutions for analysis. Public (non-collaborator) access is only through
 downloads from NERSC, or through Jupyter servers at the NOIRLab Astro Data Lab, which
 host a subset of the public DESI data. Many collaborators have expressed a preference for
 downloading subsets of data to use locally; however, DESI lacks developed tools for easy
 management of that remote analysis workflow. This is currently achieved through ad hoc
 downloads with Globus, scp, or https. [Section 6.2]

 • The USDF will provide raw and processed data to Rubin Observatory authorized users,
 including DESC, and other science collaborations investigating dark energy in other
 participating countries. The USDF will distribute data to one or more data access centers in
 Europe and elsewhere. The scope of these centers and their reliance on the USDF is currently
 being worked out. It is worth noting that the data volume of an annual release is very significant,
 with just the catalogs of detected objects beginning at PB-scale. [Section 6.3]

 • All the Rubin collaborations, as well as independent scientists, will access and analyze data
 through either the hybrid cloud-based US DAC (cloud-based RSP and USDF back-end data
 services) or IDACs operated by in-kind contributor communities. [Section 6.3]

 • The RSP is a set of web applications and services that will be used by the data rights community
 to access, visualize, interact with, and analyze Rubin Observatory data. The RSP is being
 designed to be simple enough to engage general users and flexible enough to meet the needs of
 experienced users. Data will be exposed to users through the web portal (interactive use cases),
 the Jupyter Notebook interface (custom user use cases), and machine-accessible application
 program interfaces (APIs; remote tools/analyses use cases). [Section 6.3]

 • DESC’s current analysis model involves bringing collaborators to deploy their analyses at
 NERSC to run at scale and access collaboration data products. DESC is planning to expand
 these capabilities and has had successful tests and large campaigns at the UK and France data
 facilities for Rubin, though details for securing these resources for DESC science purposes
 are being settled. These resources could potentially be used for DESC workflows that require
 Rubin imaging products available at these sites. [Section 6.4]

 • DESC transfers have largely been via HTTP, rsync, and Globus for data sets moving from
 NERSC to and from collaboration sites. DESC will explore in this period the use of Rucio over
 FTS following the steps of the Rubin project for SLAC-to-NERSC transfers, and
 possibly for its own purposes in interactions with IDACs. DESC is currently using Parsl for
 workflow management of image reprocessing tasks as well as certain simulation and analysis
 workflows. [Section 6.4]

 • CMS applications and the infrastructure that distributes and launches them support multiple
 types of data access: [Section 6.10]

 ° Traditional top-down data placement at Tier-1 and Tier-2 centers combined with
 applications specifying the dataset they need, and being automatically routed and executed
 at the sites that have it.

 ° CMS supports streaming data access to any data on disk across the WLCG facilities from
 any location with an internet connection at any time. This is called AAA, for “any data,
 anytime, anywhere” within CMS.

 ° Bottom-up data placement, as is implicit in caching. Here the applications are routed to
 sites with caches, applications access the cache locally, and cache misses are handled by the
 CMS XRootD data federation.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 37

4.6 Multifacility Computational Workflows
 • The data products generated by simulation groups can be created at any number of DOE-or
 NSF-funded HPC facilities, or other institutions, with sufficient resources to execute and store
 simulation codes. These data products are used “downstream” by many users, who are members
 of science working groups in cosmological surveys and experiments. A common use pattern is to
 build a mock survey from the simulation data, then perform a clustering analysis on that survey,
 potentially using multiple facilities for computation and storage. [Section 6.1]

 • DESI data from KPNO are transferred in 10-minute intervals to NERSC using rsync. This
 rsync tool is not known for high performance; however, the cadence of the experiment dictates
 that nightly data collection is less than 100 GB and must reach NERSC via network that is
 limited to 1 Gbps between the telescopes at KPNO and the base station; use of more advanced
 tools will not improve the overall process of science. [Section 6.2]

 • DESI is fundamentally a multisite experiment, with data from a telescope in Arizona (KPNO),
 a primary computing center in California (NERSC), and a worldwide collaboration of scientists.
 DESI is currently limited in its ability to utilize non-NERSC DOE computing facilities for a
 variety of reasons, including: [Section 6.2]

 ° The ability to manage accounts for hundreds of users across different sites .

 ° Creating a system to synchronize PB-scale datasets of millions of files between
 multiple sites.

 • Nightly data from the Rubin Observatory are accumulated and processed with science pipelines
 at the USDF as well as partner data facilities in France and the UK, producing deep stacked
 images and source catalogs. These “annual data-release” products are served to the user
 community via an RSP hosted in Google Cloud and backed by data-access services hosted at
 the USDF. Rubin expects a significant amount of data will be moved in bulk to other analysis
 facilities. Data will be moved in conjunction with the distributed data-release processing efforts.
           [Section 6.3]

 • Rubin includes a program of in-kind contributions from international participant communities,
 some of which take the form of IDACs. Large amounts of data will be moved to other
 computing facilities to support custom analysis by large science collaborations (e.g., DESC);
 this will likely amount to the mirroring of a significant fraction of each annual data release from
 SLAC to NERSC. Additional mirroring efforts to support science analysis may be initiated for
 centers such as the ALCF and the TACC. Rubin anticipates a key role for ESnet in supporting
 these data transfers. [Section 6.3]

 • DESC’s primary data source is the Rubin USDF at SLAC. Workflows will primarily involve
 heterogeneous analysis operations over either the processed data products from the alert
 stream of transient events, or the data set extracted from the accumulated images and catalogs.
 Nominally, most of DESC’s computing will take place at NERSC. As the survey proceeds,
 DESC will likely need to obtain additional resources elsewhere through specific programs or
 through international collaborations. [Section 6.4]

 • The anticipated start of operations at the Rubin Observatory is FY25Q4. In this period DESC
 expects to bulk download from the primary data source (USDF at SLAC) to NERSC the
 released datasets corresponding to the commissioning and science verification periods. The
 specifics of the data set sizes, files, etc. are uncertain due to the nature of these pre-operations’
 activities and final scope. DESC expects the resulting data size will be of a similar size as
 Rubin’s recent data preview, and of the order of 10 TB of catalogs, with the possibility of
 transferring up to 1–2 PB of imaging data. DESC’s main computing resource will continue to be
 NERSC. [Section 6.4]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 38

 • CMB-S4 raw data will be archived at NERSC and ALCF, and a subset of recent data will be
 stored on disk. Daily data-quality statistics and maps will be produced at NERSC, ALCF, NSF
 ACCESS centers, and possibly FABRIC. Bulk reprocessing will be performed at NERSC,
 ALCF, and NSF ACCESS centers. Simulated data will be generated at NERSC and ALCF and
 typically reduced to maps to avoid I/O and storage overheads. In both cases, the resulting maps
 will be stored on disk and archived at NERSC and ALCF. Map-level data will be analyzed at
 NERSC and on local compute resources across the collaboration. Published data (primarily
 maps and derived scientific data) will be made available to the scientific community at NERSC
 and Legacy Archive for Microwave Background Data Analysis (LAMBDA) located at the NASA
 Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC). The raw data and the software used to characterize and
 reduce them will also be made available to the scientific community at NERSC. [Section 6.5]

 • During the CMB-S4 construction phase, all the significant data will be simulated. Simulations
 will be run at NERSC or ALCF, and the data copied between them, peaking at O(10) PB in
 2029. Reductions to maps will be run at NERSC, ALCF, NSF ACCESS centers, and possibly
 FABRIC. Maps will be made available to the collaboration at NERSC, with the bulk of the
 analyses performed there. Small amounts of data may be moved to collaborators’ local resources
 for analysis. [Section 6.5]

 • Mu2e will utilize most of the existing computational and storage resources at Fermilab during
 production, but has used several DOE HPC facilities (i.e., ALCF and NERSC in particular)
 during simulation construction. Currently the project produces on the order of hundreds of TB
 of simulation output per year using OSG-connected resources at Fermilab, the HPC facilities,
 and other collaboration sites. [Section 6.6], [Section 8]

 • Mu2e expects to use resources at several DOE-supported sites. At Fermilab Mu2e will use
 local interactive machines provided by the lab, Fermigrid, the Fermilab Elastic Analysis
 Facility, and the data storage resources at Fermilab. Mu2e has demonstrated the ability to use
 big CPU cycles at HPC centers, and does not foresee a need for significant GPU resources
 currently. [Section 6.6]

 • SBN currently uses the Polaris supercomputer facility at ANL in addition to computing
 resources at Fermilab. Globus-based transfers of SBND neutrino data to ANL are up and
 running, and sustained access to Polaris over the next few years for ongoing data processing
 will be needed to ensure that physics results can be obtained with maximum efficiency. SBN is
 also investigating whether other DOE SC user facilities, such as NERSC, may provide unique
 advantages that could complement the present workflows mentioned previously. [Section 6.8]

 • DUNE expects to incorporate the use of HPC centers, like Perlmutter at NERSC, for
 performing simulation and data reconstruction general processing on the demonstrator data, as
 well as for executing dedicated AI/ML processing workflows. [Section 6.8]

 • During the DUNE Prototyping phase, prototype detectors running at CERN and Fermilab
 send their data to DUNE storage sites worldwide. As more and more services come online at
 the DUNE Far site (SURF), data will begin to flow from SURF in South Dakota to Fermilab
 and onward to DUNE collaboration sites worldwide for additional processing. When the first
 far detector module is operational in mid-2029, supernova data will need to be transferred in
 real-time from SURF to US HPCs for fast turnaround processing. [Section 6.8]

 • The primary data-related resource constraint for DUNE deals with the supernova use case;
 the data from South Dakota must be transmitted to DOE HPC facilities in a matter of hours,
 and then be in a place where they can be easily accessed by the job processing software. Once
 the first far detector of DUNE is online, currently estimated to be 2029, supernova triggers are
 expected regularly, albeit some may be false alarms; the estimate is currently one per month.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 39

 DUNE will require a set of machines fast enough to source and sink the data, and a distributed
 file system to make it accessible to the computational jobs. [Section 6.8]

 • The US ATLAS Tier-1 is hosted at BNL’s Scientific Data and Computing Center (SDDC). The
 ATLAS connection to ESnet is shared with other programs hosted at the SDCC. The US Tier-1
 is the largest of the ATLAS experiment: it represents about 25% of the computing resources of
 ATLAS at Tier-1s. [Section 6.9]

 • Four ATLAS Tier-2 centers are in the US: Northeast Tier-2 (NET2), Great Lakes Tier-2
 (AGLT2), Midwest Tier-2 (MWT2), and Southwest Tier-2 (SWT2). These centers are used for
 all distributed production and user analysis workloads. Each Tier-2 center consists of multiple
 university-based clusters. In 2023 to 2024 ATLAS also added a new Tier-2 outside the US that
 contributes to the US ATLAS cloud. This site (TW-FTT) is derived from the former Tier-1 site
 in Taiwan. ESnet has helped to provide connectivity for this new site into LHCONE. However,
 this site has limited bandwidth (3 Gbps) and is only running tasks that are not data intensive.
           [Section 6.9]

 • Two ATLAS Analysis Facilities (AFs) are currently located at DOE national laboratories (BNL
 and SLAC). A third AF has been set up and is operational at University of Chicago. The data
 accessing model at these AFs includes both Rucio-managed data transfers to the AFs and using
 XCache to access ATLAS data remotely. [Section 6.9]

 • Having reliable mechanisms to transfer data into HPC facilities from the CMS Tier-1 and
 Tier-2 centers is of growing importance. HPCs are different from other resources used by CMS
 primarily because they provide significant compute (CPU and GPU) resources but very limited
 disk resources, and because network access to or from HPC compute nodes is typically limited
 or not allowed. The broader LHC community has considered how to best utilize these resources
 within operational constraints. Unlike most HPC users, CMS cannot concentrate its efforts on
 using one or a handful of HPC facilities, but is instead asked to use HPC facilities worldwide.
 Network access and data management are important aspects of this. [Section 6.10]

4.7 Networking for Local and Wide-Area Data Mobility
 • The network speeds between major DOE HPC centers are not a limitation for cosmological
 simulation, and transferring PB-sized data sets is effectively routine. The data set sizes are
 expected to increase in the coming years, but will be within the capabilities of ESnet and the
 DOE HPC resources. [Section 6.1]

 • DESI’s infrastructure relies on two major components linked via network infrastructure: KPNO
 and NERSC. A number of other instruments are at the KPNO facility, and all share a common 1
 Gbps-capable network connection from the summit to a base station. A larger 10 Gbps network
 then links the base station to the rest of the R&E community. Each of these connections has a
 different operator, and each has experienced trouble in the past. Natural disasters (e.g., wildfire)
 have severed connectivity, and bandwidth limitations imply that all scientific operations must
 share the common connection fairly. This can limit productivity, given there is no back-up option,
 which can impact real-time requirements. DESI has ways to buffer data, but is otherwise stalled
 without alternative paths. LEO satellites have been used for some back-up capability in the past,
 but this is not a complete solution to support DESI. [Section 6.2], [Section 8]

 • International networking has a role in supporting Rubin Observatory production processes.
 Annual data releases will be computed at the USDF, and at the satellite computing facilities
 in France and the UK. This generates a need for networking to support continuous data
 production, in addition to distribution of data for scientific data analysis. By agreement,
 CC-IN2P3 is the responsible institution for arranging connectivity between CC-IN2P3 and the
           US. [Section 6.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 40

 • A memorandum of agreement (MOA) has been established between IN2P3, the LSST
 Corporation (LSSTC), the Rubin Observatory, and the University of Illinois for the
 IN2P3 Computing Center (CC-IN2P3) in Lyon, France to provide 40% of the computing
 capacity needed for annual data-release processing during LSST operations and to host a
 complete backup of the Rubin Observatory data archive. The MOA requires that France will
 provide the TA network connectivity to ESnet needed to support data transport to and from
           CC-IN2P3. [Section 6.3]

 • The Rubin Observatory UK Data Facility (UKDF) will be a distributed entity. Its computing
 hardware will be provisioned through Institute for Research and Innovation in Software for
 High Energy Physics (IRIS), a national organization providing computing resources for projects
 funded by the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC). RIS sites are well integrated
 into national and international networks, for the transfer of LHC and other data, and have
 a wealth of experience supporting a wide range of international science collaborations. The
 UKDF will be hosted by the University of Edinburgh. [Section 6.3]

 • The required peak bandwidth from the Rubin Observatory Base Facility in La Serena to the
 USDF is established by the need to transfer the images for prompt processing. For the USDF
 to release alerts of transient and variable sources within 60 seconds of image readout from the
 camera electronics, seven seconds of this time budget is allocated to data transfer, including
 compression/decompression. Two seconds of that budget is in the Summit to Base Facility
 transfer, and the other five seconds is in the Base Facility to Archive Transfer and compression/
 decompression. This equates to a minimum of 40 Gbps bandwidth. [Section 6.3]

 • DESC’s major data movement activity, occurring on a yearly basis, is a bulk data download
 from SLAC to NERSC. The network infrastructure in place between the facilities (via ESnet)
 is sufficient to handle the expected volume of data, and SLAC is in parallel moving to larger
 400 Gbps capabilities to support other efforts. Since this is not a real-time operation, there is no
 time limit (or performance expectation) for transfer. [Section 6.4], [Section 8]

 • DESC is open to the idea of working on structured data challenges, as other communities have
 done in the past. This could involve simulation data to start, and characterize performance
 between SLAC, NERSC, and the IDACs. Poor performance to some sites in the EU from
 NERSC has been observed, but given this is not a part of the critical path of science, it is a
 lower priority for DESC to address. [Section 6.4], [Section 8]

 • CMB-S4 will leverage networking resources that exist in Chile today. The Simons
 Observatory (SO)8 and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA)9 invested
 heavily into the networking infrastructure over prior years, and have a clean fast path to
 national and international computing resources. Networking to support experimentation
 includes multiple strands of fiber optic cables, as well as a perfSONAR monitoring
 infrastructure. A 10 Gbps dedicated fiber link from the site, to the ALMA, is being installed
 by Simons Observatory currently and already receives support from ESnet to ensure global
 connectivity. ESnet will continue to work with CMB-S4 on networking and the overlap with
 the existing projects. [Section 6.5], [Section 8]

 • Mu2e networking needs are relatively straightforward; a maximum of 10 Gbps may be required
 to handle intensive times of activity to support external computing needs. Given that most of
 the computation and storage is allocated to Fermilab, and connectivity to other WLCG sites
 will follow the same patterns as the LHC computation, additional networking support is not
 currently required. [Section 6.6], [Section 8]

9 https://www.almaobservatory.org/en/about-alma/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 41

 • Belle II, hosted by KEK Japan, relies on a similar software infrastructure and grid-computing
 model to that of the LHC experiments, and has converted to use Rucio as a data management
 platform. Because of this sharing of infrastructure, networking and data movement work well
 for the current volumes. International connectivity is provided by partners Science Information
 NETwork (SINET)10 and TransPAC11, via multiple direct and indirect paths. Belle II also
 participates in the LHCONE network to enable consistent performance between facilities.
 [Section 6.7], [Section 8]

 • The BNL network perimeter has two diverse 800 Gbps (2 x 400 Gbps) circuits that peer with
 ESnet routers. These circuits are utilized by all scientific and administrative communities at
 BNL. All traffic to and from BNL flows through either of these circuits. The BNL Network
 Perimeter on average ingests and egresses between 10 and 15 PB of data monthly. [Section 6.7]

 • DUNE relies heavily on Fermilab networking for a variety of tasks, including data archiving,
 replication, and batch processing. Two geographically diverse 100 Gbps links between the far
 detector complex at SURF and Fermilab are in the process of being acquired to provide WAN
 connectivity for the far detector. The target deployment date for these links is 2027. DUNE is
 approved for use of LHCONE, and has been making use of LHCONE and LHCOPN at certain
 grid sites that also have an LHC presence. [Section 6.8]

 • ATLAS data volumes can average 5 PB a day, with volumes exceeding this during busy periods
 when the LHC is in full operation. The Tier-1 and Tier-2s within the US can see data flows of
 tens to hundreds of Gbps on a routine basis. Most are connected via 100 Gbps or 400 Gbps
 diverse connections to ESnet, or regional networking providers. BNL (the US ATLAS Tier-1)
 sees most of this traffic coming directly from CERN, then distributing outward toward other
 Tier-2s at US universities. All US Tier-2 sites are strongly encouraged to provide at least
 100 Gbps connectivity, preferably with resilience. The intent is to have multiple 400 Gbps
 connectivity for each Tier-2 by the time HL-LHC starts. [Section 6.9], [Section 8]

 • ESnet will investigate ways to integrate resources into LHCONE at non-LHC-affiliated sites.
 DOE HPC centers (e.g., NERSC) and AFs (e.g., SLAC) could benefit from being connected to
 better identify and prioritize traffic. [Section 6.9], [Section 8]

 • Fermilab’s WAN architecture utilizes LHCOPN connectivity to support movement of raw data
 from the T0 (CERN), as well as production data movement with some of the other CMS T1s. In
 terms of aggregate WAN capacity out of the site, Fermilab currently has provisioned 2.4 Tb/s of
 link capacity to ESnet, via geographically diverse connections. A link aggregation group (LAG)
 of four 400 Gbps links is used to support the science data network paths, including LHCOPN
 and LHCONE. A second 2 x 400 Gbps LAG supports Fermilab’s general internet traffic, which
 includes some portion of science traffic. [Section 6.10]

 • Much of the LAN and WAN networking infrastructure to and within a CMS Tier-2 site has been
 an institutional contribution to the US CMS Operations Program, i.e., it has not for the most
 part been directly funded by the program. All CMS Tier-2s connect to the LHCONE at least
 100 Gbps, through partnership with regional networking infrastructure. In some cases, a Tier-2
 facility may have multiple connections either as a backup, or for active use. [Section 6.10]

 • The LHC community is currently a major user of the ESnet TA network links. Activities
 including the archival of raw data, initial copies of analysis data samples, and user-derived data
 sets using CERN or other non-US facilities are clear use cases for TA network usage. LHC
 tools do not prioritize site proximity (in the networking sense) when scheduling data transfers.
 Streaming data across the TA link is allowed (if discouraged). [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]
