High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 42

 • Networking has been fundamental to the success of ATLAS and CMS computing to date,
 enabling the exploitation of globally distributed resources for computationally limited science.
 This will remain the case to meet the budget-constrained computing challenges of HL-LHC.
 Strategies for HL-LHC computing are based on extensive use of powerful networks to reduce
 data replication by streaming over the network, and consolidating distributed resources into
 cohesive virtual federations such as data lakes. HL-LHC data and processing scales are large
 enough that optimizing for efficient bandwidth use will be essential. The ability to mark
 network packets to identify sources of traffic, and to route traffic to control speed and cost, may
 become vital. [Section 6.12]

 • As a rough guide as to the network bandwidth that facilities in US CMS will require in the
 HL-LHC era for the purpose of reconstructing the raw data and producing corresponding
 simulation datasets, one can take the following estimate. From the 250 PB of raw data collected
 per year, about 40% (e.g., 100 PB) is expected to be reconstructed in the US. That these
 large-scale reconstruction campaigns take approximately 10 weeks is desired, implying a data
 input rate to processing facilities of 10 PB/week, and an output rate of 4 PB/week. In parallel,
 simulation production campaigns will be executed continuously throughout the year, producing
 another 40% of the total 240 PB of output data (e.g., 96 PB) to be persisted on tape and/or
 disk storage within the US. In total, these workflows will require a sustained rate of up to 130
 Gbps between processing and storage facilities. To account for burst traffic, and to support data
 analysis workloads at AFs discussed later, it is desired that all major processing facilities, namely
 the Fermilab Tier-1 and US CMS Tier-2 centers, are provisioned to 400 Gbps. [Section 6.12]

 • At present, it is assumed that the general LHC Tier-2 network requirements as specified
 previously will be sufficient to support AFs at the Tier-2s. A user at an AF may expect to process
 a year’s worth of MiniAOD data and simulation (27 PB) in a timescale of a week. If the data are
 not cached at the AF, that amounts to a sustained 400 Gbps network load from the data origin
 site. In practice, it is unlikely a user would read the entirety of the data catalog, though the exact
 fraction will vary significantly depending on the analysis goals. [Section 6.12]

 • Global R&E network use will have different characteristics on the timescale of the HL-LHC,
 compared to the situation the WLCG experienced in Runs 1, 2, and 3. Specifically, the
 experiments foresee other science domains (astronomy, biology, engineering, and others)
 becoming global network users at scales equaling or exceeding the LHC users. In such an
 environment, it is not wise to assume the experiments can continue to treat the network as an
 infinite resource. The LHC community must explore options for effectively operating within a
 bandwidth constrained environment. [Section 6.12]

 • The network link that supports SNOLAB from the underground portion to the surface is made
 of 2 x 10 Gbps aggregate links shared by about 10 experiments. Only ~0.2% is expected to be
 needed by SuperCDMS during peak usage. From the surface, the data are copied to SLAC
 through the SNOLAB network link to the Ontario Research and Innovation Optical Network
 (ORION) of 1 Gbps. From there, ESnet routes become available. SNOLAB is looking into
 upgrading the outgoing bandwidth to 10 Gbps. [Section 6.13]

 • NERSC features 1 Tbps aggregate bandwidth to ESNET via 2 x 400 Gbps links and 2 x 100
 Gbps links. NERSC will be expanding to a 4 x 400 Gbps architecture in future years, in addition
 to considering a migration to 800 Gbps technology. [Section 7.1]

 • ORNL has two 400 Gbit connections to ESnet and OLCF will have two 400 Gbps connections
 to the Information Technology Services Directorate (ITSD) of ORNL. Additionally, a 100 Gbps
 dedicated WAN connection is between Defiant, an HPC cluster on the Advanced Computing
 Ecosystem (ACE) testbed, and the ESnet testbed for IRI activities. [Section 7.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 43

 • The WLCG recommendation for large Tier-1s, such as Fermilab, at HL-LHC startup is a
 minimum of 1 Tb/s. Fermilab is currently provisioned at 1.6 Tbps for science traffic and 800
 Gbps for general-purpose traffic. The latter does include the fraction of Fermilab’s science not
 carried via the science networks. This configuration is expected to be adequate to satisfy the
 currently known requirements for 2024 to 2028. If needed, additional 400G connections can be
 added to the existing LAG interfaces. Switching to 800G Ethernet technology might become
 justifiable in 2028 to 2030. [Section 7.4]

 • The DUNE experiment extends across two facilities ~1,300km apart. One site is Fermilab in
 Batavia, Illinois, and the second site, the far detector (FD) location, is SURF, in Lead, South
 Dakota. The Fermilab-managed perimeter network will provide connectivity for the DUNE
 FD site to Fermilab. Sufficient capacity to move ~30 PB of science data annually is required.
 The perimeter network equipment will reside in two geographically diverse buildings at SURF:
 the Ross Dry Building and the Yates Administration Building. Each building has a shaft that
 provides access to the underground facilities at the 4,850 ft level (4850L). WAN connectivity is
 to be provided and managed by ESnet. [Section 7.4]

 • The BNL Network Perimeter consists of two redundant routers that support interface speeds
 of 10 GbE, 40 GbE, 100 GbE, and 400 GbE. These routers are split between BNL’s two data
 centers. Each BNL router connects to a local ESnet router at 800 Gbps (2 x 400 GbE) totaling
 1.6 Tbps of Internet/WAN connectivity. Each 800 Gbps circuit is utilized by all scientific and
 administrative communities at BNL: all data traffic to and from BNL flows through either of
 these circuits. To support the large data flows to and from A Toroidal LHC ApparatuS (US
 ATLAS) resources, BNL offsets the LHCOPN and LHCONE primary circuits so each service
 in theory could transfer 800 Gbps of data. [Section 7.5]

 • The SLAC networking core currently operates at multiple 100 GbE for connected enclaves
 and groups. The networking core of S3DF operates at 100 GbE, with a pair of 2 x 100 GbE links
 to the SLAC core. SLAC connects to ESnet via two pairs of 100 GbE links; these
 link pairs typically operate as primary/secondary. No general load balancing or dual use of the
 links occurs. One pair of the SLAC/ESnet connections is dedicated for use by the Rubin
 Observatory Virtual Routed Network (Rubin Long-Haul Network, LHN) over ESnet. Within
 the next two years, SLAC expects to augment the SLAC/ESnet connections with a pair of 400
 GbE links. [Section 7.6]

 • External network connectivity to ANL is provided by ESnet, Metropolitan Research and
 Education Network (MREN), Internet2, and Internet2 Peering Exchange (I2PX). ESnet
 has optical transport and routers deployed on the ANL campus in a redundant configuration
 supporting up to 400 gigabits per second (Gbps) connections. The connections to MREN are 2 x
 100 Gbps. The border routers are connected to each other with 4 x 100 Gbps connections. The
 connections to the campus core network are 2 x 40 Gbps and 40 Gbps to the perimeter firewall.
 By the end of FY25, the perimeter firewall will be replaced with a Palo Alto PA-5450 with 100
 Gbps connectivity. [Section 7.7]

4.8 Emerging Needs
 • Commercial cloud resources are an intriguing addition to the possible cosmology simulation
 workflow structure. While the cost of using these resources remains high, augmenting existing
 resources during periods of heavy use and justifying the increased expenditure may be possible.
 One could imagine a situation where the use of AI/ML frameworks becomes an instantaneous
 source of large-scale data; if difficulty exists in allocating local computational and storage
 resources to meet the demand, these workflows may need to be integrated with commercial
 cloud infrastructure that can expand as needed. [Section 6.1], [Section 8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 44

 • Future cosmological simulation data sets may be too large to store locally by individual research
 groups, necessitating the use of streaming workflows developed to facilitate on-the-fly analysis;
 use of that new paradigm may lead to repeated downloads and analyses. This situation may be
 exacerbated as AI/ML frameworks can be essentially instantaneous sources of large-scale data;
 at the same time this difficulty could be ameliorated if only the models were sent over and local
 computational and storage resources were sufficient to meet the demand. In the future, these
 workflows could be integrated with commercial cloud infrastructure. [Section 6.1]

 • Cosmological simulation resource usage becomes a question of latency, bandwidth, amount of
 associated computing, and cost for computing, data transfer, and storage. Primarily due to cost
 issues with commercial clouds, the cosmological simulation community does not see this option
 as being viable currently, but the situation could change very quickly. Initial tests with cloud
 vendors are expected in the coming years to address some aspects of the experimental workflow.
 An anticipated advantage is the ability to make data available, with server-side compute, while
 placing the cost of using the data onto the end user, who may be supported by a different
 funding agency/source or country. Hybrid-cloud solutions that bridge to DOE facilities could be
 very beneficial, as other HEP experiments like Rubin have explored. [Section 6.1]

 • A possible disruptive element for cosmological simulation is the role of AI/ML in low-level
 simulation and analysis code, as well as at the catalog-analysis level. Since such
 techniques are typically very data intensive, the associated network requirements could
 conceivably be significant, especially if compute resources are not local to where the data are
 available. [Section 6.1]

 • DESI does not currently use cloud services for data processing or serving core data products.
 Exploratory work for sharing DESI data through the Amazon Open Data program has occurred,
 though this is not used by the collaboration itself. There has been interest in deploying the
 data-processing pipeline on Amazon Web Services (AWS) as an alternate site to be used during
 outages of the primary computing resource; data transfer and hosting costs make this option
 prohibitive. [Section 6.2]

 • DESI makes some use of AI/ML for its data-processing pipeline through standard methods that
 do not require any special resources. More active cutting-edge work is happening on using AI/
 ML for DESI science analyses, particularly using generative AI to create simulated datasets
 faster than traditional simulations. This experimentation uses standard toolkits available via
 NERSC’s Perlmutter, and does not require additional hardware or software support. [Section 6.2]

 • DESI has used emerging LEO satellites, such as Starlink, at the remote telescope site as a
 back-up connection for when the primary Internet is down. This was especially critical in 2022
 after a wildfire resulted in a multi-month outage of the fiber optic connection to the mountain.
 The LEO connection was sufficient for command and control of the telescope, but was not
 sufficient for transferring observational data, which required driving hard disks up and down
 the mountain. [Section 6.2]

 • Currently the Rubin Data Management system does not make heavy use of AI/ML for data
 production or distribution. Members of the scientific community are expected to deploy their
 own AI/ML techniques in analysis of Rubin’s scientific data products for modeling, inference,
 and anomaly detection. This expectation is a major driver for bulk download capabilities for
 Rubin data products, and may also influence the development roadmap for Rubin-supported
 analysis platforms on five-year timescales. Multiple community alert brokers currently provide
 users with AI/ML capabilities for classification and anomaly detection. [Section 6.3]

 • DESC has no concrete plans for using any DESC-specific cloud applications. Initial
 engagement by DESC scientists will happen in the US DAC, through the RSP. [Section 6.4]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 45

 • Due to the large variety of science applications and multiple approaches and stages of DESC’s
 analyses, ML will be applied in many instances of large-scale computation (CPU and GPU) at
 NERSC. [Section 6.4]

 • CMB-S4 has flexibility in how it approaches aspects of computing and networking. The project
 will explore all available options for the software used in data management, as well as available
 computational resources (HPC, grid, or cloud). [Section 6.5], [Section 8]

 • CMB-S4 has no plans to purchase dedicated AI/ML hardware or services. Possible applications
 of ML exist in areas of low-level data cleaning (detection of classes of “glitches” in the data), and
 for improvements in observing strategies / planning. In both cases the evaluation of such models
 is cheap, and model training can be performed at existing centers such as NERSC. [Section 6.5]

 • The CMB-S4 project has no intention of using WiFi, cellular, or satellite connectivity at
 the site in Chile. Some of this equipment can generate a request for information (RFI) that
 impacts science measurements. CMB-S4 may make use of an existing dedicated point-to-point
 microwave link to the nearby town. This link has been shown not to interfere with existing
 experiments and is a useful back-up connection for remote access. [Section 6.5]

 • New features for DUNE in two to five years related to networking are related to further use
 of HPC centers, like Polaris at ANL or Perlmutter at NERSC, for performing simulation and
 data reconstruction general processing, as well as for executing dedicated AI/ML processing
 workflows. This could amount to a sustained average rate of >1 TB/hr to and from that facility
 over a production campaign period (~60 days). Similarly, transfers of dedicated data formats for
 AI/ML processing to SLAC (temporary location) and then the DOE HPC centers (where the
 workflow is run) will also require approximately a rate of 1 TB/hr. [Section 6.8]

 • DUNE has followed the strategic direction of Fermilab in using cloud approaches only for those
 new hardware types which DUNE cannot quickly acquire. Examples include tests of
 inference servers on Triton (e.g., a commercial entity), NERSC Perlmutter as part of the
 ongoing SONIC project, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP). With one of the above tests with
 compute workers at Fermilab and the inference server at Google cloud in Iowa, DUNE was
 able to saturate the Fermilab general off-site network bandwidth, which at the time was limited
           to 100 Gbps. [Section 6.8]

 • DUNE has several scientists who are actively exploring ML use in reconstruction analysis.
 Currently, most of them run locally on Fermilab’s Elastic Analysis Facility. [Section 6.8]

 • Google Cloud and AWS computing services have been successfully integrated within the
 ATLAS workflow and data management systems PanDA and Rucio. The solutions may be
 considered in the implementation of AFs for HL-LHC, with all the added values and
 services offered by the commercial cloud providers. In future work, data exports from cloud
 data centers to WLCG sites will have to be optimized, involving research network providers.
 In 2024 the Google Cloud is used for MC production processing as an extension of a
 US Tier-2 center. [Section 6.9]

 • ML is used in a wide range of applications in ATLAS, including physics analysis, simulation,
 and physics object identification. Models trained for classification and regression, as well as
 generative models, are core components of the software and analysis chain. Most models used
 by the collaboration are trained on private resources due to the modest resource requirements
 and satisfactory availability of institutional GPU resources. ATLAS does not expect any
 significant changes in network load or the distributed computing software stack design during
 the ongoing analysis of Run 3 data. [Section 6.9]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 46

 • Given the size, complexity, and fully distributed nature of ATLAS computing, all workflow and
 data distribution could eventually be optimized and managed with AI. [Section 6.9]

 • The use of in-network caching has had some impact on network use for the LHC community.
 Much of the R&D efforts in the recent years have been determining where caches may be
 beneficial for placement, how large they need to be to be effective, and what strategy should be
 used to store and replace data sets. Questions remain about deployment strategies to work out
 for both CMS and ATLAS. Regional caches were found to not be as effective (since the overlap
 of data use was not high enough), but caches within a facility, and ensuring that the workflow
 management tools know to check the caches, produced the most reliable results. The adoption
 and more widespread use of the NanoAOD format is anticipated to have some impact on cache
 performance over time. [Section 6.10], [Section 8]

 • CMS does not currently use cloud resources to any significant extent. Previous studies have
 shown them to be a more costly model than the owned-resource model that CMS currently
 relies on. A notable exception would be the case of needed resource bursts for either CPU or
 network. The resources available for either CPU or TA networking in the cloud far exceed those
 available to CMS. At this point, CMS tools are generally able to use cloud services, typically
 via infrastructure at one of the tiered sites, but CMS does not have plans to use cloud services
 extensively in the near or longer term. [Section 6.10]

 • CMS has an increasing use of AI/ML in its production workflows. Analysis use cases
 have evolved even more quickly with greater freedom to adopt new toolkits and approaches.
 Both the Fermilab Tier-1 and Tier-2 facilities have GPU capabilities for CMS use,
 and the CMS community also relies on national resources. CMS is also researching a dedicated
 AI/ML training facility (at Vanderbilt) in recognition that AI/ML brings two distinct use
 cases, training and inference, that both require substantial resources (but in differing
 access patterns). CMS expects to predominantly use on-site and HPC resources rather than
 commercial cloud. [Section 6.10]

 • Reliable networking can be used to reduce disk replica requirements either by using tape recall
 or caching. By the end of Run 4, a copy of the entire CMS MiniAOD will be around 100 PB. If
 10% of this is used during any given month in a caching system, one can estimate the need for
 10 PB/month of transfers to keep the cache up to date with the most recently used data. Cache
 network needs will be typically bursty because users read full data sets rather than just a file or
 two from one. Understanding and expanding caching use cases and needs are part of ongoing
 R&D. It is expected that investments into disk space at Tier-2s against network utilization
 will become more critical in the long term. Other forces may also push higher network
 requirements, such as how spinning disk technology evolves in terms of cost per terabyte and
 I/O capabilities relative to CMS needs. [Section 6.10]

 • ATLAS and CMS are exploring advanced techniques for improving data transfer and monitoring
 capabilities across the WLCG. New technologies such as SciTags and packet marking are being
 tested and deployed to enhance network monitoring, traffic differentiation, and optimized data
 flow across high-speed networks. The deployment of SciTags and packet marking is in progress
 across several sites, which will lead to better traffic differentiation and resource management
 across the network. [Section 6.11]

 • SENSE (SDN for End-to-End Networked Science at the Exascale) uses SDN to dynamically
 manage network paths, prioritize traffic, and provide optimized routing. This setup is ideal
 for data-intensive tasks, as it can allocate resources in real time based on network conditions
 and experimental priorities. Rucio, developed by CERN, complements SENSE by managing
 large-scale data distribution across the network. Its features include automated data replication,

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 47

 strategic data placement, and support for geographically distributed resources, which streamline
 the movement and availability of critical datasets. [Section 6.11]

 • Many of the LHC experiments have explored cloud services and are using them as part of
 their global set of resources. Two primary modes of operation are envisioned: a particular site
 contracts with a cloud provider and resources are (transparently) added as part of the site from
 their experiment’s perspective, and an alternative method where a new site is created within
 a cloud provider, utilizing the various provisioning, management, and resilient infrastructure
 available. While the first option has been used with varying degrees of success, the second is not
 yet feasible for several reasons: [Section 6.11]

 ° The entity setting up a site within a cloud provider needs to be able to control costs to make
 it feasible, but policies and tools are not usually available to allow them to do so.

 ° Egress charges from cloud providers are usually expensive and may vary depending upon
 where the egress goes.

 ° Connecting to resources like LHCONE is very challenging because of the acceptable use
 policy (AUP) requirement that all traffic from the advertised subnets for LHCONE must be
 LHC related.

 • During HL-LHC the tracking algorithms used in event reconstruction are expected to see
 increased use of GPUs. Parts of the events may need to be shipped to data centers (HPCs,
 cloud vendors, WLCG data centers) for GPU processing, with the results sent elsewhere for
 recombination with the data processed on CPU-only resources. Future DOE HPC machines
 are focusing on support for AI/ML, with large numbers of GPUs and other accelerators. ML
 training requires large amounts of data transferred into the HPCs for use during the training.
 This will have an impact on the WAN network, as data are transferred from WLCG data centers
 to HPCs in the US for ML training and inference. [Section 6.12]

 • The global infrastructure is currently relatively uniform, with approximately 70 compute
 and storage elements presenting an identical interface to CMS. The data distribution model
 proposed by WLCG for the HL-LHC is commonly referred to as the “data lake model.” This
 model envisions fewer regional entry points, allowing internal optimizations and potentially
 reducing the operational burden. Data transfer between two lakes is a top-down-controlled
 activity governed by Rucio and executed via FTS. Access to data from processing elements
 inside the lake is mediated either via caches or streaming directly from one of the data lake
 origins. [Section 6.12]

 • ESnet and the LHC experiments (ATLAS and CMS) have started an R&D project that makes
 use of in-network data caches operated by ESnet using XRootD software. The pilot project
 focuses on caching of PHYSLITE data products to see if the time to reach physics results can
 be shorted, and the overall network traffic reduced for data analysis (only used parts of data files
 cached and reused). [Section 6.12]

 • SuperCDMS SNOLAB will make minimal or no use of cloud storage. Only a few services will
 be cloud-based, including Slack and GitLab. [Section 6.13]

 • SLAC is building support for the execution of AI/ML workflows with substantial investment in
 GPU. The SuperCDMS SNOLAB reconstruction working group (WG) is looking into taking
 advantage of the GPUs for event reconstruction. TensorFlow is also used in some analyses.
 One use case is for datasets severely limited by noise coming from vibrations. With ML we can
 remove the noise effectively while saving the low-energy signal events, which are important for
 low-mass data management (DM) search. The same method can be used to predict the energy
 deposited in the crystals, which works well in low energies where other techniques do not
 perform well. [Section 6.13]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 48

 • AMS does not leverage any commercial cloud services for its computing or storage
 needs. [Section 6.14]

 • AMS does not require any connectivity to be provided by wireless or satellite connectivity,
 beyond its core networking use case that leverages TDRS. [Section 6.14]

 • For NERSC-10 and beyond, NERSC will consider incorporating “cloud” technologies that add
 significant value to the NERSC user community and are affordable. This approach to provide
 cloud-like services includes NERSC Spin, a container-based platform where users can build
 their own websites, API endpoints, databases, and other network services that can integrate
 with center networks and data storage systems. In the next two to five years, NERSC is
 exploring deeper hybridization of Spin with the HPC system itself, which will open possibilities
 for performing computational tasks in a more cloud-like environment. [Section 7.1]

 • OLCF anticipates more integration with outside clouds for certain applications. OLCF has been
 testing integration with things such as weights and biases; this is an ML/distribution layer (DL)
 analytics dashboard. The heavy computations happen on Frontier, but the analytics dashboard
 is off-site and integrated through API mechanisms. OLCF is surveying cloud resource
 performance for HPC workloads, particularly for large-scale leadership-class systems. Current
 constraints around data in the cloud play a large role in limiting its use, particularly cost. With
 IRI, the High-Performance Data Facility (HPDF),12 and Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence for
 Science, Security and Technology (FASST),13 things will continue to change and become more
 distributed. [Section 7.3]

4.9 IRI Responsiveness
 • All the factors that exacerbate the issue of long-term storage for cosmological simulation may
 not have a single solution, and may require a variety of approaches. If a single location cannot
 become the home for data sets, efforts must be made to unify a cataloging system to enable
 locality searches, despite the distributed nature of the data. [Section 6.1]

 • Long-term storage of large-scale cosmological simulation data remains a critical problem to
 address, as many of these data sets are connected to ASCR Leadership Computing Challenge
 (ALCC) and the Innovative and Novel Computational Impact on Theory and Experiment
 (INCITE) programs,14 which have finite lifetimes. The advent of the IRI program and HPDF
 facility should present a global solution to this problem, to be deterministic about the way
 that long-running simulation efforts can be cataloged, stored, and found by the global
 community. [Section 6.1]

 • An area of friction for a number of scientific efforts (e.g. DESC, and DESI in particular) remains
 the mechanisms used to manage identity and permissions for the large population of scientific
 users. A common problem is the management of credentials to access computation and storage
 across facilities (e.g., DOE HPC centers), and how these may differ from accounts used to
 manage other aspects of the scientific workflow (e.g., home institutional accounts). [Section 6.2],
 [Section 8]

12 https://www.hpdf.science/
13 https://www.energy.gov/fasst/
14 https://doeleadershipcomputing.org/about/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 49

 • The DESI data lifecycle involves all three IRI patterns: [Section 6.2]
 ° Time-sensitive analysis to detect operations problems and update the survey plan.

 ° Data integration–intensive work to combine PB-scale data from multiple other
 collaborations and funding agencies for analysis.

 ° Long-term campaigns to process data for the five-year DESI survey, with proposed
 extensions and follow-up programs through at least 2042.

 • The Rubin-LSST science enterprise exhibits all three IRI patterns to some degree: [Section 6.3]
 ° Time sensitive: Rubin images are transferred in near-real time from the Summit to the
 USDF, where they are promptly processed to generate alerts.

 ° Data integration intensive: Many Rubin science analyses will require extensive integration
 between multiple data sets both internal to Rubin (images, catalogs, light curves) and
 external (data from complementary surveys at other wavelengths, spectroscopic facilities,
 and space-based telescopes). This data integration is likely to involve a range of different
 AFs both within the DOE system (e.g., SLAC, NERSC, ALCF) and beyond.

 ° Long-term campaign: Rubin has a 10-year primary survey mission and a potentially longer
 horizon in an extended mission mode. Successful scientific operation over this horizon
 requires sustained access and integration between Rubin’s experimental-support computing
 facility at SLAC and the DESC analysis facility at NERSC.

 • Rubin operations employs a model of distributed data management and processing across
 multiple sites. The current baseline plan calls for using a combination of the Rucio software
 system to coordinate multisite data movement and the PanDA software system for orchestrating
 distributed processing jobs. This use case is highly aligned with the vision for multisite
 interoperability under IRI. [Section 6.3]

 • DESC sees a potential for certain workflows that are more compute intensive to branch out
 across multiple sites in the future. In the past, working across different facilities usually meant
 specific workflow setups tailored to the infrastructure/hardware available at each facility. The
 IRI vision will help overcome this hurdle and provide users with a very similar environment
 across facilities to ease moving across platforms. [Section 6.4]

 • DESC workflows are heterogeneous but primarily fall under two categories: [Section 6.4]
 ° The great majority (>90%) both in terms of compute and storage will correspond to long-
 term campaigns. These will include the processing and reprocessing of LSST data releases
 to extract data vectors, analyze systematics, model the signal, and infer cosmological
 parameters. These require sustained access to resources at scale over a longer time to
 accomplish a well-defined objective.

 ° Some of our workflows are time sensitive. These rely on the Rubin “alert stream,” or
 intermediary brokers, for astrophysical events and generate actions or outputs that need to
 be processed within some period.

 • CMB-S4 will leverage aspects of IRI including federated login and access across facilities, as
 well as tools for job submission and management that can span domains of operation. Ideally,
 these integrated tools would allow job management not only on HPC centers but also on HTC
 or Grid-computing resources. [Section 6.5]

 • Mu2e has one example of the time-sensitive IRI pattern. Mu2e plans to perform initial
 processing of data from the experiment within several hours of the data being taken. The time
 constraint is driven by the need to produce high-precision, high-statistics information sensitive
 to subtle effects below the sensitivity of the instruments themselves. [Section 6.6]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 50

 • DUNE exhibits all the IRI patterns in design and operation. The full DUNE near detector
 simulation and reconstruction stack has been run at NERSC Perlmutter, as well as many
 simulations for the DUNE FD. Patterns exhibited include: [Section 6.8]

 ° Time sensitive: The supernova pointing workflow will be time sensitive and requires the
 analysis of as much of 320 TB from the first two detector modules in the span of 4 hours
 or less.

 ° Data integration intensive: It will be necessary to bring data from the DUNE near and far
 detectors together into a common analysis format. This is an extremely I/O intensive job.

 ° Long-term campaign: DUNE intends to be taking data for at least two decades, and during
 that time our computing model calls for reconstructing all the data we have taken to date at
 least once a year.

 • The LHC experiments can benefit from IRI, especially if the DOE HPC centers and the newly
 awarded HPDF are seamlessly integrated into the existing HTC (grid) infrastructure. IRI would
 provide the opportunity to implement near real-time workflows for critical payloads, such as
 High-Level Trigger, which should produce results in a timely manner. IRI would benefit all
 HEP by providing a uniform interface to disparate resources in an easier to integrate with way,
 and to better fit the variety of HEP workflows. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]

 • The LHC experiments have proactively pursued opportunities at US HPC sites, and currently
 have many allocations available for use. Typical workflows run on these allocations are like
 the IRI concept of a long-term campaign, which relies on sustained access at scale. New HPC
 resources typically come with some, potentially substantial, work to set up given facility specific
 configurations and constraints. A common interface (or access requirements) across DOE HPC
 sites and models for sustained access are potential IRI benefits. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]

 • Globally, many funding agencies are responsible for both HPCs and the LHC’s WLCG
 experiments, and a natural outcome is to try to support WLCG needs via HPCs. As an example,
 Germany has consolidated many of its Tier-2 sites into a new HPC allocation. For the US, the
 DOE HPC facilities becoming “standardized” would be very beneficial, allowing collaborations
 to utilize resources without having to dedicate staff to operate on a bespoke basis. Without
 something like IRI driving this uniform interface, the experiments are also forced to engage
 with each HPC as it is designed to help ensure it is usable for that experiment. [Section 6.11]

 • From the ATLAS and CMS point of view, the IRI long-term campaign pattern best fits the LHC
 use case. Historically, the collaboration expects a full year’s worth of reconstructed data and
 simulation to be produced on a few-month timescale, so there is relatively little time sensitivity.
 Online data-quality monitoring and time-sensitive calibration procedures are handled by a
 separate coordination area of the ATLAS and CMS experiments and have dedicated resources
 at CERN, the host laboratory. In addition, since each particle collision event is an independent
 identically distributed quantity, the HL-LHC science workflow is trivially parallelizable and
 does not need large-scale data shuffle operations to execute. [Section 6.12]

 • If, under the IRI, HPC centers could provide some of the services found at the WLCG data
 centers, both ATLAS and CMS will be able to make better use of these resources. [Section 6.12]

 • Many of the workflows that the LHC experiments will use during HL-LHC under the IRI
 category of data-intensive workflows (event reconstruction and ML) or long-term campaign
 (large-scale MC simulations). IRI will also provide the opportunity to implement some near-
 real-time workflows for critical payloads. [Section 6.12]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 51

 • For the LHC experiments, the US provides ~30–40% of the global computing and storage
 capacity. If this community is to effectively engage with IRI, it will be necessary to ensure that
 the interface to computing and storage resources made available by IRI is compatible with
 the global infrastructure, including university and international partners. The current WLCG
 interface is expected to evolve in preparation for HL-LHC, though the exact nature of this
 evolution is not yet determined. [Section 6.12]

 • SuperCDMS SNOLAB is not equipped, so far, to work in an IRI workflow. Its data structure,
 data taking, and data-processing patterns are simple enough that the need for advanced
 solutions has not appeared. It would instead require additional personnel and resources that are
 not accessible with the current funding level. [Section 6.13]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 52

5 Review Actions
ESnet recorded a set of high-level actions from the HEP user facilities and ESnet requirements review that
extend ESnet’s ongoing support of HEP-funded collaborations. Based on the key findings, the review identified
several actions for HEP, ASCR, and ESnet to jointly pursue. These items are listed as guidance for future
collaboration, and do not reflect formal project timelines. ESnet will review these with HEP participations on a
yearly basis, until the next requirements review process begins.

These are also organized by topic area for simplicity and follow common themes:

 • Facility management and readiness.
 • Scientific data management.
 • Scientific workflow.
 • Computational and storage requirements.
 • Remote collaboration and operational requirements.
 • Multifacility computational workflows.
 • Networking for local and wide-area data mobility.
 • Emerging needs.
 • IRI responsiveness.

5.1 Facility Management and Readiness
 • The HL-LHC will produce over 2,000 hours of data collection every year when the HL-LHC
 starts running in 2030. The HL-LHC program is expected to last for a decade or more (through
 the 2040s). Large improvements in networking, throughout the R&E community, will be
 required to enable the ambitious physics goals of the HL-LHC. [Section 6.12]

 • The current members of the LHC collaborations are not expected to encounter major changes
 during HL-LHC operation. The collaborators will continue to be distributed worldwide,
 which puts strong requirements on global networking, and cooperation between entities that
 operate R&E networks. Computing resources will continue to be globally distributed, with
 no centralized data or computing location, implying that physicists will need access to the
 distributed resources. [Section 6.12]

 • In the HL-LHC era, it is expected that the US will continue to provide two Tier-1s and more
 than a dozen Tier-2 facilities, funded via DOE and NSF respectively, as resources for ATLAS
 and CMS. Both experiments will make use of any HPC centers funded by either DOE or NSF
 that will grant allocations to community science projects. Commercial cloud providers are not
 expected to be a major component of computing infrastructure, but may provide some capacity.
 R&E networking providers are critical to connecting all these resources. [Section 6.12]

 • HL-LHC predictions show a mismatch between the computing and storage resources the
 experiments can afford, versus the resources needed to reach science goals. In response to
 this gap, the experiments are exploring alternatives in how to utilize storage, computing, and
 network infrastructure. The network baseline currently being planned is composed of terabit-
 scale (1–2 Tbps) backbone networks with the largest resource sites connected at multiple 400G
 scale (800 Gbps+). Network use will be at least a factor of 10 larger than Run 3. [Section 6.12]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 53

5.2 Scientific Data Management
 • The cosmological community is interested in advancing a model that would help reduce
 the number of times and locations that need to be involved to archive long-term data
 products, and is looking for assistance in scoping and realizing this design goal. Establishing
 permanent storage facilities would allow the community to establish a more regular
 pattern of collaboration: a smaller set of data portals that can be used to catalog and retrieve
 long-term campaigns of products along with a simplified way to support analysis activities,
 potentially leveraging interactive computing approaches, at a well-known number of
 sites. [Section 6.1], [Section 8], [Section 5.2]

 • DC24 was widely successful for the LHC community, and several important outcomes came
 from the exercise including understanding bottlenecks in the network configuration at the
 Tier-1 centers and the ways many of the tools were improved and replaced since Run 2. The
 LHC community is interested in developing a program to test the effectiveness of transfers
 both to benchmark methods at increased capacity, and integrate new functionality into existing
 tools. Such tests should be done in collaboration with ESnet. For example, one lesson learned
 from the most-recent data challenge organized by WLCG (DC24) was that it is necessary to
 utilize a given link at full capacity to determine whether it has any performance abnormalities.
 It is desirable to develop a process of regular testing of network capacities (e.g., relying on
 perfSONAR) to test connections to the maximum and identify problems before they become a
 bottleneck in production. [Section 6.10], [Section 8]

 • The LHC community will conduct a full analysis of the observed results of DC24, and discuss
 ways to both capture and act on observational data in near-real time for DC27. An in-depth data
 analysis will be needed, and this may lead to a process of evaluating each networking link in the
 ecosystem, and ways that both LHC monitoring data, and that from ESnet, can be captured and
 used to evaluate overall system performance. [Section 6.11], [Section 8]

 • A common theme across many of the HEP case studies was the surrounding challenges of
 data access as collaboration space grows larger. The LHC collaboration has a highly structured
 ecosystem that facilitates access to groups, and individuals, through a number of tools that
 manage identity and permissions across a federated grid infrastructure. Other collaborations
 that have less structure may struggle with the available tools to manage collaboration size long
 term and are attempting other solutions (e.g., neutral site hosting through cloud providers, or
 adopting the policies of the strictest member of a collaboration). [Section 8]

 • The DC24 exercise provided critical insight into the behaviors of all layers of the technology
 stack for the LHC communities: data management and ability software, computation and
 storage, as well as local- and wide-area networking. The DC27 is expected to be a crucial
 preparation step for the HL-LHC operation. Beyond the major milestones of a full DC, the
 mini-DC activities in the run-up to a full DC will be useful ways to validate specific portions
 of technology support structure. ESnet plans to engage with the LHC community on ways to
 participate in all these. [Section 8]

5.3 Scientific Workflow
 • DESI uses Globus for transfers of collaboration data, and users report good experiences with
 Globus when they want to download an entire directory tree. But they have found the interface
 lacking for the more common use case of selecting a subset of data from a complex directory
 tree (e.g., all files matching a given regex regardless of where they appear in the directory
 structure). Discussions with Globus may be useful to help facilitate ways to address this use
 case. [Section 6.2]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 54

 • The Rubin Observatory faces several challenges, some of which are outside the control
 of ESnet and DOE. Like other large facilities, it must take cybersecurity into heavy
 consideration. NOIRLab has been responsive to recent threats and has put in place controls
 that can make collaboration harder. In addition, the theme of federated identity management
 is also present for Rubin, and represents a barrier to the use of some of the tools that were
 selected during design. As a result, Rubin is looking to adopt tools used elsewhere in HEP for
 data mobility and workflow management, including Rucio. The integration steps to have this
 work in Rubin’s own environment have been challenging, and Rubin will be looking for help
 and advice. [Section 6.3], [Section 8]

 • Known or potential data-related resource constraints for Rubin as of FY24 are: [Section 6.3]
 ° Insufficient computing resources available to meet the full analysis demand from the
 Rubin scientific user community, and/or difficulty in co-locating Rubin data products with
 available computing resources. This includes unbounded or unscoped demand for AI- and
 ML-based analysis of Rubin data.

 ° Changing cybersecurity threats and policy landscapes that can present barriers to
 planned data-access and data-sharing services, and/or can introduce new costs, technical
 requirements, and schedule impacts.

 ° Challenges associated with implementing and routinely operating the distributed
 processing model for annual data-release processing.

 ° Challenges and constraints of operating in a shared data facility with other experiments.

 ° Network and I/O performance impacts of transferring a very large number of relatively
 small files.

 • DUNE’s software stack will leverage many of the tools already in use within the HEP
 community, including Rucio, FTS, and XrootD. DUNE is also looking into facilitating
 Globus as a transport mechanism with the workflow managers, such as Rucio and XrootD.
 DUNE has converted to use containers, which has greatly increased the ability to make the
 analysis work portable across available resources, particularly at DOE HPC centers like
 NERSC. [Section 6.8], [Section 8]

 • Limitations are imposed by the various SuperCDMS collaborator sites depending on
 firewall rules, use of virtual private networks (VPNs), and multifactor authentication (MFA)
 requirements that often limit the amount of automation of the transfer tools. The lack of
 uniformity in the availability of tools (e.g., not all sites have Globus endpoints) and the different
 network protection stances also imply the need to develop data-transfer tools tailored for each
 site. For a computing group of a small experiment like SuperCDMS, the lack of standardization
 creates additional overhead. [Section 6.13]

5.4 Computational and Storage Requirements
 • Within the NERSC computing center, DESI is limited by I/O performance stability of the
 “community file system”: median performance is fine, but semi-rare outlier events can cause
 multi-minute delays or even lead to job hangs or timeouts. The Perlmutter scratch disk
 performance is better, but the difficulties of constantly syncing datasets between the scratch
 filesystem and CFS has been human-error prone and effort-prohibitive. [Section 6.2]

 • The inability to pragmatically synchronize constantly evolving PB-scale datasets between
 multiple locations is a limiting factor for DESI. That includes internal to a data center (e.g.,
 between CFS and the scratch filesystem) and external (e.g., between NERSC and another DOE
 HPC facility). [Section 6.2]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 55

 • For the full-fledged Rubin Observatory data releases, expected in the two- to five-year time
 frame, DESC will see a limitation in some of the science cases that require full access to the
 complete single-visit image data set (only available at SLAC or CC-IN2P3, but not NERSC as
 currently planned) rather than just the galaxy catalogs. DESC is currently looking for mitigations
 to this problem, such as limiting the size of transferred data to NERSC but enabling the
 analyses nonetheless, or shipping software containers to run remotely at these facilities instead.
 In addition, large-scale image simulations produced at NERSC or elsewhere would possibly
 stress DESC’s small-latency storage allocation at NERSC, as well as compete with computing
 allocation for its analyses in parallel to real data analyses. The transition to NERSC-10 in
 this period and its unknown impact on established pipelines also introduces some uncertainty.
           [Section 6.4]

 • The SBN program anticipates using more DOE HPC resources for its simulation
 workflows. SBN does anticipate needing more disk space during this process, which
 limits output. [Section 6.8], [Section 8]

 • SBN’s primary concern is not network bandwidth, but rather I/O performance. The project
 relies heavily on tape-based storage, which causes a bottleneck when reading out older
 data. Fixes are being explored to rely less on this approach, and may increase expected data
 volumes. [Section 6.8], [Section 8]

 • The barrier to using DOE HPC resources within the LHC community remains,
 particularly in integrating the systems as resources into the software components, and
 normalizing the way the resources could be accounted for (expected versus ad hoc or
 opportunistic). More specifically, there is a desire to create agreements or other forms of
 arrangements, similar to an SLA, with DOE HPC facilities such that resources can be
 considered pledged, like how Tier-1s and Tier-2s operate. This helps with planning for both
 the HEP community and the ASCR resources. Some of this may require discussion at the
 programmatic level. [Section 6.12], [Section 8]

 • The LHC community experiences friction with supporting a streaming-based workflow at
 large HPC facilities. Workarounds have been established to support this, either by allowing
 the worker nodes to stream directly or by leveraging caches and data lakes that are deployed
 close topologically. All these design choices come with trade-offs, which implies a set of R&D
 activities that will extend in the coming years. [Section 6.12], [Section 8]

 • The changes to hardware at LHC Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites will impact some of the performance
 aspects of future DC activities, but the schedule of hardware upgrades is hard to predict. Some
 sites plan on upgrading hardware yearly, so their upgrades appear more “rolling”; when a DC
 happens they will go with what is available. Others may be able to schedule larger hardware
 purchases, and plan to install and test prior to the DC27 activity. Many sites will not get funding
 until closer to DC27 (e.g., end of 2026, start of 2027); thus they may not be able to upgrade
 anything before the next major challenge. [Section 8]

5.5 Remote Collaboration and Operational Requirements
 • Broadly speaking, DESI is not limited by raw bandwidth but by the convenience of tools for
 managing cross-site data flow. Globus is efficient for one-off data transfers, but issues such as
 expiring certificates, multi-factor authentication, data discovery, and data filtering (i.e., selecting
 what needs to be downloaded) limit convenience for day-to-day random access of huge datasets.
 It is desirable to consider if computing centers and end users would be able to subscribe to
 datasets from each other, with automatic efficient syncing of the subsets of the data actively
 being used, with the toolkits managing purging unused data to stay within the local quota limits.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 56

 The faster the network is, the more viable this becomes, since it reduces the barrier to having to
 re-download data. [Section 6.2]

5.6 Multifacility Computational Workflows
 • Using a single centralized facility to support DESI provides benefits of a single ecosystem to
 learn, and minimal overhead for sharing results with collaborators from other institutions. At
 the same time, it becomes a single point of failure during NERSC outages, leading to ongoing
 interest in multisite computing operations in the future. The limiting factors are not networking
 for data transfer, but rather the tools for making that data sharing automated and transparent
 for hundreds of users accessing PBs of data stored in millions of files. DESI could transfer
 its major data release to another site, but that is of little use unless the hundreds of DESI
 users at NERSC can also get accounts at that site, and the outputs of their daily work can be
 transparently synced back and forth between the two sites. [Section 6.2]

 • SuperCDMS is evaluating options for network outages and how to proceed with operations. In
 case of extensive, site-wide outages at SLAC, it would also be important to have another data
 path from SNOLAB to an alternative computation site, namely DRAC and/or Texas A&M, to not
 interrupt the processing flow. The criteria needed to temporarily switch from SLAC to another site
 for storage and processing needs to be carefully evaluated and the process tested. [Section 6.13]

5.7 Networking for Local and Wide-Area Data Mobility
 • ESnet will follow up with international partners to include up-to-date networking maps of the
 international paths, namely TransPAC,15 which is operated by International Networks at Indiana
 University, and Americas Pathway (AMPATH),16 which is operated by Florida International
 University, for updated connectivity diagrams and information regarding support for networking
 in the region with other partners. [Section 6.7], [Section 8]

 • The DOE HEP and DOE ASCR program offices are working out the specifics of the
 connectivity to SURF that ESnet will need to complete for the proper connection. The efforts
 are planned to converge by the end of fiscal year 2026. [Section 6.8], [Section 8]

 • The LHC experiments anticipate network needs will grow gradually. Increasing network
 capacity and performance will be needed at Tier-1, Tier-2, and Tier-3 facilities. The exact
 magnitude of future network provisioning is expected to be determined jointly by the
 experiments, ESnet, the R&E networking community, facilities and campuses, funding
 agencies, and other involved parties. [Section 6.9], [Section 6.10]

 • CMS would like to develop a program to test the effectiveness of transfers both to benchmark
 methods at increased capacity and integrate new functionality into existing tools. Such
 tests should be done in collaboration with ESnet. For example, one lesson learned from the
 most-recent data challenge organized by WLCG (DC24) was that it is necessary to utilize a
 link at full capacity to learn if a given link has any performance abnormalities. It is desirable
 to develop a process of regular testing of network capacities (e.g., relying on perfSONAR) to
 test connections to the maximum and identify problems before they become a bottleneck in
 production. [Section 6.10]
