High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 57

 • Networking support at BNL and Fermilab, to support the ATLAS and CMS Tier-1 computing
 facilities, respectively, has increased and is approaching an aggregate of 1 Tbps through all
 connectivity. Both sites are exploring ways to move toward 800 Gbps native connections in
 the coming years, when the technology is ready to be supported. As of 2024, multiple 400G
 connections have been installed to the Fermilab and Brookhaven national labs as well as HPC
 facilities used by HEP, and the upgrades to 400G (or N X 400G) at some US CMS campuses are
 either in place or imminent. [Section 6.11]

 • One place that R&E networks could help would be in jointly negotiating with various cloud
 providers to create a template contract that would support no egress charges if the R&E
 providers bring high-bandwidth links to the cloud providers, as well as defining policies and
 associated tools to allow LHC site creators to manage costs by, for example, controlling how data
 flow to only use the zero (or low cost) egress connections globally. [Section 6.11]

 • The HL-LHC requirements for LHCOPN links approach 1 Tbps and have pushed sites to
 explore more affordable technologies to achieve it. IT-INFN-CNAF, the Italian Tier-1, has
 deployed a pilot connection using Data Center Interconnect (DCI) equipment at the Tier-1
 (CNAF) and Tier-0 (CERN) sites, which use four light channels on the dark-fibers of two
 different providers, GÉANT and GARR. The solution can provide 4 x 400 Gbps link for a total
 of 1.6 Tbps. Spectrum sharing is achieved by interconnecting the reconfigurable optical add-
 drop multiplexer (ROADM) device of the two providers. It saves on the cost of more expensive
 router interfaces, since most of the existing LHCOPN links are provided as Multiprotocol Label
 Switching (MPLS) Layer 2 virtual circuits. [Section 6.11]

 • During the 2020–2021 studies of LHC network requirements, the LHC experiments estimated
 that Tier-1 centers would need terabit/sec connections and Tier-2 sites would require 400G
 connections. That was driven by estimates of some (but not all) data-related operations of
 CMS and ATLAS, leading to an estimated bandwidth need of 4.8 terabits/sec (Tbps) across
 the Atlantic for CMS and ATLAS alone in a so-called “minimal model” and 9.6 Tbps in a more
 “flexible” and realistic model. [Section 6.11]

 • The LHC experiments have defined two models to predict bandwidth needs into the era of
           HL-LHC: [Section 6.11]

 ° Minimal model:

 • Sum (ATLAS,ALICE,CMS,LHCb)*2(for bursts)*2(safety-margin) = 4.8 Tbps expected
 HL-LHC bandwidth.

 ° Flexible model:

 • Experiments may need to reprocess and reconstruct the collected data during the year.
 • This requires doubling the bandwidth of the minimal model: 9.6 Tbps expected
 HL-LHC bandwidth.

 • All the major Tier-1s are expected to have at least 800 Gbps LHCOPN links at the start of Run
 4 with the ability to grow to 1.2 Tbps or even 1.6 Tbps during the Run. Tier-1s should also
 have an equivalent amount of bandwidth to LHCONE to serve Tier-2s. The LHC experiments
 predict the following bandwidth estimate for sites during HL-LHC: [Section 6.11]

 ° Each major Tier-1:

 • 1 Tbps to the Tier-0 (LHCOPN).
 • 1 Tbps to the Tier-2s (aggregated, LHCONE).
 ° Each major Tier-2:

 • >400 Gbps (LHCONE) and resilient.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 58

 • The individual LHC experiments are interested in discussing the set of features that must be
 present in future network designs. If identifying a minimum set of capabilities in switches
 and routers is possible to ensure the next generation of network components can meet the needs
 of the community, it would simplify the procurement and installation process. The sooner
 those capabilities are in place, the sooner prototyping and testing future capabilities will be
 possible. [Section 6.12]

 • For HL-LHC networking, four main requirements, beyond connectivity, have been
 identified: [Section 6.12]

 ° Understanding the impact of new features in networking (SDN/NFV) by testing,
 prototyping, and evaluating impact is necessary. The experiments will need to evolve
 applications, facilities, and computing models to meet the HL-LHC challenges; this will
 take time.

 ° The ability to understand WAN network flows is limited. New methods to mark and
 monitor network use are needed. Packet marking is viewed as a high priority so that
 everyone (experiments, sites, and R&E networks) can understand the origin and intent of
 network flows at any point along their path.

 ° Developing, prototyping, and testing network features at suitable scale will be needed.
 Having at-scale network testbeds will be very important to understand the potential impact
 changes might have on operations.

 • The LAN connectivity for SNOLAB is 2 x 10 Gbps, and the WAN connectivity consists of
 a 1 Gbps link that is also shared with 10 other experiments. This limitation implies that
 SuperCDMS must plan to work within a budget of no more than 10% of either of these
 connections during operation. This link allows SNOLAB to reach Laurentian University,
 which is then connected to ORION (the provincial R&E network of Ontario), and Canadian
 Network for the Advancement of Research, Industry and Education (CANARIE, the national
 R&E network of Canada). CANARIE peers with ESnet, which facilitates the connectivity to
 reach SLAC. The network limitations were explored during a project review in 2022. At the
 time, the cost was considered too high to upgrade the 1 Gbps WAN link, which will cause the
 experiments that share this resource to be more austere in their use. SuperCDMS will consider
 this in the design of their trigger mechanism and computing and storage strategy. ESnet can
 discuss options with SuperCDMS regarding the use of other connectivity options. [Section
           6.13], [Section 8]

 • The network connectivity between SNOLAB and SLAC is a critical component, given that all
 workflows and all scientific analysis happen off-site. And the bandwidth bottleneck between
 SNOLAB and the ORION network could present a challenge in the future if no upgrades to
 the bandwidth occur, given the tendency of data volumes from current and future experiments
 to grow rather than shrink. SNOLAB and SLAC could explore alternative network paths (e.g.,
 those that do not rely on a terrestrial link) to address the critical need to keep networking active
 during experimentation. [Section 6.13]

 • Strategic planning (five+ years) for OLCF shows LAN traffic will be increased to 800 GbE
 for Science DMZ and data-movement networks with individual 1.6 Tbit links for network
 interconnects. This will also imply that DMZ traffic (e.g., related to data-movement) will scale
 to 6–12Tbit/sec. All other LAN traffic will have multiple 800 Gbit connections. Firewalls in
 this time frame will be 4–6 Tbit/second in throughput. WAN capabilities at ORNL could have
 multiple 800 Gbit connections to ESnet, and OLCF could have multiple 800 Gbit connections
 to ITSD. The connections between the ESnet testbed and OLCF resources could be further
 expanded to multiple 400 Gbit interfaces. [Section 7.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 59

 • ESnet and Fermilab network engineering teams have drafted a plan for connectivity back to
 Fermilab to support DUNE. The plan calls for redundant, geographically diverse, vendor-
 diverse, 100 Gbps circuits from SURF to ESnet points-of-presence (PoPs) in Chicago and
 Denver, respectively. ESnet backbone services (On-demand Secure Circuits and Reservation
 System [OSCARS]) would then extend those L2 paths back to Fermilab. Deployment of both
 100 Gbps circuits should occur by the 2026–2027 time frame. Both pathways will be connected
 to ESnet in a production capacity. Currently, a dedicated 10 Gbps circuit between SURF and
 ESnet’s Kansas City PoP provides DUNE FD connectivity back to the Fermilab campus.
 This circuit, provided by South Dakota’s Research Education and Economic Development
 Network (REED), will revert to a tertiary back-up role once the two 100 Gbps circuits are
 procured and deployed. [Section 7.4]

 • Fermilab is concerned about not having the capability to adequately stress test the WAN
 infrastructure as network technology step-increases push bandwidth capacities to terabit
 scale. The ability to generate traffic at 400 GE, 800 GE, and 1.6 TE is challenging. Fermilab
 desires to be able to routinely stress test the WAN infrastructure to ensure it is performing as
 expected. The complexity of having multiple types of virtual network services sharing the same
 physical infrastructure adds another level of difficulty to this. It is desirable to consider this
 as a capability to concurrently generate high traffic loads across various virtual network
 services (LHCOPN, LHCONE, default routed Internet Protocol [IP] path, etc.). This capability
 is a critical tool in Fermilab’s ability to troubleshoot aggregate data bottlenecks where multiple
 virtual network services are involved. Fermilab proposes that this should be developed as a
 service that ESnet provides to all its sites. [Section 7.4]

 • To adhere to the LHCONE and LHCOPN AUP, various complex routing policies and features
 must be implemented on BNL Network Perimeter. This AUP states only specific HEP
 resources at BNL (e.g., US ATLAS, Belle II, DUNE, etc.) should have access to the LHCONE
 and LHCOPN services, which leaves all other resources at BNL able only to traverse the
 general Internet services. To provide this exclusivity for LHCONE and LHCOPN, separate
 campus Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instances have been created on both perimeter
 routers. Policies are then applied to only import default, black hole, and local BNL routes into
 the campus VRFs. Then policy-based routing (PBR) policies are configured on all perimeter
 downstream ingress interfaces. In short, these PBR policies state that all private IPv4 and IPv6
 and HEP subnets forward to the default routing table, which has full visibility to all WAN
 circuits, while all other BNL subnets should forward to the campus VRF instance, which can
 only see the general Internet services. [Section 7.5]

 • Within the next five years, SLAC expects to upgrade the 2 x 400 GbE links to 2x or 4x 800 GbE
 links. LCLS-II has a requirement for 1–2 Tbps capacity between SLAC and NERSC. This
 requirement is expected to be met with the N x 800 GbE upgrades. The SLAC core network
 will also be upgraded to N x 800 GbE. [Section 7.6]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 60

 • Several data-related resource constraints were identified for ANL’s support of scientific efforts:
           [Section 7.7]

 ° Within the Computing, Environment, and Life Sciences (CELS) directorate, the recent
 upgrades to 400G WAN & Science DMZ paths, which very seldom exceed 25% sustained
 utilization, have resulted in very few concerns on data-related constraints.

 ° Outside of the Science DMZ, the replacement of 40G firewall paths with 100G should
 provide room for future growth of non-CELS scientific divisional network traffic.

 ° The perfSONAR infrastructure, used for network monitoring and testing, has not been
 upgraded in a number of years and in some cases, it was decommissioned without
 immediate replacement due to operating system support factors.

 ° Rebuilding the fleet of perfSONAR nodes throughout campus is necessary for us to
 proactively identify data-related constraints. However, this has been a challenge to
 prioritize due to other initiatives.

 • During DC24, ESnet directly assisted several sites in “full capacity” testing of their network
 links. This was done using multiple perfSONAR servers to generate traffic, and changing
 routing policy on both the network and the site end. This testing helped to reveal configuration
 bottlenecks, and was invaluable in gaining an understanding of the maximum expected
 performance. Future DC activities can take a similar approach, but there are also capabilities
 that ESnet’s High Touch servers (that feature Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs)) could
 assist with. Several High Touch servers could conceivably be programmed to create network
 traffic and direct it at resources located within a lab or facility perimeter. ESnet will follow up
 with interested sites on this prototype concept. [Section 8]

 • The LHC community and ESnet are collecting an enormous amount of data on the performance
 of data mobility tools, the networks that are a part of data transfer, and the individual
 hardware components (routers, switches, servers, storage). These data were incredibly useful
 during the DC24 activity, and helped to identify transfer bottlenecks and other gaps to
 delivering the requirements for HL-LHC operation. Despite having visibility, it is not possible
 to review and act on all the collected telemetry data. Cultivating or hiring a data analyst to
 review the data and suggest ways they can be better incorporated in future tools would benefit
 both efforts. [Section 8]

 • Several facilities are not connected to LHCONE currently, despite being heavily involved in
 LHC-affiliated computation and storage activities. These include major computational sites
 (e.g., NERSC and TACC) used for simulation workflows, SLAC (which has operated Afs in the
 past), and when applicable, commercial clouds. No formal agreement with any of these facilities
 exists now to be part of the LHC collaboration in a structured way, but investigating their ability
 to connect to LHCONE to support several important use cases is recommended. [Section 8]

 • LHCONE runs a hybrid approach to supporting IPv6 currently. The upcoming government
 mandate (e.g., M-21-07) will imply that Fermilab and BNL will move toward IPv6 capabilities,
 and subsequently the Tier-2s will have to move toward dual stack support at a minimum. One
 critical issue that cannot be solved by the US community will be the ability of CERN to deliver
 IPv6 capabilities from its service infrastructure; some capabilities may be IPv4 only in the
 coming years. ESnet will continue to work with US collaborators on this to ease the transition to
 IPv6 operation. [Section 8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 61

 • Several international networking partners factored heavily into the discussions this year;
 connectivity to Europe, South America, and the Asia-Pacific region is accomplished through
 relationships with several R&E partners. ESnet maintains peering relations with most of these
 partners, and their connectivity carries significant amounts of HEP traffic daily (e.g., LHC and
 ProtoDUNE traffic from Europe, Rubin Observatory and CMB-S4 traffic from South America,
 Belle II traffic from Japan, etc.). ESnet will include current network capability diagrams into
 this report to document the current state of international networking. [Section 8]

5.8 Emerging Needs
 • ATLAS has raised a concern regarding a lack of sufficiently fine-grained network monitoring
 and performance information to help debug and automate data transfers in real time between
 various sites. Better visibility is being worked on through various entities including WLCG
 Site Network Monitoring, the SciTags initiative (labeling network flows and IPv6 packets with
 owner/purpose), and improved monitoring from the various tools and infrastructures, but
 ATLAS has significant gaps in monitoring. [Section 6.9]

 • CMS has treated the global network of sites as a mesh with identical links when it comes to
 bulk transfers. The XrootD data federation was designed from the beginning to be cognizant
 of the TA links being limited, but treated links within the US as identical. The data lake model
 currently discussed in WLCG makes clear regional distinctions. The concept of creating a data
 lake has progressed slowly due to challenges around how increased latency due to the longer
 international links will affect application performance. [Section 6.10]

 • CMS would like to continue exploring with ESnet how to contribute towards global R&D
 projects such as the Global P4 Lab testbed, use of ESnet High Touch services, and evolving
 technologies such as Smart NICs. [Section 6.10]

 • The next several years are critical to transition managed network R&D by CMS, including
 results of the SENSE project, into production for the HL-LHC. The SENSE, Caltech,
 and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) teams are close to 400G throughput with
 production infrastructure using XrootD, FTS, and XrootD. [Section 6.10]

 • ESnet will continue to work with the LHC community on co-design efforts like SENSE and
 Rucio, SciTags, and other potential opportunities. The experiments need to be specific in
 what they are hoping to achieve, however. The aim of joint projects could be to “co-design” an
 effective system that makes best use of the available network resources, coordinated with the
 site resources, and manage joint site and network operations cooperatively. This needs to be
 spelled out in more detail and discussed with ESnet leadership. [Section 6.11], [Section 8]

 • For LHC experiments in general, the resource requirements are growing beyond what flat
 budgets can support. This leads the experiments to work very hard at optimizing their data
 and analysis processes to maximize what the available resources can do. Various trade-offs are
 continually being explored (network use vs multiple replicas of data, data format changes vs
 number of required datasets to meet various needs, exploitation of nonstandard computing
 capacity, reconstructing data on demands vs storing them), to try to achieve the time to science
 target with constrained resources. [Section 6.11]

 • Because of recent changes to technology drivers, the evolution of ATLAS and CMS’s “process
 of science,” and the outlook for 2030 when the HL-LHC era will begin, it appears that the
 actual networking requirements may be somewhat larger than foreseen during the 2020 HEP
 Requirements Review. Detailed projections are difficult at this point, but should be tracked
 and updated every two years or so to make quantitative estimates and (re-)establish the
 requirements in both network capacity and capability. [Section 6.11]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 62

 • One interesting option to explore on the timescale of HL-LHC is the joint ATLAS and CMS
 use of Rucio for distributed data management. This could provide a mechanism to interact with
 ESnet (and other R&E networks), communicating near-term data-movement intents and perhaps
 negotiating for any required quality of service (QoS) or deadline requirements. [Section 6.12]

 • GPU use to support some aspects of AI and ML within the LHC community is expected to
 continue; unknown currently is how this may impact WAN usage. Experiments like DUNE
 have shown that bursting to a commercial cloud to utilize GPUs is possible, but leveraging
 DOE HPC resource would allow better control over the WAN components. Opportunities
 could exist to schedule network use (e.g., using mechanics like SENSE and Rucio) to coincide
 with the availability of resources at an HPC facility. [Section 6.12], [Section 8]

 • The LHC work on data lakes will continue, and LHC has learned several things from the years
 of R&D and use during activities like DC24. An effort to reduce the number of “entry points”
 into storage resources has begun. The XrootD tool right now is not bound by factors such as
 network capacity or distance/latency, and may find nonoptimal answers to requests for data
 from clients. The overall goal of a data lake should be to simplify the way data are accessed,
 along with providing the most performant ways to access and retrieve them. Data lakes can
 also leverage some of the work on caching, and allow the caches (which often do have more
 intelligence) to assist in making optimal choices about retrieval. [Section 6.12], [Section 8]

 • The use of in-network caching was discussed at length to identify ways that ESnet and the LHC
 community can work together more efficiently to design and operate an effective service. ESnet
 has some previous work in attempting to create a Content Delivery Network (CDN) for science
 with others in the DOE, but the usage patterns never amounted to a measurable increase in
 performance. A core R&D question to address remains how large the caches should be, and
 what policies on data retrieval and retention will be valuable to implement to keep cache hit
 rates high. ESnet would like to gain better monitoring insight into the caching work, either by
 having access to LHC data (e.g., MONIT) or by having more network layer visibility integrated
 into Stardust. [Section 6.12], [Section 8]

 • As in the discussion after the LHC Operations use case, ESnet will continue to work with
 the LHC community to advance R&D efforts that support the HL-LHC operations era. This
 includes the already mentioned efforts (e.g., SENSE and Rucio, SciTags), but also ways that
 HPC resources can be integrated and utilized more efficiently. The use of ESnet High Touch
 data, and integration with Stardust, may be critical in passing along network-level telemetry to
 the storage and computational components of the LHC community. [Section 6.12], [Section 8]

 • Fermilab has a strong interest in making use of ESnet High Touch Services to generate data for
 AI/ML-based analysis of network traffic patterns. Fermilab is currently working cooperatively
 with ESnet on distinguishing between streaming-based CMS data movement and file-transfer-
 based CMS data movement. It is desirable not just to continue with this effort but also to look
 toward additional opportunities to expand use of ESnet High Touch Service capabilities in
 analyzing WAN traffic. [Section 7.4]

 • ANL has interest in learning how to leverage the MetrANOVA platform, like how perfSONAR
 has been adopted. [Section 7.7]

 • Authentication, authorization, and accounting approaches have limitations. Typically, it is
 possible to specify who can do what and keep a record of what has happened. Within an
 organizational structure this is not too much of a challenge, but across organizations with
 different policies it can be complicated, as different implementations and validation methods
 are employed. [Section 8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 63

 • Several HEP case studies outlined their production, proto-duction, and experimental use of
 commercial cloud resources. ESnet, as a network carrier, is identifying ways to assist with the
 execution of the scientific mission, and will continue to help with connectivity and peering
 when applicable. During some HEP evaluations of cloud solutions for portions of analysis
 workflows, the network was identified as a bottleneck in certain situations: mainly when traffic
 remained within a cloud versus being allowed to egress and use more predicable R&E routing
 and transit. In situations like this, ESnet could serve as a valuable partner between connected
 end sites and cloud resources, to try to force routing choices that take advantage of R&E WAN
 paths versus the internal networking a cloud may use. [Section 8]

5.9 IRI Responsiveness
 • The cosmological simulation community expects that future workflows, especially in the IRI
 context, may see the dataflow controlled from a central location, or distributed to a few “trunk”
 sites. As simulations become more integral to the work of individual researchers, potential exists
 to investigate: [Section 6.1]

 ° The concept of distributed analysis sites that will better adjust to the workflow demands.

 ° On-demand data-intensive analysis capabilities at the DOE computing centers as an IRI/
 HPDF development.

 • DESC analyses will eventually employ the galaxy catalogs, but also the full imaging data of
 approximately 10 PB, in the later years of the project. Replicating even the high-level imaging
 data at NERSC is inefficient and unfeasible, due to the scale of the expected allocation. DESC
 expects to embrace a fully distributed analysis at different facilities. Workflows will be adapted,
 preferably through IRI approaches, to a more flexible computing environment. [Section 6.4]

 • Future DESC needs, more than five years out, will likely require that the analysis process
 employ not only the complete galaxy catalogs, but also the full imaging data of O(10s) PB.
 Replicating even the high-level imaging data at NERSC is inefficient and unfeasible, due to the
 scale of the expected allocation. Thus, embracing a fully distributed analysis at different IRI and
 international sites, through grid solutions such as Distributed Infrastructure with Remote Agent
 Control (DIRAC), could be an option to offset some of these allocation difficulties. [Section 6.4]

 • DESC has two outstanding issues to work through in the coming years: [Section 6.4]
 ° DESC needs technical support in implementing data distribution solutions (Rucio,
 DIRAC). Standing up these web services requires close interaction with the facilities (e.g.,
 NERSC). Built-in facility support for this software (e.g., just like the facilities provide
 built-in support for Globus) would be very beneficial.

 ° DESC faces complex issues with identity and account management across various services/
 sites. Two broad classes of sites exist. First are sites like NERSC, where a DESC member
 has a NERSC account that lets them access both NERSC and Globus. Second are sites like
 in the UK, France (CC-IN2P3), and Rubin IDACs, where the DESC needs to deploy a
 proper Virtual Organization (VO) and have a proper grid certificate. These items are needed
 to enable interactions with grid software like Rucio and DIRAC. Ideally, the VO and
 certificates would be linked to each member’s NERSC account. Further, we would ideally
 want to be able to target the NERSC queues using grid software like DIRAC so that we can
 run jobs, move data, etc., across multiple sites transparently.

 • DUNE can take advantage of some aspects of the IRI design approaches, and the collaboration
 is currently exploring using NERSC and ALCF for aspects of simulation and analysis workflows.
 GPU resources required for parts of the workflow may need to be used at the DOE HPC

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 64

 facilities. DUNE has not fully identified a long-term location for the storage of its public data
 archive. This may also fall into the realm of an IRI workflow, or an emerging use case for HPDF
 to assist with. [Section 6.8], [Section 8]

 • The DOE IRI effort has identified “cybersecurity and federated access practice” as one of the
 six core practice areas for future work. This practice area will focus on creating novel solutions
 that enable seamless scientific collaboration within a secure and trusted IRI ecosystem.
 The discussions within this effort are nascent, but a core understanding will be recognizing that
 the security posture and policies of participating facilities may differ, and there must be a
 way to determine and agree on appropriate mechanisms to implement identity and access
 control. [Section 8]

 • The discussions within the HEP community touched on several factors that should be
 considered by the IRI effort. A first step will be to establish a hierarchy of needs: an example
 being that accessing a set of resources or tools that spans administrative boundaries is very
 different than the ability to use different tools and resources within the same location. A similar
 policy language and control structure could solve both, if ways to differentiate the needs and
 articulate the required control structures exist. [Section 8]

6 HEP Case Studies
The case studies presented in this document are a written record of the current state of scientific process, and
technology integration, for a subset of the projects, facilities, and principal investigators (Pis) funded by the Office
of HEP of the DOE SC. These case studies were discussed between July 2024 and December 2024.

The case studies were presented, and are organized in this report, in a deliberate format to present an overview
based on individual experiments, larger facilities, and in some cases the encompassing laboratory environments
that provide critical resources for operation. The case studies profiled include:

 • Cosmological Simulation Research
 • DESI
 • Vera C. Rubin Observatory
 • DESC
 • CMB
 • Muon Experimentation at Fermilab: Muon g-2 and Mu2e
 • Belle II Experiment
 • Neutrino Experiments at Fermilab: SBN and DUNE
 • LHC: ATLAS Experiment
 • LHC: CMS Experiment
 • LHC: LHC Operations
 • LHC: HL-LHC & Network Research
 • SuperCDMS
 • AMS Experiment
Each of these documents contains a complete set of answers to the questions posed by the organizers:

 • How, and where, will new data be analyzed and used?
 • How will the process of doing science change over the next 5–10 years?
 • How will changes to the underlying hardware and software technologies influence
 scientific discovery?
A summary of each will be presented prior to the case study document, along with a “Discussion Summary” that
highlights key areas of conversation from authors and attendees. These brief write-ups are not meant to replace a
full review of the case study, but will provide a snapshot of the discussion and focus during the in-person review.

6.1 Cosmological Simulation Research
Cosmological simulations are used to provide detailed theoretical predictions to understand dark matter and
dark energy, cosmological constraints on neutrino physics, and the nature of primordial fluctuations. These data
products are essential for analyzing and interpreting results from physical cosmological surveys, as well as aiding
in survey design and optimization, and in the estimation and control of statistical errors. The level of resolution
and volume required of the simulations has been, and will continue, to increase in the coming years, driving
data volumes significantly upwards. Additionally, as increased computational power has become available in the
exascale era, large-volume simulations with gas dynamics and subgrid modeling of astrophysical mechanisms

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 66

have become possible in regimes which were previously the domain of gravity-only simulations. Similarly, the
increased computational power will also enable large-scale ensemble simulations that can be used directly for
inference or to construct generative models using AI/ML techniques that can be then used for this purpose.

6.1.1 Discussion Summary
The cosmological community is interested in advancing a model that would help reduce the number of times and
locations that need to be involved to archive long-term data products. Establishing permanent storage facilities
would allow the community to establish a more regular pattern of collaboration; a smaller set of data portals
that can be used to catalog and retrieve long-term campaigns of products along with a simplified way to support
analysis activities, potentially leveraging interactive computing approaches, at a well-known number of sites.

Removing the need to worry about where the data resides allows researchers focused on developing cosmological
simulation to invest more time on the science, versus spending energy in activities to stage data and allocate
technology resources. It also prevents half-measures that are being used today to create mechanisms to perform
analysis on partial data sets, or adopt streaming approaches which are not always successful on some of the larger
computational resources that are not designed to support that mode of operation.

Cosmology data sets are typically owned by the team that generated them, unless the work was specifically part of
a collaboration and/or commissioned by the relevant collaboration. But the increasing requirements toward open
science — as well as a sense that such simulations are useful for a wide range of applications — has led to more
interest in placing simulation results in the public domain. Funding agencies often have requirements for subsets
to be made publicly available. The primary barrier in making simulation data sets public is the lack of available
storage and/or server-side public-access compute capability. This is an excellent opportunity for an interaction
with the IRI effort. Simulation datasets would typically exercise the Data integration–Intensive and Long-Term
Campaign patterns.

Cosmology simulations tend not to lose value over time, in fact older simulation catalogs continue to have high
value and are being used in emerging work that utilizes AI and ML to construct generative models. Simulations
can never truly be reproduced, even if the original codes and inputs are retained: differences in the underlying
behavior of the systems that are used to generate are common, resulting in almost entirely new simulations. Thus,
older simulations will always have an intrinsic value, since they are unique and nonreproducible. This being said,
the community understands that it is infeasible to keep every data set around forever, and there are mechanisms
to archive sets that may not receive as much use as others.

Cloud resources are an intriguing addition to the possible cosmology simulation workflow structure. While
the cost of using these potential locations remains high now, they may become a way to augment resources
during periods of heavy use. One could imagine a situation where the use of AI/ML frameworks become an
instantaneous source of large-scale data; if there is difficulty in allocating local computational and storage
resources to meet the demand, it becomes possible that these workflows will need to be integrated with
commercial cloud infrastructure that can expand as needed to fit the needs.

 • Cosmological simulations are used to provide theoretical predictions to understand dark matter
 and dark energy, cosmological constraints on neutrino physics, and the nature of primordial
 fluctuations. These data products are essential for analyzing and interpreting results from
 physical cosmological surveys, as well as aiding in survey design and optimization, and in the
 estimation and control of statistical errors. [Section 4.1]

 • Results from major cosmological simulation runs can be useful for many years, up to a decade or
 more in some cases. [Section 4.2]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 67

 • Data storage needs for cosmological simulations post mid-2020s are likely to be in the 300PB
 range of spinning disk equivalent, requiring transfer rates of >300 Gbps on an intermittent
 basis when data mobility is required. [Section 4.2]

 • Simulation data streams typically involve moving between 10–100 TB of bulk data when entire
 data sets are needed. The much smaller “user” downloads for individual analysis of a smaller
 subset to local storage typically involve <1 TB chunks of data. Progress in remote visualization
 methods is allowing real-time visualization of many large data sets. [Section 4.3]

 • Over the next two to five years, there will be an evolution in cosmological simulation workflow
 tools to manage local and remote simulation data analysis. This area is in flux, and community
 desires are only slowly being captured in a design process, mostly because of the complex
 nature of the requirements and the dynamic nature of the use cases. [Section 4.3]

 • Typically, the cosmological simulation dataflow consists of two stages, with the understanding
 that the data motion may be staged in a scheduled manner or can be highly bursty, depending
 on the use case: [Section 4.3]

 ° Within the facility where the simulation is run (supercomputer, storage, analysis system) and

 ° From the host facility to a remote analysis/archive site.

 • As increased computational power becomes available in the exascale era of HPC, large-volume
 cosmological simulations with gas dynamics and subgrid modeling of astrophysical mechanisms
 have become possible, which were previously the domain of gravity-only simulations. Similarly,
 the increased computational power will also enable large-scale ensemble simulations that can
 be used directly for inference or to construct generative models using AI/ML techniques that
 can be then used for this purpose. The level of resolution and volume required of cosmological
 simulations has been, and will continue, to increase in the coming years, driving data volumes
 significantly upwards due to these factors. [Section 4.4]

 • Cosmological simulations can, in principle, easily generate far more data than optical and
 microwave observations. This is expected to be the case even when data becomes
 available from the Rubin Observatory, the largest of the imaging surveys, which is expected to
 begin operations in 2026. Estimation of statistical errors relies on hundreds to tens of thousands
 of simulated examples, and cosmologists often need to simulate results obtained from dozens
 to hundreds of varying simulation input conditions. While the on-sky pixel-level data can in
 some cases be larger, the simulated catalogs are already at the level of PBs for large simulation
 suites. [Section 4.4]

 • The size, sophistication, and realism of simulated sky catalogs has improved significantly
 since the 2020 ESnet Requirements Review on the HEP program, and this puts further stress
 on storage and data-transfer capabilities. Typical simulation products can be a TB in size,
 approaching a PB for some of the wide-ranging simulations or those that contain more detail
 due to improvements in the modeling techniques. [Section 4.4]

 • Cosmological simulation continues to be substantially limited by the availability of storage,
 particularly when considering how to distribute the simulation data beyond the group
 that performed the simulation. Further, the need for storage beyond the initial computing
 project is critical; the lifetime of the need is often set by the life cycle of the analysis, which
 is happening in larger collaborations, and as the projects become more complex, over longer
 timelines. [Section 4.4]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 68

 • Storage for cosmological simulation will continue to be a critical issue over time. Some projects
 are more storage-limited than they are compute-limited. This issue has several associated
 dimensions to consider: [Section 4.4]

 ° Sizes and numbers of simulations will increase.

 ° Locations producing simulations are expected to increase.

 ° Funding spans different agencies.

 ° Usefulness over time, and to different communities, is increasing.

 • Data movement of cosmological simulation data between facilities is not a critical problem, but
 broad access for the user community remains challenging. Simplifying access with updated
 portal software, or tools like Globus, has improved data mobility. The next step is to combine
 this with dynamic access to computing resources. [Section 4.5]

 • The ratio of the simulation user community, to the size of the simulation groups, will increase
 as the role of simulations continues to increase; dataflow patterns will likely become more
 diverse and there will be increased pressure on data-transfer facilities that serve the resulting
 simulation outputs. Although the main focus is the continental US, the geographical locations
 of the endpoints are worldwide. The diversity of endpoints and the number of geographical
 locations is expected to grow significantly. [Section 4.5]

 • The data products generated by simulation groups can be created at any number of DOE- or
 NSF-funded HPC facilities or other institutions with sufficient resources to execute and store
 simulation codes. These include all major DOE HPC facilities and a number of other HEP-
 affiliated laboratories. These data products generated are used “downstream” by a large number
 of users who are members of science working groups in cosmological surveys and experiments.
 A common use pattern is to build a mock survey from the simulation data, then perform a
 clustering analysis on that survey. [Section 4.6]

 • The network speeds between major centers are not a limitation for cosmological simulation,
 and transferring PB-sized data sets is effectively routine. This size is expected to increase in the
 coming years, but within the capabilities of ESnet and the DOE HPC resources. [Section 4.7]

 • It is possible that future cosmological simulation data sets will be too large to store locally
 by individual research groups, necessitating streaming workflows the data are developed
 to facilitate on-the-fly analysis, which can then lead to repeated downloads and analyses
 coordinated with the data flow. This situation may be exacerbated as AI/ML frameworks can
 be essentially instantaneous sources of large-scale data; at the same time this difficulty can be
 ameliorated if only the models were sent over and local computational and storage resources
 were sufficient to meet the demand. In future, these particular workflows could be integrated
 with commercial cloud infrastructure. [Section 4.8]

 • Cosmological simulation resource usage becomes a question of latency, bandwidth, amount of
 associated computing, and cost for computing, data transfer, and storage. Primarily due to cost
 issues with commercial clouds, the cosmological simulation community does not see this option
 as being viable currently, but this situation could change very quickly. Some initial tests with
 cloud vendors are expected in the coming years to address some aspects of the experimental
 workflow. An anticipated advantage is the ability to make data available, with server-side
 compute, while placing the cost of using the data onto the end user, who may be supported by a
 different funding agency/source or country. On-premise cloud availability at the DOE facilities
 would be very beneficial, as other HEP experiments like Rubin have explored. [Section 4.8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 69

 • A possible disruptive element for cosmological simulation is the role of AI/ML in low-level
 simulation and analysis code, as well as at the catalog analysis level. Since such techniques
 are typically very data intensive, it is conceivable that the associated network requirements
 might be significant, especially if compute resources are not local to where the data are
 available. [Section 4.8]

 • Long-term storage of large-scale cosmological simulation data remains a critical problem to
 address, since much of it is often connected to ALCC and INCITE programs that have finite
 lifetimes. IRI and HPDF should present a global solution to this problem, to be deterministic
 about the way that long-running simulation efforts can be cataloged, stored, and found by the
 global community. [Section 4.9]

 • All of the factors that exacerbate the issue of long-term storage for cosmological simulation may
 not have a single unified solution, and may require a variety of approaches. If a single location
 cannot become the home for data sets, there must be efforts to unify a cataloging system to
 enable locality searches, despite the distributed nature of the data. This would be an excellent
 IRI project candidate. [Section 4.9]

 HPDF development.

6.1.2 Cosmological Simulation Research: Experiment Profile
For the purpose of this case study, supercomputers function as data-generating instruments running flagship-
scale simulations. Indeed, cosmological simulations can, in principle, easily generate far more data than optical
and microwave observations. This is expected to be the case even when data becomes available from the Rubin
Observatory, the largest of the imaging surveys, which is expected to begin operations in 2026. Halo/galaxy
catalogs from simulations are typically far larger than their on-sky counterparts: estimation of statistical errors
relies on hundreds to tens of thousands of simulated examples (or more), and cosmologists often need to simulate
results obtained from dozens to hundreds of varying simulation input conditions. While the on-sky pixel-level
data can in some cases be larger, the simulated catalogs are already at the level of PBs for large simulation
suites — in fact they could be larger, but storage constraints have been a continuing limitation. The size,
sophistication, and realism of simulated sky catalogs has improved significantly since the last report and this puts
further stress on storage and data-transfer capabilities. As mentioned above, many simulations are also needed
whenever one wants to match the simulations to the actual data, by reconstruction of initial conditions. In this
inverse problem application, one iterates on the initial guess, and after convergence one wants to sample from the
posterior, where each operation is a separate simulation.

6.1.2.1 Science Background
Typically, the dataflow consists of two stages: (1) within the facility where the simulation is run (supercomputer,
storage, analysis system) and (2) from the host facility to a remote analysis/archive site. The data motion may be
staged in a scheduled manner or can be highly bursty, depending on the use case. In the future, especially in
the IRI context, control of the dataflow may be centralized or distributed to a few “trunk” sites. As simulations
become more integral to the work of individual researchers, there is a potential to investigate 1) the concept of
distributed analysis sites that will better adjust to the workflow demands, or 2) on-demand data-intensive analysis
capabilities at the DOE computing centers as an IRI/HPDF development. Further, if the data sets are too large
to store locally by individual research groups, then it may be necessary to stream the data for on-the-fly analysis,

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 70

which can then lead to repeated downloads and analyses coordinated with the data flow. This situation may be
exacerbated as AI/ML frameworks can be essentially instantaneous sources of large-scale data; at the same time
this difficulty can be ameliorated if only the models were sent over and local computational and storage resources
were sufficient to meet the demand. In future, it is possible that these workflows will need to be integrated with
commercial cloud infrastructure.

The data generated from the simulations exist at multiple levels, from the basic representation used in the codes
(particles, fields), to science-level information (e.g., dark matter density and velocity fields, gas distribution,
velocities and temperatures, halo and galaxy information), to catalog-level information (properties of simulated
galaxies). The usage pattern varies from the group that generated the data analyzing them, to working within
distributed collaborations, and to making the results publicly available. Results from major simulation runs can be
useful for many years, up to a decade or more in some cases.

Data sets are typically owned by the team that generated them, unless the work was specifically part of a
collaboration and/or commissioned by the collaboration. But the increasing requirements toward open
science — as well as a sense that such simulations are useful for a wide range of applications — has led to more
interest in placing simulation results in the public domain. Funding agencies can put requirements on the data
sets corresponding to making subsets publicly available. The primary barrier to making simulation data sets
public is the lack of available storage and/or server-side public-access compute capability. This is an excellent
opportunity for an interaction with the IRI effort.

6.1.2.2 Collaborators
All the HEP Labs (Argonne, BNL, Fermilab, LBNL, and SLAC) participate in this work, as well as other labs
(Los Alamos National Laboratory, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, ORNL) and a large number of
collaborating universities, including the University of California, Berkeley, the University of Chicago, Harvard
University, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the University of Pennsylvania, Stanford University, the
University of Washington, Yale University, and many others. Many of the collaborations involve directly working
with the associated experiments (e.g., Cosmic Microwave Background Stage IV (CMB-S4), Dark Energy Survey
(DES), (DESI, Rubin Observatory LSST — Dark Energy Science Collaboration (LSST DESC), South Pole
Telescope (SPT). Computational facilities used include ALCF, NERSC, and OLCF as well as NSF computing
facilities, along with institutional resources available at the participating institutions.

The data products generated by simulation groups are used downstream by a large number of users who are
members of science working groups in cosmological surveys and experiments. A common use pattern is to build a
mock survey from the simulation data, then perform a clustering analysis on that survey. In the future, the ratio of
the user community to the size of the simulation groups will only increase as the role of simulations continues to
become more important. Thus, the dataflow pattern will likely become more diverse and there will be increased
pressure on data-transfer facilities. Although the main focus is the continental US, the geographical locations of
the endpoints are worldwide. The diversity of endpoints and the number of geographical locations is expected to
grow significantly.

The data sources are major computing centers and the major analysis endpoints are typically also the same
centers. Large DOE collaborations have accounts at these centers, especially at NERSC. Data access for local
analysis at secondary sites is provided by the primary data-holding facilities. Public data sets from other efforts
can also be made available through these sites.

The number of users can vary considerably depending on the use cases. Analysis of individual simulation outputs
may involve small teams, but curation and use of synthetic catalogs by survey teams may involve multiple projects
with hundreds of people across the projects. Cosmological survey collaborations are growing in size and are
almost at the same scale as high energy physics experiments (Rubin’s LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration
has, for example, more than a thousand members). Another trend is the use of multiple data sources (cross-
correlation) in cosmology. Simulations are now designed to provide outputs for multiple types of observations so
that they can be of use to multiple surveys.

There are too many potential endpoints to list individually in Table 6.1.1. The science collaborations typically
have a large number of members (hundreds), from a large number of institutions (~100) all of whom have the
right to specific simulation data products. Each consumer endpoint also varies significantly in how much data
throughput and volume it can support (from individual desktops to institutional clusters, to cloud usage). Another
thing to keep in mind is that in future there may be the need to support a much larger number of users, for
example, as part of Rubin Observatory’s user base, but this remains to be negotiated. Automation of data transfer
with analysis workflows will be an important feature of future applications, which is not properly captured in
Table 6.1.1.

6.1.2.3 IRI Readiness
The cosmological simulation community is extremely interested in working with the IRI given the multiple DOE
facilities that are used, and have major interests in expanding the coordination across sites that is potentially
possible. There are a number of areas, such as integrated workflows (including computation and wide-area data
movement), federated identity management, and single-point data management that can be significant early use
case examples for IRI. In these scenarios, simulation datasets would typically exercise the Data Integration–
Intensive and Long-Term Campaign patterns.

6.1.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
The work performed is primarily computational — the major facilities used are primarily those at the ALCF
(Polaris and Frontier, once accepted), NERSC (Perlmutter), and OLCF (Frontier). The use case consists of
running large simulations on the primary systems, carrying out analyses on these as well as smaller satellite
machines, and making the data available for downstream work. Smaller local resources are available at a number
of participating institutions. Institutional storage ranges from ~100 TB to a few PB, and internal data-transfer
rates are typically hundreds of Gbps bandwidths, but can sometimes be lower. This level of storage is significantly
smaller than the total storage available at the HPC centers, which, it is important to note, is increasing relatively
slowly. Additionally, long-term storage of large-scale simulation data remains a problem since much of it is often
connected to ALCC and INCITE programs that have finite lifetimes. An exception is the availability of Kronos at
OLCF; eventually IRI/HPDF should present a global solution to this problem.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 72

The cosmological simulation community does not foresee a change in the modus operandi over the next five years
(and even beyond, unless cloud facilities — which are otherwise very capable and currently dwarf DOE HPC
resources — become cost-competitive). Transfer rates are expected to improve as infrastructure upgrades
are made. Data storage needs post mid-2020s are likely to be in the ~300 PB range of spinning disk
equivalent (although given how slowly the accessible storage has grown, this may be unrealistic), requiring
transfer rates of >300 Gbps (intermittent).

6.1.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
The simulation results can be viewed as corresponding to three levels of data that are used for science. Level 1 is
the raw data from the simulations, level 2 is intermediate-level analysis data, and level 3 is level 2 data reduced
to the level of catalogs/databases (when possible), including large-scale sky maps covering a wide range of
observables. Level 1 analysis can be performed both in in situ or post-processing modes, while level 2 and level 3
analyses are primarily in post-processing mode, although this is changing to in situ modes in some cases. All three
levels are part of the local and remote “process of science.” Level 1 and 2 data analyses involve batch processing,
while level 3 analyses can have a significant level of interactivity, so the data access patterns can be quite different
(in the future, this last case may have some interesting IRI-related consequences).

In situ analysis uses the supercomputer’s own network, or co-scheduled computational resources, whereas level 2
and level 3 analyses can be conducted locally or remotely and may involve moving data from file systems back to
the host supercomputer or to analysis resources. This is where the networking support is most important. Level
2/3 data may also be moved over in batches to remote sites where they can be locally analyzed. Note that the
actual mass of data at the three levels is roughly similar, except that the granularity increases significantly from
level 1 to level 3.

Future activity will be along the lines mentioned previously, and this effort should not change significantly over
the next five years.

6.1.2.6 Remote Science Activities
As already stated, the major computational facilities used are primarily those at the ALCF, NERSC, and OLCF.
Storage is provided at the facilities at the level of hundreds of TB to low PB per sub-project of disk (potentially
larger, in some instances) and substantially more on tape. The larger allocations have included special dispensations
for the ALCC and INCITE program projects. Some pre-IRI activities might also be given relatively large
allocations. The major data sources are the supercomputers and other associated compute resources (analysis and
visualization clusters). The use of cloud resources may also be considered in the near future, both commercial and
institutional. WAN is typically via Internet2 and ESnet. This mode of operation is expected to remain unchanged
over the next five years.

The current data stream involves typically moving ~10–100 TB of bulk data, with larger transfers carried out on
occasion. The much smaller “user” downloads to local storage typically involve <1 TB chunks of data. Progress
in remote visualization methods should allow (almost) real-time visualization of many large data sets. Examples of
this capability already exist but are not being used in production.

As to the supercomputers themselves, significant architectural changes are unlikely over the next five years, but
in any case, these will not be disruptive with respect to the networks.

Over this time span, a few major simulation data archive/analysis centers will emerge (e.g., increase in size of
the community file systems at the leadership computing facilities (LCFs) and NERSC, potential on-pre/remote
cloud services). Most of the data will eventually be hosted there; they should also have substantial local analysis
computing available (since computing must follow the data) — this is essentially an argument for the HPDF and
would be a good example case for an HPDF pilot (of course, the HPDF timeline is uncertain).

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 73

The data stream will consist of two major types:

 • “Feeders” to the data centers, moving ~PB, and
 • Data center to “user” links which would typically move <100 TB data chunks (possibly
 interactive and part of a wider workflow).
Remote visualization methods should allow real-time visualization of many large data sets.

6.1.2.7 Software Infrastructure
There will be some changes to simulation software, but these are unlikely to be very significant (at least partly
due to inertia, because of the size of the current software base). Most of the changes that were expected beyond
the early 2020s (e.g., ECP-related) have been made already. Additionally, architecture changes in next-generation
supercomputers are expected to be evolutionary, with a corresponding situation for developing tool infrastructure.

Software infrastructure for data management varies widely. The use of code repositories is now widespread.
Higher-level workflow tools to manage simulations and simulation analysis (including remote analysis) are slowly
emerging, although most of this work is still performed by hand-written scripts. Software containers are seeing
more use for complex software stacks. Data transfer is primarily through Globus, which has proven very effective
both within institutions and externally as a graphical tool or when coupled with a portal. A number of tools are
used to process data sets, including embedded capabilities (e.g., data compression within I/O). The use of data
containers (HDF5, PnetCDF) is sometimes limited by their reliance on message passing interface (MPI) -IO;
HDF5 is also considered to be too complex by some users. Native I/O tools written for simulation codes still
obtain the best performance.

Over the next two to five years, there will be an evolution in workflow tools to manage local and remote
simulation data analysis. This area is still in flux, and community desires are only slowly being captured in a
design process, mostly because of the complex nature of the requirements and the dynamic nature of the
use cases.

6.1.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
These factors are highly specific to individual programs and facilities. Much of the simulation activity involves the
use of DOE HPC centers that ESnet has already constructed sufficient network capabilities. For purposes of this
review, networking and data architecture features are not foreseen to be a major source of requirements versus
future HPC center/university compute and storage requirements.

6.1.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.1.2.9.1 Cloud Services
As far as cloud computing and storage are concerned, usage is primarily a question of latency, bandwidth, amount
of associated computing, and cost for computing, data transfer, and storage. Primarily due to cost issues with
commercial clouds, the cosmological simulation community does not see this option as being viable currently, but
this situation could change very quickly. Some initial tests with cloud vendors are expected shortly.

There are several attractive features of the cloud model, including virtualization and resource elasticity; there
is an expectation that these will become ever more important with time and to drive increased use of cloud
resources. Another advantage is the ability to make data available, with server-side compute, while placing the
cost of using the data onto the end user, who may be supported by a different funding agency/source or country.
On-premise cloud availability at the DOE facilities would be very beneficial.

More recently, cloud hosting of supercomputing (CPU/GPU) at massive scales and specialized AI/ML-optimized
hardware, such as Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), has added a new layer of capability that has potential benefits
for cosmological simulations and the associated data analysis, especially since the AI/ML capabilities can be easily

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 74

exploited with productivity languages such as Python. Cost concerns remain the key issue given the scale of the
operational requirements.

6.1.2.9.2 Artificial Intelligence and ML
The cosmological simulation community uses a broad set of ML tools, such as classic approaches embodied
by principal component analysis (PCA) and Gaussian Processes. Additionally, there has been an explosion of
interest in modern AI/ML for a variety of applications, especially in the area of generative models, inference, and
speeding up simulations by replacing traditional compute kernels by AI/ML “look-up” methods. There is also
considerable interest in applying these techniques for analyses that go beyond conventional summary statistics.
Since DOE supercomputers are all based (mostly) on GPUs, they are highly suited to large-scale AI/ML training
and inference — it is easy for the simulation community to utilize these resources for AI/ML applications.

6.1.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
There are no use cases that involve these types of activities.

6.1.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
This work continues to be substantially limited by the availability of storage, particularly when considering how
to distribute the simulation data beyond the group that performed the simulation. Further, the need for storage
beyond the initial computing project is critical; the lifetime of the need is often set by the life cycle of the analysis,
which is happening in larger collaborations, and as the projects become more complex, over longer timelines.

The network speeds between major centers are not a limitation, and transferring PB-sized data sets is effectively
routine. This size is expected to increase in the coming years but not by a large factor. User-level transfer remains
smaller, as downloading entire catalogs is still not a typical use case.

6.1.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
The cosmological simulation community is using the DTNs at ALCF, NERSC, and OLCF for most of the large-
scale traffic.

6.1.2.12 Outstanding Issues
The following factors are considered to be high priority for the long-term success of this community:

 • A possible disruptive element is the role of AI/ML in low-level simulation and analysis code,
 as well as at the catalog analysis level. Since such techniques are typically very data intensive,
 it is conceivable that the associated network requirements might be significant, especially if
 compute resources are not local to where the data are available.

 • Storage for simulations will continue to be a critical issue over time. Some projects are more
 storage-limited than they are compute-limited. This issue has several associated dimensions
 to consider:

 ° Sizes and numbers of simulations will increase.

 ° Locations producing simulations are expected to increase.

 ° Funding spans different agencies.

 ° Usefulness over time, and to different communities, is increasing.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 75

 • All of the factors that exacerbate the issue of long-term storage may not have a single unified
 solution, and may require a variety of approaches. If a single location cannot become the home
 for data sets, there must be efforts to unify a cataloging system to enable locality searches,
 despite the distributed nature of the data. This would be an excellent IRI project candidate.

 • Data movement between facilities is not a critical problem, but broad access to the user
 community remains challenging. Simplifying the access method to use updated portal software,
 or tools like Globus, has improved data mobility. The next step is to combine this dynamic
 access to computing resources.
