6.2 DESI
DESI is a DOE-led international cosmology collaboration which is creating the world’s largest 3D map of the
universe. A five-year survey started in 2021 to observe the spectra of tens of millions of galaxies, quasars, and
stars. These data are used to construct the map to study the origins of the accelerated expansion of the universe
and test models of gravity.

6.2.1 Discussion Summary
DESI’s infrastructure relies on two major components that are linked via network infrastructure: KPNO and
NERSC. There are a number of other instruments at the KPNO facility, and all share a common 1 Gbps-capable
network connection from the summit to a base station. A larger 10 Gbps network then links the base station to
the rest of the R&E community. These connections have experienced trouble in the past; natural disasters (e.g.,
wildfire) have severed connectivity, and bandwidth limitations imply that all scientific operations must share
the common connection fairly. Beyond the network, computing at a single site (e.g., NERSC) means that all
associated operations can be brought to a halt should there be planned or unplanned maintenance. This can limit
productivity, given there is no back-up option, which can impact real-time requirements. DESI has ways to buffer
data when NERSC is unavailable, but is otherwise stalled without alternative computing mechanisms.

Despite the challenges of network availability, the network requirements are relatively modest. An entire night’s
observation can reach 100 GB or more (and the tooling understands to rsync the last 40 TB of collected data,
in the event of network interruption), which is typically sent in bursts every 10 minutes via tools like rsync. In
a worst-case scenario, use of transportable media could be used to take an evening’s worth of data manually
down to the base station, or through a slower network path such as a LEO Satellite (e.g., Starlink). This could
potentially disrupt the nightly calibration. ESnet will work with DESI, and the partners of KNPO to investigate
the network connectivity, and offer pathways to increase the reliability, capacity, or develop alternative methods.

DESI computing is done using interactive computing methods at NERSC, namely Jupyter Notebooks. DESI
has considered moving to more widely available computing options not tied to a single facility, such as a cloud
platform (similar to those that the Rubin Observatory has adopted); a core concern lies in the user community
however, who are slow to adopt new approaches to computing and are making do with legacy tools for a lot of the
analysis process. Investment into a new system halfway through an experiment is not feasible to consider.

One area of friction that could be addressed is an easier method to manage data mobility outside of the NERSC
facilities. Data can be egressed via approaches like Globus, but this typically only is an option for users who are
familiar with the tool, and have the necessary credentials to manage it. An efficient tool that works like more
commercial tools (e.g., Dropbox, iPhoto, etc.) may appeal to the users. Typically, users do not want to be bothered
with the functional details of a data mobility tool, and just want things to work efficiently and simply; rsync is easy
enough to understand wherein data appears in the correct folders without much thought. For this reason, it is
unlikely that DESI would adopt some of the other tools that the HEP community has championed (e.g., Rucio),
as the cultural shift required to do so is not very strong.

Another related area of friction remains the mechanisms that are used to manage identity and permissions for
users. A common problem is the management of credentials to access computation and storage (e.g., NERSC)
and how these may differ from accounts used to manage other aspects of the scientific workflow (e.g., home
institutional accounts, NOIRLab accounts, etc.). DESI is a firm supporter of the work IRI is investigating to
simplify this aspect of the scientific workflow.

 • DESI is a DOE-led international cosmology collaboration that started in 2021, and will operate
 for five years. The project will create the world’s largest 3D map of the universe. DESI utilizes
 the Mayall 4-meter telescope, located at KPNO outside of Tucson, AZ. [Section 4.1]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 77

 • NERSC in Berkeley, CA, is used as the primary scientific analysis center for DESI, and the
 facility hosts the ~1000-person international collaboration of scientists, who access the data the
 cosmology analyses. [Section 4.1]

 • At NERSC, the data volume is projected to grow at a rate of ~1 PB/year from 2020-2025,
 reaching ~10 PB by the end of 2026. The data are stored in a hierarchy of thousands of
 directories with millions of files. Extensions to the DESI have been proposed and received
 positive reviews; if approved these would continue the data growth at a similar rate through the
           mid-2030s. [Section 4.2]

 • Public datasets will be curated beyond the timescale of DESI by the Astro Data Lab
 at NOIRLab. The intention is to also host the public DESI data via the Cosmology Data
 Repository at NERSC, though long-term funding commitment for that is not
 guaranteed. [Section 4.2]

 • Science analyses using DESI data are primarily performed at NERSC, with the scale of
 analyses varying from single-core Jupyter Notebooks to large parallel-batch jobs. Many of the
 analyses make use of simulated datasets generated at NERSC, while some others are generated
 at their DOE HPC facilities and transferred to NERSC. [Section 4.3]

 • Every ~15 minutes, DESI obtains spectra of 5000 astronomical objects, resulting in 1–2 GB of
 raw data per exposure. Data is processed at NERSC in semi-real time (minutes to hours after
 capture), and results in a processed file size of ~10 GB per exposure. DESI projects that the
 total data volume will grow to O(10 PB) by the end of the survey. [Section 4.3]

 • Every one to two years, DESI reprocesses all the data taken to date using the latest data-
 processing code and calibrations. These serve as reference datasets for cosmology
 papers and are publicly released six months after the key cosmology projects have been
 published. [Section 4.3]

 • Transfers of processed data from NERSC to the NOIRLab and University of Utah mirrors use
 Globus for the initial bulk transfer, then rsync to pick up any later differences. [Section 4.3]

 • The DESI collaboration space at NERSC will eventually host 10PB of experimental data. These
 data are processed nightly, and analyzed by users that access NERSC from remote locations.
 Backups are performed to HPSS at NERSC, and mirrored to partner facilities (NOIRLab in
 Tucson, AZ, and the University of Utah). [Section 4.4]

 • Collaborators primarily access the data through direct login to NERSC, or through NERSC’s
 Jupyter server. Many collaborators have expressed a preference for downloading subsets of
 data to use locally, though DESI lacks developed tools for easy management of that remote
 analysis workflow. This is currently achieved through ad hoc downloads with Globus, scp, or
 https. [Section 4.5]

 • The primary data access mode for DESI is for collaborators to directly login to NERSC directly,
 and perform work at the location of the data. It is possible for collaborators to download a subset
 of data, for processing at local institutions for analysis. Public (noncollaborator) access is only
 through downloads from NERSC, or through Jupyter servers at the NOIRLab AstroData Lab,
 who host a subset of the public DESI data. [Section 4.5]

 • DESI data from KNPO is transferred in 10-minute intervals to NERSC using rsync. This rsync
 tool is not known for high performance, however the cadence of the experiment dictates that
 nightly data collection is less than 100 GB and must reach NERSC via network that is limited to
 1 Gbps between the telescopes at KPNO and the base station; use of more advanced tools will
 not improve the overall process of science. [Section 4.6]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 78

 • DESI is fundamentally a multisite experiment, with data from a telescope in Arizona (KPNO),
 a primary computing center in California (NERSC), and a worldwide collaboration of scientists.
 DESI is currently limited in its ability to utilize non-NERSC DOE computing facilities for a
 variety of reasons, including: [Section 4.6]

 ° The ability to manage accounts for hundreds of users across different sites

 ° Creating a system to synchronize PB-scale datasets of millions of files between
 multiple sites

 • Raw data are directly downloaded from KPNO to NERSC, which routes via the University of
 Arizona in Tucson where it picks up Internet2. The bandwidth limited step is the KPNO to
 Tucson 1 Gbps fiber link leased from the Tohono O’odham Utility Authority. [Section 4.7]

 • As a remote mountain site, KPNO has occasional network outages so a key operational
 requirement is that observations can continue without network connectivity. As an extreme case,
 in 2022 a wildfire melted the internet fiber optic cables to the telescope. Operations proceeded
 for several months with a minimal Starlink connection for instrument command and control, and
 external hard drives with data shuttled up and down the mountain by car. The hard drives were
 connected to computers in Tucson each day to initiate the data transfer to NERSC. [Section 4.7]

 • DESI does not currently use cloud services for data processing or serving core data products.
 There has been exploratory work for sharing DESI data through the Amazon Open Data
 program, though this is not used by the collaboration itself. There has been interest in deploying
 the data-processing pipeline on AWS as an alternate site during NERSC outages, though data
 transfer and hosting costs make this prohibitive as a primary computing solution. [Section 4.8]

 • DESI makes some use of AI/ML for its data-processing pipeline through fairly standard
 methods that do not require any special resources. There is more active cutting-edge work on
 using AI/ML for DESI science analyses, in particular using generative AI to create simulated/
 mock datasets faster than traditional simulations. At the same time, these use standard toolkits
 and NERSC Perlmutter computing and do not require novel hardware or tools. [Section 4.8]

 • DESI has used Starlink at the remote telescope site as a back-up connection solution for when
 the primary internet is down. This was especially critical in 2022 after a wildfire resulted in
 a multi-month outage of the fiber optic connection to the mountain. The Starlink bandwidth
 was sufficient for command and control of the telescope, but was not sufficient for transferring
 observational data, which required driving hard disks up and down the mountain. [Section 4.8]

 • The DESI data lifecycle involves all three of the IRI patterns: [Section 4.9]
 ° Time-Sensitive analysis to detect operations problems and update the survey plan;

 ° Data Integration–Intensive work to combine PB-scale data from multiple other
 collaborations and funding agencies for analysis;

 ° Long-Term Campaigns to process data for the five-year DESI survey, with proposed
 extensions and follow-up programs through at least 2042.

 • DESI uses Globus for transfers of collaboration data. DESI users report good experiences
 with Globus when they want to download an entire directory tree, but have found the interface
 lacking for the more common use case of selecting a subset of data from a complex directory
 tree, e.g., all files matching a given regex regardless of where they appear in the directory
 structure. [Section 5.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 79

 • Within the NERSC computing center, DESI is limited by I/O performance stability of
 the “community file system” — median performance is fine, but semi-rare outlier events can
 cause multi-minute delays or even lead to job hangs/timeouts. The Perlmutter scratch disk
 performance is better, but the difficulties of constantly syncing datasets between the scratch
 filesystem and CFS has been human-error prone and effort-prohibitive. [Section 5.4]

 • The inability to pragmatically synchronize constantly evolving PB-scale datasets between
 multiple locations is a limiting factor for DESI. That includes internal to a data center (e.g.,
 between CFS and the scratch filesystem) and external (e.g., between NERSC and another DOE
 HPC facility). [Section 5.4]

 • Broadly speaking, DESI is not limited by raw bandwidth, but is limited by the convenience of
 tools for managing cross-site data flow. Globus is efficient for one-off data transfers, but issues
 such as expiring certificates, multi-factor-authentication, data discovery, and data filtering (i.e.,
 selecting what needs to be downloaded) limit convenience for day-to-day random access of
 huge datasets. It is desirable to consider if computing centers and end users would be able to
 subscribe to datasets from each other, with automatic efficient syncing of the subsets of the data
 that are actively being used, with the toolkits managing purging unused data to stay within the
 local quota limits. The faster the network is, the more viable this becomes since it reduces the
 barrier to having to re-download data. [Section 5.5]

 • Using a single centralized HPC facility to support a given HEP experiment is beneficial, since
 there’s a single ecosystem to learn and it requires minimal overhead to share results with
 collaborators from other institutions. At the same time, it becomes a single point of failure
 during NERSC outages leading to ongoing interest in multisite computing operations in the
 future. The limiting factors are not networking for data transfer, but rather the tools for making
 that data sharing automated and transparent for hundreds of users accessing PBs of data stored
 in millions of files. DESI could transfer its major data release to another site, but that is of little
 use unless the hundreds of DESI users at NERSC can also get accounts at that site, and the
 outputs of their daily work can be transparently synced back and forth between the two sites.
           [Section 5.6]

6.2.2 DESI: Experiment Profile
Observations begin at the Mayall 4-meter telescope at KPNO outside of Tucson, AZ. Every ~15 minutes, DESI
obtains spectra of 5000 astronomical objects, resulting in 1–2 GB of data per exposure. These data are transferred
in semi-real time to the NERSC in Berkeley, CA, where they are processed in a real-time queue such that results
from each night are available to collaboration scientists each morning. Processed data are ~10 GB/exposure.
Results from each night are used to update the observing plan for the following night. Real-time quality assurance
(QA) analysis is performed at both KPNO and NERSC to guide observers throughout the night. Hosting the QA
at KPNO allows DESI to be robust to network and NERSC outages, while simultaneously processing at NERSC
enables read-only access for all collaborators without requiring secure access to the mission-critical operations
at KPNO.

6.2.2.1 Science Background
NERSC is also used as the primary scientific analysis center for the ~1000-person international collaboration of
scientists, who access the data at NERSC for the cosmology analyses. Every one to two years, DESI reprocesses
all the data taken to date using the latest data-processing code and calibrations. These serve as reference datasets
for cosmology papers and are publicly released six months after the key cosmology projects have been published.
DESI projects that the total data volume will grow to O(10 PB) by the end of the survey. The primary data access
mode is for collaborators to directly login to NERSC and perform their work there. Some collaborators download
a subset of the data to their local institutions for analysis. Public (noncollaborator) access is only through
downloads from NERSC, or through Jupyter servers at the NOIRLab AstroData Lab, who host a subset of the
public DESI data.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 80

6.2.2.2 Collaborators
DESI is an international collaboration with O(1000) collaborators from over 70 institutions in 10 countries
spanning North and South America, Europe, Asia, and Australia. The primary data access and sharing occurs
through direct logins to NERSC. This is motivated both by the scale of the data (PBs), and through the need for a
centralized location to share results between collaborators from many institutions.

Some DESI collaborators also download subsets of the data for analysis at their local institutions. Small volumes
of data are typically accessed via scp or https, while more expert users download larger datasets using Globus.

Public (noncollaborator) access is either through direct download from NERSC (Globus or https), or through
Jupyter Notebooks at the NOIRLab AstroData Lab, who host a subset of the DESI public data.

A mirror of the raw data is kept at the Astro Data Lab at the NSF’s National Optical Infrared Astronomy
Research Laboratory (NSF’s NOIRLab) in Tucson, AZ, and a mirror of a subset of the processed data is kept
at the University of Utah. These provide a geographically separated copy of the data for safety in case of a
catastrophic event at NERSC, but they are not used for primary analyses.

Most of DESI’s data are still proprietary, though an “Early Data Release” in 2023 provided pre-survey data to the
scientific community. Future data releases (approximately every two years) will expand the user base of
DESI data.

6.2.2.3 IRI Readiness
The DESI data lifecycle involves all three of these patterns: Time-Sensitive analysis to detect operations
problems and update the survey plan; Data Integration–Intensive work to combine PB-scale data from multiple
other collaborations and funding agencies for analysis; and Long-Term Campaigns to process data for the five-year
DESI survey, with proposed extensions and follow-up programs through at least 2042.

DESI is fundamentally a multisite experiment, with data from a telescope in Arizona, a primary computing center
in California (NERSC), and a worldwide collaboration of scientists. DESI is currently limited in its ability to
utilize non-NERSC DOE computing facilities for a variety of reasons including

 ° Account management for hundreds of users across different sites (ideally this would be a
 single approval + account, allowing access to all sites with the same credentials)

 ° How to real-time sync PB-scale datasets of millions of files between multiple sites

 ° Ecosystem differences in queue policy, web servers, Jupyter access, etc., i.e., a workflow (or
 even a single Jupyter Notebook) that works at one site requires significant overhead to port
 to another DOE facility.

6.2.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
Data originates from the DESI spectrographs at the Mayall 4-meter telescope at the KPNO near Tucson, AZ.
Raw data are transferred to NERSC for processing and science analysis, with subsets of the processed data
downloaded to individual institutions for further customized/ad hoc analysis. Raw and processed data are backed
up to NERSC’s HPSS tape system. Raw data are also mirrored to NOIRLab in Tucson, AZ and a subset of
processed data are mirrored to the University of Utah as geographically separated sites from NERSC. Raw data
are retained at KPNO until they are verified to be at NERSC disk, NERSC tape, and NOIRLab disk.

Raw data are directly downloaded from KPNO to NERSC, which routes via the University of Arizona in Tucson
where it picks up Internet2. The bandwidth limited step is the KPNO to Tucson 1 Gbps fiber link leased from the
Tohono O’odham Utility Authority, though this is sufficient for the needs of DESI and other telescopes operating
at KPNO. A small cluster of computers at KPNO supports observations, but this is not provided as a general
resource to the collaboration for data analysis. As a remote mountain site, KPNO has occasional network outages
so a key operational requirement is that observations can continue without network connectivity. As an extreme
case, in 2022 a wildfire melted the internet fiber optic cables to the telescope. Operations proceeded for several
months with a minimal Starlink connection for instrument command and control, and external hard drives with
data shuttled up and down the mountain by car. The hard drives were connected to computers in Tucson each day
to initiate the data transfer to NERSC.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 82

At NERSC, the data volume is projected to grow at a rate of ~1 PB/year from 2020 to 2025, reaching ~10 PB by
the end of 2026. The data are stored in a hierarchy of thousands of directories with millions of files. Extensions to
the DESI have been proposed and received positive reviews; if approved these would continue the data growth
at a similar rate through the mid-2030s.

Public datasets will be curated beyond the timescale of DESI by the Astro Data Lab at NOIRLab. The intention
is to also host the public DESI data via the Cosmology Data Repository at NERSC, though long-term funding
commitment for that is not guaranteed.

DESI uses the full ecosystem of services available at NERSC: data transfer nodes; the real-time queue for rapid
processing; the interactive queue for data analysis by collaborators; the regular queue for large reprocessing runs;
database servers; webservers for data distribution and visualization; and a Jupyter server for data exploration.

6.2.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
Science analyses using DESI data are primarily performed at NERSC, with the scale of analyses varying from
single-core Jupyter Notebooks to large parallel-batch jobs. Networking is used to get raw data to NERSC,
to make off-site backups of processed data, and for some users to download subsets of the data to their local
institutions. Many of the analyses also make use of simulated datasets. Most of these are directly generated at
NERSC, while some others are generated elsewhere (e.g., Oakridge) and transferred to NERSC.

Using a single centralized facility provides benefits of a single ecosystem to learn, and minimal overhead for
sharing results with collaborators from other institutions. At the same time, it becomes a single point of failure
during NERSC outages leading to ongoing interest in multisite computing operations in the future. The limiting
factors are not network bandwidth for data transfer, but rather the tools for making that data sharing automated
and transparent for hundreds of users accessing PBs of data stored in millions of files. E.g., DESI could transfer
its major data release to another site, but that is of little use unless the hundreds of DESI users at NERSC can
also get accounts at that site, and the outputs of their daily work can be transparently synced back and forth
between the two sites.

6.2.2.6 Remote Science Activities
The data are obtained at KPNO (near Tucson, AZ), processed at NERSC (in Berkeley, CA), and accessed by a
worldwide collaboration, so the workflow is fundamentally and permanently multisite. Although the total data
volume will grow to be rather large at NERSC (~10 PB), the real-time bandwidth requirements to support the
operations are relatively modest (e.g., transferring a burst of 1 to 2 GB every 15 minutes from KPNO to NERSC
throughout the night). Remote collaboration access to the data is more limited by the convenience of the tools
than raw network bandwidth.

6.2.2.7 Software Infrastructure
Data transfer from KPNO to NERSC is performed with rsync spawned by a custom daemon-like python script
that checks for new data every 10 minutes. Backups to NERSC HPSS tape use HPSS Tape Archiver (HTAR).
Transfers of processed data from NERSC to the NOIRLab and University of Utah mirrors use Globus for the
initial bulk transfer, then rsync to pick up any later differences. Transfers of data within the NERSC center use a
combination of Globus, rsync, and Unix cp.

Collaborators primarily access the data through direct login to NERSC, or through NERSC’s Jupyter server.
Many collaborators have expressed a preference for downloading subsets of data to use locally, though DESI
lacks developed tools for easy management of that remote analysis workflow. This is currently achieved through
ad hoc downloads with Globus, scp, or https.

Data processing is performed at NERSC using Python scripts, leveraging numpy, scipy, cupy, numba, and mpi4py
for efficiency and parallelism. The workflow is entirely file-based and does not rely upon a centralized database or
workflow server for job coordination.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 83

6.2.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.2.2.9.1 Cloud Services
DESI uses AWS for hosting their wiki, svn repository, mailing lists, document repository, publication database,
desi.lbl.gov website, and a public-facing version of the imaging data browser.17

DESI does not currently use cloud services for data processing or serving core data products. There has been
exploratory work for sharing DESI data through the Amazon Open Data program, though this is not used by the
collaboration itself.

There has been interest in deploying the data-processing pipeline on AWS as an alternate site during NERSC
outages, though data transfer and hosting costs make this prohibitive as a primary computing solution.

17 http://viewer.legacysurvey.org

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 84

6.2.2.9.2 AI and ML
DESI makes some use of AI/ML for its data-processing pipeline through fairly standard methods of random
forests and convolutional neural networks that do not require any special resources. The most custom aspect
is that DESI wrote its own pure-numpy evaluators of these models that do not rely upon external libraries
like scikitLearn or TensorFlow. This provides long term (5–10+ years) reproducibility in a way that is not
possible with the rapidly evolving landscape of AI/ML libraries that do not guarantee decade-level backwards
compatibility.

There is more active cutting-edge work on using AI/ML for DESI science analyses, in particular using generative
AI to create simulated/mock datasets faster than traditional simulations. At the same time, these use standard
toolkits and NERSC Perlmutter computing and do not require novel hardware or tools.

6.2.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
DESI has used Starlink at the remote telescope site as a back-up connection solution for when the primary
internet is down. This was especially critical in 2022 after a wildfire resulted in a multi-month outage of the
fiber optic connection to the mountain. The Starlink bandwidth was sufficient for command and control of the
telescope, but was not sufficient for transferring observational data, which required driving hard disks up and
down the mountain.

6.2.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
Within the NERSC computing center, DESI is limited by I/O performance stability of the “community file
system” — median performance is fine, but semi-rare outlier events can cause multi-minute delays or even lead
to job hangs/timeouts. The Perlmutter scratch disk performance is better, but the difficulties of constantly syncing
datasets between the scratch filesystem and CFS has been human-error prone and effort-prohibitive.

More generally, the inability to pragmatically sync constantly evolving PB-scale datasets between multiple
locations is a limiting factor for DESI. That includes internal to a data center (e.g., between CFS and the scratch
filesystem) and external (e.g., between NERSC and another DOE computing facility).

Although astronomy datasets are made publicly available, this is done through https servers providing individual
files for download, not through systems designed for accessing and jointly processing entire datasets from
different sites, and it is rare for data portals to provide any significant amount of computing resources to process
their data by external users. This leaves users on their own to download and process data at different data centers
in an uncoordinated manner.

6.2.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
DESI uses the “NERSC DTN” Globus endpoint for transfers of proprietary collaboration data, and the “DESI
Public Data” Globus endpoint (also served from NERSC) for public data.

Overall users report good experiences with Globus when they want to download an entire directory tree, but
have found the interface lacking for the more common use case (for DESI users) of wanting to download a subset
of data from a complex directory tree, e.g., all files matching a given regex regardless of where they appear in the
directory structure.

6.2.2.12 Outstanding Issues
Broadly speaking, DESI is not limited by raw bandwidth — organizations like ESnet and Internet2 have stayed
ahead of the curve such that bandwidth is not a problem — Thanks! DESI is limited by the convenience of tools
for managing cross-site data flow. Globus was a huge step forward for efficient one-off data transfers, but issues
such as expiring certificates, multi-factor-authentication, data discovery, and data filtering (i.e., selecting what
needs to be downloaded) limit its convenience for day-to-day random access of huge datasets.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 85

Ideal would be something like Apple’s iCloud Photos — devices have access to a library of photos much larger
than can fit on the device, and all syncing back and forth between the device and the iCloud storage happens
transparently to the user. Ideally computing centers and end users would be able to subscribe to datasets from
each other, with automatic efficient syncing of the subsets of the data that are actively being used, with the
toolkits managing purging unused data to stay within the local quota limits. The faster the network is, the more
viable this becomes since it reduces the barrier to having to re-download data.

6.3 Vera C. Rubin Observatory
Rubin Observatory will carry out the LSST, using the Simonyi Survey Telescope and the Rubin Observatory
LSST Camera. It will take repeated images over more than 18,000 deg2 of the southern sky in six broad-band
optical filters (ugrizy). The resulting dataset will provide a static census of approximately 40 billion objects as
well as a dynamic time-domain census over an unprecedented range of time scales and flux limits. The primary
deliverables for Rubin Observatory include a real-time stream of “alerts” of transient events, prompt data
products, annual data-release data products, and a science platform specifically developed to reduce the barrier
of entry to Rubin Observatory data and to shorten the path to science for the user community.

6.3.1 Discussion Summary
Rubin does face several challenges, some of which are outside of the control of ESnet and DOE. Like other large
facilities, they must take cybersecurity into consideration. NOIRLab has been responsive to recent threats, and
has put in place controls that sometimes make collaboration harder. In addition, the theme of federated identity
management is also present for Rubin, and represents a barrier to the use of some tools. Rubin is looking to
adopt some of the tools used elsewhere in HEP for data mobility and workflow management, including Rucio.
The steps to integrate this work in their own environment have been challenging, and Rubin will be looking for
additional assistance and advice.

ESnet will follow up with international partners to include up-to-date networking maps of the corresponding
international paths.

 • Rubin Observatory will carry out the LSST, using the Simonyi Survey Telescope and the Rubin
 Observatory LSST Camera. It will take repeated images of the southern sky, and the resulting
 dataset will provide a static census of approximately 40 billion objects. The primary deliverables
 for Rubin Observatory include a real-time stream of “alerts” of transient events, prompt data
 products, annual data-release data products, and a science platform. [Section 4.1]

 • Rubin Observatory is an NSF-DOE funded partnership. Operations partners are NSF’s
 NOIRLab and SLAC, whose managing organizations are Association of Universities for
 Research in Astronomy, Inc. (AURA) and Stanford University, respectively. There are four
 operations affiliate partners: [Section 4.1]

 ° Chile, host country of the telescope facility

 ° Brazil, providing high-bandwidth network connectivity from Santiago to Saõ Paulo

 ° CC-IN2P3 physics institute in France, providing 40% of the annual data-
 processing capacity

 ° IRIS Network in the United Kingdom, providing 25% of the annual data-
 processing capacity

 • The operations of Rubin Observatory are broken into three phases: [Section 4.1]
 ° FY19–FY25 (pre-operations)

 ° FY26–FY35 (main survey)

 ° FY36–FY37 (post operations)

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 87

 • Rubin pre-operations ran early versions of all the data production elements, and between
 2021–2023 some of this was done in a commercial cloud (e.g., the IDF) deployment using
 precursor data sets. Transition from the IDF to the USDF was completed in FY24. Pre-
 operations will culminate with data production at full-scale testing in FY25. The full LSST will
 run for 10 years and final data processing will take place after that for two years. Survey data
 taking ends in FY35. [Section 4.1]

 • Rubin expects ~30 TB of continuous image and metadata to flow from Chile to the US each
 night. Real-time transfer over dedicated high-bandwidth segments is required to analyze each
 image at the USDF (hosted at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory) and broadcast alerts to
 the community. [Section 4.2]

 • The USDF at SLAC will curate 5 PB/yr of data, with ancillary and other image data products
 that could add up to 500 PB by end of survey in 2035. [Section 4.2]

 • Rubin Observatory data are collected from the 3.2 gigapixel LSSTCam mounted on the
 8.4m Simonyi Survey Telescope located on the summit of Cerro Pachón in Chile. Data are
 transported via an encrypted tunnel over a long-haul network from the observatory summit to
 the USDF at SLAC. Data are routed at modest bandwidth over time to the French Data Facility
 at IN2P3 in Lyon for geographically distributed backup. [Section 4.3]

 • Rubin alerts are required to be broadcast via community-developed brokers in 60 seconds
 from the time the camera shutter closes on the mountain top in Chile. Other “prompt data
 products” are made available to the community after an 80-hour embargo period. The embargo
 period is implemented to prevent prompt detection of artificial satellites in the LSST data
 stream. [Section 4.3]

 • All image data will be carried to the project’s Archive Center at the USDF, hosted within the
 SLAC Shared Science Data Facility (S3DF). The total northbound data from Rubin to the
 Archive Center is approximately 30 TB/night. A very demanding application using these flows is
 Alert Production, where 12.7 GB (uncompressed) of pixel data need to be transferred from the
 Base Facility in La Serena Chile to the Archive Center in 7 seconds bursts. There are two such
 bursts approximately every minute of nighttime observing. The bursts need to be sustained for
 approximately 355 days in each year. The required reliability level for these flows is very high,
 and is seen to require a path-diverse network with nearly lossless networking. [Section 4.3]

 • The Rubin prompt processing will generate a nightly stream of sources which vary in
 brightness. This stream will be made available to at least seven community brokers. These
 brokers allow (outside Rubin) access to the alert stream including the tools needed to filter the
 stream for specific science cases. At least some of the brokers will be open to any member of the
 worldwide science community. [Section 4.3]

 • Rubin community-provided alert brokers will be the worldwide community access avenue for
 alerts. At least one community alert broker will provide access to the worldwide community.
 In 2021, Rubin completed selection of the community alert brokers, these include seven
 international teams: ANTARES (NOIRLab), ALeRCE (Chile), Lasair (UK), Pitt-Google (U of
 Pittsburgh), Fink (France), AMPEL (Germany), BABAMUL (CALTECH). Two downstream
 brokers that operate off one of the primary brokers were also endorsed by the SAC: SNAPS
 (Northern Arizona University) and POI (Vanderbilt). [Section 4.3]

 • The Rubin Data-Release Production system will be executed approximately annually , and will
 ingest and process all data which has been taken to date. By co-adding and combining data
 taken at multiple epochs, it will provide a more detailed characterization of fainter astrophysical
 objects than is provided by the Prompt Data Products. [Section 4.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 88

 • Over its 10 years of planned operations, Rubin Observatory will produce annual data releases.
 Each data release will include reprocessing of all data from the start of the survey up to the
 cutoff date for that release. [Section 4.3]

 • Given the volume of data involved, it is not feasible to make all Rubin releases available on fast
 storage for the duration of the project. Instead, Rubin will keep the two most-recent releases
 available for rapid access, and archive older releases to tape. Users will not be able to perform
 database queries against these archived releases. However, they would be made available for
 bulk download. [Section 4.4]

 • In FY24 the IDF transitioned to the hybrid-cloud US DAC model, with the user-facing RSP
 remaining in Google Cloud and the back-end data holdings and data services hosted at the
 USDF at SLAC. The RSP is implemented in a virtualization framework that is portable across
 cloud providers or Kubernetes-based on-premises infrastructure. Multiple other scientific
 services, applications, and databases (including a staff-facing instance of the RSP) run within a
 Kubernetes cluster environment at the USDF. [Section 4.4]

 • Rubin requires a constant 1,188 CPU cores throughout the survey period to perform Prompt
 Processing. These cores will be used during the night for alert generation, and during the day
 for catch-up (where necessary) and solar system processing. Each core will have access to 5 GB
 of memory, and all these cores are located at the USDF. [Section 4.4]

 • The RSP is a set of web applications and services that will be used by the data rights community
 to access, visualize, interact with, and analyze Rubin Observatory data. The RSP is being
 designed to be simple enough to engage general users and flexible enough to meet the needs of
 experienced users. Data will be exposed to users through the web portal (interactive use cases),
 the Jupyter Notebook interface (custom user use cases), and machine-accessible application
 program interfaces (APIs; remote tools/analyses use cases). [Section 4.5]

 • All the Rubin collaborations, as well as independent scientists, will access and analyze data
 through either the hybrid cloud-based US DAC (cloud-based RSP and USDF back-end data
 services) or IDACs operated by in-kind contributor communities. There will also be a data
 access center (DAC) at the base facility in Chile. Chileans will have priority access to this DAC,
 but others can use it as well. [Section 4.5]

 • The USDF will provide raw and processed data to Rubin Observatory authorized users,
 including the DOE Dark Energy Science Collaboration and their international collaborators,
 including science collaborations investigating Dark Energy in other participating countries.
 The USDF will distribute data to one or more data access centers in Europe and elsewhere.
 The scope of these centers and their reliance on the USDF is currently being worked out. It is
 worth noting that the data volume of an annual release is very significant, with just the catalogs
 of detected objects beginning at PB-scale. [Section 4.5]

 • Nightly data from the Rubin Observatory are accumulated and processed with science pipelines
 at the USDF as well as partner data facilities in France and the UK, producing deep stacked
 images and source catalogs. These “annual data-release” products are served to the user
 community via a RSP hosted in Google Cloud and backed by data-access services hosted at the
 USDF. [Section 4.6]

 • Rubin expects a significant amount of data will be moved in bulk to other Afs. Data will be
 moved back and forth between the USDF and the FrDF+ UK Data Facility (UKDF) in
 conjunction with the distributed data-release processing efforts. [Section 4.6]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 89

 • Rubin also includes a program of in-kind contributions from international participant
 communities, some of which take the form of IDACs. Additionally, large amounts of data will be
 moved to other computing facilities to support custom analysis by large science collaborations.
 In particular, for the DESC this will likely amount to the mirroring of key data products from
 each annual data release from SLAC to NERSC. Additional mirroring efforts to support science
 analysis may be initiated for centers such as ALCF, OLCF and TACC. Rubin anticipates a key
 role for ESnet in supporting these data transfers. [Section 4.6]

 • International networking has a role in supporting Rubin Observatory LSST production
 processes. LSST annual releases will be computed at the USDF and at the satellite computing
 facilities in France and the UK. This generates a need for networking to support continuous
 data production, in addition to distribution of data for scientific data analysis. By agreement,
 CC-IN2P3 is the responsible institution for arranging connectivity between CC-IN2P3 and the
           US. [Section 4.7]

 • A memorandum of agreement (MOA) has been established between IN2P3, the LSST
 Corporation (LSSTC), the Rubin Observatory, and the University of Illinois for the
 IN2P3 Computing Center (CC-IN2P3) in Lyon, France to provide 40% of the computing
 capacity needed for annual data-release processing during LSST operations and to host a
 complete backup of the Rubin Observatory data archive. The MOA requires that France will
 provide the TA network connectivity to ESnet needed to support data transport to and from
           CC-IN2P3. [Section 4.7]

 • The UKDF will be a distributed entity. Its computing hardware will be provisioned through
 IRIS, a national organization providing computing resources for projects funded by the STFC.
 RIS sites are well integrated into national and international networks, for the transfer of LHC
 and other data, and have a wealth of experience supporting a wide range of international science
 collaborations. The UKDF will be hosted by the University of Edinburgh. [Section 4.7]

 • The required peak bandwidth from the Base Facility in La Serena to the USDF is established
 by the need to transfer the images for prompt processing. In order for the USDF to release
 alerts of transient and variable sources within 60 seconds of image readout from the camera
 electronics, seven seconds of this time budget is allocated to data transfer, including compression/
 decompression. Two seconds of that budget is in the Summit to Base transfer, and the other five
 seconds is in the Base to Archive Transfer and compression/decompression. This equates to a
 minimum of 40 Gbps bandwidth. [Section 4.7]

 • Currently the Rubin Data Management system does not make heavy use of AI/ML for data
 production or distribution. The scientific community is expected to deploy their own AI/ML
 techniques in analysis of Rubin’s scientific data products for modeling, inference, and anomaly
 detection. This expectation is a major driver for bulk download capabilities for Rubin data
 products, and may also influence the development roadmap for Rubin-supported analysis
 platforms on five-year timescales. Multiple community alert brokers currently provide users
 with AI/ML capabilities for classification and anomaly detection. [Section 4.8]

 • The Rubin-LSST science enterprise exhibits all three IRI patterns to some degree: [Section 4.9]
 ° Time Sensitive: Rubin images are transferred in near-real time from the Summit to the
 USDF, where they are promptly processed to generate alerts on objects that have changed
 in brightness, moved, or newly appeared.

 ° Data Integration Intensive: Many Rubin science analyses will require extensive integration
 between multiple data sets both internal to Rubin (images, catalogs, light curves) and
 external (data from complementary surveys at other wavelengths, spectroscopic facilities,

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 90

 and space-based telescopes). This data integration is likely to involve a range of different
 Afs both within the DOE system (e.g., SLAC, NERSC, ALCF) and beyond (e.g., partner
 data-processing facilities in France and the UK, NSF-funded computing centers like
 TACC, NASA archive and science processing centers hosting data from the Roman Space
 Telescope, and Rubin IDACs in other partner countries).

 ° Long-term Campaign: Rubin has a 10-year primary survey mission, and a potentially longer
 horizon in an extended mission mode. Successful scientific operation over this horizon
 requires sustained access and integration between Rubin’s experimental-support computing
 facility at SLAC and the DESC analysis facility at NERSC.

 • Rubin operations employs a model of distributed data management and processing across three
 main sites (USDF, FrDF, UKDF). The current baseline plan calls for using a combination of the
 Rucio software system to coordinate multisite data movement and the PanDA software system
 for orchestrating distributed processing jobs. This use case is highly aligned with the vision for
 multisite interoperability under IRI, and Rubin expects to follow IRI development both as an
 exemplar experiment and as a future beneficiary of new infrastructure in the future. [Section 4.9]

 • Known or potential data-related resource constraints for Rubin as of FY24 are: [Section 5.3]
 ° Insufficient computing resources available to meet the full analysis demand from the
 Rubin scientific user community, and/or difficulty in co-locating Rubin data products with
 available computing resources. Includes unbounded/unscoped demand for AI/ML-based
 analysis of Rubin data.

 ° Changing cybersecurity threat and policy landscape can present barriers to planned data-
 access and data-sharing services, and/or can introduce new costs, technical requirements,
 and schedule impacts.

 ° Challenges associated with implementing and routinely operating the distributed
 processing model for annual data-release processing.

 ° Challenges and constraints of operating in a shared data facility with other experiments.

 ° Network and I/O performance impacts of transferring a very large number of relatively
 small files.

6.3.2 Vera C. Rubin Observatory: Facility Profile
Rubin expects ~30 TB of image and metadata to flow from Chile to the US each night. Real-time transfer over
dedicated high-bandwidth segments is required to analyze each image at the USDF (hosted at SLAC National
Accelerator Laboratory) and broadcast alerts to the community of all sources in the image that have varied
in brightness by more than 5 sigma compared to a reference image. Alerts are required to be broadcast via
community-developed brokers that receive a stream from Rubin in 60 seconds from the time the camera shutter
closes on the mountain top in Chile. Other “prompt data products” are made available to the community after an
80-hour embargo period. The embargo period is implemented to prevent prompt detection of artificial satellites
in the LSST data stream.

6.3.2.1 Science Background
Nightly data are accumulated and processed with science pipelines at the USDF as well as partner data facilities
in France and the UK (FrDF and UKDF respectively), producing deep stacked images and source catalogs.
These “annual data-release” products are served to the user community via a RSP hosted in Google Cloud and
backed by data-access services hosted at the USDF.

Rubin expects a significant amount of data will be moved in bulk to other Afs. First, large amounts of data will be
moved back and forth between the USDF and the FrDF+UKDF in conjunction with the distributed data-release

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 91

processing efforts. Second, Rubin includes a program of in-kind contributions from international participant
communities, some of which take the form of IDACs in those countries serving copies of either subsets or
full copies of LSST data releases. Third, large amounts of data will be moved to other computing facilities to
support custom analysis by large science collaborations. In particular, for the DESC this will likely amount to the
mirroring of key data products from each annual data release from SLAC to NERSC. Additional mirroring efforts
to support science analysis may be initiated for centers such as the ALCF and the TACC. Rubin anticipates a key
role for ESnet in supporting these data transfers.

All Rubin data are proprietary for two years except the alert stream which is world public. After two years, the
data are shareable with any one, but no specific mechanism for making these data public and serving them is
yet defined.

6.3.2.2 Collaborators
Rubin Observatory is an NSF-DOE funded partnership. Operations partners are NSF’s NOIRLab and SLAC
whose managing organizations are AURA and Stanford University, respectively. Rubin counts with four
operations affiliate partners:

 1. Chile, host country of the telescope facility
 2. Brazil, providing high-bandwidth network connectivity from Santiago to Saõ Paulo
 3. CC-IN2P3 physics institute in France, providing 40% of the annual data-processing capacity
 4. IRIS Network in the United Kingdom, providing 25% of the annual data-processing capacity
The primary science community includes data scientists, astronomers and physicists in the USA and Chile.
International participants in Europe, Asia, and North America who have approved in-kind contributions to the
Rubin science enterprise will also be collaborators with equal access and rights to work with Rubin data. All these
collaborators can work independently or through self-governed science collaborations. Presently, Rubin engages
with eight such science collaborations who largely drive the discussion about the science needs of the community.

Depending on the size of the in-kind contribution, International members may have agreements with DOE or
NSF directly or with AURA or SLAC.

The total worldwide Rubin science user community is estimated to comprise of order 10,000 individuals.

6.3.2.2.1 North-South Networking
All image data will be carried to the project’s Archive Center at the USDF, hosted within the SLAC Shared
Science Data Facility (S3DF). The total northbound data from the observatory to the Archive Center is

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 93

approximately 30 TB/night. A very demanding application using these flows is Alert Production, where
12.7 GB (uncompressed) of pixel data need to be transferred from the Base Facility in La Serena Chile to
the Archive Center in 7 seconds bursts. There are two such bursts approximately every minute of nighttime
observing. The bursts need to be sustained for approximately 355 days in each year. The required reliability level
for these flows is very high, and is seen to require a path-diverse network with nearly lossless networking.

This same network carries substantial traffic from the USDF to the Rubin Observatory Base Facility La Serena,
in the form of Calibration data and annual Data Releases, but the aggregate volume is not as large as the South-
North traffic, nor is there a near-real-time latency requirement for that traffic. Establishing duplex service at
the level required for the South–North traffic should more than suffice for the North–South traffic. Lesser, but
operationally significant volumes of data will flow from the Base Facility to the Rubin Observatory Headquarters
site in Tucson and to other sites involved in Rubin operations.

Collaboration among the participating network operators supporting the Rubin North-South network connection
is convened under the auspices of the Americas Lightpaths Express & Protect (AmLight-ExP) consortium and the
South American–African Astronomy Coordination Committee (SA3CC).

6.3.2.2.2 National and International Networking
The USDF will provide raw and processed data to Rubin Observatory authorized users, including the DOE
DESC and their international collaborators, including science collaborations investigating Dark Energy in
other participating countries. The USDF will distribute data to one or more data access centers in Europe and
elsewhere. The scope of these centers and their reliance on the USDF is currently being worked out. It is worth
noting that the data volume of an annual release is very significant, with just the catalogs of detected objects
beginning at PB-scale.

International networking has a role in supporting Rubin Observatory LSST production processes. LSST annual
releases will be computed at the USDF and at the satellite computing facilities in France and the UK. This
generates a need for networking to support continuous data production, in addition to distribution of data
for scientific data analysis. By agreement, CC-IN2P3 is the responsible institution for arranging connectivity
between CC-IN2P3 and the US.

6.3.2.3 IRI Readiness
The Rubin-LSST science enterprise exhibits all three IRI patterns to some degree:

 • Time Sensitive: As soon as they are collected, Rubin images are transferred in near-real time
 from the Summit to the USDF, where they are promptly processed to generate alerts on objects
 that have changed in brightness, moved, or newly appeared. These alert packets are broadcast,
 also in near-real-time, to a network of “alert broker” software platforms in the community.
 These broker systems enable scientists to implement their own filters on the alert stream to find
 objects of greatest interest, and to trigger follow-up observing with other telescopes during the
 same night.

 • Data Integration Intensive: Many Rubin science analyses will require extensive integration
 between multiple data sets both internal to Rubin (images, catalogs, light curves) and external
 (data from complementary surveys at other wavelengths, spectroscopic facilities, and space-
 based telescopes). This data integration is likely to involve a range of different Afs both within
 the DOE system (e.g., SLAC, NERSC, ALCF) and beyond (e.g., partner data-processing
 facilities in France and the UK, NSF-funded computing centers like TACC, NASA archive
 and science processing centers hosting data from the Roman Space Telescope, and Rubin
 IDACs in other partner countries). Rubin will also deliver a cornerstone dataset for the coming
 generations of multimodal AI foundation models in astronomy and cosmology.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 94

 • Long-term Campaign: Rubin has a 10-year primary survey mission, and a potentially longer
 horizon in an extended mission mode. Successful scientific operation over this horizon requires
 sustained access and integration between Rubin’s experimental-support computing facility at
 SLAC and the DESC analysis facility at NERSC, as well as a long-term effort to evolve and
 maintain software and workflow tools to take advantage of changing technology platforms and
 opportunities. Rubin data itself must be curated and preserved over this same time frame, as
 each successive analysis campaign draws on the cumulative data set since the start of the survey.

 • Rubin operations employs a model of distributed data management and processing across three
 main sites (USDF, FrDF, UKDF). The current baseline plan calls for using a combination of the
 Rucio software system to coordinate multisite data movement and the PanDA software system
 for orchestrating distributed processing jobs (see Rubin DMTN-21318 for details). This use case
 is highly aligned with the vision for multisite interoperability under IRI, and Rubin expects
 to follow IRI development both as an exemplar experiment and as a future beneficiary of new
 infrastructure in the future.
In the near term, time-critical aspects of Rubin commissioning and early operations may limit the extent to
which current project data management activities can engage with IRI prototype capabilities. Rubin should
nevertheless serve as an important IRI use case, and major aspects of Rubin data management could be
candidates for migration into IRI frameworks on the five-year timescale of Rubin’s planned mid-survey
hardware refresh.

6.3.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
Rubin Observatory data are collected from the 3.2 gigapixel LSSTCam mounted on the 8.4m Simonyi Survey
Telescope located on the summit of Cerro Pachón in Chile.

Data are transported via an encrypted tunnel over a long-haul network from the observatory summit to the
USDF at SLAC. Data are routed at modest bandwidth over time to the French Data Facility at IN2P3 in Lyon for
geographically distributed backup.

The Rubin Observatory Data Management System and Facilities are described in detail in Sections 6.3.2.7 and
6.3.2.8 below, via excerpted content from the current detailed 10-year Operations Plan. To preserve subsection
reference correctness, the original Chapter and section numbering is preserved in the excerpt content:

 • FY26–FY35 (main survey)
 • FY36–FY37 (post operations)
