High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 95

Pre-operations will run early versions of all the data production elements described above. In 2021–2023 some
of this was done in a commercial cloud IDF deployment using precursor data sets (simulated or from other
telescopes). Transition from the IDF to the USDF was completed in FY24. Pre-operations will culminate with
data production at full-scale testing in FY25, ideally using science validation survey data from the telescope and
LSSTCam obtained in the last part of commissioning.

The full LSST will run for 10 years and final data processing will take place after that for two years. Survey data
taking ends in FY35.

6.3.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
The Rubin LSST is a public survey. The Rubin team itself is not responsible for the delivered science. The DOE
is chiefly involved in Rubin for dark matter and dark energy science. The DOE supports the DESC and their
science is described in a separate case study.

For NSF, the science goals are based on studies of the nature and distribution of Solar System bodies, the halo
of the Milky Way, galaxy formation and evolution, and the transient and variable universe. Each of these science
areas has an associated science collaboration. These are self-governed and only DESC has a direct funding
connection to one of the agencies (DOE).

All the collaborations as well as independent scientists will access and analyze data through either the hybrid
cloud-based US DAC (cloud-based RSP and USDF back-end data services) or IDACs operated by in-kind
contributor communities. There will also be a DAC at the base facility in Chile. Chileans will have priority access
to this DAC, but others can use it as well.

All scientists will have compute and storage resources at the US DAC or Chilean DAC. Tools available will allow
complex queries of the object and source catalogs as well as statistical and other common analyses.

The prompt processing will generate a nightly stream of sources which vary in brightness. This stream will be
made available to seven community brokers. These brokers allow (outside Rubin) access to the alert stream
including the tools needed to filter the stream for specific science cases. At least some of the brokers will be open
to any member of the worldwide science community.

Solar System objects will be identified in the nightly processing and new and repeat observations of these bodies
will be sent to the Minor Planet Center (MPC)19 for further orbit determination and cataloging. Scientists can
access the latest information from the MPC or the RSP.

A subset of Rubin Data will be managed by the Rubin and NOIRLab education teams. This cloud-based resource
will support public engagement and citizen science.

6.3.2.6 Remote Science Activities
All observational data are collected at the Rubin Observatory summit facility on Cerro Pachón in Chile, which is
remote from the main data archiving and processing site.

Most science users will do their data exploration and analysis through the RSP, hosted in Google Cloud and
backed by data services through the USDF at SLAC. Users will access the RSP from their own local computers
through an online portal.

Other science analysis campaigns will be conducted at IDACs in partner countries, or at other computing centers
in the US such as NERSC.

The model of an observatory that is remote from the data facility is foundational to the Rubin experimental design
and is not expected to change in the foreseeable future. The role of IDACs and other Afs can be expected to
evolve and may be significantly different over strategic planning horizons (five years and beyond).

19 http://www.minorplanetcenter.org

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 96

6.3.2.7 Software Infrastructure
This section excerpts Chapter 18 of the current version of the 10-year Rubin Observatory Operations plan,
describing the Observatory’s data and software products. The content and internal references have been lightly
edited to make this Case Study document self-contained, however the numbering of subsections and figures is
preserved from the original document.

6.3.2.7.1 Data Products and Community Support

Rubin Observatory Data Management is required to deliver science-ready, calibrated data products to the
Rubin Observatory data rights community (i.e., scientists at US and Chilean institutions and named international
member scientists who receive access in return for contributions to Rubin Observatory operations). The Rubin
Observatory data rights community will have access to all data products with no proprietary period. Anyone who
is not a member of this data rights community will have limited rights to Rubin Observatory’s data products,
as described in Section 6.3.2.7.1.2. Rubin Observatory is also required to deliver the software used to generate
the data products and the documentation necessary to understand and reproduce the generation of Rubin
Observatory data products.

The data products to be produced by the Rubin Observatory Data Management System (DMS) are defined
in the Rubin Observatory Data Products Definition Document (LSE-16320; the DPDD). Broadly, these are
categorized into prompt data products, which are designed to enable rapid identification of transient and variable
astrophysical objects, and detection and tracking of moving objects within the solar system, and data-release
data products, which are generated annually with the goal of deep detection and precise characterization
of astrophysical phenomena. Note that all prompt data products (with the exception of real-time alerts) are
regenerated during data-release processing: it is expected that most scientific use cases, with the key exception of
those which are dependent on low-latency notifications, will be best served by data-release products.

The fundamental inputs to both the prompt and data-release processing systems are single-visit images — which
may be either “standard visits,” consisting of a pair of successive 15 second exposures called snaps, or “alternate
standard visits,” consisting of a single 30 second exposure — delivered by Rubin Observatory LSST Camera to
the DMS. Details of how these inputs are processed are provided in the subsequent sections.

After the Single Frame Processing step is completed, the pixel values and their variances are not modified any
more. These processed visit images (PVIs) are used downstream to produce coadded and difference images. The
rest of the processing is essentially a model-based interpretation of imaging observations that includes numerous
astrophysical and other assumptions.

6.3.2.7.1.1 Data and Software Products
6.3.2.7.1.1.1 Prompt Products Production
6.3.2.7.1.1.1.1 Prompt Products Processing Sketch
Prompt Products Processing is designed to provide time-critical data products to the community at low latency.
As such, it is designed to work on a per charge-coupled device (CCD) basis: as each image is received from the
LSSTCam, it is rapidly transferred to the USDF and immediately processed. Processing of each image proceeds
as follows:

 • The image is processed by the Single Frame Processing pipeline. Single Frame Processing
 consists of an instrument signature removal (ISR) step, in which calibration reference data
 are used to remove artifacts resulting from the instrument or detector electronics, followed
 by determination of the image’s background, point spread function, and photometric and
 astrometric calibration. The result of the Single Frame Processing pipeline is a PVI.

 • The PVI is differenced against a deep “template,” constructed from previous observations of the
 area being observed.
20 https://docushare.lsst.org/docushare/dsweb/Get/LSE-163

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 97

 • Source detection is performed on the difference image, resulting in a collection of DIASources.
 The flux and shape of each DIASource is measured.

 • DIASources are positionally associated with previous detections of both astrophysical
 (DIAObject) and solar system (SSObject) objects. If no association can be made, a new
 DIAObject is created.

 • If a DIASource is associated with an SSObject it is flagged for further processing during
 the following day. At this point, artificial satellites are also largely filtered out, with any
 remaining confounding contaminants excluded from the alert stream by the Alert Verification
 System (AVS).

 • Otherwise, the DIAObject — which provides aggregated and derived quantities describing the
 astrophysical object — is updated based on measurements made on the DIASource.

 • An alert is issued, which includes the complete DIAObject or SSObject record, the DIASource
 record, and all previous measurements of that object from the last twelve months of observing.

 • Within 24 hours of observing, precovery forced photometry will be performed on any difference
 image overlapping the position of new DIAObjects. Alerts will not be issued with precovery
 photometry information but the resulting DIAForcedSource measurements will be included in
 future alerts from this DIAObject.
Solar System Processing proceeds during the day. In brief, the daytime processing will:

 • Analyze all DIASources seen during the previous night which are not associated with previously
 known objects in an attempt to fit tracks between them.

 • Designate tracks which are consistent with Keplerian orbit around the sun as new SSObjects
 and submit them to the IAU MPC.

 • Retrieve an updated orbit catalog for all known Solar System bodies from the MPC and
 recompute properties of all SSObjects.

6.3.2.7.1.1.1.2 Prompt Data Products: Alert Stream, Filtering Service, Images, Catalogs
The Prompt Products Processing system, sketched in the previous section, will identify transient, variable and
moving objects observed by the Rubin Observatory. Examples of source types that will be detected by this
process are (i) moving objects in the Solar System and (ii) supernovae superimposed on bright extended galaxies.
In total, Rubin expects to detect around 10,000,000 such sources per night.

To enable follow-up observations, each of these 10,000,000 sources will be transmitted to seven Community
Brokers via an “alert stream,” where they will be accessible by the worldwide astronomical community with no
proprietary period. Two specialized downstream brokers receive subsets of alerts from other brokers. Each alert
is designed to provide as complete a description as possible of the observation, so as to enable informed decisions
on follow-up. This will include the time of detection, position, flux, size and shape. The shape parameters will
include weighted second moments and fits to trailed and dipole source models. The alert stream also will include
prior variability information and data from the same night, if available, including low order light-curve moments
and the probability that the object is variable. Additionally, alert packets will provide the IDs for nearby Objects
in the latest LSST Data Release catalog (i.e., potential host galaxies for transients).

Community-provided alert brokers (e.g., ANTARES, Section 7.1.5) will be the worldwide community access
avenue for alerts. At least one community alert broker will provide access to the worldwide community. More
information on the current plans for alert production and community brokers is given in LDM-612.21 In 2021,
Rubin completed selection of the community alert brokers through a formal review led by a sub-committee of the
SAC. These include seven international teams: Arizona–NOIRLab Temporal Analysis and Response to

21 https://docushare.lsst.org/docushare/dsweb/Get/LDM-612

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 98

Events System (ANTARES), ALeRCE (Chile), Lasair (UK), Pitt-Google (U of Pittsburgh), Fink (France),
AMPEL (Germany), BABAMUL (CALTECH). Two downstream brokers that operate off one of the primary
brokers were also endorsed by the SAC: SNAPS (Northern Arizona University) and POI (Vanderbilt).

In addition to the alert stream, the images (PVIs and difference images) and catalogs (of DIASources,
DIAObjects, and SSObjects) generated during Prompt Processing will be made available through the RSP to
members of the data rights community within a specified period from the time the corresponding observation
was completed.

6.3.2.7.1.1.2 Data-Release Production
6.3.2.7.1.1.2.1 Data-Release Processing Sketch
In contrast to the Prompt Products Processing system, described above, the Data-Release Production system
will be executed approximately annually,22 and will ingest and process all data which has been taken to date. By
co-adding and combining data taken at multiple epochs, it will provide a more detailed characterization of fainter
astrophysical objects than is provided by the Prompt Data Products. Data-Release Processing proceeds
as follows:

 • The Image Characterization and Calibration system is used to generate PVIs for each input
 image. There are two parts to this system:

 ° An equivalent of the Single Frame Processing system described in Prompt Processing is
 used to perform ISR and to estimate the point spread function (PSF) and astrometric and
 photometric calibration for each image.

 ° The global simultaneous calibration system combines source catalogs derived from multiple
 images to arrive at a refined photometric and astrometric calibration.

 • These steps are iterated: the refined calibration is passed back to Single Frame Processing,
 where it is used to improve the PSF estimate and generate new source catalogs, which are,
 in turn, used in global calibration to further refine the calibration. Depending on available
 resources, this cycle may either be iterated to convergence, or for a set number of cycles.

 • The PVIs are combined to produce coadded images. A suite of coadds are produced, including
 deep, seeing-optimized, short-period, and multi-band. Great care is taken to properly set the
 background levels and to remove image artifacts during coaddition.

 • A difference image is generated for each PVI, using an appropriate coadd as the template.
 • Source detection is performed on coadds and difference images, generating CoaddSources and
 DIASources, respectively. The source detection algorithm identifies regions of connected pixels,
 known as footprints, above the signal-to-noise threshold in the PSF-likelihood image of the visit.
 An additional technique will be used to detect extended low surface brightness objects.

 • The complete set of sources detected to date (coadds and difference images) is associated and
 deblended to synthesize a list of unique astrophysical objects. This process makes use of all
 information available at this stage, including, for example, the knowledge of peak positions,
 bands, time, time variability, and galactic longitude and latitude.

 • Objects are characterized by measuring their properties — fluxes, adaptive moments, etc.; refer
 to the DPDD (LSE-163) for a complete list — on the coadded images.

 • Detailed measurements of the shape of each object, appropriate for weak lensing shear analysis,
 are made. The details of this procedure are still being refined in response to ongoing work in
 the community on algorithms such as meta calibration (Zuntz et al., 2018). The plan is to use a
 third-party shear estimation algorithm that runs on small-cell, edge-free coadds.

22 In fact, eleven times over the course of the survey

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 99

 • Source fluxes will be measured on every visit (PVIs and image differences) with the position
 and motion parameters characterized in previous steps kept fixed. This process of “forced
 photometry” results in the ForcedSource catalog, which is used to measure the light-curve of
 each object in the survey.

6.3.2.7.1.1.2.2 Catalog and Image Data Releases
Over its 10 years of planned operations, Rubin Observatory will produce annual data releases. Each data release
will include reprocessing of all data from the start of the survey up to the cutoff date for that release.

Data releases include catalogs of Sources, Objects, DIASources, DIAObjects, and ForcedSources, as well as the
raw image data, generated and retained image data (PVIs, coadded images),23 and all ancillary data necessary
to regenerate the release (e.g., calibration frames, telemetry, configuration metadata). Some information is
provided in more than one format: for example, catalog data are provided as both Apache Parquet24 tables,
which are designed to facilitate next-to-data processing and map-reduce style operations, and loaded into the
Qserv database (Section 6.3.2.8.1.4.2.2, excerpted in the next major section of this case study), which provides
a relational query capability. The expected growth of the total data volume of each release (including this
duplication) with time is shown in 6.3.1.

Figure 6.3.1: Total size of a Rubin Observatory data release, as a function of survey year.

Given the volume of data involved, it is not feasible to make all releases available on fast storage (“spinning disk”)
for the duration of the project. Instead, Rubin will keep the two most-recent releases available for rapid access,
and archive older releases to tape. Users will not be able to perform database queries against these archived
releases. However, they would be made available for bulk download through appropriate interfaces (see Section
7.1.4 below). Database software and data loading scripts will be provided for users who wish to set up a running
copy of an older (or current) data-release database on their systems.

Rubin anticipates keeping small, overlapping samples of data from older data releases loaded in the database to
assist with data-quality monitoring and assessment. A sample of a few percent of the older data releases, with
larger samples early on, would be sufficient for characterization of the same data for monitoring variations from
release to release.

23 Members of the data rights community will be able to access all image data generated over the course of a data release, but it may not all
be materialized on physical storage as part of the release; rather, some data products may be regenerated on demand.
24 https://parquet.apache.org

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 100

The Operations Team recognizes that the strong scientific drivers maximize the amount of data stored in online
databases, and the feasibility of increasing the amount of data available on fast storage is currently under study
by the construction DM team. Given the relatively small size of early data releases, storing additional early data
releases would not bear much cost impact. In later years of operations, armed with real-time knowledge of fast
storage costs in the mid-2020s, the Operations Team will be able to revisit this analysis.

Data products will only be made available after thorough science data-quality assessment has been performed by
the System Performance Department, and with the approval of the directorate. Data products will be distributed
using common community standards where available and appropriate. In particular, Rubin Observatory’s data
access services make extensive use of International Virtual Observatory Alliance standards, including Table
Access Protocol (TAP)25 and Astronomical Data Query Language (ADQL)26 for catalog access, and ObsCore27,
SIA28, and Hierarchical Progressive Survey (HiPS)29 for image access.

6.3.2.7.1.1.3 Calibration and Ancillary Data
Calibration data and engineering telemetry (available from the Engineering Facility Database, Engineering &
Facility Database [EFD] through the RSP) will be available to the Rubin Observatory community. Calibration
data products include the raw calibration images such as flat fields, bias frames, spectra of standard stars obtained
using the spectrograph on the Auxiliary Telescope, and images from the all-sky camera. Substantial volumes of
low-level telemetry will be obtained and archived from the guiders as well as instruments such as the weather
station, anemometers, and temperature sensors used throughout the observatory. Although these data are
generally used for engineering purposes and to support operations, these data also will be stored and made
available to the community.

6.3.2.7.1.1.4 Education and Public Outreach (EPO) Data Products
Rubin Observatory DMS will produce data products that will populate the EPO program (outside the scope of
this ESnet case study.)

6.3.2.7.1.1.5 Software and Documentation
Rubin Observatory regards reproducibility and transparency as key to achieving the best possible scientific
results. As such, it is a requirement on the construction project, and a policy Rubin intends to continue into
operations, that all data-processing software is to be written in publicly accessible repositories and be released
under an open-source license. At present, all the Science Pipelines software (see the science pipelines design
document, LDM-15130) which is being written to perform the data processing described above is available on
GitHub31 and licensed under Open-Source Initiative-approved licenses (generally the GNU General Public
License version 3, with a few exceptions for administrative reasons). Note that all relevant project-authored
tooling will come preinstalled and ready for use within Rubin Observatory Science Platform’s Notebook
Environment. It is expected that the details of distribution and licensing may vary over the course of the
operational period, but the principles will remain constant.

Given the extent and complexity of the deliverables — both in software and in data products — produced by
Rubin Observatory, documentation is regarded as essential to enable to effectively and responsibly analyze
and interpret the Observatory’s output. All software and data releases will be accompanied by extensive and
appropriate documentation to make this possible.

6.3.2.7.1.2 Data Rights
Rubin Observatory data policy is fully described in the document RDO-01332. RDO-013 describes a number
of scientist communities with rights to access and use Rubin Observatory proprietary data. The communities
include US and Chilean scientists, so-called builders from Rubin Observatory construction project and
pre-operations, international members with agreements to provide in-kind contributions, and the public.
See section 4 of RDO-013. It is expected that Rubin Observatory will make public data (i.e., data after the
two-year proprietary period) accessible to the worldwide community. Such access may require non-data rights
communities to support the costs of data transfer.

6.3.2.7.1.3 Science Platform
The RSP is a set of web applications and services that will be used by the data rights community to access,
visualize, interact with, and analyze Rubin Observatory data. The RSP is being designed to be simple enough to
engage general users and flexible enough to meet the needs of experienced users. The RSP also needs to enable
users to access contextual knowledge of Rubin Observatory survey and data, facilitating their understanding of
the relationships among the data products.

The platform consists of three primary user-facing elements: the web Portal, the Notebook analysis environment,
and a set of network-addressable Application Programming Interfaces (APIs).

Figure 6.3.2: A layered view of the RSP.

As illustrated in Figure 6.3.2, Rubin Observatory data will be exposed to users through the web portal (interactive
use cases), the Jupyter Notebook interface (custom user use cases), and machine-accessible application program
interfaces (APIs; remote tools/analyses use cases). The Portal component will provide the essential data access
and visualization services common to present-day archives, e.g., Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and NOIRLab
Data Lab holdings. The Notebook component, based on the Jupyter family of technologies (JupyterHub
and JupyterLab) will enable more sophisticated next-to-the-data analysis. These user-visible services will be
supported by the user database, storage, computing, and tools components, enabling the users to access, sub-
select, and perform added-value processing of the data products.

The Portal component is a web portal designed to provide the essential data access and visualization services
through a simple-to-use website. Through the Portal, users will be able to view Rubin Observatory images,
request subsets of data via simple web forms or SQL queries, store the results of such queries to their personal
workspaces, construct and customize plots, and generally explore the LSST dataset in a way that allows them to
identify and access (subsets of) data required by their science case. It will enable browsing and visualization of
the available datasets in ways the users are accustomed to at archives such as NOIRLab Data Lab, IRSA, MAST,
or SDSS with an enhanced level of interactivity in line with expectations for then-contemporary archive portals.
The database serving the data products will support asynchronous queries.

The Notebook environment, based (at least) initially on the Jupyter family of technologies (e.g., JupyterHub and
JupyterLab), will enable sophisticated data selection, analysis, and creation of added-value user-generated data
products. The Notebook environment will come preinstalled with a library of commonly used and useful software
32 https://docushare.lsst.org/docushare/dsweb/Get/RDO-013

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 102

tools such as AstroPy, the Rubin Observatory Science Pipelines software stack, Anaconda Scientific Python
Distribution, and others. Users will be able to upload and install their own tools as well.

The Notebook user experience will be nearly identical to working with Jupyter Notebooks locally, except that
computation and analysis will occur at resources provided at the USDF. This is an implementation of
the “bringing computation to the data” paradigm. Rather than imposing the burden of downloading, storing,
and processing (large) subsets of Rubin Observatory data at their home institutions, the RSP will enable users to
bring their codes and perform their analysis at the USDF. This will reduce the barrier to entry by users of Rubin
Observatory data and shorten the path to science for the Rubin Observatory science community.

The RSP is being designed to facilitate collaborative work. The capabilities ranging from sharing of derived
datasets within smaller groups, collaborations, or with the broader Rubin Observatory community, to
collaborative visualization and editing capabilities that are expected to become available within the Jupyter
ecosystem. Scientists will be able to create user-generated data products from nightly and/or annual data
products in order to support particular scientific goals. Once created and with the concurrence of the creators,
user-generated data products may be associated with nightly and annual data products through database
federation. However, there is no requirement that external groups ever make their products publicly available
(see RDO-013). In rare cases, and only with initiation by the creators, community-developed algorithms used to
create user-generated data products may be incorporated into the regular Rubin Observatory data processing.

Analyses also can be performed on a variety of supported external systems. Common personal Unix
flavors such as Linux and macOS will be supported as resources allow, as well as commonly used cluster
and HPC environments.

6.3.2.7.1.3.1 Science Platform Resource Allocation
Queries, visualizations, and analysis performed through the Portal and Notebooks will be served by a shared
computing cluster, storage, and database resource. There is a high-level requirement that, in order to enable
data exploration and user-generated data product creation, Rubin Observatory provides its user community with
software and computing capability equivalent to at least 10% of total Rubin Observatory computing and data
storage capacity. The current sizing model for Rubin Observatory compute and storage is summarized in Section
8.1.2 (excerpted in the next major section of this ESnet Case Study), and described in detail in DMTN-13533.
User resources — shown in table 22 of that document — amount to 500 cores for the USDF Science Platform
and 100 cores in the Chilean DAC during the first year of operations. These correspond to 10% and 20% of the
total Data-Release processing capacity respectively, and are expected to expand as the Data Facility expands. In
year one, 2 PB of storage (corresponding to 0.4 TB for each of 5000 users) is available to the Science Platform in
the USDF; this will expand to 10 PB over the course of operations.

Each RSP user account will be provided with a baseline level of resources, to be determined based on the initial
size of the user base and the average number of concurrent users the RSP experiences, in practice. The current
plan is for 500 cores for the US DAC in 2023 (increasing annually), dedicated preliminary end-user science
analyses (e.g., working on small numbers of images), and the creation of user-generated data products. Qserv
has its own resources for catalog queries. For the RSP the minimum resource allocation, per concurrent user,
is half a core. A good analogy is one of being given a server with a few TB of disk, a few TB of database storage
that is co-located next to Rubin Observatory data, and with a chance to use tens to hundreds of cores for analysis
(depending on system load). Cluster resources beyond this baseline allocation will be requested from and approved
by a Rubin Observatory Resource Allocation Committee—analogous to a Telescope Allocation Committee.

For larger endeavors (e.g., pixel-level reprocessing of the entire LSST dataset), the users will be steered
toward resources beyond Rubin Observatory DF (e.g., national supercomputing centers, university computing
centers, or the public cloud). Clear, but evolving, guidelines will be published to familiarize scientists with
the limits of Rubin Observatory-provided computing and the information necessary to apply for non-Rubin
Observatory resources.
33 https://dmtn-135.lsst.io/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 103

Back-end RSP services, including access to databases, images, and other files, will be exposed through machine-
accessible web APIs serving community-accepted formats and protocols. This will make it easy to initiate remote
computations operating on Rubin Observatory data. Virtual Observatory interfaces will allow connection to other
archives and enable the use of standard tools such as Tool for oPerations on Catalogues And Tables (TOPCAT)
or Aladin. Rubin Observatory also will be capable of exporting images and catalogs to external computing sites
for projects with requirements that exceed the capacity constraints of Rubin Observatory DACs as provided, for
example, through in-kind contributions.

6.3.2.7.1.4 Interfaces Between Rubin Observatory and the Community
As a facility, Rubin Observatory will provide science-ready data to the community of scientists to use in their
wide-ranging astronomical investigations. These investigations will lead to new understanding of the data, beyond
that which an Operations team could ever develop alone. Therefore, the opportunity exists for the Operations
team to capture this community experience in order to feed it back into the schedule of the telescope and the
processing of the data. This section highlights the mechanisms in place to facilitate the flow of information
and knowledge into and out of the Rubin Observatory system and give some illustrative examples of how this
feedback process will work.

Interactions between the System Performance Community Science team and the Rubin Observatory LSST
Science Collaborations will be a particularly valuable interface because this is a) where active community
investigation of the Rubin LSST data is likely to take place and b) where staff are already established in good
relationships with the astronomy community. However, ensuring that the feedback from researchers who do not
have the time or resources required to sustain membership in these large collaborations is solicited, ingested, and
acted on is essential for promoting diversity and inclusion among the LSST science community. The paragraphs
below describe a range of interfaces to serve the broad community.

Community Scientists: The individual Community Scientists in the System Performance department Community
Science Team will be the primary human interface to the Science Collaborations and the wider scientific
community. They will work with the community to intake, understand, and triage the issues identified and then
activate the appropriate investigative and corrective activities within the System Performance and other relevant
departments. To best enable this work, the cumulative astronomical expertise of the Community Scientists will
cover the four LSST science pillars (at minimum).

The LSST Science Collaborations: Since 2006, the SCs have evolved and grown into eight active, self-managed
teams that represent a diverse and geographically distributed network of scientists collaboratively preparing
for science with the LSST data set. They also provide scientific expertise to Rubin Observatory, and help
to guide design and operations choices (e.g., survey strategy, in-kind contributions, algorithms). In 2021, a
Federation Charter document34 was established to recognize the contributions of the Science Collaborations to
Rubin Observatory; to establish mutually agreed-upon principles, rules, rights, and privileges of the Science
Collaborations; and to define the obligations of Rubin Observatory to the Science Collaborations to support their
activities which benefit the entire Rubin Community. During Construction, the DMS Science Team had staff
serve as liaisons to each of the Science Collaborations by, e.g., attending their regular telecons and/or face-to-face
meetings. During Operations, these liaison roles will be filled by staff with appropriate expertise from across the
Rubin departments, and the liaison program itself will be facilitated by the Community Science team.

Documentation: The collection and public dissemination of information about Rubin Observatory, the LSST
Science Pipelines, and the data products will begin during commissioning as the camera and full operational
system is first characterized as-built. Documents describing key features and software evolution specific to
each annual data release will be published approximately following the SDSS model, and made freely available
(including to non-data rights holders). During Operations, the Community Scientists will monitor and respond to
community needs for additional documentation. Document-writing will be a shared responsibility among many,

34 https://docushare.lsst.org/docushare/dsweb/Get/Agreement-241

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 104

coordinated mainly by the Community Documentation positions in the System Performance department. In
addition to formal documentation, the Community Science team will curate a suite of tutorials to illustrate usage
of the LSST data products and science pipelines.

Q&A Support: An open community forum will be provided for community members to ask questions or request
support (e.g., Science Platform tools, coding bugs) and receive assistance from project staff within a few days.
In other projects this type of support is referred to as a “Help Desk” and is implemented as a standalone web
form (or is an email address), but for Rubin Observatory this is a Support category within the Rubin Community
Forum (Community.lsst.org; see below). The Community Scientists will take primary responsibility for monitoring
Support requests and connecting users with project expertise. Embedding a “Help Desk”-style functionality in
an open forum allows users to help other users, and project staff to help users, without a bottleneck of request
processing by a “Help Desk” team.

Rubin Community Forum (Community.lsst.org35; see below): Providing an interface with which the users can
ask questions and find answers (e.g., like “Stack Overflow”) or post interesting results for discussion is of great
benefit to both the wider community and to the Rubin Observatory. During Construction the Project has fostered
a healthy multithreaded conversation about a wide range of matters at community.lsst.org, an initiative which
has enabled collaboration within the community, and between the community and Project staff. This is a public
forum; anyone anywhere can obtain an account and view or participate in discussions, including non-data rights
holders. There are also private topics restricted to Science Collaboration members and/or Project staff. This
online forum is an ever-growing archive of information that enables the community to benefit from their own
cumulative expertise, and from interactions with Operations staff.

Users Committee: The Rubin Users Committee is the formal interface between the science community and
Rubin Observatory. The User’s Committee is charged with actively using the LSST data and the RSP, soliciting
feedback from the community, and regularly reporting to the Rubin Lead Community Scientist and to the Rubin
Observatory Director with recommendations for science-driven improvements to the LSST data products and
the RSP tools and services. The Users Committee Charge (rdo-051.lsst.io36) and website37 provides more details
about membership, timescales, and responsibilities.

Survey Strategy Initiatives: Community investigations of the observing schedule and its impact on the science
are already underway and being documented in an open “Observing Strategy White Paper,”38 which was begun
as a joint effort between the Science Collaborations and the Rubin Project team. It is anticipated that evolving
into an ongoing public conversation between the science community and the System Performance department’s
Survey Scheduling Team. Detailed cadence simulations are currently underway by the Rubin construction team
that will be evaluated in 2021. The input to this cadence analysis was initially a set of 40 detailed white papers
submitted to The Rubin Observatory SAC in 2019 after an open call to the worldwide community (i.e., including
non-data rights holders). The Survey Scheduling team supports community use of Metric Analysis Framework
and interacts with both the Science Collaborations and the broader community.

Following the initial cadence white papers, the scheduling team advanced optimization of the baseline cadence
for the full survey start. Then in 2020 a Survey Cadence Optimization Committee (SCOC) was established. The
committee solicited further cadence “notes” from the community to further advance the initial cadence or survey
plan. As of this writing the SCOC and scheduling team are actively working on the draft initial survey cadence
for full survey operations. A set of recommendations from the SCOC is scheduled to be received by the Rubin
Director in December 2021. Further simulations will be completed and a revised baseline for the survey cadence
will be presented in December 2022.

6.3.2.7.1.5 Beyond Rubin Operations: Community-Based Data Analysis
In fulfilling its core operational mission, Rubin Observatory will release both real-time and static-sky data at
a scale unprecedented in optical astronomy, both in terms of rate and volume and in terms of the diversity of
scientific interests served.

The analyses of these data products will be the responsibility of the user community. In order to maximize the
scientific return of the data sets, Rubin Observatory user community will need to develop software tools targeted
toward specific research problems. A description of some high-priority capabilities needed to maximize Rubin
Observatory science can be found in the National Research Council report on Optimizing the US Ground-based
Optical and Infrared Astronomy System (NRC, 201539). A subsequent NSF-endorsed community-based study

39 https://nap.nationalacademies.org/catalog/21722/optimizing-the-us-ground-based-optical-and-infrared-astronomy-system

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 106

and workshop, sponsored by the Kavli Foundation and jointly led by Rubin Observatory and National Optical
Astronomy Observatory (NOAO, now part of NOIRLab), has further detailed and prioritized these capabilities in
a report that was released in 2016.

Some of the computational resources and software capabilities highlighted in these reports are:

 • Robust and scalable brokering systems to filter, characterize, classify, and annotate time-domain
 alerts (there are seven full brokers in development, several of which are operating now on
 Zwicky Transient Facility [ZTF]);

 • Curated catalogs of data from surveys complementary to LSST, served through interfaces
 allowing flexible and large-scale joining with Rubin Observatory catalog data;

 • Networks, resources, and workshops for training in and exchange of the data-intensive
 astronomy techniques required by Rubin Observatory science;

 • Computational resources for large-scale, high-fidelity numerical simulations to support the
 astrophysical interpretation of Rubin Observatory data products; and

 • Computational resources to permit development and running of modified Rubin Observatory
 data-processing code for the generation and distribution of data products that go beyond those
 provided by Rubin Observatory.
Examples of relevant ongoing work, outside of the scope of this operations plan, that is relevant to the
community’s use of LSST data, include:

ANTARES, the Arizona-NOAO Temporal Analysis and Response to Events System — NOIRLab and the
University of Arizona Computer Science and Mathematics Departments have collaborated to build a software
infrastructure system to process alerts generated by astronomical time-domain survey programs. ANTARES
will serve as a broker, taking in alerts, annotating them with catalog information from surveys across the
electromagnetic spectrum, diverting objects that do not require rapid follow up to a database, and ranking the
remaining sources by rarity. These alerts then can be distributed to other brokers who are working on specific
projects for more detailed characterization or classification. The goal of ANTARES is to build a system that is
scalable to the very large number of alerts that will be generated by Rubin Observatory and to serve as a resource
for the general astronomical community. ANTARES is currently running every night at ZTF scale and is under
active development to scale to Rubin Observatory size. In 2021, Rubin Observatory selected ANTARES to be
one of the seven “community brokers” which will receive and disseminate the Rubin Observatory alert stream
(LDM-61240). The other six teams include the ALeRCE broker developed by members of the Chilean community,
University of Pittsburgh+Google, Caltech, a French community broker, a German community broker, and Lasair,
a broker from the UK community.

DESC — This DOE-funded Science Collaboration will require capabilities and services tuned specifically to
their domain. The DESC is preparing its own DOE-funded operations plan that complements the activities
described in Rubin Observatory’s operations plan. Control and understanding of systematics are essential for
analyses of the probes of dark energy, and the DESC already has working groups focused on the analysis of weak
lensing, large-scale structure, supernovae, and clusters, as well as the calibration of photometric redshifts. In
addition, there are working groups on cosmological and survey simulations.

LSSTC Enabling Science Initiatives — LSSTC has sponsored a number of activities designed to prepare
scientists to work effectively with Rubin Observatory data as soon as it begins to flow. The Data Science
Fellowship Program is a training program designed to teach graduate students skills that are required for working
with the large Rubin Observatory databases — skills that are not usually addressed by current astrophysics
programs. Currently in its fourth year, the program is in high demand. Recent topics covered by LSSTC
workshops include the 2018 Cadence Hack-a-thon which paid stipends totaling 75K USD to 42 white paper

40 https://docushare.lsst.org/docushare/dsweb/Get/LDM-612

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 107

authors. These white papers are at the core of the current Rubin Observatory process to simulate and choose
the ultimate cadence for the survey. Even more recently, LSSTC supported the “Managing Follow-Up, 2019”
workshop giving seed funding and/or observing time to 15 community-based teams. In 2021, LSSTC announced
two significant community-based efforts to maximize LSST science. These are the LINCC program (LSST
Interdisciplinary Network for Collaboration and Computing) and the Catalyst Fellowship program. Both these
programs add resources and effort to LSST research within the Rubin community with particularly strong
connections to LSSTC member institutions. LSSTC and its member institutions are vital Rubin Observatory
supporters in the development of non-federal funding sources to support Rubin science in the community as well
as highly motivated members of the Rubin enterprise in their own right.

NOIRLab Community Science and Data Center —One of NOIRLab’s four programs is the Community
Science and Data Center (CSDC, the other three are Rubin, Gemini, and the Mid-Scale Observatories). The
CSDC will have two core missions: (i) facilitate and support data-intensive astronomical research and (ii)
facilitate and support O/IR System optimization. This program will focus on the skills and workflow necessary
for users of the public data holdings curated and served by NOIRLab and its constituent programs, in particular
Rubin Observatory. This role is highly complementary to the role to be delivered by Rubin Observatory’s Data
Management and System Performance departments. The requirements that these departments are structured to
meet include the generation, assurance, archiving, and delivery of science-ready products to Rubin Observatory
data rights community. Accordingly, the community scientist staffing includes community support to (i) ingest and
react to community-identified issues with the data or observing strategy and (ii) to ensure the accessibility and
usability of Rubin Observatory’s science products. Rubin Observatory itself, for example, will not provide support
for the additional time-domain infrastructure necessary to follow up on the alert stream. Rubin Observatory also
will not provide support for user training in basic programming or data analysis techniques.

Ongoing efforts at NOIRLab are laying the groundwork for this value-added support of Rubin Observatory
community during operations. In particular NOIRLab programs Gemini, SOAR, and Cerro Tololo Inter-
American Observatory (CTIO) are actively collaborating with Las Cumbres Observatory to develop a dynamically
scheduled follow-up network called AEON (Alert Event Observatory Network) and associated end-to-end
tools to maximally take advantage of limited US federal resources for follow-up of Rubin Observatory and other
transient events.

To enable broad-based community science in collaboration with Rubin Observatory, NOIRLab will build on the
software capabilities and data products to be delivered by Rubin Observatory Operations, as well as build on
current programs within NOIRLab’s CSDC, including the Data Lab project, to enable flexible data-intensive
science within large archival survey data sets. A goal of Rubin, CSDC, and NOIRLab is to evolve the combined
technologies to common solutions and approaches through the Rubin operations phase, specifically after

to DESC. Wherever these capabilities and services overlap significantly with the needs of the broader US
astronomical community, NOIRLab will explore the feasibility of leveraging DOE investment for the benefit of
the NSF-supported Rubin Observatory community.

6.3.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
This section excerpts Chapter 17 of the current version of the 10-year Rubin Observatory Operations plan,
describing the Observatory’s data systems and network architecture. The content and internal references have
been lightly edited to make this Case Study document self-contained, however the numbering of subsections and
figures is preserved from the original document.

6.3.2.8.1 Data Management System
6.3.2.8.1.1 Rubin Observatory DMS Architecture

 Figure 6.3.3: Architectural overview of the Rubin Observatory DMS. Colored boxes represent the sites
 over which the DMS is deployed; divisions within them show the deployment enclaves; white boxes indi-
 cate particular services.

41 https://lco.global/aeon/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 109

The Rubin Observatory DMS is the combined hardware and software infrastructure which will collect data from
the Rubin Observatory LSSTCam and other ancillary instrumentation, transport, archive, process it into science-
ready data products, and make the raw data and derived data products available to the community.

The DMS is structured around a number of services, which are deployed and managed within enclaves, and
hosted over three separate sites — the Chilean Data Center, the USDF, and CC-IN2P3 — connected by WANs.
This architecture is shown schematically in Figure 6.3.3.

Each site is separated into functional enclaves based on requirements for availability, access, and change
management. Enclaves are distinguished by having different users, operational timescales, interfaces, and
services. The Chilean Data Center supports four enclaves: Prompt Base, Archive Base, Commissioning
Cluster, and Chilean DAC. The US Data Facility provides Prompt USDF, Archive USDF, US DAC, and Offline
Processing USDF enclaves. A single Offline Processing Satellite enclave is deployed at IN2P3.

Each enclave supports one or more services. These services can be considered as consisting of four
tiers of components:

 1. The Science Platform, which provides a user interface and data aFs for use by both Observatory staff
 and the wider scientific community.
 2. Applications Software, which provides libraries of data structures and algorithmic code for
 representing and processing Rubin Observatory data. These libraries are available for use through
 the Science Platform, and are used to construct the Science Pipelines which are executed to
 generate the standard Rubin Observatory data products.
 3. Middleware is used to provide the environment within which the Science Pipelines execute. It
 provides a layer of isolation and abstraction between the Pipeline “payloads” and the underlying
 infrastructure on which they execute, and provides data access services to both science users and
 Observatory staff.
 4. Infrastructure — the compute hardware, storage, networking, and the low-level services and
 software which are necessary to run and manage a data center — underpins and supports all the
 above component tiers.
The various enclaves, and the services which are hosted within them, are described below.

6.3.2.8.1.2 Compute and Storage Sizing
The DMS construction team has completed an extensive evaluation of the compute and storage infrastructure
which is necessary to process and release all the data collected during the Rubin Observatory LSST (the “sizing
model”), and have further used that to estimate the total non-labor cost of the system (the “costing model”). The
full details of this evaluation are available in technical note DMTN-13542; this section presents a brief overview of
the estimation process.

The sizing and costing models described in this section have been initially developed based on the prototype
Data Facility built by the Construction Project at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at
University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (NCSA). The ultimate location of the operational Data Facility is
SLAC and this has introduced a slightly different costing. This should be clear in DMTN-135.

42 https://dmtn-135.lsst.io/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 110

6.3.2.8.1.2.1 Storage Requirements
The storage sizing model is derived on the basis of six fundamental considerations:

 • LSE-8143, which provides estimates of the total number of sources which will be observed
 by the Rubin Observatory based on the LSST Science Book44, the Science Requirements
 Document (LPM-1745), and the Observatory System Specifications (LSE-3046);

 • LSE-16347, the Data Products Definition Document, which summarizes the various types of
 image which will be made available, and describes the information which will be included
 in Rubin Observatory catalogs; and LDM-15348 which maps those catalogs onto a detailed
 database schema;

 • Practical experience of processing precursor datasets with prototype versions of the Rubin
 Observatory Science Pipelines, which helps to establish intermediate data products which
 must be stored temporarily; provides a basis for estimating how effective compression is when
 applied to Rubin Observatory data; and establishes the size of ancillary data products like
 representations of the PSF;

 • Science Platform users will have access to personal storage space for generating and storing
 their work;

 • Access requirements for data products, including ensuring that products where low-latency
 access is required are stored on fast storage; that all data releases are archived to tape; and that
 the two most-recent data releases are available on spinning disk (LPM-15149);

 • The approach taken to disaster recovery, which determines how much storage redundancy
 is required.
Based on these considerations, there are five separate classes of storage:

 • Fast storage, likely comprised of solid-state devices, is used for the Alert Production Database
 (APDB; for which low-latency access is required as part of the Prompt Products Production
 system described Section 7.1.1.1 in the Case Study section above) and the client-facing query
 management and indexing components of the distributed Qserv database (Section 8.1.4.2.2).

 • Normal storage, corresponding to networked filesystems hosted on enterprise-grade spinning
 magnetic disks, is used for initial collection of raw data, and intermediate and final data
 products which are being generated or modified during the production of a data release, and
 for user storage.

 • Object stores, hosted on consumer-grade spinning disks, are used for providing cheap and
 scalable access to read-only data. In general, it is expected data will migrate from filesystem-
 based “normal” storage to object stores when processing is completed.

 • Qserv storage is dedicated to the distributed database system which is used to manage data-
 release catalogs. The Qserv system is intrinsically fault-tolerant, so consumer-grade spinning
 disks are used.

 • Tape storage is used for archiving and back-up all data products which are hosted on other
 storage media.

Storage is also required to support the activities of the Chilean DAC (Section 6.3.2.8.1.3.2.2). The Chilean DAC is

6.3.2.8.1.2.2 Compute Requirements
Compute requirements are estimated separately for Prompt Processing (Section 8.1.1.1), Data-Release
Processing (Section 7.1.1.2, excerpted in the preceding major section of this Case Study), and the Science
Platform (Section 7.1.3, excerpted in the preceding major section of this Case Study). The Science Platform
is made available for users at the US DAC, the Chilean DAC, and for internal staff use. This analysis does not
consider other processes, such as periodic template generation or calibration products processing, which are
assumed to be negligible.

Estimated compute requirements for the Science Pipelines are derived from processing precursor data —
primarily taken from Hyper Suprime-Cam on the Subaru Telescope and DECam on the Victor M. Blanco
Telescope51 — through existing pipeline prototypes, and scaling the results based on the source counts, derived
from scientific considerations, documented in LSE-8152. Compute times are measured on existing hardware, and
converted53 into core-hours on fiducial hardware54. This estimation methodology incorporates all I/O, memory
bandwidth, cache miss, and other overheads into the core-hour measurement. Note that the fiducial hardware is
not assumed to evolve with time; in practice, it is expected that continued technology evolution will result in a
reduction of the number of core-hours required late in the survey relative to the estimates presented here.

In some cases, Rubin Observatory algorithms are still under active development, and are not yet appropriate for
making informed estimates of actual compute cost. In these cases, core-hour figures obtained for comparable jobs
from the DES55 have been used in their place. Where equivalent DES and Rubin codes are available (e.g., in
single-visit processing), run-times have been shown to be well matched, which gives us confidence in this basis
of estimate.

Based on the above considerations, Rubin requires a constant 1,188 CPU cores throughout the survey period to
perform Prompt Processing. These cores will be used during the night for alert generation, and during the day for
catch-up (where necessary) and solar system processing. Each core will have access to 5 GB of memory, and all
these cores are located at the USDF.

 Figure 6.3.6: Fiducial core-hours required for data-release processing as a function of time.

54 Intel Xeon E5-2680v3 at 2.50 GHz

The core-hours required for data-release processing increases as the volume of data collected grows, as shown
in Figure 6.3.6. One third of these cores will have access to 5 GB of memory; the remainder, to 20 GB; jobs will
be allocated to high- or low-memory core depending on their requirements (e.g., operations on a single CCD
will generally be executed on a low-memory system, while combining multiple detectors or deblending complex
scenes will require a high-memory system). These cores will be divided between the USDF and the Satellite
Data Processing (Section 6.3.2.8.1.5) to enable split-site processing.

Cores are allocated to user-driven processing in the Science Platform as a ratio of the total available compute
system, following the construction Science Requirements Document (LPM-1756). On this basis:

 • USDF user computing is sized as 10% of the total Data-Release Processing compute, amounting
 to over 500 cores at the start of operations;

 • Chilean DAC computing as sized as 20% of USDF user computing;
 • Project staff computing is sized as 10% of USDF user computing.
It will be possible to dynamically reallocate CPU cores between services at the USDF. In particular, it will be
possible to reallocate cores from Data-Release Processing to the Science Platform at times of high demand,
assuming that the long-term average level of Data-Release compute is adequate to meet the release schedule.

6.3.2.8.1.3 Chilean Data Center
The Chilean Data Center is hosted at the La Serena Base Computing Center. This center is a megawatt facility
with redundant power service provided by on-site gas generators. The Chilean Data Center has 6 x 100 Gbps
network links to the Summit Facility — to receive streamed data from the telescope and to enable remote
control — and will have dedicated dual PoP and path-diverse 100 Gbps networking to the USDF as well as
connectivity to dedicated R&E networks and the commodity (or open commercial) Internet.

Through an agreement with the other AURA centers on the NOIRLab recinto, the Computing Center will be
used to consolidate computing and network servers from CTIO, SOAR, and AURA operations (and likely Gemini
in the future).

The Chilean Data Center hosts four DMS enclaves, as described below. In addition, it will host a backup of the
entire Rubin Observatory data set.

The Chilean Data Center will be operated by the Rubin DevOps team, under the supervision of the DevOps
Manager. This team is part of the Rubin Data Management Department. Most services deployed within the
various enclaves will operate software which is developed and maintained by the Data Management Department
(primarily, the Pipeline Middleware and Science Platform and Reliability Engineering groups). The Chilean Data
Center is hosted within the physical Data Facility in La Serena which is managed by NOIRLab facilities and
ITOps. The shared space was developed under leadership of Rubin Observatory but is available for use by all
Programs in NOIRLab in Chile.

6.3.2.8.1.3.1 Prompt Base
The Prompt Base enclave exists to support services which must interact with the Observatory Control System
(OCS) or the Camera Data Acquisition System (DAQ). In several cases, these services are closely related to
counterparts in the Prompt USDF enclave (Section 6.3.2.8.1.4.1). Services in this enclave are, where possible,
designed to operate autonomously and with a high degree of fault tolerance; the enclave is designed to be
functional whenever the Observatory is taking data.

The Prompt Base enclave supports the following services.

56 https://docushare.lsst.org/docushare/dsweb/Get/LPM-17

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 114

6.3.2.8.1.3.1.1 Archiving
The Archiving Service captures raw images taken by the Observatory’s cameras (both the main LSSTCam and
the Auxiliary Telescope spectrograph), including data from wavefront and guide sensors. These are augmented by
metadata and telemetry captured by the Header Service, which forms part of the Archiving Service. Image data
and metadata are then supplied to the Observatory Operations Data Service (OODS; Section 6.3.2.8.1.3.1.4) and
staged for ingestion into the Data Backbone (Section 6.3.2.8.1.6).

The Archiving Service also includes a “catch-up” capability, which can stage any data to the OODS and Data
Backbone that was missed by the primary archiving system due to network or other outages.

6.3.2.8.1.3.1.2 Planned Observation Publication
The Planned Observation Publication Service retrieves telemetry from the OCS describing the location of the
next visit, and the scheduler’s predictions of future visits. It makes these available as a globally accessible web
page for human inspection, and via machine readable web APIs.

6.3.2.8.1.3.1.3 Prompt Processing Ingest
The Prompt Processing Ingest Service captures images from the LSSTCam data system together with selected
metadata from the OCS and forwards it directly to the Prompt Processing Service in the Prompt USDF enclave
(Section 6.3.2.8.1.4.1.1).

6.3.2.8.1.3.1.4 Observatory Operations Data
The OODS provides access to files and metadata to Observatory systems. It is designed to provide lower-latency
than the Data Backbone (Section 6.3.2.8.1.6) to facilitate fast turnaround analyses by the team in Chile.

6.3.2.8.1.3.1.5 Observatory Control System Driven Batch
The OCS Driven Batch Service provides a batch computing service capable of executing science payloads.
It is used for processing daily calibration data. Data is read from and written to the Data Backbone (Section
6.3.2.8.1.6).

6.3.2.8.1.3.2 Archive Base
The Archive Base enclave provides a single service: an endpoint for the Data Backbone. The Data Backbone is
described in Section 6.3.2.8.1.6.

6.3.2.8.1.3.3 Commissioning Cluster
The Commissioning Cluster enclave provides a single service: an interactive computing environment for rapid
turnaround of human-driven ad hoc analysis of data during any recommissioning of the system. In addition, this
enclave supports human-driven quality control activities undertaken in Chile.

The Commissioning Cluster runs an instance of the LSST Science Platform (Section 6.3.2.7.1.3, excerpted in the
preceding major section of this Case Study) with low-latency access to the OODS (Section 6.3.2.8.1.3.1.4).

6.3.2.8.1.3.4 Chilean DAC
The Chilean DAC is responsible for providing science-user-facing data access and analysis services to the Chilean
community. It will contain all raw data on disk and probably a cache of other data. See LDM-57257 for details.
The primary user access and interface to the DAC is through an instance of the LSST Science Platform (Section
6.3.2.7.1.3). The DAC will enforce authorization and authentication policies set by the Rubin Observatory for
access to compute and data resources.

57 https://ldm-572.lsst.io/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 115

6.3.2.8.1.4 US Data Facility
The USDF, sited at SLAC, acts as the primary processing and distribution site for all Rubin Observatory data
products. This includes responsibility for Prompt Processing and alert distribution (Section 6.3.2.7.1.1.1, Case
Study section above), 35% of Data-Release Processing (Section 6.3.2.7.1.1.2; the remainder of the processing is
carried out at CC-IN2P3 (40%) and in the UK (25%), as described in Section 6.3.2.8.1.5), archiving the results of
processing, and making them available to the data rights community through a DAC. The USDF will also provide
for user-generated data product production. .

The USDF is configured with a high-reliability IT service model that ensures professional, secure, and consistent
operation. Systems at the USDF have been designed to allow for dynamic reallocation of resources between
Observatory operations, batch processing, and DAC subsystems in response to shifting peak demand.

The USDF will be operated by the Infrastructure and Support team within the Data Management Department,
under the supervision of the USDF Lead. Generation of data products using Data Facility infrastructure will
be carried out by the Data Management Department’s Execution group, under the leadership of the Lead
Production Scientist. These groups will work closely with the Data Abstraction and Algorithms and Pipelines
teams, which will provide the execution middleware and the science payloads, which will be used to generate
data products, and with the Science Platform and Reliability Engineering team, which will develop and support
the Science Platform which provides the primary mechanism by which Observatory staff and members of the
data rights community will access and work with data stored in the facility.

The USDF hosts four DMS enclaves.

6.3.2.8.1.4.1 Prompt USDF
The Prompt USDF enclave is responsible for compute-intensive processing for all near-real time operations
and other operations closely tied with the Observatory. The services provided by this enclave feedback status
information to the OCS through the Telemetry Gateway (Section 6.3.2.8.1.3.1.6); as such, they form an important
part of the overall Rubin Observatory system, and are generally expected to be available whenever observing
is ongoing.

6.3.2.8.1.4.1.1 Prompt Processing
The Prompt Processing Service receives images and accompanying metadata from the Prompt Processing Ingest
Service (Section 6.3.2.8.1.3.1.3), executes one of a number of possible algorithmic payloads upon them, and stores
resulting data products to the Data Backbone (Section 6.3.2.8.1.6).

Algorithmic payloads include:

 • Alert Production pipelines, as described in Section 6.3.2.7.1.1.1.1 (Use Case section above).
 Alerts are generated for point sources detected in the difference images, and also from certain
 “streak” features consistent with Near Earth Objects. (Artificial satellites are largely filtered
 out by the Rubin Science Pipelines. Any remaining confounding contaminants are excluded
 from the alert stream by Rubin’s AVS). Science alerts are passed to the Alert Distribution
 Service (Section 6.3.2.8.1.4.1.2) for distribution. In this mode, data from two visits is processed
 simultaneously to meet the throughput and latency requirements resulting from the duration
 of each visit being 30 seconds, and alert distribution taking place within 60 seconds of visit
 completion.

 • Calibration Product Production pipelines. These data taken by the LSSTCam and/or ancillary
 information to generate calibration products, such as bias, flat, and dark frames, which are used
 to calibrate the telescope during Alert Production processing.

 • Exposures may be grouped and processed by specially configured pipelines based on the above
 when deep-drilling fields are being observed.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 116

6.3.2.8.1.4.1.2 Alert Distribution
The Alert Distribution Service receives alert packets generated by the Prompt Processing Service (Section
6.3.2.8.1.4.1.1) and distributes them to consumers. A number — at least five — of community-provided “brokers”
will receive all alerts generated (expected to amount to around 10,000,000 per night). In addition, the Alert
Distribution Service provides a limited capacity and capability Alert Filtering Service, which will allow individual
members of the data rights community to receive alerts directly from the Observatory.

6.3.2.8.1.4.1.3 Prompt Quality Control
The Prompt Quality Control Service will monitor the execution of the Prompt Processing Service (Section
6.3.2.8.1.4.1.1) and will post-process data products written to the Data Backbone (Section 6.3.2.8.1.6) to generate
additional measurements. Warnings are provided to the responsible Observing Specialists and Data Facility
Production Scientists when these measurements cross predefined thresholds.

6.3.2.8.1.4.2 Archive USDF
The Archive USDF enclave provides bulk storage for file and catalog data which are used by other enclaves
within the US Data Facility. It provides the following services.

6.3.2.8.1.4.2.1 Data Backbone Endpoint
The Archive USDF enclave provides an endpoint for the Data Backbone. The Data Backbone is described in
Section 6.3.2.8.1.6.

6.3.2.8.1.4.2.2 Qserv Distributed Database
Over the course of the operational period, Data-Release Production (Section 6.3.2.7.1.1.2, Use Case section
above) will generate catalogs consisting of tens of trillions of rows and tens of PBs of data (Section 6.3.2.7.1.1.2.2).
These will be made available for data rights holders to access and query through the Science Platform (Section
6.3.2.7.1.3). Catalogs will be stored and queried using Qserv, a bespoke massively parallel relational database
system (LDM-13558). Qserv makes intelligent use of replication, chunking, vertical partitioning, and shared scans
to provide a system which is fault tolerant and capable of scaling to meet the variety and complexity of anticipated
queries, which range from simple object lookups to complex full-sky correlations over billions of elements.
Although Qserv is being developed directly to meet Rubin Observatory’s needs, it builds upon the mature open-
source technologies MariaDB59 and xRootD60.

The Qserv instance is hosted in the Archive USDF and provides the primary source-of-truth for released data —
this is where catalogs are ingested when Data-Release processing is complete — and provides query capabilities
to users of the US DAC (Section 6.3.2.8.1.4.4). Additional Qserv instances may be deployed locally by other
DACs as required.

6.3.2.8.1.4.3 Offline Production USDF
The Offline Production USDF enclave is responsible for all long-period data processing carried out at the US
Data Facility. This includes the largest and most complex science payloads executed by the Rubin Observatory
system, used to generate calibration products and data releases. This enclave also includes systems for monitoring
and quality control of ongoing processing jobs, and for bulk distribution of data to partner institutions.

Services in the Offline Production USDF enclave are expected to manage long-running processing jobs—
spanning weeks or months of real time — efficiently and reliably. They track the execution of millions or billions
of individual tasks, and ensure output data are collected and saved to the Archive USDF enclave. Services are
designed for autonomous operation where possible, although provisions are made for manual intervention
where appropriate.

59 https://mariadb.org

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 117

In general, low-latency processing is not critical in this enclave. However, because the enclave is sized to provide
appropriate capacity for generating data releases on schedule, downtime must be minimized to ensure data are
released on time.

The Offline Production USDF enclave provides the following services.

6.3.2.8.1.4.3.1 Batch Production
The Batch Production Service executes processing “campaigns,” where each campaign consists of a given science
pipeline, configuration, and set of inputs and outputs. Various different campaigns can be executed on different
cadences, including:

 • Periodic calibration product generation;
 • Annual data-release processing;
 • Daily solar system processing;
 • As needed alert catch-up processing and special programs processing.
More than one campaign can be executed simultaneously. In particular, data-release processing will largely
be scheduled as a single campaign which runs for much of the year, while other, smaller, campaigns execute in
parallel with it.

This service can coordinate with its peer at the IN2P3 Satellite Data Processing Center (Section 6.3.2.8.1.5; also,
potentially, with other facilities) to enable split-site processing of data releases.

6.3.2.8.1.4.3.2 Offline Quality Control
The Prompt Quality Control Service will monitor the execution of the Batch Production Service (Section
6.3.2.8.1.4.3.1) and will post-process data products written to the Data Backbone (Section 6.3.2.8.1.6) to generate
additional measurements. Warnings are provided to the responsible Observing Specialists and Data Facility
Production Scientists when these measurements cross predefined thresholds.

6.3.2.8.1.4.3.3 Bulk Distribution
The Bulk Distribution Service is used to provide Prompt and Data-Release products to major facilities and
partners such as Science Collaborations. It extracts data products from the USDF Archive and transmits them
over high-bandwidth connections to designated recipients. It is not available for direct access by science users,
who will, instead, access data through the DAC (Section 6.3.2.8.1.4.4).

6.3.2.8.1.4.4 US Data Access Center
The US DAC is responsible for providing science-user-facing data access and analysis services to the worldwide
Rubin Observatory data rights community. It will be hosted on the Cloud while all raw data, all file-based
data-release products, and all databases will be held at SLAC. The primary user access and interface to the
DAC is through an instance of the RSP, Section 6.3.2.7.1.3, Case Study section above). The DAC will enforce
authorization and authentication policies set by the Rubin Observatory for access to compute and data resources.
The RSP has been shown to be portable, having been operated in multiple situations, including the Google
Cloud. The success of the IDF has motivated hosting the RSP in the Google cloud moving forward.

In operations, Rubin envisions CC-IN2P3 and the UK as integrated parts of the Data Management Department.

and the USDF will meet regularly with the Data Management AD to ensure smooth co-processing of data. This
