the department.

6.3.2.8.1.5.1 IN2P3 Data Facility
A memorandum of agreement has been established by IN2P3, LSSTC, Rubin Observatory, and the University
of Illinois for the IN2P3 Computing Center (CC-IN2P3) in Lyon, France to provide 40% of the computing
capacity needed for annual data-release processing during LSST operations, as estimated at the time of the MOA,
and to host a complete backup of the Rubin Observatory data archive. CC-IN2P3 is a highly data-intensive
supercomputer center with an established history of data management for high energy physics experiments,
including the LHC at CERN, and in which large-scale astronomy experiments are a future strategic priority.
The MOA requires that France will provide the TA network connectivity to ESnet needed to support data
transport to and from CC-IN2P3.

During the current construction phase, this collaboration is managed by a Joint Coordination Committee chaired
by NCSA. This committee is charged with preparing for combined processing which will take place during
survey operations.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 119

6.3.2.8.1.5.2 UKDF
The UKDF will be a distributed entity. Its computing hardware will be provisioned through IRIS61, a national
organization providing computing resources for projects funded by the STFC with large-scale computing
requirements. At the moment, IRIS provides the UK’s contribution to the WLCG, as well as computational
support for preparatory work for a number of future astronomy projects, including the Square Kilometer Array
and Euclid. IRIS sites are already well integrated into national and international networks, for the transfer
of LHC and other data, and have a wealth of experience supporting a wide range of international science
collaborations.

The UKDF will be hosted by the University of Edinburgh, with hardware at its Advanced Computing Facility,
which is home to the UK’s national academic supercomputing service, and staff working with the Wide-Field
Astronomy Unit, located at the Royal Observatory Edinburgh, which hosts a number of existing sky survey
archives. The location of the UKDF staff contributing to Data-Release Processing will be determined by the
range of roles required to support the UK’s quarter share of the Data-Release Processing workload, which is
currently being discussed by Rubin operations management and the LSST:UK Consortium.

6.3.2.8.1.5.3 Offline Processing Satellite
The Offline Processing Satellite enclave provides a single service.

6.3.2.8.1.5.3.1 Batch Production
The Batch Production Service offered at the Satellite Data Processing Center offers a similar range of capabilities
to that at the USDF (Section 6.3.2.8.1.4.3.1). It will be used to perform 40% of the annual data-release processing.

6.3.2.8.1.6 Backbone Services
The Data Backbone is responsible for data storage, transport, and replication, including transferring files between
the constituent facilities of the Rubin Observatory system. Specifically, the Data Backbone is responsible for:

 1. Management of files and data resident in designated database management systems in Chile and at
 the USDF;
 2. Enforcing data retention and redundancy policies set by Rubin Observatory for data products at
 all levels;
 3. Providing disaster recovery capabilities for data;
 4. Transporting data as needed between the observatory sites; and
 5. Meeting data service levels specified for all users (e.g., members of the scientific community) and
 other consumers of Rubin Observatory data services (e.g., alert brokers).
To meet these responsibilities, the Data Backbone provides policy-based replication of files (including images)
and databases (including metadata about files as well as other miscellaneous databases but not including the
Qserv data-release database) across multiple physical locations. It provides for caching of data at each endpoint,
and automatic persistence of data to long-term archival storage when appropriate.

The Data Backbone has “endpoints,” where data may be stored or retrieved, at the USDF (Section 6.3.2.8.1.4.2.1)
and the Chilean Data Center (Section 6.3.2.8.1.3.2).

6.3.2.8.1.7 Wide Area Networks
6.3.2.8.1.7.1 Network Requirements
The Rubin Observatory’s WANs (6.3.2.8) are responsible for transferring data and control information among
the distributed observatory sites, and also provide connectivity to data centers for scientists and non-scientists
alike. As such, the requirements are complex, being drawn not just from the Observatory System

61 http://www.iris.ac.uk/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 120

Specifications (LSE-3062) as flowed down through the DMS Requirements (LSE-6163), but also from
memorandums of agreement between the Observatory and key partners. These requirements are summarized in
the Network Design Document (LSE-7864) for convenience.

These requirements necessitate data transfers on a wide range of timescales, including:

 • Order of milliseconds within the OCS and the control systems of each subsystem (the
 Telescope, Camera, and DMS);

 • Order of seconds in acquiring and processing the raw image stream from the Camera through
 Data Production to create transient alerts;

 • Order of days in archiving the raw image stream and other metadata for subsequent use in the
 production of astronomical catalogs and other data-release products;

 • Order of weeks to months in producing and deploying data necessary for calibration of the
 Telescope and Camera; and

 • Order of years in producing and deploying Data Releases of processed images and catalogs.
In addition, there are large geographical distances between the various sites, which imply non-trivial latency in
certain data transfers. There are also data-transfer requirements associated with supporting user access in DACs
in Chile and the United States, and in the Education and Public Outreach Data Center (EDC) in the United
States. In the case of Chile, these requirements are derived from MOAs between Rubin Observatory and AURA
(Document-11647), and between AURA and Chile (Document-11622) that require providing a DAC in Chile in
return for authorization to site Rubin Observatory in that country.

Considering continuity and criticality, Rubin has explicitly planned for certain levels of outages and failures, and
has replaced or augmented existing systems to enhance reliability. For example, before the start of construction a
microwave link was the only connection between the mountain and the base site. This did not meet the reliability
requirements for Rubin Observatory operations, and so the project has installed fiber optic-based networks while
retaining the microwave system as a backup. The system also has redundancy and “diverse” paths in every link
from La Serena to the USDF.

6.3.2.8.1.7.2 Network Architecture and Design

Figure 6.3.8: Rubin Observatory network paths and capacities.

6.3.2.8.1.7.2.1 Summit to Base Link
The key driving requirements for the Summit to Base communications are the bandwidth and reliability required
to transfer the image data and associated EFD metadata for alert processing, to transfer the raw image data to the
Base Facility, and to handle OCS commands and control traffic (see Figure 6.3.9 below).

Rubin Observatory has installed an optical fiber pair between the Summit and Base Facility utilizing dense
wavelength division multiplexing technology to provide 6 x 100 Gbps lambdas with end nodes owned and
operated for Rubin Observatory by NOIRLab COS-ITOps.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 122

 Figure 6.3.9: Nightly flow of data to support prompt processing. Data products are described in detail in
 Section 18 (Case Study section above).

This capacity is divided into a minimum of 100 Gbps for image data transfer and 100 Gbps for OCS command
and control data. A second pair of fibers carrying non-Rubin AURA traffic will be available for failover.

The historical data for fibers in north-central Chilean mountainous areas since 2018 suggest a mean time between
failures of 340 days and a mean time to repair of 2 days. The availability estimate on this segment is 98%.
Therefore, the summit facility is capable of storing a week’s worth of data to mitigate network downtime events
between the summit and the base. During such downtime, the existing microwave backup link will be used as a
survival link to check on the status of core network devices. Rubin has deployed a wireless link to the summit to
provide basic internet services (no data link) as an out of bounds service independent of the fiber.

6.3.2.8.1.7.2.2 Base to USDF Link
The required peak bandwidth from the Base Facility in La Serena to the USDF is established by the need to
transfer the images for prompt processing (see Figure 6.3.9).

In order for the USDF to release alerts of transient and variable sources within 60 seconds of image readout from
the camera electronics, seven seconds of this time budget is allocated to data transfer, including compression/
decompression. Two seconds of that budget is in the Summit to Base transfer, and the other five seconds is in the
Base to Archive Transfer and compression/decompression. This equates to a minimum of 40 Gbps bandwidth.

Current agreements between NOIRLab and other South American observatories have secured dual, PoP- and
path-diverse leased 100 Gbps links between Chile and the US and an additional 100 Gbps spectrum link. The
latter is expandable with purchased equipment upgrades at Rubin Observatory’s discretion. The non-spectrum
links are shared and have a guaranteed minimum for Rubin of 2 x 40 Gbps during observing and 2 x 20 Gbps
during non-observing times. These agreements have been achieved at the equivalent cost of a single 10 Gbps link
if acquired via non-partner commercial leased services.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 123

Networking between the Base and the USDF rests on provisioning initially provided by the Major Research
Equipment and Facilities Construction construction project and is sustained and enhanced as needed by the
operations project. This networking includes

 • One 100 Gbps lambda and one 40–100 Gbps lambda on physically distinct footprints from the
 Base Facility to Santiago, Chile;

 • One 100 Gbps lambda running up the west coast of South America, landing in a nuclear- and
 hurricane-hardened facility in Miami, Florida;

 • One 100 Gbps lambda from Santiago up the eastern side of South America, landing in a nuclear-
 and hurricane-hardened facility in Miami, Florida;

 • One 100 Gbps spectrum65 from Santiago up the eastern side of South America, landing in Boca
 Raton, Florida;

 • Networking provided by Florida LambdaRail to a demarcation point for national backbone
 research networks;

 • Networking provided by ESnet national research backbone network to SLAC, via Atlanta; and
 to CC-IN2P3;

 • The networks will be hardware encrypted on each end (Summit, USDF).
All the network links are being tested by Rubin Observatory and Network Partners at multiple levels during
construction/commissioning, including Installer tests supervised by Rubin and Partners (test reports available),
demonstrations and end-to-end tests (Rubin Observatory Network End-to-End Test Plan, Document-14789),
Verification tests (Rubin Observatory Network Verification Plan, LDM-732), and Commissioning tests (Rubin
Observatory Commissioning Plan, LSE-79).

This infrastructure provides general research connectivity to the US for Rubin Observatory. The networking
supports creation of bandwidth-protected channels that provide a guaranteed minimum rate with extra idle
bandwidth available to the channel. Networking to and from the computing center in France is provided by
ESnet in the US, and by both GÉANT and Renater in Europe.

65 Spectrum refers to the right to use a given frequency band on a fiber, using end equipment of one’s choosing, such that the capacity of the
link can be increased by the deployment of more capable equipment. This choice is up to the “owner” of the spectrum.

6.3.2.8.1.7.2.3 Archive to DAC and EPO Center to User Links

 Figure 6.3.10: Data flows during processing and distribution of calibration and data-release products.

Rubin Observatory must provide data access to the US, Chilean, and international contributor scientific
communities and to a worldwide community of non-specialist users whose curiosity may be triggered by Rubin
Observatory education and public outreach (see Figure 6.3.10). User access to the DACs and EPO Data Center
will be via public and R&E network connections (e.g., Internet and Internet2, NSF ACCESS, ESnet), and the
aggregate bandwidth will be limited only by the connectivity of the hosting and using institutions. In cases of
standalone DACs or science centers funded outside the project, the entity developing and operating the center
will be responsible for providing network connectivity to Rubin Observatory USDF to enable data transfer.

Rubin Observatory network architecture will include identity management, cybersecurity management, and
privilege limitations on usage of any resources (e.g., computing, storage, networks, software, and data) in a
resource management layer on top of the network. Rubin Observatory network management will include “taps,”
firewalls, and other security mechanisms to enable this resource management.

6.3.2.8.1.8 Configuration Control, Test, and Release Procedures
The Data Management Configuration Control Board (CoCB), which will be chaired by the AD of Data
Management or their designate, is responsible for change control and establishing testing and release procedures
across the Data Management department.

The CoCB is responsible for managing changes to the Data Management configuration baseline, which specifies
which technologies and which versions of software are deployed within the DMS. Any changes to the baseline,
including deploying new releases of scientific processing pipelines, must be approved by the CoCB. The CoCB
will maintain the software release schedule, and will evaluate bug and problem reports, determining if fixes
must be deployed immediately, or if they can be deferred until a future scheduled software release or
maintenance window.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 125

All changes will go through the full set of automated testing. Each data facility will have an efficient (and, where
possible, self-service) method for deployment of any released software to test systems in the data facility. These
will support at least two types of test:

 1. Full regression testing for normal releases—a process that may take many days; and
 2. Bug testing for specific quick fixes with a limited regression.
In exceptional circumstances, “quick fix” deployments may be made which bypass regular CoCB procedures and/
or avoid full regression testing; these would always require explicit approval from the AD of Data Management.

6.3.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.3.2.9.1 Cloud Services
As mentioned above, in pre-operations, Rubin Operations deployed a commercial cloud-based IDF on the
GCP. Rubin Data Production software and precursor data sets were deployed to the IDF to allow Rubin staff to
develop processes and train for operations readiness.

The three-year IDF program was also used to deploy pre-operations data sets known as Data Previews:
early previews of what operations annual data releases will look like, including data products, science analysis
tools, user support, and documentation. The first Data Previews have been based on simulated “Data
Challenge 2” (DC2) data from the DESC. Subsequent previews will include data obtained in commissioning
and science verification.

In FY24 the IDF transitioned to the hybrid-cloud US DAC model, with the user-facing RSP; see Sec. 7.1.3 in
Case Study Section 7 above) remaining in Google Cloud and the back-end data holdings and data services hosted
at the USDF at SLAC (as described in Sec. 8.1.4.4 under Case Study Section 8 above.) The RSP is implemented
in a virtualization framework that is portable across cloud providers or Kubernetes-based on-premises
infrastructure. Multiple other scientific services, applications, and databases (including a staff-facing instance of
the RSP) run within a Kubernetes cluster environment at the USDF.

6.3.2.9.2 AI and ML
Currently the Rubin Data Management system does not make heavy use of AI/ML for data production or
distribution. The scientific community is expected to deploy their own AI/ML techniques in analysis of Rubin’s
scientific data products for modeling, inference, and anomaly detection. This expectation is a major driver for
bulk download capabilities for Rubin data products, and may also influence the development roadmap for Rubin-
supported analysis platforms on five-year timescales. Multiple community alert brokers currently provide users
with AI/ML capabilities for classification and anomaly detection.

It is possible that some elements of the Rubin Science Pipelines may be migrated in the future to use AI/ML
techniques and/or hardware acceleration such as with GPUs.

6.3.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
Rubin staff use wireless networking extensively for routine productivity and communications purposes. In
addition to wireless networks in standard laboratory / office spaces, Rubin requires wireless networking at
the (remote) summit facility. This networking is currently provided by the Rubin project itself, in conjunction
with NSF NOIRLab.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 126

6.3.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
Known or potential data-related resource constraints as of FY24 are:

 • Insufficient computing resources available to meet the full analysis demand from the Rubin
 scientific user community, and/or difficulty in co-locating Rubin data products with available
 computing resources. Includes unbounded/unscoped demand for AI/ML-based analysis of
 Rubin data.

 • Changing cybersecurity threat and policy landscape can present barriers to planned data-
 access and data-sharing services, and/or can introduce new costs, technical requirements, and
 schedule impacts.

 • Challenges associated with implementing and routinely operating the distributed processing
 model for annual data-release processing.

 • Challenges and constraints of operating in a shared data facility with other experiments.
 • Network and I/O performance impacts of transferring a very large number of relatively
 small files.

6.3.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
Information about data mobility and sharing is given above in Section 2 (Collaborators), Section 3 (IRI
Readiness), Section 7 (Software Infrastructure), and Section 8 (Network and Data Architecture).

Plans for bulk download of Rubin data are currently under development. The baseline expectation is to use the
Rucio software framework to distribute science data from the USDF to other data-access centers and aFs. A draft
plan for supporting bulk downloads is available as RTN-086.66

6.3.2.12 Outstanding Issues
Rubin will be in a commissioning phase during FY25, with multiple major milestones still remaining in advance
of regular survey operations. In addition, “unknown unknowns” will continue to arise.

A high-level view of commissioning milestones can be found in DMTN-23267. This document is regularly updated.

6.4 DESC
DESC is the international science collaboration that will make high-accuracy measurements of fundamental
cosmological parameters using data gathered from the LSST produced by Vera C. Rubin Observatory, and
investigate the nature of dark energy and dark matter. Over ten years, the observatory will image the southern sky
(18,000 deg2) hundreds of times in six broad-band filters, accumulating a time-lapse ‘movie’ of the sky, as well as
obtaining extremely sensitive measurements of billions of galaxies in the coadded image data. The observatory,
with an 8.2 m primary mirror, a remarkably large field of view (approximately 10 square degrees), and the largest-
ever digital camera (3.2 gigapixel, with a two-second readout), is designed to enable Rubin through its LSST to
revolutionize optical cosmology and many fields of astronomy. DESC will make high-accuracy measurements of
fundamental cosmological parameters, and derive cosmological constraints, using data from the LSST.

6.4.1 Discussion Summary
The DESC project is investigating the use of Rucio and FTS, as is the Rubin Observatory, to see if it would be a
good fit for the data management aspects of the project. The use of any software comes with risks: the project is
striving to ensure that individual users can easily interact with the systems they create, and will gravitate toward
things that are easy to install, use, and support long term. The latter observation holds true for managing access
for scientific users: the lack of a cohesive multi-institutional method to manage credentials is also a challenge
for this collaboration. DESC hopes this is an outcome of IRI, as they stand to have numerous users that will be
impacted by this issue as they use computing and storage resources that could span facilities.

DESC is exploring ways to perform multimodal analysis using other streams of research data. Some possibilities
include the European Space Agency’s Euclid mission, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. The
effort is still in its early stages, and there are open questions about ways to get access to the data, and how it can
be integrated through software and computational hardware. A general question that was raised was that the
portal system for these three data products (and in general, all individual collaborations that produce a data set
that others may want to use) is that there will be no uniformity in how the data can be retrieved. This causes a
challenge for the greater scientific community.

DESC’s major data movement activity, occurring on a yearly basis, is a bulk data download from SLAC to
NERSC. The network infrastructure in place between the facilities (via ESnet) is sufficient to handle the
expected volume of data, and SLAC is in parallel moving to larger 400 Gbps capabilities to support other efforts.
Since this is not a real-time operation, there is no time limit (or performance expectation) for transfer. DESC is
open to the idea of working on structured data challenges, as other communities have done in the past. This could
involve simulation data to start, and characterize performance between SLAC, NERSC, and the IDACs. There
has been observed poor performance to some sites in the EU from NERSC, but given this is not a part of the
critical path of science, it is a lower priority for DESC to address.

 then need to be moved to NERSC). In the next two to five years, NERSC will be migrating to
 NERSC-10, and DESC will be testing the incorporation of IDACs and other IRI platforms to

 these resources. [Section 4.4]

 • NERSC is the main computing platform for DESC, and SLAC is the primary data source for
 Rubin Observatory data. The most critical component of this activity is an efficient transfer
 between these sites. ESnet current connectivity between these sites is sufficient for DESC's
 early needs, and planned upgrades in future years should ensure the data volumes are managed
 efficiently. [Section 4.4]

 • DESC transfers have largely been via HTTP, rsync, and Globus for data sets moving from

 • All DESC science activities are intrinsically ‘remote’ as the project is reliant on data obtained
 by the Rubin Observatory, processed and distributed from the USDF at SLAC, with subsidiary
 copies in other points of the world (France, Chile, UK). In the general case DESC will be
 pulling data from SLAC to NERSC with a yearly cadence; a smaller volume alert stream will
 be monitored coming from diverse brokers that cull the original kHz stream of transient source
 alerts from the Observatory. [Section 4.5]

 • DESC’s current analysis model involves bringing collaborators to deploy their analyses at
 NERSC to run at scale and access collaboration data products. DESC is planning to expand
 these capabilities and has had successful tests and large campaigns at the UK and France Data
 Facilities for Rubin, though details for securing these resources for DESC science purposes
 are being settled. These resources could potentially be used for DESC workflows that require
 Rubin imaging products available at these sites. [Section 4.5]

 • DESC's primary data source is the Rubin USDF at SLAC. Workflows will primarily involve

 stream of transient events, or the data set extracted from the accumulated images and catalogs.
 Nominally, most of DESC's computing will take place at NERSC; moving selected datasets
 from the Rubin USDF at SLAC to NERSC is a priority. As the survey proceeds, DESC will
 likely need to obtain additional resources elsewhere through specific programs or through
 international collaborations. [Section 4.6]

 • The anticipated start of operations at the Rubin Observatory is FY25Q4. In this period DESC
 expects to bulk download from the primary data source (USDF at SLAC) to NERSC the
 released datasets corresponding to the commissioning and science verification periods. The
 specifics of the data set sizes, files, etc. are uncertain due to the nature of these pre-operations’
 activities and final scope. DESC expects the resulting data size will be of a similar size as
 Rubin’s recent data preview, and of the order of 10 TB of catalogs, with the possibility of
 transferring up to 1–2 PB of imaging data. DESC's main computing resource will continue to be
 NERSC Perlmutter, as well as the Spin platform as a database to store selected streamed data
 from the alerts brokers. [Section 4.6]

 • DESC has no concrete plans for using any DESC-specific Cloud applications. It is worth noting
 that a good part of the initial engagement with the data by DESC scientists, in terms of image
 visualization, exploratory analysis, will happen in the US DAC, through an interface called the
 RSP. [Section 4.8]

 • Due to the large variety of science applications and multiple approaches and stages of DESC’s
 analyses, ML will be applied in many instances of large-scale computation (CPU and GPU) at
 NERSC. [Section 4.8]

 • DESC sees a potential for certain workflows that are more compute intensive (such as image
 simulations and Markov Chain MC analyses of cosmology parameter space) to branch out across
 multiple sites in the future. In the past, working across different facilities usually meant specific
 workflow setups tailored to the infrastructure/hardware available at each facility. The IRI
 vision will help overcome this hurdle and provide users with a very similar environment across
 facilities to ease moving across platforms. [Section 4.9]

 • DESC workflows are heterogeneous but primarily fall under two categories: [Section 4.9]
 ° The great majority (>90%) both in terms of compute and storage will correspond to long-
 term campaigns. These will include the processing and reprocessing of LSST data releases
 to extract data vectors, analyze systematics, model the signal, and infer cosmological
 parameters. They will be complemented by cosmological and image simulations in a similar
 amount. Therefore, these require “sustained access to resources at scale over a longer time

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 130

 to accomplish a well-defined objective.” Reliability and reproducibility of results at our
 computing platforms are key for the success of DESC. In this regard, compute-intensive
 multisite workflows would be an enormous benefit given possible allocation constraints to
 reach enhanced goals for DESC science.

 ° Some of our workflows are time sensitive. These rely on the Rubin ‘alert stream’, or
 intermediary brokers, for astrophysical events and generate actions or outputs that need
 to be processed within some time period (typically few minutes to few days, depending on
 the nature of the source). If the sources are not monitored reliably through our selected
 computing platform(s) in the best case the result will be a delay or degradation of the
 information obtained about the source, and in the worst case, the loss of a relevant or
 unique astronomical event.

 • For the full-fledged Rubin Observatory data releases, expected in the two- to five-year time
 frame, DESC will see a limitation in some of the science cases which require full access to the
 complete single-visit image data set (only available at SLAC or CC-IN2P3, but not NERSC
 as currently planned) rather than just the galaxy catalogs. DESC is currently looking for
 mitigations to this problem such as limiting the size of transferred data to NERSC but enabling
 the analyses nonetheless or shipping software containers to run remotely at these facilities
 instead. In addition, large-scale image simulations produced at NERSC or elsewhere
 would possibly stress DESC's small-latency storage allocation at NERSC, as well as compete
 with computing allocation for its analyses in parallel to real data analyses. The transition to
 NERSC-10 in this period and its unknown impact on established pipelines also introduces some
 uncertainty. [Section 5.4]

 • DESC has two outstanding issues to work through in the coming years: [Section 5.9]
 ° DESC needs technical support in implementing data distribution solutions (Rucio,
 DIRAC). Standing up these web services requires close interaction with the facilities (e.g.,
 NERSC). Built-in facility support for this software (e.g., just like the facilities provide
 built-in support for Globus) would be very beneficial.

 ° DESC faces complex issues with identity and account management across various services/
 sites. There are two broad classes of sites. First, there are sites like NERSC where a DESC
 member has a NERSC account that lets them access both NERSC and Globus. Second,
 there are sites like in the UK, France (CC-IN2P3), and Rubin IDACs where the DESC
 needs to deploy a proper VO and have a proper grid certificate. These items are needed
 to enable interactions with grid software like Rucio and DIRAC. Ideally, the VO and
 certificates would be linked to each member’s NERSC account. Further, we would ideally
 want to be able to target the NERSC queues using grid software like DIRAC so that we can
 run jobs, move data, etc., across multiple sites transparently.

 • DESC analyses will eventually employ the galaxy catalogs, but also the full imaging data of
 approximately 10PB, in the later years of the project. Replicating even the high-level imaging
 data at NERSC is inefficient and unfeasible, due to the scale of the expected allocation.
 DESC expects to embrace a fully distributed analysis at different facilities. Workflows will
 be adapted, preferably through IRI approaches, to adapt to a more flexible computing
 environment. [Section 5.9]

 • Future DESC needs, more than five years out, will likely require that the analysis process
 employ not only the complete galaxy catalogs, but also the full imaging data of O(10s) PB.
 Replicating even the high-level imaging data at NERSC is inefficient and unfeasible, due to the
 scale of the expected allocation. Thus, embracing a fully distributed analysis at different IRI and
 international sites, through grid solutions such as DIRAC, could be an option to offset some of
 these allocation difficulties. [Section 5.9]

6.4.2 DESC: Experiment Profile
Key planned DESC analyses of LSST include cosmological constraints on the matter content and amplitude
of clustering from the combination of correlation functions of the weak lensing and clustering observables (the
so-called ‘3x2pt’ analysis), and constraints from only the weak lensing shear and clustering 2-point correlation
function; cosmological constraints on the equation of state of dark energy and the matter density from the large
LSST supernova sample; and parameter constraints from the abundance of clusters and cluster lensing. DESC
will also test for tensions in inferred parameters from LSST to those derived from other experiments (such as
those seen today in estimates of the Hubble parameter and clustering amplitude derived from different probes).

6.4.2.1 Science Background
As was the case with precursor photometric surveys, the image dataset is extremely rich and offers various
avenues for exploring the core science cases. In particular, the Rubin LSST will provide DESC the ability to do
cosmology in the time domain on an unprecedented scale. Millions of transient events are generated and selected
per night of observation to provide O(106) of cosmologically relevant objects at the end of the survey. In addition,
the analysis of wide and deep accumulated images will lead to static catalogs of galaxies that will be released
yearly by the Rubin Observatory, probing large volumes and enabling cross-correlation science with other
current and planned surveys in different wavelengths.

The primary data source is the Rubin USDF at SLAC. Workflows will primarily involve heterogeneous analysis
operations over either the processed data products from the alert stream of transient events, or the data set
extracted from the accumulated images and catalogs. Nominally, most of the computing will take place at
NERSC, so moving selected datasets from the Rubin USDF at SLAC to NERSC is a priority. However, as the
survey proceeds, DESC will likely need to obtain additional resources elsewhere through specific programs or
through international collaborations.

6.4.2.2 Collaborators
The collaboration currently comprises some 1,270 members, of whom about 250 are full members. These
originate in 23 countries and more than 200 institutions. Of the members, about 50% are from the United States,
9% from the United Kingdom and 7% from France. About 520 of the members are graduate students or postdocs.

DESC’s current analysis model involves bringing collaborators to deploy their analyses at NERSC to run at scale
and access collaboration data products. DESC is planning to expand these capabilities and has had successful
tests and large campaigns at the UK and France Data Facilities (CC-IN2P3) for Rubin, though details for securing
these resources for DESC science purposes are still being settled. These resources could potentially be used
for DESC workflows that require Rubin imaging products available at these sites. Some of the computing and
storage allocation at NERSC could then be offloaded. Additional potential resources for DESC are the IDACs
for the Rubin observatory, which are being developed as in-kind contributions to Rubin Observatory by a
number of institutions around the world. Some of the IDAC resources will be made available to DESC and other
LSST science collaborations for science analyses and could potentially provide specialized capabilities (e.g.,
complementary databases, Hadoop platforms, opportunistic resources for peak times at NERSC).

Until now, data sets (generally simulations) have been produced at the US and France Data Facilities (CC-IN2P3)
and transferred through http, rsync and Globus. As detailed later, DESC foresees changing the model to use
Rucio over FTS to integrate better with the Rubin Project’s systems. DESC has begun working directly with
Rubin on this, capitalizing on their expertise.

DESC has detailed the current approach to the IRI in the IRI-specific section below. Of particular note, DESC
utilizes DOE LCFs (both ALCF and Oak Ridge Leadership Facility, OLCF) for large simulation campaigns. The
simulation products are currently transferred to NERSC via Globus.

6.4.2.3 IRI Readiness
NERSC is the primary computing resource for DESC. However, as the needed computing time and expected
available NERSC allocation are anticipated to diverge in a few years’ time, DESC is exploring available
complementary resources. Some are from the international community — in the past DESC has undertaken
simulations and image processing in France at CC-IN2P3. In the past, DESC has also used other DOE
computing resources for specific, well-suited needs, such as the ALCF Theta (and other) platforms for large-scale
simulation efforts.

As for IRI, DESC sees a potential for certain workflows that are more compute intensive (such as image
simulations and Markov Chain MC analyses of cosmology parameter space) to branch out across multiple sites. In
the past, working across different facilities usually meant specific workflow setups tailored to the infrastructure/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 133

hardware available at each facility. IRI is supposed to help overcome this hurdle and provide users with a very
similar environment across facilities to ease moving across platforms. With regard to data movement, Globus has
helped immensely across US facilities to provide an easy-to-use interface that is the same at all facilities. DESC
very much hopes that this also will be the case in the future (though only a small number of DESC-relevant
facilities support Globus currently). With regard to workflow implementation, there is a lot of work ahead. DESC
will follow IRI developments closely and make use of infrastructure developed wherever possible.

DESC workflows are quite heterogeneous but primarily fall under two categories:

 • The great majority (>90%) both in terms of compute and storage will correspond to long-term
 campaigns. These will include the processing and reprocessing of LSST data releases to extract
 data vectors, analyze systematics, model the signal, and infer cosmological parameters. They will
 be complemented by cosmological and image simulations in a similar amount. Therefore, these
 require “sustained access to resources at scale over a longer time to accomplish a well-defined
 objective.” Reliability and reproducibility of results at computing platforms are key for the
 success of DESC. In this regard, compute-intensive multisite workflows would be an enormous
 benefit given possible allocation constraints to reach enhanced goals for DESC science.

 • Some of the workflows are time sensitive. These rely on the Rubin ‘alert stream’, or
 intermediary brokers, for astrophysical events and generate actions or outputs that need to be
 processed within some time period (typically few minutes to few days, depending on the nature
 of the source). If the sources are not monitored reliably through selected computing platform(s)
 in the best case the result will be a delay or degradation of the information obtained about the
 source, and in the worst case, the loss of a relevant or unique astronomical event.

6.4.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
DESC will be responsible only for analyzing data collected by the Rubin Observatory with possible
enhancements coming from the addition of legacy data or concurrent missions through agreements to perform
joint processing. DESC is not directly involved in the development of the instrument or in the data-taking
process. DESC also has no influence on the facility’s computing capabilities. DESC defers to the Vera C. Rubin
observatory case study for some of the requested details.

Present-FY26Q4: The anticipated start of the survey is FY26Q1. In this period DESC expects to bulk
download from the primary data source (USDF at SLAC) to NERSC the released datasets corresponding to
the commissioning and science verification periods (also called Data Previews). The specifics of the data set
sizes, files, etc. are uncertain due to the nature of these pre-operations’ activities and final scope, but DESC can
estimate it will be of a similar size as Rubin’s recent Data Preview 0.2 (DP0.2), of the order of 10 TB of catalogs,
with the possibility of transferring up to 1–2 PB of imaging data to understand how much DESC will eventually
use. In this period, the main computing resource will continue to be NERSC Perlmutter. DESC will be using
the Spin platform at NERSC as a database to store selected streamed data from the alerts brokers, the yearly data
volume expected to be stored this way is 1–2 TB.

FY27-FY31: Major Rubin data releases for static cosmology analyses will be generated in this period. DESC may
incorporate other complementary data sets to enhance the science (both legacy, with small impact in relative data
volume, and concurrent data sets, from the Euclid and Roman space observatories, with likewise minor impact
in data volume as they will be limited to relatively small areas of the sky). The bulk of data will still originate with
Rubin, and will be of the order of 1–2 PB to be transferred every two to three years, and, assuming some data
reduction strategies, could eventually be yearly.

FY32 onward: Eventually, analyses would employ fully not only the galaxy catalogs, but the full imaging data of
O(10s) PB. Replicating even the high-level imaging data at NERSC is inefficient and unfeasible, due to the scale
of the expected allocation. Thus, embracing a fully distributed analysis at different IRI and international sites,
through grid solutions such as DIRAC, could be an option to offset some of these allocation difficulties. This

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 134

would enable enhanced goals for analyses, such as more thorough exploration of cosmological parameter space
through Markov Chain MC processes, or forward modeling of pixel-level data of supernovae and host galaxies —
scene modeling photometry — to produce more accurate uncertainties and reduce the systematic error budget
on supernova analysis. Another enhanced goal would combine fully the Rubin and Euclid data sets at the imaging
level assuming an agreement is reached for this processing.

6.4.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
Present–FY26Q4: This period will see mainly preparatory work for cosmology analyses in DESC, as the first
relevant Data Release from the Rubin Observatory for cosmology (key projects) will not be delivered until at
least FY27Q4. However, plenty of scientific publications will precede this milestone, e.g., comparative work with
previous surveys, calibration work relevant for cosmology, validations of data and methods. These analyses will be
carried out at NERSC primarily.

Most of the computational work will still be in the form of simulations and analyses on simulated or precursor
datasets (in most cases, without need of massive data movement). An example is forecasting for analysis
choices: the analysis of the data will require us making choices on the scales to be analyzed and the impact of
marginalization over survey and astrophysical systematics. Soon, DESC expect that the collaboration will run a
series of simulated analyses to inform these choices. This is computationally intensive because it requires testing
of many different scenarios through realistic likelihood evaluation for many of the probes.

Some very early science cases will run at the end of this period over science verification data, as precursor
analysis runs, mainly constrained to NERSC with data-intensive and compute-intensive workflows. For example,
the analysis of the alert stream will be used to find faint nearby supernovae very early in Rubin data (ideally
within hours of explosion). At these phases, the supernova ejecta will plough through any circumstellar material
or binary companion, and the resulting emission can contain signatures of the progenitor system. Identifying
these systems rapidly and scheduling target-of-opportunity follow-up will yield insights into the explosion
physics, and can potentially refine the models used to infer supernova distances at high redshift, as well as shed
light into other modes of stellar death. Targeted spectroscopic follow-up of a sample of low-to-intermediate
redshift supernovae can be used to build a small sample of objects with reduced systematic error. These small
samples can be used to validate the entire supernova analysis pipeline for Year 1 and Year 2 data.

FY27-FY31: A high-level overview of plans for science with the first full-blown data releases follows:

 1. A key project analysis process primarily starts from the annual object catalogs from the Data Release
 (starting with DR2) or database information built up by DESC from the culled transient stream
 (known as the FAST DB).
 2. For weak lensing analyses, galaxy shapes are the main observable used, combined with redshift
 measurements inferred from multi-band photometry. Three summary statistics are currently
 envisaged which correlate galaxy shapes with each other; correlate galaxy shapes with positions; and
 correlate galaxy positions with each other. These are combined into a set of three 2-pt correlations
 (data-intensive). DESC also anticipates higher-order statistics being needed to capture non-
 Gaussian information. This analysis task includes running large-scale image and source injection
 simulation studies to estimate and account for systematic effects.
 3. Analysis of supernovae is based on identifying SNIa from the transients’ stream, followed by using
 the apparent brightness and redshift to determine a recession velocity.
 4. Strong lensing is based on finding lensed quasars and supernova systems and then measuring the
 time delays for various paths of the lensed object using multiyear light curves.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 135

 5. Finally, clusters of galaxies are used to predict cosmological parameters based on the relationships
 between cluster properties and halo mass. These parameters are obtained via a likelihood analysis
 using mass function predictions obtained from simulations. Many of these analyses are followed up
 by compute-intensive analysis to explore a multi-dimensional parameter space with
 Bayesian statistics.
These analyses will be carried out primarily at NERSC. As mentioned in other sections, during this period DESC
foresees testing and carrying out workflows across multiple sites as supplementary computing, trying to minimize
data movement. Specific tasks might be run completely outside of NERSC, such as those related to imaging,
details still to be defined (and summary data products or results would then need to be moved to NERSC).

During this period, NERSC will be migrating to NERSC-10, and DESC will be testing the incorporation of
IDACs and other IRI platforms to these analyses. Large efforts in simulations in parallel to data analyses will be
required using all these resources.

FY32 onward: DESC expects workflows to eventually be distributed across multiple sites, with the exact
technology to be determined (see also next section). Major cosmology analyses will be undertaken with LSST
year 4 and year 10 data releases (starting in approximately 2032 and 2038, respectively and extending for two
or three years). DESC also anticipates an increasing level of joint analyses of LSST data with survey data from
space-based observatories Euclid and Roman Space Telescope during this period, the scope of which remains to
be determined.

6.4.2.6 Remote Science Activities
As mentioned above, all DESC science activities are intrinsically ‘remote’ as DESC is reliant on data obtained
by the Rubin Observatory, processed and distributed from the USDF at SLAC, with subsidiary copies in other
points of the world (France, Chile, UK). In the general case DESC will be pulling data from SLAC to NERSC
with a yearly cadence approximately (keeping in general only the latest data release). In addition, an alert stream
will be monitored coming from diverse brokers that cull the original kHz stream of transient source alerts from
the Observatory.

Present-FY26Q4: Most of the current work in DESC is being done with simulated data which already exist
at NERSC or are being created at NERSC or at other computing facilities. In general, the simulation data are
already curated where the simulation is carried out to reduce transferred data volumes considerably. However, in
this time frame, simulation campaigns will need to be created for DESC to explore cosmological parameters and
to generate covariance estimates. This will mean that data will have to be moved from other computing centers
to NERSC. Data transfers will be O(100) TB. During FY25 and FY26, data from the Rubin Observatory will start
appearing at SLAC and DESC will perform test data transfers at first (Data Preview 1, O(10) TB, expected May
2025) and fully run the data transfer system with Data Preview 2 (O (100 TB), expected in early 2026). In this
period, DESC would exercise small transfers (O(10 TB) in 2025, progressively towards 1–2 PB scale) and possibly
coordinated workflows (2026) with international collaborators, in preparation for full production.

FY27-FY31: In this period DESC will transfer the first dataset relevant for the DESC Key Projects as described
in the Science Plan. This data set is expected to be of the order of 1–2 PB, after some optimization. These data
transfers will happen more or less yearly. Most of the primary work will happen at NERSC but supplemented
with information transferred from other experiments. In most cases, these will be O(10) TB sized catalogs (real
data and simulations) and on occasion smaller imaging datasets. As for analysis workflows, though the primary
work will happen at NERSC, DESC will explore grid-like approaches and multisite workflow management with
previous, smaller data sets, and effectively deploy them in this period.

FY32 onward: Full implementation of multisite workflows, for image processing, Markov Chain MC to benefit
from the Rubin/IRI computing ecosystems. For example, DESC conceives using DIRAC as a grid-based option
for this. IDACs will be used to offload cycles for debugging or complementing NERSC jobs, which would still be
the primary facility.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 136

6.4.2.7 Software Infrastructure
Present-FY26Q4: With simulated data totaling a few hundred TB, transfer has largely been via HTTP, rsync, and
Globus for data sets moving from NERSC to and from CC-IN2P3 (France), ALCF, OLCF, and SLAC. DESC
will explore in this period the use of Rucio over FTS following the steps of the Rubin project for SLAC-to-
NERSC transfers, and possibly for its own purposes in interactions with IDACs. DESC is currently using Parsl
for workflow management of image reprocessing tasks as well as certain simulation and analysis workflows, and
DESC has funded support for this. DESC has good experience with other workflow tools and has been able to
work closely with the Parsl team on desired features to run distributed processing with minimal human oversight.

FY27-onward: DESC has no concrete plans for workflow management tools beyond the ad hoc tools DESC has
built and Parsl, which will need to be tested at scale with realistic data sets and use cases.

6.4.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
NERSC is the main computing platform and SLAC the data source for Rubin Observatory data. The most critical
component is an efficient transfer between these sites. Today, there are at least a pair of 100 Gbps connections
between SLAC and NERSC, via ESnet. NERSC has a sum of 1Tb/s connection to ESnet, so if SLAC upgrades
their site connection then a higher bandwidth is possible. These upgrades are expected at SLAC in the coming
five-year period, as detailed in the SLAC Site Technology profile.

As complementary information, DESC has tested Globus transfers of tens and hundreds of TB between NERSC
and international sites in France (CC-IN2P3) and Spain, with transfer rates of 400 MB/s and 180
MB/s respectively.

6.4.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.4.2.9.1 Cloud Services
DESC has no concrete plans for using any DESC-specific Cloud applications. It is worth noting that a good part
of the initial engagement with the data by DESC scientists, in terms of image visualization, exploratory analysis,
will happen in the US DAC, through an interface called the RSP. DESC defers to the Rubin Observatory case
study for technical details.

6.4.2.9.2 Artificial Intelligence and ML
Due to the large variety of science applications and multiple approaches and stages of DESC’s analyses, there
are many instances where ML will be applied. For large-scale computation at NERSC as the primary computing
facility, DESC benefits from its large investment in GPU platforms (1792 GPU-accelerated nodes in the current
platform Perlmutter). Many of the most widely used packages and libraries are available (TensorFlow, PyTorch
and others).

6.4.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
DESC has no wireless networking requirements.

6.4.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
Present-FY26Q4: In this period DESC does not expect major bottlenecks in either the data-transfer throughput
or available computing time. In the maximal case, DESC might expect up to O(1–2) PB of data transfer between
SLAC and NERSC (Rubin’s Data Previews 1 and 2, corresponding to commissioning and science verification
data, including images and intermediate products) and a moderate increase in compute allocation to deal with
first exploratory and proof of principle analyses.

FY27-FY31: For the full-fledged data releases, DESC will see a limitation in some of the science cases which
require full access to the complete single-visit image data set (only available at SLAC or CC-IN2P3, but not
NERSC as currently planned) rather than just the galaxy catalogs. DESC is currently looking for mitigations

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 137

to this problem such as limiting the size of transferred data to NERSC but enabling the analyses nonetheless
or shipping containers to run at these facilities instead. In addition, large-scale image simulations produced at
NERSC or elsewhere would possibly stress small-latency storage allocation at NERSC, as well as compete with
the computing allocation for its analyses in parallel to real data analyses. The transition to NERSC-10 in this
period and its unknown impact on established pipelines also introduces some uncertainty.

FY32 onward: A full-fledged implementation of multisite processing and possibly increased computing
allocations at the USDF or France (CC-IN2P3) would be the final goal to realize the full scale of DESC analyses.

6.4.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
Major transfers from data sources (currently, mostly simulated data) has happened through https from the Google
Cloud (where the Rubin USDF was being hosted temporarily), and through rsync and Globus from CC-IN2P3
in France. The current plan is to adopt Rucio and FTS in a way similar to what the Vera Rubin Observatory has
done to manage its data sets, for two purposes:

 • Transfer data from the USDF to NERSC after each yearly data release.
 • Synchronize subsets of data or value-added data sets DESC generates across sites with which
 DESC has an agreement to cooperate in analysis or host copies of data for DESC scientists.
The back-up plan, however, is to use Globus. DESC would use NERSC DTN as the main endpoint which has
access to the filesystems of interest.

6.4.2.12 Outstanding Issues
There are two outstanding issues.

 • DESC needs technical support in implementing some of data distribution solutions (Rucio,
 DIRAC). Standing up these web services requires close interaction with the facilities (e.g.,
 NERSC). Built-in facility support for this software (e.g., just like the facilities provide built-in
 support for Globus) would be very beneficial.

 • Second, the DESC faces complex issues with identity and account management across various
 services/sites. There are two broad classes of sites. First, there are sites like NERSC where a
 DESC member has a NERSC account that lets them access both NERSC and Globus. Second,
 there are sites like in the UK, France (CC-IN2P3), and Rubin IDACs where the DESC needs
 to deploy a proper VO and have a proper grid certificate. These items are needed to enable
 interactions with grid software like Rucio and DIRAC. Ideally, the VO and certificates would be
 linked to each member’s NERSC account. Further, we would ideally want to be able to target
 the NERSC queues using grid software like DIRAC so that DESC can run jobs, move data,
 etc., across multiple sites transparently.

6.5 CMB
The CMB consists of the photons created in the Big Bang, propagated through the universe until detected today.
As a consequence, the photons that make up the CMB trace the entire history of the universe and provide a
unique window on fundamental physics and cosmology. In addition, CMB data sets are extraordinarily sensitive
mm-wave surveys, incidentally supporting a wealth of astrophysics and astronomy. The full scope and scale of
CMB science is laid out in the CMB-S4 Decadal Survey Report.68

CMB-S4 is the “Stage 4” ground-based CMB experiment, bringing the entire US community together to build a
single experiment capable of detecting the faintest CMB signals.69 The four design-driving science cases are:

 1. To detect (or very tightly constrain) primordial gravitational waves to test theories of inflation.
 2. To detect (or very tightly constrain) additional species of light relic particles.
 3. To map the matter in the universe and elucidate the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters.
 4. To detect mm-wave transients and add mm-wave data to multi-messenger astronomy.
 5. Note that meeting these will necessarily also enable the full scope of other CMB science.

6.5.1 Discussion Summary
CMB-S4 will leverage resources that exist in Chile today. The Simons Observatory (SO) and Atacama Large
Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) invested heavily into the networking infrastructure over prior years, and
has a clean fast path to national and international computing resources. Networking to support experimentation
includes multiple strands of fiber optic cables, as well as a perfSONAR monitoring infrastructure. ESnet will
continue to work with CMB-S4 on networking capabilities, as well as any overlap with the existing projects.

CMB-S4 is still early in its design and development, and has flexibility in the way it approaches aspects of
computing and networking. The project plans to attempt data challenges in the coming years (with ESnet
support), and will also explore all available options for the software used in data management, as well as available
computational resources (HPC, Grid, or Cloud). They are interested in aspects of IRI, in particular how federated
identity may ease the transition between multiple ways to compute and store research data for a distributed set
of users.

 • The CMB consists of the photons created in the Big Bang, propagated through the universe
 until detected today. As a consequence, the photons that make up the CMB trace the entire
 history of the universe and provide a unique window on fundamental physics and cosmology.
 CMB-S4, a joint project between the NSF and the DOE, is the “Stage 4” ground-based CMB
 experiment, bringing the entire US community together to build a single experiment capable of
 detecting the faintest CMB signals. [Section 4.1]

68 https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.04473
69 Scientific research using CMB data continues to be a priority for DOE and NSF, an initiative that provides crucial information on the
fundamental nature of matter and energy in the universe. However, DOE and NSF jointly decided in calendar year 2025 that they can no
longer support the P5-envisioned CMB-S4 project. Nevertheless, DOE and NSF will continue to partner with the CMB science community
to explore the potential science that can be achieved with limited upgrades to existing experiments to further this important U.S.-led research.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 140

 • In mid-2024, the NSF was not able to commit to funding for portions of the project that
 involved experimentation to be conducted at the South Pole. Thus, the information provided
 by CMB-S4 in this report assumes the entirety of the observatory will be based in Chile.
 The experimentation will produce three coordinated surveys from Chile between 2028 to
           2035. [Section 4.1]

 ° A wide and deep survey of ~70% of the sky using 2 x 6m telescopes that operates with a
 with a daily cadence

 ° An ultra-deep survey of ~3% of the sky using 18 x 0.5m telescopes

 ° An ultra-deep survey of the same ~3% of the sky using a different 5m telescope.

 • The CMB-S4 collaboration currently consists of 520 members at 142 institutions in 24 countries
 and 26 US states. The institutions include DOE, NASA, and Department of Commerce
 laboratories, as well as a host of universities. [Section 4.1]

 • In operations, CMB-S4 will gather 1.9 x 10^8 samples per second, corresponding to a
 compressed data rate of 2.0 Gbps. Data will be transferred in real time over fiber networks to
 the primary data center at the DOE’s NERSC and copied to the secondary data center at the
 DOE’s ALCF. All data are archived at both NERSC and ALCF. 20 TB of data are expected daily
 during operations (~7PB of data annually). [Section 4.2]

 • CMB-S4 will deploy a number of resources (2 x 6m telescopes, 1 x 5m + 18 x 0.5m
 telescopes) starting in 2030. These resources have the potential to produce 8 PB/year of data,
 sent to the United States nightly in 20 TB sets. Local computation and storage resources
 (670TB) can support storing a buffer of data for up to a month due to network degradation or
 downtime. [Section 4.2]

 • Along with the raw data files CMB-S4 will create, the primary data products will be the
 frequency maps: [Section 4.2]

           °    Daily (7 years x 365 days): 150 TB in 51,000 files.

           °    MC (1,000 realizations x 7 years): 450 TB in 150,000 files.

 • CMB-S4 will conduct a series of data challenges, starting in 2025 and running yearly through
 2029, to help prepare for the operational challenge of data mobility from Chile to the US, and
 the analysis pipeline being constructed using DOE- and NSF-funded computing resources.
 Outcomes include: [Section 4.2]

 ° Validate and verify the experiment design at the degree needed at each DOE/NSF
 review gate.

 ° Validate and verify the project data management and collaboration data analysis pipelines.

 ° Demonstrate scaling the data volume the simulation/reduction tools can process to achieve
                100% by 2030.

 ° Demonstrate porting and sufficient optimization of the data management software stack to
 each new generation of HPC and HTC architecture deployed by the DOE/NSF.

 • Current and near-term work in data movement will focus on building a test stand for both data
 and metadata into the baseline data-movement tool (Rucio). These tests will primarily involve
 local operations within NERSC: running Rucio as a service on the Spin container-based service
 and ingesting simulated data into CFS. CMB-S4 will also practice moving data between local
 filesystems using Rucio. By the end of this time frame, transfers between NERSC and ALCF, or
 another large computing center, will be tested to validate performance expectations.
           [Section 4.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 141

 • Each day’s data are immediately reduced to a map of the observed sky, using US agency
 computing resources (DOE HPC, NSF HTC, and potentially FABRIC). These maps are
 analyzed to identify transient sources, with alerts issued to the entire scientific community via
 the Community Alert Broker, and for data quality and telescope health checks. [Section 4.3]

 • Given the size and complexity of the CMB-S4 data set (~100 PB), collecting, transporting, and
 reducing the raw data from timestreams of detector samples to well-characterized sky maps is
 the responsibility of the CMB-S4 project. Given the extraordinary range of science these maps
 support and their relatively small size (~100 TB), analyzing these maps is the responsibility of
 the CMB-S4 collaboration and the scientific community at large. [Section 4.3]

 • CMB-S4 raw data will be archived at NERSC and ALCF, and a subset of recent data will
 be stored on disk at those centers. Daily data-quality statistics and maps will be produced at
 NERSC, ALCF, NSF ACCESS, and possibly FABRIC. Bulk reprocessing will be performed at
 NERSC, ALCF, and NSF ACCESS. Simulated data will be generated at NERSC and ALCF
 and typically reduced to maps on the fly to avoid I/O and storage overheads. In both cases, the
 resulting maps will be stored on disk and archived at NERSC and ALCF. Map-level data will
 be analyzed at NERSC and on local compute resources across the collaboration. Published data
 (primarily maps and derived scientific data) will be made available to the scientific community
 at NERSC and LAMBDA located at the NASA GSFC. The raw data and the software used
 to characterize and reduce them will also be made available to the scientific community at
 NERSC. [Section 4.6]

 • During the construction phase, all the significant data will be simulated. Simulations will be
 run at NERSC or ALCF, and the data copied between them, peaking at O(10) PB in 2029.
 Reductions to maps will be run at NERSC, ALCF, NSF ACCESS centers, and possibly
 FABRIC. Maps will be made available to the collaboration at NERSC, with the bulk of the
 analyses performed there. Small amounts of data may be moved to collaborators’ local resources
 for analysis. [Section 4.6]

 • CMB-S4 will build upon existing infrastructure established by the Simons Observatory
 pathfinder experiment, which produces approximately 10% of the expected CMB-S4 data
 volume. A 10 Gbps dedicated fiber link from the site, to the ALMA, is being installed by
 Simons Observatory currently and already receives support from ESnet to ensure global
 connectivity. [Section 4.7]

 • The fiber connection from the CMB-S4 experiment site, to the broader network, consists of a
 fiber pair from the Simons Observatory to the Red Universitaria Nacional (REUNA)
 PoP at the ALMA observatory. The fiber pair has an eight-channel passive optical multiplexer
 installed at each end, providing eight optical channels. Each of those channels can
 support 1 Gbps or 10 Gbps Ethernet with off-the-shelf pluggable optics. The Simons
 Observatory is using one channel today. CMB-S4 intends to use two of those channels for
 production operations. [Section 4.7]

 • CMB-S4 has no plans to purchase dedicated AI/ML hardware or services. There are
 possible applications of ML in areas of low-level data cleaning (detection of classes of “glitche”
 in the data), and for improvements in observing strategies / planning. In both cases the
 evaluation of such models is cheap and model training can be performed at existing centers such
 as NERSC. [Section 4.8]

 • The CMB-S4 project has no intention of using WiFi / Cellular / Satellite connectivity at the site
 in Chile. Some of this equipment can generate RFI that impacts science measurements. CMB-
 S4 may make use of an existing dedicated point-to-point microwave link to the nearby town. This
 link has been shown not to interfere with existing experiments and is a useful back-up connection
 for remote access / debugging if the nominal fiber connection goes down. [Section 4.8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 142

 • By design, the CMB-S4 project plans to leverage multiple DOE SC user facilities and is
 a natural fit for consideration as an IRI workflow. Data will be replicated and analyzed
 across multiple DOE HPC facilities, with real-time requirements on results to help guide
 experimental outcomes. The results are broadly interesting to a wide community of users across
 the HEP community, and must be available decades into the future. [Section 4.9]

6.5.2 CMB: Experiment Profile
CMB-S4 was case-studied in 2020 with South Pole and Chile Atacama observatory sites. In the time after this
initial case study, the experiment design is in the process of being revisited to site the observatory wholly in
Chile. Since the process is incomplete, a conservative approach to the design is being taken, where all the 2020
assets will be deployed in Chile for the sake of this report. Revised data rates and requirements are anticipated by
the midterm review.

6.5.2.1 Science Background
CMB-S4 is a joint DOE and NSF project, recommended by the Particle-Physics Project Prioritization
Panel (P5)70 in 2014 and 2023 and the Astronomy and Astrophysics Advisory Committee71 in 2017. It adds
the capacities and capabilities of ANL, Fermilab, LBNL, and SLAC under the DOE Office of HEP to the
longstanding NSF university program spanning the Division of Astronomical Sciences (MPS/AST) and the
Division of Physics (MPS/PHY) in the Directorate of Mathematical and Physical Sciences and the Office of Polar
Programs in the Directorate of Geosciences. Other partners include NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and
GSFC, the Department of Commerce’s National Institute of Standards and Technology, Associated Universities
Incorporated, and the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. Collaborative discussions are underway with the
Cerro Chajnantor Atacama Telescope (CCAT-prime) and the Simons Observatory and its supporting Simons and
Heising-Simons foundations. CMB-S4 also anticipates international partners and in-kind contributions, especially
from Australia, Canada, Europe, and Japan.

Here and throughout the document, CMB-S4 is discussing a temporary project plan that will change as the
mission design is optimized for the Chilean observing site. Note that while CMB-S4 anticipate their availability,
none of the off-project network and computing resources that are planned for use have yet been secured as
writing of this report (November, 2024)

To meet the CMB-S4 science goals (and all the other science that this will be enable) three coordinated surveys
will be conducted from 2028 to 2035 at the high altitude Chilean site in the Atacama desert:

 1. A wide/deep survey of ~70% of the sky with O(270,000) detectors spanning sixmm-wave
 frequencies on 2 x 6m telescopes with a daily cadence.
 2. An ultra-deep survey of ~3% of the sky with O(150,000) detectors spanning 8 mm-wave frequencies
 on 18 x 0.5m telescopes.
 3. An ultra-deep survey of the same ~3% of the sky with O(120,000) detectors spanning 7 mm-wave
 frequencies on 1 x 5m telescope.

70 https://www.usparticlephysics.org
71 https://www.nsf.gov/events/event_summ.jsp?cntn_id=299907&org=NSF

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 143

In operations, CMB-S4 will gather 1.9 x 10^8 samples per second, corresponding to a compressed data rate
of 2.0 Gbps. Data will be transferred in real time over fiber networks to the primary data center at the DOE’s
NERSC and copied to the secondary data center at the DOE’s ALCF. All data are archived at both NERSC
and ALCF.

Each day’s data are immediately reduced to a map of the observed sky, using US agency computing resources
(DOE HPC, NSF HTC, and potentially FABRIC72). These maps are analyzed to identify transient sources,
with alerts issued to the entire scientific community via the Community Alert Broker, and for data quality and
telescope health checks.

The bulk data are analyzed on US agency resources to:

 1. Characterize the instruments (e.g., determine their exact pointing, measure their beams and band-
 passes, etc.).
 2. Identify systematic effects in and develop software mitigations sufficient for their residuals to be less
 than the tiny CMB signals.
 3. Reduce them to maps at each observing frequency for a multitude of different data cuts over time
 and/or detectors, together with a statistical characterization of each map (e.g., a noise correlation
 matrix or a MC suite of simulated raw data sets reduced to equivalent sets of maps).
These well-characterized frequency maps are then passed to the various collaboration analysis working groups for
the full range of scientific analyses.

Given the size and complexity of the CMB-S4 data set (~100 PB), collecting, transporting, and reducing the raw
data from timestreams of detector samples to well-characterized sky maps is the responsibility of the CMB-S4
project. Given the extraordinary range of science these maps support and their relatively small size (~100 TB),
analyzing these maps is the responsibility of the CMB-S4 collaboration and the scientific community at large.

6.5.2.2 Collaborators
The CMB-S4 collaboration currently consists of 520 members at 142 institutions in 24 countries and 26 US states.
The institutions include DOE, NASA, and Department of Commerce laboratories, as well as a host
of universities.

Currently all data are simulated, and the primary site for creation, storage, sharing, and analysis of these is
NERSC, although this will expand to ALCF and NSF ACCESS as the construction project proceeds.

CMB-S4 raw data will be archived at NERSC and ALCF, and a subset of recent data will be stored on disk at
those centers. Daily data-quality statistics and maps will be produced at NERSC, ALCF, NSF ACCESS and
possibly FABRIC. Bulk reprocessing will be performed at NERSC, ALCF, and NSF ACCESS. Simulated
data will be generated at NERSC and ALCF and typically reduced to maps on the fly to avoid I/O and storage
overheads. In both cases, the resulting maps will be stored on disk and archived at NERSC and ALCF. Map-
level data will be analyzed at NERSC and on local compute resources across the collaboration. Published data
(primarily maps and derived scientific data) will be made available to the scientific community at NERSC and
LAMBDA73 located at the NASA GSFC74. The raw data and the software used to characterize and reduce them
will also be made available to the scientific community at NERSC.

6.5.2.3 IRI Readiness
During operations, the CMB-S4 project plans to leverage multiple DOE SC facilities in the following ways:

 1. A copy of all raw data will be replicated across at least two computing facilities (e.g., NERSC
 and ALCF).
 2. Near real-time QA tests will be run on raw data. To avoid interruptions due to facility maintenance,
 it must be possible to run these tests on any HPC or HTC compute resources available to the
 project. (time-sensitive pattern)
 3. Prior to data releases, a large volume of archival data may be reprocessed. This requires
 substantial compute resources and jobs may be distributed across multiple HPC centers.
 (long-term campaign pattern)
For points (2) and (3) above, CMB-S4 will leverage aspects of IRI including federated login / access across
facilities and also tools for job submission and management. Ideally, these integrated tools would allow job
management not only on HPC centers (i.e., running slurm), but also on HTC / Grid-computing resources. HTC
resources are ideally suited for rapid data-quality testing.
