6.5.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
Present / Next Two to Five Years: During the construction phase, all the significant data will be simulated
(although small amounts of laboratory data will be generated, primarily at the national laboratories, some of which
may be transferred to NERSC).

Simulations of raw data will be run at NERSC or ALCF and the data copied between them, peaking at O(10) PB
in 2029. Reductions to maps will be run at NERSC, ALCF, NSF ACCESS, and possibly FABRIC. Maps will be
made available to the collaboration at NERSC, with the bulk of the analyses performed there. Small amounts of
data may be moved to collaborators’ local resources for analysis.

Beyond: During the operations phase, data will be transferred to NERSC and ALCF over the network, with the
exact mechanics (including failsafe processes for system downtimes) still to be determined.

Daily reductions to maps will be run at NERSC, ALCF, NSF ACCESS, and possibly FABRIC. Bulk-data
reductions to maps will be run at NERSC, ALCF, and NSF ACCESS.

MC simulations will be used for uncertainty quantification and debiasing of the instrument data. Such simulations
will be generated at NERSC and ALCF and reduced to maps on the fly. The maps will be archived at both sites
and made available to the collaboration at NERSC.

6.5.2.6 Remote Science Activities
The observing site (Chilean Atacama) is remote.

Present / Next Two to Five Years: Precursor experiment (Simons Observatory in Chile) will exercise many of the
systems CMB-S4 plans to use, albeit at ~10% of the data volume.

Beyond: In operations, the Chilean telescopes will generate 2.0 Gbps, and will be connected with a robust 10
Gbps network to the United States.

6.5.2.7 Software Infrastructure
6.5.2.7.1 Data Movement
Present / Next Two to Five Years: Current and near-term work in data movement will focus on building a test
stand for ingesting data / metadata into the baseline data movement tool (Rucio). These tests will primarily
involve local operations within NERSC: running Rucio as a service on the Spin container-based service and
ingesting simulated data into CFS. CMB-S4 will also practice moving data between local filesystems using Rucio.
By the end of this time frame, transfers between NERSC and ALCF, or another large computing center, will be
tested to validate performance expectations.

Separate from data-movement tests internal to the project, CMB-S4 will also increase the number of datasets
(both simulations and legacy public datasets) that are hosted through the portal hosted at NERSC. This portal
supports data downloads using globus.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 147

Beyond Five Years: Prior to operations, a review of the Rucio baseline selection will occur. Even if a new
baseline software tool is chosen, the same basic transfer patterns would persist. During operations, continuous
transfer of data from Chile to NERSC would occur using Rucio over globus. Data would then be replicated with
the same tools to ALCF or another computing facility.

6.5.2.7.2 Data Simulation and Reduction
CMB-S4 currently uses (and plan to continue using) two software frameworks for simulation and analysis of
experimental data. The Time Ordered Astrophysics Scalable Tools (TOAST) framework75 is focused on use in an
HPC context. The SPT-3G framework76 is focused on HTC computing environments. Both are open source and
interoperability work is ongoing.

6.5.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
In the context of the CMB-S4 project, the “local” experiment / facility network describes the infrastructure in
place at the site in Chile and the interfaces from this location to the broader internet. The raw experimental data
consists of compressed “data frames” that are packed into binary files (with a tunable size) prior to transmission
to North America. These binary files have historically been around a Gigabyte in size, which strikes a balance
between file size and number of files.

Present / Next Two to Five Years: During the construction phase of the project, minimal CMB-S4 data will be
transferred from the experiment site back to North America. One of the proposed sites in Chile (Cerro Toco) has
established infrastructure and a currently operating experiment (the Simons Observatory). CMB-S4 will leverage
that existing connection to run some tests with perfSONAR and also transfer some small simulated data files.
Connectivity to the broader Internet is via REUNA, the Chilean NREN. CMB-S4 has an excellent collaborative
relationship with REUNA.

Beyond Five Years: The fiber connection from the experiment site to the broader Internet consists of a fiber pair
from the Simons Observatory site to the REUNA PoP at the ALMA observatory. The fiber pair has an eight-
channel passive optical multiplexer installed at each end, providing 8 optical channels. Each of those channels is
capable of supporting 1 Gbps or 10 Gbps Ethernet with off-the-shelf pluggable optics. The Simons Observatory is
using one channel today. CMB-S4 intends to use two of those channels for production operations.

Although the exact telescope configuration is currently being re-baselined, if a maximal set of 27 small aperture
telescopes and 4 large aperture telescopes is assumed, the sustained data rate is approximately 2 Gbps. CMB-S4
plans to have a 5x margin to allow for “catch-up” transfers in the event of an outage. Although this could fit into
a single optical channel on the multiplexer, there is a plan to use two of the eight channels to allow for service
activities on one channel at a time if needed (and/or reduce catch-up time).

76 https://github.com/CMB-S4/spt3g_software

6.5.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.5.2.9.1 Cloud Services
Although CMB-S4 has no plans to pursue traditional cloud compute resources, cloud-based services for software
development and deployment (github / github actions, conda-forge, docker hub, etc.) will be utilized. CMB-S4
has also explored the use of the FABRIC nearline testbed (described below).

Present / Next Two to Five Years: CMB-S4 has explored the use of FABRIC for several time-critical tasks.
These nodes have reasonable core counts and memory for tasks such as detecting transient astrophysical sources
in small maps made of the raw data. The appeal of using a platform like this is the immediate access to a small
amount of compute cycles and the ability to stream data to these nodes in near real time.

Beyond: Although the baseline plan for real-time computing needs is a combination of HPC centers and HTC
resources, CMB-S4 will explore other possibilities for the redesigned, all-Chile configuration. This might include
limited computing resources on-site, novel solutions like FABRIC, or small dedicated compute nodes in North
America. Commercial cloud solutions are not likely to play a future role, simply due to the cost of transferring /
streaming substantial data volumes to those providers.

6.5.2.9.2 AI and ML
CMB-S4 has no plans to purchase dedicated AI/ML hardware or services. There are possible applications of
ML in areas of low-level data cleaning (detection of classes of “glitches” in the data), and for improvements in
observing strategies / planning. In both cases the evaluation of such models is cheap and model training can be
performed at existing centers such as NERSC.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 149

6.5.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
The CMB-S4 project has no intention of using WiFi / Cellular / Satellite connectivity at the site in Chile. Some
of this equipment can generate RFI that impacts science measurements. CMB-S4 may make use of an existing
dedicated point-to-point microwave link to the nearby town. This link has been shown not to interfere with
existing experiments and is a useful back-up connection for remote access / debugging if the nominal fiber
connection goes down.

6.5.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
The biggest overall data-related challenge is the capacity and capability of HPC and HTC systems, especially
in their total system memory and their available cycles and the efficiency with which CMB-S4 can use them
(especially in the post Moore’s law epoch of energy-constrained computing).

6.5.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
CMB-S4 maintains a data portal at data.cmb-s4.org which has the capability of delivering data both to the CMB-
S4 collaboration and to the wider CMB community through Globus.

The portal is just a statically generated website that contains metadata and links to documentation for data, mostly
in Flexible Image Transport System (FITS) files, hosted on Globus. Data is accessible either through HTTPS,
convenient for quickly downloading individual files to personal machines, or through the Globus application
itself, suitable for batch downloading of data to Supercomputers.

Data is hosted on the NERSC Community File System accessible from all NERSC Supercomputers in specific
folders which are made available on Globus through Globus Guest Collections. The CMB-S4 team is admin of
the Guest Collections but the entire infrastructure is maintained by NERSC.

The NERSC Share Endpoint has id 5dbafbb3-578b-4fb5-aa2f-2b60ad18072d and the two Guest Collections
CMB-S4 maintains are for CMB-S4 specific data, and for public datasets.

CMB-S4 is currently hosting about 30 TB of data mostly as 2-GB-sized uncompressed FITS files.

6.5.2.12 Outstanding Issues
There are no outstanding issues to report at this time beyond continuing to work with ESnet on wide-area/
international bandwidth strategies that will become a factor in the future.

6.6 Muon Experimentation at Fermilab: Muon g-2 and Mu2e
Muons are a potential window to new physics. Extreme precision measurements and searches for extraordinarily
rare phenomena offer comparisons to the Standard Model (SM) that may reveal discrepancies that will narrow
down the models beyond the Standard Model (BSM) that are viable. In contrast to many LHC studies that search
for new BSM particles, these studies are indirect searches for new physics and require very intense beams.

6.6.1 Discussion Summary
The muon g-2 experiment will complete its studies with nearly 7 PB of raw experimental data, and an additional
1.5 PB of processed results. All data are planned to remain on tape at Fermilab, and at current time there is
no backup planned or required. Once the aforementioned processing is complete, the collaboration does not
anticipate reprocessing will happen at this time.

Mu2e will utilize most of the existing computational and storage resources at Fermilab during production, but
has used a number of DOE HPC facilities (i.e., ALCF and NERSC in particular) during simulation construction.
Currently the project produces on the order of hundreds of TB of simulation output per year using OSG-
connected resources at Fermilab, the HPC facilities, and other collaboration sites.

The first aspect of operational Mu2e science will be to handle cosmic-ray events, which are expected to produce
up to 500 TB of event data per year. The majority of this effort will be computed through Fermilab, but there
is possibility that some computation will occur at other WLCG sites; a project goal is to consider up to half of
computing needs occurring off-site. Regular operational data from Mu2e will top 7PB or raw data a year. All
data will be stored at Fermilab, with back-up copies stored at partner sites in Europe (locations are still being
determined).

Mu2e networking needs are relatively straightforward; a maximum of 10 Gbps may be required to handle
intensive times of activity to support external computing needs. Given that a majority of computation and
storage is allocated to Fermilab, and connectivity to other WLCG sites will follow the same patterns as the LHC
computation, additional networking support is not required at this time.

Mu2e will be adopting Rucio and other tools that are well-known to the HEP community to manage workflow
and data mobility. The project is limited in exploration of alternative software and computational platforms
namely due to funding and staff. Adopting new workflows is not something the collaboration has the time or
resources do explore currently, but they have been able to make their simulation and analysis code work at
locations like NERSC and ALCF. During long shutdowns, or extended technical stops, it may be possible to
explore other use cases.

 • The Muon g-2 experiment at Fermilab collected data from 2018 until summer of 2023 and has
 two major releases of results: the first in 2021 based on Run 1 data and the second in 2023 based
 on Runs 2+3 data. The collaboration is analyzing the remaining data (Runs 4–6) and expects to
 make a final measurement during FY25. [Section 4.1]

 • The Muon to Electron Conversion Experiment at Fermilab (Mu2e) will search for the
 neutrinoless decay of a muon into an electron in the Coulomb field of an atomic nucleus.
 Mu2e will start taking cosmic-ray commissioning data early in mid CY 2025 and will begin
 commissioning with beam operations late in calendar 2026. The first physics run will begin early
 in CY 2027 and will continue to the end of CY 2027. During 2028 and 2029 Fermilab accelerator
 operations will pause for upgrades to the accelerator complex in preparation for LBNF. Mu2e
 will resume running in 2030 and continue until the 2033 summer shutdown. [Section 4.1]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 152

 • The Muon g-2 collaboration comprises 181 collaborators from 33 institutions located in 7
 countries: China, Italy, Russia, South Korea, Germany, United Kingdom, and the United
 States. [Section 4.1]

 • The Mu2e collaboration features a total of 239 scientists from 39 institutions in 6 countries:
 China, Germany, Italy, Russia, the UK and the US. [Section 4.1]

 • The full Muon g-2 analysis data set, is approximately 1.3 PB. These data are processed at
 Fermilab to generate much smaller summary files (e.g., histograms in files on order of GB) that
 are transferred to collaborators for analysis at their institutions. [Section 4.2]

 • Mu2e expects that many institutions will request copies of analysis-format datasets and that these
 will be stored locally at each institution. At this time, it is estimated that one copy of the analysis-
 format dataset for the full experiment will be, at most, on the scale of 50 TB. [Section 4.2]

 • At design rate the Mu2e experiment will produce about 7 PB/year of raw data, including physics
 data, calibration data and special runs. The current projection is that Mu2e will achieve the
 physics goals of the experiment taking about 4 PB/year of raw data. For most of these data two
 copies will be stored on tape, but a subset will have only one copy. All tape resident copies will
 be stored at Fermilab. The details of how many events will be selected for calibration, how
 many events will be written out by reconstruction and the size per event of these datasets are
 not well understood at this time. The current estimate is that an additional 5 PB/year will be
 needed for intermediate data sets, repeat processing and for storage of simulated events. This
 brings the total tape needs to about 13 PB/year. [Section 4.2]

 • All Mu2e data can be processed on Fermigrid, but for planning purposes it is assumed that
 about half of it will be processed on Fermigrid and half on opportunistic OSG. On average
 Mu2e expects to process each event twice, leading to an estimate of 4 TB/year of outbound data
 and 2.5 TB/year of inbound data. Discussions have taken place that may lead to some
 calibration work being done in the UK or at INFN, using resources provided by their funding
 agencies. For this exercise Mu2e assumes that about 0.5 PB/year will be transferred to each
 location. [Section 4.3]

 • As Mu2e will be under construction in CY 2025 and 2026, the project will be commissioned with
 cosmic rays. During this period, MC data volumes are likely to remain constant and experimental
 data volumes will be small, likely much less than 0.5 PB/year. On the time scale of three to five
 years Mu2e will commission with beam and have a one-year run. This will be followed by the
 two-year-long shutdown. During the run there will be nominal data volumes. During the two-
 year-long shutdown reprocessing of the full dataset with the latest calibrations and algorithms is
 expected. On a timescale of more than five years Mu2e will restart data taking following the long
 shutdown, complete data taking and begin final analysis. A significant increase in network needs
 compared to the three- to five-year forecast is not expected. [Section 4.3]

 • Simulations for Mu2e will be run on Fermigrid, OSG, at NERSC and ALCF. The simulated
 events, and reconstructed simulated events will be stored at Fermilab. Mu2e expects that
 many institutions will request copies of the analysis-format datasets derived from the simulated
 events; these datasets are likely to be about a few times the volume of the corresponding
 experimental datasets. [Section 4.3]

 • The primary data store for raw Mu2e data and intermediate datasets will be in the computing
 centers on the Fermilab site. Most of the calibration jobs, and all the reconstruction jobs, will be
 run on Fermigrid or use opportunistic cycles on OSG. Mu2e currently has no collaborators with
 access to dedicated cycles on OSG. [Section 4.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 153

 • The current computing needs of Mu2e are dominated by simulation campaigns to provide
 datasets of simulated events for the purpose of value engineering the design, validating the
 design, and providing input for the development of trigger, reconstruction, calibration and
 analysis algorithms. At first the simulations were done on OSG, including Fermilab, but in
 recent years resources on Theta at ALCF and on Cori and Perlmutter at NERSC have been
 used. The output of each of these simulation campaigns is on the scale of 250 TB. [Section 4.4]

 • Mu2e has had preliminary discussions with groups in Italy and in the UK to provide computing
 resources for the calibration of subsystems. If these plans are realized, outbound datasets will
 be on the scale of 0.5 PB/year to each location, and inbound datasets would accumulate to tens
 of TB/year. If additional computing resources are available in collaborating institutions, Mu2e
 plans to use them for simulation campaigns; in this case there will be little outbound traffic and
 inbound traffic of up to a few hundred TB/year. [Section 4.4]

 • Mu2e expects to use resources at several DOE supported sites. At Fermilab Mu2e will use
 local interactive machines provided by the lab, Fermigrid, the Fermilab Elastic Analysis
 Facility, and the data storage resources at Fermilab. Mu2e has demonstrated the ability to use
 big CPU cycles at HPC centers, and does not foresee a need for significant GPU resources
 at this time. [Section 4.6]

 • Mu2e has one example of the time-sensitive IRI pattern. Mu2e plans to perform initial
 processing of data from the experiment within several hours of the data being taken. This will
 be used to select events for several different calibration streams and to produce Data-Quality
 Monitoring (DQM) information. The time constraint is driven by the need to produce high-
 precision, high-statistics DQM information that is sensitive to subtle effects that are below the
 sensitivity of online DQM. [Section 4.9]

6.6.2 Muon Experimentation at Fermilab: Experiment Profile
6.6.2.1 Science Background
Measuring the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon (g-2) has been an enterprise for the last seven decades,
with each experiment achieving better precision and probing the SM more deeply.

The Muon to Electron Conversion Experiment at Fermilab (Mu2e) will search for the neutrinoless decay of a
muon into an electron in the Coulomb field of an atomic nucleus. Observation of this process would provide
unambiguous evidence for physics BSM. The projected single event sensitivity of Mu2e is 2.87 x 10-17,
approximately four orders of magnitude more sensitive than the previous best experiment, SINDRUM-II. For the
quoted sensitivity the projected background level is about 0.4+/-0.2 events. More information77 may be found in
the Mu2e Technical Design Report (TDR)78.

77 https://mu2e.fnal.gov
78 https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.05241

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 154

6.6.2.1.1 Muon g-2 Science Background

 Figure 6.6.1: Data taking for the Muon g-2 experiment at Fermilab

The Muon g-2 experiment at Fermilab collected data, as shown in Fig. 6.6.1, from 2018 until summer of 2023 and
has two major releases of results: the first in 2021 based on Run 179 data and the second in 2023 based on Runs
2+3 data.80 The Runs 2+3 analysis achieved a systematic uncertainty of 70 ppb, exceeding the design goal of the
entire experiment. Fig. 6.6.2 shows the latest results, including the Fermilab 2023 release and the world average,
the latter dominated by the Fermilab result. The discrepancy between the experiment measurement and the SM
prediction81 exceeds five-sigma.

 Figure 6.6.2: Latest results from Muon g-2 experiments

However, there are new predictions from the lattice quantum chromodynamics (QCD) community82 that are
much less discrepant compared to the measurements. The Muon g-2 Theory Initiative is in the process of
evaluating these predictions and the possibility of updating their consensus.

The collaboration is analyzing the remaining data (Runs 4–6) and expects to make a final measurement during

results that require the full dataset, including the electric dipole moment of the muon and tests of Lorentz
invariance, will likely follow shortly thereafter.

6.6.2.1.2 Mu2e Science Background
Mu2e raw data will flow from sensors in five subsystems, through the data acquisition system (DAQ) and trigger
to storage on tape in the Fermilab central computing facility. The raw data will be processed into analysis-
format datasets in a multistep process with a latency of a few weeks. The analysis-format data sets will be small
and widely distributed to collaborating institutions; the intermediate datasets will be used by members of the
collaboration to improve calibrations and algorithms. From time to time Mu2e will reprocess all data using the
most up-to-date calibrations and algorithms; when this is done, intermediate datasets older than a few iterations
will be retired83.

Mu2e is still under construction. Mu2e will start taking cosmic-ray commissioning data early in mid CY 2025
and will begin commissioning with beam operations late in calendar 2026. The first physics run will begin early
in CY 2027 and will continue to the end of CY 2027. During 2028 and 2029 Fermilab accelerator operations will
pause for upgrades to the accelerator complex in preparation for LBNF. Mu2e will resume running in 2030 and
continue until the 2033 summer shutdown. This called the Long Shutdown. Additional information is available in
section 3, below.

In the past years, the computing needs of Mu2e were dominated by simulation campaigns to provide datasets of
simulated events for the purpose of value engineering the design, validating the design, and providing input for
the development of trigger, reconstruction, calibration and analysis algorithms. A typical scale is 25 million core
hours once every few years plus 10 million hours per year for developing the code to produce these datasets and
extracting results from these datasets. This will remain the computing driver until the start of beam data in late
calendar 2026.

At first the simulations were done on OSG, including Fermilab, but in recent years resources on Theta at ALCF
and on Cori and Perlmutter at NERSC have been used. The output of each of these simulation campaigns is on
the scale of 250 TB.

The “story of the data” is similar for both Fermilab muon experiments (and, for that matter, most other Fermilab
experiments) and is depicted in Fig. 6.6.3. The main components relevant to this case study are the Mass
Storage and Compute systems and especially the network connecting them. These components are described in
subsequent sections and elsewhere. The Fermilab network is described in Section 7.4.

 Figure 6.6.3: The flow of data from raw data to analysis results.

6.6.2.2 Collaborators
6.6.2.2.1 Muon g-2 Collaborators
The Muon g-2 collaboration comprises 181 collaborators from 33 institutions located in 7 countries: China, Italy,
Russia (very limited access to data), South Korea, Germany, United Kingdom, United States. As mentioned, large-
scale data processing is nearly complete. The full analysis data set, even with data reduced, is about 1.3 PB. These
data are processed at Fermilab to generate much smaller summary files (e.g., histograms in files on order of GB)
that are transferred to collaborators for analysis at their institutions. Given that the experiment is no longer taking
data and data analysis is nearing the end, the collaboration is not expected to grow in size.

Muon g-2 has no contribution to the table below. The collaboration is no longer executing large data transfers, as
currently only histogram files are needed for final analysis. These files are small (~GB scale).

6.6.2.2.2 Mu2e Collaborators
The Mu2e Collaboration list may be found here84. There are a total of 239 scientists from 39 institutions in six
countries: China, Germany, Italy, Russia, the UK and the US.

The primary data store for raw data and intermediate datasets will be in the computing centers on the Fermilab
site. Most of the calibration jobs, and all the reconstruction jobs, will be run on Fermigrid or use opportunistic
cycles on OSG. Mu2e currently has no collaborators with access to dedicated cycles on OSG.

There have been preliminary discussions with groups at INFN in Italy and in the UK for them to provide
computing resources at the level of a few million CPU hours per year that would be used for the calibration of
subsystems for which they have the primary responsibility. Mu2e expects firm commitments from the Italian
groups for CY 2025. Should these plans be realized, Mu2e estimate that outbound datasets will be on the
scale of 0.5 PB/year to each location and that inbound datasets will be small, at most a few tens of TB/year; the
inbound datasets will be calibration sets and DQM information. If additional computing resources are available
in collaborating institutions Mu2e plans to use them for simulation campaigns. In this case there will be little
outbound traffic and there will be inbound traffic of up to a few hundred TB/year.

Mu2e expects that many institutions will request copies of analysis-format datasets and that these will be stored
locally at each institution. At this time, it is estimated that one copy of the analysis-format dataset for the full
experiment will be, at most, on the scale of 50 TB; it may be considerably smaller.

Simulations will be run on Fermigrid, OSG, at NERSC and ALCF. The simulated events, and reconstructed
simulated events will be stored at Fermilab. Mu2e expects that many institutions will request copies of the
analysis-format datasets derived from the simulated events; these datasets are likely to be about a few times the
volume of the corresponding experimental datasets.

Mu2e will run four classes of jobs:

 • Data Production: this is a multi-stage process: select events for calibration, perform
 calibrations, main reconstruction pass, optional secondary reconstruction passes and creation
 of analysis-format data sets. From time to time the secondary reconstruction will be repeated
 and perhaps once every few years the full dataset will be reprocessed; in both cases the goal is
 to take advantage of improved calibrations and algorithms. Mu2e plans to run these jobs using
 dedicated Fermigrid resources and opportunistic OSG or HPC resources. The breakdown is
 not known at this time. For purposes of this study, it is assumed that 50% of the work is done on
 Fermigrid and that other 50% is done on OSG or at HPC centers.

 • End-user Analysis: The input to this work is the analysis-format data sets that are the final
 product of data production. This work will likely be distributed across Fermigrid, opportunistic
 OSG and resources at remote institutions.
84 https://mu2e.fnal.gov/mu2e_collaboration_list.shtml

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 157

 • MC Production pre-data: These jobs create simulated events and process them through
 the same reconstruction chain as for experimental data. These jobs have no data inputs, only
 configuration input. An unusual feature of Mu2e compared to other HEP experiments is
 that the output of these datasets is small per unit CPU. A simulation campaign of 10 million
 hours will produce somewhere between 50 TB and 250 TB, depending on what processes are
 simulated, and what level of intermediate results are retained. The reason is that simulation of
 the signal is trivial and does not require significant resources. What takes time is the simulation
 of pileup processes; Mu2e has exploited all the opportunities to sculpt these processes at the
 generator level but the reality is that many corners of generator phase space must be included
 that produce very rare, but still important backgrounds. Therefore, most simulated events fail
 the selection criteria and are not written to the output file. The dominant workload in these
 jobs is Geant4 and Mu2e has demonstrated the ability to use multithreaded Geant4 on “Knights
 Landing” architecture for Intel CPUs (KNL) based HPC resources. Mu2e has run these jobs
 on Fermigrid, OSG, on Theta and BeBop at ALCF, and on Cori and Perlmutter at NERSC.
 The analysis-format data sets generated from these simulations are on the scale of 2 TB per 10
 million hours of computing.

 • MC Production with data: once Mu2e has data, random triggers will be used as the pileup
 model. The project will overlay random trigger events on simulated signal and signal-like
 background tracks, and will also select signal-like tracks from off-spill running. Mu2e will
 take the hits from these tracks and overlay random triggers over them to study reconstruction
 efficiency and resolution tails in the presence of pileup. This will greatly reduce the need for
 simulation of pileup, which is the driver for the simulation CPU needs. Mu2e anticipates still
 needing to simulate pileup in order to understand features that are observed in the random
 trigger events; MC production CPU will remain the same during data taking was needed
 pre-data.

6.6.2.3 IRI Readiness
6.6.2.3.1 Muon g-2 IRI Readiness
The Muon g-2 collaboration is currently performing the final analysis on local machines, the Fermilab Elastic
Analysis Facility, and laptops and only involves simple workflows evaluating histograms. An IRI notebook based
analysis facility may be an interesting resource, though the timing is not right for use.

6.6.2.3.2 Mu2e IRI Readiness
Mu2e expects to use resources at several DOE supported sites. At Fermilab Mu2e will use local interactive
machines provided by the lab, Fermigrid, the Fermilab Elastic Analysis Facility and the data storage resources at
Fermilab. Mu2e has demonstrated the ability to use big CPU cycles at HPC centers, and does not foresee a need
for significant GPU resources at this time.

Mu2e has one example of the time-sensitive pattern. Mu2e plans to perform initial processing of data from the
experiment within several hours of the data being taken. This will be used to select events for several different
calibration streams and to produce DQM information. The time constraint is driven by the need to produce
high-precision, high-statistics DQM information that is sensitive to subtle effects that are below the sensitivity of
online DQM. This will inform the calibration work.

At this time Mu2e does not foresee examples of the data integration intensive pattern.

Regarding the long-term campaign pattern. Including commissioning and the planned Fermilab accelerator
shutdown Mu2e expects to take data from 2025 to 2033. This will be followed by several more years of final
analysis where continuous access to the resources discussed above will be required.

6.6.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
6.6.2.4.1 Muon g-2 Instruments and Facilities
The experiment ceased collecting data in July 202385, and does not plan any further simulation campaigns.
Therefore, no data are expected to be generated except for small files associated with analyses. the final result
from the experiment are expected in FY25, and some ancillary results to appear soon thereafter. By FY26 or
FY27, all Muon g-2 computing activity will end.

6.6.2.4.2 Mu2e Instruments and Facilities
For full information about the Mu2e apparatus see the Mu2e TDR86.

The parts of the apparatus that generate data are a straw tube tracking system, a caesium iodide calorimeter, a
plastic scintillator based Cosmic Ray Veto System, a pixel telescope-based Beam Extinction Monitor System and
a Stopping Target Monitor comprising two crystals, one high purity Germanium and the other LaBr. The data
generated by these systems are processed by the Trigger and Data Acquisition System (TDAQ).

Other major subsystems include the proton delivery system, including an extinction insert, and the Muon
Beamline comprising the three large superconducting magnets, the production target, a collimator system, the
stopping target and the muon beam stop. One can also consider the detailed arrangement of shielding materials
as a subsystem in its own right.

All these subsystems are located in the Muon Campus at Fermilab.

The operational cycle of Mu2e is 1.4s, divided into an on-spill period of approximately 0.4s and on off-spill period
of approximately 1.0s. During the on-spill period a proton pulse hits the production target every 1695 ns and the
apparatus is configured to record one event for every proton pulse. During the off-spill period the apparatus will
85 B. Abi et al., (Muon g−2 Collaboration), Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 141801 (2021)
86 https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1501.05241

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 159

be configured to record cosmic rays and to perform in-band calibration tasks; off-spill events will have a duration
of 100 �s, which is a tradeoff between several competing requirements. Data from the five data-generating
subsystems flows into a streaming, deadtime-less Data Acquisition system and from there into a software based
Trigger system that will inspect every event. During on-spill data taking, the trigger will accept approximately 1
in 400 events. During off-spill data taking, the trigger will select cosmic-ray events in the tracker and calorimeter
at a rate of order 10 Hz and will prescale other events to collect unbiased samples that are needed to optimize the
time-dependent trade-offs between efficiency and fake rates.

At the design rate of protons on target, Mu2e TDAQ system will produce 7 PB/year of raw data, which will be
copied to the Fermilab computer center for processing and long-term storage.

Mu2e is currently under construction. Mu2e will start taking cosmic-ray commissioning data early in mid
calendar 2025 and first commissioning beam data late in calendar 2026. When the proton beam data begins, the
rate of protons on target (POT), will be about 55% of the design rate and the experiment will ramp up towards
the design POT rate during early calendar 2027. Starting in January 2028 there will be a two-year shutdown
of Fermilab accelerator operations to allow building the LBNF beamline. Mu2e will resume operations at full
design POT rate in the fall of calendar 2030 and run until summer 2033.

Accelerator operations for Mu2e will be managed by the Fermilab Accelerator Division while the operation of the
Mu2e apparatus will be managed by staff from the collaboration and two Fermilab directorates, Particle Physics
Directorate and Applied Physics and Superconduction Technologies Directorate. Operation of computing for
Mu2e will be managed by the collaboration, drawing on resources, services and staff supplied by the Fermilab
Computational Science and Artificial Intelligence Directorate (CSAID).

For the Snowmass 2021 planning exercise, members of Mu2e performed preliminary design studies for an
upgrade of the apparatus, named Mu2e-II. The work is ongoing, The goal is to identify the minimal set of
modifications to the apparatus that will improve the physics reach by a factor of 10, using the proton beam
that will be available from the Fermilab PIP-II Linac. The technically limited schedule would be to begin
commissioning Mu2e-II about two years after the end of Mu2e data taking.

Throughout all these periods Mu2e expects to use computing resources supplied by CSAID. On the time scale
of now to five years from now it is expected that the primary resource for data production will be Fermigrid
and OSG. For MC production Mu2e will also use HPC facilities that are available, and resources provided by
members of the collaboration.

The comments in the above paragraph also apply to the Mu2e-II design work that will be done during
this period.

Mu2e can also run reconstruction code on the big core HPC resources. The code is not thread safe and is not
designed to run on GPUs. Mu2e has no short-term plans to address these issues because it would divert limited
human resources from critical preparations for data taking. Once operations are established, the project will have
effort available for making the code thread-safe, porting selected components to GPU based architectures and
reimplementing algorithms to exploit resources that will then be available or in the pipeline. This effort could
begin in calendar 2027 and is likely to be well underway during the LBNF shutdown of fiscal 2028-2029. Once
Mu2e has this capability, a large fraction of reconstruction work will be well suited to GPU based HPC centers.

One could also imagine upgrading the trigger hardware to a new architecture. The return on this investment
would be a greater physics reach accompanied by a reduction in the resources required for offline reconstruction,
including network resources. It is very likely such a trigger system could be in place for Mu2e-II and one could
imagine testing components of that system during the later stages of Mu2e. At this time, it seems unlikely that this
work would converge on time for an upgrade of the Mu2e trigger compute servers during the LBNF shutdown.

In summary, on the 2 year time horizon Mu2e’s computing needs will be dominated by simulations with needs
similar to recent years. Towards the end of that period the project will begin to take cosmic-ray data, which will

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 160

mean a modest increase in data processing needs. In the period two to five years from now, Mu2e will complete
commissioning and will have one-year physics data taking. Towards the end of that period Mu2e will begin the
effort of porting code to run on new architectures. On the time scale of 5 to 10 years from now Mu2e will have 3
year run at nominal POT and, if Mu2e-II is funded, construction of Mu2e-II will begin. The Mu2e-II trigger will
be in an excellent position to exploit then-available technologies.

6.6.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
6.6.2.5.1 Muon g-2 Process of Science
There is no substantial large-scale computing expected, as the collaboration is in the final analysis stage. There is
a possibility that it may be necessary to reprocess or re-evaluate a systematic uncertainty, and that could revive
part of the production workflow. This activity could mean the following,

 • Re-running the reconstruction program on some of the raw data, involving staging potentially
 several PBs of data from tape and processing. The collaboration already has workflows in place
 centered around the local grid facility at Fermilab (FermiGrid). A small fraction of jobs may use
 nodes on the OSG, which could entail moving TBs of files.

 • Running a deep analysis to determine a systematic uncertainty. The workflow is similar to the
 above, but running over the reduced reconstructed dataset, which is much smaller than the raw
           data (1.3 PB).

 • Running a simulation campaign to understand a detector effect or systematic. A large-scale
 simulation campaign may produce ~1 PB of data. Simulation workflows would likely be run on
 FermiGrid but could potentially run at NERSC, as has been performed in the past. The latter
 would potentially involve moving that data back to Fermilab.
At this time, none of the above activities are anticipated.

6.6.2.5.2 Mu2e Process of Science
At design POT rate the Mu2e experiment will produce about 7 PB/year of raw data, including physics data,
calibration data and special runs. The current projection is that Mu2e will achieve the physics goals of the
experiment taking about 4 PB/year of raw data. For most of these data two copies will be stored on tape but
a subset will have only one copy. All tape resident copies will be stored at Fermilab. The details of how many
events will be selected for calibration, how many events will be written out by reconstruction and the size per
event of these datasets are not well understood at this time. The current estimate is that an additional 5 PB/year
will be needed for intermediate data sets, repeat processing and for storage of simulated events. This brings the
total tape needs to about 13 PB/year.

When data arrives at the computer center the goal is to complete the first processing step with a turnaround
of less than six hours 95% of the time. This step will select events to be used for calibration and will produce
nearline monitoring of data quality. It will also split the event stream into several sub-streams based on trigger
information. The datasets used as input to calibration will be quite small. First, most events will not be interesting
for calibration. Second, the output events will be much smaller than the input events! In a typical Mu2e on-spill
event, the duration of the live window is about 1 �s, during which time the tracker will record about 3000 hits;
most triggered events will contain a single reconstructable track and only small fraction will contain more than
one track. A typical reconstructed track will have 30 to 50 hits on it and the time that a track is “live” in the
apparatus is about 100 ns. The vast majority of the hits are not associated with any reconstructable track and are
not relevant for most calibration purposes. Therefore, the calibration datasets will be stripped of uninteresting
hits, making them much smaller per event than the raw data. Mu2e can perform a similar compression on the hits
in the calorimeter and CRV. A subset of the events will be written out without this compression so that they can
serve as input to other studies.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 161

Once the calibration workflows are complete, the raw data will then be processed through the main
reconstruction pass. There are many open questions here: will the full raw data be read, or one of the sub-streams
of the raw data? How will prescale events that have good reconstructable tracks that are of no value for physics
but have value for monitoring be treated? For what fraction of the dataset will uninteresting hits be removed? The
net result is that Mu2e expects the size of the output of the main reconstruction pass to be smaller than the size of
the raw data.

For the first few months of data taking, the POT rate will be about 55% of nominal. For some of this time Mu2e
may open up some prescales to study events that would normally be discarded but it is believed that for most of
this period the computing needs will scale with the POT rate.

Not all intermediate datasets will be written to tape. For example, the datasets produced by iterations over the
same data several times in order to derive a calibration set will likely be disk resident only and be discarded once
the calibration information is extracted.

As discussed above, the present plan is that it would be possible to process all these data on Fermigrid, but for
planning purposes it is assumed that about half of it will be processed on Fermigrid and half on opportunistic
OSG. On average Mu2e expects to process each event twice, leading to an estimate of 4 TB/year of outbound data
and 2.5 TB/year of inbound data.

Discussions have taken place that may lead to some calibration work being done in the UK or at INFN, using
resources provided by their funding agencies. For this exercise Mu2e assumes that about 0.5 PB/year will be
transferred to each location.

Figure 6.6.4 shows an estimate of the time dependence of Mu2e network bandwidth needs from now until the
end of analysis.

6.6.2.6 Remote Science Activities
6.6.2.6.1 Muon g-2 Remote Science Activities
The collaboration is performing the final analysis at this time. Large-scale use of remote resources is not
anticipated. Possibilities that could occur were covered in the previous section.

6.6.2.6.2 Mu2e Remote Science Activities
As discussed in section 2.2 Mu2e plans to use remote resources in the following ways:

 1. MC generation on OSG, HPC centers and at collaborating institutions, definitely at INFN and
 possibly in the UK.
 2. Data reconstruction and calibration on FermiGrid, OSG and possibly at HPC centers, particularly
 NERSC and ALCF.
 3. Calibration activities at INFN and possibly in the UK.
 4. All collaborating institutes are likely to have their own copies of the analysis-format datasets of both
 experimental data and simulated events.
During the next two years Mu2e will be under construction and will be commissioned with cosmic rays. During
this period, MC data volumes are likely to remain constant and experimental data volumes will be small, likely
much less than 0.5 PB/year.

On the time scale of three to five years Mu2e will commission with beam and have a one-year run. This will be
followed by the two-yearlong shutdown. During the run there will be nominal data volumes. During the two-
yearlong shutdown reprocessing of the full dataset with the latest calibrations and algorithms is expected.

On a timescale of more than five years Mu2e will restart data taking following the long shutdown, complete
data taking and begin final analysis. A significant increase in network needs compared to the three- to five-year
forecast is not expected.

6.6.2.7 Software Infrastructure
All of the data movement and management for the Intensity Frontier Fermilab experiments, which includes
Muon g-2 and Mu2e, are handled by the Fermilab FabrIc for Frontier Experiments (FIFE) project. Components
include Security Account Manager (SAM) for data management, transport, and cataloging; Jobsub/HEPCloud
for job submission; and Fermi-FTS for automated and robust file transfer management. (Warning: Some of these
names, like SAM and FTS, are used in other projects and may lead to confusion. See the FIFE web page for the
meanings here). All of these components are open source and use standard open-source tools such as xRootD.

FIFE and subcomponents are significant projects at Fermilab and are managed by the Fermilab CSAID. Note
that Mu2e is in the process of migrating to Rucio.

Both experiments use Geant4 to simulate the interaction of particles with materials and are following the
development of improvements to Geant4 and the development of GeantV. Mu2e has already demonstrated the
ability to use multithreaded Geant4, thereby opening up running on memory poor machines such as KNL-based
HPC machines.

Both experiments write their own C++ code for processing raw data into processed products (by the
reconstruction program). Muon g-2 and Mu2e write their code within the art event processing framework87. At
this time, both experiments write out data as ROOT Tree files. Many experiments are moving to Python based
analysis codes. This choice is generally left to the individual analyzers.

87 https://art.fnal.gov

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 163

The general evolution of these software tools is an important open discussion for the intensity frontier
experiments and especially DUNE. Muon g-2 is likely to remain with its current system of art and C++ code
given the lifetime of the experiment. Mu2e will likely take advantage of progress spearheaded or in collaboration
with DUNE. Fermilab has been tasked with writing a new software framework for DUNE; that project is in the
requirements gathering phase.

6.6.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
The network and data architecture supporting Mu2e and Muon g-2 can be found in Section 7.4.

6.6.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.6.2.9.1 Cloud Services
In general, use of Cloud services is not a decision made by the experiment, but rather by Fermilab CSAID if a
proposed processing task is deemed suitable and other resources are not available or not compatible. Currently,
and for the foreseeable future, Mu2e and Muon g-2 will not use Cloud resources explicitly. A future feature of
HEPCloud is that it may choose to use Cloud resources if the pricing is competitive and other resources are full.

6.6.2.9.2 AI and ML
Fermilab CSAID has been slowly building a local GPU resource attached to the Elastic Analysis Facility for use
in AI efforts.

Muon g-2 never found a need for large-scale AI in reconstruction nor analysis. There were attempts to use ML
to improve tracking efficiencies, showing some promise. Unfortunately, the effort needed to evaluate the gains
further and integrate the techniques into the production workflows could not be sustained.

Mu2e uses AI in several places in the reconstruction workflow. All of it is small scale and would not significantly
benefit from GPU resources. At present an AI based classifier is used to decide whether time clusters of hits are
signal-like or background-like. Pattern recognition proceeds only on signal-like time clusters. Mu2e also uses
AI to produce a track quality metric that decides if a given track is well reconstructed and is suitable for use in
analysis, and more small scale uses are expected in the future. A graduate student is working on an AI based
algorithm to replace the existing Mu2e pattern recognition algorithms. That work has just begun and it is much
too early to tell if that effort will produce results that improve on the existing algorithms.

6.6.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
These activities do not apply to Muon g-2 or to Mu2e.

6.6.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
Muon g-2 does not anticipate constraints on performing the final analyses beyond sustaining the needed human effort.

Mu2e expects to be able to complete its full scientific program with currently available resources.

6.6.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
Data mobility endpoints are managed by the appropriate operations team in CSAID and not by the
experiments themselves.

6.6.2.12 Outstanding Issues
This section does not apply to Muon g-2 or to Mu2e.

6.7 Belle II Experiment
The Belle II experiment collects data at the SuperKEKB asymmetric electron-positron collider at KEK in
Tsukuba, Japan. SuperKEKB operations at and near the Y(4S) resonance to produce pairs of B mesons. Other
heavy flavor particles, such as charm mesons and tau leptons, are also copiously produced. Belle II precision
measurements of rare decays and charge conjugation parity violation (matter-antimatter asymmetry) in heavy
quarks and leptons provide a unique probe of physics beyond the SM.

6.7.1 Discussion Summary
Belle II, hosted by KEK Japan, relies on a similar software infrastructure and grid-computing model as that of
the LHC experiments, and has converted to use Rucio as a data management platform. Because of this sharing
of infrastructure, networking and data movement work well for the current volumes. International connectivity
is provided by partners Science Information NETwork (SINET) and TransPAC , via multiple direct and indirect
paths. Belle II also participates in the LHCONE network to enable consistent performance between facilities.

Belle II was an active participant in the LHC DC24 activities, and presented expected results for its operations
during this period. A primary reason for their participation was to test new software components that are
common and shared with the LHC experiments. At the current time, the experiment does not anticipate
participating in DC26, but may still monitor the situation to ensure that the increased data volumes are not
disruptive to Belle II operations.

ESnet will follow up with International networking partners, namely TransPAC which is operated by
International Networks at Indiana University, for updated connectivity diagrams and information regarding
support for networking in the region with other partners.

 • The Belle II experiment collects data at the SuperKEKB asymmetric electron-positron collider
 at KEK in Tsukuba, Japan. Belle II’s goal is to accumulate about 50 times more data than Belle,
 the predecessor experiment. Operations began in 2019 and about half as much data as Belle has
 been collected. The plan is to increase the amount of data collected per year to reach the goal by
           the 2030s. [Section 4.1]

 • Belle II recently resumed data taking in March 2024 after a 19-month shutdown to replace the
 innermost vertex detector and a portion of the particle-identification detector as well as complete
 an upgrade of the DAQ. A SuperKEKB upgrade with a corresponding ~1.5 year shutdown,
 tentatively scheduled for 2029, will be required to reach the design goal. [Section 4.1]

 • The Belle II collaboration comprises 1183 members from 125 institutions and 28 countries around
 the world. There are 118 US collaborators from 16 institutions, including BNL. [Section 4.1]

 • Two copies of the raw data coming out of the Belle II DAQ at KEK are permanently stored; one
 copy at KEK and a second copy distributed between BNL (30%), Canada (15%), France (15%),
 Germany (20%) and Italy (20%). All raw data centers are connected to LHCONE. BNL houses
 approximately 3PB of Belle II data, and anticipates having 5PB of tape and 5PB of disk storage
 available approaching 2028. [Section 4.2]

 • The transfers between sites are monitored and classified. Belle II participated in the DC24
 LHC Data Challenge and managed to reach 250 TB/day which is more than six times the
 maximum throughput expected at the end of the decade. [Section 4.2]

 • There is no current or future network or data-related constraint expected for Belle II. The Data
 Challenge performed in February 2024 demonstrated that the current network will be able to
 handle the Belle II needs, including safety factors, until the end of the decade. [Section 4.2]

6.7.2 Belle II: Experiment Profile
Belle II’s goal is to accumulate about 50 times more data than Belle, the predecessor experiment. Operations
began in 2019 and about half as much data as Belle has been collected. The plan is to increase the amount of data
collected per year to reach the goal by the 2030s. The Belle II collaboration comprises 1183 members from 125
institutions and 28 countries around the world. There are 118 US collaborators from 16 institutions, including
BNL. The US contribution to Belle II is funded by DOE OS HEP.

6.7.2.1 Science Background
Belle II has a grid-computing model with a three-level hierarchical structure (“tiers”) of computing sites: raw
data centers (Tier-1), regional data centers(Tier-2) and MC(simulated data) production centers(Tier-3). Raw data
centers are also regional data centers and MC production centers. Regional data centers are also MC production
centers. The raw data coming out of the Belle II DAQ at KEK are permanently stored, calibrated and processed
at raw data centers. Two copies of the raw data are stored. One copy at KEK and a second copy distributed
between BNL (30%), Canada (15%), France (15%), Germany (20%) and Italy (20%). All raw data centers are
connected to LHCONE.

The fully reconstructed events, coming from the raw data-processing step, are stored in the miniDST (mDST)
format. MC events are simulated and reconstructed using the same software used to process detector events and
then also stored in mDST format. Detector and MC mDST are stored in regional data centers. User analysis
is generally performed on filtered subsets of the mDSTs dubbed uDSTs. Generally, two replicas of mDSTs and
uDSTs are stored. In addition, Belle II retains replicas of the results of processing with a previous major software
release, which are expected on a yearly basis.

The use and allocation of Belle II computing resources is re-evaluated annually, taking into account past
performance and experience as well as expected changes in data rates. The computing model is periodically
updated to ensure efficient usage of resources.

Belle II recently resumed data taking in March 2024 after a 19-month shutdown to replace the innermost vertex
detector and a portion of the particle-identification detector as well as complete an upgrade of the DAQ. A
SuperKEKB upgrade with a corresponding ~1.5 year shutdown, tentatively scheduled for 2029, will be required
to reach the design goal. The data volume and resource estimates take these events into account.

6.7.2.2 Collaborators

separately (e.g., Italy holds both a primary and secondary copy and thus appears twice). Transfer to primary
storage is constant during data taking (up to nine months per year) and minimal otherwise. Transfer to secondary
storage occurs during production of simulated data or processing of raw data which nominally occurs throughout
the year with an 83% duty factor. Distributed data management techniques, discussed later in this case study,
enable “grid” access.

6.7.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
The different workflows used by Belle II are briefly explained in this section. Details are provided in the next section.

All raw data produced at KEK are archived at KEK and one of the Tier-1 (raw data centers) sites (Section 6.7.2.1)
to ensure that these data, that cannot be reproduced, can be recovered in case one of the copies is corrupted or
lost. A subset of the raw data is used for detector calibration. The calibration is applied to process the data (aka
prompt reconstruction) to produce files that can be used by the end users to conduct their analyses. In addition to
real data, MC data are also constantly generated.

Reprocessing campaigns based on improved calibration run typically once per year or biyearly. Reprocessing will
be every other year beginning 2025.

The final important workflow is the user analysis where end users use the reconstructed data coming from the
detector as well as the MC data to extract physics results.

6.7.2.6 Remote Science Activities
Belle II uses a grid model initially developed at the turn of the millennium to support the computing needs of the
LHC experiments. This model has a hierarchical structure with a Tier-0 site that produces and hosts a primary
copy of the raw data produced by the experiment (KEK in the Belle II case), Tier-1 sites (also known as raw Data
Centers) that host a secondary copy of the raw data and that are used for prompt processing and reprocessing and
Tier-2 sites (Table 1) that are mainly dedicated to MC production and user analysis.

Many of the Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites in Belle II are part of the WLCG collaboration and shared with LHC
experiments. This also includes the network connecting these sites, in particular the ones connected by LHCOne.
The sites without LHCOne connection are small and can be used without LHCOne. Because of these resources
sharing, Belle II is an associate member of WLCG. This grid-based computing model is not foreseen to change
for the lifetime of the experiment.

In this grid model framework, the raw data produced at KEK are exported from KEK to the raw data centers
according to the shares in Table 6.7.2. The sharing is implemented by Rucio.

As described in the previous section, a fraction of raw data (calibration skims, raw data format) is, in addition,
exported and processed at BNL to derive calibration constants. The calibration proceeds in several stages with
an important reusable intermediate data product, the cDST, being a byproduct: many re-calibrations can reuse
this data format. The raw data are approximately 70 kB/event, while a cDST is approximately 120 kB/event but is
produced on only a fraction of the data. Calibration constants are uploaded to the Conditions database at BNL.

Once calibration constants are available, the raw data can be reconstructed to produce the mDST that can, in
principle, be used for physics analysis; it has a size of approximately 15 kB/event. As the retention rate of most
analyses is on the order of 1%, a subsequent processing step produces uDSTs for several event selections. The
event size of this data format is approximately 20 kB/event as information is added to the mDST information.
Physicists process the uDST files with a grid-based analysis framework (gbasf2) to produce ntuples that they
download to their local resources for subsequent analysis.

 Figure 6.7.2: Belle II computing model

In the Belle II computing model (see Figure 2 ), raw data processing only occurs at raw data centers. The output
mDST is distributed across seven regional data centers. uDST files are distributed across many more sites.
For simulation, the picture is similar but simpler: mDST is produced directly across the more numerous MC
production sites, and uDST distribution follows. A key input to simulation are samples of background data taken
from real data. These background files must be distributed across the MC production sites to respect the MC
production policy.

The processing of the MC or data files is always done on the site that hosts the data (no WAN access) except for
the small sites that do not host a Storage Element. The jobs always go to the data; data are not moved to sites with
empty computing sites. The output of the jobs are also stored locally, except for the sites without storage elements
or if the storage element is temporarily inaccessible. Additional copies are created based on the replication
policies using the Rucio subscription mechanism.

The transfers between sites are monitored and classified into different “activity” as shown in Figure 3. As shown
in this figure, Belle II participated in the DC24 Data Challenge and managed to reach 250 TB/day which is more
than six times the maximum throughput expected at the end of the decade. The other activities have much lower
throughput. The second highest throughput is the staging activity that only occurs during staging campaigns
(once per year before 2025, then once every two years after) which do not involve WAN transfers since the
data are only staged at the Tier-1 sites. Since the migration to Rucio in 2021, no network bottlenecks have been
observed. Although DC24 showed satisfactory results for Belle II for the rest of the decade, Belle II plans to
participate in future Data Challenges because many Belle II sites are co-located with LHC sites, which might
affect throughput in the future.

Other remote science activities include :

 • Downloading of job output by the end users. This activity fluctuates significantly with time
 day/night, weekend, confrence, etc. However, the volume for these transfers is negligible with
 respect to the intersite transfers.

 • Access to condition database. The condition database service (see next section) is hosted at BNL
 and accessed by each job, but direct access to the service is limited by local and remote caching.

6.7.2.7 Software Infrastructure
6.7.2.7.1. Rucio
Rucio, initially developed by and for the ATLAS collaboration, is now a common Distributed Data Management
solution within the HEP community and beyond. It is used in production by many big collaborations (e.g.,
ATLAS or CMS) at scale well above the one from Belle II (e.g., ATLAS currently manages 1 EB which is much
more than the 25-30 PB stored by Belle II). Rucio now enjoys large community support.

Belle II chose to migrate from its bespoke data management solution to Rucio in January 2021. Since then, Rucio,
with FTS as back-end transfer system, has managed all production and analysis data production on the grid.
Rucio ensures the replication of raw data from KEK to the other raw Data Centers according to the defined share
detailed in the previous section. It also ensures the replication of the dataset output generated by the production
system, again according to predefined share, takes care of the staging for the reprocessing campaigns, and makes
a second copy of user or group data to other sites.

In January 2024, it was decided that Rucio will also become the official metadata service for Belle II to replace
the old metadata service called ARDA Metadata Grid Application (AMGA) hosted and operated at KEK. This
transition is expected to occur in 2025.

This critical service is operated at BNL.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 173

6.7.2.7.2. DIRAC
Belle II uses DIRAC as a Workflow and Workload Management system. It allows users to interact with all grid
resources to schedule and run production and analysis jobs, etc. DIRAC was initially developed by LHCb and,
similarly to Rucio, it is now used by a large community. In order to fit Belle II needs, an extension to DIRAC,
called BelleDIRAC, was developed. In particular, this extension implements a Production system that enables
large-scale MC production as well as an interface to Rucio.

Most of the BelleDIRAC services are operated at KEK. A single service for Data Management certification is
operated at BNL.

6.7.2.7.3. Conditions Database
BNL operates the Belle II Conditions Database (CDB) service. The CDB supports data processing on the Belle
II computing grid. In addition, as part of the detector’s calibration cycle, the CDB serves as persistent storage
for selected data collected by the Belle II DAQ at KEK which is properly formatted for CDB injection. The
CDB system is composed of two sub-services: the payload service and the metadata service. The payload service
is accessed if the client-side software cannot find a copy of the payload on CERN Virtual Machine File System
(CVMFS)(payloads are migrated to CVMFS with a latency of hours) or on the client’s local caches such that the
load on the CDB payload service at BNL for reading is typically modest. Writing new calibration data payloads,
which can only proceed via the CDB service at BNL, is also typically modest as the CDB service is a mostly read
service. The CDB metadata service provides the list of which conditions data payloads needed for a given data-
processing job. This service also has a selective backup on CVMFS but, unlike for payloads, the metadata service
is the primary source. The data transfer to or from this (metadata) service per query is also modest. Nevertheless,
bursts of requests to the CDB system have been observed and successfully supported. Squid caches have been
set up at the major data centers to intercept part of the load going to the CDB service, reducing even further the
traffic to the service.

A migration to a new CDB service based on the recommendations of the HEP Software Foundation is foreseen in
the next few years. This new service should not significantly change the network needs for this service.

6.7.2.7.4. CVMFS
CernVM Files System(CVMFS) is a well-known service that enables distribution of software. In addition to
software distribution, CVMFS is also used to distribute the CDB payload as explained in the previous subsection.

6.7.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
6.7.2.8.1 Domestic Connectivity
The SDCC at BNL has implemented a vendor agnostic, resilient, scalable, and modular Tbps High-Throughput
Science Network (HTSN) which serves as the primary network transport for all data-intensive collaborations at
BNL (Figures 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8). It provides high-throughput connectivity to all HPC and HTC collaborations and
supports the timely transfer of large amounts of scientific data via the internet.

The HTSN has five key components:

 1. Network Perimeter

 ° Two diverse 800 Gbps (2 x 400 GbE) circuits that peer with ESnet routers within the BNL
 515 and 725 data centers. These circuits are utilized by all scientific and administrative
 communities at BNL. All traffic to and from BNL flows through either of these circuits.

 ° The BNL Network Perimeter on average ingests and egresses between 10–15 PB of
 data monthly.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 174

 2. Science DMZ

 ° Supports open, high-speed WAN/Internet) access for all scientific collaborations
 throughout the BNL campus.
 3. Science Core

 ° A Tbps Science and Data Center Interconnect for data intensive collaborations at BNL.
 This Science Interconnect enables high-speed connectivity between collaborations such as
 ATLAS, STAR, sPHENIX, CAD, Center for Functional Nanomaterials (CFN), NSLS-II,
 High-Performance Computing Clusters and SDCC.

 ° Intelligence and routing policies are applied within the Science Core to restrict or grant
 access to specific resources within the SDCC.
 4. Spine

 ° A Tbps network Spine that interconnects all Leaf switches. Leaf switches can consist
 of top of rack (ToR) or chassis-based switches that connect compute, storage or general
 infrastructure service servers.

 ° The responsibility of the Spine is fast packet forwarding and flexibility, not policy insertion
 or server termination.

 ° The External Border Gateway Protocol (eBGP) is utilized throughout the HTSN, and was
 chosen for its ability to immensely scale and to create modularity and fault domain isolation
 down to the rack level. Each Spine group shares the same Autonomous System Number
 (ASN) but does not have Internal Border Gateway Protocol (IBGP) peering between them.
 Each Leaf or pair of Leaves will require their own ASN.
 5. Storage Core

 ° A redundant terabit per second switching block that aggregates high-performance
 storage services.

 (DNS) architecture.

6.7.2.8.2 International Connectivity
The success of Belle II relies on transpacific networking capacity provided by a number of partners that
participate in the LHCONE overlay network. Belle II relies heavily on network access, thus the partnerships
that underpin LHCONE are critical for ongoing operations. LHCONE delivers service using physical resources
operated by a number of different entities:

 • Belle II is connected to SINET,89 a Japanese academic backbone network that works in
 collaboration with APAN.90

 • SINET is connected to the United States via multiple direct and indirect paths:
 ° 100 Gbps is available via the NSF-funded PacificWave (PacWave)91 project to
 Los Angeles, California.

 ° 100 Gbps is available via the NSF-funded TransPAC link,92 operated by Indiana University
 International Networks to Seattle, Washington.

 ° 100 Gbps via the National Institute of Communications Technology R&D testbed network:
 JGN93 that connects to the United States via Hong Kong and Guam. This connectivity is
 operated in partnership with the Pacific Islands Research (PIREN) project94 and TransPac.

 ° 100 Gbps to Singapore operated with JGN, where alternate peering arrangements can
 function as backups to carry traffic to the United States via Guam or Australia.

 • The PacWave exchange points in the United States are located in Seattle ,Washington; Los
 Angeles, California; and Sunnyvale, California. Domestic networks such as Internet2, ESnet,
 and CENIC,95 as well as other international partners, maintain peering here.

6.7.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.7.2.9.1 Cloud Services
In 2022 BNL moved to using Microsoft Office 365 for email, calendar service, Sharepoint, and OneDrive cloud
storage. Although, bandwidth to and from these services is much lower than that required for scientific data,
the reliance of the laboratory on cloud services for day-to-day business has made the resilience of Internet
connectivity critical. During periods of peak scientific data movement, cloud data for day-to-day work has been
affected, and QoS and other traffic engineering controls were put in place to protect the business traffic from
being affected by the scientific data flows.

6.7.2.9.2 AI and ML
Belle II makes use of ML applications for triggering, track reconstruction, particle identification, etc., but Belle II
does not expect significant network impact or noteworthy changes to the distributed computing software stack.

6.7.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
Not applicable to Belle II.

6.7.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
There is no current or future network or data-related constraint expected. The Data Challenge performed in
February 2024 demonstrated that the current network will be able to handle the Belle II needs, including safety
factors, until the end of the decade.

Not applicable to Belle II.

6.8 Neutrino Experiments at Fermilab: SBN and DUNE
Fermilab features a number of experiments focused on neutrinos, often hard to detect particles that will help to
understand the origin of matter as well as the unification of forces. This detection can be done over both short
and long distances. The two experiments profiled are examples of this: SBN and DUNE. Both focus on the study
of neutrino oscillations, and use a similar set of scientific technology for observation. It is also expected that both
experiments will share similar approaches to their implementations of computational and storage infrastructures
at Fermilab, and their approach to wide-area networking. The work of SBN and the ProtoDUNE experiments at
CERN will prepare for DUNE, which is scheduled to start in several years’ time. Both experiments will utilize
grid-computing approaches provided by OSG, WLCG, and HEP-community software for data movement,
cataloging, simulation, and analysis.

6.8.1 Discussion Summary
The SBN program anticipates using more DOE HPC resources for their simulation workflows. The program does
anticipate needing more disk space during this process, which limits their output.

SBN’s primary concern is not network bandwidth, but rather I/O performance. The project relies heavily on
tape-based storage, which causes a bottleneck when reading out older data. Fixes are being explored to rely less
on this approach, but which may increase the expected data volumes.

DUNE can take advantage of some aspects of the IRI design approaches, and the collaboration is currently using
NERSC and exploring using ALCF for some aspects of their simulation and analysis workflows. In particular, it
is expected that GPU resources required for some parts of the workflow may need to be used at the DOE HPC
facilities. DUNE has not fully identified a long-term location for the storage of their public data archive. This may
also fall into the realm of an IRI workflow, or an emerging use case for HPDF to assist with.

DUNE’s software stack will leverage many of the tools that are already in use within the HEP community
including Rucio, FTS, and xRootD. DUNE is also looking into facilitating Globus as a transport mechanism with
the workflow managers such as Rucio and xRootD. DUNE has converted to use containers, which has greatly
increased the ability to make the analysis work portable across available resources, particularly at DOE HPC
centers like NERSC.

DUNE participated in the DC24 activities with the LHC sites, and learned a lot about their approach to software
and data management. They anticipate participating in future DCs as well, due to the overlap they have with
other WLCG computing resources. DUNE will also conduct their own DC activities on an annual basis. In
particular, being able to handle production traffic from the detector, as well as a supernova activity, will be an
area of focus. This particular part of the DC will rely on the connection between SURF and Fermilab when the
network is provisioned (expected 2026 or 2027). For the DC activities prior to this, BNL will currently serve as a
stand-in for SURF.

DOE’s HEP and ASCR program offices are still working out the specifics of the connectivity to SURF that
ESnet will need to complete for the proper connection. The efforts are planned to converge by the end of fiscal
year 2026.

 • The SBN program studies properties of neutrinos and neutrino interactions using beams
 of accelerator-generated neutrinos at Fermilab. In total three detectors—- the SBND,
 MicroBooNE, and the short baseline far detector (ICARUS T600)—- detect neutrinos from
 Fermilab’s BNB. The SBN detectors can measure important properties of neutrino interactions
 on argon that will be critical for the future long-baseline neutrino experiment DUNE.
           [Section 4.1]
