 • The three international SBN collaborations comprise of approximately 250 scientists from
 more than 50 institutions, and include members from across the US, CERN, Italy, the UK,
 Switzerland, Spain, Turkey, and Brazil. [Section 4.1]

 • The work of SBN and the ProtoDUNE experiments at CERN will prepare for DUNE, which
 is scheduled to start in several years’ time. Both experiments will utilize grid-computing
 approaches provided by OSG, WLCG, and HEP-community software for data movement,
 cataloging, simulation, and analysis. [Section 4.1]

 • DUNE will study the fundamental nature of neutrinos through measurements of neutrino
 oscillations from both neutrino beam and other natural neutrino sources. In addition to studying
 neutrino oscillations, DUNE has a broader physics program that includes searches for proton
 decay, detection of neutrinos from supernova collapse, and other exotic phenomena. The core
 facilities of DUNE are the near and far detectors, located on-site at Fermilab (Illinois) and in
 SURF (South Dakota). The detectors are placed such that they are on-axis with the beam of the
 future LBNF at Fermilab. The separation of the DUNE near and far detectors means that the
 experiment is relying on a WAN that originates at SURF in South Dakota, and must transfer
 all data back to Fermilab: this emphasis on near-constant network connectivity is shaping the
 choices made for buffering, storage, and analysis at both locations. [Section 4.1]

 • The DUNE Collaboration comprises approximately 1500 scientists from more than 200
 institutions in 39 countries around the world. These institutions include both national
 laboratories and universities. [Section 4.1]

 • DUNE has built two prototype cryostats at CERN for testing of final far detector technology
 designs, ProtoDUNE-HD and ProtoDUNE-VD. These two cryostats provide an opportunity
 to test both the detector technology but also the offline computing resources and software.
 ProtoDUNE-HD has just completed a three-month beam run at CERN, and ProtoDUNE-VD
 is anticipated to start a roughly yearlong test period in late 2024. The ProtoDUNE-VD test run
 will comprise both beam and cosmic-ray data taking. [Section 4.1]

 • The SBN detectors (ICARUS and SBND) will produce approximately 5 PB of data per year that
 will be stored at Fermilab, and at backups sites. [Section 4.2]

 • The SBN ICARUS detector has been taking data since 2021. The raw data rate from the
 detector is 2 PB, with raw data being stored at Fermilab and a backup for a significant portion of
 ICARUS data stored at CNAF. The SBND detector is completing the commissioning phase and
 is expected to take physics-quality data in fall 2024. The current expected raw data rate from
 the detector is 3 PB. Data management and processing will follow similar strategies as ICARUS,
 complementing the primary Fermilab resources with additional off-site data centers. SBN is
 expected to end operations at the end of FY27. [Section 4.2]

 • ICARUS data are expected to be approximately 100 MB per event at the raw data stage, but
 then only 40 MB/event after first stage reconstruction. The second stage of reconstruction will
 increase that size by approximately a factor of 2, but then high-level reconstruction objects can
 be summarized to then create a final size of approximately 50 kB per event. [Section 4.2]

 • For normal data taking from the ICARUS detector, raw data arrives at a steady rate of
 approximately 370 GB/hr (~100 MB/s), and from SBND at approximately 320 GB/hr (~90
 MB/s). These data are delivered to Fermilab, and is made available for immediate processing via
 xRootD to run on-site at Fermigrid, but can be accessed and run on OSG sites as available. Raw
 data backups are ~75 GB/hr (~20 MB/s) to CNAF for ICARUS, and 130 GB/hr (~35 MB/s) for
 SBND (Polaris at ANL). [Section 4.2]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 181

 • When operating, the DUNE FD will produce approximately 30PB of data per year, and the
 near detector will produce approximately 5PB of data per year that will be stored at Fermilab,
 and back-up sites. ProtoDUNE efforts have produced approximately 5PB of data per year at
 CERN during the initial run, and will exhibit a similar pattern for a second run between 2025
           and 2026. [Section 4.2]

 • Transfer of the raw data produced from the DUNE detectors is likely to be the largest single
 network task for the experiment. The data must be transferred from the detectors to archival
 storage at Fermilab and at least one additional archival location geographically separate from
 storage at Fermilab. It is anticipated that along with initial processing, there will be annual
 reprocessing of all data accumulated to date. In addition to beam and calibration data, the signal
 of neutrinos produced from a nearby supernova burst present a significant challenge due to the
 large volume of data collected in a very short period of time (up to 600 TB in 100 seconds) and
 the time-critical nature of analyzing that data for optical astronomical observations. [Section 4.2]

 • The first full DUNE Far Detector, FD-VD, is slated to begin full operation at SURF in Lead,
 SD in mid-2029. A second module will come online in 2030-31. These systems will require
 significant testing and calibration and are projected to produce 10–15 PB of data per year per
 module to start, and will be capped at 30 PB/year when in full operation. This includes tests of
 supernova burst sensitivity that will produce around 320 TB over a few hours (they are actually
 produced over 100s but are constrained by local network speeds). Early calibration runs will
 also produce significant data volumes over short time periods. Steady rates of 100TB/day are
 anticipated. [Section 4.2]

 • DUNE, as a whole, will produce 45PB of data per year at full operation. This includes the near
 and far detectors, and 10PB of processed data. [Section 4.2]

 • DUNE data are expected to be approximately 8 GB per event at the raw data stage, but then
 only 20 MB/event after first stage reconstruction. The second stage of reconstruction will
 increase that size by approximately a factor of 2, but then high-level reconstruction objects can
 be summarized to then create a final size of approximately 20kB per event. [Section 4.2]

 • There are three DUNE prototype detectors that will be active during the next two years:
 ProtoDUNE-HD, ProtoDUNE-VD, and ND-lAr 2x2 demonstrator. The ProtoDUNE detectors
 are located at CERN, while the demonstrator is located at Fermilab. The raw data arrive from
 the ProtoDUNE detectors at a steady rate of approximately 1 TB/hr (~300 MB/s), and from the
 2x2 detector at approximately 42 GB/hr (~15 MB/s). The ProtoDUNE data are delivered to
 CERN on-site, and a second copy of the ProtoDUNE data is also transferred to Fermilab. The
 raw data are made available for immediate processing, which is accessed via xRootD to run on
 the WLCG. For the 2x2 demonstrator, the data are automatically stored at Fermilab, and then
 transferred in batches to a DUNE allocation at NERSC for processing. [Section 4.3]

 • In addition to detector data, DUNE will produce large quantities of simulation that in some
 cases will rival the size of the detector data. This data will be produced at distributed compute
 facilities and be cataloged and stored in storage elements around the globe. DUNE is currently
 using more than 50 compute facilities, and more than 10 storage facilities to achieve its
 computing tasks. It is expected that this number will grow between now and late 2028 when the
 first far detector module will become operational. [Section 4.3]

 • DUNE data acquisition for the first far detector module will commence post 2029, and the
 output of the module will be roughly 30 PB/year going to archival storage. Offline processing
 and data flows will look very similar to prototype operations but with slightly different
 endpoints. (e.g., instead of data coming from CERN, data will be created at SURF). There is no
 significant change in the software or process of science between the activities of the prototypes

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 182

 and the actual DUNE detectors, and this is by design. It is anticipated that the current design
 of the DUNE computing model implemented with the prototypes will scale and be sufficient to
 achieve the science goals of DUNE. [Section 4.3]

 • For data management software DUNE uses the Rucio replica management service which has
 wide support in the high energy physics community. This is combined with the MetaCat data
 catalog which tracks the provenance of the data and can also interface to other databases such as
 the run conditions database. Rucio can work with the FTS system which in turn uses primarily
 https-based transfers to actually move the data sets to and from remote data sets. It can also use
 Globus as a transport mechanism and DUNE expects to get data to and from the leadership
 facilities. There is a distributed global disk model in which current data sets are hosted at a set
 of 15 storage elements in the US and Europe. [Section 4.3]

 • For ICARUS reconstruction processing, computing jobs need to have data delivered at a
 consistent average rate of up to 2 TB/hr to satisfy demands during data production campaigns
 (~60 days in length). Data write rates back to Fermilab for storage is ~1 TB/hr. Data need to
 be delivered to wherever that production is running: SBN expects this to be largely Fermilab
 computing resources, but it will include some fraction of jobs to available OSG sites across
 the US and Europe, and to CNAF computing in Italy. For SBND, these numbers will peak
 at approximately 1 TB/hr for data reading and ~0.8 TB/hr for data write-back in this similar
 two-year period. [Section 4.4]

 • ICARUS simulation will use off-beam data events for base simulation, which will require a data
 delivery rate of ~2 TB/hr to computing nodes over a production campaign period (~60 days),
 with a similar rate for data to write back to send back to Fermilab storage. [Section 4.4]

 • In addition to use of Fermilab central computing, SBN will onboard computing at CNAF,
 CERN, and the UK to further facilitate general production and analysis work. SBN also plans
 to make use of HPC facilities like Polaris at ANL and Perlmutter at NERSC/LBNL to further
 enable general production processing (e.g., event simulation, signal processing, and event
 reconstruction at ANL) [Section 4.4]

 • For reconstruction processing of data, DUNE needs to have an amount of outbound network
 traffic from the disk elements equal to the output of the detectors so that processing can keep up
 with the production of raw data. Data write rates back to disk storage elements from production
 processing are roughly 1/10 of the raw data rates. Data need to be delivered to wherever that
 production is running: we expect this to be a combination of computing resources from around
 the world, but they will be located close to storage elements. DUNE expects data input/output
 rates to be tape/disk I/O limited for the foreseeable future. [Section 4.4]

 • SBN currently uses the Polaris supercomputer facility at Argonne in addition to computing
 resources at Fermilab. Globus-based transfers of SBND neutrino data to Argonne are up and
 running, and sustained access to Polaris over the next few years for ongoing data processing
 will be needed to ensure that physics results can be obtained with maximum efficiency. SBN is
 also investigating whether other DOE SC user facilities, such as NERSC, may provide unique
 advantages that could complement the present workflows mentioned above. [Section 4.6]

 • DUNE expects to continue to incorporate the use of HPC centers, like Perlmutter at NERSC,
 for performing simulation and data reconstruction general processing on the 2x2 demonstrator
 data, as well as for executing dedicated AI/ML processing workflows. [Section 4.6]

 • During the DUNE Prototyping phase, prototype detectors running at CERN and Fermilab
 send their data to DUNE storage sites worldwide. As more and more services come on line at
 the DUNE Far site–- SURF, data will begin to flow from SURF in South Dakota to Fermilab

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 183

 and onward to DUNE collaboration sites worldwide for additional processing. When the first far
 detector Module is operational in mid-2029 supernova data will need to be transferred real-time
 from SURF to US HPC’s for fast turnaround processing. [Section 4.6]

 • The primary data-related resource constraint for DUNE deals with the supernova use case; the
 data from South Dakota must be transmitted to DOE HPC facilities in a matter of hours, and
 then have it in a place where it can be easily accessed by the job processing software. Once the
 first FD of DUNE is online, currently estimated to be 2029, supernova triggers are expected
 regularly, albeit some may be false alarms; the estimate is currently one per month. DUNE will
 require a set of machines fast enough to source and sink the data, and a distributed file system
 to make it accessible to the computational jobs. [Section 4.6]

 • DUNE relies heavily on Fermilab networking for a variety of tasks, including data archiving,
 replication, and batch processing. Two geographically diverse 100 Gbps links between the
 FD complex at SURF and Fermilab are in the process of being acquired to provide WAN
 connectivity for the FD. The target deployment date for these links is 2027. DUNE is approved
 for use of LHCONE, and has been making use of LHCONE and LHCOPN at certain grid sites
 that also have an LHC presence. [Section 4.7]

 • DUNE has followed the strategic direction of Fermilab in using cloud only for those new
 hardware types which DUNE cannot quickly acquired. Examples include tests of inference
 servers on Triton (e.g., a commercial entity), NERSC Perlmutter as part of the ongoing SONIC
 project, and GCP. With one of the above tests with compute workers at Fermilab and the
 inference server at Google cloud in Iowa, DUNE was able to saturate the Fermilab general
 off-site network bandwidth which at the time was limited to 100 Gbps. [Section 4.8]

 • DUNE has several scientists who are actively exploring ML use in reconstruction, analysis. At
 the moment most of them run locally on Fermilab’s Elastic Analysis Facility. [Section 4.8]

 • New features for DUNE in the two- to five-year time period related to networking are related
 to further use of HPC centers, like Polaris at ANL or Perlmutter at NERSC, for
 performing simulation and data reconstruction general processing, as well as for executing
 dedicated AI/ML processing workflows. This could amount to a sustained average
 rate of >1 TB/hr to and from that facility over a production campaign period (~60 days).
 Similarly, transfers of dedicated data formats for AI/ML processing to SLAC (temporary
 location) and then the DOE HPC centers (where the workflow is actually run) will also require
 approximately a rate of 1 TB/hr. [Section 4.8]

 • DUNE exhibits all the IRI patterns in design and operation. The full DUNE near detector
 simulation and reconstruction stack has been run at NERSC Perlmutter, as well as many
 simulations for the DUNE FD. The various near detector software has also been run at ALCF
 at least at the proof of principle status. Short-Baseline software has also been run at ALCF.
 Patterns exhibited include: [Section 4.9]

 ° Time-sensitive: The Supernova pointing workflow will be time sensitive and requires the
 analysis of as much of 320 TB from the first two detector modules in the span of 4 hours
 or less.

 ° Data Integration Intensive: It will be necessary to bring data from the DUNE near and far
 detectors together into a common analysis format. This is an extremely I/O intensive job.

 ° Long-term Campaign: DUNE intends to be taking data for at least two decades, and during
 that time our computing model calls for reconstructing all the data we have taken to date at
 least once a year.

6.8.2 Neutrino Experiments at Fermilab: Experiment Profile
DUNE will study the fundamental nature of neutrinos through measurements of neutrino oscillations from both
neutrino beam and other natural neutrino sources. In addition to studying neutrino oscillations, DUNE has a
broader physics program that includes searches for proton decay, detection of neutrinos from supernova collapse,
and other exotic phenomena. The core facilities of DUNE are the near and far detectors, located on-site at
Fermilab (Illinois) and in SURF (South Dakota), respectively. The detectors are placed such that they are on-axis
with the beam of the future LBNF at Fermilab. The separation of the DUNE near and far detectors means that
the experiment is relying on a WAN that originates at SURF in South Dakota, and must transfer all data back to
Fermilab: this emphasis on near-constant network connectivity is shaping the choices made for buffering, storage,
and analysis at both locations.

The SBN program studies properties of neutrinos and neutrino interactions using beams of accelerator-generated
neutrinos at Fermilab. In total three detectors — the SBND, MicroBooNE, and the short baseline far detector
(ICARUS T600) — detect neutrinos from Fermilab’s BNB, with the major goal of conclusively identifying or
ruling out anomalous neutrino oscillations hinted at by many other measurements. The detectors are all Liquid
Argon Time Projection Chambers (LArTPCs), which combine great position and calorimetric resolution to enable
precise event reconstruction and particle identification. In addition to searching or ruling out ‘new physics’ in
neutrino oscillations, the SBN detectors can measure important properties of neutrino interactions on argon that
will be critical for the future long-baseline neutrino experiment DUNE.

6.8.2.1 Science Background
6.8.2.1.1 DUNE Science Background
Transfer of the raw data produced from the DUNE detectors is likely to be the largest single network task for
the experiment. The LBNF beam will produce pulses of neutrinos at roughly a 1 Hz repetition rate, but there
are additional triggers for data recording beyond beam interactions produced from the detectors. Estimates of
those data volumes are presented in Section 6.8.2.4. The data must be transferred from the detectors to archival
storage at Fermilab and at least one additional archival location geographically separate from storage at Fermilab.
This data must then be processed through production reconstruction software packages before it can be analyzed
by collaboration members and utilized for measurements. The distribution of the data to compute facilities and
transfer back of the resulting datasets is the next largest network activity. It is anticipated that along with initial
processing, there will be annual reprocessing of all data accumulated to date. In addition to beam and calibration
data, the signal of neutrinos produced from a nearby supernova burst present a significant challenge due to the
large volume of data collected in a very short period of time (up to 600 TB in 100 seconds) and the time-critical
nature of analyzing that data for optical astronomical observations.

DUNE has built two prototype cryostats at CERN for testing of final far detector technology designs,
ProtoDUNE-HD and ProtoDUNE-VD. These two cryostats are 1:20 scale of the final far detector designs,
and provide an opportunity to test both the detector technology but also the offline computing resources and
software. ProtoDUNE-HD has just completed a 3 month beam run at CERN, and ProtoDUNE-VD is anticipated
to start a roughly yearlong test period in late 2024. The ProtoDUNE-VD test run will comprise both beam and
cosmic-ray data taking. These detectors produce significant amounts of data for archival storage at CERN and
Fermilab, along with considerable need for distributed computing in order to analyze the data.

In addition to detector data, DUNE will produce large quantities of simulation that in some cases will rival the
size of the detector data. This data will be produced at distributed compute facilities and be cataloged and stored
in storage elements around the globe. DUNE is currently using more than 20 compute facilities, and more than
10 storage facilities to achieve its computing tasks. It is expected that this number will grow between now and
late 2028 when the first far detector module will become operational.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 185

6.8.2.1.2 SBN Science Background

Figure 6.8.1: The layout of the SBN Program detectors along the BNB at Fermilab.

All three detectors are located on Fermilab’s campus at distances of a few hundred meters apart, and record
interaction events at an approximately 1 Hz rate. Event data are dominated by the data from the LArTPCs
themselves: each detector has thousands to tens of thousands of sensing wires that sample and record charge
signals over a period of milliseconds for each interaction event. In each detector, the LArTPC data are combined
by the data acquisition system (DAQ) with data from other detector systems that record scintillation light signals
and the passage of cosmic rays through the detectors, and then written to a local computing cluster at each
detector building site. The complete ‘raw data’ are then transferred to Fermilab’s central computing, where it is
staged and then written to archival tape.

Raw data must then be processed for analysis. A simple view of the processing chain is as follows: raw data goes
through a signal processing and hit-finding stage to filter out noise, deconvolve electronics and electric field
response, and identify areas of detected charge; then, higher-level reconstruction algorithms perform pattern
recognition and image analysis combining data across all views of the detector to reconstruct 3D charged particle
tracks and electromagnetic showers and perform calorimetric energy measurements; and, finally, those higher-
level objects are used in analysis to identify neutrino interactions and reconstruct their topologies and final-
state particles.

Collected data are typically compared to simulations to assess reconstruction efficiencies, systematic
uncertainties, and ultimately to test predicted models of new physics or of neutrino interactions. Simulated data
goes through the same processing chain as above, but first must go through a generation process to produce
equivalent raw data. Neutrino interactions are modeled using calculations available in software packages, particle
interactions in matter are then modeled using GEANT496, and then detector modeling is applied through
custom-written software. Because each detector is located near the surface of the earth, cosmic-ray backgrounds
are a constant presence: they can be simulated through software, but for final analyses the detectors will take data
events taken out-of-time with the beam which offers a random snapshot of activity induced by cosmic rays in the
detector, and then neutrino interaction simulations are ‘overlaid’ on top of this raw data. A library of ‘out-of-time’
data events is collected to allow for this overlay simulation.

The SBN97 detectors detect millions of neutrino interactions, collect many more events that are simply cosmic-
ray-induced background interactions, and also need to simulate tens of millions of neutrino interactions to
achieve its physics goals. Typically, simulation and the two stages of reconstruction (signal processing and

96 https://geant4.web.cern.ch/
97 https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.01520

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 186

3D reconstruction) are run centrally by the experiment data production teams, and produce files containing
3D reconstruction information with a size on the order of 50 kB per event. These files are stored centrally
at Fermilab, then accessed by analyzers across the collaboration to perform the final physics measurements.
Alternative workflows for 3D reconstruction based on AI/ML methods run at HPC centers are being integrated
in the SBN operations.

As improvements in the simulation and reconstruction are always ongoing, the SBN experiments plan a
roughly yearly data production cycle. Raw data are collected from the detectors throughout the year and stored
permanently, but derived data will be reproduced each year. Simulation and signal-processing outputs will be
produced roughly once per year, while 3D reconstruction outputs will be produced roughly twice per year (using
the previous stages as inputs). The output of 3D reconstruction will then be accessed through the year for the
performance of physics analysis. SBN currently has a data lifetime model of saving the bulk of derived data for
two years, and the much smaller analysis data used for publications permanently.

6.8.2.2 Collaborators
6.8.2.2.1 DUNE Collaborators
The DUNE Collaboration comprises approximately 1500 scientists from more than 200 institutions in 39
countries around the world. These institutions include both national laboratories (Fermilab, CERN, BNL, LBNL,
IN2P3, CNAF, NIKHEF, RAL, etc.) and universities. The center of activity is Fermilab, but there are clusters
of both scientists and resources located at national labs that are being utilized for both compute, storage, and
collaboration. Some examples of these clusters are located across the US, CERN, France, Brazil, the UK, Spain,
and Italy.

Currently, there are two major endpoints for raw data archival storage (tape): Fermilab and CERN. There are
currently test instances for archival storage in the UK and France that are expected to ramp up capacity as activity
at the near and far detector increases. DUNE extensively uses disk storage facilities as part of the distributed
computing model to make sure that compute facilities are efficiently utilized. For disk storage, DUNE currently
has close to 30 active facilities spread across the US, the UK, France, the Netherlands, Spain, CERN, Czechia,
and India. The addition of more disk storage endpoints is expected as DUNE expands its compute resources in
the next 5–10 years.

6.8.2.2.2 SBN Collaborators
The SBN international collaborations comprise of approximately 250 scientists from more than 50 institutions,
and include members from across the US, CERN, Italy, the UK, Switzerland, Spain, Turkey, and Brazil. Member
institutions critically include both scientific laboratories and universities. While the center of activity is typically
at Fermilab, where many collaborators (particularly young researchers) locate themselves for some period of time,
analysis and data activities span across these institutions, with significant/large clusters of researchers and activity
centered around the UK, CERN, and Italy.

Typically, the collaborations have relied on the computing infrastructure at the host lab (Fermilab) for data storage
and the bulk of computing. Dedicated backups of raw data are planned to be sent and stored at the INFN-
CNAF facility in Bologna, Italy, and investigations on a possible additional back-up location will be underway
soon. Computing resources at other institutions have been and will continue to be added to be used in central
processing much like sites are added to the OSG: those sites will be used to augment computing resources as
much as possible, and will likely be used for dedicated purposes on top of general computing: for example, the
generation of dedicated or specialized datasets.

The ICARUS data backups to CNAF are about 1 PB per year, collected and sent roughly continuously during
beam data-taking periods (which is generally consistently over 9 months of the year). Similarly, SBND data will
be transferred to Polaris at ANL. Transfers will be managed via Rucio or Globus subscriptions, and be validated
through checksums. While data should be transferred in a timely fashion (to avoid a pileup of data needing to be
backed up), there is not currently a strict latency requirement.

6.8.2.3 IRI Readiness
6.8.2.3.1 DUNE IRI Readiness
The full DUNE near detector simulation and reconstruction stack has been run at NERSC Perlmutter, as well as
many simulations for the DUNE FD. The various near detector software has also been run at ALCF at least at
the proof of principle status. Short-Baseline software has also been run at ALCF. These are workflows that make
extensive use of GPU and thus DUNE will need to make use of multiple DOE SC resources.

Time-sensitive: The supernova pointing workflow, described in more detail below, will be very time sensitive,
requiring the analysis of as much of 320 TB from the first two detector modules in the span of 4 hours or less.
Thus, DUNE is planning for robust network links from the DUNE FD to the DOE supercomputing centers.

Data Integration-Intensive: It will be necessary to bring data from the DUNE near and far detectors together
into a common analysis format. This is an extremely I/O intensive job.

Long-term Campaign: DUNE intends to be taking data for at least two decades and during that time the
computing model calls for reconstructing all the data taken to date at least once a year.

6.8.2.3.2 SBN IRI Readiness
SBN currently uses the Polaris supercomputer facility at Argonne in addition to computing resources at Fermilab.
Globus-based transfers of SBND neutrino data to Argonne are up and running, and sustained access to Polaris

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 189

over the next few years for ongoing data processing (i.e., a “long-term campaign”) will be needed to ensure that
physics results can be obtained with maximum efficiency. GPU-accelerated machine-learning algorithms are
actively being developed for SBN physics analysis, and the availability of both GPUs and CPUs at Polaris makes
it an ideal site for related processing to take place.

SBN is also investigating whether other DOE SC user facilities, such as NERSC, may provide unique advantages
that could complement the present workflows mentioned above.

6.8.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
6.8.2.4.1 DUNE Instruments and Facilities
Assets that generate data

DUNE consists of several related components located across the US and in Europe.

Offline data processing is done worldwide, including multiple sites in Europe and sites in India and Brazil.

Present: Prototypes - Running now

Prototypes located at Fermilab, CERN and collaborating institutes. These are currently running. A 700-ton
ProtoDUNE-HD detector running at CERN has already generated close to 5 PB of data in 2024 and DUNE will
perform another run of a different prototype of similar scale in 2025-2026.

Processing of these data is done worldwide using conventional grid resources. File sizes are kept between 1 and 8
GB and there are several million such files.

A smaller prototype of a novel pixel detector (the 2x2) is running at Fermilab and generated ~ 15 TB in its first 1
week run. It will run again in 2025.

Up to 2029: Analysis of Prototype data and start of DUNE commissioning and calibration

On the two- to five-year time scale, DUNE will be processing and analyzing the data from the prototypes.

The first full DUNE far detector, FD-VD, is slated to begin full operation at SURF in Lead, SD in mid-2029
with significant testing of DAQ and data-movement systems starting one to two years earlier. A second module
will come online in 2030-31. These systems will require significant testing and calibration and are projected
to produce 10–15 PB of data per year per module. This includes tests of supernova burst sensitivity that will
produce around 320 TB over a few hours (they are actually produced over 100s but are constrained by local
network speeds). Early calibration runs will also produce significant data volumes over short time periods.
Steady rates of 100TB/day are anticipated. Files will be kept to 1–8 GB that implies ~100,000 files produced in a
supernova candidate or large calibration run.

Longer term 2029–2040

In 2030-31 the second far detector module and the near detectors located at Fermilab will come on board. Near
detector data volumes are expected to be in the few PB/year range, while DUNE will plan to cap the total raw
data from the far detectors at 30 PB/year. At this time, the plan is to store data in Europe and in the US near
processing resources.

The near detector groups are already developing code optimized for reconstruction and simulation using GPU/
accelerators and will likely make significant use of national class compute facilities. Efforts are also underway to
optimize algorithms to process FD data using parallel compute facilities.

6.8.2.4.2 SBN Instruments and Facilities
Present-2 years:

The MicroBooNE detector took data from 2015 until 2020. The data are stored centrally at Fermilab and is
actively being analyzed by the Collaboration. Further processing of the data is being planned for the upcoming
years, and will support the legacy results of the experiment.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 191

The ICARUS detector has been taking data for three years. The raw data rate from the detector is 2 PB. Raw data
are stored at Fermilab, with a backup for a significant portion of ICARUS data stored at CNAF. For large-scale
processing, Fermilab computing and OSG sites will be used.

The SBND detector is completing the commissioning phase and is expected to take physics-quality data in
the fall. The current expected raw data rate from the detector is 3 PB. Data management and processing will
follow similar strategies as ICARUS, complementing the primary Fermilab resources with additional off-site
data centers.

Two to five years:

The data taking period will be completed within this time frame, with an expected end of operations at the end
of FY27. DUNE expects significant activities related to storage and processing of the data, as well as simulation.
In addition to use of Fermilab central computing, SBN will onboard computing at CNAF, CERN, and the UK to
further facilitate general production and analysis work. SBN also plans to make use of HPC facilities like Polaris
at ANL and Perlmutter at NERSC/LBNL to further enable general production processing (e.g., event simulation,
signal processing, and event reconstruction at ANL) and final-fits/sensitivity estimation (e.g., Feldman-Cousins
analysis at NERSC). There is no major change expected in the detector infrastructure or basic computing
envisioned, though DUNE hopes to continue to evolve the ability to rely less on tape for data storage, and have
a greater availability of disk for data that has an expected lifetime less than a few years (e.g., much of the bulky
derived data from simulation and first-stage reconstruction output).

Beyond five years:

The SBN program will be finished with data taking at this timeline, and will likely be in the final stages of
physics exploitation. This will hopefully reduce significant computing load for taking new data, but larger scale
production and analysis are likely to continue for some time in this period. It is very unlikely that significant
changes in data sources or workflows will occur in this time.

6.8.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
6.8.2.5.1 DUNE Process of Science
Data is generated either from the detector (“raw data”) or is simulated. The former is managed by the online
DAQ and data management team in the collaboration, while the latter is managed by the offline production team.
Data then proceeds through two stages of reconstruction (signal processing, and 3D reconstruction), managed by
the offline production team. The output of the reconstruction includes slimmed ‘analysis tuples’ that will be read
by analyzers across the collaboration.

Data reduction is largely accomplished through the reconstruction processing. After signal processing, algorithms
to identify regions of interest are employed to reduce the search region for hit reconstruction in waveforms. For
example, DUNE data are expected to be ~8 GB per event at the raw data stage, but then only 20 MB / event
after first stage reconstruction. The second stage of reconstruction will increase that size by approximately a factor
of 2 (largely to hold detailed charged particle track trajectories), but then high-level reconstruction objects can be
summarized to then create a final analysis tuple with the goal of a size of ~20 kB per event.

Present to two years:

There are at least three prototype detectors that will be active during the next two years, ProtoDUNE-HD,
ProtoDUNE-VD, and ND-lAr 2x2 demonstrator. The ProtoDUNE detectors are located at the Neutrino Platform
in the North area of CERN, while the 2x2 demonstrator is located in the main injector neutrino oscillation
search (MINOS) hall at Fermilab. The raw data arrive from the ProtoDUNE detectors at a steady rate of about
1 TB/hr (~300 MB/s), and from the 2x2 detector at about 42 GB/hr (~15 MB/s). The ProtoDUNE data are
delivered to CERN Exabyte Object Storage (EOS) (disk) and Cloud Tiering Appliance (CTA) (tape) on-site, and a
second copy of the ProtoDUNE data are also transferred to Fermilab for archival storage. The raw data are made

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 192

available for immediate processing which is accessed via xRootD to run on OSG and WLCG compute nodes. For
immediate processing, data files are still in disk cache and so do not need to be accessed from tape. For the 2x2
demonstrator, the data are automatically transferred to Fermilab Enstore (tape) on-site, and then transferred in
batches to a DUNE allocation at NERSC for processing on HPC.

For reconstruction processing of data, DUNE needs to have an amount of outbound network traffic from the disk
elements equal to the output of the detectors so that processing can keep up with the production of raw data.
Data write rates back to disk storage elements from production processing are roughly 1/10 of the raw data rates.
Data need to be delivered to wherever that production is running: DUNE expects this to be a combination of
computing resources from around the world, but they will be located close to storage elements.

While the collaboration pushes for most analysis to use the slimmed analysis tuples (hosted at Fermilab, but small
and able to be copied easily elsewhere), there will be a need for calibration and event selection tasks to access
reconstruction datasets. These will be several 100 TB datasets staged from central storage locations and delivered
to computing nodes at Fermilab or OSG sites.

New features in this period related to networking are related to further use of HPC centers, like Perlmutter at
NERSC, for performing simulation and data reconstruction general processing on the 2x2 demonstrator data,, as
well as for executing dedicated AI/ML processing workflows.

Two to five years:

Generally, the situation for the present to two years is repeated for the two- to five-year case, with similar
operations of the prototype detectors during that time. The first far detector module is expected to operate in late
2028 and so is included in the final section.

General needs for production processing will increase year-to-year in a generally stable way: data reconstruction
and simulation (and its corresponding reconstruction) scale with the total amount of data taken/neutrino
interactions collected. DUNE expects data input/output rates to not be network bound, but rather tape/disk I/O
limited, and so the peak rates above should not increase by more than a factor of 2, and can be offset by longer
production campaign timelines (e.g., moving from 60 to 90 days)

In this period, slimmed analysis tuples should be almost exclusively the files that most collaboration data
analyzers will access (necessary to keep total data I/O rates under control).

Beyond five years:

At this time period, data acquisition for the first far detector module will commence and the output of the module
will be roughly 30 PB/year going to archival storage. It is anticipated that the offline processing and data flows
will look very similar to prototype operations but with slightly different endpoints. (e.g., instead of data coming
from CERN, data will be created at SURF). There is no significant change in the software or process of science
between the activities of the prototypes and the actual DUNE detectors, and this is by design. It is anticipated
that the current design of the DUNE computing model98 implemented with the prototypes will scale and be
sufficient to achieve the science goals of DUNE. For details of the updated rates during DUNE operations,
please see Section 6.8.2.4.1

6.8.2.5.2 SBN Process of Science
Data is generated either from the detector (“raw data”) or is simulated. The former is managed by the online
DAQ and data management team in the collaboration, while the latter is managed by the offline production team.
Data then proceeds through two stages of reconstruction (signal processing, and 3D reconstruction), managed by
the offline production team. The output of the reconstruction includes slimmed ‘analysis tuples’ that will be read
by analyzers across the collaboration.

98 https://lss.fnal.gov/archive/design/fermilab-design-2022-01.pdf

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 193

Data reduction is largely accomplished through the reconstruction processing. After signal processing, algorithms
to identify regions of interest are employed to reduce the search region for hit reconstruction in waveforms. For
example, ICARUS data are expected to be ~100 MB per event at the raw data stage, but then only 40 MB / event
after first stage reconstruction. The second stage of reconstruction will increase that size by approximately a factor
of 2 (largely to hold detailed charged particle track trajectories), but then high-level reconstruction objects can be
summarized to then create a final analysis tuple with the goal of a size of ~50 kB per event.

Present-2 years:

For normal data taking from the detector, raw data arrive from ICARUS at a steady rate of about
370 GB/hr (~100 MB/s), and from SBND at about 320 GB/hr (~90 MB/s). These data are delivered to Fermilab
dCache and Enstore tape storage on-site, and is made available for immediate processing which, for the most
part, is accessed data via xRootD to run on-site at Fermigrid, but can be accessed and run on OSG sites as
available. For immediate processing, data files are still in disk cache and so do not need to be accessed from tape.
Raw data backups are ~75 GB/hr (~20 MB/s) to CNAF for ICARUS, and 130 GB/hr (~35 MB/s) for
SBND (Polaris at ANL).

For reconstruction processing of data, ICARUS computing jobs need to have data delivered at a consistent
average rate of up to 2 TB/hr to satisfy demands during data production campaigns (~60 days in length).
Data write rates back to Fermilab for storage is ~1 TB/hr. Data need to be delivered to wherever that production
is running: SBN expects this to be largely Fermilab computing resources, but it will include some fraction of
jobs to available OSG sites across the US and Europe, and to CNAF computing in Italy. For SBND, these
numbers will peak at approximately 1 TB/hr for data reading and ~0.8 TB/hr for data write-back in this similar
two-year period.

In this two-year period, ICARUS simulation should begin using off-beam data events for its base simulation (see
Section 6.8.2.1.2), which will require a data delivery rate of ~2 TB/hr to computing nodes over a production
campaign period (~60 days), with a similar rate for data to write back to send back to Fermilab storage. SBND
may not be doing these ‘overlay’ simulations as a default at this point, and so would see a much reduced need for
reading data when starting simulation generation; however, data write-back rates will still be large, approximately
1.25 TB/hr during a production campaign period.

ICARUS and SBND production campaigns overlap with each other in time, and typically include data
reconstruction processing alongside simulation. Thus, total data delivery rates coming out from Fermilab data
storage at a sustained rate of 5 TB/hr over a period of 60 days (if possible), and with data back to data storage at a
rate of ~3.8 TB/hr over a similar period.

While the collaboration pushes for most analysis to use the slimmed analysis tuples (hosted at Fermilab, but small
and able to be copied easily elsewhere), there will be a need for calibration and event selection tasks to access
reconstruction datasets. These will be several 100 TB datasets staged from central storage locations and delivered
to computing nodes at Fermilab or OSG sites.

New features in this period related to networking are related to further use of HPC centers, like Polaris at ANL
or Perlmutter at NERSC, for performing simulation and data reconstruction general processing, as well as for
executing dedicated AI/ML processing workflows. Significant fractions of the SBND data inputs for simulation
and reconstruction could be sent to Polaris for more efficient processing. Following the numbers above, this could
amount to a sustained average rate of >1 TB/hr to and from that facility over a production campaign period (~60
days). Similarly, transfers of dedicated data formats for AI/ML processing to SLAC (temporary location) and then
the HPC centers (where the workflow is actually run) will also require approximately a rate of 1 TB/hr.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 194

Two to five years:

Generally, the situation for the present to two years is repeated for the two- to five-year case. Detector operations/
data acquisition will continue at the steady rates presented there until the end of FY27.

General needs for production processing will increase year-to-year in a generally stable way: data reconstruction
and simulation (and its corresponding reconstruction) scale with the total amount of data taken/neutrino
interactions collected. SBN expects data input/output rates to not be network bound, but rather tape/disk I/O
limited, and so the peak rates above should not increase by more than a factor of 2, and can be offset by longer
production campaign timelines (e.g., moving from 60 to 90 days)

In this period, slimmed analysis tuples should be almost exclusively the files that most collaboration data
analyzers will access (necessary to keep total data I/O rates under control).

Beyond five years:

At this time period, data acquisition will be over, and this time period will see general production processing slow
down as the reconstruction and simulation reaches its final state. Most activity will be centered around analysis,
which will depend on many analyzers accessing small analysis tuples.

6.8.2.6 Remote Science Activities
The DUNE computing infrastructure is inherently distributed. Data centers are classified as Computing Site
(High Throughput Computing (HTC) or HPC), Data site (disks), Archive site (tapes). DUNE uses data centers
spread globally. Some DUNE sites only provide compute, others compute and storage and a few provide
compute, disk and tape to DUNE. During the DUNE Prototyping phase, prototype detectors running at
CERN and Fermilab send their data to DUNE storage sites worldwide. As more and more services come on
line at the DUNE Far site - SURF, data will begin to flow from SURF in South Dakota to Fermilab and onward
to DUNE collaboration sites worldwide for additional processing. When the first far detector Module is
operational in mid-2029 supernova data will need to be transferred real-time from SURF to US HPC’s for fast
turnaround processing.

In 2030-31, the second far detector module will come online along with the near detectors located at Fermilab,
their data will be sent worldwide for processing. A copy of all processed data will come back to Fermilab for
archival storage. The near detector data will be sent to national class compute facilities for processing using the
GPU/accelerators already there.

6.8.2.7 Software Infrastructure
6.8.2.7.1 DUNE Software Infrastructure
For data management software DUNE uses the Rucio replica management service which has wide support in the
high energy physics community. This is combined with the MetaCat data catalog which tracks the provenance
of the data and can also interface to other databases such as the run conditions database. Rucio can work with
the FTS system which in turn uses primarily https-based transfers to actually move the data sets to and from
remote data sets. It can also use Globus as a transport mechanism and DUNE expects to get data to and from the
leadership facilities. There is a distributed global disk model in which current data sets are hosted at a set of 15
storage elements in the US and Europe.

The task of moving raw data into final and intermediate formats is accomplished by the DUNE offline software,
for which a new framework is currently being written.

Present-2 years: DUNE continues using Rucio and Metacat for data management and movement, and the legacy
framework (ART) for data reduction

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 195

Two to five years: DUNE continues using Rucio and Metacat, adding the Globus transport, and the new offline
framework

Beyond five years: DUNE will continue using Rucio and Metacat, adding the Globus transport, and the new
offline framework

6.8.2.7.2 SBN Software Infrastructure
SBN experiments use much of the resources offered through FIFE at Fermilab. SBN largely follows the
software infrastructure being developed for general experiments and for DUNE (including SAM, Rucio,
CVMFS, xRootD, dCache).

6.8.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
The network and data architecture supporting DUNE and SBN can be found in Section 7.4.

6.8.2.8.1 DUNE Network and Data Architecture
DUNE relies heavily on Fermilab networking for a variety of tasks, including data archiving, replication, and
batch processing. Two geographically diverse 100 Gbps links between the FD complex at SURF and Fermilab are
in the process of being acquired to provide WAN connectivity for the FD. The target deployment date for these
links is 2027. DUNE is approved for use of LHCONE, and has been making use of LHCONE and LHCOPN at
certain grid sites that also have an LHC presence.

6.8.2.8.2 SBN Network and Data Architecture
SBN has no additional information to provide for this section.

6.8.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.8.2.9.1 Cloud Services
DUNE has used minimal cloud services, mostly in test of inference servers such as Triton in which the bulk of
the computing is done on commodity resources but the GPU, FPGA or tensor unit is located in the cloud, and is
accessed by a call-out over the network. DUNE has for the most part followed the strategic direction of Fermilab
in using cloud only for those new hardware types which DUNE cannot quickly acquire. Even for this application,
tests of running the inference server on NERSC Perlmutter as part of the ongoing Services for Optimized
Network Inference on Coprocessors (SONIC) project are being performed.

With one of the above tests with compute workers at Fermilab and the inference server at Google cloud in Iowa,
DUNE was able to saturate the Fermilab general off-site network bandwidth which at the time was 100 gBit/s.

DUNE expects to continue to have just a minimal or token use of the cloud going forward in the above three
time frames.

6.8.2.9.2 Artificial Intelligence and ML
6.8.2.9.2.1 DUNE AI & ML
DUNE has several scientists who are actively exploring ML use in reconstruction, analysis. At the moment most
of them run locally on Fermilab’s Elastic Analysis Facility.

6.8.2.9.2.2 SBN AI & ML
SBN collaborators developed an end-to-end AI/ML data reconstruction workflow, currently outperforming more
traditional reconstruction approaches [arXiv:2102.01033]. This workflow is based on data presented in an image
format, after signal-processing steps. The input data are stored in “larcv” files [arXiv:2209.04023], which take 35
MB/event in ICARUS. These files are transferred to SLAC directly from the OSG or Fermigrid worker nodes

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 196

using Rucio. Once stored at SLAC, they are further transferred to HPC centers where they are processed using
the massive GPU resources available. The choice of HPC centers is driven by the allocations obtained by the PI
leading the effort, or by the Collaboration as a whole. Results of the workflow are stored in hdf5 files, typically of
size 1 MB/event. These hdf5 files are transferred back to Fermilab where their content is merged into the analysis
data format files which are already used by the Collaboration. These data transfers are included in the rate
estimates provided in Section 6.8.2.5.2.

6.8.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
No specific needs for increased wireless capabilities for SBN or DUNE.

6.8.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
6.8.2.10.1 DUNE Data-Related Resource Constraints
DUNE has run significant amounts of simulation of the far detector at NERSC. The analysis and simulation for
the DUNE near detector Liquid Argon 2x2 prototype as well as for the full near detector at the moment requires
GPU capabilities which are currently supplied at NERSC Perlmutter. This MLReco code has also been run at
ANL Polaris.

The main data-related constraint deals with the supernova use case in which DUNE must get the data from
South Dakota to one or the other of the computing centers in a matter of hours, and then have it in a place where
it can be easily accessed by the jobs.

For the present two years DUNE will only be doing tests with data of that size and shape.

Once the first FD of DUNE is full of liquid argon and functional, currently estimated to be 2029 (five years from
now) then DUNE will be having supernova triggers to deal with regularly, albeit mostly false alarms. Estimate is
currently one per month.

By that time DUNE will need a set of machines fast enough to source and sink the data that fast, and a
distributed file system to make it accessible to the workers.

6.8.2.10.2 SBN Data-Related Resource Constraints
SBN’s major concern, based on MicroBooNE production experiences, is the performance of data storage I/O,
rather than networking. SBN currently relies on tape storage for the bulk of data storage needs, and staging
back and forth from tape can generally be the main obstacle for data production workflows. SBN is working to
update the computing model to better handle this: if so, this may change some calculations presented in previous
sections and put more strain on networking needs. SBN and Fermilab computing experts will need to keep a
close eye on how modifications in production workflows have impacts on the whole system.

6.8.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
6.8.2.11.1 DUNE Data Mobility Endpoints
Fermilab currently has a proof of principle Globus end point set up for SBN program. (if-globusdtn-01.fnal.gov)
Planning for a more permanent and scalable Globus end point in future. The main DUNE data are accessed via
dCache, a.k.a. fndcadoor.fnal.gov. Fermilab is the archival point for all DUNE data, i.e., at least one copy ends up
on tape there for all raw and processed data.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 197

6.8.2.11.2 SBN Data Mobility Endpoints
A Globus endpoint has been established for transferring SBN files from Fermilab to Argonne for processing
on Polaris. At present, the endpoint is only used by SBND, but it will likely be used by ICARUS as well in the
future. The endpoint’s name is currently “Fermilab-SBND” with Unique Identifier (UID) d868b0a3-3883-44ff-
bd0e-7e1d2110d6dd. Technical details about how the setup compares with others are available upon request.

6.8.2.12 Outstanding Issues
SBN and DUNE do not have any to report at this time.

6.9 LHC: ATLAS Experiment
The LHC at CERN99 is the most powerful particle accelerator in the world. Highly energetic protons, traveling
almost at the speed of light around a 27 kilometer long ring in both directions, are steered to collide head-on,
creating new particles and new interactions to probe fundamental natural laws.

6.9.1 Discussion Summary
The Data Challenges (the last being DC24) were incredibly useful for the ATLAS experiment, as well as the
entire LHC community. A number of issues were identified, including with the FTS tool, which was limiting
productivity because it was not aware of throughput capabilities. Simply stated, poor performance of some
transfers limited the deployment of more to better-connected sites. Additional work to move from VOMS, which
is based on x.509 certificates, to HTTP-based tokens is also underway. FTS (and Rucio) are developed at CERN,
and have limited resources to implement fixes. The timing of the next DC is currently being discussed, and
tentatively is scheduled for 2027.

ATLAS data volumes can average 5PB a day, with volumes exceeding this during busy periods when the LHC
is in full operation. The Tier-1 and Tier-2s within the United States can see data flows of tens to hundreds of
Gbps on a routine basis. Most are connected via 100 Gbps or 400 Gbps diverse connections to ESnet, or regional
networking providers. BNL (the US ATLAS Tier-1) sees a majority of this traffic coming directly from CERN),
then distributing outward toward other Tier-2s at US Universities.

ESnet will investigate ways to integrate resources into LHCONE at non-LHC-affiliated sites. In particular DOE
HPC centers (e.g., NERSC) and aFs (e.g., SLAC) could benefit from being connected to better identify and
prioritize traffic.

 • The LHC at CERN is the most powerful particle accelerator in the world. Highly energetic
 protons, traveling almost at the speed of light around a 27 kilometer long ring in both
 directions, are steered to collide head-on, creating new particles and new interactions to probe
 fundamental natural laws. [Section 4.1]

 • ATLAS is the largest of four particle detectors that measure and record the particle collisions at
 the LHC. The primary scientific goal is to quantitatively measure and discover properties of the
 SM of particle physics. [Section 4.1]

 • ATLAS is a global collaboration of physicists, engineers, technicians, students and support staff
 from around the world. It is one of the largest collaborative efforts ever attempted in science,
 with over 5500 members and almost 3000 scientific authors. [Section 4.1]

 • The LHC collides protons more than a billion times every second, out of which the detector
 experiments select interesting collisions for recording at a rate of a thousand times every
 second. With over two thousand hours of data collection every year when the LHC is running,
 a huge data sample for physicists to analyze from the completed Runs (1 and 2) is already
 available. Run 3 started data collection in 2022 and is planned to continue until the end of 2025.
 Run 4 (High Luminosity) is anticipated in 2030. [Section 4.1]

 • ATLAS is designed to observe up to 1.7 billion proton-proton collisions per second, with a
 combined data volume of more than 60 million megabytes per second (480 Tbps). However,
 only some of these events will contain interesting characteristics that might lead to new
 discoveries. [Section 4.2]

99 https://home.cern/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 199

 • Datasets in ATLAS are collections of files organized by category/workflow. These datasets are
 the fundamental units in ATLAS, fully integrated into the Rucio DMS, and used for workflow,
 transfers and user analysis. Individual datasets vary largely in size: [Section 4.2]

 ° raw datasets are in the range of 1 TB to about 250 TB

 ° AOD datasets are in the range of 1 GB to about 100 TB

 ° DAOD datasets are in the range of 1 GB to about several TB

 ° HITS datasets are in the order of several TBs

 • The ATLAS grid infrastructure consists of the Tier-0 computing site at CERN, 9 Tier-1’s, 70
 Tier-2’s and about 50 Tier-3 sites distributed worldwide. All workflows are executed at all Tiers
 with MOUs: the Tier-0, Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites. Tape storage to store raw and AOD files is
 available at the Tier-0 and Tier-1 sites and a small subset of Tier-2 sites. [Section 4.3]

 • ATLAS Tier-3 sites at most universities are usually smaller local CPU clusters with several
 TBs of disk storage attached. At these sites individual end-user analysis happens without any
 production activity. [Section 4.3]

 • Data from the ATLAS detector is calibrated, reconstructed and automatically distributed all
 around the world by the ATLAS DMS. The ATLAS Production System then filters through
 these events and selects the ones needed for a particular type of analysis. This brings the data
 set down to a manageable size for someone doing an analysis on their laptop. All members of the
 ATLAS Collaboration have equal access possibilities to all ATLAS data, independently of their
 geographical location, thanks to the WLCG. [Section 4.3]

 • The open-source software framework Rucio is used to organize, manage, and access the ATLAS
 data. The data are distributed across heterogeneous data centers at widely distributed locations
 worldwide. [Section 4.3]

 • The PanDA ecosystem manages all workflows and workloads in ATLAS. It is designed to handle
 complex multistep workflows, running over thousands of files, using many different application
 workloads, and optimization to process over a large number of distributed sites deployed
 worldwide. PanDA uses the HTCondor system for job submission to a majority of computing
 resources. [Section 4.3]

 • ATLAS has a long history of successfully using HPC resources during Run 2 and Run 3 at the
 LHC. From 2016 to 2020, US-based HPC resources supported 10–25% of ATLAS simulation
 production. This share decreased after several HPC resources were commissioned in Europe.
 In the first half of 2024, 21% of the worldwide ATLAS CPU resources came from HPC
 resources with 70% of them from the European HPC Vega in Slovenia, 8% from Perlmutter
 at NERSC, and 5% from CSCS (the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre) in Switzerland.
 European HPC resources are mostly used through grid interfaces. US resources at NERSC
 and Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC) require special edge services to run ATLAS
 jobs. Only simulations were carried out, since they are not data intensive. In the future, ATLAS
 plans to adapt all workloads to run on HPC resources. This will put much higher demands on
 networking. [Section 4.4]

 • ATLAS computing is fully distributed. All processing and reprocessing of the data is managed
 by PanDA, and Rucio is used for data cataloging and data transfer. All computing activities are
 free to occur at any site, irrespective of their Tier, and based on intelligent brokering of tasks
 and jobs. Distributed analysis jobs are also brokered by site capability—- users are discouraged
 from choosing a specific site. The distributed nature of ATLAS computing drives the network
 performance requirements between ATLAS sites. All ATLAS workloads and workflows may be
 run on demand at any time. [Section 4.4]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 200

 • There are four distinct storage types used by ATLAS computing environments; disk, tape, cloud
 and cache storage. [Section 4.4]

 ° Disk storage is the main bulk of the storage: 1042M files with the volume of 412 PB are
 stored in the disk storage. In the US, 198M files with the volume of 98.5 PB are stored in
 the disk storage.

 ° Tape storage is used as a main data archival system: 370M files with the volume of 639 PB
 are stored in the tape archive system. In the US, 63M files with the volume of 107 PB are
 stored in the BNL Tier-1 HPSS system.

 ° S3 type storage is used for temporary output of event service jobs.

 ° xRootD xCache storage is used for unmanaged disk data cache for input of user
 analysis jobs.

 • BNL has implemented a vendor agnostic, resilient, scalable and modular terabit-per-second
 (Tbps) HTSN which serves as the primary network transport for all data-intensive collaborations
 at BNL. It provides high-throughput connectivity to all High-Performance Computing (HPC)
 and HTC collaborations and supports the timely transfer of large amounts of scientific data via
 the Internet through two diverse 800 Gbps (2 x 400 GbE) circuits that peer with ESnet routers.
           [Section 4.4]

 • The WLCG collects resources worldwide and enables their usage by the LHC experiments
 as a distributed computing facility. The mission of the WLCG is to provide global computing
 resources to store, distribute and analyze the ~50-70 PB of data expected every year of
 operations from the LHC at CERN. WLCG is coordinated by CERN. It is managed and
 operated by a worldwide collaboration between the experiments (ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and
 LHCb) and the participating computer centers. [Section 4.4]

 • Depending on the size of the site (irrespective of the Tier label) there are 100 to 200k CPUs and
 0.5 to 50 PB of disk storage available. In total ATLAS has a pledged disk space of 378 PB and a
 tape space of 625 PB at all sites worldwide combined in summer 2024. [Section 4.4]

 • The US ATLAS Tier-1 is hosted at BNL’s SDDC. The ATLAS connection to ESnet is
 shared with other programs hosted at the SDCC. The US Tier-1 is the largest of the ATLAS
 experiment, it represents about 25% of the computing resources of ATLAS at Tier-1s.
           [Section 4.6]

 • There are four ATLAS Tier-2 centers in the US—- NorthEast Tier-2 (NET2), Great Lakes Tier-2
 (AGLT2), MidWest Tier-2 (MWT2), and SouthWest Tier-2 (SWT2). These centers are used for
 all distributed production and user analysis workloads. Each Tier-2 center consists of multiple
 university-based clusters. [Section 4.6]

 • In 2023-2024 ATLAS also added a new Tier-2 outside the US that contributes to the US ATLAS
 cloud. This site (TW-FTT) is derived from the former Tier-1 site in Taiwan and has a relatively
 small number of job slots (2200) and about 3 PB of storage. ESnet has helped to provide
 connectivity for this new site into LHCONE. However, this site has limited bandwidth (3 Gbps)
 and is only running tasks that are not data intensive. [Section 4.6]

 • There are two ATLAS aFs currently located at DOE National Laboratories (BNL and SLAC). A
 third AF has been set up and is operational at University of Chicago (UC). Each AF consists of
 a few PB of storage and about 1000 cores provisioned as a local batch system. They also support
 Jupyter based interactive analysis, and provide some GPU or/and Acorn RISC Machine (ARM)
 resources. In general, more than 500 individual users are using AF. The data accessing model
 at these aFs includes both Rucio-managed data transfers to the aFs, and using xCache to access
 ATLAS data remotely. The popular Jupyter interactive analysis model presents a different kind
 of need for high bandwidth, low latency, and on demand networking. [Section 4.6]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 201

 • All US Tier-2 sites are strongly encouraged to provide at least 100 Gbps connectivity, preferably
 with resilience. The intent is to have multiple 400 Gbps connectivity for each Tier-2 by the time
 HL-LHC starts. [Section 4.7]

 • Google Cloud and AWS computing services have been successfully integrated within the
 ATLAS workflow and data management systems PanDA and Rucio. Scaling to more than
 100k concurrently running vCPUs in PanDA has been demonstrated. The solutions may be
 considered for example in the implementation of aFs for HL-LHC, with all the added values
 and services offered by the commercial cloud providers. In future work, data exports from cloud
 data centers to WLCG sites will have to be optimized, involving research network providers. In
 2024 the Google Cloud is used for MC production processing as extension of a US Tier-2 center,
 and was able to scale of up to 15k job slots. [Section 4.8]

 • ML is used in a wide range of applications in ATLAS, including physics analysis, simulation
 and physics object identification. Models trained for classification and regression, as well as
 generative models, are core components of the software and analysis chain. Most models used
 by the collaboration are trained on private resources due to the modest resource requirements
 and satisfactory availability of institutional GPU resources. ATLAS does not expect any
 significant changes in network load or the distributed computing software stack design during
 the ongoing analysis of Run 3 data. [Section 4.8]

 • Given the size, complexity, and fully distributed nature of ATLAS computing, all workflow and
 data distribution could eventually be optimized and managed with AI. [Section 4.8]

 • The LHC experiments can benefit from IRI, especially if the DOE HPC centers and the newly
 awarded HPDF are seamlessly integrated into the existing HTC (grid) infrastructure. IRI would
 provide the opportunity to implement near real-time workflows for critical payloads, such as
 High-Level Trigger, which should produce results in a timely manner. IRI would benefit all
 HEP by providing a uniform interface to disparate resources in a way that is easier to integrate
 with, and to better fit the variety of HEP workflows. [Section 4.9]

 • ATLAS anticipates network needs will grow gradually. Increasing network capacity and
 performance will be needed at US ATLAS Tier-1, Tier-3 and Tier-3 aFs. The exact magnitude
 of future network provisioning is expected to be determined jointly by US ATLAS, ESnet and
 other involved parties. [Section 5.7]

 • The primary concern for ATLAS is lack of sufficiently fine-grained network monitoring and
 performance information to help us debug and automate data transfers in real time between
 various sites. Better visibility is being worked on through various entities including WLCG
 Site Network Monitoring, the SciTags initiative (labeling network flows and IPv6 packets with
 owner/purpose) and improved monitoring from the various tools and infrastructures, but ATLAS
 still have significant gaps in monitoring. [Section 5.8]

6.9.2 ATLAS: Experiment Profile
ATLAS100 is the largest of four particle detectors that measure and record the particle collisions at the LHC. The
primary scientific goal is to quantitatively measure and discover properties of the SM of particle physics. ATLAS
took a giant step in this with the discovery of the Higgs Boson in 2012, which led to the 2013 Nobel Prize in
Physics for Peter Higgs and Francois Englert.

100 http://atlas.cern/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 202

6.9.2.1 Science Background
In addition to the paper announcing the discovery of the Higgs Boson, ATLAS has published over a thousand
new results in particle physics. A major emphasis of the ongoing Run 3 at the LHC will be the precision
measurement of Higgs properties.

The SM of particle physics is considered to be an incomplete theory. In order to explain many observations
and measurements like dark matter and Higgs mass hierarchy, new phenomenology remains to be discovered
experimentally. ATLAS physics goals combine a strong program of SM measurements with search for new
phenomena like Supersymmetry.

Datasets in ATLAS are collections of files organized by category/workflow. In the table above, the range of
ATLAS dataset sizes (not the size of the full data sample since those are never stored at any single site) are shown.
Datasets are the fundamental units in ATLAS, fully integrated into the Rucio DMS, and used for workflow,
transfers and user analysis. Individual datasets vary largely in size:

 • raw datasets are in the range of 1 TB to about 250 TB
 • AOD datasets are in the range of 1 GB to about 100 TB
 • DAOD datasets are in the range of 1 GB to about several TB
 • HITS datasets are in the order of several TBs

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 212

The ATLAS grid infrastructure consists of the Tier-0 computing site at CERN, 9 Tier-1’s, 70 Tier-2’s and about
50 Tier-3 sites distributed worldwide. Basically, all workflows are executed at all Tiers with MOUs: the Tier-0,
Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites. Tape storage to store raw and AOD files is available at the Tier-0 and Tier-1 sites and
selected Tier-2 sites (DESY and NET2) . The US Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites are described in Section 6.9.2.3. Plots of
computing usage broken down by activity/workflow (data processing, MC, analysis etc.) are described in Section
6.9.2.4.1.

The setup and scope of Tier-3 sites vary significantly. There are dedicated AFs with all Grid components at
MWT2, SLAC and BNL (denoted as either Shared Tier-3s or AFs). Here, similar activities at a reasonable
fraction of a Tier-2 site can be expected. The role and number of AF sites across BNL and ATLAS will be defined
over the next few years, and it is foreseen that bulk user access to the AF will be needed in the future, perhaps
with shared storage between all the AFs. This may require a review of some networking parameters. Tier-3 sites
at most universities are usually smaller local CPU clusters with several TBs of disk storage attached. At these sites
individual end-user analysis happens without any production activity.

Depending on the size of the site (irrespective of the Tier label) there are 100 to 200k CPUs and 0.5 to 50 PB of
disk storage available. In total ATLAS has a pledged disk space of 378 PB and a tape space of 625 PB at all sites
worldwide combined in summer 2024. There is a CPU pledge of approximately 4300 kHS23 (about 500k batch
cores) for the full year 2024.

ATLAS requests additional CPU resources “beyond pledge” from all sites to generate simulated events which
are crucial for physics studies. On average, a substantial amount (~3700 kHS23) is delivered as a beyond pledge
resource. About 2/3 of this came from HPC site Vega in the past year. In terms of number of cores, the baseline is
around 500k CPU cores constantly used worldwide. Further details about the breakdown of the number of cores
used concurrently by different workflow at US facilities is presented in Section 6.9.2.4.

6.9.2.3 IRI Readiness
ATLAS and HEP experiments in general can benefit from IRI, especially if LCF and HPDF are seamlessly
integrated into the existing HTC (grid) infrastructure (including OSG). IRI will also provide the opportunity to
implement near real-time workflows (WF) for critical payloads such as High-Level Trigger WF, which should
produce results in a timely (near real time) manner. The BNL network infrastructure has been designed with IRI
patterns in mind. This is shown in the network design of the external Science DMZ network for data transfer and
a firewalled science portals network for services. IRI benefits HEP by providing a uniform interface to disparate
resources in a way that is easier to integrate with, better fit to HEP workflows. The ATLAS workflows that benefit
most from an IRI approach are those currently running at LCF and HPCs.

6.9.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
6.9.2.4.1 LHC
The LHC collides protons more than a billion times every second, out of which ATLAS selects interesting
collisions for recording at a rate of a thousand times every second. With over two thousand hours of data
collection every year when the LHC is running, ATLAS has a huge data sample for physicists to analyze from
the completed Run 1 and Run 2. Run 3 started data collection in 2022 and is planned to continue until the end of
2025. Table 6.9.2 shows typical LHC parameters.
