All of the equipment needed for the High-Luminosity LHC, the LHC’s successor, and its experiments
will be installed during Long Shutdown 3, between 2026 and the end of 2028. The High-Luminosity LHC is
scheduled to come into operation at the end of 2029, though this could shift to 2030 with the outcome decided
in October 2024.

Stable beam time for 2024 (with a duty cycle of 50%) will continue with an average pileup of <μ>=55 and
luminosity leveling at μ=64 , leading to a projected 110 fb-1 of delivered integrated luminosity. Additionally,
about 4 weeks of heavy ion collisions are expected. In 2025 a similar data taking setup is planned.

6.9.2.4.2 ATLAS
ATLAS is the largest of four particle detectors that measure and record the particle collisions at the LHC.
Selected highlights from this web page are shown below. The primary scientific goal is to combine a strong
program of SM measurements with search for new phenomena like Supersymmetry.

The four major components of the ATLAS detector are the Inner Detector, the Calorimeter, the Muon
Spectrometer and the Magnet System. Integrated with the detector components are: the Trigger and Data
Acquisition System, a specialized multi-level computing system, which selects physics events with distinguishing
characteristics; and the Computing System, which develops and improves computing software used to store,
process and analyze vast amounts of collision data at 130 computing centers worldwide.

ATLAS is designed to observe up to 1.7 billion proton-proton collisions per second, with a combined data volume
of more than 60 million megabytes per second. However, only some of these events will contain interesting
characteristics that might lead to new discoveries. To reduce the flow of data to manageable levels, ATLAS
uses a specialized two-level online event selection system — the Trigger System — which selects events with
distinguishing characteristics that make them interesting for physics analyzes.

The ATLAS trigger system carries out the selection process in two stages. The Level-1 hardware trigger,
constructed with custom-made electronics, works on a subset of information from the calorimeter and muon
detectors. The decision to keep the data from an event is made less than two-and-half microseconds after the
event occurs, and the event is then retrieved from pipelined storage buffers. The Level-1 trigger can save at most
100,000 events each second for the High-Level Trigger (HLT).

The HLT is a large farm of CPUs — i.e., a software-based trigger — which refines the analysis of the hardware-
based Level-1 trigger. It conducts a very detailed analysis either by performing overall examination of the whole
event for selected layers of the detector (for example calorimeters, trackers, muon detectors), or, by utilizing
the data in smaller and isolated regions of the detector. About 1000 events per second are selected by the HLT
analysis and are fully assembled into an event record. These events are passed on to a data storage system for
offline analysis.

The ATLAS Computing System analyzes the data produced by the ATLAS detector, developing and improving
computing software used to store, process and analyze vast amounts of collision data.

Data from the ATLAS detector is calibrated, reconstructed and automatically distributed all around the world by
the ATLAS DMS. The ATLAS Production System then filters through these events and selects the ones needed
for a particular type of analysis. This brings the data set down to a manageable size for someone doing an analysis
on their laptop.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 215

All members of the ATLAS Collaboration have equal access possibilities to all ATLAS data, independently of
their geographical location, thanks to the WLCG. ATLAS computing infrastructure and software are constantly
evolving — with the help of members of the Collaboration.

ATLAS has over 130 computing centers worldwide — located on every inhabited continent — nursed around the
clock by members of the Collaboration.

6.9.2.4.3 WLCG
The WLCG collects resources worldwide and enables their usage by the LHC experiments as a distributed
computing facility. The mission of the WLCG project is to provide global computing resources to store,
distribute and analyze the ~50-70 PB of data expected every year of operations from the LHC at CERN on
the Franco-Swiss border.

The scale and complexity of data from the LHC is unprecedented. These data need to be stored, easily retrieved
and analyzed by physicists all over the world. This requires massive storage facilities, global networking, immense
computing power, and, of course, funding.

CERN does not have the computing or financial resources to crunch all the data on-site, so in 2002 it turned to
grid computing to share the burden with computer centers around the world. The WLCG builds on the ideas of
grid technology initially proposed in 1999 by Ian Foster and Carl Kesselman.

WLCG is coordinated by CERN. It is managed and operated by a worldwide collaboration between the
experiments (ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb) and the participating computer centers. It is reviewed by a
board of delegates from partner country funding agencies, and scientifically reviewed by the LHC Experiments
Committee. The WLCG is partnered with EGI, OSG, and NeIC (Nordic e-Infrastructure Collaboration).

6.9.2.4.4 US ATLAS T1 at BNL
The US ATLAS Tier-1 is hosted at BNL’s SDDC. The ATLAS connection to ESnet is shared with other programs
hosted at the SDCC. The US Tier-1 is the largest of the ATLAS experiment, it represents about 25% of the
computing resources of ATLAS at Tier-1s.

The infrastructure of the US ATLAS Tier-1 site at BNL consists of the following three large blocks, currently
physically located in the existing SDCC datacenter based on B725 building at BNL site:
 • ATLAS Tier-1 Linux Farm including HTCondor and Grid CE / Gatekeeper infrastructure (CPU
 resource),

 • ATLAS Tier-1 dCache storage system, including a Ceph testbed and GridFTP / SRM / XRootD
 DTNs (disk resource),

 • Oracle SL8500 based part of the SDCC HPSS complex devoted to ATLAS (tape resource).
 ° some tape libraries with LHC Run1 data are based in the ‘old’ computing center in B515
The network architecture and the high-level service layout of the US ATLAS Tier-1 site is described in the
Section 6.9.2.8.1.

6.9.2.4.5 US ATLAS T2 Infrastructure
There are four ATLAS Tier-2 centers in the US: NorthEast Tier-2 (NET2), Great Lakes Tier-2 (AGLT2), MidWest
Tier-2 (MWT2), and SouthWest Tier-2 (SWT2). These centers are used for all distributed production and user
analysis workloads. Each Tier-2 center consists of multiple university-based clusters. The ATLAS Great Lakes
Tier-2 clusters are located at the University of Michigan and Michigan State University. The MidWest Tier-2
clusters are at University of Chicago, Indiana University and the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. The
NorthEast Tier-2 is run by the University of Massachusetts at Amherst (which collaborates with Harvard for the
storage operations) and is located in the Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center (MGHPCC),
in Holyoke, Massachusetts. Finally, the SouthWest Tier-2 center has clusters at the University of Texas at
Arlington, and Oklahoma University. The MWT2 is funded at a level 50% higher than the other Tier-2 sites in the
US, and therefore provides 50% more resources.

Note that in 2023-2024 ATLAS also added a new Tier-2 outside the US that contributes to the US ATLAS cloud.
This site (TW-FTT) is derived from the former Tier-1 site in Taiwan and has a relatively small number of job slots
(2200) and about 3 PB of storage. ESnet has helped to provide connectivity for this new site into LHCONE.
However, this site has limited bandwidth (3 Gbps) and is only running tasks that are not data intensive.

The resources provisioned at each US Tier-2 center is based on the WLCG pledges, which are set by ATLAS/
WLCG Resource Review Board and Computing Resource Scrutiny Group annually. These pledges provide the
baseline for the minimal CPU and Storage resources to be made available by each Tier-2 center in ATLAS. The
pledges are set in the April of every year, and are tracked monthly.

In addition, ATLAS officially requests additional CPU cycles from all sites, in order to accommodate MC
simulations in support of physics publications, equivalent to the pledged amount. Finally, ATLAS adds 20% to
both compute and storage pledges to accommodate the physics analysis of US users — dedicating a higher share
to analysis queues than the ATLAS average. Combining all these factors, the US Tier-2 sites aim to provide 220%
of the CPU pledge, and 120% of the storage pledge. The extra amounts for US physicists are subject to changes
based upon funding and needs.

6.9.2.4.6 US ATLAS Analysis Facilities
Final stages of analysis (statistical inference, weighting, signal/background calculations, plots etc.) are usually
not done on the Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites using grid tools. US physicists typically copy the selected smaller data
products from the grid to local facilities for final analysis leading to publications. These local analysis sites are
called Tier-3 (T3) or/and AFs.

US ATLAS consolidated the user analysis resource and supports, and currently maintains three common and
shared AFs, available for all US ATLAS physicists. These sites require good network bandwidth to WLCG sites,
including US Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites.

There are two AFs currently located at DOE National Laboratories (BNL and SLAC). A third AF has been set
up and is operational at University of Chicago (UC). Each AF consists of a few PB of storage and about 1000
cores provisioned as a local batch system. They also support Jupyter based interactive analysis, and provide some
GPU or/and ARM resources. In general, more than 500 individual users are using AF. The data accessing model
at these AFs includes both Rucio-managed data transfers to the AFs, and using XCache to access ATLAS data
remotely. The popular Jupyter interactive analysis model presents a different kind of need for high bandwidth,
low latency, and on demand networking.

The future development of the AF and number of AF in US ATLAS depends very much on the WLCG-wide
policy. In 2024 the LHC Coordinating Committee (LHCC) defined a list of questions to be answered by all
LHC experiments.

6.9.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
6.9.2.5.1 Computation
The main activities in terms of CPU usage are:
 • MC event generation. Different event generators are used to repeatedly generate proton-proton
 or heavy ion collision events and particularly interesting particle decays. There are usually no or
 very small input file sizes in the order of GBs required and the output file sizes in the order of a
 few MBs per job.

 • MC data simulation. The outputs of the event generation are used to simulate the particle
 decays in a detailed or parameterized ATLAS detector simulation. These are the most CPU

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 219

 demanding tasks with event processing times of in the range of 1 to 30 minutes. The output file
 sizes are in the order of several 100 MBs to a few GBs per job.

 • MC simulation reconstruction. Individual physics objects like electrons, muons, photons etc.
 of the previously simulated particle decays in the collision events are reconstructed for a later
 analysis and stored in AOD files. The processing times per event are in the range of 10-30
 seconds and the output file sizes are in the range of 1–10 GB per job.

 • Detector data reconstruction. Physics objects are reconstructed from raw detector data and
 stored in AOD files. The processing times per event are in the range of 10-30 seconds. The
 input file sizes are in the range of 2 to 5 GB and the output file sizes are in the range of 1 to 10
 GB per jobs.

 • Production of derived analysis formats (derivation production) as inputs for physics and
 performance analysis. The physics object files are augmented with additional calibrated
 information and events are filtered based on interesting event patterns and stored in DAOD
 files. About 80 different individual DAOD formats are written. The input and output file sizes
 are in the range of 100 MB to 10 GB per job.

 • Individual and group analysis. Individual physicists are processing the filtered physics objects
 files to filter out highly specialized information. The input and output files are in the range of
 100 MB to 10 GB per job.
All of the above activities process datasets with sizes between 10 GB and 250 TB consisting of 10–100k event data
files and file sizes up to 15-25 GBs each. The processing of these datasets is broken down into individual jobs by
the Workflow Management System PanDA and each job processes only a fraction of the datasets in each job.

During Run 3 the so-called data carousel came into production that synchronizes data staging from tape and its
delivery with job submission through the PanDA workflow management system. This allows a more efficient
usage of disk storage at the grid sites.

6.9.2.5.1.1 High-Performance Computing
ATLAS has a long history of successfully using HPC resources during Run 2 and Run 3 at the LHC. From 2016-
2020, US-based HPC resources supported 10-25% of ATLAS simulation production. This share decreased after
several HPCs were commissioned in Europe (Slovenia, Spain and Czechia) as part of the EU Exascale project. In
the first half of 2024 21% of the worldwide ATLAS CPU resources came from HPCs, with 70% of them from the
European HPC Vega in Slovenia, 8% from Perlmutter at NERSC and 5% from CSCS in Switzerland.

European HPC resources are mostly used through grid interfaces. US resources at NERSC and TACC require
special edge services through Harvester to run ATLAS jobs. Only simulations were carried out, since they are
not data intensive. In the future, ATLAS plans to run all workloads at HPCs. This will put much higher demands
on networking.

 Figure 6.9.13: Amount of data produced per day at NERSC since March 2024 that
 is directly transferred from the jobs from NERSC to BNL storage

6.9.2.5.1.2 Distributed Computing
ATLAS computing is fully distributed, as soon as the raw data are transferred out of CERN. The first step in raw
data distribution is planned to the 10 Tier-1 sites, according to MOU pledges. This allows for a complete second
copy of the raw data. After this archival step, all processing and reprocessing of the data is managed by PanDA,
based on the current availability of resources. Rucio is used for data cataloging and data transfer. All computing
activities are free to occur at any site, irrespective of their Tier, and based on intelligent brokering of tasks and
jobs. Distributed analysis jobs are also brokered by site capability: users are discouraged from choosing a specific
site. The distributed nature of ATLAS computing drives the network performance requirements between ATLAS
sites. All ATLAS workloads and workflows may be run on demand at any time.

6.9.2.5.2 Storage
ATLAS storage usage

 • There are four distinct storage types used by ATLAS computing environments; disk, tape, cloud
 and cache storage.

 ° Disk storage is the main bulk of the storage used by ATLAS. Currently, 1042M files with
 the volume of 412 PB are stored in the disk storage. In the US, 198M files with the volume
 of 98.5 PB are stored in the disk storage.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 223

 ° Tape storage is used as a main data archival system. Currently, 370M files with the volume
 of 639 PB are stored in the tape archive system. In the US, 63M files with the volume of
 107 PB are stored in the BNL Tier-1 HPSS system.

 ° S3 type storage is used for temporary output of event service jobs. The files in S3 are small
 and will be merged to produce the large files before they are written to the disk storage
 described above.

 ° XRootD XCache storage is used for unmanaged disk data cache for input of user analysis
 jobs. These small cached data are created on demand by user jobs. And, their data are
 copied from the disk storage described above and stay in the cache for the duration of the
 user analysis jobs.

 • The main disk storage is split into a few different areas. The largest fraction (~90%) of the
 disk storage is assigned to DATADISK space where the production system uses it for inputs
 and outputs of the jobs. GROUPDISK area is used for Physics group production while
 SCRATCHDISK area is used mainly by inputs and outputs of user analysis jobs.

 • Files are categorized as primary or secondary depending on if they are the main copy of the
 data or duplicate copy of the data. Roughly, 75% of the data in the disk storage are primary
 while 25% of the data are secondary. In addition, files are classified by their data types such as
 raw, HITS, AOD and DAOD, etc. raw data are unprocessed data from the detectors. They are
 stored mainly in tape storage for archiving purposes. But they can be brought to disk storage for
 production of AOD. AOD are further processed, and resulted in DAOD, Derived AOD. AOD
 and DAOD data types occupy the largest fraction of the disk storage with ~40% and ~25%
 respectively.

 • Storage usage at US T1 and T2 sites are shown in Figures 6.9.14 through 6.9.18.
 • Changes in Run 3: Due to the usage of the data carousel less AODs remain persistent on disk
 storage and are staged back from tape on demand.

6.9.2.6 Remote Science Activities
As described in previous sections, ATLAS computing is fully distributed, and therefore remote from CERN.
The raw data are collected exclusively at CERN. All other activities leading to the final published products are
done remotely.

6.9.2.7 Software Infrastructure
6.9.2.7.1 Rucio
The open-source software framework Rucio is used to organize, manage, and access the ATLAS data. The data
are distributed across heterogeneous data centers at widely distributed locations worldwide. Rucio is built in
different components:

A central database hosted at CERN contains the so-called dataset catalog. This catalog groups individual files of a
detector run or MC simulation process into datasets together with their file location information. These datasets
are stored on disk or tape storages at more than 100 sites worldwide.

Dataset files are not accessed from remote, but are moved between storages and sites asynchronously
before a processing job request. Currently ATLAS is moving approximately 4–5 PB per day aggregated
between sites worldwide.

The middleware to establish direct storage to storage transfers over the network, commonly called third-party
copy, is provided by the FTS. FTS establishes connections between storage systems using the required protocols
and ensures that the files are correctly transferred over the networks. Rucio decides which files to move, groups
them in transfer requests, submits the transfer requests to FTS, monitors the progress of the transfers, retries in
case of errors, and notifies the clients upon completion. If there are multiple FTS servers available, Rucio is able
to orchestrate transfers among them for improved parallelism and reliability.

The input files for individual jobs are accessed through the LAN from a worker node to the local disk storage.

Remote access to analysis job inputs with network latency hiding is used at several ATLAS grid sites using
XRootD and file caching though XCache at the sites.

The outputs of individual user analysis jobs in the order of 1 GB - 50 TB is downloaded to university clusters.

6.9.2.7.2 PanDA
The PanDA ecosystem manages all workflows and workloads in ATLAS. It is designed to handle complex
multistep workflows, running over thousands of files, using many different application workloads, and
optimization to process over a large number of distributed sites deployed worldwide. The main components of
PanDA include ProdSys which translates the physics workflows to executable tasks. Deft provides an intelligent
user interface to create workflows. Job Execution and Definition Interface (JEDI) transforms tasks into jobs
that can run on single cores, single nodes or a single HPC. The execution steps managed by JEDI range from
simulations, data processing, to distributed ML. Harvester provides an integrated interface to computing
resources, with edge services that can transparently manage execution of workflows across all types of resources
- grids, clouds and HPCs. Finally, the most important element of job execution is the PanDA pilot system, which
manages job executions that are orchestrated by PanDA. All of these components are deeply integrated with the
ATLAS DMS, Rucio.

The highly customizable PanDA system not only manages clusters and storage, but also optimizes workflow
over existing networks. Over the years, many capabilities to optimize network performance have been built into
PanDA and Rucio. However, direct integration with network layers have remained elusive over the past decade.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 231

6.9.2.7.3 Frontier
The ATLAS model for remote access to database resident information relies upon a limited set of dedicated and
distributed Oracle database repositories complemented with the deployment of Frontier system infrastructure
on the WLCG. ATLAS clients with network access can get the database information they need dynamically by
submitting requests to a squid server in the Frontier network which provides results from its cache or passes new
requests along the network to the launchpads located at CERN since 2023. Since the beginning of LHC Run
1, the system has evolved in terms of client, squid, and launchpad optimizations but the distribution model has
remained fundamentally unchanged.

6.9.2.7.4 CVMFS
The ATLAS software for simulation and reconstruction is distributed via the CernVM files system (CVMFS).
CVMFS is implemented as a Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX) read-only file system in user space (a
Filesystem in Userspace [FUSE] module). Files and directories are hosted on standard web servers and mounted
in the universal namespace /cvmfs. Internally, CVMFS uses content- addressable storage and Merkle trees in
order to maintain file data and metadata. CVMFS uses outgoing HTTP connections only. It transfers data and
metadata on demand and verifies data integrity by cryptographic hashes.

In addition, ATLAS is currently exploring the usage of docker containers for software distribution. These
containers are distributed via the CVMFS files system.

6.9.2.7.5 HTCondor
PanDA uses the HTCondor system for job submission to a majority of computing resources. This allows the
Harvester to use a reliable and well-defined HEP standard. While Advanced Resource Connector (ARC), native
cloud interfaces, or direct interface to batch systems are sometimes used, HTCondor is used for the vast majority
of job submissions.

6.9.2.7.6 ROOT
ROOT is a software framework with building blocks for:

 • Data processing
 • Data analysis
 • Data visualization
 • Data storage
ROOT is written mainly in C++ (C++20 standard) and has bindings for Python available as well. It is highly
adopted in high energy physics and other sciences but also in industry. More than 1 EB of data are stored in
ROOT format.

6.9.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
6.9.2.8.1 US ATLAS T1 at BNL
BNL has implemented a vendor agnostic, resilient, scalable and modular terabit per second (Tbps) HTSN which
serves as the primary network transport for all data-intensive collaborations at BNL. It provides high-throughput
connectivity to all High-Performance Computing (HPC) and HTC collaborations and supports the timely transfer
of large amounts of scientific data via the Internet.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 232

The HTSN has five key components:

 1. Network Perimeter
 a. Two diverse 800 Gbps (2 x 400 GbE) circuits that peer with ESnet routers within the BNL
 515 and 725 data centers. These circuits are utilized by all scientific and administrative
 communities at BNL. All traffic to and from BNL flows through either of these circuits.
 b. The BNL Network Perimeter on average ingests and egresses between 10-15 PB of data
 monthly.
 2. Science DMZ
 a. Supports open, high-speed WAN/Internet) access for all scientific collaborations throughout
 the BNL campus.
 3. Science Core
 a. A Tbps Science and Data Center Interconnect for data intensive collaborations at BNL.
 This Science Interconnect enables high-speed connectivity between collaborations such as
 ATLAS, STAR, sPHENIX, CAD, CFN, NSLS-II, High-Performance Computing Clusters
 and SDCC.
 b. Intelligence and routing policies are applied within the Science Core to restrict or grant
 access to specific resources within the SDCC.
 4. Spine
 a. A Tbps network Spine that interconnects all Leaf switches. Leaf switches can consist of
 ToR or chassis-based switches that connect compute, storage or general infrastructure
 service servers.
 b. The responsibility of the Spine is fast packet forwarding and flexibility, not policy insertion
 or server termination.
 c. External Border Gateway Protocol (eBGP) is utilized throughout the HTSN. EBGP was
 chosen for its ability to immensely scale and to create modularity and fault domain isolation
 down to the rack level. Each Spine group shares the same ASN but does not have Internal
 BGP (iBGP) peering between them. Each Leaf or pair of Leaves will require their own ASN.
 5. Storage Core
 a. A redundant terabit per second switching block that aggregates high-performance
 storage services.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 233

6.9.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.9.2.9.1 Cloud Services
Google Cloud and AWS computing services have been successfully integrated within the ATLAS workflow
and data management systems PanDA and Rucio. State-of-the-art technologies like Kubernetes, nonstandard
processors like ARM or GPUs and cloud storage are used and have been operated at the scale of a current
medium-sized Grid site. Scaling to more than 100k concurrently running vCPUs in PanDA has been
demonstrated. The solutions may be considered for example in the implementation of AFs for HL-LHC, with all
the added values

and services offered by the commercial cloud providers. In future work, data exports from cloud data centers to
WLCG sites will have to be optimized, involving research network providers.

In 2024 the Google Cloud is used for MC production processing as extension of the SWT2 at the scale of up to
15k job slots as shown in Section 6.9.2.5.1101.

In 2022 BNL (as some other labs) moved to using Microsoft Office 365 for email, calendar service, Sharepoint,
and OneDrive cloud storage. Although, bandwidth to and from these services is much lower than that required
for scientific data, the reliance of the laboratory on cloud services for day-to-day business has made the resilience
of Internet connectivity critical. During periods of peak scientific data movement, cloud data for day-to-day work
has been affected, and QoS and other traffic engineering controls were put in place to protect the business traffic
from being affected by the scientific data flows.

6.9.2.9.2 Artificial Intelligence and ML
From the ATLAS Run3 software and computing paper: ML is used in a wide range of applications in ATLAS,
including physics analysis, simulation and physics object identification within the reconstruction and trigger
system. Models trained for classification and regression, as well as generative models, are core components of the
software and analysis chain.

Although deep neural networks are reliant on GPUs for training, inference is performed almost exclusively on
CPUs. In addition to supporting inference of modern ML models, training infrastructure is available through
WLCG with support for job submissions using PanDA, including access to many GPUs. However, most models
used by the collaboration are trained on private resources due to the modest resource requirements and
satisfactory availability of institutional GPU resources.

ATLAS does not expect any significant changes in network load or the distributed computing software stack
design during the ongoing analysis of Run 3 data.

6.9.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
No wireless capability studies or capability upgrades are planned at present. Some users may do their work from
systems connected via wireless, but this is not currently an area of concern for ATLAS because most such users
use wireless to access remote systems that are doing the actual data transfers or access.

6.9.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
The primary concern for ATLAS is lack of sufficiently fine-grained network monitoring and performance
information to help us debug and automate data transfers in real time between various sites. Better visibility
is being worked on through various entities including WLCG Site Network Monitoring, the SciTags initiative
(labeling network flows and IPv6 packets with owner/purpose) and improved monitoring from the various tools
and infrastructures, but ATLAS still have significant gaps in monitoring.

101 https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41781-024-00128-x

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 241

6.9.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
BNL SDCC operates Globus and FTS endpoints. These File transfer services have access to the HEP storage
systems such as dCache which is connected to the ESnet network at the bandwidth of 1.6 Tbps. Together with
ESnet and various site network and storage administrators, FTS service was used to generate the network load
during Data Challenge 24 and various mini-Data Challenges in the preparation for the Data Challenge.

A related note is that the idea of DTNs were not the basis for how ATLAS distributed data management was
originally architected. Instead, the focus was on using many flows from many servers at each end of a site-to-site
transfer. The distributed data management infrastructure could benefit from incorporating tools and architectures
targeting higher performance, but the cost-benefit analysis needs to be continually evaluated.

6.9.2.12 Outstanding Issues
The primary wish list consists of capabilities to monitor and manage data transfers automatically. Given the size,
complexity, and fully distributed nature of ATLAS computing, all workflow and data distribution needs to be
optimized and managed with AI.

ATLAS anticipates network needs will grow gradually, following the patterns described in this document.
Increasing network capacity and performance will be needed at US ATLAS Tier-1, Tier-3, and Tier-3 AFs. The
exact magnitude of future network provisioning is expected to be determined jointly by US ATLAS, ESNET and
other involved parties.

6.10 LHC: CMS Experiment
This case study functions as a high-level introduction describing the process of science within the larger context
of the global CMS collaboration: how data are produced, how science is derived from these data, its computing
facilities, and its requirements process. This case study also provides more details about the networking
implications of performing LHC particle physics specifically at the Tier-1 site at Fermilab, the seven Tier-2 sites
at US universities, and the numerous other “sites” used to process data and to perform analysis. CMS researchers
also utilize campus or research group facilities at about 50 US institutions, the largest of which are Tier-3 sites, as
well as individually managed computing resources of each of the approximately 700 researchers within US CMS.

6.10.1 Discussion Summary
DC24 was successful for the CMS experiment, and several important outcomes came from the exercise.
Understanding bottlenecks in the network configuration at Fermilab were important, along with the way that
many of the tools that were improved and replaced since LHC Run 2. CMS would be interested in developing a
program to test the effectiveness of transfers both to benchmark methods at increased capacity, and integrate new
functionality into existing tools. Such tests should be done in collaboration with ESnet. For example, one lesson
learned from the most-recent data challenge organized by WLCG (DC24) was that it is necessary to utilize a link
at full capacity, to learn if a given link has any performance abnormalities. It is desirable to develop a process
of regular testing of network capacities (e.g., relying on perfSONAR) to test connections to the maximum and
identify problems before they become a bottleneck in production.

Changes made to analysis formats have also had a large impact on network traffic. The NanoAOD format, which
was introduced late in Run 2, is becoming more widely used. The format is smaller, and thus occupies less
network bandwidth and can run faster on CPUs. More than 50% of all physics analysis activities are now based
on NanoAOD, with another 40% or more to be based on MiniAOD. The use of the larger AOD format is now
minimal, despite occupying a lot of disco space. At future HL-LHC scales, CMS expects not be able to afford to
keep AOD on disk any more. These may be relegated to tape archives.

The data rates that CMS originally estimated for Run 3 (i.e., in 2020 just prior to run beginning) were smaller
than what was witnessed by a factor of two to three times beyond the 2018 values, and four to six times beyond
the 2017 values. This increase in size has not translated directly into increased traffic on network connections;
however, some of the R&E efforts to improve data mobility tools and workflow management has helped to
mitigate big spikes in traffic.

The use of Caching has had some impact on network use, and CMS credits ESnet’s role in the development
and deployment as being critical to understanding what is possible and how it can be leveraged for Run 3 and
the latter run comprising the HL-LHC operating period. Much of the R&D efforts in the recent years have
been determining where caches may be beneficial for placement, how large they need to be to be effective, and
what strategy should be used to store and replace data sets. Nevertheless, there are still open questions about
deployment strategies that need to be worked out for both CMS and ATLAS. Regional caches were found to not
be as effective (since the overlap of data use was not high enough), but caches within a facility, and ensuring that
the workflow management tools know to check the caches, produced the most reliable results. The adoption
and more widespread use of the NanoAOD format is anticipated to have some impact on cache performance
over time.

 • The CMS experiment at the LHC is designed to probe new phenomena at the energy frontier.
 The CMS collaboration is made up of more than 3000 members from more than 50 countries.
 Researchers at US institutions comprise about 30% of the collaboration. [Section 4.1]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 243

 • CERN facilities are used to provide the initial CMS data reconstruction, to support detector
 commissioning work as well as physics analysis work. Then globally distributed Tier-1 and
 Tier-2 facilities are responsible for data archiving (at the Tier-1 only), simulated data generation,
 analysis data storage, and physics analysis activities (primarily at the Tier-2s). The US operates
 one Tier-1 facility (Fermilab) and seven Tier-2 facilities (Univ. of Florida, UC-San Diego,
 Caltech, Massachusetts Institute of Technology [MIT], Univ. of Wisconsin, Univ. of Nebraska,
 and Purdue University). Data also moves from these facilities to other universities as analysis
 data sets are reduced and refined during the analysis process. [Section 4.1]

 • Analyses are done by small and large groups that share data either at a CMS TIer-2 center, at
 a local Tier-3 or on other local computing facilities. An “average” event collected by CMS is
 processed 50–100 times by analysts. That means that CMS analysts are processing hundreds
 of PB each year just to carry out the initial analysis steps which process data created by the
 production system. [Section 4.2]

 • CMS devotes 30% of its disk storage to derived data sets, or around 100 PB. These data are
 typically used much more frequently as the size for any given analysis is smaller, and can be
 more quickly processed as the analysis process evolves. [Section 4.2]

 • CMS distinguish three types of data: Data from collisions in the accelerator, data from
 simulations, and user produced data. The first two are centrally produced, while the third is
 produced by the physicists themselves as part of their analysis workflow. [Section 4.2]

 • The LHC provides data to CMS in roughly ten-hour data taking periods with minimal
 downtime (typically a few hours) between periods. As such, a roughly constant stream of data is
 available during operation. Event rates of around 1 kHz of physics events are typical
 today and for Run 3, and 7.5 kHz is expected for HL-LHC. This translates into raw data
 volumes of: [Section 4.2]

           °    Run 2: 45 PB written during 4 years (2015-2018)

           °    Run 3: approximately 120 PB (2022-2024)

           °    Run 4: 270 PB/yr (estimated in 2022)

 • CMS has produced simulations that scale in size with the luminosity collected. CMS has about
 70 PB (170 PB) of Run 3 (Run 2) MC simulation datasets stored on tape, representing around 75
 billion (250 billion) MC events. [Section 4.2]

 • The centrally produced data from CMS comes in multiple formats ranging from the most
 versatile and complete (raw and AOD) to the easiest, smallest, and fastest to use ones (MiniAOD
 and NanoAOD). CMS has been moving to toward the use of NanoAOD, a data format designed
 for interactive end-user analysis, and produced centrally. CMS adoption of this format has
 already grown in Run 3 to around 50% of analyses using the NanoAOD as their primary data
 tier. [Section 4.3]

 • The CMS Tier-0 is at CERN, and has two primary functions. It is responsible for “prompt
 calibration and reconstruction” and archiving of all the raw data at CERN. When the LHC is
 not running, the Tier-0 compute cluster may be used for other processing by CMS. [Section 4.3]

 • CMS globally has 7 Tier-1s, including Fermilab in the US The collection of the Tier-1s are
 responsible for operating a distributed archive of all centrally produced data, including a second
 copy of the raw. The copy of the raw across the Tier-1s is considered the “active copy,” i.e., the
 raw copy at CERN is considered strictly a backup. In addition, the Tier-1s provide computing
 resources to the experiment that are primarily used for centrally organized processing. The US
 CMS Tier-1 Center at Fermilab is the largest of CMS Tier-1 facilities, currently providing 40%
 of the total CMS Tier-1 capacity. [Section 4.3]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 244

 • CMS has roughly 50 Tier-2s globally. The collection of the Tier-2s is responsible for all data
 analysis, and some simulations. Tier-2s also provide disk space to host data for analysis, and a
 moderate amount of disk space for staging in data for processing. [Section 4.3]

 • Tier-3 sites are typically university-hosted clusters that are smaller than Tier-2 sites and are
 typically without dedicated support to ensure high resource availability. Those in the US are
 not funded through the Operations Program. Tier-3 sites can be part of the DMS of CMS and
 receive official datasets, or can access data through streaming. These sites can also provide disk
 space to hold user data as required by the local community. [Section 4.3]

 • CMS uses compute resources beyond the tiered computing centers. These include HPC centers
 in the US During 2023, the CMS usage of shared HPC facilities funded by DOE and NSF
 amount to about 10% of the overall computing budget globally. This has increased substantially
 in the recent past: by around 4x in relative fraction of CMS compute since 2020 (and a
 substantially greater increase in absolute terms), and has substantially increased again in 2024.
 CMS expects that this model will change for the HL-LHC to include larger allocations on
 HPC facilities. The size and locations of future facilities is not fully predictable; however, CMS
 would rely on excellent network connectivity to any HPC facility from its Tier-1 and Tier-2
 facilities. [Section 4.3]

 • HPC centers funded by DOE and NSF as shared facilities across multiple science domains do
 not generally provide the full functionality required from a Tier-2 or Tier-1 center, e.g., they
 normally do not provide any substantial amount of storage under the control of the experiment.
 Data access at HPC centers relies on either temporarily staging in input data on storage at
 the HPC site, or streaming access if the site setup allows for access to the wider network.
 In general, HPC centers only run compute dominated applications that have modest IO/
 CPU requirements, e.g., the central production workflows involved in central processing and
 simulations. Output is archived back to the Tier-1 sites, either directly from the application or
 through other mechanisms. [Section 4.3]

 • CMS currently uses Rucio for bulk-data transfer activities, having fully switched from its
 previous system based on PhEDEx and Dynamo tools, to manage dataset storage and dataset
 transfers. Rucio has become a community solution for data management. Rucio uses the FTS to
 manage scheduling and file transfer. For bulk transfers via Rucio and executed by FTS, US CMS
 has moved to TPC https implemented via XRootD servers and away from gridFTP. [Section 4.3]

 • Failures in data streaming are a large source of job failures in CMS. This has also become an
 issue for analysis-facing activities, where a greater variety of tools are used to access CMS data.
 While CMS can instrument its centrally maintained software with retry mechanisms and other
 fallback logic, it is more difficult to extend this to community-developed tools. Reliable and
 high-capacity streaming of input data, either raw or pileup simulation, considerably reduces the
 disk requirements of CMS at HPC and other nondedicated computing facilities. [Section 4.3]

 • CMS acknowledges that the data volume that can be handled by the networks within and
 coming out of the CMS detector facility far exceeds what can be handled offline within current
 CPU, storage and networking infrastructures. This bottleneck will remain for the foreseeable
 future, as network growth patterns move faster than storage and computation. [Section 4.4]

 • The LHC computing and storage infrastructure is organized in a tiered computing model
 including four tiers, 0-3. Originally, when the connectivity among the sites was extremely
 limited, the tiers were hierarchical in that Tier-N+1 was connected only to an associated Tier-N
 above and associated Tier-N+2 below. Data was not allowed to flow from Tier-N+2 to Tier-N.
 This rigid concept has been eliminated over the last decade as network capacity and capability
 progressed. [Section 4.4]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 245

 • The global CMS collaboration, together with WLCG and OSG, will define services that sites
 perform. Today the service profile defines the site to belong to a certain tier. In the future,
 centers of a given tier today may no longer provide all the services that today would be expected
 from that tier. In addition, it is likely that the HL-LHC data and processing infrastructure will
 no longer support the full global mesh of data flows among all tiers. These changes are part of an
 ongoing R&D program. [Section 4.4]

 • CMS applications and the infrastructure that distributes and launches them support multiple
 types of data access: [Section 4.5]

 ° Traditional top-down data placement at Tier-1 and Tier-2 centers combined with
 applications specifying the dataset they need, and being automatically routed and executed
 at the sites that have it.

 ° CMS supports streaming data access to any data on disk across its the WLCG facilities from
 any location with an internet connection at any time. This is called AAA, for “Any Data,
 Anytime, Anywhere” within CMS.

 ° Bottom-up data placement, as is implicit in caching. Here the applications are routed to
 sites with caches, applications access the cache locally, and cache misses are handled by the
 CMS XRootD Data Federation.

 • Having reliable mechanisms to transfer data into HPC facilities from the CMS Tier-1 and
 Tier-2 centers is of growing importance. HPCs are different from other resources used by CMS
 primarily because they provide significant compute (CPU and GPU) resources but very limited
 disk resources, and because network access to or from HPC compute nodes is typically limited
 or not allowed. The broader LHC community has considered how to best utilize these resources
 within operational constraints. Unlike most HPC users, CMS cannot concentrate its efforts on
 using one or a handful of HPC facilities, but is instead asked to use HPC facilities worldwide.
 Network access and data management are important aspects of this. [Section 4.6]

 • CMS is currently a major user of the TA network link. Activities including the archival of raw
 data, initial copies of analysis data samples, and user-derived data sets using CERN or other
 non-US facilities are clear use cases for TA network usage. CMS tools do not prioritize site
 proximity (in the networking sense) when scheduling data transfers. Streaming data across the
 TA link is allowed (even if discouraged). [Section 4.7]

 • The US CMS Tier-1 facility at Fermilab has local network infrastructure consists of fully
 redundant, high-performance switching fabric distributed across multiple Fermilab data
 centers. That switching fabric is based on 400 GE network technology for inter-switch
 connectivity, with 10 GE and 100 GE connectivity available for host system connectivity. The
 LAN provides approximately 10 Tb/s of network capacity in total. [Section 4.7]

 • Fermilab’s WAN architecture utilizes LHCOPN connectivity to support movement of raw data
 from the T0 (CERN), as well as production data movement with some of the other CMS T1s. In
 terms of aggregate WAN capacity out of the site, Fermilab currently has provisioned 2.4Tb/s of
 link capacity to ESnet, via geographically diverse connections. A LAG of four 400 Gbps links is
 used to support the science data network paths, including LHCOPN and LHCONE. A second 2
 x 400 Gbps LAG supports the Laboratory’s general internet traffic, which includes some portion
 of science traffic. [Section 4.7]

 • Much of the LAN and WAN networking infrastructure to and within a CMS Tier-2 site has been
 an institutional contribution to the US CMS Operations Program, i.e., it has not for the most
 part been directly funded by the program. [Section 4.7]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 246

 • All CMS Tier-2s connect to the LHCONE at least 100 Gbps, through partnership with regional
 networking infrastructure. In some cases, a Tier-2 facility may have multiple connections either
 as a backup, or for active use. [Section 4.7]

 • CMS does not currently use cloud resources to any significant extent. Previous studies have
 shown them to be a more costly model than the owned-resource model that CMS currently
 relies on. A notable exception would be the case of needed resource bursts for either CPU or
 network. The resources available for either CPU or TA networking in the cloud far exceed those
 available to CMS. At this point, CMS tools are generally able to use cloud services, typically
 via infrastructure at one of the tiered sites, but CMS does not have plans to use cloud services
 extensively in the near or longer term. This can evolve depending on largely external factors
 (e.g., cost evolution, or government policies). [Section 4.8]

 • CMS has an increasing use of AI/ML in its production workflows. Analysis use cases have
 evolved even more quickly as there is greater freedom to adopt new toolkits and approaches.
 Both the Fermilab Tier-1 and Tier-2 facilities have GPU capabilities for CMS use, and the
 CMS community also relies on national resources. CMS is also researching a dedicated AI/ML
 training facility (at Vanderbilt) in recognition that AI/ML brings two distinct use cases, training
 and inference, that both require substantial resources (but in differing access patterns). CMS
 expects to predominantly use on-site and HPC resources rather than commercial
 cloud. [Section 4.8]

 • Reliable networking can be used to reduce disk replica requirements either by the use of tape
 recall or caching. By the end of Run 4, a copy of the entire CMS MiniAOD will be around 100
 PB. If 10% of this is used during any given month in a caching system, one can estimate the
 need for 10 PB/month of transfers to keep the cache up to date with the most recently used
 data. Cache network needs will be typically bursty because users read full data sets rather
 than just a file or two from one. Understanding and expanding caching use cases and needs
 are part of ongoing R&D. It is expected that investments into disk space at Tier-2s against
 network utilization will become more critical in the long term. Other forces may also push in
 the direction of higher network requirements, such as how spinning disk technology evolves in
 terms of cost per terabyte and I/O capabilities relative to CMS needs. [Section 4.8]

 • US CMS has proactively pursued opportunities at US HPC sites, and currently has many
 allocations available for use. Typical workflows run on these allocations are similar to the
 IRI concept of a “long-term campaign,” that relies on sustained access at scale. New HPC
 resources typically come with some, potentially substantial, work to set up given facility specific
 configurations and constraints. A common interface (or access requirements) across DOE HPC
 sites, as well as models for sustained access, are potential IRI benefits. [Section 4.9]

 • CMS would like to develop a program to test the effectiveness of transfers both to benchmark
 methods at increased capacity, and integrate new functionality into existing tools. Such tests
 should be done in collaboration with ESnet. For example, one lesson learned from the most-
 recent data challenge organized by WLCG (DC24) was that it is necessary to utilize a link at full
 capacity, to learn if a given link has any performance abnormalities. It is desirable to develop a
 process of regular testing of network capacities (e.g., relying on perfSONAR) to test connections
 to the maximum and identify problems before they become a bottleneck in production. [Section 5.7]

 • CMS has treated the global network of sites as a mesh with identical links when it comes to
 bulk transfers. The XRootD data federation was designed from the beginning to be cognizant
 of the TA links being limited, but treated links within the US as identical. The data lake model
 currently discussed in WLCG makes clear regional distinctions. The concept of creating a data
 lake has progressed slowly due to challenges around how increased latency due to the longer
 international links will affect application performance. [Section 5.8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 247

 • CMS would like to continue exploring with ESnet how to contribute towards global R&D
 projects such as the Global P4 Lab testbed, use of ESnet High Touch services, and evolving
 technologies such as Smart NICs. [Section 5.8]

 • The next several years are critical to transition managed network R&D by CMS, including
 results of the Software-Defined Network for End-to-end Networked Science at the Exascale
 (SENSE) project, into production for the HL-LHC. The SENSE, Caltech, and UCSD teams
 are close to 400G throughput with production infrastructure using XRootD, FTS and XRootD.
           [Section 5.8]

6.10.2 CMS: Experiment Profile
The content presented in this case study is written from the perspective of networking and data. CMS identifies
two primary periods: Run 3 and Run 4. These map roughly on the time periods 2022-2025 and 2029-2031. The
time period from 2026 through 2028 is a transition period where the detector, together with the LHC accelerator
complex, is undergoing a major upgrade that is presently hard to predict in terms of computing activities. It will
probably include some large-scale data challenges that are discussed in the third case study.

The CMS experiment at the LHC is designed to probe new phenomena at the energy frontier. Since starting
operations in 2010, CMS has collected nearly 200 fb-1 of luminosity at center-of-mass energies between 7 and 13 TeV.

6.10.2.1 Science Background
The CMS collaboration is made up of more than 3000 members from more than 50 countries. Researchers at US
institutions comprise about 30% of the collaboration. The collaboration has published more than 1000 papers
with scientific findings across a broad physics program enabled by all collaborators having access to the entire
data sample for their work. No previous HEP experiment has produced this many publications. The success of
the physics program of CMS depends on the availability of sufficient computing resources to store, process and
analyze the data in an efficient fashion.

The LHC provides proton-proton bunch crossings (where each crossing produces many proton-proton
interactions) in CMS at a rate of nearly 40 MHz at a duty cycle of about 50% during 8 months of a typical running
year. CMS commonly uses the word “event” to refer to all the data that corresponds to a single bunch crossing,
both for collision data and simulated data. The interactions that result from each beam crossing are independent
of those from other beam crossings. This means that CMS can reduce, model and analyze each event as being
independent from all other events.

40 MHz worth of detector data (called “raw” data in this document) cannot all be saved for analyst use, in part
because raw events are nearly 1 MB in size. CMS uses a two-step filtering system (“Level-1” and HLT) to reduce
the data rate down to approximately 7.5 kHz of events to be processed and made available to the collaboration
for analysis. This event rate has increased considerably since Run 2, and during Run 3, driven by physics
opportunities and available computing resources.

Part of this online data reduction process is to broadly categorize events into “datasets” according to the physics
signatures observed during the filtering process. Datasets are also separated according to the data-taking period
to ensure that any large changes in LHC conditions, CMS detector operations or software used can be treated
separately by analysts. A typical CMS publication requires analysis of a few datasets of detector data, and a few
dozen simulation datasets for each year of data taking it includes. Larger endeavors may require up to 50% of
the entire detector data, and corresponding simulations. Analysts nearly always aim to analyze as much of the
available integrated luminosity as possible (e.g., using as much run time as possible). There are more than a
hundred analyses ongoing in CMS at any given time, each engaging between a handful and up to dozens of
researchers who are actively involved in the analysis of data (either directly from production, or using samples
derived from it).

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 248

CMS executes a variety of tasks on its distributed computing infrastructure, for reconstructing collision data
recorded by the detector, simulating collision data, and analyzing both. The CMS computing system relies
on infrastructure distributed worldwide, and as such relies heavily on excellent network connectivity among
its dedicated computing centers, and increasingly its connections to shared facilities at universities, high-
performance computing (HPC) centers and potentially cloud resources when economically viable. Beyond the
substantial real-time facility for data taking that is co-located with the CMS detector, CERN facilities are used
to provide the initial data reconstruction, to support detector commissioning work as well as physics analysis
work. Then globally distributed Tier-1 and Tier-2 facilities are responsible for data archiving (at the Tier-1 only),
simulated data generation, analysis data storage, and physics analysis activities (primarily at the Tier-2s). The US
operates one Tier-1 facility (Fermilab) and seven Tier-2 facilities (Univ. of Florida, UC-San Diego, Caltech, MIT,
Univ. of Wisconsin, Univ. of Nebraska, and Purdue University). Data also moves from these facilities to other
universities as analysis data sets are reduced and refined during the analysis process.

In a nutshell, one may think of the science publication process of the CMS experiment as starting with detector
operations to collect data, then central production to process and do initial data reduction and validation,
followed by a decentralized (but coordinated) data analysis process that derives results by using progressively
improved reconstruction and analysis methods, as well as new approaches and ideas that come from across
the collaboration. This is followed by a convergence of those results through multiple stages of discussion and
sometimes refinements of the analysis, leading to publications via a centrally organized internal review process.
Publications are then passed onwards to the peer review processes of the respective journals.

The CMS production and analysis process is quite storage and data-movement intensive. Data sets are replicated,
moved or deleted according to their usage patterns, site and resource availability and experiment priorities.
Individual analysts or analysis groups create and manage further derived data sets for their analysis workflows.
Analyses are done by small and large groups that share data either at a CMS TIer-2 center, at a local Tier-3 or
on other local computing facilities. An “average” event collected by CMS is processed 50–100 times by analysts.
That means that CMS analysts are processing hundreds of PB each year just to carry out the initial analysis steps
which process data created by the production system.

CMS devotes 30% of its disk storage to derived data sets, or around 100 PB. These data are typically used much
more frequently as the size for any given analysis is smaller, and can be more quickly processed as the analysis
process evolves. In addition to these resources, final analysis steps are done locally on the laptops, desktops
or computing clusters of individual researchers or groups. Reliable distribution of data to these researchers
is essential to the CMS analysis process. It enables researchers to work outside of a centrally managed and
maintained system, and it thus reduces the complexity and management difficulty that the central system would
otherwise have to face.

The infrastructure to support this process is largely developed and operated by CMS experts, including a
significant number of computing professionals as well as physicists that have specialized in software and
computing technologies. However, the experiment strives to be sufficiently open in the infrastructure such
that computing and storage resources at individual universities can be integrated and used in both the central
production and decentralized analysis parts of this process.

As the entire CMS data flow and analysis process relies on collaboration and data sharing, the CMS research
program and methods are discussed in the next section.

6.10.2.2 Collaborators
The CMS experiment is designed, built, and operated by a collaboration of close to 200 institutions across more
than 50 countries, and comprises roughly 3,000 members, of which close to ⅔ are physicists with authorship
privileges on all CMS physics papers. The US makes up about 30% of the authors at about 50 institutions.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 249

The collaboration as a collective produces official data samples via a central production team. Applications
composed of algorithms developed by the collaboration convert and reduce the raw detector data into derived
formats ready for analysis. These data are distributed across the CMS computing facilities on reliable disk,
with topical and popular data sets having the greatest accessibility (e.g., largest number of replicas across
the distributed system). Tools and support are provided to facilitate the use of these data. All members of the
collaboration have access to all centrally produced data, and are free to pursue any kind of physics analysis that
is supported by these data. Researchers use everything from local computing facilities to laptops to interact with
these organized resources typically via custom approaches developed according to research group interests,
abilities and prior experience.

Typically, physicists self-organize into small groups of a few to a few dozen researchers to collaborate on one
or more physics publications. Here again reduced data samples are shared amongst members of these groups,
or often between groups with related interests. Due to the sheer size of the data CMS, the processing of these
reduced data samples often require substantial resources both to produce and to store. CMS nominally devotes
30% of its disk resources to data samples derived by data analysis groups.

Researchers target conference results and subsequently journal publications for discussion and peer review of
their results. Conferences do bring a set of seasonal deadlines that impact the way resources are used in the
collaboration. Most researchers have a peak of activity for the main spring (i.e., March) and summer (i.e., July)
conferences. As such, production campaigns may be scheduled to make data available with the best available
algorithms and calibrations in advance of these deadlines. Given the already very substantial Run 2 data set, this
practice has reduced during Run 3 and analysis practices have become more balanced. This is simply driven
by the scientific reach of most analyses, scaling only with the square root of the luminosity used. In addition
to conference deadlines, CMS schedules are now driven by software and calibration readiness and other
experimental aspects.

Results are peer reviewed via a process that is agreed upon by the entire collaboration, and in which every
member of the collaboration is asked to participate. Typically, there are multiple stages of work and review.
Analyses are initially discussed and reviewed by physicists who are expert in related analyses (e.g., analysis
working groups), experts in various reconstruction, event selection and signal-vs-background separation
methods, experts specialized in “statistics” (hypothesis testing), and subsequently more broadly by the CMS
analysis community. The resulting publications that come out of this process carry the names of all members
with authorship privileges. There is a well-defined process for somebody new to the collaboration to obtain and
maintain authorship privileges.

CMS researchers collaborate broadly on technical and physics research topics. For example, CMS works closely
with software authors, infrastructure providers and the theoretical particle-physics community. However, as CMS
data are largely internal to the collaboration, the impact on network use of these collaborations is minimal. The
vast majority of network use is thus networks that connect the close to 200 collaborating institutions within CMS.

The term “data streaming” is defined to mean remote file open, and direct reads to remotely opened files. The
term “data transfer” is defined to mean transfer of entire files, most often in bulk.

6.10.2.3 IRI Readiness
US CMS has proactively pursued opportunities at US HPC sites and currently has allocations on numerous sites
as described in the previous section. Typical workflows run on these allocations are typically long-term campaigns
that rely on sustained access at scale. New HPC resources typically come with some, potentially substantial, work
to set up given facility specific configurations and constraints. A common interface (or access requirements) across
US HPC sites as well as models for sustained access at HPCs are potential IRI benefits. This is discussed in more
detail in Section 6.12.

6.10.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
The LHC computing and storage infrastructure is organized in a tiered computing model including four tiers,
0-3. Originally, when the connectivity among the sites was extremely limited, the tiers were hierarchical in that
Tier-N+1 was connected only to an associated Tier-N above and associated Tier-N+2 below. Data was not
allowed to flow from Tier-N+2 to Tier-N. This rigid concept has been eliminated over the last decade as network
capacity and capability progressed.

Data now flows across the full mesh, among all sites of all tiers. Today, and in the future, the global CMS
collaboration together with WLCG and OSG will define services that sites perform. Today the service profile
defines the site to belong to a certain tier. For the HL-LHC, even that might change. In the future, centers of a
given tier today may no longer provide all the services that today would be expected from that tier. In addition, it
is likely that the HL-LHC data and processing infrastructure will no longer support the full global mesh of data
flows among all tiers. These changes are part of an ongoing R&D program towards an updated computing model
for HL-LHC, and will be discussed in the HL-LHC document in more detail.

In the following, CMS will describe the current services profile for each of the tier, starting with the High-Level
Trigger compute cluster (HLT).

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 252

6.10.2.4.1 HLT
The Run 3 HLT computing system is a roughly 30,000-core x86 plus GPU cluster. There are 200 nodes each
with two Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) EPYC “Milan” 7763 processors and two Nvidia T4 GPUs, as well as
18 nodes each with 2 AMD EPYC “Bergamo” 9754 processors and three Nvidia L4 GPUs. Its primary purpose
is to perform the last stage of the online filtering of events. All events that pass this filter will be stored forever in
the archive as raw data. It is located at the site of the CMS detector roughly 10 miles away from the main CERN
site, on the other side of the LHC ring. The HLT is part of LHC’s trigger and data-acquisition system (TriDAS),
the CMS trigger and data acquisition system that is responsible for all the real-time data reduction and collection
for CMS. Its size, architecture and components are reviewed annually, independently of the annual offline and
computing requirements process discussed further below.

CMS also continues to run the HLT computing system used during Run 2 as a permanent offline “cloud”
resource for processing MC simulations and prompt reconstruction. On average this contributes around 25,000
x86 cores to the CMS offline processing capability at CERN.

6.10.2.4.2 Tier-0
The Tier-0 is at CERN, and has two primary functions. It is responsible for “prompt calibration and
reconstruction” and archiving of all the raw data at CERN. When the LHC is not running, the Tier-0 compute
cluster may be used for other processing by CMS.

6.10.2.4.3 Tier-1
CMS globally has seven Tier-1s, including Fermilab in the US The collection of the Tier-1s are responsible for
operating a distributed archive of all centrally produced data, including a second copy of the raw. The copy of the
raw across the Tier-1s is considered the “active copy,” i.e., the raw copy at CERN is considered strictly a backup.
In addition, the Tier-1s provide computing resources to the experiment that are primarily used for centrally
organized processing. Historically, each Tier-1’s computing was responsible for all the reprocessing of the data it
archives. The computing and storage capacity of a given Tier-1 center was thus directly related to the amount of
data it pledged to archive. More information on pledges follows below.

One change in the Tier-1 facilities since 2020 is that given the ongoing sanctions that impact network and other
aspects of infrastructure in Russia, the JINR Tier-1 is now used as a purely opportunistic CPU resource for CMS.
This is in agreement with WLCG and CERN policies with respect to JINR. This means that the substantial tape
resource at JINR is no longer used.

CMS is also exploring the possibility of adding additional Tier-1 centers. Serbia has signed an MOU with CERN
to provide a Tier-1 facility for CMS and is expected to be operational in the coming year or two.

6.10.2.4.4 Tier-2
CMS has roughly 50 Tier-2s globally. The collection of the Tier-2s is responsible for all data analysis, and some
simulations. Tier-2s also provide disk space to host data for analysis, and a moderate amount of disk space for
staging in data for processing.

6.10.2.4.5 CMS Computing Capacity and Planning
The Tier-0, -1, and -2 resources are subject to an annual needs planning process. CMS offline and computing
management makes a needs assessment every year that projects out two years into the future. After internal
review, the annual needs are reviewed externally by the LHCC twice a year. After sign-off by the LHCC, the
needs determined in this way are used to guide the funding agencies in the various member countries, leading to
annual computing resource pledges. In the US, the LHC operations programs, jointly funded by DOE and NSF,
are responsible for the US pledges, and coordinate them annually with the funding agencies.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 253

Throughout the year, the actual delivered computing capacity is measured from all Tier-1s and Tier-2s via the
WLCG accounting system. For the US, the propagation of usage into this accounting system is the responsibility
of OSG. This will be described in Section 6.12.

6.10.2.4.6 Tier-3
Tier-3 sites are typically university-hosted clusters that are smaller than Tier-2 sites and are typically without
dedicated support to ensure high resource availability. Those in the US are not funded through the Operations
Program. Tier-3 sites can be part of the DMS of CMS and receive official datasets, or can access data through
streaming. These sites can also provide disk space to hold user data as required by the local community. However,
they are not part of the annual requirements review process. As such, the total Tier-3 resources of CMS are
presently modest compared to the other tiers.

6.10.2.4.7 HPC facilities
CMS also uses compute resources beyond the dedicated resources located in one of the tiered computing
centers. These include HPC centers in the US During 2023, the CMS usage of shared HPC facilities funded by
DOE and NSF amount to about 10% of the overall computing budget globally, and are not part of any pledges.
This has increased substantially in the recent past: by around 4x in relative fraction of CMS compute since 2020
(and a substantially greater increase in absolute terms), and has substantially increased again in 2024. Recent
allocations include 1.2 million node-hours at NERSC, 600k node-hours on TACC Frontera, 229k node-hours on
Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center Bridges-2, 236k node-hours on San Diego Supercomputing Center (SDSC)
Expanse and 260k node-hours on Purdue Anvil. CMS expects that this model will change for the HL-LHC to
include larger allocations on HPC facilities. The size and locations of future facilities is not fully predictable;
however, CMS would rely on excellent network connectivity to any HPC facility from its Tier-1 and Tier-2
facilities. Current DOE HPC facilities are well-connected to ESnet, while NSF-supported HPC facilities have
excellent connectivity to Internet2. For example, NSF facilities typically take just one or two years from proposal
acceptance to being in production. For more details on this see the HL-LHC case study.

Today, HPC centers funded by DOE and NSF as shared facilities across multiple science domains do not
generally provide the full functionality required from a Tier-2 or Tier-1 center, e.g., they normally do not provide
any substantial amount of storage under the control of the experiment. Data access at HPC centers relies on
either temporarily staging in input data on storage at the HPC site, or streaming access if the site setup allows for
access to the wider network. In general, HPC centers only run compute dominated applications that have modest
IO/CPU requirements, e.g., the central production workflows involved in central processing and simulations.
Output is archived back to the Tier-1 sites, either directly from the application or through other mechanisms.

This infrastructure setup defines the data flows. raw and official datasets flow from the Tier-0 to the Tier-1s for
archival storage. Simulations are produced on all tiers and are transferred from everywhere to the Tier-1s for
archival. Datasets that are needed for input to analysis are distributed across the Tier-1 and Tier-2 disk resources.
The distribution is automatic and follows rules defined by the collaboration. The automatic distribution has
the ability to increase the number of replicas of datasets to allow for more processing resources to have access
to the data, as well as to decrease replication when demand for datasets is decreasing. All disk resources in
CMS are accessible through the AAA federated data access system, implemented via XRootD, and can stream
data to remote applications. CMS production jobs have a typical output rate of 1 Megabyte/sec per processing
hyperthread; compute nodes with 128 Hyperthreads (HT) or more will require more than just a 1 Gbps LAN
connection to the worker nodes. Accordingly, most worker nodes at Tier-1 and Tier-2 are connected at 1 Gbps or
more to their LAN.
