6.10.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
For the purpose of this discussion, CMS distinguish three types of data: Data from collisions in the accelerator,
data from simulations, and user produced data. The first two are centrally produced, while the third is produced
by the physicists themselves as part of their analysis workflow. In the following the three types of data to
illuminate their fundamental differences are described.

6.10.2.5.1 Collision Data
The LHC operates at a typical cadence of three running years, followed by two shutdown years. Within a running
year, collisions start around March to May, and end in November or December. Software releases are prepared
for the beginning of data taking each year. Changes from one year to the next within a running period are
typically more modest than changes from one multiyear running period to the next.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 256

The LHC provides data to CMS in roughly ten-hour data taking periods with minimal downtime (typically a
few hours) between periods. As such, a roughly constant stream of data comes out of the TriDAS, the combined
Trigger and Data Acquisition system. Event rates of around 1 kHz of physics events are typical today and for Run
3, and 7.5 kHz is expected for HL-LHC. Detector level correction (“calibrations”) processes are run within 48
hours to allow for a “prompt reconstruction” to start. Beyond the baseline program, there are also targeted data
taking periods with higher data taking rates. This translates into raw data volumes of:

      • Run 2: 45 PB written during 4 years (2015-2018)
      • Run 3: ~120 PB (2022-2024, as of September 2024)
 • Run 4: 270 PB/yr (Only baseline program as estimated in 2022)
It is important to note that to capture the total CMS data volume or flow, these figures are to be multiplied by
several factors. For example, data are typically processed by multiple software versions, multiple replicas of
important data are kept on disk, and multiple formats for analysis data are provided to researchers.

During the annual running period, bug fixes to the software are introduced into both the online and the prompt
reconstruction. In some years, these changes are significant due to the discovery of features of the CMS detector
that were not expected nor foreseen (i.e., things break occasionally requiring adjustments in software because the
instrument is inaccessible until shutdowns).

Towards the end of the annual running period, a final software release with the best possible calibrations,
alignments and reconstruction methods is prepared, and the entire years’ worth of data are processed a second
time. During the shutdown between two running periods the entire data from that period is then processed one
more time to arrive at a dataset that is as consistent as possible across the three-year running period.

CMS is working to evolve its data processing pipelines to avoid or at least minimize the need for either an end-
of-year reprocessing or a final processing during shutdowns. This has so far been achieved with moderate success
during Run 3, and needs for a full Run 3 (or Run 2 plus Run 3) processing during the long shutdown after Run 3
have not yet been determined.

Data analysis may start at any moment in this cycle, and thus may be performed on any of the three versions of
the collision data. A given version of the data thus has a “lifecycle” from the time it is produced until it is retired.
All centrally produced data are archived in a distributed tape archive across the Tier-0 and the Tier-1 Centers
from the time it becomes available until it is retired. Only raw data and the most-recent reprocessing are archived
forever, and raw data are archived at the Tier-0 and the Tier-1 sites to achieve two physically separated copies.
CMS refers to the last reprocessing as the “legacy” version of the data.

The retirement date is subject to negotiations within the global collaboration with a tension between wanting to
retire data to free tape resources, and wanting to retain versions necessary to support ongoing analyses until they
are accepted for publication.

There are about 50 “data streams” coming out of the TriDAS. These streams are designed to take into account
online trigger decisions and minimize overlaps among streams. The target is to allow at most 10% overall overlap
among all streams, i.e., the sum of all collisions in these streams is no more than 10% larger than the sum of
all collisions exiting the TriDAS. These data streams vary in size by about a factor of 70 from the largest to the
smallest and are sometimes limited in size by offline constraints on per file sizes and luminosity accounting
(which is done in approximately 23 second intervals that must be kept together as one file per data stream to
ensure proper accounting).

In addition, depending on the stability of the detector throughout the annual running period, there may be 5–10
distinct “epochs” within a year. Epochs are typically similar in duration, one or two months, varying by at most
a factor of five in duration. During an epoch, the raw data from a given data stream is transferred consistently to
a particular Tier-1 site for archival purposes. Rebalancing of archival sites happens only at epoch breakpoints.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 257

Multiplying the 50 trigger streams by the 3–5 epochs by the three versions, CMS observes that there are O(500)
unique datasets from collisions for a given year’s data collection. Each of these is managed separately across the
CMS computing infrastructure.

The collaboration has developed two additional data collection modes that allow it to increase the effective trigger
rate without the need for proportionately scaling up the complete computing infrastructure.

 1. The “scouting” stream consists of only properties calculated during the trigger decision and does
 not contain the full information content of all detector hits. It is thus much smaller in size per
 event, allowing many more events to be saved for the same total bandwidth and saved volume of
 data. Therefore, the scouting stream can be written at much higher rates than the physics streams.
 The scouting stream can be stored on minimal disk and tape resources and analyzed directly by
 the collaboration. Reprocessing of scouting stream data is not possible as not enough information
 per event is kept. CMS is commissioning a second type of scouting, in this case based on the first
 level trigger information. This scouting provides data with no trigger selection aside from a minimal
 prescale. Thus, it gives analysts a view at the full 40 MHz data rate of LHC collisions.
 2. In addition to the scouting streams, the collaboration can “park” data produced by the TriDAS
 directly, while skipping the following processing steps. In its design, the raw data are stored on tape
 and recalled at a later time, most commonly in between the running periods when the accelerator
 and detectors are maintained and upgraded. At that point, the full processing is done on these data
 and the output is provided to the collaboration for analysis just like any other data produced by the
 CMS detector. In practice, CMS has used the CERN and Tier-1 resources to process the parked
 data during the prompt reconstruction during Run 3. Parked data significantly increases the total
 tape archiving requirements but has less of an impact on the total computing and storage needs until
 it is processed. In addition, CMS keeps the raw parked data only on tape at the CERN Tier-0 in
 order to minimize the impact it has on the distributed computing system.

6.10.2.5.2 Simulation Data
In addition to data from the detector, CMS has produced simulations that scale in size with the luminosity
collected. The planning assumption is 400 million events per fb-1, however given HPC and other compute
resources available to CMS that are beyond its request, more events are typically produced. Around 100-150
billion events have been produced per year in the run 3 era. For the HL-LHC, it is currently envisioned to
have roughly the same number of simulated events per unit luminosity as currently planned. This means the
number of simulated events will increase considerably. The compute needed to produce a simulated event will
also grow substantially. For this reason, CMS is investigating parameterized and AI/ML-based approaches to
replace some or even most of the simulation production. Simulated data serves all aspects of the CMS scientific
process. Simulations are needed to commission detectors, develop detector calibration and alignment procedures,
design algorithms that define higher-level physics objects from lower-level instrument readings, determine their
efficiency and resolution, and to develop data analysis strategies for obtaining results. A mix of simulation and
carefully designed measurements based on detector data are used to determine the backgrounds to the expected
or hypothesized signal for any given physics analysis. Simulations are thus of central importance to the physics
program of CMS.

In total, CMS has about 70 PB (170 PB) of Run 3 (Run 2) MC simulation datasets stored on tape, representing
around 75 billion (250 billion) MC events. While some intermediate clean up campaigns have taken place, this is
representative of the total four-year production of simulation. Below the parameters that drive the evolution of
data volumes from Run 2 to Run 3 to the HL-LHC are discussed.

As the nature of the known, yet to be detected, and hypothesized new physics processes explored at the LHC
is very diverse, spanning more than ten orders of magnitude of production rate between common and rare
processes, the simulations are correspondingly diverse. This is a fundamental difference between the collision

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 258

data described above and simulations. For collision data the TriDAS decides how datasets are put together, while
for simulations it is the configuration of the physics generator, the software that produces the simulated energy-
momentum four vectors of the particles in an event at or near their point of origin, that determines a dataset. As a
result, there are 10,000 to 20,000 distinct datasets in a typical annual simulation campaign compared to about 50
distinct datasets from the detector. The size of the simulation samples varies by orders of magnitude from roughly
10,000 to 100 million simulated collisions per sample. While 70% of all simulation datasets created for the 2016
data taking era (a typical data taking year during Run2) had fewer than 100,000 collision events in them, 80% of
all the simulated collision events were in datasets with more than 10 million events per dataset.

Simulation data have the same data lifecycle issues for the same reasons as detector data. In fact, CMS typically
produces mostly the same set of physics processes for every software release used in detector data processing.
Simulated samples that correspond to the legacy processing are kept in the archive.

CMS has changed the way it produces most simulation samples in recent years. The simulation process is a
multistep one, where separate applications run different simulation aspects (e.g., physics generator, detector
simulation, digitization, reconstruction). Instead of running each of these on separate worker nodes (or
separate condor jobs) and staging out the results, most CMS simulation is now performed by running a chain of
applications and staging out only the results to be saved for analysis. This has reduced the local and WAN usage
as well as disk requirements for MC production.

6.10.2.5.3 User Data
As they are the starting point of all physics publications, the data collections or “streams” within the centrally
produced CMS data are defined to ease and increase the efficiency of data access for the analyses. A specific
analysis typically uses only a fraction of the events collected by the experiment; it uses only certain data streams,
and only a subset of the objects that characterize the events within those streams that are available from central
production. The first step of most analysis efforts is thus the extraction and formation of user defined datasets
that will become the basis of further analysis. This is most often a massive down select of PBs of official data into
Terabytes of user data. It also often involves a format conversion from formats that are relatively slow to process,
e.g., an event processing rate of a few to 10 Hz per CPU core, to a “custom Ntuple” that is afterwards processed
at multiple kHz. This supports the nature of end-user analysis which is interactive in nature and needs rapid
repetition of making plots and tables.

Until recently, it has been up to the user community to produce and manage their custom “Ntuples.” CMS has
made a first step towards simplifying this process by introducing the NanoAOD, a data format designed for
interactive end-user analysis, and produced centrally. CMS adoption of this format has already grown in Run 3 to
around 50% of analyses using the NanoAOD as their primary data tier. For the HL-LHC era, additional R&D is
being pursued, especially within the context of IRIS-HEP103, to further simplify and streamline this process. For
more details see the HL-LHC use case document.

Managing the disk space to host the user data is only partly within the scope of the global CMS collaboration.
20% of the disk resources pledged to global CMS are for user data, under the assumption that national entities
provide more user disk space to enable the local community. The US exceeds this as detailed below in the
section on Tier-2 facilities. User data are not necessarily registered in the central CMS file catalog, or replicable
via the CMS DMS. Now that CMS has moved to Rucio104 for its data management, it does have the needed
infrastructure support to include user data. However, this has so far been used in only a handful of cases and is
not available for widespread use.

While CERN provides some user analysis CPU resources, member countries are expected to provide the bulk
of these resources for their national communities. The US CMS collaboration chose to place extra resources at
the US CMS Tier-1 facility and Tier-2 centers to support user data and user analysis as described in the Tier-1
103 https://iris-hep.org
104 https://rucio.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 259

and Tier-2 sections below. Each US CMS member institution is nominally assigned to one of the US CMS Tier-2
centers, or the Fermilab LPC (a Tier-3 co-located with the Fermilab Tier-1), for both CPU and disk resources.

6.10.2.5.4 Event Reconstruction and Analysis Data Creation
Figure 6.10.4 summarizes the typical process for going from raw data through to analysis data in CMS (i.e., all the
centrally run production processing steps that are performed).

 Figure 6.10.4: CMS Data Processing Steps

This multistep process differs slightly for data and simulation processing:

 • Prompt reconstruction: 48 hours after a data taking fill, a period used for deriving calibrations,
 CMS makes a first pass through the raw data to derive physics objects from the detailed
 detector information. This process is called reconstruction and happens at CERN on the Tier-0
 facility. The reconstruction produces analysis data which is distributed to Tier-1 and Tier-2 disk
 and Tier-1 tape.

 • Simulation production: Simulated samples are created across the CMS Tier-1 and Tier-2
 facilities as well as through HPC allocations. There are four processing steps: event generation,
 detector simulation, detector digitization and pileup simulation, and then event reconstruction.
 The way this has run in CMS has varied with time. Currently the generator step (which models
 the physics process and produces the particles to be simulated) is run first and saved (a few kB
 per event). The remaining steps are then run on a single compute node sequentially. This node
 reads the generator input, typically by streaming it from the site on which it was generated,
 and produces the analysis data formats. In addition to the event generator input, this process
 reads a second input file for pileup simulation. The pileup samples are pre-generated and
 then read via streaming as part of the digitization process. Currently these samples are 3.7
 (2.7) MB/event for Run 3 (Run 2), and are expected to grow to 13 MB/event for HL-LHC. The
 pileup samples are each 1 PB or more and are thus located only at Fermilab and CERN. The
 event generation, simulation, digitization and reconstruction production chain takes about one
 minute on a typical CPU, so the streaming I/O need is around 60 MB/second/1000 processing
 threads. For HL-LHC, this rate is currently estimated to be reduced given the large increase in
 reconstruction time per event. The simulation production process produces analysis data which
 is distributed to Tier-1 and Tier-2 disk and Tier-1 tape.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 260

 • Re-reconstruction: After final software and detector conditions are derived, CMS reperforms
 the event reconstruction of all data collected during a year. This processing is much like the
 prompt reconstruction; however, it relies on the Tier-1 and Tier-2 facilities instead of the
 Tier-0. raw data must be recalled from tape for this process (currently done by pre-staging
 campaigns to recall the data files from tape and distribute them to appropriate sites). It can also
 be streamed as input (1 MB/event for Run 2 and Run 3 and 6 MB/event for HL-LHC). The
 reconstruction produces analysis data which is distributed to Tier-1 and Tier-2 disk and
 Tier-1 tape.

 • Analysis-format reduction (“MiniAOD” and “NanoAOD” production): As the full event
 reconstruction takes significant resources, CMS has also developed ways to revise its smaller
 analysis formats (MiniAOD and NanoAOD), described below, using information saved in its
 larger analysis formats (as described below). In practice this processing behaves a lot like a
 re-reconstruction in that it requires its input data to be distributed on Tier-1 and Tier-2 disk,
 and analysis data formats are produced as output (however, only a subset of them are produced).
 Outputs are distributed to Tier-1 and Tier-2 disk pools and saved to Tier-1 tape.

6.10.2.5.5 Analysis Data Formats
The centrally produced data from CMS comes in multiple formats ranging from the most versatile and complete
(raw and AOD) to the easiest, smallest, and fastest to use ones (MiniAOD and NanoAOD).

Data resulting from central processing is represented in memory (aside from the NanoAOD format) by objects,
which are made persistent in files for analysis use. Data is represented in a two-dimensional structure, where one
dimension is the collision number (recorded or simulated) and the other dimension are the objects that represent
the information content for each collision. The latter can include the raw data, the simulation output, the lower-
level reconstructed objects such as tracks and jets, and the higher-level reconstructed objects such as electrons,
muons, quark-jets, etc. Persistence of data in CMS is based on the ROOT persistency implementation. CMS
makes extensive use of ROOT’s compression capabilities on storage, and thus data need to be uncompressed
during retrieval.

Data formats differ in the level of detail stored per collision. The table below shows that accordingly, the average
size of the data stored per collision differs by multiple orders of magnitude between raw and NanoAOD. The
HL-LHC numbers are presently largely event size targets, as the actual formats are not yet finalized. The Table
also shows some values for the typical processing time per event.

The use of the various data tiers has evolved considerably over the lifetime of CMS, and is expected to continue
doing so. It has become possible to use more compact event forms for an increasing fraction of the analyses, as
the experiment’s software base and the objects used in analysis matured. Run 1 analyses were primarily based
on AOD samples. MiniAOD (10x smaller) was introduced for Run 2, and is by now well established as the
primary analysis tier, used in about 90% of all analysis activity. MiniAOD includes information on physics objects
sufficient to perform various analysis-specific optimizations, and even development of physics object selections,
but is not sufficiently detailed to redo CPU intensive aspects of the event reconstruction, for example. Physics
analyses for long-lived objects that require specialized tracking algorithms thus need to fall back to AOD. The
standardized physics objects that most analyses use are derived from information in MiniAOD rather than being
stored directly in the MiniAOD format, and may require some fair amount of processing. Typical processing rates
for MiniIAOD today range from a few Hz to a few tens of Hz. The MiniAOD format is optimized to support
remote reading, as well as some partial file access. An analysis executable typically accesses O(10)% of the data in
a MiniAOD file.

NanoAOD was introduced late in Run 2 and has become the most popular data tier for analysis over the last
several years. As shown in the table above is more than an order of magnitude smaller than MiniAOD. Standard
physics objects are pre-computed and stored in a flat columnar format. Processing speeds are thus orders of
magnitudes faster than MiniAOD. This is achieved via a combination of pre-computed standard objects, smaller
event sizes, and more aggressive support of partial file reads.

More than 50% of all physics analysis activities are now based on NanoAOD, with another 40% or more to
be based on MiniAOD. The use of AOD for analysis is relatively minimal given its large footprint, however
it continues to occupy a large part of the CMS disk. At HL-LHC scales, CMS expects not be able to afford to
keep AOD on disk any more, given its size, except as a transit version that is staged from tape for a dedicated
processing application and then removed from disk. In that scenario, access to AOD would require retrieval from
archival storage.

105 For Run 4, this number is scaled down to 270 fb-1/year, according to models with a slower start of HL-LHC operations.

6.10.2.5.6 Data Access
CMS applications and the infrastructure that distributes and launches them support multiple types of data access:

 • Traditional top-down data placement at Tier-1 and Tier-2 centers combined with applications
 specifying the dataset they need, and being automatically routed and executed at the sites
 that have it. In this mode, all data access is local to the site via the site’s LAN. The figure
 below shows the global transfer rate for data set placement by CMS in 2019. Levels of 5 to 6
 Gbpsecond were typical during this non-data taking year.

 • CMS supports streaming data access to any data on disk across its grid facilities from any
 location with an internet connection at any time. This is called AAA, for “Any Data, Anytime,
 Anywhere” within CMS. CMS considers this a reasonable access modality when the application
 requires very little IO per CPU. It is used as part of the centrally organized production at some
 HPC centers simply because simulation, digitization, and reconstruction are all very CPU
 intensive, leading to small IO/CPU ratios. It is also used as a failover when the storage at a site
 is down while jobs are still running.

 • Bottom-up data placement, as is implicit in caching. Here the applications are routed to sites
 with caches, applications access the cache locally, and cache misses are handled by the CMS
 XRootD Data Federation (also referred to as the AAA federation). CMS allows access in this
 fashion for all the MiniAOD and NanoAOD formats, but neither AOD nor raw. raw is only on
 tape, and AOD is only accessible via top-down placement. Caching is expected to become the
 dominant data access for end users of MiniAOD and NanoAOD formats. Use of caches has
 also proven to be of benefit to overall CMS application performance when compared to the
 otherwise mixed system of on-prem data and remote access patterns for CMS applications.

 Figure 6.10.5: 2023 statistics for data set transfers in CMS for all sites globally

As a consequence, central production workflows use top-down data access and streaming access for workflows
that have a very small data to CPU ratio. Caching access is not (yet) used in central production except in a few
sites (specifically Caltech and UCSD in the US).

Managing data access and data distribution for a distributed storage system is different from a system with one or
a handful of sites. One challenge faced by CMS is the need to keep the available disk of each of the O(50) Tier-2
facilities full of useful data that analysts want. CMS has adopted Rucio to help manage these data. Rucio allows
both production teams and users to define rules for retaining data on disk, and on specific sites, for specified time
periods. Data not retained by any specific rule can be removed from disk as needed to make room for new data.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 263

Unlike 2020, CMS does not have a dynamic DMS that attempts to replicate data as needed for running jobs. With
Rucio such a system has proven not to be needed. As a result, 2023 data transfers are globally less than those in
2020 despite a considerable increase in Run 3 data rates.

User data may be accessed through any of these modalities, although as user data are most often Ntuples that
are by design very fast to analyze, it is unlikely to be streamed. In addition, some users reduce the size of their
ntuples to something small enough such that it can be taken outside the CMS computing infrastructure, onto
solid-state drives (SSDs) in laptops, or single standalone servers in people’s offices or departmental server rooms.

6.10.2.5.7 Analysis Group and Researcher Workflows
So far this section has focused primarily on the extensive central production system of CMS. In addition to this,
an average of about 50,000 cores across Tier-1 and Tier-2 facilities (e.g., 25% of the CMS CPU resource) are used
by individual researchers or research groups for data analysis and other compute-intensive work. CMS does not
place significant restrictions on the methods and tools used for analysis; and as such, groups have different ways
of doing their work. One workflow that will be common for Run 3 analysis work is shown in this Figure 6.10.6:

 Figure 6.10.6: CMS Analysis Workflow Example
Here, data in either MiniAOD or NanoAOD format from the production system are used as input to the analysis
workflow. Analysts then reduce these data by removing (aka skimming) events that are deemed uninteresting for
the specific physics processes being studied, and by saving only the information in the original data format that is
needed for further processing steps. These further processing steps are then performed outside of the distributed
computing system, in many cases by transferring data sets to local clusters or other nearby computing systems
where interactive access is possible.

Local compute access and smaller data formats provide a more interactive environment for researchers to
evaluate different approaches, create proper graphical representations of their data, perform systematic studies,
and to derive results. This is typically a many step process, with different codes being used through the process.
A challenge for CMS through the HL-LHC is to provide researchers with tools that both enable this interactive
research at a much larger volume of data, but also to reduce the need for intermediate processing steps that
currently consume significant storage and compute resources. R&D on this style of “Analysis Facility” is
currently quite advanced. Several US-based facility prototypes are available for users, including collocated with
the Nebraska and Purdue Tier-2 and at Fermilab (EAF). One essential aspect of AFs will be excellent data I/O
achieved by caching, fast disks and other approaches.

6.10.2.6 Remote Science Activities
CMS relies on a fully distributed computing system. In that sense, nearly all scientific activities are remote in
nature. The use and evolution of these resources are described in the previous sections. As all science in CMS is
remote, the use of HPC is by no means special in its remoteness.

Having reliable mechanisms to transfer data into HPC facilities from the CMS Tier-1 and Tier-2 centers is of
growing importance. HPCs are different from other resources used by CMS primarily because they provide
significant compute (CPU and GPU) resources but very limited disk resources, and because network access to

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 264

or from HPC compute nodes is typically limited or not allowed. CMS106 and the broader LHC community107
have considered how to best utilize these resources within operational constraints. Unlike most HPC users,
CMS cannot concentrate its efforts on using one or a handful of HPC facilities, but is instead asked to use HPC
facilities worldwide. Network access and data management are important aspects of this.

Today, the common solution found by CMS to use US HPCs is to stream any input data via XRootD/AAA. For
MC production, the biggest piece of this is the premixing library data which is 3.7 MB for about 60 CPU seconds
of processing per hyperthread, or about 0.5 MB/s for a typical eight-core MC job. This implies about 4 Gbps per
10000 cores on average at full application efficiency.

6.10.2.7 Software Infrastructure
The CMS data management software tools are more completely described in case study 12 on infrastructure
and tools.

To first approximation, there are four sources of data transfers of CMS data:

 • Bulk transfers due to top-down placement.
 • Output handling from analysis or central processing workflows.
 • XCache fetching data to handle cache misses.
 • Streaming data via XRootD protocol from remote servers to applications.
The first two use cases use CMS-developed tools that sit on top of FTS108, which is standard across the CERN
community. The last two use cases use the XRootD protocol.109

FTS to manage scheduling and file transfer. For bulk transfers, CMS currently uses Rucio110, having fully
switched from its previous system based on PhEDEx and Dynamo tools, to manage dataset storage and dataset
transfers (while still relying on FTS underneath). Rucio has become a community solution for data management.

For bulk transfers via Rucio and executed by FTS, US CMS has moved to TPC https implemented via XRootD
servers and away from gridFTP. Sites typically have multiple such servers that each provide 10 Gbps, and all have
access to the same filesystem. Large bandwidth transfers are thus accomplished by orchestrating very many flows
across many servers.

Data streaming uses the XRootD protocol to optimally support partial file reads. XCache handles immediate data
transfers, and also uses the XRootD protocol, to refresh the target cache following a cache miss. This is handled
so as to minimize latency and thus minimize idle CPU when cache misses occur. The XCache server invokes an
XRootD client that initially fetches only the vector of bytes requested by the application, and then later fills in the
rest of the file when the server is not too busy. While of course limited by cache size, the CMS experience is that
it is better to use even a cold XCache than to do remote reads in many cases (in part due to reliability of reading).

New concepts of caching are currently being established in CMS. A cache provides access to all or a subset of the
official CMS data or user data without the need for organized data movement. The AAA federation is providing
data access for the caches. Caches at the level of hundreds of TB up to a few PB are currently in place at Caltech
and UCSD. These have remained approximately the same size during Run 3 as was anticipated given the planned
Run 3 CMS data volumes.

106 https://cds.cern.ch/record/2707936/files/NOTE2020_002.pdf
107 https://zenodo.org/record/3647548
108 https://fts.web.cern.ch
109 https://xrootd.slac.stanford.edu
110 https://rucio.readthedocs.io/en/latest

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 265

To account for the complete set of all transfers it is thus sufficient to instrument and monitor XRootD and
FTS within the overall transfer software stack. CMS has recently completed an analysis of the accuracy of
the monitoring tools for both of these, and have found issues with both. CMS has started a program of work
to improve the monitoring capabilities of both in order to arrive at reliable accounting of data transfers. It is
expected this will be completed, including deployment on at least the US Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites, towards the end
of 2021.

Fully instrumented XRootD software for both the HTTPS and XRootD protocols provides some redundancy
in accounting as FTS uses HTTPS as implemented via XRootD servers at all US CMS Tier-2s. It is expected
to be useful to achieve long-term reliable accounting of transfers together with the perfSONAR updates done
at all sites leading up to the recent DC24 challenge. Moreover, FTS accounting allows transfer accounting per
end-to-end link, while XRootD servers at both source and destination will have accounting for their outgoing and
incoming traffic. CMS believes that continuing joint work with ESnet staff to regularly exchange network usage
accounting information will continue to be important now that these monitoring improvements have been put
in place.

CMS also relies on high availability for software distribution and distribution of detector conditions and
calibration data to production and analysis applications. To avoid redundant data transfers, CMS uses a squid-
caching system, built around Frontier111 for distributed database caching, and CVMFS112 for efficient global
distribution of software.

6.10.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
6.10.2.8.1 The US CMS Tier-1
The US CMS Tier-1 Center at Fermilab is the largest of CMS Tier-1 facilities, currently providing 40% of the
total CMS Tier-1 capacity. The Fermilab Tier-1 consists of dedicated computing infrastructure, which includes:

 • 370 kHS23 growing to 520 kHS23 in 2025 (approximately 40k CPU cores) of compute nodes
 • 48.8 PB growing to 63 PB of dCache distributed disk storage
 • 152 PB growing to 178 PB of archival tape storage capacity that will soon be run by CTA (in
 addition there is a separate tape archive for the CMS Heavy Ion data).
The CMS facility also supports the LHC Physics Center analysis facility, supporting several hundred physicists
with interactive computing nodes, an additional 5000 cores of batch compute, and about 9 PB of distributed
EOS storage.

The US CMS Tier-1’s local network infrastructure consists of fully redundant, high-performance switching fabric
distributed across multiple Fermilab data centers. That switching fabric has the following characteristics:

 • Currently based on 400GE network technology for inter-switch connectivity, with 10GE and
 100GE connectivity available for host system connectivity.

 • Extensive use of link aggregation (LAG) to scale bandwidth for inter-switch connectivity. At
 the present time, the US CMS Tier-1 LAN provides approximately 10Tb/s of network capacity
 in total.

 • PBR techniques to route CMS high volume traffic over special purpose networks (such as
 LHCOPN, LHCONE) utilized for WAN data movement.
Fermilab’s WAN architecture is based on separating its high-impact science data traffic from its general internet
traffic. Conceptually, this design is analogous to a Science DMZ architecture. Most traffic into and out of the
US CMS T1 is via the science data path(s). For CMS, those science data paths mean the LHCOPN, LHCONE,

111 http://frontier.cern.ch
112 https://cernvm.cern.ch/portal/filesystem

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 266

and end-to-end OSCARS circuits. Fermilab’s LHCOPN connectivity supports movement of raw data from
the T0 (CERN), as well as production data movement with some of the other CMS T1s. Fermilab’s LHCOPN
configuration consists of three OSCARS circuits (primary, secondary, and tertiary) to CERN, which provide
levels of redundancy with differing bandwidth guarantees for that traffic. LHCONE supports production data
movement between the Fermilab Tier-1 and most CMS Tier-2s, as well as CMS T1s that do not use LHCOPN for
T1-T1 data movement. Like the LHCOPN, connectivity to LHCONE is via geographically redundant (primary/
failover) paths. US CMS Tier-1 WAN traffic that does not utilize either the LHCOPN or LHCONE paths
traverses the Laboratory’s general internet path.

In terms of aggregate WAN capacity out of the site, Fermilab currently has provisioned 2.4Tb/s of link capacity
to ESnet, via geographically diverse connections. A LAG of four 400 Gbps links is used to support the science
data network paths, including LHCOPN and LHCONE. A second 2 x 400 Gbps LAG supports the Laboratory’s
general internet traffic, which includes some portion of science traffic, for example, CMS traffic to/from sites not
connected to LHCONE.

Future network enhancements:

 • Upgrade of the US CMS Tier-1 LAN infrastructure to 800GE technology is expected for
           2028–2030 time frame;

 • Upgrade of the Laboratory network perimeter infrastructure to 800GE technology is
 expected also in 2028 - 2030 time frame, likely to be aligned with availability of 800GE
 services from ESnet;

 • In 2026–2028 time frame, additional WAN capacity to ESnet will be implemented in the
 form of additional 400GE links. The 2 x 400GE general internet connection is expected to be
 upgraded to 4 x 400GE prior to the start of Run 4.

6.10.2.8.2 The US CMS Tier-2s
Current experience at US Tier-2 facilities suggests the following level of network use for various
infrastructure components:

 • FTS transfers to and from the site: 3–5 Gbps spread across a number of servers (e.g., 10 at a
 typical site).

 • I/O from compute nodes: 1.5 Mbps per thread, corresponding to an average of 40 Gbit/s at a
 current Tier-2 site.

 • XCache servers: 2 Gbps (in or out) per server. As an example, Caltech maintains 2 PB over 2
 cache servers.

 • Squids (for CVMFS content): 100 Mbps/squid. Each site runs at least two squids.
 • HTCondor gatekeepers: 2M bps/s per gatekeeper. Sites typically have three gatekeepers.
 • Other traffic: up to 1 Gbit/s for user interactive access, monitoring, sync with user’s desktops
 and laptops, etc.
CMS has a LAN requirement of 1 Megabyte/HT, i.e., nodes with 128 Hyperthreads (HT) and more will require
more than just a single 1 Gbps LAN connection to the worker nodes. Accordingly, most worker nodes at Tier-1
and Tier-2 are connected at 1 Gbps or more to their LAN. Different centers have networking hardware from
different vendors, and LAN aggregations, ranging from cluster-wide large Cisco gear to ToR switches that are
aggregated into cluster switches via multiple 10 Gbps links. Generally, much of the LAN and WAN networking
infrastructure to and within a Tier-2 site has been an institutional contribution to the US CMS Operations
Program, i.e., it has not for the most part been directly funded by the program.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 267

The Tier-2 LAN is then typically connected up to the University border switch routers via either one or more
100 Gbps links or with 400 Gbps links. Depending on location, this campus network connectivity may be shared
with others. Most sites then share their outgoing connection with other Science DMZ customers on campus.
Most sites have a regional network that must be traversed before connecting to ESnet. In all cases, that regional
network is shared with others. Thus, actual usable bandwidth to get to ESnet is generally less, and will vary over
time depending on other activities.

Figure 6.10.7 shows the ESnet network map as available on the ESnet website with the US CMS HEP Tier-1 and
Tier-2 sites overlaid. Not shown is the Vanderbilt Tier-2 as it is dedicated to Heavy Ion physics, and participated
in the nuclear physics ESnet requirements process in 2024.

 Figure 6.10.7: ESnet network map with US CMS Tier-1 (“T1”) and Tier-2 (“T2”) centers overlaid.
All Tier-2 sites are roughly the same in terms of CPU and storage capacity, and should thus be thought of as
having roughly the same networking requirements. Based on this map, CMS can identify specific links that could
be used to estimate the growth in networking as a function of time:

 • SALT - ECHO: Covers the ESnet bandwidth from UCSD and Caltech to all other Tier-2s
 and Fermilab, assuming that traffic from Southern California to the East Coast and Midwest is
 routed via this link.

 • KANS - STLO: Adds traffic from University of Nebraska-Lincoln (UNL) to Caltech and UCSD
 on its way east.

 • BOST - ALBA: Traffic to and from MIT west should travel this route.
 • JACK - ATLA: Traffic from and to University of Florida Tier-2 should travel this route.
Wisconsin and Purdue connect to ESnet at Starlight at 100 Gbps without traversing ESnet. There are thus no
obvious ESnet links to characterize traffic from these two sites. The networking for the US Tier-2 facilities is

US CMS delegates network performance measurement collection to OSG, and expects to continue to do so. At

was recently carried out as part of the recent DC24 data challenge. Sites have 100 Gbps, and most sites updated
their perfSONAR and DTNs.

6.10.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.10.2.9.1 Cloud Services
CMS does not currently use cloud resources to any significant extent. Previous studies have shown them to be
a more costly model than the owned-resource model that CMS currently relies on. A notable exception would
be the case of needed resource bursts for either CPU or network. The resources available for either CPU or TA
networking in the cloud far exceed those available to CMS. At this point, CMS tools are generally able to use
cloud services, typically via infrastructure at one of the tiered sites, but CMS does not have plans to use cloud
services extensively in the near or longer term. This can evolve depending on largely external factors (e.g., cost
evolution, or government policies).

One specific use case is the SONIC approach which enables the use of a remote (on-prem or off-prem)
accelerator resource by CMS applications. SONIC is an interesting way to adopt GPUs as it allows workers to
share a set of GPUs which can then load-balance ML models (and other GPU kernels). Data access is a clear issue
for models with large inputs (e.g., tracking applications).

6.10.2.9.2 AI and ML
As elsewhere in scientific pursuits, CMS has an increasing use of AI/ML in its production workflows. Analysis
use cases have evolved even more quickly as there is greater freedom to adopt new toolkits and approaches. Both
the Fermilab Tier-1 and Tier-2 facilities have GPU capabilities for CMS use, and the CMS community also relies
on national resources such as NRP. CMS is also researching a dedicated AI/ML training facility (at Vanderbilt)
in recognition that AI/ML brings two distinct use cases, training and inference, that both require substantial
resources (but in differing access patterns).

CMS expects to predominantly use on-site and HPC resources rather than commercial cloud. As described just
above, SONIC is one important access pattern that CMS expects for AI/ML. SONIC facilitates both on-prem
and remote GPU usage, potentially with considerable LAN/WAN requirements. As of today, these are difficult to
estimate as CMS is still in the process of R&D towards production use cases for SONIC.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 269

6.10.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
CMS does not have any work or plans in this area.

6.10.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
Several examples of resource constraints or perceived resource constraints for CMS researchers and their science
are present:

 • CMS data volume limitations: The data volume that can be handled by the networks within and
 coming out of the CMS detector facility far exceeds what can be handled offline within current
 CPU, storage and networking infrastructures.

 • TA link: CMS is currently a major user of the TA network link. Activities including the archival
 of raw data, initial copies of analysis data samples, and user-derived data sets using CERN or
 other non-US facilities are clear use cases for TA network usage. The raw data transferred to
 Fermilab alone are expected to average more than 10 Gbpsecond during HL-LHC operations.
 Today the raw data are a small part of the TA network usage by CMS. Indeed, while data rates
 have increased considerably during Run 3, the TA link traffic from FTS transfers inbound to
 the US CMS sites has not changed substantially from the end of Run 2 data taking (contrary to
 the concerns from the 2020 ESnet case study). CMS tools do not prioritize site proximity (in the
 networking sense) when scheduling data transfers. Streaming data across the TA link is allowed
 (even if discouraged).

 • Streaming reliability: Failures in data streaming are a large source of job failures in CMS.
 This has also become an issue for analysis-facing activities, where a greater variety of tools are
 used to access CMS data. While CMS can instrument its centrally maintained software with
 retry mechanisms and other fallback logic, it is more difficult to extend this to community-
 developed tools.

 • Streaming to sites beyond the CMS infrastructure: Reliable and high-capacity streaming of
 input data, either raw or pileup simulation considerably reduces the disk requirements of CMS
 at HPC and other nondedicated computing facilities.

 • Disk vs. network trade-offs: As is the case with HPCs, reliable networking can be used to
 reduce disk replica requirements either by the use of tape recall or caching. By the end of Run
 4, a copy of the entire CMS MiniAOD will be around 100 PB. If 10% of this is used during
 any given month in a caching system, one can estimate the need for 10 PB/month of transfers
 to keep the cache up to date with the most recently used data. Cache network needs will be
 typically bursty because users read full data sets rather than just a file or two from one. This
 suggests that aggregate network measures are a poor metric in this use case. Understanding
 and expanding caching use cases and needs are part of ongoing R&D. Recent focus has been on
 analysis facility use cases that have become increasingly important.

6.10.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
CMS does not currently use Globus or other endpoints for data sharing. There is ongoing R&D in the Pelican
project to allow direct transfers from XRootD Rucio Storage Element (RSE) (the software CMS sites utilize) to
Globus RSE. This would imply CMS would benefit without needing doing anything with Globus directly, and
without having the operational overheads of multi-hop transfers.

6.10.2.12 Outstanding Issues
Traditionally, the LHC community has treated the network as a free and infinite resource. As the community
prepares for the “Exabyte per year” era of the HL-LHC, it is envisioned to both make more aggressive use of the
network, and account and manage usage much more carefully:

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 270

 • Via the R&D activities in caching, it is expected to be in a position to trade investments into
 disk space at Tier-2s against network utilization in the long term. Other forces may also push in
 the direction of higher network requirements, such as how spinning disk technology evolves in
 terms of cost per terabyte and I/O capabilities relative to CMS needs.

 • CMS would like to develop a program to test the effectiveness of transfers both to benchmark
 methods at increased capacity, and integrate new functionality into existing tools. Such tests
 should be done in collaboration with ESnet. For example, one lesson learned from the most-
 recent data challenge organized by WLCG (DC24) was that it is necessary to utilize a link at full
 capacity, to learn if a given link has any performance abnormalities. It is desirable to develop a
 process of regular testing of network capacities (e.g., relying on perfSONAR) to test connections
 to the maximum and identify problems before they become a bottleneck in production.

 • Traditionally, CMS has treated the global network of CMS sites as a mesh with identical links
 when it comes to bulk transfers. The XRootD data federation was designed from the beginning
 to be cognizant of the TA link being limited, but treated links within the US as identical. The
 Data Lake model currently discussed in WLCG makes clear regional distinctions. Data Lake
 concepts have progressed slowly due to challenges around how increased latency affects
 application performance. However, it is expected that at least the existence of the Atlantic is
 likely to become an architectural feature of the data distribution architecture.

 • CMS would like to continue exploring with ESnet how to contribute towards global R&D
 projects such as the Global P4 Lab testbed, use of ESnet High Touch services, and evolving
 technologies such as Smart NICs.

 • The next several years are critical to transition managed network R&D, including results of the
 SENSE project, into production for CMS in time for HL-LHC. The SENSE and Caltech +
 UCSD teams are close to 400G throughput with production infrastructure using XRootD, FTS
 and XRootD.

 • CMS believes that national and international collaboration bringing together researchers, data
 management experts and networking experts is important for making better use of network
 resources as usage levels of research networks increase. In HEP, forums for these collaborations
 include the WLCG Networking Throughput WG, or more broadly groups including the Global
 Network Advancement Group.

6.11 LHC: LHC Operations
The experiments running at the LHC are exploring the fundamental structure of matter and the forces that
govern their interaction. The two main general-purpose collaborations at the LHC are ATLAS and CMS and
both collaborations have thousands of collaborators distributed around the globe who require access to the data
generated by their detectors at CERN and to simulated data generated at sites around the world.

6.11.1 Discussion Summary
A paper was published after DC24113 with a number of findings. The LHC collaborators’ DC24 activity revealed
several weaknesses in the software stack, namely with the way that FTS performed globally when faced with
bottlenecks at certain locations. The discussion in CMS about the use of alternative data formats, and the use
of other R&D efforts such as Caching may also influence how much bandwidth is needed between facilities,
with the TA links in particular being a main focus area. ESnet’s TA strategy has not changed substantially since
the previous HEP review, and will continue to add capacity (mainly through the use of more flexible spectrum
agreements, and sharing resources with others partners like GÉANT across multiple connections).

A final observation from the LHC collaborators’ DC24 activity was that WLCG’s hardware choices for the next
major cycles will have a huge influence on the performance of the overall computation and storage system. Since
funding requests have to be made in advance, and hardware choice and prices fluctuate, there is uncertainty
about what capabilities may exist. As a result of this, there will be a series of mini-DC activities that occur on a
regular basis to evaluate aspects of the ecosystem: computing, storage, software, and networking, culminating in
the larger complete DC activities that focus on major goal milestones. ESnet can assist with mini-DC activities
when needed, specifically by making resources like perfSONAR and ESnet High Touch available to assist with
traffic generation and results gathering.

Networking support at BNL and Fermilab, to support the ATLAS and CMS Tier-1 computing facilities,
respectively, has increased and is approaching an aggregate of 1Tbps through all connectivity. Both sites are
exploring ways to move toward 800Gbbps native connections in the coming years, when the technology is ready
to be supported.

One last positive impact of the DC24 activity, that is not fully planned for within the next DC, will be a full
analysis of the results and ways to both capture and act on these data in near-real time. A data analysis will be
needed, and this effort should begin the process of evaluating each link in the ecosystem and ways that both LHC
monitoring data, and that from ESnet, can be captured and used to evaluate overall system performance.

ESnet will continue to work with the LHC community on co-design efforts like SENSE and Rucio, SciTags,
and other potential opportunities. The experiments do need to be specific in what they are hoping to achieve,
however. The aim of joint projects could be to “co-design” an effective system that makes best use of the
available network resources, coordinated with the site resources, and manage joint site and network operations
cooperatively. This needs to be spelled out in more detail, and discussed with ESnet leadership.

 • The LHC schedule has operating periods (called “runs”) interspersed with maintenance and
 upgrade periods (called “long shutdowns”). The first run of the LHC was 2009-2012 followed by
 long shutdown 1 (LS1) from 2012-2014. The second run (Run 2) was from 2014-2018, followed
 by LS2 from 2019-2021. Run 3 has started in 2022 and will continue until 2026. The LHC will
 be upgraded to increase its luminosity during LS3, from 2026 to 2029. The new accelerator,
 HL-LHC will start producing collisions in Run 4 in 2030. ATLAS and CMS are expected to
 produce 10 times more data compared to Run 3. [Section 4.1]

 • The collaborators involved with LHC operations are the four main LHC experiments (ALICE,
 ATLAS, CMS and LHCb) as well as the technical teams running the accelerator and the
 globally distributed middleware (OSG, EGI, Rucio, perfSONAR, FTS, etc.) and infrastructures
 (the various Tier-x sites) supporting the activities of the experiments. [Section 4.1]

 • LHC Run 3 will be completed by the end of 2026 and it is expected that the network traffic will
 keep growing at the usual rate until then. In the latest years, the LHC community has seen an
 annual increase of 20-30% of traffic in LHCOPN and LHCONE, the two networks dedicated to
 transfers between WLCG sites. The current networking capacities are typically 100 Gbps WAN
 links, with many sites already having resilience (multiple) 100 Gbps connections. This will need
 to evolve as the LHC community prepares for Run 4. The expected traffic during Run 4 beyond
 2030, when the HL-LHC will come into operation, will significantly increase. ATLAS and CMS
 have estimated this increase in network traffic to be a factor of 10 compared to Run3.
           [Section 4.2]

 • All Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites are expected to have perfSONAR nodes deployed to monitor network
 performance. These nodes are integrated into a mesh configuration, enabling regular tests such
 as latency and bandwidth checks between sites. perfSONAR allows network administrators to
 identify potential network issues that could impact data transfer rates, both intersite and with
 CERN. It plays a vital role in the global transfer of data across the LCG. [Section 4.3]

 • Monitoring for CERN IT Data Centre and WLCG Infrastructure (MONIT) is CERN’s
 scalable, central monitoring system that aggregates, stores, and analyzes monitoring data from
 multiple sources across the LHC experiments. It provides a unified interface for monitoring
 the infrastructure, including network performance, storage, and computing resources. MONIT
 gathers data from various monitoring tools (e.g., perfSONAR, FTS, XRootD, and custom storage
 monitoring systems) deployed across all Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites. [Section 4.3]

 • The WLCG collects resources worldwide and enables their usage by the LHC experiments
 as a distributed computing facility. The mission of the WLCG project is to provide global
 computing resources to store, distribute and analyze the ~50-70 PB of data expected every
 year of operations from the LHC at CERN. WLCG is coordinated by CERN. It is managed and
 operated by a worldwide collaboration between the experiments (ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and
 LHCb) and the participating computer centers. [Section 4.4]

 • In terms of aggregate WAN capacity out of the site, CMS Tier-1 (Fermilab) currently has
 provisioned 2.4Tb/s of link capacity to ESnet, via geographically diverse connections. A LAG
 of four 400 Gbps links is used to support the science data network paths, including LHCOPN
 and LHCONE. A second 2 x 400 Gbps LAG supports the Laboratory’s general internet traffic,
 which includes some portion of science traffic, for example, CMS traffic to/from sites not
 connected to LHCONE. [Section 4.7]

 • BNL has two path-diverse 800 Gbps (2 x 400 GbE) circuits that peer with ESnet routers within
 their 515 and 725 data centers. These circuits are utilized by all scientific and administrative
 communities at BNL. All traffic to and from BNL flows through either of these circuits.
           [Section 4.7]

 • SENSE (SDN for End-to-End Networked Science at the Exascale) uses SDN to dynamically
 manage network paths, prioritize traffic, and provide optimized routing. This setup is ideal
 for data-intensive tasks, as it can allocate resources in real-time based on network conditions
 and experimental priorities. Rucio, developed by CERN, complements SENSE by managing
 large-scale data distribution across the network. Its features include automated data replication,
 strategic data placement, and support for geographically distributed resources, which streamline
 the movement and availability of critical datasets. The CMS & ATLAS experiments, in
 collaboration with ESnet, are integrating the SENSE/Rucio architecture to improve its network
 management and data transfer capabilities. [Section 4.8]

 • ATLAS and CMS are exploring advanced techniques for improving data transfer and monitoring
 capabilities across the WLCG. New technologies such as SciTags and packet marking are being
 tested and deployed to enhance network monitoring, traffic differentiation, and optimized data
 flow across high-speed networks. The deployment of SciTags and packet marking is in progress
 across several sites, which will lead to better traffic differentiation and resource management
 across the network. [Section 4.8]

 • Many of the LHC experiments have explored cloud services and are using them as part of their
 global set of resources. There are two primary modes of operation envisioned: [Section 4.8]

 ° A particular site contracts with a cloud provider and resources are (transparently) added as
 part of the site from their experiment’s perspective.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 274

 ° A new site is created within a cloud provider, utilizing the various provisioning,
 management and resilient infrastructure available. However, this option not feasible for the
 following reasons:

 • The entity setting up a site within a cloud provider needs to be able to control costs to
 make it feasible, but there are not usually policies and tools to allow them to do so.

 • Egress charges from cloud providers are usually expensive and may vary depending
 upon where the egress goes to.

 • Connecting to resources like LHCONE is very challenging because of the AUP
 requirement that all traffic from the advertised subnets for LHCONE must be
 LHC related.

 • Globally, many funding agencies are responsible for both HPCs and WLCG experiments and
 a natural outcome is to try to support WLCG needs via HPCs. As an example, Germany has
 consolidated many of its Tier-2 sites into a new HPC allocation. For the US, it would be very
 beneficial for the DOE HPC facilities to become “standardized,” allowing collaborations to
 utilize resources without having to dedicate approximately 0.25 FTE to operate things on a
 bespoke basis. Without something like IRI driving this uniform interface, the experiments
 are also forced to engage with each HPC as it is designed to help ensure it is usable for that
 experiment. [Section 4.9]

 • One place that R&E networks could help would be in jointly negotiating with various cloud
 providers to create a template contract they would support no egress charges if the R&E
 providers bring high-bandwidth links to the cloud providers, as well as defining policies and
 associated tools to allow LHC site creators to manage costs by, for example, controlling how data
 flows to only use the zero ( or low cost ) egress connections globally. [Section 5.7]

 • The HL-LHC requirements for LHCOPN links approach 1 Tbps and has pushed sites to
 explore more affordable technologies to achieve it. IT-INFN-CNAF, the Italian Tier-1, has
 deployed a pilot connection using DCI equipment at the Tier-1 (CNAF) and Tier-0 (CERN)
 sites, which use four light channels on the dark-fibers of two different providers, GÉANT and
 GARR. The solution can provide 4 x 400 Gbps link for a total of 1.6 Tbps. Spectrum Sharing

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 275

 is achieved by interconnecting the ROADM device of the two providers. It saves on the cost
 of more expensive router interfaces, since most of the existing LHCOPN links are provided as
 MPLS Layer 2 virtual circuits. [Section 5.7]

 • During the 2020-2021 studies of LHC network requirements, the LHC experiments estimated
 that Tier-1 centers would need terabit/sec connections and Tier-2 sites would require 400G
 connections. That was driven by estimates of some (but not all) data-related operations of
 CMS and ATLAS, leading to an estimated bandwidth need of 4.8 terabits/sec (Tbps) across
 the Atlantic for CMS and ATLAS alone in a so-called “minimal model” and 9.6 Tbps in a more
 “flexible” and realistic model. [Section 5.7]

 • As of 2024, multiple 400G connections have been installed to the Fermilab and Brookhaven
 national labs as well as HPC facilities used by HEP, and the upgrades to 400G (or N X 400G)
 at some US CMS campuses are either in place or imminent. As mentioned above, 400G-scale
 operations in production mode are already being demonstrated, and are expected to be available
 in the mass market before HL-LHC startup in 2030. [Section 5.7]

 • It is expected that all the major Tier-1s to have at least 800 Gbps LHCOPN links at the start
 of Run 4 with the ability to grow to 1.2 Tbps or even 1.6 Tbps during the Run. Tier-1s should
 also have an equivalent amount of bandwidth to LHCONE to serve Tier-2s. Details of the
 networking for ATLAS and CMS are in the experiment specific case studies (#9 and #10
 respectively). [Section 5.7]

 • For LHC experiments in general the resource requirements are growing beyond what flat
 budgets can support. This leads the experiments to work very hard at optimizing their data
 and analysis processes to maximize what the available resources can do. Various trade-offs are
 continually being explored (network use vs multiple replicas of data, data format changes vs
 number of required datasets to meet various needs, exploitation of nonstandard computing
 capacity, reconstructing data on demands vs storing it), to try to achieve the time to science
 target with constrained resources. [Section 5.8]

 • Because of recent changes to technology drivers, the evolution of ATLAS and CMS’s “process
 of science”, and the outlook for 2030 when the HL-LHC era will begin, it appears that the
 actual networking requirements may be somewhat larger than foreseen during the 2020 HEP
 Requirements Review. Detailed projections are difficult at this point, but should be tracked
 and updated every two years or so to make quantitative estimates and (re-)establish the
 requirements in both network capacity and capability. [Section 5.8]

6.11.2 LHC Operations: Profile
The LHC schedule has operating periods (called “runs”) interspersed with maintenance and upgrade periods
(called “long shutdowns”). The first run of the LHC was 2009-2012 followed by long shutdown 1 (LS1) from
2012-2014. The second run (Run 2) was from 2014-2018, followed by LS2 from 2019-2021. Run 3 has started in
2022 and will continue until 2026.

6.11.2.1 Science Background
The LHC will be upgraded to increase its luminosity during LS3, from 2026 to 2029. The new accelerator,
HL-LHC will start producing collisions in Run 4 in 2030. ATLAS and CMS are expected to produce 10 times
more data compared to Run 3. It is important to note that each succeeding run significantly increases the amount
and complexity of the data generated, requiring increased storage, network and compute capacity to
successfully exploit.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 276

6.11.2.2 Collaborators
The collaborators involved with LHC operations are the four main LHC experiments (ALICE, ATLAS, CMS
and LHCb) as well as the technical teams running the accelerator and the globally distributed middleware (OSG,
EGI, Rucio, perfSONAR, FTS, etc.) and infrastructures (the various Tier-x sites) supporting the activities of the
experiments. Sections 6.9 and 6.10 should provide the details for each collaboration’s process of science, specifics
of data volumes, and internalized hardware and software infrastructure.

6.11.2.3 IRI Readiness
For LHC operations, the use of either pledged or opportunistic HPC resources is currently very difficult because
each HPC is “special” in terms of hardware, network access, storage policies and job submission. This means
each experiment using such facilities needs to dedicate significant resources to operating and maintaining the
HPC for their use case.

However, ATLAS and CMS are the top two users of the NERSC CPU partition, on track to use over 2 million
node-hours between them. Since each HPC is special, HEP experiments have developed in-house mechanisms
like HEPCloud and Harvester to manage access to disparate resources. Therefore, the LHC community would
greatly benefit from a unified security model across DOE (and NSF) HPC facilities and a unified resource
brokering API.

Globally, many funding agencies are responsible for both HPCs and WLCG experiments and a natural outcome
is to try to support WLCG needs via HPCs. As an example, Germany has consolidated many of its Tier-2 sites
into a new HPC allocation. For the US, it would be very beneficial for the DOE HPC facilities to become
“standardized,” allowing collaborations to utilize resources without having to dedicate approximately 0.25 FTE to
operate things on a bespoke basis. Without something like IRI driving this uniform interface, the experiments are
also forced to engage with each HPC as it is designed to help ensure it is usable for that experiment.

6.11.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
6.11.2.4.1 LHC
The LHC collides protons more than a billion times every second, out of which each experiment selects
interesting collisions for recording at a variable rate, depending upon the triggering and capacity of the
experiment’s data acquisition system. Typically experiments have about two thousand hours of data collection
every year when the LHC is running, and the four main experiments have a huge data sample for physicists to
analyze from the completed Run 1 and Run 2 periods. Run 3 started data collection in 2022 and is planned to
continue to 2026. Table 6.11.1 shows typical LHC parameters.
