All of the equipment needed for the High-Luminosity LHC, the LHC’s successor, and its experiments will
be installed during Long Shutdown 3, between 2026 and the end of 2028. The High-Luminosity LHC is
scheduled to come into operation at the end of 2029, though this could shift to 2030 with the outcome decided
in October 2024.

Stable beam time for 2024 (with a duty cycle of 50%) will continue with an average pileup of <μ>=55 and
luminosity leveling at μ=64 , leading to a projected 110 fb-1 of delivered integrated luminosity. Additionally,
about 4 weeks of heavy ion collisions are expected. In 2025 a similar data taking setup is planned.

6.11.2.4.2 Globally Distributed Computing Sites
Both ATLAS and CMS have organized their resource sites following a hierarchical tiered model with their Tier-0
at CERN, national scale Tier-1 sites and regional Tier-2 sites distributed in various countries.

6.11.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
Each of the LHC experiments has its own unique requirements for its scientific processes. See Sections 6.9 and
6.10 for more details.

Generally, the experiments gather data from the LHC collisions occurring within their detectors with real-
time event selection via various hardware and software triggers to capture events of interest. These data are
initially processed at the Tier-0 (CERN) and then globally distributed to various computing centers. The further
processing and analysis become more experiment specific but generally include categorizing, thinning and
skimming data to make it more usable for physicists. Various tools are used to track data, manage workflows and
produce suitable data formats and simulated results, all leading to scientific publications for the areas of high
energy physics each experiment is exploring.

6.11.2.6 Remote Science Activities
LHC computing is fully distributed, and therefore remote from CERN. The raw data are collected exclusively at
CERN - all other activities leading to the final published products are done remotely.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 278

6.11.2.7 Software Infrastructure
The WLCG collects resources worldwide and enables their usage by the LHC experiments as a distributed
computing facility. The mission of the WLCG project is to provide global computing resources to store, distribute
and analyze the ~50-70 PB of data expected every year of operations from the LHC at CERN on the Franco-
Swiss border.

The scale and complexity of data from the LHC is unprecedented. These data need to be stored, easily retrieved
and analyzed by physicists all over the world. This requires massive storage facilities, global networking, immense
computing power, and, of course, funding.

CERN does not have the computing or financial resources to crunch all the data on-site, so in 2002 it turned to
grid computing to share the burden with computer centers around the world. The WLCG builds on the ideas of
grid technology initially proposed in 1999 by Ian Foster and Carl Kesselman.

WLCG is coordinated by CERN. It is managed and operated by a worldwide collaboration between the
experiments (ALICE, ATLAS, CMS and LHCb) and the participating computer centers. It is reviewed by a
board of delegates from partner country funding agencies, and scientifically reviewed by the LHC Experiments
Committee. The WLCG is partnered with EGI, OSG, and NeIC.

There are some common efforts to provide software that is used by more than one LHC experiment. Some
examples are summarized here and will be presented in more detail below:

 • Rucio, a distributed DMS.
 • FTS, responsible for reliably transferring data while not overloading end-systems.
 • Monitoring
 ° SciTags, to label flows and/or IPv6 packets by experiment and activity.

 ° WLCG Site Network Monitoring to track each site’s IN/OUT traffic.

 • Networking orchestration
 ° SENSE/Rucio to integrate SDN with distributed data management.

 ° NOTED a tool to identify network congestion and move large flows to other
 paths dynamically.

6.11.2.7.1 Data Management Tools
For ATLAS & CMS, the majority of data transfers over wide-area networks are facilitated through either the
FTS or XRootD. Rucio now handles all large-scale data transfers over wide-area networks. It coordinates file
movements and replication across distributed sites using FTS for third-party transfers and HTTPS for secure,
efficient data transfer. The adoption of HTTPS in Rucio marks a significant upgrade in security compared to the
old GridFTP system.

XRootD, which is still used for direct data access, works in conjunction with Rucio to ensure smooth file transfers.
Rucio uses Data Identifiers to manage and organize files, datasets, and containers, making data tracking and
management more efficient. This system ensures that data can be easily moved between different storage
locations without errors.

For both ATLAS and CMS, most data transfers over wide-area networks are managed through the FTS or
XRootD. However, CMS exhibits a slightly different data access pattern compared to ATLAS, particularly when
it comes to data streaming using XRootD, where CMS jobs read data remotely. To effectively support these
streaming access scenarios, deploying a robust network infrastructure, such as a CDN, is crucial. A CDN can
significantly enhance data streaming performance, improving the efficiency and reliability of remote data access
for CMS batch processing.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 279

A list of common ATLAS & CMS current and future tools designed to handle the high throughput and complexity
of LHC data processing and storage includes:

 1. Rucio: Rucio is a data management tool used by ATLAS and CMS (and other LHC experiments)
 to manage large volumes of distributed data. It provides automated data replication, transfer
 management, and dataset tracking across multiple storage sites. Rucio allows efficient and reliable
 data movement between Tier-1, Tier-2, and Tier-3 sites. Rucio is integrated with the experiments’
 Workflow Management Systems for production and analysis workflows. The Rucio framework is
 expected to evolve to accommodate higher data rates, improved automation, and dynamic resource
 management. Enhancements may include better integration and improved support for real-time
 data analytics.
 2. XRootD: XRootD is a high-performance, scalable data access framework. It supports fast, efficient
 remote data access, making it critical for distributed LHC data processing. Both ATLAS and CMS
 use XRootD to provide federated access to data, depending upon the site involved, enabling users to
 access files from remote locations without needing local replicas.
 3. FTS: FTS is a multiprotocol data transfer tool. It manages and schedules large-scale data transfers
 between WLCG sites. FTS plays a significant role in ensuring that the CMS & ATLAS can
 efficiently transfer data to and from CERN and other sites.
 4. dCache: A distributed storage system designed to manage large amounts of data with efficient I/O
 operations. dCache provides a hierarchical storage solution that integrates with disk, tape, and SSD,
 optimizing data access for different tiers. It is heavily used by both ATLAS and CMS, particularly for
 managing cached data between hot, warm, and cold storage.
 5. CRIC (Computing Resource Information Catalog): CRIC is a resource information system used
 to manage and describe the experiment’s computing infrastructure. ATLAS and CMS use CRIC to
 manage their resource details (e.g., storage, computing nodes, network capacity), which are crucial
 for data processing and analysis workflows.
 6. CVMFS: CVMFS is used to distribute software to computing nodes in a fast and scalable way.
 ATLAS and CMS rely on CVMFS to access software environments on both local and remote
 computing nodes. It ensures that up-to-date software versions are available globally, which is
 essential for consistent analysis and data processing across distributed resources.
 7. Frontier (Squid): Frontier is a system for retrieving condition data from databases, using a squid-
 caching layer to reduce database load. Both ATLAS and CMS use Frontier/Squid to cache and
 serve condition data used by their jobs, reducing latency and database load during analysis or
 reconstruction tasks.
 8. HTTP-TPC (used by FTS and other transfer tools): HTTP-TPC is a third-party copy mechanism
 for transferring data between storage systems using HTTP. ATLAS and CMS use HTTP-TPC for
 data transfers between different storage elements, often in conjunction with FTS, allowing more
 efficient data movements across their infrastructure.
 9. HTCondor: HTCondor is a job scheduling and management system for distributed computing used
 by both ATLAS and CMS. It targets HTC systems.
 10. Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management (SLURM): SLURM is a job scheduling and
 management system used for distributed computing by both ATLAS and CMS, typically for HPC
 systems.
 11. perfSONAR tool: perfSONAR is a network measurement tool used to monitor and troubleshoot
 network performance. It helps identify bottlenecks and optimize the paths between the experiment
 sites, ensuring efficient data flows and enabling easier identification of network problems.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 280

6.11.2.7.2 Monitoring Tools
In the CMS and ATLAS experiments, efficient network and storage monitoring across Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites is
critical for ensuring reliable, high-performance distribution of large datasets. These sites are globally distributed
and connected through high-speed scientific networks, including the WLCG infrastructure, to facilitate data
transfer and analysis. Here is an overview of various network and storage monitoring systems in place, such as
perfSONAR and CERN’s MONIT (which includes monitoring for the FTS, XRootD, and storage systems).

 • Tier-1 and Tier-2 Monitoring Using perfSONAR:
 ° perfSONAR (Performance Service-Oriented Network Architecture) is an open-source
 network monitoring system widely used across the LHC Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites for
 measuring network performance. It helps identify and resolve network bottlenecks by
 continuously monitoring network latency, packet loss, jitter, and throughput.

 ° All Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites are expected to have perfSONAR nodes deployed to monitor
 network performance. These nodes are integrated into a mesh configuration, enabling
 regular tests such as latency and bandwidth checks between sites. perfSONAR allows
 network administrators to identify potential network issues that could impact data transfer
 rates, both intersite and with CERN. It plays a vital role in the global transfer of data across
 the LCG.

 • SciTags and Packet Marking Deployment in US
 ° ATLAS and CMS are exploring advanced techniques for improving data transfer and
 monitoring capabilities across the WLCG. As the demand for large-scale data processing
 grows, driven by the High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) era, new technologies such as
 SciTags and packet marking are being tested and deployed to enhance network monitoring,
 traffic differentiation, and optimized data flow across high-speed networks.

 ° The deployment of SciTags and packet marking is in progress across several US CMS
 sites. The UNL and UCSD have already successfully implemented SciTags as part of their
 network monitoring infrastructure. Other US Tier-2 sites are currently in the process of
 deploying these technologies, which will lead to better traffic differentiation and resource
 management across the network.

 ° UNL’s deployment has been a crucial step in demonstrating the feasibility of SciTags and
 packet marking for large-scale scientific data transfers. The feedback and results from this
 deployment are helping to refine the implementation at other US sites.

 • CERN’s MONIT System:
 ° MONIT is CERN’s scalable, central monitoring system that aggregates, stores, and
 analyzes monitoring data from multiple sources across the LHC experiments. It provides a
 unified interface for monitoring the infrastructure, including network performance, storage,
 and computing resources.

 ° MONIT gathers data from various monitoring tools (e.g., perfSONAR, FTS, XRootD, and
 custom storage monitoring systems) deployed across all Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites.

 ° MONIT provides dashboards for real-time data visualization and analysis. It uses tools like
 Grafana to present a comprehensive overview of the network and storage infrastructure.
The Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites use a combination of network and storage monitoring tools, to ensure the reliable and
efficient transfer and storage of experimental data. The experiment’s monitoring efforts are tightly integrated
with CERN’s MONIT platform, enabling centralized monitoring and rapid issue resolution. This comprehensive
monitoring infrastructure is crucial for supporting the high-performance computing needs of the experiments.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 281

This monitoring setup ensures that the experiments can operate efficiently, even with the increased data demands
during the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) era. Recommendations include:

 1. Continuous Improvement of perfSONAR Testing: Regularly updating perfSONAR configurations
 and running extensive tests will ensure network issues are detected early.
 2. Storage System Expansion: As data grows, expanding storage monitoring capabilities will become
 increasingly important.
 3. Increased Use of MONIT Dashboards: LHC sites should leverage MONIT’s full potential by
 creating custom dashboards for different types of network and storage performance indicators.

6.11.2.7.3 Network Management Tools
The CMS & ATLAS experiments, in collaboration with ESnet, are integrating the SENSE/Rucio architecture to
improve its network management and data transfer capabilities. This system is designed to address the growing
data demands and transfer needs of CMS & ATLAS, ensuring faster, more reliable, and prioritized data flows
across its global network of data centers.

6.11.2.7.3.1 SENSE/Rucio Architecture Overview
SENSE (SDN for End-to-End Networked Science at the Exascale) uses SDN to dynamically manage network
paths, prioritize traffic, and provide optimized routing. This setup is ideal for data-intensive tasks, as it can
allocate resources in real-time based on network conditions and CMS & ATLAS priorities. Rucio, developed by
CERN, complements SENSE by managing large-scale data distribution across the network. Its features include
automated data replication, strategic data placement, and support for geographically distributed resources, which
streamline the movement and availability of critical datasets.

As illustrated in Figure 1, the integration of SENSE with Rucio is based on identifying data flows that require
high-priority handling. For example, if Rucio marks specific transfers as critical, SENSE allocates network paths
to prioritize them, reducing latency and enhancing throughput. This orchestration involves automated, real-
time adjustments across all parts of the data transfer stack, including FTS and XRootD systems, ensuring
end-to-end efficiency.

 Figure 6.11.1: The SENSE architecture and capabilities: to traffic engineer end-to-end flows with deter-
 ministic bandwidth guarantees across a multidomain footprint.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 282

6.11.2.7.3.2 Key Components and Functionalities
The SENSE/AutoGOLE stack incorporates Site and Network Resource Managers (RM) and an Orchestrator
to deploy Layer 2 virtual circuits globally. Layer 3 topology support also enables managing multi-subnet flows,
which enhances flexibility in accessing various overlays and managing data across complex network structures.
The architecture uses automation at the Site RM level, allowing rapid deployment of network topologies,
virtual circuit overlays, and server configurations. A Data Movement Manager further enhances automation by
responding to multiple requests and allocating bandwidth according to data transfer priority levels.

6.11.2.7.3.3 Testbeds and Site Upgrades
Testbeds at Fermilab (Fermilab), Caltech, UCSD, and the UNL play a crucial role in assessing SENSE/Rucio’s
performance. These sites are part of the CMS Tier-1 and Tier-2 data center infrastructure, handling large data
volumes from the CMS experiment. Notable upgrades, such as Fermilab’s 400 Gbps link via LHCONE and
Caltech’s 4 x 400 Gbps connections, facilitate the evaluation of SENSE/Rucio under high-throughput conditions,
especially during peak data collection and processing periods.

On the ATLAS side, the Northeast Tier-2 (NET2), operated by the University of Massachusetts at Amherst and
located in the MGHPCC, has started testing SENSE/Rucio from the ATLAS perspective in fall 2024. NET2 is in
the process of getting high-performance network connectivity to ESnet and should upgrade its 10 Gbps link to
400 Gbps by mid-November 2024. This upgrade will allow them to test SENSE/Rucio for ATLAS at
relevant scale.

6.11.2.7.3.4 Benefits Targeted
The SENSE/Rucio architecture is working towards these advantages:

 • Optimized Data Transfers: SENSE dynamically assigned network paths with low latency and
 high bandwidth for priority data transfers, reducing transfer times significantly.

 • Traffic Prioritization: SDN-based controls allowed critical data to be prioritized, ensuring
 timely delivery of high-importance datasets for real-time analysis.

 • Enhanced Resource Utilization: By adapting network paths based on real-time conditions,
 SENSE improved bandwidth utilization, avoiding static routing limitations.

 • Resilience and Reliability: The architecture dynamically rerouted traffic around network
 congestion and hardware failures, which is essential for uninterrupted data transfers during
 intensive data taking.
6.11.2.7.3.5 Future Plans and Expansion
Based upon demonstrated improvements to existing capabilities, both CMS & ATLAS are planning to expand
SENSE/Rucio integration to all Tier-2 sites, transitioning from experimental testbeds to full-scale production. As
a part of this expansion, network monitoring and telemetry tools will be deployed to track performance, identify
bottlenecks, and optimize configurations.

By enhancing network management capabilities, SENSE/Rucio helps CMS & ATLAS to maintain a scalable,
resilient infrastructure that meets the evolving data needs of its experiments. This integration not only ensures
faster data transfers but also enables the CMS & ATLAS computing system to offer more predictable, priority-
based data workflows essential for timely scientific discoveries.

6.11.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
LHC Run 3 will be completed by the end of 2026 and it is expected that the network traffic will keep growing at
the usual rate until then. In the latest years, the LHC community has seen an annual increase of 20-30% of traffic
in LHCOPN and LHCONE, the two networks dedicated to transfers between WLCG sites.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 283

The current networking capacities are typically 100 Gbps WAN links with many sites already having resilience
(multiple) 100 Gbps connections. This will need to evolve as the LHC community prepares for Run 4. The
expected traffic during Run 4 (2029/2030-2032/2033), when the HL-LHC will come into operation, will
significantly increase. ATLAS and CMS have estimated this increase in network traffic to be a factor of 10
compared to Run3.

In preparation of HL-LHC the LHC experiments have defined a calendar of “data challenges” to progressively
test the capabilities of the WLCG software and hardware infrastructure to meet the requirements. Here is the
way they have estimated the network bandwidth:

 • ATLAS & CMS T0 to T1 per experiment
 ° 350 PB raw data per year; average of 50 Gbps or 400 Gbps during LHC running time

 ° Another 100 Gbps estimated for prompt reconstruction data tiers (AOD, other derived
 output) estimated 1 Tbps for CMS and ATLAS summed

 • ALICE & LHCb T0 Export
 ° 100 Gbps per experiment estimated from Run 3 rates
From these numbers they have defined two models:

 • Minimal Model
 ° Sum (ATLAS,ALICE,CMS,LHCb)*2(for bursts)*2(safety-margin) = 4.8 Tbps expected
 HL-LHC bandwidth

 • Flexible Model
 ° Experiments may need to reprocess and reconstruct the collected data during the year

 ° This requires doubling the bandwidth of the Minimal model: 9.6 Tbps expected HL-LHC
 bandwidth
Which gives this estimate for sites:

 • Each Major Tier-1s:
 ° 1 Tbps to the Tier-0 (LHCOPN)

 ° 1 Tbps to the Tier-2s (aggregated, LHCONE)

 • Each Major Tier-2s:
 ° >400 Gbps (LHCONE) and resilient
It is expected that all the major Tier-1s to have at least 800 Gbps LHCOPN links at the start of Run 4 with the
ability to grow to 1.2 Tbps or even 1.6 Tbps during the Run. Tier-1s should also have an equivalent amount of
bandwidth to LHCONE to serve Tier-2s. Details of the networking for ATLAS and CMS are in the experiment
specific case studies (#9 and #10 respectively).

In terms of aggregate WAN capacity out of the site, CMS Tier-1 (Fermilab) currently has provisioned 2.4Tb/s of
link capacity to ESnet, via geographically diverse connections. A LAG of four 400 Gbps links is used to support
the science data network paths, including LHCOPN and LHCONE. A second 2 x 400 Gbps LAG supports the
Laboratory’s general internet traffic, which includes some portion of science traffic, for example, CMS traffic to/
from sites not connected to LHCONE.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 284

BNL has two path-diverse 800 Gbps (2 x 400 GbE) circuits that peer with ESnet routers within their 515 and 725
data centers. These circuits are utilized by all scientific and administrative communities at BNL. All traffic to and
from BNL flows through either of these circuits.

A report on the results of the last WLCG Data Challenge can be found online.114

6.11.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.11.2.9.1 Cloud Services
Many of the LHC experiments have explored cloud services and are using them as part of their global set of
resources. There are two primary modes of operation envisioned:

 1. A particular site contracts with a cloud provider and resources are (transparently) added as part of
 the site from their experiment’s perspective.
 2. A new site is created within a cloud provider, utilizing the various provisioning, management and
 resilient infrastructure available.
While option 1 above has been used with varying degrees of success, option 2 is not yet feasible for a number
of reasons.

 • The entity setting up a site within a cloud provider needs to be able to control costs to make it
 feasible, but there are not usually policies and tools to allow them to do so.

 • Egress charges from cloud providers are usually expensive and may vary depending upon
 where the egress goes to.

 • Connecting to resources like LHCONE is very challenging because of the AUP requirement
 that all traffic from the advertised subnets for LHCONE must be LHC related.
One place that R&E networks could help would be in jointly negotiating with various cloud providers to create a
template contract they would support no egress charges if the R&E providers bring high-bandwidth links to the
cloud providers, as well as defining policies and associated tools to allow LHC site creators to manage costs by,
for example, controlling how data flows to only use the zero ( or low cost ) egress connections globally.

6.11.2.9.2 AI and ML
This is an area of very active research and development using ML frameworks like but sci-kit-learn, PyTorch,
and, to a lesser extent, Keras/Tensorflow and JAX. The experiments rely upon the same Nvidia Cuda platform.
However, training tasks are also very experiment specific. See the individual case studies for details.

6.11.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
No wireless capability studies or capability upgrades are planned at present. Some users may do their work from
systems connected via wireless, but this is not currently an area of concern for LHC, because most such users use
wireless to access remote systems that are doing the actual data transfers or access.

6.11.2.9.4 Data-Centre Interconnect and Spectrum Sharing
The HL-LHC requirements for LHCOPN links approach 1 Tbps and has pushed sites to explore more affordable
technologies to achieve it. IT-INFN-CNAF, the Italian Tier-1, has deployed a pilot connection using DCI
equipment at the Tier-1 (CNAF) and Tier-0 (CERN) sites, which use four light channels on the dark-fibers of two
different providers, GEANT and GARR. The solution can provide 4 x 400 Gbps link for a total of 1.6 Tbps.

114 https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.11401877

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 285

Spectrum Sharing is achieved by interconnecting the ROADM device of the two providers. It saves on the cost
of more expensive router interfaces, since most of the existing LHCOPN links are provided as MPLS Layer 2
virtual circuits. The solution is described in detail online.115

6.11.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
For LHC experiments in general, but ATLAS and CMS in particular, the resource requirements are growing
beyond what flat budgets can support. This leads the experiments to work very hard at optimizing their data
and analysis processes to maximize what the available resources can do. Various trade-offs are continually being
explored (network use vs multiple replicas of data, data format changes vs number of required datasets to meet
various needs, exploitation of nonstandard computing capacity (GPUs, FPGAs, etc.), reconstructing data on
demands vs storing it, etc.), to try to achieve the time to science target with constrained resources.

During the 2020-2021 studies of LHC network requirements, the LHC experiments estimated that Tier-1
centers would need terabit/sec connections and Tier-2 sites would require 400G connections. That was driven
by estimates of some (but not all) data-related operations of CMS and ATLAS, leading to an estimated bandwidth
need of 4.8 terabits/sec (Tbps) across the Atlantic for CMS and ATLAS alone in a so-called “minimal model” and
9.6 Tbps in a more “flexible” and realistic model.

As of 2024, multiple 400G connections have been installed to the Fermilab and Brookhaven national labs as
well as HPC facilities used by HEP, and the upgrades to 400G (or N X 400G) at some US CMS campuses are
either in place or imminent. As mentioned above, 400G-scale operations in production mode are already being
demonstrated, and the standalone capability of individual “Gen5” (PCIe 5.0) inexpensive data servers with
multiple 400G and 200G to reach several hundred Gbps was demonstrated at SC23, with Tbps capability per
data server on the horizon. Next-generation servers (PCIe 6.0 with Compute Express Link [CXL] memory
interconnects) are emerging between now and approximately 2026, and a further technology generation is
expected to be available in the mass market before HL-LHC startup in 2030.

Given the above factors: technology drivers and the evolution of ATLAS and CMS’s “process of science,” the
outlook for 2030, the currently foreseen start of the HL-LHC era, it appears that the actual requirements may be
somewhat larger than foreseen in 2021. Detailed projections are difficult at this point, but should be tracked and
updated every two years or so to make quantitative estimates and (re-)establish the requirements in both network
capacity and capability (as in the programmability aspects summarized above).

6.11.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
Some experiments utilize Globus endpoints or, more generically, DTNs but this was not the typical design pattern
for the LHC experiments. Instead, most of them rely upon the Storage Element design which various storage
technologies in use (dCache, XRootD, STORM, EOS, etc.) support. Transfers fill capacity in the WAN by using a
many-to-many model with sites typically having ~50 storage servers that serve as either sources or destinations.
Many small transfers run in parallel to try to efficiently utilize the available network and storage IO capacity.

6.12 LHC: HL-LHC & Network Research
The High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) will collide protons more than a billion times every second, out of which
ATLAS and CMS will select interesting collisions for recording at a rate of ~ten thousand times every second.

6.12.1 Discussion Summary
The barrier to using DOE HPC resources still remains, particularly in integrating the systems as resources into
the software components, and normalizing the way the resources could be accounted for (expected versus ad hoc
or opportunistic). More specifically, there is a desire to create agreements or other forms of arrangements, similar
to an SLA, with DOE HPC facilities such that resources can be considered “pledged,” similar to how Tier-1s and
Tier-2s operate. This helps with planning for both the HEP community and the ASCR resources. Some of this
may require discussion at the programmatic level.

An additional operations concern is related to the way that the LHC resources rely on a streaming workflow,
the ability of large HPC facilities to support this remains important: either by allowing the worker notes stream
directly, or by leveraging caches and data lakes that are deployed close topologically. All of these design choices
come with trade-offs, which implies a set of R&D activities that will extend in the coming years.

WLCG’s hardware choices for the next major cycles will have a huge influence on the performance of the overall
computation and storage system. Hardware choice, and how this relates to overall cost, can fluctuate leading
to uncertainty about what capabilities may exist. Some of this leads to speculation about analysis output, data
volumes, and the roles of other technology (e.g., networking).

It is expected that GPU use to support some aspects of AI and ML within the LHC community will continue;
the challenging parts that are unknown currently are how this may impact WAN usage. Experiments like DUNE
have shown that bursting to a commercial cloud to utilize GPUs is possible, but leveraging DOE HPC resource
would allow better control over the WAN components. There could be opportunities to schedule network use
(e.g., using mechanics like SENSE and Rucio) to coincide with the availability of resources at an HPC facility.

The LHC work on Data Lakes will continue, and has learned several things from the years of R&D and use
during activities like DC24. In particular, there is now an effort to reduce the number of “entry points” into
storage resources. The XRootD tool right now is not bound by factors such as network capacity or distance/
latency, and may find nonoptimal answers to requests for data from clients. The overall goal of a data lake should
be to simplify the way data are accessed, along with providing the most performant ways to access and retrieve
it. Data lakes can also leverage some of the work on caching, and allow the caches (which often do have more
intelligence) to assist in making optimal choices about retrieval.

The use of in-network caching was discussed at length to identify ways that ESnet and the LHC community
can work together more efficiently to design and operate an effective service. ESnet has some previous work in
attempting to create a “CDN for Science” with others in the DOE, but the usage patterns never amounted to a
measurable increase in performance. A core R&D question to address remains: how large should the caches be,
and what policies on data retrieval and retention will be valuable to implement to keep cache hit rates high. To
date there are not many good answers due to the sometimes chaotic nature of the uses of the cache. For example,
user analysis between facilities may focus on completely different portions of a larger data set; within a facility it
may be more relevant and can take advantage of caching. Workflow tools that are integrated to use a cache get
a small uptick in performance in these cases, but may also use nonoptimal reasoning when retrieving data sets.
ESnet would like to gain better monitoring insight into the caching work, either by having access to LHC data
(e.g., MONIT) or by having more network layer visibility integrated into Stardust.

As in the discussion after the LHC Operations use case, ESnet will continue to work with the LHC community to
advance R&D efforts that support the HL-LHC operations era. This includes the already mentioned efforts (e.g.,

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 288

SENSE and Rucio, SciTags), but also ways that HPC resources can be integrated and utilized more efficiently.
The use of ESnet High Touch data, and integration with Stardust, may be critical in passing along network-level
telemetry to the storage and computational components of the LHC community.

 • The CMS experiment anticipates the following annual data volume for each data type during
 HL-LHC operation: [Section 4.2]

 ° raw Data: 250 PB

 ° AOD Data: 210 PB

 ° MiniAOD Data: 27 PB

 ° NanoAOD Data: 0.6 PB

 • The ATLAS experiment anticipates the following annual data volume for each data type during
 HL-LHC operation: [Section 4.2]

 ° raw Data: 168 PB

 ° AOD Data: 200 PB

 ° Derived AOD (DAOD) Data: 76 PB

 ° DAOD_PHYSLITE Data: 2.6 PB

 • The exact computing model for the HL-LHC has not been finalized, given that the LHC Run
 is not expected to start till 2030. It is assumed that the current computing models will be the
 baseline model, with some small improvements. There will be no fixed hierarchy of computing
 sites for most data processing and data access services. In order to improve usage efficiency, sites
 will be primarily categorized by size, service level, and capability. Hence the location of datasets
 and users is not deterministic. Tier-1s will need additional capacity to handle worldwide traffic,
 and Tier-2s will be scoped larger for national traffic needs. The network capacity should be
 provisioned to match the scale of the available resources at each site. [Section 4.3]

 • PanDA, ProdSys and Rucio are being extended for the demands of HL-LHC. Rucio has been
 adopted as the LHC and WLCG standard. A notable difference between the two collaborations
 is that CMS more heavily relies on streaming data from storage endpoints to remote processing
 centers via the XRootD protocol. CMS is currently re-evaluating its workflow management
 infrastructure solution, which may lead to changes in network usage patterns if a new system is
 adopted. [Section 4.3]

 • ATLAS has chosen to evaluate two scenarios based on how aggressively it is anticipated that the
 HL-LHC storage and computing R&D program will deliver improvements: [Section 4.3]

 ° “Conservative” R&D is a program where work can be completed with the existing person-
 power. The R&D activities currently underway to support Run 3 will be put into place, and
 will encourage an almost universal adoption of the DAOD_PHYSLITE format.

 ° A full program of “aggressive” higher-risk R&D can only be completed with new person-
 power. ATLAS implements new developments that very significantly improve the speed
 and storage volumes of workflows that currently are heavy consumers of resources.

 • There have been significant efforts made to understand the computing and storage
 requirements for HL-LHC. The process began by extrapolating current methods forward,
 accounting for the data increases from HL-LHC and the additional complexity associated with
 high-luminosity operations of the collider. Further assumptions about the initially conservative

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 289

 estimates of computing and storage capacities would be increased for fixed cost and additionally
 assumed the notion of a “flat budget” for the foreseeable future. To decrease the gap, significant
 efforts were made to better optimize how less resources could be utilized to do the same
 amount of science. This has helped decrease the difference between what is needed and what
 is affordable. While there are potentially some optimistic assumptions in this estimate, it is
 known that the planning process must change to ensure resource availability on the time scale
 of HL-LHC. At this point there is still a significant gap in the amount of storage believed to be
 needed versus what can be provisioned with current budget projections. [Section 4.4]

 • The impact of HL-LHC on ATLAS and CMS storage and compute resources is significant. As
 previously noted, the increase in luminosity not only generates significantly more data but also
 significantly more complex events which require more processing to resolve. [Section 4.4]

 • The expanded use of High-Performance Computers (HPC) will also have an impact on the
 compute resources (storage and networking). These HPC centers are increasing in computing
 power and several exaflop-scale machines will be operational during the start of the HL-LHC.
 These centers are more capable of processing larger and larger volumes of data; this means that
 the workloads that will run on these machines will evolve. HPC’s will be capable of producing a
 large volume of simulated data. [Section 4.4]

 • Global R&E network use will have different characteristics on the timescale of the HL-LHC,
 compared to the situation the WLCG experienced in Runs 1, 2, and 3. Specifically, the
 experiments foresee other science domains (astronomy, biology, engineering, and others)
 becoming global network users at scales equaling or exceeding the LHC users. In such an
 environment, it is not wise to assume the experiments can continue to treat the network as an
 infinite resource . The LHC community must explore options for effectively operating within a
 bandwidth constrained environment. [Section 4.7]

 • Networking has been fundamental to the success of ATLAS and CMS computing to date,
 enabling the exploitation of globally distributed resources for computationally limited science.
 This will remain the case to meet the budget-constrained computing challenges of HL-LHC.
 Strategies for HL-LHC computing are based on extensive use of powerful networks to reduce
 data replication by streaming over the network, and consolidating distributed resources into
 cohesive virtual federations such as data lakes. HL-LHC data and processing scales are large
 enough that optimizing for efficient bandwidth use will be essential. The ability to mark
 network packets to identify sources of traffic, and to route traffic to control speed and cost may
 become vital. [Section 4.7]

 • As a rough guide as to the network bandwidth that facilities in US CMS will require in the
 HL-LHC era for the purpose of reconstructing the raw data and producing corresponding
 simulation datasets, one can take the following estimate: from the 250 PB of raw data collected
 per year, about 40% (e.g., 100 PB) is expected to be reconstructed in the US. It is desired that
 these large-scale reconstruction campaigns take approximately 10 weeks, implying a data
 input rate to processing facilities of 10 PB/week, and an output rate of 4 PB/week. In parallel,
 simulation production campaigns will be executed continuously throughout the year, producing
 another 40% of the total 240 PB of output data (e.g., 96 PB) to be persisted on tape and/or disk
 storage within the US. In total, these workflows will require a sustained rate of up to 130 Gbps
 between processing and storage facilities. To account for burst traffic, and to support data analysis
 workloads at AFs discussed below, it is desired that all major processing facilities, namely the
 Fermilab Tier-1 and US CMS Tier-2 centers, are provisioned to 400 Gbps. [Section 4.7]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 290

 • At present, it is assumed that the general LHC Tier-2 network requirements as specified above
 will be sufficient to support AFs at the Tier-2s. A user at an AF may expect to process a year’s
 worth of MiniAOD data and simulation (27 PB) in a timescale of a week. If the data are not
 cached at the AF, that amounts to a sustained 400 Gbps network load from the data origin site.
 In practice, it is unlikely a user would read the entirety of the data catalog, though the exact
 fraction will vary significantly depending on the analysis goals. [Section 4.7]

 • The global infrastructure is currently relatively uniform, with approximately 70 compute
 and storage elements presenting an identical interface to CMS. The data distribution model
 proposed by WLCG for the HL-LHC is commonly referred to as the “Data Lake Model.” The
 data lake model envisions fewer regional entry points than the 70 storage elements currently
 available, allowing internal optimizations and potentially reducing the operational burden on
 international CMS. Data transfer between two lakes is a top-down-controlled activity governed
 by Rucio and executed via FTS using third-party copy HTTPS transfer protocols with capability
 token authentication. Access to data from processing elements inside the lake is mediated either
 via caches or streaming directly from one of the data lake origins. [Section 4.8]

 • ESnet and the LHC experiments (ATLAS and CMS) have started an R&D project that makes
 use of in-network data caches operated by ESnet using XRootD software. The pilot project
 focuses on caching of PHYSLITE data products to see if the time to reach physics results can
 be shorted, and the overall network traffic reduced for data analysis (only used parts of data files
 cached and reused). [Section 4.8]

 • During HL-LHC the tracking algorithms used in event reconstruction are expected to see
 increased use of GPUs. It is conceivable parts of the events will need to be shipped to data
 centers (HPC’s, Cloud vendors, WLCG data centers) for GPU processing with the results sent
 elsewhere for recombination with the data processed on CPU-only resources. Future DOE
 HPC machines are focusing on support for AI/ML, with large numbers of GPUs and other
 accelerators. ML training requires large amounts of data transferred into the HPC’s for use
 during the training. This will have an impact on the WAN network as data are transferred from
 WLCG data centers to HPCs in the US for ML training and inference. [Section 4.8]

 • From the ATLAS and CMS point of view, the IRI long-term campaign pattern best fits the
 LHC use case. Historically, the collaboration expects a full year’s worth of reconstructed data
 and simulation to be produced on a few-month timescale, so there is relatively little time
 sensitivity. Online DQM and time-sensitive calibration procedures are handled by a separate
 coordination area of the ATLAS and CMS experiments and have dedicated resources at CERN,
 the host laboratory. In addition, since each particle collision event is an independent identically
 distributed quantity, the HL-LHC science workflow is trivially parallelizable and does not need
 large-scale data shuffle operations to execute. [Section 4.9]

 • If, under the IRI, HPC centers could provide some of the services found at the WLCG data
 centers (for example proxy caches, CVMFS outbound connectivity from the worker nodes
 - through a reverse proxy), both ATLAS and CMS will be able to make better use of these
 resources. [Section 4.9]

 • Most of the workflows that ATLAS will use during HL-LHC will fall under the IRI category of
 data-intensive workflows (event reconstruction and ML) or long-term campaign (large-scale MC
 simulations). IRI will also provide the opportunity to implement some near real-time workflows
 for critical payloads. [Section 4.9]

 • For CMS, the US provides, depending on the resource type, 30-40% of the global computing
 and storage capacity. Since the international CMS collaboration is responsible for operating
 a common computing infrastructure, if CMS is to effectively use IRI, it will be necessary

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 291

 to ensure that the interface to computing and storage resources made available by IRI is
 compatible with the global infrastructure, including university and international partners.
 It is expected that the current WLCG interface (Compute and Storage Elements) that CMS
 is presented with, will evolve in preparation for HL-LHC, though the exact nature of this
 evolution is not yet determined. [Section 4.9]

 • Given the compatibility of CMS workflow pattern with IRI plans, previous experience with
 integrating HPC facilities, and the need to provide a homogenous computing interface to
 an international collaboration, CMS would be an excellent choice for a long-term campaign
 pathfinder project for the IRI.[Section 4.9]

 • The current members of the collaborations are not expected to encounter major changes to
 the membership for the HL-LHC. The collaborators will continue to be distributed worldwide,
 which puts strong requirements on global networking. Specifically, it is expected that computing
 resources will continue to be globally distributed, with no centralized data or computing
 location. Physicists will need access to the distributed resources from all corners of the
 world. [Section 5.1]

 • In the HL-LHC era, it is expected that, in terms of the current computing model, the US will
 continue to provide one of the Tier-1 and several Tier-2 facilities, fully funded via DOE and
 NSF respectively, as resources for CMS. It is expected that US CMS will make use of any HPC
 centers funded by either DOE or NSF that will grant allocations. Commercial cloud providers
 are not expected to be a major component of the CMS computing infrastructure. [Section 5.1]

 • The High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) will collide protons more than a billion times every
 second, out of which ATLAS and CMS will select interesting collisions for recording at a rate
 of ~ten thousand times every second. With over two thousand hours of data collection every
 year when the HL-LHC starts running in 2030, ATLAS and CMS will have a huge data sample
 for physicists to analyze worldwide. The HL-LHC program is expected to last for a decade.
 Large improvements in networking will be required to enable the ambitious physics goals of
 the HL-LHC. The entire HL-LHC era will last for 10 years of data taking, with 12-24 month
 maintenance periods interspersed roughly every three years. [Section 5.1]

 • For the HL-LHC era, the predictions show a mismatch between the computing and storage
 resources the experiments can afford versus the resources needed to reach science goals.
 In response to this gap, the experiments are exploring alternatives in how to utilize storage,
 computing and network infrastructure. The network baseline currently being planned is
 composed of terabit-scale (1–2 Tbps) backbone networks with the largest resource sites
 connected at multiple 400 G scale (800 Gbps+). Network use will be at least a factor of 10 larger
 than Run 3. [Section 5.1]

 • The individual LHC experiments are interested in discussing the set of features that must be
 present in future network designs. If it is possible to identify a minimum set of capabilities in
 switches and routers, to ensure the next generation of network components can meet the needs
 of the community, it would simplify the procurement and installation process. The sooner
 those capabilities are in place, the sooner prototyping and testing future capabilities will be
 possible. [Section 5.7]

 • For HL-LHC networking, four main requirements have been identified: [Section 5.7]
 ° Run 3 is moving to multiple 100G links for large sites, while Run 4 (HL-LHC) is targeting
 Tbps links, perhaps based upon either 400G or 800G waves.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 292

 ° It is necessary to understand the impact of new features in networking (SDN/NFV)
 by testing, prototyping and evaluating impact. The experiments will need to evolve
 applications, facilities and computing models to meet the HL-LHC challenges; it will
 take time.

 ° The ability to understand WAN network flows is limited. New methods to mark and
 monitor network use are needed. Packet marking is viewed as a high priority so that
 everyone (experiments, sites and R&E networks) can understand the origin and intent of
 network flows at any point along their path.

 ° Developing, prototyping, and testing network features at suitable scale will be needed.
 Having at-scale network testbeds will be very important to understand the potential impact
 changes might have on operations.

 • One interesting option to explore on the timescale of HL-LHC is the joint ATLAS and CMS
 use of Rucio for distributed data management. This could provide a mechanism to interact
 with ESnet (and other R&E networks), communicating near-term data-movement intents and
 perhaps negotiating for any required QoS or deadline requirements. [Section 5.8]

6.12.2 HL-LHC: Network Research Profile
With over two thousand hours of data collection every year when the HL-LHC starts running in 2030, ATLAS
and CMS will have a huge data sample for physicists to analyze worldwide. The HL-LHC program is expected to
last for a decade. Large improvements in networking will be required to enable the ambitious physics goals of the
HL-LHC.

6.12.2.1 Science Background
As shown in Figure 6.12.1, the HL-LHC era starting in 2030 will accumulate roughly the same integrated
luminosity of data in three years of LHC running as the entire period of running of the LHC has produced up
to then. All of that data will be accumulated at a center of mass energy of 14 TeV. This implies that the science
capabilities of the first years of HL-LHC data taking at design luminosity, in 2030-2032, is expected to be roughly
equivalent to the data taking from 2010-2025, or Runs 1, 2, and 3 combined.

The entire HL-LHC era will last for 10 years of data taking, with 12-24 month maintenance periods interspersed
roughly every three years116. Each data taking year, the accelerator expects to deliver 250 fb-1 of data117 to the
ATLAS and CMS experiments.

the two experiments result from different choices of analysis procedures and are largely driven by sociology.

events, 6e6 seconds live time per year, and a 4.3 MB (CMS) or 2.8 MB (ATLAS) event size.

6.12.2.2 Collaborators
The current members of the ATLAS collaboration are described in Section 6.9. It is not expected that major
changes to the membership will occur for the HL-LHC. The collaborators will continue to be distributed
worldwide, which puts strong requirements on global networking. Specifically, it is expected that computing
resources will continue to be globally distributed, with no centralized data or computing location. Physicists will
need access to the distributed resources from all corners of the world.

The international nature of CMS, location of its facilities, and location of any shared HPC centers is essentially
unchanged over time. Refer to Section 6.10 for more details.

The exact computing model for the HL-LHC has not been finalized, given that the LHC Run is not expected
to start till 2030. It is assumed that the current ATLAS computing model will be the baseline model, with some
small improvements. There will be no fixed hierarchy of computing sites for most data processing and data
access services. In order to improve usage efficiency, sites will be primarily categorized by size, service level, and
capability. Hence the location of datasets and users is not deterministic - ATLAS expects worldwide distribution
of all resources and users. ATLAS also expects about seven large sites in the US, which will all be required to
have a full range of distributed computing capabilities. They will store both primary and secondary data, will
provide access to hundreds of users, and will participate in continuous data transfers. These sites will include
the BNL Tier-1, the current Tier-2’s (Great Lakes, Midwest, Northeast, and Southwest), SLAC, and the larger
DOE and NSF HPC’s. It is expected that a few 400 Gbps links will be needed between them when the HL-LHC
starts. BNL Tier-1 will need additional capacity to handle worldwide traffic. The network capacity should be
provisioned to match the scale of the available resources at each site.

6.12.2.3 IRI Readiness
The IRI envisions three primary workflow patterns: time-sensitive; data-integration intensive; and long-term
campaign. From the ATLAS and CMS point of view, the long-term campaign pattern best fits the LHC use case.
Historically, the collaboration expects a full year’s worth of reconstructed data and simulation to be produced on
a few-month timescale, so there is relatively little time sensitivity. Online DQM and time-sensitive calibration
procedures are handled by a separate coordination area of the ATLAS and CMS experiments and have dedicated
resources at CERN, the host laboratory. In addition, since each particle collision event is an independent
identically distributed quantity, the HL-LHC science workflow is trivially (or, pleasantly) parallelizable and does
not need large-scale data shuffle operations to execute.

HEP experiments in general can benefit from IRI, especially if LCF and HPDF are seamlessly integrated into
the existing HTC (grid) infrastructure (including OSG). The IRI will provide a unified programmatic interface to
both compute and data flow. This standardization of interfaces across the DOE HPC centers will make it possible
to use these resources by the time of HL-LHC.

If, under the IRI, HPC centers could provide some of the services found at the WLCG data centers (for example
proxy caches, CVMFS outbound connectivity from the worker nodes - through a reverse proxy), both ATLAS and
CMS will be able to make better use of these resources.

Most of the workflows that ATLAS will use during HL-LHC will fall under the category of data-intensive
workflows (event reconstruction and ML) or long-term campaign (large-scale MC simulations). IRI will also
provide the opportunity to implement some near real-time workflows (WF) for critical payloads such as High-
Level Trigger WF, which should produce results in a near-real-time manner. As an example, the BNL network
infrastructure has been designed with IRI patterns in mind. This is shown in the network design of the external
Science DMZ network for data transfer and a firewalled science portals network for services. IRI benefits HEP
by providing a uniform interface to disparate resources in a way that is easier to integrate with, better fit to HEP
workflows. The ATLAS workflows that benefit most from an IRI approach are those currently running at LCF
and HPCs.

CMS has extensive experience integrating HPC sites within the US In particular, the Fermilab Tier-1 computing
site uses the HEPCloud interface to extend its computing capacity provided to CMS by roughly double through
use of the NERSC Perlmutter and TACC Frontera supercomputers. CMS expects that, in IRI, long-term
campaign workflows will be at risk of pre-emption to make room for time-sensitive workflows, and prefers a
service level agreement characterized by the integrated core-hours made available over some time window. For
example, an allocation might provide a total of 100M core-hours with a minimum 20M core-hours over a one-
month window. This allows for reliable long-term campaign planning. R&D to increase the resilience of CMS
workflows to pre-emption will be needed to fully exploit such an infrastructure.

For CMS, the US provides, depending on the resource type, 30–40% of the global computing and storage
capacity. Since the international CMS collaboration is responsible for operating a common computing
infrastructure, if CMS is to effectively use IRI, it will be necessary to ensure that the interface to computing and
storage resources made available by IRI is compatible with the global infrastructure, including university and
international partners. It is expected that the current WLCG interface (Compute and Storage Elements) that
CMS is presented with, will evolve in preparation for HL-LHC, though the exact nature of this evolution is not
yet determined.

Given the compatibility of CMS workflow pattern with IRI plans, previous experience with integrating HPC
facilities, and the need to provide a homogenous computing interface to an international collaboration, CMS
would be an excellent choice for a long-term campaign pathfinder project for the IRI.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 295

6.12.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
The impact of HL-LHC on ATLAS and CMS storage and compute resources is significant. As previously noted,
the increase in luminosity not only generates significantly more data but also significantly more complex events
which require more processing to resolve.

The expanded use of High-Performance Computers (HPC) will also have an impact on the compute resources
(storage and networking). These HPC centers are increasing in computing power and several exaflop-scale
machines will be operational during the start of the HL-LHC. These centers are also becoming more capable of
processing larger and larger volumes of data than they did in the past. This means that the workloads that will
run on these machines will evolve. HPC’s will be capable of producing a large volume of simulated data. This
simulated data will be reconstructed at the HPC where it was produced. The output files from the simulation step
and the reconstruction step will need to be quickly transferred to ATLAS and CMS data centers for subsequent
processing. During HL-LHC the tracking algorithms used in event reconstruction are expected to see increased
use of GPUs. The foreseen reconstruction processing will be a mix of CPU and GPU codes. It is conceivable
parts of the events will need to be shipped to data centers (HPC’s, Cloud vendors, WLCG data centers) for GPU
processing with the results sent elsewhere for recombination with the data processed on CPU-only resources.
The DOE HPC machines are being designed to be very efficient at AI/ML with large numbers of GPUs and
other accelerators. ML training requires large amounts of data transferred into the HPC’s for use during the
training. This will have an impact on the WAN network as data are transferred from WLCG data centers to HPCs
in the US for ML training and inference.

To upgrade to HL-LHC will involve numerous changes to the accelerator. The LHC particle beam will need to
be more intense and more focused than at present. New or upgraded components will need to be installed in
various sections of the LHC’s 27 kilometers ring. In addition to the accelerator upgrades, the ATLAS and CMS
experiments also need to implement significant upgrades and detector replacements to handle the much more
challenging environment of the HL-LHC.

6.12.2.4.1 ATLAS Computing Infrastructure
The HL-LHC refers to the upgraded LHC configuration that will be implemented during Long Shutdown
3 (LS3). Luminosity is a measure of the number of collisions per unit area for a given period of time. More
luminosity means more particle collisions and more opportunities to measure new, interesting physics. A good
way to measure discovery potential is by integrated luminosity which is measured in inverse femtobarns (fb−1).
An inverse femtobarn equates to 100 trillion collisions. The integrated luminosity for all LHC Runs 1 and 2 was
about 150 inverse femtobarns of data and during the ongoing Run 3 also about 150 inverse femtobarns have
been recorded so far. The HL-LHC will produce more than 250 inverse femtobarns of data per year and will be
capable of collecting up to 3000 inverse femtobarns.

One of the significant challenges posed by HL-LHC is the increase in the average number of particle collisions
each time particle bunches cross each other (which happens around 40 million times per second). The Run 3
average number of collisions per crossing is around 50 but HL-LHC will increase that to 150-200. It is important
to note that the impact of this increase in processing power is worse than linear and a priori exponential,
primarily because of the increased combinatorics involved in assigning particles to collisions.

In the ATLAS Software and Computing HL-LHC Roadmap, ATLAS has chosen to evaluate two scenarios
based on how aggressively it is anticipated that the HL-LHC storage and computing R&D program will deliver
improvements. They are useful straw-men to discuss model uncertainties and development costs.

The two scenarios, defined in terms of the R&D program activities described in the next section, are as follows:

Conservative R&D: “Conservative” R&D is assumed to be work that can be completed with the existing person-
power in the ATLAS software and computing community, as long as the overall staffing levels are maintained
and key experts remain in ATLAS. The research and development activities currently underway for Run 3

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 296

are assumed to be successful, including the data carousel, fast track reconstruction, and most of the detector
simulation being performed with fast simulation. Almost universal adoption by the physics groups of DAOD_
PHYSLITE would also fall into this category.

Aggressive R&D: The full program of “aggressive” higher-risk R&D can only be completed with new person-
power, either in the form of new individuals, or existing contributors being permitted to spend a higher fraction
of their time on software and computing development for ATLAS. There are a number of higher-risk projects
where work is ongoing already with the available person-power. Since there is significant uncertainty in the
impact on resources these projects might have, their potential impact is included in the “aggressive” R&D
projection. ATLAS implements new developments that very significantly improve the speed and storage volumes
of workflows that currently are heavy consumers of resources. For example, porting of high-precision generators
to GPUs, sharing events with CMS, or speeding up the full simulation either by software efficiencies or porting
parts of the code to GPUs. Developments of very high quality fast simulation that could replace full simulation in
almost all cases, would also fall into this category. Some R&D activities in the aggressive category cannot yet be
quantified in their impact and so are not yet included in the model. An example is ML models for fast simulation
and reconstruction.

Figures 6.12.2 and 6.12.3 show the estimated CPU and storage needs under these different scenarios, to be
compared with provisioned resource curves based on flat funding for CPU and storage, and capacity growth
per unit cost of 10% and 20% per year. US ATLAS in its current best-estimate budget planning assumes 10%
growth (the lower curve) for the years out to HL-LHC, based on an assessment of the technology landscape.
Other estimates within the HEP community range from 5% to 20%. These studies demonstrate that ATLAS (and
US ATLAS) must pursue vigorously aggressive R&D options to be able to meet the HL-LHC challenges in a
sustained budget model.

6.12.2.4.2 CMS Computing Infrastructure
In the HL-LHC era, it is expected that, in terms of the current computing model, the US will continue to provide
one of the Tier-1 and several Tier-2 facilities, fully funded via DOE and NSF respectively, as resources for CMS.
They are run as coordinated facilities via the US CMS Operations Program for central processing, generation
of simulated datasets, and, at a smaller scale, data analysis. CERN will operate the Tier-0, a tape archive, and
a Tier-2 for CERN-resident physicists. In addition, it is expected that US CMS will make use of any HPC
centers funded by either DOE or NSF that will grant allocations. As discussed in section 6.12.2.9, commercial
cloud providers are not expected to be a major component of the CMS computing infrastructure. The global
infrastructure is currently relatively uniform, with approximately 70 compute and storage elements presenting an
identical interface to CMS.

The data distribution model proposed by WLCG for the HL-LHC is commonly referred to as the “Data Lake
Model.” The data lake model envisions fewer regional entry points than the 70 storage elements currently
available, allowing internal optimizations and potentially reducing the operational burden on international
CMS. In a data lake, behind each entry point are generally multiple storage endpoints that are geographically
distributed. These storage endpoints will be referred to as “data origins.” An entry point may support multiple
levels of QoS, depending on the cluster. QoS differences may include data access performance, latency, levels of
protections against data loss, etc. The exact definitions of the QoS categories and their expected implementations
are still a subject of R&D and discussions. Data transfer between two lakes is a top-down-controlled activity
governed by Rucio and executed via FTS using third-party copy HTTPS transfer protocols with capability token
authentication. Access to data from processing elements inside the lake is mediated either via caches or streaming
directly from one of the data lake origins.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 298

This vast quantity of data must be distributed around the globe for processing and physics analysis. The data
distribution model for the HL-LHC is commonly referred to as the “Data Lakes Model.” A lake is defined as a
cluster of storage and nearby computing facilities that have a single entry point for interactions outside of the
lake. Figure 6.12.4 shows this model as a graphic with two lakes, though many more lakes will be needed to
meet CMS needs for processing and analysis worldwide. Further details on the data lake model are presented in
Section 6.12.2.4.
