6.12.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
The computing workflows and workloads described in Sections 6.9 and 6.10 for simulation, data processing,
derivations and analysis will continue to be required, with some significant improvements noted below.

The HL-LHC, commencing with Run 4 in 2029, will deliver unprecedentedly complex events, with up to 200
interactions per proton-proton bunch crossing. These events will be collected at a prodigious rate: ATLAS and
CMS expects to record data at 10kHz, approximately five to ten times more than during previous runs. By the
end of Run 6 in 2041, the HL-LHC is expected to have delivered an integrated luminosity of up to 3000 fb-1,
several times more than all previous runs combined. As well as the challenges involved in collecting, storing,
reconstructing and analyzing such a colossal volume of data, MC simulation events will need to be produced in
similar numbers. Taken together, the data and MC requirements of the HL-LHC physics program are formidable,
and if the computing costs are to be kept within feasible levels, substantial improvements must be made in both
compute and storage.

Networking has been fundamental to the success of ATLAS and CMS computing to date, enabling the
exploitation of globally distributed resources for computationally limited science. This will remain the case to
meet the budget-constrained computing challenges of HL-LHC. Strategies for HL-LHC computing are based on
extensive use of powerful networks to reduce data replication by streaming over the network, and consolidating
distributed resources into cohesive virtual federations such as data lakes. HL-LHC data and processing scales are
large enough that optimizing for efficient bandwidth use will be essential.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 299

As part of this optimization, the ability to mark network packets to identify sources of traffic, and to route
traffic to control speed and cost may become vital. To this end, ATLAS initiated the HEPiX Network Function
Virtualization WG in collaboration with other experiments and national entities including ESnet. US ATLAS
will play central roles in the R&D in this area, drawing on the close relationship with ESnet, the long standing
networking expertise within the facilities, and distributed computing leadership in PanDA and its Rucio
integration; shaping network traffic through Rucio and PanDA will be crucial.

Economizing storage is an important goal for HL-LHC computing. Unlike CPU, the requirements for which
will become approximately constant once the LHC reaches its design luminosity, storage needs will continue
to increase during the lifetime of the HL-LHC. And while opportunistic computational resources exist,
opportunistic storage does not. Innovative ideas for optimizing storage by breaking out of the disk/tape paradigm
to a finer grained spectrum of storage cost-reliability-latency are being pursued. In particular, the US-driven
ATLAS data carousel project is developing a mechanism to stage data (such as AODs) from tape to a sliding
window disk buffer when they are required for processing, reducing by 50% or more the input sample volume
resident on disk. The data carousel leverages the managed ‘train production’ approach already utilized by ATLAS
to drive a tightly integrated orchestration of workflow and workload management that processes data with
file-level granularity as soon as it appears from tape, keeping its disk residency to a minimum. With tape facilities
at only ~10 sites, and processing resources distributed across over 100 sites, remote processing requiring remote
data delivery is an essential element of the approach.

Remote data delivery reliant on powerful networks will in general be essential to minimize data replication
and disk storage footprint while fully utilizing distributed processing resources. In order to most efficiently use
bandwidth and minimize latencies, ATLAS (largely US ATLAS) is developing new services and workflows to
deliver across the network only the data needed by the consuming workload, with fine granularity that avoids the
inefficiencies and latencies of data pre-staging and enables the use of processing resources to be highly dynamic
while remaining efficient. The intelligent data delivery service (iDDS) provides support for such fine-grained
workflows, with its ServiceX component providing intelligent data transformations and filters to deliver just the
needed data.

As a rough guide as to the network bandwidth that facilities in US CMS will require in the HL-LHC era for
the purpose of reconstructing the raw data and producing corresponding simulation datasets, one can take the
following estimate: from the 250 PB of raw data collected per year, about 40% (e.g., 100 PB) is expected to be
reconstructed in the US. It is desired that these large-scale reconstruction campaigns take approximately 10
weeks, implying a data input rate to processing facilities of 10 PB/week, and an output rate of 4 PB/week. In
parallel, simulation production campaigns will be executed continuously throughout the year, producing another
40% of the total 240 PB of output data (e.g., 96 PB) to be persisted on tape and/or disk storage within the US. In
total, these workflows will require a sustained rate of up to 130 Gbps between processing and storage facilities. To
account for burst traffic, and to support data analysis workloads at AFs discussed below, it is desired that all major
processing facilities, namely the Fermilab Tier-1 and US CMS Tier-2 centers, are provisioned to 400 Gbps.

6.12.2.5.1 Analysis Facilities
A significant user-facing component of HL-LHC computing is distributed physics analysis, which is expected to
be centered at a variety of AFs. These are dedicated pieces of infrastructure designed to provide access to large
data sets and computational resources that enable rapid iterative analysis of physics data. Figure 3 shows how
the Analysis Facility concept fits into the Data Lakes model. The AF is a relatively new concept discussed within
IRIS-HEP, HSF, and WLCG. A motivation for this concept is the fact that columnar analysis of data formats like
the NanoAOD promise to provide a very large increase in data analysis speed, as measured in number of events
analyzed per second. Typical analyses of MiniAOD in Run 2 achieve processing rates O(10Hz) while columnar
analysis of NanoAOD promises to achieve O(1–10kHz) or more, both per hyperthread. As such, these new
processing paradigms allow an interactive feel. The AF enables physicist users to interact with their data in a

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 300

scalable way without sending several-hour-long batch jobs and waiting for their completion before digesting the
results and preparing the next iteration. Several salient features are:

 • One or more analysis software frameworks that take care of selecting the appropriate data access
 method, planning the query, and scaling out the resulting workflow to be executed. At present,
 users are largely responsible for hand-crafting each of these components.

 ° Data access and query planning may also involve requesting data from the edge of a data
 lake nearby to the AF, potentially through the ServiceX platform. This pattern is much the
 same as predicate pushdown in local clusters, but targeting a reduction of WAN bandwidth.

 • A modern user interface such as JupyterHub, while still retaining shell and scriptable access
 through well-designed APIs

 • Facility hardware, provided by the US CMS operations program, including high-performance
 disk or NVMe caches and sufficient processing capabilities to provide a target “15-minute
 HL-LHC analysis turnaround time on NanoAOD”

 Figure 6.12.5: Depicts the AFs concept, how it fits into Data Lakes Model, and lists some of its features.

At present, it is assumed that the Tier-2 network requirements as specified above will be sufficient to support AFs
at the Tier-2s. A user at an AF may expect to process a year’s worth of MiniAOD data and simulation (27 PB) in
a timescale of a week. If the data are not cached at the AF, that amounts to a sustained 400 Gbps network load
from the data origin site. In practice, it is unlikely a user would read the entirety of the data catalog, though the
exact fraction will vary significantly depending on the analysis goals. From Run2 experience, a typical analysis
requires between 5–30% of a given data release version’s data. As long as the use of a lake-edge query service
such as ServiceX is structured such that it uses MiniAOD as an add-on to NanoAOD rather than as a replacement
of NanoAOD, the IO requirements of ServiceX will probably be within 100 Gbps steady state and 400 Gbps burst
capacity during the first three-year running period of HL-LHC. The reasoning is as follows: 10% of 27PB for an
annual MINI version is 3PB. Reading this 10% in a week is a more modest 40 Gbps. If MiniAOD information was
added only to a subset of filtered events, or only a few floats per event needed to be fetched via the WAN, then
the bandwidth requirements could be very comfortably within the 400 Gbps burst capacity.

6.12.2.5.2 Inference As a Service
A novel network requirement CMS expects in the HL-LHC era is sourced from planned use of a disaggregated
CPU-GPU architecture that allows to dynamically adjust the number of GPUs that facilities will require as the
reconstruction software evolves to incorporate more algorithms amenable to GPU acceleration. These algorithms,
presently in development, fall into two classes: ML algorithms for reconstruction trained on simulated data; or
classical algorithms rewritten within performance portability frameworks such as Sycl or Alpaka. The SONIC

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 301

project has introduced a module that extends CMS reconstruction software to asynchronously send subsets of
input data to a remote server with GPUs running the Nvidia Triton service for processing. It is an open question
whether these coprocessors will only be located within the LAN or if CPU workflows running on a site can
offload portions of the tasks to GPUs at another site over the WAN. In the latter case, it must be understood if
the latency and bandwidth permits the CPU workflows to continue with good efficiency while waiting for the
inference result to be returned.

6.12.2.6 Remote Science Activities
The HL-LHC computing infrastructure is inherently distributed. In other sections ATLAS has described the
LHC computing model, with a central site at CERN (the Tier-0) and national scale centers around the globe
(Tier-1s) as well as many regional centers (Tier-2s). This basic model is being evolved to meet the needs of
HL-LHC, and it will certainly augment this infrastructure with additional resources that might be used, like HPC
sites, commercial and research clouds and additional institutional resources. In practice you can consider all users
as “remote” and almost all the resources that they use to pursue their science goals as “remote.”

6.12.2.7 Software Infrastructure
6.12.2.7.1 ATLAS
The ATLAS Distributed Computing (ADC) system and organization today is a sophisticated ensemble of software
systems, computing facilities and people that make it possible for ATLAS processing to run 24x7x365 on about
750k cores (in 2024) across over 100 worldwide sites and a wide range of resource types including grid clusters,
HPCs, LCFs and clouds, processing in total about 2.8 exabytes (in 2024) of data per year.

The new HL-LHC directed capabilities and workflows described in previous sections are being developed on
the proven and scalable foundation of this system, particularly the PanDA workload management system, Prodsys
production management system and the Rucio distributed DMS (which were described in Section 6.9).

Beginning with Run 1 in the case of PanDA and Run 2 with ProdSys and Rucio, these systems have met the
capability and scaling requirements of ATLAS, and have steadily been enhanced and hardened based on
running experience. ATLAS has confidence that they have the scalability and robustness to continue to serve
ATLAS through Run 4. Hence ATLAS has been able to focus on adding new HL-LHC directed capability to
these systems.

PanDA, ProdSys and Rucio are being extended for the demands of HL-LHC in such projects as the data carousel
and the intelligent data delivery service (iDDS). Rucio has been adopted as the LHC and WLCG standard. The
iDDS service is in production use ATLAS and was developed to support fine-grained workflows like the ATLAS
data carousel. ServiceX is being developed in a joint effort between ATLAS and IRIS-HEP to support fine-
grained workflows with intelligent data transformations and filters to dynamically deliver just the needed analysis
data across the network, where and when it is needed. While iDDS and ServiceX both work in close concert with
ADC services like PanDA and Rucio, they are implemented as experiment-agnostic services.

6.12.2.7.2 CMS
At present, it is expected that a large portion of the software infrastructure described in Case Study 10 and 11
will continue to be used in the HL-LHC era. Notably, CMS and ATLAS now both use Rucio data management
software, and have for some time both used the CERN FTS. A notable difference between the two collaborations
is that CMS more heavily relies on streaming data from storage endpoints to remote processing centers via the
XRootD protocol. CMS is currently re-evaluating its workflow management infrastructure solution, which may
lead to changes in network usage patterns if a new system is adopted.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 302

6.12.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
For the HL-LHC era, the predictions show a mismatch between the computing and storage resources the
experiments can afford versus the resources needed to reach science goals. In response to this gap, the
experiments are exploring alternatives in how to utilize storage, computing and network infrastructure. The
network baseline currently being planned is composed of terabit-scale (1–2 Tbps) backbone networks with the
largest resource sites connected at multiple 400G scale (800 Gbps+). Network use will be at least a factor of 10
larger than Run 3.

Global R&E network use will have different characteristics on the timescale of the HL-LHC, compared to the
situation the WLCG experienced in Runs 1, 2, and 3. Specifically, the experiments foresee other science domains
(astronomy, biology, engineering, and others) becoming global network users at scales equaling or exceeding the
LHC users. In such an environment, it is not wise to assume the experiments can continue to treat the network
as an infinite resource . The LHC community must explore options for effectively operating within a bandwidth
constrained environment.

For HL-LHC four main requirements have been identified:

 • Capacity: Run 3 is moving to multiple 100G links for large sites, while Run 4 (HL-LHC) is
 targeting Tbps links, perhaps based upon either 400G or 800G waves.

 ° Capacity is fundamental for science at HL-LHC scales.

 ° As noted, in a capacity constrained environment, it will be important to manage the
 capacity to do the most science possible.

 • Capability: It is necessary to understand the impact of new features in networking (SDN/NFV)
 by testing, prototyping and evaluating impact. The experiments will need to evolve applications,
 facilities and computing models to meet the HL-LHC challenges; it will take time.

 ° Traffic shaping activities underway in the Research Network Technical WG are a good
 capability example.

 ° Network orchestration between sites is another good example and something that could
 help us more effectively exploit available resources.

 • Visibility: As the ESnet Blueprinting meetings have shown, the ability to understand WAN
 network flows is limited. New methods to mark and monitor network use are needed.

 ° Packet marking is viewed as a high priority so that everyone (experiments, sites and
 R&E networks) can understand the origin and intent of network flows at any point along
 their path.

 ° The LHC community needs better mechanisms to coordinate the available monitoring
 resources from the sites, experiments and networks, to allow us to have a better
 understanding of how complex infrastructures are using the network.

 • Testing: Developing, prototyping, and testing network features at suitable scale will be needed.
 ° Networks of the future will likely have new features, capabilities and services that could be
 leveraged to do more with the resources that are available.

 ° The LHC community challenge is identifying which features might be beneficial to try
 to integrate into operations, noting that such integration can require significant effort
 to realize.

 ° Having at-scale network testbeds will be very important to understand the potential impact
 changes might have on operations.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 303

These requirements should also motivate and guide network infrastructure upgrades and replacements and it will
be critical to understand the bigger picture of R&E networking and its evolution, to ensure the experiments are
able to take advantage of capacity and services available.

6.12.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.12.2.9.1 Cloud Services
As demonstrated in the ATLAS-Google project in 2022-23 and also in a smaller project with Amazon,
PanDA+Rucio can use commercial cloud resources interchangeably with grid-based WLCG resources and also
integrate new setups for interactive and parallel data analysis. Bulk MC production with bursts of up to 100k
concurrently running jobs in Google Cloud have been demonstrated. The baseline plan for HL-LHC is to use
grid and HPC resources. If some grid resources are set up as cloud resources, they will also be used. ATLAS will
require a good network pipe between grid sites and commercial clouds when used. In this model, the network
needs will be similar to university-based US Tier-2 sites.

CMS expects to have the ability to make use of Cloud resources, but at present, budgets to do so are not present,
given the current business models of cloud providers. It is unclear whether or not such budgets will exist in
the future. CMS has in the past evaluated the use of commercial cloud both for processing, and for TA transfer.
US CMS finds that both are not cost-effective, at present. Experimentation has shown that making large-scale
use of cloud resources if the cost structure were to change is possible. A key component of the cloud cost
structure that makes this approach unattractive is the egress bandwidth charges. If ESnet were to be able to
negotiate a favorable peering arrangement with cloud providers, the cost competitiveness of cloud resources
would increase substantially.

6.12.2.9.2 AI and ML
From the ATLAS Run3 software and computing paper: ML is used in a wide range of applications in ATLAS,
including physics analysis, simulation and physics object identification within the reconstruction and trigger
system. Models trained for classification and regression, as well as generative models, are core components of the
software and analysis chain.

During the HL-LHC era, it is expected that AI/ML tools and techniques will be used more frequently than
is done during Run 3. The need for GPU resources will grow beyond the current levels provided by private
local institutional resources . ATLAS is using GPU resources at NERSC HPC using a small but growing GPU
allocation for AI/ML training.

As discussed in section 4, CMS plans to offload a portion of the event reconstruction algorithms to GPUs, both
via ML and classical algorithms. The use of ML within CMS for reconstruction and data analysis is very well
advanced, and underpins many of the major measurements and searches for new physics the collaboration has
performed over the past years. A full review of these uses is outside the scope of this document.

Usage of ML within CMS workflow and data management, in contrast, is less well developed. R&D initiatives
are underway to rectify this situation, with goals of reduced resource usage and personnel requirements through
automation. ML anomaly detection approaches are actively being investigated for DQM in CMS as well, and
some lessons learned from these activities may also be useful for monitoring computing infrastructure.

6.12.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
No wireless capability studies or capability upgrades are planned at present since wireless use cases are only
users accessing remote services that do the actual data operations.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 304

6.12.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
One interesting option to explore on the timescale of HL-LHC is the joint ATLAS and CMS use of Rucio for
distributed data management. This could provide a mechanism to interact with ESnet (and other R&E
networks), communicating near-term data-movement intents and perhaps negotiating for any required QoS or
deadline requirements.

There have been significant efforts made to understand the computing and storage requirements for HL-LHC.
The process began by extrapolating current methods forward, accounting for the data increases from HL-LHC
and the additional complexity associated with high-luminosity operations of the collider. Further assumptions
about the initially conservative estimates of computing and storage capacities would be increased for fixed cost
and additionally assumed the notion of a “flat budget” for the foreseeable future.

To decrease the gap, significant efforts were made to better optimize how less resources could be utilized to
do the same amount of science. This has helped decrease the difference between what is needed and what is
affordable. While there are potentially some optimistic assumptions in this estimate, it is known that the planning
process must change to ensure resource availability on the time scale of HL-LHC. At this point there is still
a significant gap in the amount of storage believed to be needed versus what can be provisioned with current
budget projections.

Another concern is the potential constraints in R&E network capacity on the timescale of the HL-LHC. One of
the options that has been considered in addressing the gap in resources noted above, is taking more advantage of
high-performance networks to help reduce storage requirements. However, this implicitly assumes the network
continues to be unconstrained and free of cost to the HL-LHC collaborations. As noted elsewhere, network
providers serving global high energy physics collaborations have been very successful in providing network
capacities beyond the requirements of existing use cases, giving collaborations whatever bandwidths they have
required. This is likely not going to be feasible for the HL-LHC era, not because of the significant growth in
HL-LHC data, but, rather due to the expected rise in use from other global, data-intensive science domains.

The LHC collaborations have not faced such an environment to date and, if such a situation were to arise, the
tools or methodologies to work effectively are not present. Capabilities like SENSE/Rucio, NOTED, and others,
will help to provide potentially critical capabilities for a potential oversubscribed network environment.

ESnet and the LHC experiments (ATLAS and CMS) have started an R&D project that makes use of in-network
data caches operated by ESnet using XRootD software. The pilot project focuses on caching of PHYSLITE data
products to see if the time to reach physics results can be shorted, and the overall network traffic reduced for data
analysis (only used parts of data files cached and reused).

6.12.2.11 Data Mobility Endpoints
On the timescale of HL-LHC, it is expected that the LHC experiments will evolve their computing models,
hardware, software and architecture, guided by mini-challenges and the two remaining WLCG Network Data
Challenges. So, even though “Data Mobility Endpoints” (e.g., Globus nodes or DTNs) are not currently a central
component of the experiment’s architecture, they could very well become a core component of WLCG. US
ATLAS has already developed a proof of concept to use Rucio to manage transfers via Globus. US ATLAS, Rucio
Core team and HEP-CCE (w/ HEP-CCE contributing a python code developer) are all collaborating testing such
a setup at scale. This will be driven by architecture evolutions coupled with testing and at-scale validation. One
side effect is that it may make WLCG infrastructure more compatible with other global science infrastructures.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 305

6.12.2.12 Outstanding Issues
The individual LHC experiments are interested in discussing the set of features that must be present in future
network designs. If it is possible to identify a minimum set of capabilities in switches and routers, to ensure the
next generation of network components can meet the needs of the community, it would simplify the procurement
and installation process. The sooner those capabilities are in place, the sooner prototyping and testing future
capabilities will be possible.

Another important consideration is how to identify appropriate hardware and software configurations that can be
used to optimize the ability to use the procured resources. In many cases, the information about such tunings can
easily apply to many science domains and sharing the work to test and benchmark across different components
would benefit all the LHC experiments and beyond.

6.13 Super Cryogenic Dark Matter Search (SuperCDMS SNOLAB)
Numerous astrophysical and cosmological observations indicate that nearly 85% of the mass content of the
universe does not emit electromagnetic radiation at any wavelength, therefore being called dark matter. The
composition of dark matter is unknown, and its properties imply that it cannot be made of known elementary
particles. For this reason, dark matter is one of the strongest evidences of new fundamental physics. To
date, experiments have set stringent constraints on the existence of dark matter particles with masses in the
GeV regime, but the sub-GeV regime, that is also well-motivated from the theoretical side, has been much
less explored.

SuperCDMS SNOLAB is a next-generation experiment aiming to detect sub-GeV dark matter particles. In the
spring of 2015, SuperCDMS SNOLAB was selected by the DOE and the NSF as one of the three Generation
2 dark matter experiments. SuperCDMS SNOLAB is an experiment funded and operated under the DOE OS
HEP program in the Cosmic Frontier, and co-funded by NSF. Non-US funding is provided through the CFI, and
other smaller funding resources.

6.13.1 Discussion Summary
The LAN connectivity for SNOLAB is 2 x 10 Gbps, and the WAN connectivity consists of a 1 Gbps link that
is also shared with 10 other experiments. This limitation implies that SuperCDMS must plan to work within
a budget of no more than 10% of either of these connections during operation. This link allows SNOLAB to
reach Laurentian University, which is then connected to ORION (the provincial R&E network of Ontario),
and CANARIE (the national R&E network of Canada). CANARIE peers with ESnet, which facilitates the
connectivity to reach SLAC. The network limitations were explored during a project review in 2022, at the
time the cost was considered too high to upgrade the 1 Gbps WAN link, which will cause the experiments that
share this resource to be more austere in their use. SuperCDMS will consider this in the design of their trigger
mechanism, and computing and storage strategy. ESnet can discuss options with SuperCDMS regarding the use
of other connectivity options.

6.13.2 SuperCDMS: Experiment Profile
SuperCDMS SNOLAB consists of an array of monocrystalline germanium and silicon detectors operating at
cryogenic temperatures (~30 mK). Particle interactions occurring in SuperCDMS SNOLAB detectors produce
recoiling nuclei or electrons, that in turn create prompt phonons (quanta of vibrations of the crystalline structure)
and ionization charges. An external electric field is applied over the detector volume to drift the ionization
charges that produce additional phonons through the Neganov-Trofimov-Luke (NTL) effect. The detectors are
classified in two categories depending on their instrumentation: 1) iZIP detectors, that measure both phonon and
ionization charge signals, enabling enhanced background rejection; and 2) high-voltage detectors, that measure
the NTL phonons from charges drifting in an increased electric field, enabling lower energy thresholds.118, 119

6.13.2.1 Science Background
The SuperCDMS SNOLAB experiment is currently in the installation phase at SNOLAB (Canada), 2 km
underground. Commissioning is expected to start in fall 2025, and science operations are expected to start at the
beginning of 2026 and to last for at least three years, leaving open the possibility of upgrades (more detectors and/
or new technology in order to leverage the cryogenic facility).

119 P. N. Luke et al., Calorimetric ionization detector. Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A 289, 406–409 1990

collaborators), processed data will be also copied on the OSN and the DRAC.

The Collaboration will retain ownership of the data, except for small datasets released in support of publications.

data sets will be also accessible at OSN and DRAC (due to the limited disk resources available). At SLAC, the
SuperCDMS collaboration has ~100 active users from all SuperCDMS institutions. Most collaborators have
accounts both at SLAC and on the Canadian DRAC.

6.13.2.3 IRI Readiness
SuperCDMS SNOLAB is not equipped, so far, to work in an IRI workflow. Its data structure, data taking, and
data-processing patterns are simple enough that the need for advanced solutions has not presented itself, and
would instead require additional personnel and resources that are not accessible with the current funding level.

6.13.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
The SuperCDMS SNOLAB DAQ and Trigger system is based on the MIDAS data acquisition (DAQ) framework,
with off-the-shelf computers and custom trigger electronics. MIDAS is a flexible C++-based DAQ system,
developed at Paul Scherrer Institute and TRIUMF. A custom software package manages all the underlying
custom MIDAS front-ends and clients that control SuperCDMS DAQ hardware, data flow, and triggering system
(which consists of two subsystems, the L1 firmware trigger and the L2 software trigger). These include the Online
Data Base layout, device drivers, and low-level tools for data acquisition.

The DAQ and Trigger system is deployed on a cluster underground in a dedicated subnetwork. The gateway
computer is connected to another dedicated SuperCDMS subnetwork on the surface to allow for data transfers
from underground.

The lifetime goal is to be taking usable dark matter search data 80% of the time. To meet this high rate of
experimental lifetime, the SNOLAB DQM system is designed to (1) promptly alert shifters as problems arise
and (2) provide efficient access to data needed during debugging. In addition, data-quality information is used in
the offline analysis to determine which data are reprocessed for science results and to inform analyzers of
special conditions during particular runs. The DQM system is located on the underground cluster and it is
mirrored on the surface and at SLAC.

The DAQ and DQM systems have redundant disk space both underground and on the surface. The surface
server is used as data buffer, data transfer, underground database mirroring, and DQM.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 311

Both the surface and underground computers have enough disk space to host about 3 weeks of data in case
network problems occur. Additional surface resources include experimental control workstations for on-site
shifters, a disk and CPU allocation on the shared SNOLAB Nearline Computing System, and lightweight virtual
machines provided by SNOLAB IT.

On the surface, the data are automatically transferred to SLAC.

The raw data, in compressed MIDAS format, will be processed at SLAC, and the reconstructed output data, in
ROOT format, can be directly used for data analyses. Collaborators will access and analyze processed data stored
at SLAC using local computing resources. The data will also be transferred from SLAC to Fermilab, where it will
be stored on tape for additional backup. Simulated data are generated at Texas A&M, transferred to SLAC, and
then transferred to Fermilab for tape backup and to other sites as needed.

The estimated data volume is 350 TB/year, including calibration data and simulated data.

SLAC is the leading lab for the computing of the experiment, and it will host the full set of data (real and
simulated), supports data processing, data analysis, user accounts, and web applications, including job
management and bookkeeping. SLAC also hosts the public website, and collaborative tools. All SuperCDMS
applications at SLAC are containerized and deployed through Kubernetes.

Software releases are deployed as Apptainer containers and are used at all participating SuperCDMS institutions
for data analysis, software development, processing, and data simulation.

The major packages for simulation, reconstruction and calibration are written in C++ OO. Simulations are based
on the Geant4 toolkit, and in particular SuperCDMS developed the open source Geant4 package G4CMP120 to
simulate the phonon and charge transport in cryogenic semiconductor crystals. SuperCDMS also has extensive
software written in python to support workflows and analysis.

The full chain, from data acquisition, data transfers, data processing and analysis has been tested through data
challenges and a test run with a quarter of the final detector payload at the Cryogenic Underground TEst Facility
at SNOLAB (CUTE) facility121. All the stages, from data taking to making the processed data accessible to the
analyzers are automated and functional.

6.13.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
SuperCDMS SNOLAB will not rely on SNOLAB for data analysis. Data analysis will happen primarily at SLAC,
DRAC, the OSN, NSF ACCESS facilities, and at other smaller institutions.

Data are going to be processed at SLAC to extract quantities that can be directly used in physics analyses. During
data processing, reconstruction software will extract various quantities from the raw pulses such as the pulse
amplitude, area and start time, that provide information of the deposited energy and the interaction position
within the detectors. These quantities from the processing are stored in Reduced Quantities files. After the data
processing, the analyzers are going to apply a set of cuts to select only the relevant data for dark matter searches.
A complete background model (including radiogenic, cosmic, and cavern sources) is being developed and it will
be generated using DRAC resources while detector response simulation production based on Geant4 will happen
at Texas A&M. After that, SuperCDMS SNOLAB analyzers will compare the processed data with the simulated
background model, with a profile likelihood ratio statistic test.

120 Nuclear Instruments and Methods A 1055 (2023) 168473 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05998)
121 “CUTE: A Cryogenic Underground TEst Facility at SNOLAB,” https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.07930 , 2023

6.13.2.6 Remote Science Activities
The main network connections are going to be between:

 • SNOLAB underground laboratory to SNOLAB surface (raw data)
 • SNOLAB surface to SLAC, through the ORION network
 • SLAC to Fermilab (tape backup site for all data, raw, processed, simulated)
 • SLAC to OSN and DRAC (secondary sites for analysis, transfer of main processed datasets and
 other data on demand)

 • Texas A&M to SLAC (simulated data)
In addition to that, SuperCDMS SNOLAB has some database replication between SNOLAB and SLAC that will
require network usage. While the amount of replication data should be considered negligible, it may not actually
be so for the limited bandwidth at SNOLAB toward the rest of the world.

6.13.2.7 Software Infrastructure
Data transfers between SuperCDMS sites happen with a variety of tools, depending on the availability of such
tools at the source or destination site.

SNOLAB is minimally equipped with software (no Globus, XRootD, …) and each experiment has a dedicated
subnetwork with limited bandwidth. Given the small amount of data that SuperCDMS will move from SNOLAB
to SLAC, automated transfer tools based on rsync (single stream) with the option to move to bbcp (multiple
streams, 4 by default) are currently in use, if needed. The limited outgoing bandwidth and the single destination
make the use of such simple approaches ideal for this scenario.

SLAC is fully equipped with every possible transfer tool and SuperCDMS uses a variety of those. Transfers
between SLAC and Texas A&M happen via Globus.

Transfers between SLAC and OSN happen via S3 (other technologies can be available).

Transfers between SLAC and DRAC happen via rsync, Globus or https (small datasets ~10–100TB).

Transfers between SLAC and Fermilab have not been tested yet but SuperCDMS has a large choice of tools, from
rsync to Globus.

6.13.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
The network link from underground to the surface is made of 2 x 10 Gbps aggregate links shared by about 10
experiments. Only ~0.2% is expected to be needed by SuperCDMS during peak usage. From the surface, the
data are copied to SLAC through the SNOLAB network link to the ORION of 1 Gbps. From there, ESnet
routes become available and, given the amount of data moved, SuperCDMS does not generally experience
any problems.

Once the data reaches SLAC, all subsequent main data transfers happen between SLAC and other laboratories
with very large network capabilities (Fermilab, Texas A&M, OSN, DRAC).

6.13.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.13.2.9.1 Cloud Services
SuperCDMS SNOLAB will make minimal or no use of cloud storage. Only a few services will be cloud-based,
these include Slack and GitLab.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 313

6.13.2.9.2 AI and ML
SLAC is building support for the execution of AI/ML workflows with substantial investment in GPU.
SuperCDMS SNOLAB reconstruction working group (WG) is looking into taking advantage of the GPUs for
event reconstruction. TensorFlow is also used in some analyses. One use case is for datasets severely limited by
noise coming from vibrations. With ML we can remove the noise effectively while saving the low energy signal
events, which are important for low-mass data management (DM) search. The same method can be used to
predict the energy deposited in the crystals, which works well in low energies where other techniques do not
perform well.

6.13.2.9.3 Wireless or Distributed Location Science Activities
SuperCDMS SNOLAB does not require any connectivity to be provided by wireless or satellite connectivity, but
could investigate this as an optional back-up strategy.

6.13.2.10 Data-Related Resource Constraints
The network link at SNOLAB from underground to surface (2 x 10 Gbps) is sufficient for the needs of the facility
but it is subject to instabilities and interruptions, while the outgoing SNOLAB network is limited to a 1 Gbps
link.

While there are no plans yet, SNOLAB is looking into upgrading the outgoing bandwidth to 10 Gbps.

Once the data reaches the US network the data distribution and accessibility problem becomes the dominant one.

Limitations are imposed by the various sites depending on firewall rules, use of VPNs, and MFA requirements
that often limit the amount of automation of the transfer tools. The lack of uniformity in the availability of tools
(e.g., not all sites have Globus endpoints) and the different network protection stances also imply the need to
develop data transfer tools tailored for each site. For a computing group of a small experiment like SuperCDMS,
the lack of standardization creates additional overhead.

6.13.2.12 Outstanding Issues
The network connectivity between SNOLAB and SLAC is a critical component, given that all workflows and
all scientific analysis happen off-site. And in particular, the bandwidth bottleneck between SNOLAB and the
ORION network could present a challenge in the future if there are no upgrades to the bandwidth, given the
tendency of data volumes from current and future experiments to grow rather than shrink.

In case of extensive, site-wide outages at SLAC, while SuperCDMS has on-site storage for a few weeks of
data taking, it would also be important to have another data path from SNOLAB to an alternative computation
site, namely DRAC and/or Texas A&M, in order to not interrupt the processing flow. The criteria needed to
temporarily switch from SLAC to another site for storage and processing needs to be carefully evaluated and the
process tested.

Finally, SuperCDMS need to also ensure the flow of processed data to secondary storage sites (OSN and DRAC).

6.14 Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS) Experiment
AMS is a precision particle physics detector installed on the ISS in May 2011, conducting a unique, long-duration
mission of fundamental physics research in space. Figure 6.14.1 shows AMS on the ISS.

6.14.1 Discussion Summary
Due to limitations in the available bandwidth that TDRS can deliver, and the number of use cases that exist on
the ISS, AMS is only able to access about 14Mbps of space-to-ground transmission. This limitation has not forced
the adoption of high-speed data migration tools, as the data volumes will always remain small for this aspect of
the workflow. NASA has been evaluating if the use of other satellite technologies (e.g., Starlink) could serve as an
augmented communication mechanism, or a replacement for TDRS, but this would not be something AMS has
any control over.

The AMS project creates a large number of simulations during their process of science, over 20PB have been
produced since the start of the project. With the pending upgrade to AMS hardware in the coming years, it is
anticipated that all produced MC will have to be reprocessed.

AMS occupies a unique space in the HEP portfolio, and is capturing a valuable set of research data that is not
replicable on earth at the current time.

 • AMS is a precision particle physics detector installed on the ISS in May 2011, conducting
 a unique, long-duration mission of fundamental physics research in space. It is the largest
 instrument, and is scheduled to run until the ISS project ends, currently expected to be after
 2030. Since 2011, AMS has collected more than 200 billion events. [Section 4.1]

 • Construction, integration, testing and operation of the AMS is carried out by an international

 and organizations from 14 countries. [Section 4.1]

 • AMS produces ~40 TB of raw data per year, which are transmitted to CERN, and then

 there are changes to reconstruction software. [Section 4.2]

 • Each version of full reproduction is called ”pass.” Currently, AMS acquired over 500 TB of raw
 data, from which a 2PB of pass 8 data were produced and copied to collaborators institutions for

6.14.2.4 Instruments and Facilities
AMS has more than 300K readout channels and 1500 temperature sensors. The acquisition rate goes up to 2 kHz.
There are more than 500 microprocessors onboard which reduce data rate from 7 Gbps to 10 Mb/s. Data taken
on board of the ISS by AMS consist of raw events, where each event is the collection of the information read out
from relevant AMS sub-detectors electronics after the latter are triggered by particle(s) crossing AMS sensitive
volumes. Raw events are logically grouped in sequences called runs, each run having a unique 32 bit identifier.
Events inside one run are numbered in sequence.

Every quarter of the orbit a scientific run starts. The duration of each run corresponds to 23 minutes, and every
run contains on average 700k events. On orbits which are close to the Earth magnetic poles, the number of events
in a run can exceed 2 million. The average size of raw event is 2 KB, thus yearly raw data yield is 40 TB.

On top of this data volume additional calibration information, like the AMS electronics parameters, as well as
various temperatures, pressures and other health and status data are recorded regularly. This calibration related
information corresponds to less than 1% of the total data volume.

Recorded data are packed to fixed length packets, or frames, and transmitted via the TDRS satellites to ground at
White Sands, NM, and then relayed to NASA MSFC, AL. At MSFC data are firstly transferred to the AMS relay
computers using the UDP protocol and finally to the AMS SOC at CERN, Geneva, Switzerland with bbftp124
software, the latter using multiple Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) streams between client and server to
speed up data transfer. The sustained transferring speed from MSFC to SOC up to 50 Mbit/sec is achieved.

Data arrived at SOC are de-framed and checked for consistency. Then events are indexed and reassembled
into the AMS raw files, one file per run. Resulted files are moved to permanent storage and registered in the
AMS database.

The AMS Data Production, i.e., massive data reconstruction is organized in two stages. Firstly, freshly arrived
data are put into first production. It runs in a fully automated manner and produces the data summary files for the
quick detector performance evaluation. The detector performance is monitored in 24/7 regime at AMS POCC at
CERN. First production requires computing power of ~450 CPU cores (including 100% contingency) to cope
with the data rate and to ensure nearly real-time processing. Usually, the reconstructed data are available for the
analysis in two hours after the raw data arrive in SOC.

The data summary files from the first production are used subsequently to produce detector calibrations,
which are required for second production. Second production uses all the available calibrations, alignments
and ancillary data from the ISS as well as monitoring values (temperatures, pressures, and voltages) to produce
physics analysis ready dataset. Second production usually runs every six months incrementally. However, in case
there are significant changes in reconstruction software, a full reproduction may be needed.

Each version of full reproduction, performed with updated software is called “pass.” Currently, pass 8 data are
available for analysis. Second production uses the computing power of both CERN and remote computing
centers. Data transfer between CERN and remote computing centers are performed with GridFTP and bbftp
protocols. Calibration data are also available via cvmfs125.

The typical AMS raw file size is 1.5 GB, while the AMS data file in pass 8 production is 7 GB. At the moment,
there are 250K pass 8 files were produced.

124 Farrache G. bbftp. URL: http://ccweb.in2p3.fr/bbftp
125 cvmfs . URL: https://cvmfs.readthedocs.io/en/stable/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 322

By the end of 2025, AMS will undergo a significant upgrade on the ISS, carried out by astronauts. This upgrade
will involve the addition of a new tracker layer at the top of the instrument, as illustrated in Figure 3. The new
layer will enhance the instrument’s acceptance of high energy particles by 300% and increase the AMS sensitivity
to high-Z nuclei. These advancements are essential for progressing dark matter searches and improving
precision measurements of sub-Iron nuclei, which play a crucial role in refining cosmic-ray propagation models.
Additionally, they enable the study of rare and exotic particles, such as strange quark matter, heavy antimatter
nuclei, and supersymmetry (SUSY)T particles.

The new configuration of AMS will require a complete overhaul of simulations and data analysis tools, which
will be developed over the next three to five years. Additionally, a new data analysis and computing center at
UH Manoa, USA, will be established within the next two to three years. This center will handle extensive MC
simulations, data production, and analyses. With both the current and upgraded geometries requiring simulated
datasets, the total volume of data is expected to increase to 50 PB over the next five years.

 Figure 6.14.3: AMS instrument with new layer 0 added to the existing nine tracker layers

6.14.2.5 Generalized Process of Science
The general process of science is described in the previous section. Data are either reconstructed from AMS or
simulated. Both are managed by SOC team at CERN. Raw data proceed through two stages of reconstruction,
and analysis tuples after the second stage are available for transfer and offline analysis across the collaboration.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 323

 Figure 6.14.4: AMS data Levels. Level 1 data are raw data reconstructed from frame files. Level 2
 data are produced with information from raw data and Detector Calibrations. Level 3 data, both for the
 actual detector and MC, include the number of particles per second (particle rates) of specific species
 with detector efficiency information to calculate the final flux. Level 4 data are the final product of the
 analysis, including flux and systematic errors, ready for publication.

The first stage of production is performed at AMS SOC and takes two or three hours after data frames are
de-framed by checking raw events for consistency. Then, raw files are assembled, validated, and registered
in the database as AMS Level 1 data, as shown in Figure 3. One raw file corresponds to one AMS run. The
production jobs assemble data in ROOT files and Time-Dependent Variables (TDV) files. TDV files contain the
environmental variables that are important for data analysis: for example, the temperature variations of the silicon
Tracker sensors affect the alignment parameters and particle tracking efficiency. TDV files are stored on the
Andrew File Service (AFS) and published to CVMFS weekly.

The AMS Level 1 data are processed every six months with a delay of 1 to 7 months since acquisition to create
AMS Level 2 data. To produce Level 2 data, all the information in the TDV files, including detector calibrations,
is necessary. MC simulations for all particle species are produced in parallel at Level 2. The AMS Level 3 data
are generated by different groups, each of them selecting and analyzing different particle species at different time
scales. Level 3 data includes the number of particles per second (particle rates) of specific species with detector
efficiency information to calculate the final flux. Level 3 data are produced for both real detector data and MC
data. Depending on the type of particle, Level 3 is produced with a time lag ranging anywhere from one to two
years after acquisition. The AMS Level 4 data include full analysis of particle spectra after detector efficiency
studies, MC corrections, and systematic error calculations. Extensive analyses and crosschecks between different
groups are necessary to produce the Level 4 data that are finally ready for publication. Level 4 data are produced
with a time lag of two to five years after acquisition. The software to generate Level 3 and Level 4 is not shared
between the groups within the AMS collaboration; each group develops its own software independently.

6.14.2.6 Remote Science Activities
The AMS data arrives at CERN (Geneve), de-framed and processed at AMS SOC, making available detector
calibrations. AMS SOC transfers raw data with calibrations to remote centers, listed in Table 1 for distributed
production of AMS Level 2 data. After production all data are copied back to CERN, stored at EOS and archived
on CTA. The full reprocessing of current AMS dataset takes about 1 month using 35,000-40,000 CPU cores.
Between rounds of AMS data production remote centers are employed for MC simulations of the various cosmic-
ray species interactions with AMS instrument. The simulated events then undergo the same reconstruction
procedure as used for events collected by AMS detector on ISS. These data are also copied to CERN. The
collaborators are free to copy all available data for further analyses.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 324

6.14.2.7 Software Infrastructure
6.14.2.7.1 Data Resource Management
AMS SOC has developed its own software infrastructure to manage the primary data resources, i.e., the data at
CERN. The data arrive at AMS POCC which is located at CERN in the format of “frame” files. The frame files
are shared to AMS SOC by Network File System (NFS). The frame files are de-framed and re-packed into raw
files, and the latter is put into EOS and CTA storage by XRDCP, at the same time, metadata are registered at
Oracle database.

After raw files are registered, automatic job requesting software (also developed by AMS SOC) requests first
production jobs through the Apache webserver. Jobs are distributed by the SOC production server to its
producers, and in case local computing resources are not enough, jobs may be submitted to CERN
LXBATCH computing farm using HTCondor. When first production jobs are done, SOC validating scripts
check the produced ROOT files and copy them to EOS, and these data are backed up to CTA storage using the
FTS platform.

Secondary “pass-N” production shares almost the same procedure except that more data moving may be involved
which will be discussed in the next section.

6.14.2.7.2 Data mobility
Secondary “pass-N” production usually requires data transferring between CERN EOS and remote sites. AMS
used to use Globus and GridFTP for cross-site data moving, but as CERN dropped Globus and GridFTP support,
XRDCP is now used to transfer data across sites.

6.14.2.7.3 Data Process
GBATCH is a common software package, developed by AMS collaboration and used for data production from raw
to AMS Level 2 data and MC simulations. It is linked against ROOT, Geant4, CERNLib, and some other HEP
libraries and serves as a common framework for all collaboration data analyses.

The above-mentioned software tools may evolve over time, however, as AMS uses EOS and CTA as primary data
storage, it is necessary to use the software tools supported by CERN IT.

6.14.2.8 Network and Data Architecture
6.14.2.8.1 The LAN Capabilities
AMS science data, including raw data and ROOT data ready for physics analysis, are stored at CERN EOS, so
there is no LAN capability to be reported.

6.14.2.8.2 The Local Network Configuration
AMS science data, including raw data and ROOT data ready for physics analysis, are stored at CERN EOS, so
there is no local network configuration to be reported.

6.14.2.8.3 Network Bandwidth Connection Speed
AMS science data, including raw data and ROOT data ready for physics analysis, are stored at CERN EOS, so
the connection speed is determined by the bandwidth of CERN computing facilities.

6.14.2.9 Emerging Technology Use
6.14.2.9.1 Cloud Services
AMS does not leverage any commercial cloud services for their computing or storage needs.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 325

7 Technology Profiles
The technical profiles presented in this document are a written record of the current state of support offered by
DOE SC–funded laboratories and user facilities in collaboration with HEP-funded activities. These case studies
were discussed between July 2024 and December 2024. The profiled laboratories and user facilities include:

 • NERSC
 • ALCF
 • OLCF
 • Fermilab
 • BNL
 • SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory
 • ANL
A summary of each will be presented prior to the case study document, along with a “Discussion Summary” that
highlights key areas of conversation from authors and attendees. These brief write-ups are not meant to replace a
full review of the case study, but will provide a snapshot of the discussion and focus during the in-person review.

7.1 NERSC
The mission of NERSC is to accelerate scientific discovery at the DOE OS through HPC and data analysis.

As the primary scientific computing facility for the US DOE SC, NERSC is the principal provider of HPC and
data resources and services. Fundamental to the mission of NERSC is enabling computational science of scale,
in which large, interdisciplinary teams of scientists attack fundamental problems in science and engineering that
require massive calculations and have broad scientific and economic impacts.

7.1.1 Discussion Summary

 • NERSC supplies supercomputing, data storage, networking, auxiliary equipment and technical
 consulting to more than 10,000 users and 1,000 projects conducting research support by
 the DOE SC. NERSC supports approximately 100 HEP projects, both simulation and data
 focused. [Section 4.1]

 • NERSC-10 is expected in the 2027 time frame, and is anticipated to be 10X the aggregate
 performance of Perlmutter. NERSC-10 is expected to offer more flexibility toward assembling
 and composing the required set of capabilities on a per-user basis, will be able to support
 urgent and interactive workflows from DOE SC’s experimental and observational facilities,
 and provide seamless performance across converged networks, accelerators, and storage
 components. [Section 4.1]

 • NERSC features 1 Tbps Aggregate Bandwidth to ESNET via 2 x 400 Gbps links and 2 x 100
 Gbps links. NERSC will be expanding to a 4 x 400 Gbps architecture in future years, in addition
 to considering a migration to 800 Gbps technology. [Section 4.7]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 327

 • For NERSC-10 and beyond, NERSC will consider incorporating “cloud” technologies that add
 significant value to the NERSC user community and are affordable. This approach to provide
 cloud-like services includes NERSC Spin; a container-based platform where users can build
 their own websites, API endpoints, databases, and other network services that can integrate
 with center networks and data storage systems. In the next two to five years, NERSC is
 exploring deeper hybridization of Spin with the HPC system itself, which will open possibilities
 for performing computational tasks in a more cloud-like environment. [Section 4.8]

7.1.2 NERSC: Technology Profile
NERSC supplies supercomputing, data storage, networking, auxiliary equipment and technical consulting to
more than 10,000 users and 1,000 projects conducting research support by the DOE SC.

7.1.2.1 Facilities Operated and Supported
7.1.2.1.1 Computing
Perlmutter is a HPE (Hewlett Packard Enterprise) Cray EX supercomputer, named in honor of Saul Perlmutter,
an astrophysicist at Berkeley Lab who shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for his contributions to research
showing that the expansion of the universe is accelerating.

Perlmutter, based on the HPE Cray Shasta platform, is a heterogeneous system comprising both CPU-only and
GPU-accelerated nodes, with a performance of three to four times the previous Cori system.

Perlmutter consists of 1536 GPU-accelerated nodes with 1 AMD Milan processor and 4 Nvidia A100 GPUs, and
3072 CPU-only nodes with 2 AMD Milan processors.

7.1.2.3 Computational and Storage Infrastructure
NERSC offers a robust infrastructure for efficient data handling, including high-performance DTNs, squid
servers, a dedicated CVMFS cache for each compute node, and Frontier cache130, along with a suite of data
transfer tools such as Globus, XRootD TPC over HTTPS, scp, bbcp, and GridFTP.

The DTNs are specialized servers with dual 100-gigabit Ethernet links for fast external transfers over the
ESnet WAN and 10-gigabit links for internal NERSC transfers. These nodes provide seamless access to storage
resources like the CFS, Perlmutter Scratch and HPSS, ensuring high-speed data movement between NERSC
and external sites.

Globus, as a widely used data transfer tool at NERSC, is configured with specific endpoints to support different
workflows and storage requirements:

 • NERSC DTN: A multi-node endpoint that enables high-speed access to all major NERSC
 file systems, including CFS, Global Homes, Global Common, and Perlmutter Scratch. This
 endpoint is ideal for most transfers into and out of NERSC.

 • NERSC Perlmutter: Another multi-node endpoint similar to NERSC DTN, serving as a backup
 for Perlmutter-related transfers when the primary DTN endpoint is unavailable.

 • NERSC HPSS: A single-node endpoint optimized for direct access to the HPSS tape archive,
 useful for archival data transfers though potentially slower for large volumes.

 • NERSC SHARE: A read-only, single-node endpoint offering access to specific shared file
 systems for data distribution.

 • NERSC S3: Designed for transferring data directly to and from Amazon S3 buckets, facilitating
 cloud integration and hybrid workflows.
Over the next two to five years, NERSC plans to maintain its current suite of data management tools while
leveraging the expected evolution of these tools. As tools evolve, it is anticipated that improved capabilities for
facilitating complex, multifacility workflows, real-time processing, and network QoS adjustments to prioritize
critical data flows will be available.

7.1.2.4 Cloud Services
For NERSC 10 and beyond, NERSC will consider incorporating “cloud” technologies that add significant value
to the NERSC user community and are affordable. The NERSC 10 system itself will be located at Berkeley Lab
in the machine room of Shyh Wang Hall (Building 59).

NERSC Spin, a container-based platform where users can build their own websites, API endpoints,
databases, and other network services that can integrate with center networks and data storage systems.
Over 80 NERSC projects are using Spin to complement their use of batch HPC e.g., data dissemination
to their research communities or to automate complex research workflows. In the next two to five years,
NERSC is exploring deeper hybridization of Spin with the HPC system itself, which will open possibilities for
performing computational tasks in a more cloud-like environment by a) making HPC resources accessible to
containerized workloads and b) providing a platform for NERSC to deploy novel user-facing capabilities such as
Function-as-a-Service

130 https://docs.nersc.gov/services/frontiercache/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 333

7.1.2.5 AI and ML
NERSC has been involved in modern deep learning and AI for the last 10 years. This includes activities related
to deployment of system hardware and software optimized for AI; deep application engagement with science
teams; and broad empowerment of the community, through for example training and schools.

Current examples in this area include deployment of Perlmutter a system with over 7000 A100 GPUs (which was
the optimum AI accelerator at time of deployment) and work with Nvidia and HPE to ensure performant large-
scale deep learning training using NVIDIA Collective Communication Library (NCCL) with HPE slingshot
interconnect. Application engagement has been through for example the NERSC Exascale Scientific Applications
Program (NESAP) that has resulted in multiple publications in domain science and ML venues. Training events
have included over 20 deep learning at-scale tutorials with thousands of participants, including at the SC
conference (and made publicly available) since 2018.

In the next two to five years NERSC-10 will be deployed. This will provide significant improvements in
performance for AI workloads as well as the integration of AI with traditional simulation and data pipelines. This
will be complemented with software and services to facilitate the reuse of AI models, and continued work on
applications, focused on large-scale training and the integration of fine-tuning and inference into science codes.

Starting in this period and moving beyond five years, NERSC’s strategy is towards pervasive AI. This means
enabling AI to accelerate science and HPC operations wherever and whenever it is able to do so. This is expected
to include NERSC being available for the training, hosting and fine-tuning of mission-science ‘foundational’ AI
models as well as AI-ready datasets, but also the operation of highly instrumented “self-driving” HPC systems,
and providing an AI ecosystem for science including AI-assisted interfaces.

7.1.2.8 Data Mobility Endpoints
The DTNs are NERSC servers dedicated to performing transfers between NERSC data storage resources such
as HPSS, the Community File System, Perlmutter Scratch, and storage resources at other sites. These nodes are
being managed (and monitored for performance) as part of a collaborative effort between ESnet and NERSC to
enable high-performance data movement over the high-bandwidth 100 Gb ESnet WAN. The most up-to-date
documentation can be found online.131

7.1.2.8.1 Configuration
All DTNs have :

 • Two 100-gigabit ethernet links for transfers to internet
 • Two 10-gigabit ethernet links to transfer to NERSC internal resources (HPSS)
 • Two FDR IB connections to the global file system
Similar to other NERSC systems, users will maintain their own shell configuration files (“dot files”).

7.1.2.8.2 Access
There are four DTNs available for interactive use (e.g., via ssh) at dtn0[1-4].nersc.gov, and a pool of nodes used
for automated transfer services like Globus.

131 https://docs.nersc.gov/systems/dtn/

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 334

All NERSC users are automatically given access to the DTNs. The nodes support both interactive use via Su–
Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) (direct login) or data transfer using GridFTP services; however, it is recommended to
use Globus for large data transfers.

7.1.2.8.3 Available File Systems
The NERSC DTNs provide access to Global Homes, Global Common, the CFS, Perlmutter Scratch, and HPSS.
On the DTNs Perlmutter Scratch is mounted at /global/pscratch and can be accessed using the $SCRATCH
environment variable.

7.1.2.8.4 File Transfer Software
For most cases, it is recommended to use Globus because it provides the best transfer rates. It makes transfers
trivial so users do not have to learn command line options for manual performance tuning. Globus also does
automatic performance tuning and has been shown to perform comparable to -- or even better (in some cases)
than -- expert-tuned GridFTP. Users can also use GridFTP to transfer large files by hand.

For smaller files you can use Secure Copy (scp) or Secure file transfer protocol (sftp) or rsync to transfer files
between two hosts.

7.1.2.8.5 Restrictions
In order to keep the DTNs performing optimally for data transfers, NERSC requests that users restrict
interactive use of these systems to tasks that are related to preparing data for transfer or are directly related to
data transfer of some form or fashion. Examples of intended usage would be running python scripts to download
data from a remote source, running client software to load data from a file system into a remote database, or
compressing (gzip) or bundling (tar) files in preparation for data transfer. Examples of what should not be done
include running a database on the server to do data processing, or running tests that saturate the nodes resources.
The goal is to maintain data transfer systems that have adequate memory and CPU available for interactive user
data transfers.

7.2.2 ALCF: Technology Profile
ALCF computing resources—available to researchers from academia, industry, and government agencies—
support large-scale, computationally intensive projects aimed at solving some of the world’s most complex
and challenging scientific problems. Through awards of supercomputing time and support services, the ALCF
enables its users to accelerate the pace of discovery and innovation across disciplines.

The ALCF’s team of computational scientists, data scientists, performance engineers, system administrators,
software developers, visualization experts, and support staff help ensure users get the most out of the facility’s
HPC systems. The ALCF also provides training and expertise to prepare researchers for the next generation of
leadership computing resources.

7.2.2.1 Facilities Operated and Supported
The ALCF operates multiple supercomputing systems:

 • Polaris is a 560 node HPE Apollo 6500 Gen 10+ based system. Each node has a single 2.8 GHz
 AMD EPYC Milan 7543P 32 core CPU with 512 GB of DDR4 RAM and four Nvidia A100
 GPUs connected via NVLink, a pair of local 1.6TB of SSDs in RAID0 for the users’ use, and a
 pair of Slingshot 11 network adapters. There are two nodes per chassis, seven chassis per rack,
 and 40 racks. More details about Aurora can be found on the ALCF Polaris page132.

132 https://docs.alcf.anl.gov/polaris/hardware-overview/machine-overview

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 336

 • Sophia is a 24-node Nvidia DGX A100-based system. The DGX A100 comprises eight Nvidia
 A100 GPUs that provide a total of 320 gigabytes of memory for training AI datasets, as well as
 high-speed Nvidia Mellanox ConnectX-6 network interfaces. More details about Sophia can be
 found on the ALCF Sophia page.133
Systems that are in flight:

 • Aurora is a 10,624 node HPE Cray Ex based system. It has 166 racks with 21,248 CPUs and
 63,744 GPUs. Each node consists of 2 Intel Xeon CPU Max Series (codename Sapphire Rapids
 or SPR) with on-package high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and six Intel Data Center GPU
 Max Series (codename Ponte Vecchio or PVC). Each Xeon has 52 physical cores supporting 2
 hardware threads per core and 64 GB of HBM. Each CPU has 512 GB of DDR5. The GPUs are
 connected all-to-all with Intel XeLink interfaces. Each node has 8 HPE Slingshot-11 NICs, and
 the system is connected in a dragonfly topology. More details about Aurora can be found on the
 ALCF Aurora page.134

 • Crux - No documentation is available currently. Crux is an approximately 1PF CPU-only system
 that is being repurposed.

ALCF operates multiple Globus endpoints for data movement in general. To enable sharing of data more publicly,

Globus users, or publicly via https.

 Eagle filesystem)

 • alcf#dtn_hpss for HPSS
7.2.2.9 Outstanding Issues
ALCF has deployed a variety of services to support the IRI initiative, under the Argonne Nexus effort:

 • Service accounts to support long-running experimental campaigns that integrate ALCF
 computing at experiment time. For example, in the same way that a user can obtain an account
 at ALCF, a light source beamline can have a dedicated account.

 • On-demand queue for immediate access to compute nodes at ALCF. This queue is intended for
 near real-time computing, frequently required by experimental facilities but also useful in other
 time-sensitive scenarios.

 • Globus Sharing allows ALCF users to share data directly to named collaborators with an ALCF
 account, or publicly via Globus to users without an ALCF account.

7.3 OLCF
The OLCF is charged with helping researchers solve some of the world’s most challenging scientific problems
with a combination of world-class HPC resources and world-class expertise in scientific computing.

As a US DOE SC User Facility, the OLCF offers leadership-class computing resources to researchers from
government, academia, and industry who have many of the largest computing problems in science. Every year,
researchers use OLCF resources to achieve breakthroughs ranging from understanding the smallest building
blocks of matter to how supernovae spread elements across the universe. The OLCF supports research in biology,
chemistry, seismology, engineering, energy, and many other fields. OLCF simulations have improved the safety
and performance of nuclear power plants, turbomachinery, and aircraft; accelerated development of new drugs
and advanced materials; and informed design of an international fusion reactor. The simulations have explored
hurricanes, biofuels, neurodegenerative diseases, and clean combustion for power and propulsion. Research
challenges remain, and OLCF resources can help.

7.3.1 Discussion Summary

 • OLCF Frontier has been in operation since its debut as the first exaflop supercomputer on May
 2022. Its predecessor, Summit, was decommissioned in November 2024, as OLCF prepares for
 the commissioning of the next HPC system, OLCF-6 and titled “Discovery.” The next system is
 expected in the 2027-2028 time frame. [Section 4.1]

 • To support Frontier, OLCF-6, and DOE programs and initiatives such as IRI and FASST, the
 OLCF has developed application, computing technology, and infrastructure pilots under the
 Advanced Computing Ecosystem (ACE) strategic initiative. ACE is a strategic computing
 framework to support domain science efforts by providing infrastructure to enhance research
 capabilities. [Section 4.1]

 • ORNL has two 400 Gbit connections to ESnet and OLCF will have two 400 Gbps connections
 to the ITSD of ORNL. Additionally, there is a 100 Gbps dedicated WAN connection between
 Defiant, an HPC cluster on the ACE testbed, and ESnet testbed for IRI activities. [Section 4.7]

 • OLCF anticipates more integration with outside clouds for certain applications. OLCF has
 been testing integration with things such as weights and biases; this is an ML/DL analytics
 dashboard. The heavy computations happen on Frontier, but the analytics dashboard may be
 onsite or off-site and integrated through API mechanisms. OLCF is surveying cloud resource
 performance for HPC workloads, particularly for large-scale leadership-class systems.138
 Current constraints around data in the cloud play a large role in limiting its use, particularly cost
 and performance of tightly-coupled parallel calculations. Having said that, with IRI, HPDF and
 FASST, data sources and destinations are expected to become more distributed. [Section 4.8]

 • Strategic planning (five+ years) for OLCF shows LAN traffic will be increased to 800 GbE
 for Science DMZ and data-movement networks with individual 1.6 Tbit links for network
 interconnects. This will also imply that DMZ traffic (e.g., related to data-movement) will scale
 to 6–12Tbit/sec. All other LAN traffic will have multiple 800 Gbps connections. Firewalls in
 this time frame will be 4–6 Tbit/second in throughput. WAN capabilities at ORNL could have
 multiple 800 Gbps connections to ESnet, and OLCF could have multiple 800 Gbps connections
 to ITSD. The connections between the ESnet testbed and OLCF resources could be further
 expanded to multiple 400 Gbps interfaces. [Section 5.7]

138 Evaluating the Cloud for Capability Class Leadership Workloads" https://www.osti.gov/biblio/2000306

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 342

7.3.2 OLCF: Technology Profile
The OLCF is a multi-enclave facility operated by ORNL that supports researchers solving the most challenging
scientific problems. OLCF has a long history in delivering, operating, and conducting research on world-leading
supercomputers. The most recent being Frontier, the world’s first exascale system139. The multi-enclave nature
of the OLCF provides various levels of security, policies, and capabilities to researchers with diverse computing
needs. These enclaves include open data, useful for domain-specific data portal development, supercomputing
(or medium enclave) which provides the leadership-class computing environment, protected data enclave for
ensuring a secure and protected computing infrastructure, and the testbed enclave, that supports exploring
and developing future capabilities, workflows, interfaces, and technology and fits into the US DOE IRI
program landscape.

7.3.2.1 Facilities Operated and Supported
The foremost system operated at OLCF, Frontier, debuted in 2022 and is based on HPE Cray’s EX architecture
and slingshot interconnect with optimized 3rd Gen AMD EPYC CPUs and AMD Instinct 250X GPUs. Frontier
consists of ~9,856 nodes containing a hybrid node architecture design of 1 CPU to 4 GPU achieving 1.2 exaflop/
sec performance. Further description of the architecture and specifications of Frontier are available140. Frontier
has been accelerating innovation in research and technology and is expected to be operational for the next four to
five years.

The predecessor to Frontier, Summit, was decommissioned in November 2024, as OLCF prepares for the
commissioning of the next HPC system, OLCF-6 and titled “Discovery.” The next system is expected in the
2027-2028 time frame. OLCF-6 is expected to further extend the limit of exascale leadership-class computing
and support DOE through increased computational and data science capabilities, interoperate with leadership
scale IRI, and be at the forefront in supporting domain scientists and application developers as they explore and
integrate transformational AI technologies.

To support Frontier, OLCF-6, and DOE programs and initiatives such as IRI and FASST, the OLCF has
developed application, computing technology, and infrastructure pilots under the Advanced Computing
Ecosystem (ACE) strategic initiative. ACE is a strategic computing framework to support domain science
efforts by providing infrastructure to enhance research capabilities141. ACE is the integration of Frontier, Odo
(a small-scale HPC training system), and the ACE testbed. ACE supports advancing scientific research through
four primary facets, 1) developing and deploying science projects and workflows that leverage IRI, 2) enabling
testbeds for a controlled environment for testing and validating new technologies, 3) advancing technologies that
support future computing systems, and 4) evaluating new computing strategies and technologies.

Access to the OLCF resources is limited to approved projects through the INCITE program, ALCC, or
Director’s Discretionary projects. Access to the ACE testbed is provided through a testbed project application
and collaboration with OLCF staff. Many resources are made available to OLCF users across the government,
academia, and industrial sectors to help facilitate the project’s goals and maximize the utilization of
computational resources.

Lastly, the OLCF supports quantum computing research efforts, including the Quantum Computing User
Program (QCUP). This program is managed by the OLCF and connects researchers with quantum computing
resources through ORNL’s vendor partners. The OLCF is positioned at the forefront of high-performance
computing to support the diverse and evolving scientific landscape at the international stage.
