7.3.2.2 Network and Data Architecture
The OLCF network has redundancy to remove single points of failure and contains various technologies to take
advantage of all network paths. These technologies include link aggregation control protocol (LACP), equal
cost multipath (ECMP), multi-chassis link aggregation (MLAG), and first hop redundancy protocol. Therefore,
losing part of the network only results in loss of bandwidth. Currently, ESnet is working on bringing dark fiber
to ORNL. This capability would allow multiplexing technology such that the fiber can be turned into many pairs
of fibers dynamically and enables greater flexibility as capacity can be increased quickly when needed without
waiting for new fiber to run underground. The networking capabilities at the OLCF are outlined with time
frames following current (present to two years), forecasted technology horizon (two to five years), and strategic
planning (five+ years). It is challenging to forecast some of the details, as the continued development of the
future OLCF-6 system will dictate the network and data architecture.

Current OLCF LAN contains multiple 400 GbE connections for the Science DMZ and data movement. A 1.6
Tbit path is available for moving data between scratch storage (Orion/Wolf) and archive (Kronos/Themis) storage
using moderate and open security DTNs and can be scaled up to two to three times that. All other network traffic
is managed with multiple 100 GbitE connections. OLCF’s firewalls are capable of 1.1 Tbit of aggregate traffic
and can carry 100 Gbps streams. In terms of WAN, ORNL has two 400 Gbps connections to ESnet and OLCF
will have two 400 Gbps connections to the ITSD of ORNL. Additionally, there is a 100 Gbit dedicated WAN
connection between Defiant, an HPC cluster on the ACE testbed, and ESnet testbed for IRI activities.

In the forecasted technology horizon (two to five years), OLCF expects LAN traffic will be 400/800 GbE for
Science DMZ and data-movement networks. Data streaming nodes (DSN) could exist on the LAN in this time
frame with possibly 200 or 400 Gbit connections. For all other traffic, there will be the availability of multiple 400
Gbps or 800 Gbps connections. It is expected that the firewalls will be in the 3 TB range of aggregate traffic and
connected via multiple 400 GbE or possibly 800 GbE interfaces. WAN capabilities at ORNL could be increased
to have four or more 400 Gbit connections to ESnet, and OLCF could have four or more 400 Gbit connections to
ITSD. The connections between the ESnet testbed and OLCF resources could be expanded to multiple 100 Gbit
Interfaces in the next few years to support the IRI program.

Strategic planning (five+ years) for OLCF is expecting LAN traffic will be increased to 800 GbE for Science
DMZ and data movement networks with individual 1.6 Tbit links for network interconnects. This will DMZ data-
movement traffic to scale 6–12 Tbit/sec. All other LAN traffic will have multiple 800 Gbit connections. Firewalls
in this time frame will be 4–6 Tbit/second in throughput. WAN capabilities at ORNL could have multiple 800
Gbit connections to ESnet and OLCF could have multiple 800 Gbit connections to ITSD. The connections
between the ES.net testbed and OLCF resources could be further expanded to multiple 400 Gbit interfaces.

components, a node-local storage and a center-wide parallel file system using Lustre (named Orion142). The

The Orion system has a capacity of ~700 PB and allows a tiered archival system (disk + tape) with a distribution

7.3.2.4 Cloud Services
In the present- to two-year time frame OLCF provides access to an on-premise cloud resource. This is the
OpenShift k8s-based resource called “Slate.” OLCF projects are able to develop and deploy cloud-native
applications on this resource. OLCF-staff also develop and deploy services for users on this system. Currently,
OLCF provides JupyterHub as a service from this resource to enable a python portal for workflows. It has been
possible to integrate the Dask workflow system from this JupyterHub, which has clients on supercomputing
resources, in order to drive workflows across HPC systems.

OLCF provides cloud-based access to external quantum resources in the current time frame. This is through the
QCUP. OLCF is the centralized onboarding point, which then enables access to an array of back-end vendor-
provided quantum resources hosted outside of OLCF.

Going beyond the two-year time frame, more integration with the outside clouds for certain applications is
possible. OLCF has been testing integration with things such as weights and biases for instance. This is an ML/
DL analytics dashboard. The heavy computations happen on Frontier, but the analytics dashboard is off-site and
integrated through API mechanisms.

Going beyond five years, it is possible things get even more distributed. Especially with AI. OLCF is surveying
cloud resource performance for HPC workloads, particularly for large-scale leadership-class systems. Current
constraints around data in the cloud play a large role in limiting its use, particularly cost and performance of
tightly-coupled parallel calculations. Having said that, with IRI, HPDF and FASST, data sources and destinations
are expected to become more distributed.

7.3.2.5 AI and ML
There are several options for various kinds of ML, deep learning, and data analytics tasks on OLCF systems.

 • PyTorch on Frontier: PyTorch is a library for Python programs that pairs well with HPC
 resources and facilitates building DL projects. PyTorch emphasizes the flexibility and human-
 readableness of Python and allows deep learning models to be expressed in a similar manner.
 Compared to other frameworks and libraries, it is one of the more “beginner friendly” ML/DL
 packages due to its dynamic and familiar “Pythonic” nature. PyTorch is also useful when GPUs
 are involved because of its strong GPU acceleration ability. On Frontier, PyTorch is able to take
 advantage of the many AMD GPUs available on the system.

 • JAX: a Python library for accelerator-oriented array computation and program transformation,
 designed for high-performance numerical computing and large-scale ML. JAX provides a
 familiar NumPy-style API that can execute on either CPUs, GPUs, or TPUs.

7.3.2.7 Data-Related Resource Constraints
Most constraints revolve around open and integrated access. Science projects funded by DOE science
programs (BER, BES, HEP, etc..) in the DOE seem to be moving towards web-based applications, distributed
across user facilities and cloud. How the data and analysis pipelines integrate with ASCR HPC facilities is
certainly a challenge, from a security and automation perspective. Policies are a constraint limiting integration
between web-based applications and ASCR HPC facilities on the back end.

In the present to two years at OLCF, the openShift k8s-based resource called “Slate” will be operational.
Currently, most ASCR user facilities provide a peripheral resource like this for either workflows or facility-hosted
web applications. This infrastructure is very useful for enabling data sharing capabilities. This will be used in the
Open enclave to enable domain-specific data portals for projects that live at OLCF. Challenges still exist when
projects want to host data at OLCF and share that data publicly.

In the next two to five years, OLCF anticipates more distributed and seamless access to data across the DOE
landscape. This revolves around IRI. Additionally, there needs to be more integrated and automated access
to leadership computing resources from within data portal applications, so users can search data and launch
computational tasks seamlessly. The challenges of building trust for these integrations and workflows between
the cloud and HPC user facilities will hopefully be more well established in this time frame. This will require
supplemental interfaces and policies to enable this integrated future.

7.3.2.8 Data Mobility Endpoints
DTNs are hosts specifically designed to provide optimized data transfer between OLCF systems and systems
outside of the OLCF network. These nodes perform well on local-area transfers as well as the wide-area data
transfers for which they are tuned. The OLCF recommends that users use these nodes to improve transfer speed
and reduce load on computational systems’ login and service nodes. OLCF provides two sets of DTNs: one for
systems in the moderate enclave and a second for systems in the open enclave. More information about DTNs
can be found online.144

7.3.2.8.1 Interactive Access
DTN access is automatically granted to all enabled OLCF users. For interactive access to DTNs (ssh/scp/sftp),
connect to dtn.ccs.ornl.gov (for the moderate enclave) or opendtn.ccs.ornl.gov (for the open enclave).

7.3.2.8.2 Access From Globus Online
DTNs are also accessible via the “OLCF DTN” (for moderate) and “NCCS Open DTN” (for open)
Globus endpoints.

7.4 Fermilab
Fermilab is America’s particle physics and accelerator laboratory. We bring the world together to solve the
mysteries of matter, energy, space and time. Since 1967, Fermilab has worked to answer these and other
fundamental questions and enhance our understanding of everything we see around us. As the United States’
premier particle physics laboratory, we do science that matters. We work on the world’s most advanced particle
accelerators and dig down to the smallest building blocks of matter. We also probe the farthest reaches of the
universe, seeking out the nature of dark matter and dark energy.

7.4.1 Discussion Summary

 • Fermilab is the DOE’s particle physics and accelerator laboratory. It is a single purpose
 laboratory, with a mission to support DoE-sponsored HEP experiments and activities. Fermilab
 is the US Tier-1 center for the LHC/CMS experiment, hosting roughly 40% of CMS experiment
 data. The Laboratory is also the host institution for the DUNE experiment and supports the
 Tier-0 center for the experiment. Other active Fermilab-based experiments include SB/ND,
 NOvA, Mu2e, Muon g-2, ICARUS, and MicroBoone. [Section 4.1]

 • The WLCG recommendation for large Tier-1s, such as Fermilab, at HL-LHC startup is a
 minimum of 1Tb/s. Fermilab is currently provisioned at 1.6 Tbps for science traffic and 800
 Gbps for general-purpose traffic. The latter does include the fraction of the Laboratory’s science
 that is not carried via the science networks. It is expected that this configuration should be
 adequate to satisfy the currently known requirements for 2024- 2028. If needed, additional
 400G connections can be added to the existing LAG interfaces. It is expected that switching to
 800G Ethernet technology might become justifiable in 2028–2030. [Section 4.7]

 • In terms of aggregate WAN capacity out of the site, Fermilab currently has provisioned 2.4Tb/s
 of link capacity to ESnet, via geographically diverse connections. A LAG of four 400 Gbps links is
 used to support the science data network paths, including LHCOPN and LHCONE. A second 2
 x 400 Gbps LAG supports the Laboratory’s general internet traffic, which includes some portion
 of science traffic, for example, CMS traffic to/from sites not connected to LHCONE. [Section 4.7]

 • The DUNE experiment extends across two facilities ~1300km apart. One site is Fermilab
 in Batavia, IL, and the second site, the FD location, is SURF, in Lead, South Dakota. The
 Fermilab-managed perimeter network will provide connectivity for the DUNE FD site
 to Fermilab. Sufficient capacity to move ~30PB of science data annually is required. The
 perimeter network equipment will reside in two geographically diverse buildings at SURF —
 the Ross Dry Building and the Yates Administrivia Building. Each building has a shaft which
 provides access to the underground facilities at the 4850ft level (4850L). WAN connectivity is to
 be provided and managed by ESnet. [Section 4.7]

 • ESnet and Fermilab network engineering teams have drafted a plan for connectivity back to
 Fermilab to support DUNE. The plan calls for redundant, geographically diverse, vendor-
 diverse, 100 Gbps circuits from SURF to ESnet PoPs in Chicago and Denver, respectively.
 ESnet backbone services (OSCARS) would then extend those L2 paths back to Fermilab.
 Deployment of both 100 Gbps circuits should occur by the 2026–2027 time frame. Both
 pathways will be connected to ESnet in a production capacity. Currently, a dedicated 10 Gbps
 circuit between SURF and ESnet’s Kansas City PoP provides DUNE FD connectivity back to
 the Fermilab campus. This circuit, provided by South Dakota’s REED, will revert to a tertiary
 back-up role once the two 100 Gbps circuits are procured and deployed. [Section 5.7]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 348

 • Fermilab is concerned about not having the capability to adequately stress test the WAN
 infrastructure as network technology step-increases push bandwidth capacities to terabit
 scale. The ability to generate traffic at 400GE, 800GE, & 1.6TE is challenging in its own
 right. Fermilab desires to be able to routinely stress test the WAN infrastructure to ensure it
 is performing as expected. The complexity of having multiple types of virtual network services
 sharing the same physical infrastructure adds another level of difficulty to this. It is desirable
 to consider this as a capability to concurrently generate high traffic loads across various virtual
 network services (LHCOPN, LHCONE, default routed IP path, etc.). This capability is a
 critical tool in Fermilab’s ability to troubleshoot aggregate data bottlenecks where multiple
 virtual network services are involved. Fermilab proposes that this should be developed as a
 service that ESnet provides to all its sites. [Section 5.7]

 • Fermilab has a strong interest in making use of ESnet High Touch Services to generate data for
 AI/ML-based analysis of network traffic patterns. Fermilab is currently working cooperatively
 with ESnet on distinguishing between streaming-based CMS data movement and file-transfer-
 based CMS data movement. It is desirable not just to continue with this particular effort,
 but also to look toward additional opportunities to expand use of ESnet High Touch Service
 capabilities in analyzing WAN traffic. [Section 5.8]

7.4.2 Fermilab: Technology Profile
Fermilab is the DOE’s particle physics and accelerator laboratory. It is a single purpose laboratory, with a mission
to support DoE-sponsored HEP experiments and activities. Fermilab is the US Tier-1 center for the LHC/CMS
experiment, hosting roughly 40% of CMS experiment data. The Laboratory is also the host institution for the
DUNE experiment and supports the Tier-0 center for the experiment. Other active Fermilab-based experiments
include SB/ND, NOvA, Mu2e, Muon g-2, ICARUS, and MicroBoone. In addition, Fermilab hosts one of the
elements of the DOE’s national Lattice QCD computational infrastructure. However, the Lattice QCD cluster is
standalone infrastructure with no significant Fermilab WAN requirements and is not factored into this case study.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 349

Figure 7.4.1: Fermilab Experiments Schedule 2022-2032

Computing resources to support these experiments are divided into two distinct entities, the US CMS Tier-1
facility for CMS computation, and a shared computation infrastructure for all the other experiments. The
significantly higher computing, storage, and networking requirements for CMS computation are more easily
and economically met with separate infrastructure than attempting to scale all Fermilab experiment computing
infrastructure up to meet CMS’s needs. As a result, CMS traffic into and out of Fermilab is relatively easy to
identify, based on network addresses used. The rest of Fermilab’s experiments share computing, storage, and
network resources. Identifying specifically what WAN traffic belongs to which of those experiments presents
a challenge.

Computing resources, whether part of the US CMS Tier-1 facility or the shared use infrastructure, are distributed
across two data centers, the Feynman Computing Center (FCC) and the Grid Computing Center (GCC). Each
computer center supports multiple computer rooms. The two data centers are approximately 2km apart, and
heavily interconnected (>1000pr) with geographically diverse optical fiber. FCC has both uninterruptible power
supply (UPS) and back-up generator support, while GCC has only limited UPS deployment and generator
support. Storage nodes and other sensitive servers are normally located in FCC, while CPU worker nodes are
normally located in GCC. This holds true for both the US CMS Tier-1 and the shared computing infrastructure
for the rest of the Laboratory’s experiments. The end result is virtual work group LANs that straddle both FCC
and GCC data centers for both the US CMS Tier-1 facility and the shared computing infrastructure used by the
rest of the Fermilab-supported experiments.

Future Computing Facility Upgrades/Expansion

While there has been discussion and very preliminary planning for a next-generation data center at Fermilab
to meet its future local computation needs, there is nothing currently in place with a funding or construction
roadmap. The existing FCC and GCC data centers are expected to accommodate planned expansion of local
computing resources to meet HL-LHC and DUNE/FD startup requirements up to 2029-2030.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 350

7.4.2.2 Network and Data Architecture
The Laboratory’s network architecture is organized into a modular model. Each module consists of network
resources dedicated to specific tasks and can be represented by logical groupings of subnets. These modules are
typically structured based on organizational divisions, experiment affiliations, or, in some cases, geographical
locations. Examples of network modules include:

 • Fermilab’s network perimeter
 • Data center network spanning multiple buildings
 • US CMS-Tier-1 network
 • DUNE network architecture
 • NOvA far detector network
All network modules connect to a central component known as the Site Interconnect, which facilitates
connectivity between modules and enforces inter-module security policies. Modules can also have direct
connections to one another, enabling certain traffic to bypass the Site Interconnect, provided that adequate
security controls are in place. For instance, the US CMS-Tier-1 module has a direct link to the Perimeter module
for high-impact data transfers, bypassing the Site Interconnect. However, general-purpose traffic from the US
CMS-Tier-1 module, such as email and web traffic, still must pass through the Site Interconnect.

Network modules may be protected by dedicated firewalls at the module boundary to address specific security
needs. The Network Perimeter module includes border firewalls that inspect general-purpose traffic before the
traffic reaches the Site Interconnect. High-impact scientific data traffic may bypass these border firewalls to reach
its destination module directly. Additionally, computing resources in commercial clouds can be integrated into
Fermilab’s network, functioning as an extension of the network modules connected to either the Site Interconnect
or the Perimeter module. The conceptual network architecture is depicted in the figure below.

Figure 7.4.2: Fermilab Network Diagram

7.4.2.2.1 Network Perimeter
Currently, the Network Perimeter consists of:

 • Two (2) Arista 7800 routers, each consisting of:
           °    2x 48-port 100G LC, 2x 36-port 400G LC

 ° Deep buffers, 800G enabled

 ° 2x 400G and 4x 400G off-site connections to ESnet at the geographically diverse GCC and
 FCC data centers respectively

 • Two Palo Alto PA-7050 with 100G line cards, at the geographically diverse GCC and FCC data
 centers respectively

 • DMZ Arista switches (not shown in diagram) with 10/100/400G ports
Fermilab off-site traffic is asymmetric by design, with science networks (LHCOPN, LHCONE, E2E circuits,
etc.) traffic using one ESnet connection (FCC), and general routed internet traffic using the other ESnet
connection (GCC). This inherently creates a situation for one (FCC) ESnet connection to require significantly
larger bandwidth capacity than the other. If one connection fails, traffic will automatically switch to the other
connection. This leads to a potential bottleneck if all scientific traffic shifts to the general IP path where lower
bandwidth is provisioned. However, based on the previous experience, Fermilab can tolerate temporary
congestion on one link. Additionally, with 800G of provisioned bandwidth on the lower capacity WAN link
(GCC), there is currently ample capacity to manage this type of situation.

The WLCG recommendation for large Tier-1s at HL-LHC startup is 1Tb/s, with the largest Tier-1s (Fermilab
specifically noted) needing significantly more than 1Tb/s. Fermilab is currently provisioned at 1.6 Tbps for
science traffic and 800 Gbps for general-purpose traffic. The latter does include the fraction of the Laboratory’s
science that is not carried via the science networks. It is expected that this configuration should be adequate to
satisfy the currently known requirements for 2024- 2028. If needed, additional 400G connections can be added to
the existing LAG interfaces. It is expected that switching to 800G Ethernet technology might become justifiable
in 2028–2030.

requirements, and which utilize common computing and storage facilities such as FermiGrid, public dCache
and public EnStore. The networks used in these experiments are typically directly connected to the general data
center to streamline the path for collecting, commuting, and storing experimental data. This setup is illustrated in
the diagram below for the SBN-FD/ND network. The general data center is built as the following:

 • Three distribution switches in computer rooms in different buildings ~2km apart:

 • ToR access switches dual-homed to two distribution switches:
 ° Large-scale deployment of 100GE host connections

 ° Abundant of fiber utilized in dual-homing between computer rooms

 ° Default 10GbaseT connection for all worker servers’ (1350 connections)

 ° 200 storage servers with 100G connections

 ° 44x 1G connections

 ° 92 / 20 mix of 100/400G uplinks respectively

7.4.2.2.3 The US CMS-Tier-1 Network
The US CMS Tier-1 Center at Fermilab is the largest of CMS Tier-1 facilities, currently providing 40% of the
total CMS Tier-1 capacity. The Fermilab Tier-1 consists of dedicated computing infrastructure. For the details on
computing and storage requirements, please see Section 6.11.

The US CMS Tier-1’s local network infrastructure consists of fully redundant, high-performance switching fabric
distributed across the Laboratory’s two data centers. That switching fabric has the following characteristics:

 • Currently based on 400GE network technology for inter-switch connectivity, with 10GE and
 100GE connectivity available for host system connectivity.

 • Extensive use of link aggregation (LAG) to scale bandwidth for inter-switch connectivity. At the
 present time, the US CMS Tier-1 LAN provides approximately 10Tb/s of network capacity
 in total.

 • PBR techniques to route CMS high volume traffic over special purpose networks (such as
 LHCOPN, LHCONE) utilized for WAN data movement.
Fermilab’s WAN architecture is based on separating its high-impact science data traffic from its general internet
traffic. Conceptually, this design is analogous to a Science DMZ architecture. Most traffic into and out of the
US CMS T1 is via the science data path(s). For CMS, those science data paths mean the LHCOPN, LHCONE,
and end-to-end OSCARS circuits. Fermilab’s LHCOPN connectivity supports movement of raw data from
the T0 (CERN), as well as production data movement with some of the other CMS T1s. Fermilab’s LHCOPN
configuration consists of three OSCARS circuits (primary, secondary, and tertiary) to CERN, which provide
levels of redundancy with differing bandwidth guarantees for that traffic. LHCONE supports production data
movement between the Fermilab Tier-1 and most CMS Tier-2s, as well as CMS T1s that do not use LHCOPN for

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 353

T1-T1 data movement. Like the LHCOPN, connectivity to LHCONE is via geographically redundant (primary/
failover) paths. US CMS Tier-1 WAN traffic that does not utilize either the LHCOPN or LHCONE paths
traverses the Laboratory’s general internet path.

In terms of aggregate WAN capacity out of the site, Fermilab currently has provisioned 2.4Tb/s of link capacity
to ESnet, via geographically diverse connections. A LAG of four 400 Gbps links is used to support the science
data network paths, including LHCOPN and LHCONE. A second 2 x 400 Gbps LAG supports the Laboratory’s
general internet traffic, which includes some portion of science traffic, for example, CMS traffic to/from sites not
connected to LHCONE.

Future network enhancements:

 • Upgrade of the US CMS Tier-1 LAN infrastructure to 800GE technology is expected for
            2028–2030 time frame;

 • Upgrade of the Laboratory network perimeter infrastructure to 800GE technology is
 expected also in 2028 - 2030 time frame, likely to be aligned with availability of 800GE
 services from ESnet;

 • In 2026–2028 time frame, additional 400GE links deployed to WAN capacity. The 2 x 400GE

7.4.2.2.4 DUNE Network Architecture
The DUNE experiment extends across two facilities ~1300km apart. One site is Fermilab in Batavia, IL, and the
second site, the FD location, is SURF, in Lead, South Dakota. The local network at SURF to support the DUNE
FD is made up of several components:

 • Perimeter network — Fermi-managed infrastructure to provide connectivity for the DUNE FD
 site to Fermilab. Sufficient capacity to move ~30PB of science data annually is required. The
 perimeter network equipment will reside in two geographically diverse buildings at SURF —
 the Ross Dry Building and the Yates Administrative Building. Each building has a shaft which
 provides access to the underground facilities at the 4850ft level (4850L). WAN connectivity is to
 be provided and managed by ESnet.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 354

 • Experiment (DAQ/DCS) network - provides network services for the DAQ and the detector
 control systems. The experiment network moves data from the detectors down at the 4850L
 in the Ross cavern to the computing room in the Ross Dry main control room on the surface.
 The Experiment network is designed to have a high level of resilience to meet the DAQ
 requirements, even in the event of extended failure scenarios such as a complete fiber cut in
 one shaft.

 • Technical network — provides network services for cryogenic control devices, building and
 computer room controls, and monitoring systems. The technical network extends from the
 surface to the cavern.

 • General-purpose network - provides essential network services such as DNS, DHCP, KDC, and
 other IT services required at the FD location, both in the cavern and on the surface.

 • Network management network - a separate network infrastructure to manage all
 DUNE networks.
The DUNE FD network at SURF is logically an extension of Fermilab site network. It is designed as a distinct
network module within the Fermilab network architecture. The DUNE FD network module connects to the
Site Interconnect module at the Fermilab Batavia site via the site-to-site WAN circuits. The high-level network
architecture for DUNE is depicted in figure below:

 • Logically within the network perimeter of Fermilab.
 • Fully redundant, high-performance switching fabric, both down in the cavern and up on
 the surface.

 • Based on 100GE/400GE network technologies for inter-switch connectivity, with redundant
 10GE and 100GE connectivity available for host system connectivity.

 • Fully redundant and geographically separated fiber connectivity between the cavern and the
 computing facilities up on the surface in Ross.

 • Redundant essential network services (DNS. NTP, DHCP)
 • A redundant network perimeter at SURF, with the border devices in both the Ross and
 Yates buildings.

7.4.2.2.5 NOvA (NuMI Off-axis νe Appearance)
The NOvA experiment utilizes two detectors: a 300-metric-ton near detector at Fermilab and a much larger
14-metric-kiloton far detector at Ash River, Minnesota, just south of the US-Canada border. Although NOvA has
surpassed its initial planned schedule, it remains an active experiment, and a decommissioning date has not yet
been set.

Currently, ESnet and the University of Minnesota jointly provide two geographically separate 1G OSCARS
circuits (Vlan 201 & 203) between Batavia and the NOvA Far Detector, ensuring redundancy across ESnet and
partially through University of Minnesota (UMN). From the UMN router in Duluth, these circuits are merged
and provisioned through a single physical pipe to Ash River provided by a local Internet service provider
(ISP). These connections need to be maintained and kept operational during the lifetime of the experiment.
Additionally, the Fermilab public dCache prefix is advertised on LHCONE for the NOvA experiment. This
service is primarily used for production NOvA computing performed at FZU (Prague, Institute for Physics of the
Czech Academy of Sciences).

7.4.2.3 Computational and Storage Infrastructure

7.4.2.3.1 Storage
The US-CMS Tier-1 has dedicated storage, both disk and tape. The dCache distributed storage system is used
to provide disk storage for production CMS computing. CMS dCache servers are (nearly...) all connected to
the network with 100GE NICs. There is also a much smaller EOS storage system for derived data objects used
in analysis by physicists. The EnStore tape system currently provides tape storage for archiving and back-end
storage of production CMS computing data. The rest of the experiments supported at Fermilab use shared storage
facilities. Disk storage for them is provided on the public dCache storage facility. The EnStore tape system is
used for tape storage by those experiments, although the storage elements are separate from CMS. Table 7.4.4
depicts the approximate current capacity/capabilities of Fermilab storage systems used to support its experiments.

fluctuate. The rest of the Fermilab-supported experiments use a shared compute infrastructure, named the

for more casual use and as a development environment. Wilson does include a modest level of GPU capabilities.

7.4.2.3.3 Future Storage/Compute Resource Upgrades/Expansion
Modest incremental growth in storage and compute is expected over the short-term time frame (~2 yr). Starting
in roughly the 2028-2030 time frame, the US-CMS Tier-1 storage and compute facilities will need to expand
significantly to meet the demands of High-Luminosity LHC. In addition, DUNE/FD will be ramping up to take
beam data. This expansion of compute and storage resources will continue into the early 2030s.

In addition, Fermilab networking has an interest in applying AI/ML techniques to its WAN network traffic data.
Potential applications for AI/ML-based analysis include:

 • Active network flow performance analysis, in terms of identifying sub-optimal performance
 within individual data transfer flows, and predicting whether said performance problems are
 likely to be network-related or end system-related;

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 359

 • Network path asymmetry detection, and predicting whether this is or is not significantly
 affecting data-movement performance;

 • Jumbo frame use/non-use, and predicting whether jumbo frames are/will significantly impact
 performance, either positively or negatively.
Fermilab has a strong interest in making use of ESnet High-Touch Services to generate data for AI/ML-based
analysis of network traffic patterns. Fermilab is currently working cooperatively with ESnet on distinguishing
between streaming-based CMS data movement and file-transfer-based CMS data movement. It is desirable not
just to continue with this particular effort, but also to look toward additional opportunities to expand use of High-
Touch Service capabilities in analyzing WAN traffic.

7.4.2.6 Wireless Capabilities
No programmatic uses of wireless technologies beyond normal user connectivity are currently planned. There
have been several R&D investigations with use of 5G technologies for both beamline operations activities and
advanced detector design. However, none of those efforts have gone beyond the early R&D stage. There are no
roadmaps for deployment of either at this time.

7.4.2.9 Outstanding Issues
Fermilab is concerned about not having the capability to adequately stress test the WAN infrastructure as
network technology step-increases push bandwidth capacities to terabit scale. The ability to generate traffic
at 400GE, 800GE, & 1.6TE is challenging in its own right. Fermilab desires to be able to routinely stress test
the WAN infrastructure to ensure it is performing as expected. The complexity of having multiple types of
virtual network services sharing the same physical infrastructure adds another level of difficulty to this. It is
desirable to consider this as a capability to concurrently generate high traffic loads across various virtual network
services (LHCOPN, LHCONE, default routed IP path, etc.). This capability can be seen as being a critical tool
in Fermilab’s ability to troubleshoot aggregate data bottlenecks where multiple virtual network services are
involved. Fermilab proposes that this should be developed as a service that ESnet provides to all its sites.

7.5.2.2 Network and Data Architecture
7.5.2.2.1 BNL Network Architectures
The BNL network infrastructure’s purview is to provide data communications that are highly available and robust
in order to facilitate and support operations and research at BNL. It provides the foundation underlying the
critical services within the enterprise and scientific computing such as, HTC, phone service, security and safety
and monitoring.

The success of the BNL network infrastructure in supporting its critical services can be attributed to the
following fundamental principles, reliability and resiliency, modularity and hierarchy. These fundamental
principles are architected and implemented throughout all the various network infrastructures at BNL.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 362

 1. Reliability and Resiliency

 ° A highly available and reliable network that can survive any component failure without
 human intervention.
 2. Modularity

 ° A network divided into multiple functional modules, each serving a specific role in the
 network. Modules should be easy to replicate, redesign and expand. Modularity helps
 promote, ease of network manageability, adaptability, scalability and creates fault isolation
 domains.
 3. Hierarchy

 ° Provides the ability to have more choke points within the network to aggregate traffic,
 reachability and topology information.
As of today, the BNL network infrastructure is separated into three main areas, the Network Perimeter, Campus
Network and the HTSN. Each of these areas support different critical BNL services:

 1. Network Perimeter

 ° A highly available, Terabit per second (Tbps) network infrastructure to support the timely
 transfer of large amounts of scientific data from various systems or experiments to remote
 locations via the Internet or WAN.
 2. Campus Network

 ° Foundation underlying the critical services within the enterprise such as workstations,
 phone service, security, safety and monitoring and enterprise computing.
 3. HTSN

 ° A centralized, highly available, fault-tolerant, scalable, Terabit per second network
 infrastructure to support all collaborations compute and storage requirements.

7.5.2.2.2 BNL Network Perimeter
The BNL Network Perimeter consists of two redundant Nokia Routers which support interface speeds of 10
GbE, 40 GbE, 100 GbE and 400 GbE. These routers are split between BNL’s two data centers, one in building
515 and the other in building 725. Each BNL router connects to a local ESnet router at 800 Gbps (2 x 400
GbE) totaling 1.6 Tbps of Internet/WAN connectivity. Each 800 Gbps circuit is utilized by all scientific and
administrative communities at BNL, all data traffic to and from BNL flows through either of these circuits.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 363

 Figure 7.5.1: High-Level Overview of the BNL Network Perimeter and DNS Architecture (FY24)

7.5.2.2.2.1 BNL WAN and Internet Circuits
As of today, the BNL Network Perimeter supports various WAN circuits along with its Internet circuits. These
WAN/Internet circuits all share the same 1.6 Tbps of total connectivity to ESnet. There is no QoS, traffic shaping
or prioritization on any data sources over the BNL WAN/Internet circuits. The following are BNL’s current
WAN/Internet circuits:

 1. General IPv4 Internet
 2. General IPv6 Internet
 3. LHCONE Service
 4. LHCOPN Service
Each WAN/Internet circuit provided from ESnet is redundantly connected to each BNL Network Perimeter
router for resiliency. Only one circuit from each service is active at any given time. To support the large data flows
to and from US ATLAS resources BNL offsets the LHCOPN and LHCONE primary circuits so each service in
theory could transfer 800 Gbps of data.

All WAN/Internet circuits terminate on the BNL Network Perimeter and utilize EBGP and Bidirectional
Forwarding Detection (BFD). BNL does not allow any Layer-2/VPLS (ESnet OSCARS) circuits to traverse the
Network Perimeter since Layer-3 routing is strictly enforced.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 364

 Figure 7.5.2: High-Level Overview of the BNL’s WAN and Internet Circuits provided from ESnet (FY24)

7.5.2.2.2.2 Connectivity to Science DMZ(s) and Campus Network
The BNL Network Perimeter strictly utilizes Layer-3 routing protocols such as OSPF/OSFPv3 and BGP.
Between both Perimeter routers Open Shortest Path First (OSPF0 / OSPFv3 and iBGP) are utilized but when
connecting to other downstream devices (e.g., Science DMZ(s), Campus Network) EBGP and BFD are used. All
downstream devices utilizing EBGP are configured with a private ASN, since these ASNs are private and should
not be advised externally they are stripped when their routes are advertised to ESnet or any other
WAN peering’s.

The utilization of EBGP between the Network Perimeter and downstream devices allows for better traffic
engineering and provides BNL with the ability to steer large data flows to the correct Perimeter router that has
the active Internet/WAN peering. Utilizing EBGP also eliminates the need to redistribute BGP routes into and
Interior Gateway Protocol such as OSPF.

As depicted above in “High-Level Overview of the BNL Network Perimeter and DNS Architecture” the
following connectivity is provided to downstream devices:

 1. BNL Campus
 a. 40 Gbps in aggregate (4 x 10 GbE)
 2. HTSN Science DMZ
 a. 1.6 Tbps in aggregate (4 x 400 GbE)
 3. NSLS-II Science DMZ
 a. 400 Gbps in aggregate (4 x 100 GbE)
7.5.2.2.2.3 BNL’s Support for LHCOPN and LHCONE Services
To adhere to the LHCONE and LHCOPN AUP, various complex routing policies and features must be
implemented on BNL Network Perimeter. This AUP states only specific HEP resources at BNL (e.g., US ATLAS,
Belle II, DUNE, etc.) should have access to the LHCONE and LHCOPN services, which leaves all other
resources at BNL able only to traverse the general Internet services.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 365

To provide this exclusivity for LHCONE and LHCOPN, separate campus Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF)
instances have been created on both perimeter routers. Policies are then applied to only import default, black
hole, and local BNL routes into the campus VRFs. Then policy-based routing (PBR) policies are configured on
all perimeter downstream ingress interfaces. In short, these PBR policies state that all private IPv4 and IPv6 and
HEP subnets forward to the default routing table, which has full visibility to all WAN circuits, while all other
BNL subnets should forward to the campus VRF instance, which can only see the general Internet services.

7.5.2.2.3 BNL Campus Network
The BNL Campus Network supports critical services within the enterprise such as workstations, phone service,
security, safety and monitoring and enterprise computing. The BNL campus is over 5,000 acres and contains over
300 buildings with over 100 of these buildings connected to the BNL Campus Network through various types
of Layer-1 technologies such as, DSL, wireless point-to-point bridges or through the large campus fiber optic
cabling infrastructure. The BNL Campus Network is comprised of over 800+ switches, 800+ wireless access
points and numerous pairs of firewalls and load balancers from various vendors.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 366

 Figure 7.5.4: High-Level Overview of the BNL’s Campus Network Topology (FY24)

7.5.2.2.3.1 BNL Campus Architecture
The BNL Campus Network architecture follows the same fundamental principles as discussed in the beginning of
the section: modularity, resiliency and hierarchy. The Campus architecture follows a well-defined and traditional
three-tiered model comprising the Core, Distribution, and Access layers.

 1. Core Layer
 a. Is the least complex layer yet the most critical part of the Campus Network.
 b. It provides a limited set of services and is designed to be highly resilient.
 c. The responsibility of the Core is fast packet forwarding and flexibility, not policy insertion or
 server termination.
 d. Serves as Area 0 in the OSPF and OSPFv3 topologies.
 2. Distribution Layer (DL)
 a. Connects directly to the Campus Core via OSPF/OSPFv3 via Area 0.
 b. Defines a summarization boundary for OSPF and OSFPv3 since each DL is a separate
 OSPF Area.
 c. Each distribution switch pair is configured as a MLAG cluster, which creates one logical
 Spanning-Tree and LACP switch from the access layer switches perspective. This allows
 access layer switches to redundantly connect to both DL switches via LACP in an active/
 active fashion.
 d. Acts as an active/active default gateway for all Non-Firewalled Switch Virtual Interfaces
 (SVIs) and Spanning-Tree root bridge for all virtual LANs (VLANs) that are defined within
 the DL.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 367

 e. Is an aggregation point for all the access switches.
 f. Services and control boundary between the access layer and Campus Core.
 g. Each DL usually has a pair of firewalls for various services that require access control from
 other internal BNL subnets.
 3. Access Layer
 a. Is where devices (e.g., workstations, access points, phones, printers, etc.) connect to the
 network.
 b. Various interfaces speeds and duplex’s must be supported (e.g., 10 Mbps, 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps,
 half duplex, full duplex).
 c. Must support Power over Ethernet (PoE) for phones, access points and other devices
 requiring power over the network.

7.5.2.2.4 HTSN
BNL’s HTSN is a vendor agnostic, resilient, scalable and modular Terabit Per Second (Tbps) network
infrastructure which serves as the primary network transport for all data-intensive collaborations at BNL. It
provides high-throughput connectivity to all High-Performance Compute (HPC) and HTC collaborations and
supports the timely transfer of large amounts of scientific data via the Internet.

The HTSN has five key components:

 1. Network Perimeter
 a. Discussed in section 2.1
 2. Science DMZ
 a. Supports open, high-speed WAN and Internet access for all scientific collaborations
 throughout the BNL campus.
 b. Is configured as an MLAG cluster which allows all DTNs to redundantly connect to each
 chassis in an active/active fashion via LACP.
          c. Supports 10, 25, 40, 50, 100 and 400 GbE interface speeds.
 3. Science Core
 a. A Tbps Science and Data Center Interconnect for data-intensive collaborations at BNL.
 This Science Interconnect enables high-speed connectivity between collaborations such as
 ATLAS, STAR, sPHENIX, CAD, CFN, NSLS-II, HPC Clusters and the SDCC.
 b. Intelligence and routing policies are applied within the Science Core to restrict or grant
 access to specific resources within the SDCC.
 c. Supports 10,25,40 and 100 GbE interface speeds.
 4. Spine
 a. A Tbps network Spine that interconnects all Leaf switches. Leaf switches consist of ToR
 or chassis-based switches that connect compute, storage or general infrastructure service
 servers.
 b. The responsibility of the Spine is fast packet forwarding and flexibility, not policy insertion
 or server termination.
 c. EBGP is utilized throughout the HTSN. EBGP was chosen for its ability to immensely scale
 and to create modularity and fault domain isolation down to the rack level. Each Spine group

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 368

7.5.2.2.5 NSLS2 Network Infrastructure
The NSL2 network infrastructure comprises of three functional areas:

 1. NSLS2 Science Network (aka N2SN)
 a. A highly available Terabit per second (Tbps) network infrastructure to support the operation
 of science experiments performed at the individual Beamlines.
 2. NSLS2 Accelerator Network (aka Controls)
 a. A highly available Gigabit per second (Gbps) network infrastructure to support the
 operations and monitoring of the medium-energy electron storage ring.
 3. NSLS2 Network Management
 a. A highly available Gigabit per second (Gbps) network infrastructure to support the
 operations and monitoring of the network switches and firewalls which comprise of the
 NSLS2 Infrastructure.
7.5.2.2.5.1 NSLS2 Science Network (N2SN) Components
 1. N2SN Core
 a. Supports the connectivity between the N2SN components, the NSLS2 Accelerator network,
 NSLS2 Network Management as well as the HTSN Science Core.
 2. N2SN Beamline block (1 per Beamline)
 a. Supports services for the operation of individual Beamline experiments.
 3. N2SN Data Services block
 a. Supports data services such as DNS, DHCP, etc., as well as Storage.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 370

 4. N2SN DMZ block
 a. Supports connectivity to the Perimeter routers for Internet and BNL Campus traffic from
 both the N2SN and Controls functional areas.
7.5.2.2.5.2 NSLS2 Accelerator/Controls Network Components
 1. High-Availability pair of firewalls
 a. Used to separate and enforce policy for traffic to/from the Accelerator/Controls network.
 2. Accelerator Aggregation block
 a. Supports the connectivity between the Accelerator components, as well as Storage.
 3. Accelerator Data Services block
 a. Supports data services such as DNS, DHCP, VM IOC servers, etc.
 4. Accelerator Mezzanine cell block (30)
 a. Supports the individual cells comprising of the accelerator ring.
 5. Accelerator RF Cavity block
 a. Supports the function of the accelerator ring.
 6. Accelerator Injection Service Building block
 a. Supports the function of the accelerator ring.
 7. Accelerator Control Room
 a. Supports the operations and monitoring of the accelerator ring.
7.5.2.2.5.3 N2SN Core
Supports the connectivity between the N2SN components, the NSLS2 Accelerator network, NSLS2 Network
Management as well as the HTSN Science Core.

 1. Consists of redundant Tbps chassis configured in an MLAG configuration capable of supporting 10
 GbE, 25 GbE, 40 GbE and 100 GbE interface speeds.
 2. Connectivity between the N2SN Core and the Beamlines is done via a 20 Gbps (2 x 20 GbE) or 200
 Gbps (2 x 100 GbE) connection.
 3. Connectivity between the N2SN Core and the N2SN Data Services block is done via a 400 Gbps (4
 x 100 GbE) connection.
 4. Connectivity between the N2SN Core and the N2SN DMZ is separated by a redundant pair of
 firewalls at 80 Gbps (2 x 40 GbE).
 a. Only required traffic is permitted between these areas.
 b. Static routes are used between N2SN Core and the N2SN DMZ firewall.
 5. Connectivity between the N2SN Core and the HTSN Science Core is done via redundant 400 Gbps
 connections.
 a. 4 x 100 GbE to B515 Data Center
 b. 4 x 100 GbE to B725 Data Center
 c. Only required traffic is permitted between these areas which are controlled by ACLs.
 6. EBGP routing protocol with BFD is utilized to support connectivity to the N2SN Beamline
 blocks, N2SN Data Services block, the NSLS2 Network Management block, as well as the HTSN
 Science Core.

 7. Connectivity between the N2SN Core and the NSLS2 Accelerator network is separated by
 redundant pair of firewalls at 80 Gbps (2 x 40 GbE).

7.5.2.2.5.4 N2SN Beamline Network
Supports services for the operation of individual Beamline experiments. Each beamline has its own network
infrastructure. There are currently 30+ beamline network infrastructures.

Each of the 30+ individual beamline infrastructures consist of the following:

 1. A High-speed aggregation switch capable of supporting 10 GbE, 25 GbE, 40 GbE and 100 GbE
 interface speeds. Redundant High-speed aggregation switches is available should the beamline
 require it.
 2. Multiple low-speed switches capable of supporting 10 MbE, 100 MbE and 1 GbE interface speeds
 with PoE.
 3. Connectivity between the N2SN Core and a Beamline is done via redundant 20 Gbps (2 x 10 GbE)
 or 200 Gbps (2 x 100 GbE) connection.
 4. EBGP routing protocol with BFD is utilized to support connectivity to the N2SN Core.
 5. BGP EVPN VxLAN is utilized to transport L2 EPICS, Camera, and Instrumentation traffic between
 the N2SN Beamlines and ESXi VM IOC servers residing on the N2SN Data Services block.
 6. Local ACLs are used to limit traffic between individual Beamlines.

 a. Storage nodes via 100 Gbps (4 x 25 GbE) connection
 b. Redundant High-speed switches also in an MLAG configuration capable of supporting 10

 100 GbE)
 4. EBGP routing protocol with BFD is utilized to support connectivity to the N2SN Core

7.5.2.2.5.7 NSLS2 Accelerator/Controls Infrastructure

block, an Injection Service Building block, and a Controls room block. This infrastructure is comprised of 220+
Layer 2 switches interconnected using fiber optic cabling.

 1. Connectivity between the N2SN Core and the NSLS2 Accelerator network is separated by

 both downstream and upstream.
 b. Multiple low-speed switches capable of supporting 10MbE, 100MbE and 1 GbE interface
 speeds with PoE.
 2. This infrastructure consists of a large Layer 2 network with Layer 3 SVIs terminating on the main
 aggregation switch or the firewall depending on security requirements.

7.5.2.3 Computational and Storage Infrastructure
The SDCC at Brookhaven Lab began in 1997 when the RHIC and ATLAS Computing Facility was established.
Then called RACF, the full-service scientific computing facility has since supported some of the most notable
physics experiments, including BRAHMS, Pioneering High Energy Nuclear Interaction eXperiment (PHENIX),
PHOBOS Collaboration, and Solenoidal Tracker at RHIC (STAR), by providing dedicated data processing,
storage, and analysis resources for these diverse, expansive experiments with general computing capabilities and
support for users.

Today, this history of providing useful, resilient, and large-scale computational science, data management, and
analysis infrastructure has grown, and the SDCC has evolved to support additional facilities and experiments.
These include the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II) and CFN at Brookhaven Lab, as well as other
DOE SC user facilities; the ATLAS experiment at CERN’s LHC in Europe; and Belle II at KEK in Japan and
DESY in Germany. SDCC also is planning for its role in future experiments with the sPHENIX, DUNE, and
Electron-Ion Collider.

For users, SDCC offers a single-point facility with high-throughput, high-performance, and data-intensive
computing along with data management, storage, analysis, and preservation capabilities that support scientific
programs in domains spanning physics, biology, climate, and energy. SDCC also serves as the core for
Brookhaven Lab’s institutional computing needs, connecting scientists and researchers at home and abroad.

SDCC maintains a 1,050,000 HEPSPEC 2006 (HS06) unit processing farm (currently with 110,000 processing
cores), a distributed and centralized disk storage farm (more than 80 PB of online disk storage), robotic tape
storage silos (250 PB of storage), a 400 terabit-per-second internal network with up to 2 x 400 gigabits per second
of WAN connectivity, and data grid and cloud computing software infrastructure. The hardware is a combination
of commodity-based processing servers, enterprise-class Unix servers, and highly specialized mass storage
systems, all connected by high-speed network infrastructure.

7.5.2.6.2 LoRaWAN Remote Monitoring
The BNL Energy and Utilities division has several wells located across the site. Many of these locations have no
network connectivity available. The need to monitor the level of these wells has been needed for some time as
operators currently have to do a visual inspection of the sites. It would be far too costly to install traditional wired
network services to these locations, so another solution was needed. LoRaWAN was chosen due to its long range,
ease of integration and relatively low cost to fill this need.

LoRa gateways are currently being deployed in three locations throughout the site to cover the needed areas.
These gateways will receive data from various Lora sensors which will be sent back to an on-premises server. The
server has native integration with the Modbus protocol, so the BNL energy and utilities division can poll these
data points using their building management software.

The vendor for this project is Activity. They provide the application server, ThingPark Enterprise and the Long
Range Relay (LRR) software for the gateways. The gateways are Kerlink Wirnet iStations.

The most challenging aspect of this project has been sourcing the necessary components. Originally, BNL was
looking to Cisco for this before they decided to exit the LoRa business. Cisco directed BNL towards Actility for
the software components. Special arrangements were made with vendors to purchase the necessary hardware,
which was difficult since the technology was not being resold at the time.

 Figure 7.5.7: High-Level LoraWan Architectures
 This project is currently in production, so the final architecture is subject to change.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 375

7.5.2.6.3 Site Cellular Network Connectivity
Various locations throughout the BNL campus have network connectivity through legacy DSL uplinks. Due
to growing bandwidth consumption in these areas, the need for modern network connectivity has been long
overdue. After being unable to procure the necessary funds to have fiber connectivity brought to these locations
the idea of using a form of wireless connectivity for these areas was thought to be the best solution. Ultimately
cellular capable network routers were used to provide the needed connectivity to these buildings.

There are basically two use cases for these routers. A use case where connectivity is required back to the BNL
campus network and another where just internet connectivity is required. Where connectivity is required back to
the BNL campus network, the routers build a VPN tunnel to BNL’s VPN concentrator via the cellular network.
Using this method, BNL can deploy wireless access points, VoIP phones, and additional drop-down switches
to provide network connectivity. Other buildings, such as the apartments simply require connectivity to the
internet, so for these use cases a cellular router and a wireless access point is deployed for user connectivity to
the internet.

 Figure 7.5.8: Cellular Router Connectivity to BNL Campus Network via VPN

7.5.2.6.4 NSLS2 Wireless Network
As described previously, the enterprise wireless network is an open SSID authenticated via a captive portal with
limited access to the BNL networks. The need for additional access to the BNL network via a wireless has arisen
over time, specifically in the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS2) facility. Many of the devices needing
this type of connectivity are headless devices and unable to authenticate through the captive portal. The answer
to this was to provision a new hidden SSID using a pre-shared key for authentication with specific access to parts
of the BNL network at NSLS2 and the internet. The SSID is hidden to prevent normal users from attempting to
connect to it and the passkey is only shared with authorized users.

7.6 SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory
SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, originally named the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, is located in
Menlo Park, California. Founded in 1962, the laboratory is sponsored by the US DOE and administrated by
Stanford University.

7.6.1 Discussion Summary

 • The primary scientific computation and storage facilities at SLAC are provisioned in the
 S3DF (SLAC Shared Scientific Data Facility). The S3DF is a compute, storage and network
 architecture designed to support massive-scale analytics required by all SLAC experimental
 facilities and programs, including LCLS/LCLS-II, UED, cryo-EM, the accelerator, and the
 Rubin observatory. The S3DF infrastructure is optimized for data analytics and is characterized
 by large, massive throughput, high-concurrency storage systems. [Section 4.1]

 • The SLAC networking core currently operates at multiple 100 GbE for connected enclaves and
 groups. The networking core of S3DF operates at 100 GbE, with a pair of 2 x 100 GbE links
 to the SLAC core. SLAC connects to ESnet via two pairs of 100 GbE links; these link pairs
 typically operate as primary/secondary. There is not general load balancing or dual use of the
 links. One pair of the SLAC/ESnet connections is dedicated for use by the Rubin Observatory
 Virtual Routed Network (Rubin Long Haul Network - LHN) over ESnet. [Section 4.7]

 • Within the next two years, SLAC expects to augment the SLAC/ESnet connections with a pair
 of 400 GbE links. These two links are expected to replace two of the 100 GbE connections,
 while the two 100 GbE connections for Rubin LHN remain in place specifically for the Rubin
 traffic. Thus, SLAC/ESnet will be a pair of 400 GbE links and a pair of 100 GbE links. The
 SLAC core network will also be upgraded to N x 400 GbE to accommodate higher speed
 connectivity among the enclaves and groups, including S3DF. [Section 4.7]

 • Within the next five years, SLAC expects to upgrade the 2 x 400 GbE links to 2x or 4x 800 GbE
 links. LCLS-II has a requirement for 1–2 Tbps capacity between SLAC and NERSC. This
 requirement is expected to be met with the N x 800 GbE upgrades. The SLAC core network
 will also be upgraded to N x 800 GbE. [Section 5.7]

7.6.2 SLAC: Technology Profile
The primary scientific computation and storage facilities at SLAC are provisioned in the S3DF (SLAC Shared
Scientific Data Facility). The S3DF is a compute, storage and network architecture designed to support massive-
scale analytics required by all SLAC experimental facilities and programs, including LCLS/LCLS-II, UED,
cryo-EM, the accelerator, and the Rubin observatory. The S3DF infrastructure is optimized for data analytics
and is characterized by large, massive throughput, high-concurrency storage systems. More information is
available online.145

7.6.2.1 Facilities Operated and Supported
SLAC Shared Science Data Facility (S3DF) offers:

 • Modern hardware for massive-scale analytics in a modern data center designed ground-up for
 research computing

 • High-speed networking storage solutions for data-intensive pipelines/applications
 ° Scale up to Tb/s links with hundreds of PBs online

145 http://s3df.slac.stanford.edu

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 378

 • Support for the entire data pipeline from detector input through to results publication
 • Funding plans that incorporate hardware lifecycle
TID Scientific Computing Systems division at SLAC is responsible for delivering S3DF. Funding is provided
by SLAC for both core staff and core infrastructure, and all science directorates will be supported. The S3DF
has the strategic goal of effectively replacing legacy siloed infrastructure. To this end, goals are to create high-
throughput pipelines by leveraging existing technology, but also centralizing services that can be shared by the
entire SLAC ecosystem.

7.6.2.2 Network and Data Architecture
The SLAC networking core currently operates at multiple 100 GbE for connected enclaves and groups. The
networking core of S3DF operates at 100 GbE, with a pair of 2 x 100 GbE links to the SLAC core. SLAC
connects to ESnet via two pairs of 100 GbE links; these link pairs typically operate as primary/secondary. There is
not general load balancing or dual use of the links. One pair of the SLAC/ESnet connections is dedicated for use
by the Rubin Observatory Virtual Routed Network (Rubin Long Haul Network - LHN) over ESnet.

Within the next two years, SLAC expects to augment the SLAC/ESnet connections with a pair of 400 GbE links.
These two links are expected to replace two of the 100 GbE connections, while the two 100 GbE connections
for Rubin LHN remain in place specifically for the Rubin traffic. Thus, SLAC/ESnet will be a pair of 400 GbE
links and a pair of 100 GbE links. The SLAC core network will also be upgraded to N x 400 GbE to accommodate
higher speed connectivity among the enclaves and groups, including S3DF.

Within the next five years, SLAC expects to upgrade the 2 x 400 GbE links to 2x or 4x 800 GbE links. LCLS-II
has a requirement for 1–2 Tbps capacity between SLAC and NERSC. This requirement is expected to be met
with the N x 800 GbE upgrades. The SLAC core network will also be upgraded to N x 800 GbE.

7.6.2.3 Computational and Storage Infrastructure
There are three different ways of utilizing S3DF:

 • Interactive: Commands that you issue are executed immediately. This is the most common
 approach for activities like building and debugging code, running simple analysis which require
 limited resources and/or require interaction with plots and logs. There are two modes for doing
 interactive work in S3DF: through a terminal, by opening a shell on one of the interactive pools,
 or through a browser, via OnDemand.

 • Batch: Jobs are submitted to a queue and are executed as soon as resources become available.
 This is the most common approach for running large jobs or for executing many jobs. Note that
 this is the most efficient mechanism form a facility perspective because it provides the best use
 of the available resources. Also, note that, by far, the largest fraction of S3DF computing cycles
 is in the batch system. S3DF uses SLURM as workload manager for batch jobs.

 • Service: This approach is for running long-lived jobs that run in the background waiting for data
 to analyze. This method is for service activities and require specific resources. These resources
 may be dedicated hardware acquired by your organization or may be dynamically allocated from
 a larger pool. For the latter approach, S3DF uses Kubernetes, an open-source framework for
 automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications.

7.6.2.4 Cloud Services
SLAC uses the following cloud services for mission support (infrastructure and services that are not directly part
of science/HEP programs or projects).;

 • Azure
 • AWS
In addition, there are is considerable use for collaboration, documentation, and related efforts among both
mission support and science projects:

 • Google Cloud
In 2024, the bandwidth requirements to/from these services is fairly modest (a few Gbps for connections between
SLAC and the provider). Some of these services are implemented with VPN tunnels, some use public addresses,
via ESnet.

During the next two years, SLAC expects to move more support services into Azure and AWS, and anticipates
bandwidth increase of two to four times during that time period, perhaps sporadically reaching peaks of 10 Gbps.

7.6.2.5 AI and ML
SLAC is working toward use of Yurts.AI for knowledge base and searching/cataloging of a broad variety of
online information resources, including scientific papers, technical notes, SLAC provided web content, and
other sources.

Individual project teams are exploring use of ML and AI technologies directed at their specific needs. Much of
that effort is coalesced within the resources provided in S3DF.

7.6.2.6 Wireless Capabilities
SLAC implements WiFi throughout the facility using Cisco Access Points and Wireless LAN Controllers. Some
areas of SLAC do not have WiFi coverage due to types of building construction or distance/terrain. Outdoor
coverage is limited. Most use of WIFI is in 2.4G and 5G bands, although 2.4G is being phased out in some areas
due to interference and noise from non-WiFi equipment. A WiFi lifecycle process implements ongoing upgrades,
including WiFi-6 support and future technologies as they become available.

The primary linear beamline tunnel has WiFi coverage via remote antennas. This facilitates service operations
during planned maintenance activities, when the beamline is not in operation.

Commercial cellular coverage is available in numerous areas around SLAC, but that coverage is more limited
than WiFi, due to terrain and building construction. Three carriers maintain a macro site on the roof of the
primary SLAC communications building (B050).

7.6.2.8 Data Mobility Endpoints
s3dfdtn.slac.stanford.edu is a load-balanced DNS name which points to a pool of dedicated DTNs. It is open to
everyone with an S3DF account. Common tools like scp/sftp/rsync are available for casual data transfers. For
serious large-volume data transfer, you may consider bbcp and globus.

7.6.2.8.1 bbcp
This is a high-performance multi-stream data transfer tool developed at SLAC. In its simplest form, the bbcp
command line is similar to that of scp.

7.7 ANL
Argonne is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center, where talented scientists and engineers
work together to answer the biggest questions facing humanity, from how to obtain affordable clean energy to
protecting ourselves and our environment. Ever since we were born out of the University of Chicago’s work on
the Manhattan Project in the 1940s, our goal has been to make an impact — from the atomic to the human to the
global scale.

The laboratory works in concert with universities, industry, and other national laboratories on questions and
experiments too large for any one institution to do by itself. Through collaborations here and around the world,
we strive to discover new ways to develop energy innovations through science, create novel materials molecule-
by-molecule, and gain a deeper understanding of our planet, our climate, and the cosmos.

7.7.1 Discussion Summary

 • External network connectivity to ANL is provided by ESnet, MREN, Internet2, and Internet2
 Peering Exchange (I2PX). ESnet has optical transport and routers deployed on the Argonne
 campus in a redundant configuration supporting up to 400 gigabits per second (Gbps)
 connections. The connections to MREN are 2 x 100 Gbps. The border routers are connected to
 each other with 4 x 100 Gbps connections. The connections to the campus core network are 2 x

7.7.2 ANL: Technology Profile
ANL is a multidisciplinary science and engineering research center, where scientists and engineers work together
to answer the biggest questions facing humanity, from how to obtain affordable clean energy to protecting
ourselves and the environment.

The laboratory works in concert with universities, industry, and other national laboratories on questions and
experiments too large for any one institution to do by itself. Through collaborations here and around the world,
ANL strives to discover new ways to develop energy innovations through science, create novel materials
molecule-by-molecule, and gain a deeper understanding of the planet, climate, and the cosmos.

7.7.2.1 Facilities Operated and Supported
ANL capabilities span 18 of the 24 institutional strengths that the DOE defines for national laboratories:

 • Propel discovery through national user facilities
 • Produce new understanding of the world through basic research
 • Drive advances in computation and analysis to solve the toughest problems
 • Shape and secure the energy infrastructure future by applying science and engineering
Partnerships and teamwork, within and outside Argonne, are integral to success in achieving these outcomes.
Active multidisciplinary collaborations across the laboratory, with the University of Chicago and other leading
research institutions, are a cornerstone of ANL’s approach to science and engineering.

ANL supports scientific use of networking in a number of core ways:

 • Argonne’s CELS directorate co-manages a pair of border routers with the Business Information
 Services Directorate (BIS).

 • CELS HPC resources (including ALCF) are behind a Juniper QFX10002-60C switch
 configured in a manner similar to that of the Science DMZ “Supercomputer Center
 Network” architecture.

 • Scientific directorate HPC resources outside of CELS (Advanced Energy Technologies, Nuclear
 Technologies and National Security, Photon Sciences, Physical Sciences & Engineering) along
 with all laboratory operations IT assets are behind a high-availability pair of Cisco Firepower
 9300 firewalls running Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) software. The firewalls and campus
 core switches are managed by BIS, and HPC resources themselves are managed by scientific
 directorate IT administrators.

 • Argonne’s HEP division is a member of the Physical Sciences & Engineering directorate.
 • Both CELS HPC resources and Physical Sciences & Engineering directorate IT resources are
 used for HEP work at Argonne.

 • The non-CELS scientific directorate HPC clusters are typically less than six <25kVA cabinets,
 running a wide variety of operating systems to support user needs. Scientific directorate
 IT administrators typically manage all cluster + storage interconnects using a wide variety
 of infrastructure. The BIS networking team manages all uplinks from these small HPC
 deployments into the campus network switches.

 • Approximately 100 buildings and 12 datacenters are interconnected in the Argonne campus via
 a new, robust, single-mode fiber cable plant with capacity and ability to expand.

 • Most CELS directorate infrastructure is located in Argonne Building 240, with a purpose-built
 datacenter for HPC. The focus in this building is supporting ultra-high-density, non-redundant
 cabinets of scientific computing equipment.

 • Most non-CELS scientific directorate infrastructure is located at Argonne Building 386, a
 purpose-built datacenter for mission-critical data services. The focus in this building is low to
 medium density, redundant cabinets of enterprise computing equipment.

 • All ESnet equipment, border routers and campus core switches at the Argonne campus are
 co-located with the fiber plant terminating in buildings 221 and 541b.

 • A small number of legacy datacenters outside of Buildings 221, 240, 541b and 386 are being
 used throughout campus.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 385

Research in the High Energy Physics division is driven by the goal of understanding the fundamental
constituents of matter and energy, and illuminating the ultimate nature of space and time.

In their search for scientific discovery, high energy physicists have built some of the world’s largest, most complex
and sophisticated devices, including powerful accelerators, massive particle detectors and sensitive cosmological
survey instruments. Theorists in the field have contributed to the deep level of understanding of the natural
world. Cutting-edge computing has long been associated with high energy physics, from extreme-scale number-
crunching with supercomputers to handling enormous amounts of data produced by the experiments. Because
of the size and complexity of many projects, which can involve many institutions, the national laboratories have a
special role to play in high energy physics.

Argonne maintains two state-of-the-art facilities for high energy physics. The Argonne Wakefield Accelerator
Facility146 aims to achieve high accelerating gradients for next-generation particle accelerators. The 4 Tesla
Magnet Facility reuses hospital MRI magnets for prove and detector testing under high magnetic fields. It
provides benchmarking for muon experiments that will be performed at Fermilab. Additionally, the ATLAS
Support Center provides computing and training facilities for members of the ATLAS collaboration.

Additionally, ANL supports a number of research groups (some of which are profiled as case studies in
this review):

 • The Accelerator Physics Group carries out research to enable the next generation of
 particle accelerators.

 • The ATLAS at the LHC experiment will enable us to learn about basic universal forces and
 allow us to further probe possible extra dimensions of space, the unification of fundamental
 forces, and evidence for dark matter candidates in the universe.

 • The Cosmological Physics and Advanced Computing group studies some of the most exciting
 fundamental science problems: dark energy, dark matter, and the nature of primordial
 fluctuations—uniting theorists, observers, computer and computational scientists, applied
 mathematicians, and statisticians.

 • The Experimental Cosmology Group focuses on studies of the CMB, the relic radiation left over
 from the early universe. Group members work on cutting-edge sensor development and related
 technologies.

 • The Instrumentation Research Group is involved in the development of new instrumentation,
 particularly detector technology, provides a common thread that links together a wide range of
 high energy physics projects and programs.

 • Researchers at the Intensity Frontier investigate some of the rarest processes in nature,
 including unusual interactions of fundamental particles and subtle effects that require large data
 sets to observe and measure.

 • The Theoretical High Energy Physics Research Group concentrates on the interplay between
 theory and experiment. The Argonne Theory Group is active in exploring the particle physics
 SM and in searching for avenues to go beyond it.

7.7.2.2 Network and Data Architecture
7.7.2.2.1 Overview
External network connectivity is provided by ESnet, MREN, Internet2, and Internet2 Peering Exchange (I2PX).
ESnet recently migrated Argonne to the new ESnet6 network and has optical transport and routers deployed on
the Argonne campus in a redundant configuration supporting up to 400 gigabits per second (Gbps) connections.

146 https://www.anl.gov/awa

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 386

There are two primary networking node locations distributed between the north (Building 221) and south
(Building 541B) sides of the campus to provide network redundancy. Generally, all buildings and data centers
have connections to each of these networking nodes. The fiber used to connect to off-site providers is diverse and
exits on the east and west sides of the campus.

Argonne networks support many connection speeds. The WAN currently consists of 100 Gbps and 400 Gbps
paths. The campus core network supports speeds of 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, 40 Gbps, and 100 Gbps. Building
connections are generally multiple 10-Gbps links with some 40-Gbps links, and data centers are 10 Gbps, 40
Gbps, and 100 Gbps. LAN connections within buildings are generally 1 Gbps and 10 Gbps.

7.7.2.2.2 WAN
The Argonne WAN network connectivity is provided by ESnet and MREN (Internet2) gateway, Peer Exchange
(I2PX)). ESnet has optical and routing equipment on the Argonne campus. Argonne has two Juniper MX960
border routers that are split between Building 221 and Building 541B for redundancy and diversity. These will
most likely be replaced in FY26 due to a significant amount of the MX960 cards going end of life in June 2026.

The Argonne connections to ESnet are 2 x 400 Gbps. The connections to MREN are 2 x 100 Gbps. The border
routers are connected to each other with 4 x 100 Gbps connections. The connections to the campus core network
are 2 x 40 Gbps and 40 Gbps to the perimeter firewall. By the end of FY25, the perimeter firewall will be
replaced with a Palo Alto PA-5450 with 100 Gbps connectivity.

7.7.2.2.3 Science DMZ
The Argonne Science DMZ is composed of Juniper QFX series equipment in Building 240 that is connected
directly to the Argonne border routers with redundant 4 x 100 Gbps links. The Science DMZ provides high-
speed connectivity between scientific organizations for the exchange of data without taking the traditional path
through a firewall.

Connections into the Science DMZ are a minimum of 100 Gbps with most facilities connecting at 4 x 100 Gbps.
This allows collaborators to exchange data in a high-speed environment that does not affect commodity network
connectivity.

7.7.2.2.4 Core
The Argonne core network is provided by two Cisco Nexus 7710s spread across Buildings 221 and Buildings
541B for redundancy. These switches offer network speeds at 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, 40 Gbps, and 100 Gbps. The core
provides connections to buildings and many of the data centers on the Argonne campus.

7.7.2.2.5 LAN
The Argonne LAN consists of the building access and aggregation switches. The Laboratory has standardized on
Cisco and Aruba switches in the LAN. There is a combination of 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, and 40 Gbps network speeds
in the LAN. Desktops are connected at 1 Gbps.

7.7.2.6 Wireless Capabilities
Many experiments utilizing both WiFi and 5G CBRS are occurring within the Argonne campus.

Within the CELS directorate, the Waggle sensor project147 has deployed sensors both on-site and off-campus for
initiates148. In some cases, sensors are pre-configured at Argonne on the eduroam wireless infrastructure, and
automatically join the same eduroam SSID at their final location (such as Northwestern University) seamlessly. A
number of 5G projects have been launched at Argonne, including an end-to-end open-source 5G testbed.

The APS operates their own Aruba WiFi deployment for their experiment hall and directly attached Lab/Office

becoming available for general use. There is no estimated time of arrival for when 6ghz wireless will become
widely available on-site due to the large number of end-of-life WiFi 5 (and earlier) access points which must be
replaced first.
