High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 389

8 Group Discussion
In September 2024, an in-person review was held that invited participation from the HEP community, HEP
activity host institutions, DOE SC staff spanning ASCR and HEP, and ESnet staff. The purpose of this review was
to go over the case studies presented in [Section 6] and the technical profiles discussed in [Section 7], and discuss
common findings and potential actions for the future support of the HEP community by ESnet.

8.1 Topic Summary
Discussion centered on four broad topic areas, heavily based on the early finding and actions identified through
case study review, and the interests of the representatives present for the in-person review:

 • IRI and the HEP community.
 • HEP R&D efforts.
 • Data challenges.
 • LHCONE support and international networking.
The notes that follow are a summary of the discussions, many of which led to the drafting of additional findings
and recommendations for ESnet, ASCR, and HEP.

8.1.1 IRI and the HEP Community
A common theme across many of the HEP case studies was the surrounding challenges of data access as
collaboration space grows larger. This is not purely a technical problem; the LHC collaboration numbers in the
thousands and has a structured ecosystem that facilitates access to groups and individuals through several tools
that manage identity and permissions across a federated grid infrastructure. Other collaborations that have less
structure may struggle with the available tools to manage collaboration size long term. DESI, for example, has
users from around the world attempting to use resources at NERSC, and each will have to apply and be granted
access to NERSC systems; access may not be allowed due to political factors such as citizenship and country of
origin. A potential way to address this later concern is brokering through neutral sites like cloud providers; the
RSP approach149 offers a layer of policy and identity between the users and the collaboration systems directly
managing the data. The approach of using a cloud-based front-end may see more consideration in future
collaborations that span international boundaries, and may be present for future work within the IRI effort as
they define standards and approaches to address federated identity and permissions that span facility boundaries.

The DOE IRI effort has identified “cybersecurity and federated access practice” as one of the six core practice
areas for future work. This practice area will focus on creating novel solutions that enable seamless scientific
collaboration within a secure and trusted IRI ecosystem. The discussions within this effort are nascent, but a
core understanding will be recognizing that the security posture and policies of participating facilities may
differ, and there must be a way to determine and agree on appropriate mechanisms to implement identity and
access control.

The discussions within the HEP community touched on factors that should be considered by the IRI effort. A
first step will be to establish a hierarchy of needs: an example being that the ability to access a set of resources
or tools that spans administrative boundaries is very different than the ability to use different tools and resources
within the same location. A similar policy language and control structure could solve both if there are ways to
differentiate the needs and articulate the required control structures.

149 https://www.spiedigitallibrary.org/conference-proceedings-of-spie/13101/131012B/Rubins-hybrid-on-premises-cloud-data-access-cen-
ter/10.1117/12.3018005.short#_=_

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 390

Additionally, it must be acknowledged that authentication, authorization, and accounting approaches have
limitations. Typically, it is possible to specify who can do what and keep a record of what has happened. Within
an organizational structure this is not too much of a challenge, but across organizations with different policies this
can be complicated as different implementations and validation methods are employed.

Opportunities exist to develop potentially new, and disruptive, models for managing access across reassures.
Currently one HPC facility cannot create users, permissions, and allocation of resources for someone to
access a different HPC facility. There is a natural expectation that different accounts are needed with different
expectations, tools, and culture at each. Creating a policy layer that spans facilities is one matter, but ways to
bridge the underlying permissions, APIs, and access methods are completely different. Compounding this is the
technical debt that may be required for a facility, collaboration, or individual PI to commit to in attempting to
provide or use resources.

Suggested ways forward are to define problems and categorize the relative ease toward a solution. For example,
limited access to data, storage, and systems via web interfaces is much easier to manage than lower-level
methods, such as system account, which allows for direct access. Existing efforts to migrate permissions across
boundaries are widely accepted for some simple use cases (https://eduroam.org/), and can be built upon.

8.1.2 HEP R&D Efforts
ESnet has a long history of participation in R&D efforts with the HEP community and several ongoing efforts
with the LHC. These currently include work on SENSE and Rucio, in-network caching of experimental data,
network capacity testing, supporting cloud pilots, identification of science traffic, and the concept of data lakes
to support scientific analysis. All these R&D efforts tie together networking capabilities to the workflow of
LHC science in some meaningful way. Some are approaching a level of maturity that will see them deployed as
production services in the coming years; others are pilots providing valuable information for the development of
future services.

Integration of SENSE and Rucio, as described in the LHC case studies, is an effort to impart network control
abilities into the Rucio workflow manager. When deployed on participating networks and sites, it allows
scheduling of data-movement tasks across traffic-engineered paths, which allows for greater performance
capabilities, and less impact on other traffic flows. CMS and ATLAS have been moving this capability into
production at several of their Tier-2 sites.

In-network caching has gone through several successful trials, and is under active development. As discussed
in the LHC case studies, questions remain as to the effectiveness of the approach, and whether it will translate
into a useful production service. Early findings indicate several major differences in the operation of a cache
depending on the number of users and facilities it is designed to support. For example, an “in-facility” cache that
serves a small to medium number of users, many of which may be operating on similar subsets of data, can see
reduced WAN download benefits. As the number of users or facilities grows, e.g., a cache deployed to service a
region, the data sets analyzed rarely overlap. To see any cache benefit, the size of the cache must increase, and the
policy for replacement must be altered. Caching has many benefits, but how it is deployed, and how it interacts
with similar efforts such as the data lake project, are being worked out.

During DC24, ESnet directly assisted sites in “full capacity” testing of their network links. This was done using
multiple perfSONAR servers to generate traffic and changing routing policy on both the network and the site
end. This testing helped to reveal configuration bottlenecks and was invaluable to gain an understanding of the
maximum expected performance. Future DC activities can take a similar approach, but there are also capabilities
that ESnet’s High Touch servers (that feature FPGAs) could assist with. High Touch servers could conceivably be
programmed to create network traffic and direct it at resources located within a lab or facility perimeter. ESnet
will follow up with interested sites on this prototype concept.

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 391

A number of HEP case studies outlined their production, proto-duction, and experimental use of commercial
cloud resources. ESnet, as a network carrier, is identifying ways to assist with the execution of the scientific
mission, and will continue to assist with connectivity and peering when applicable. During some HEP
evaluations of cloud solutions for portions of analysis workflows, the network was identified to be a bottleneck
in certain situations: mainly when traffic remained within a cloud versus being allowed to egress and use more
predicable R&E routing and transit. In situations like this, ESnet could serve as a valuable partner between
connected end sites and cloud resources, to try to force routing choices that take advantage of R&E WAN paths
versus the internal networking a cloud may use.

SciTags is an initiative promoting identification of the science domains and their high-level activities at the
network level. Simply stated, these are network flow and packet marking approaches that can be applied by
scientific users and used by networks to better understand usage patterns. The approach is based on a network-
tagging mechanism that marks network packets and/or network flows using the science domain and activity
fields. The current state of use for SciTags is purely voluntary; end users can adopt this approach for their own
traffic flows, and participating networks may choose to add the information on data they observe and are able to
identify. Some networks may choose to act on this information for either monitoring or traffic prioritization, but
are not required to do so. The effort is active, and ESnet is participating with the LHC community on several
demonstrations and pilot efforts (including demonstrations at the SC conference).

The concept of a data lake, a method to access experimental data that abstracts away the locations and
technologies that will serve the data, has been prototyped within the LHC community. The concept is tied to the
notion of an AF, which offers capabilities to perform user analysis of data in different locations around the world.
Tools such as Rucio are used to manage the overall workflow, but the data lake abstraction facilitates retrieval of
the underlying dataset transparently for the user, and imparts some level of caching such that the data set could
be reused if it remains popular for other users of the same AF. To date these have been deployed within LHC
resources, and not on networks like ESnet. The R&D cycle for this effort is high, and many questions remain on
implementation: how the data lake interfaces with storage, what metrics are used to optimize retrieval, and how
the network itself plays into requests to move data. ESnet has no immediate follow-up on this R&D, but will be
available for future collaboration.

8.1.3 Data Challenges
The LHC community and ESnet are collecting an enormous amount of data on the performance of data mobility
tools, the networks that are a part of data transfer, and the individual hardware components (routers, switches,
servers, storage). These data were incredibly useful during the DC24 activity, and helped to identify transfer
bottlenecks and other gaps to delivering the requirements for HL-LHC operation. Despite having visibility,
reviewing and acting on all the collected telemetry data is not possible. Cultivating or hiring a data analyst to
review the data and suggest ways they can be better incorporated into future tools would benefit both efforts.

DC24 provided critical insight into the behaviors of all layers of the technology stack for the LHC communities:
data management and ability software, computation and storage, as well as local and wide area networking. The
previously planned DC26 challenges may slip due to the changing schedules of the LHC, but it is expected that
this activity will also be a crucial preparation step for the HL-LHC operation. Beyond the major milestones of
a full DC, the mini-DC activities150 in the run-up to a full DC will be useful ways to validate specific portions of
technology support structure. ESnet plans to engage with the LHC community on ways to participate in all these.

ESnet requested additional clarifications on the organized, and unorganized, nature of DC activities within the
HEP community. Full data challenges will also be coordinated, and could involve more than just the core LHC
experiments: affiliated efforts like DUNE and Belle II may choose to participate as well given the overlap in
operational technology they share with the LHC experiments. Mini-DC activities are also organized, but to a
lesser extent. Any site can choose to run DC activities (alone, or with partners) with the intention of making small
150 https://indico.cern.ch/event/1374962/contributions/5778763/attachments/2921661/5128230/Mini-Challenges_%20Building%20from%20
DC24.pdf

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 392

incremental changes to hardware, software, or network configuration and analyzing the resulting performance.
For example, ATLAS will be performing US-based load testing at the end of 2024 between BNL and the Tier-2
sites. This will be done on an individual basis first, and then to all simultaneously. ATLAS within Europe will
do the same shortly after. The ISIS HEP effort will conduct a series of tests in early 2025. Each test has a set of
deliverables and milestones that lead into the preparation for the larger DC efforts.

Uncertainly remains regarding the schedule of the next DC. Tentatively this was set for the end of 2026, but
the LHC operational schedule has shifted and the LHC DOMA group will be meeting at the end of 2024 to
adjust schedules accordingly. Once the dates are decided, an effort will be required within the greater US R&E
community to prepare as we did in the run-up to DC 24. ESnet will request some visibility of this topic in the
upcoming community meetings (The Quilt, Internet2, etc.).

Lastly, the changes to hardware at Tier-1 and Tier-2 sites will impact some of the performance aspects of future
DC activities, but the schedule of hardware upgrades is hard to predict. Some sites plan on upgrading hardware
yearly, so their upgrades appear more “rolling”; when a DC happens they will use what is available. Others may
be able to schedule larger hardware purchases and plan to install and test prior to a large DC activity. Many sites
will not get funding until closer to the DC (e.g., end of 2026, start of 2027); thus they may not be able to upgrade
anything before the next major challenge.

8.1.4 LHCONE Support and International Networking
A number of facilities are not connected to LHCONE currently, despite being heavily involved in LHC-
affiliated computation and storage activities. These include major computational sites (e.g., NERSC, and TACC)
used for simulation workflows, SLAC (which has operated AFs in the past), and when applicable, commercial
clouds. No formal agreement with any of these facilities exists now to be part of the LHC collaboration in a
structured way, but investigating their ability to connect to LHCONE to support a number of important use cases
is recommended.

LHCONE runs a hybrid approach to supporting IPv6 currently. The upcoming government mandate (e.g.,
M-21-07) will imply that Fermilab and BNL will move toward IPv6 capabilities, and subsequently the Tier-2s
will have to move toward dual stack support at a minimum. One critical issue that cannot be solved by the US
community will be CERN’s ability to deliver IPv6 capabilities from its service infrastructure; some capabilities
may be IPv4 only in the coming years. ESnet will continue to work with US collaborators to ease the transition to
IPv6 operation.

Several international networking partners factored heavily into the discussions this year; connectivity to Europe,
South America, and the Asia-Pacific region is accomplished through relationships with a number of R&E
partners. ESnet maintains peering relations with most of these partners, and their connectivity carries significant
amounts of HEP traffic daily (e.g., LHC and ProtoDUNE traffic from Europe, Rubin Observatory and CMB-
S4 traffic from South America, Belle II traffic from Japan, etc.). ESnet will include current network capability
diagrams into this report to document the current state of international networking.

8.2 Outcomes
The following discussion points, many of which are core findings and actions of this report and denoted in
[Section 4] and [Section 5], were created from the discussions in [Section 8.1]. These observations will help to
drive future collaboration.

8.2.1 Facility Management and Readiness
 • A common problem across several HEP efforts is the management of credentials to access
 computation and storage across facilities (e.g., DOE HPC centers), and how these may
 differ from accounts used to manage other aspects of the scientific workflow (e.g., home
 institutional accounts).

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 393

 • Several facilities are not connected to LHCONE currently, despite being heavily involved in
 LHC-affiliated computation and storage activities. These include major computational sites
 (e.g., NERSC, and TACC) used for simulation workflows, SLAC (which has operated AFs in the
 past), and when applicable, commercial clouds. No formal agreement with any of these facilities
 exists now to be part of the LHC collaboration in a structured way, but investigating their ability
 to connect to LHCONE to support several important use cases is recommended.

8.2.2 Scientific Data Management
 • A common theme across many of the HEP case studies was the surrounding challenges of
 data access as collaboration space grows larger. The LHC collaboration has a highly structured
 ecosystem that facilitates access to groups, and individuals, through a number of tools that
 manage identity and permissions across a federated grid infrastructure. Other collaborations
 that have less structure may struggle with the available tools to manage collaboration size long
 term and are attempting other solutions (e.g., neutral site hosting through cloud providers, or
 adopting the policies of the strictest member of a collaboration). [Section 5.2]

 • The DC24 exercise provided critical insight into the behaviors of all layers of the technology
 stack for the LHC communities: data management and ability software, computation and
 storage, as well as local and wide area networking. The DC27 is expected to be a crucial
 preparation step for the HL-LHC operation. Beyond the major milestones of a full DC, the
 mini-DC activities in the run-up to a full DC will be useful ways to validate specific portions
 of technology support structure. ESnet plans to engage with the LHC community on ways to
 participate in all these. [Section 5.2]

8.2.3 Scientific Workflow
 • Several HEP experiments and facilities have adopted a core set of tools for data and workflow
 management, including Rucio, FTS, and XRootD. Adoption of a common set of tools will greatly
 increase the ability to make the analysis work portable across available resources, particularly at
 DOE HPC centers. [Section 5.3]

8.2.4 Computational and Storage Requirements
 • The barrier to using DOE HPC resources within the LHC community remains integrating
 the systems as resources into the software components, and normalizing the way the resources
 could be accounted for (expected versus ad hoc or opportunistic). More specifically, there is a
 desire to create agreements or other arrangements, similar to an SLA, with DOE HPC facilities
 such that resources can be considered pledged. This helps with planning for both the HEP
 community and the ASCR resources. Some of this may require discussion at the programmatic
 level. [Section 5.4]

 • The LHC community experiences friction with supporting a streaming-based workflow at
 large HPC facilities. Workarounds have been established to support this: either by allowing
 the worker nodes stream directly, or by leveraging caches and data lakes that are deployed
 close topologically. All these design choices come with trade-offs, which implies a set of R&D
 activities that will extend in the coming years. [Section 5.4]

8.2.5 Remote Collaboration and Operational Requirements
 • Removing the need to worry about data locality allows researchers focused on developing
 cosmological simulation to invest more time on the science, versus spending energy in activities
 to stage data and allocate technology resources. It also prevents the half-measures being
 used today to create mechanisms to perform analysis on partial data sets, or adopt streaming
 approaches that are not always successful on larger computational resources not designed to
 support that mode of operation. [Section 8], [Section 4.5]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 394

 • Several HEP experiments rely on interactive computing methods, namely Jupyter Notebooks.
 It is desirable to be able to leverage computing options that may not be tied to a single facility,
 such as a cloud platform (like those that the Rubin Observatory has adopted). [Section 4.5]

8.2.6 Multifacility Computational Workflows
 • The HEP community is interested in moving a model that would help to reduce the number of
 times and locations that need to be involved to archive long-term data products, and is looking
 for assistance in scoping and realizing this design goal. Establishing permanent storage facilities
 would allow the community to establish a more regular pattern of collaboration; a smaller set
 of data portals that can be used to catalog and retrieve long-term campaigns of products along
 with a simplified way to support analysis activities, potentially leveraging interactive computing
 approaches, at a well-known number of sites.

8.2.7 Networking for Local and Wide-area Data Mobility
 • During DC24, ESnet directly assisted several sites in “full capacity” testing of their network
 links. This was done using multiple perfSONAR servers to generate traffic, and changing
 routing policy on both the network and the site end. This testing helped to reveal configuration
 bottlenecks, and was invaluable in gaining an understanding of the maximum expected
 performance. Future DC activities can take a similar approach, but there are also capabilities
 that ESnet’s High Touch servers (that feature FPGAs) could assist with. Several High Touch
 servers could conceivably be programmed to create network traffic and direct it at resources
 located within a lab or facility perimeter. ESnet will follow up with interested sites on this
 prototype concept. [Section 5.7]

 • The LHC community and ESnet are collecting an enormous amount of data on the performance
 of data mobility tools, the networks that are a part of data transfer, and the individual hardware
 components (routers, switches, servers, storage). These data were incredibly useful during
 the DC24 activity, and helped to identify transfer bottlenecks and other gaps to delivering the
 requirements for HL-LHC operation. Despite having visibility, reviewing and acting on all the
 collected telemetry data is not possible. Cultivating or hiring a data analyst to review the data
 and suggest ways they can be better incorporated into future tools would benefit both efforts.
           [Section 5.7]

 • LHCONE runs a hybrid approach to supporting IPv6 currently. The upcoming government
 mandate (e.g., M-21-07) will imply that Fermilab and BNL will move toward IPv6 capabilities,
 and subsequently the Tier-2s will have to move toward dual stack support at a minimum. One
 critical issue that cannot be solved by the US community is CERN’s ability to deliver IPv6
 capabilities from its service infrastructure; some capabilities may still be IPv4 only in the
 coming years. ESnet will continue to work with US collaborators on this to ease the transition to
 IPv6 operation. [Section 5.7]

 • Several international networking partners factored heavily into the discussions this year;
 connectivity to Europe, South America, and the Asia-Pacific region is accomplished through
 relationships with several R&E partners. ESnet maintains peering relations with most of these
 partners, and their connectivity carries significant amounts of HEP traffic daily (e.g., LHC and
 ProtoDUNE traffic from Europe, Rubin Observatory and CMB-S4 traffic from South America,
 Belle II traffic from Japan, etc.). ESnet will include current network capability diagrams into
 this report to document the current state of international networking. [Section 5.7]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 395

8.2.8 Emerging Needs
 • Commercial cloud resources are an intriguing addition to simulation workflows. While the cost
 of using these resources remains high, there may become a way to augment existing resources
 during periods of heavy use and justify the increased expenditure. One could imagine a
 situation where the use of AI/ML frameworks becomes an instantaneous source of large-scale
 data; if difficulty exists in allocating local computational and storage resources to meet the
 demand, these workflows may need to be integrated with commercial cloud infrastructure that
 can expand as needed to fit the needs.

 • The use of in-network caching has had some impact on network use for the LHC community.
 Much of the R&D efforts in the recent years have been determining where caches may be
 beneficial for placement, how large they need to be to be effective, and what strategy should be
 used to store and replace data sets. Questions remain about deployment strategies to work out
 for both CMS and ATLAS. Regional caches were found to not be as effective (since the overlap
 of data use was not high enough), but caches within a facility, and ensuring that the workflow
 management tools know to check the caches, produced the most reliable results. [Section 4.8]

 • ESnet will continue to work with the LHC community on co-design efforts like SENSE and
 Rucio, SciTags, and other potential opportunities. The experiments need to be specific in what
 they are hoping to achieve, however. The aim of joint projects could be to co-design an effective
 system that makes best use of the available network resources, coordinated with the site
 resources, and manage joint site and network operations cooperatively. This needs to be spelled
 out in more detail, and discussed with ESnet leadership. [Section 5.8]

 • GPU use to support some aspects of AI and ML is expected to continue; what is unknown
 currently is how this may impact WAN usage. Experiments have shown that bursting to a
 commercial cloud to utilize GPUs is possible, but leveraging DOE HPC resource would allow
 better control over the WAN components. [Section 5.8]

 • The LHC work on data lakes will continue, and several things have been learned from the years
 of R&D and use during activities like DC24. There is now an effort to reduce the number of
 “entry points” into storage resources. The XRootD tool now is not bound by factors such as
 network capacity or distance/latency, and may find nonoptimal answers to requests for data
 from clients. The overall goal of a data lake should be to simplify the way data are accessed,
 along with providing the most performant ways to access and retrieve them. Data lakes can
 also leverage some of the work on caching, and allow the caches (which often do have more
 intelligence) to assist in making optimal choices about retrieval. [Section 5.8]

 • Authentication, authorization, and accounting approaches have limitations. Typically, it is
 possible to specify who can do what and keep a record of what has happened. Within an
 organizational structure this is not too much of a challenge, but across organizations with
 different policies this can be complicated, as different implementations and validation methods
 are employed. [Section 5.8]

 • Several HEP case studies outlined their production, proto-duction, and experimental use of
 commercial cloud resources. ESnet, as a network carrier, is identifying ways to assist with the
 execution of the scientific mission, and will continue to help with connectivity and peering
 when applicable. During some HEP evaluations of cloud solutions for portions of analysis
 workflows, the network was identified to be a bottleneck in certain situations: mainly when
 traffic remained within a cloud versus being allowed to egress and use more predicable R&E
 routing and transit. In situations like this, ESnet could serve as a valuable partner between
 connected end sites and cloud resources to try to force routing choices that take advantage of
 R&E WAN paths versus the internal networking a cloud may use. [Section 5.8]

High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review: Final Report 396

8.2.9 IRI Responsiveness
 • Several HEP experiments and facilitates could take advantage of some aspects of the IRI design
 approaches: namely the use of DOE HPC facilities for aspects of their simulation and analysis
 workflows. GPU resources are expected to be incredibly valuable as the role of AI and ML
 approaches increases. Additionally, the announcement to create an HPDF may serve as a focal
 point for a long-term location for the storage of public data archives.

 • The DOE IRI effort has identified cybersecurity and federated access practice as one of the
 six core practice areas for future work. This practice area will focus on creating novel solutions
 that enable seamless scientific collaboration within a secure and trusted IRI ecosystem. The
 discussions within this effort are nascent, but a core understanding will be to recognize that the
 security posture and policies of participating facilities may differ, and that there must be a
 way to determine and agree on appropriate mechanisms to implement identity and access
 control. [Section 5.9]

 • The discussions within the HEP community touched on several factors that should be
 considered by the IRI effort. A first step will be to establish a hierarchy of needs. For example, it
 is very different to access a set of resources or tools that spans administrative boundaries versus
 having the ability to use different tools and resources within the same location. A similar policy
 language and control structure could solve both, if there are ways to differentiate the needs and
 articulate the required control structures. [Section 5.9]
